# EXPLANATION
->Of the<-
## FRONTISPIECE.

**T**he Christian Religion <note>Represented as an allegorical female figure.</note>, which keeps itself before the Tree, 
Displays the Bible with its pages turned open;
A Franciscan friar, who builds upon other foundations,
Tries, through the sound of his flute, to discourage its use,
And with one hand flutes away the Salutory Work <note>The "Salutory Work" refers to the Bible itself.</note>,
While the other points to the Book in which the Laws of the Councils
Are recorded. Thus the Authority of the Roman Church intends,
To set her arm unshakeably fast upon this ground (1).
Here rests her left hand, which has firmly grasped,
The Holy Sacrament, while the other offers as a sign
Of Peace, the branch of fresh Olive: but see how
A small snake coils around that sprout, appearing to sting
A visible Poison into her hidden innards;
Added to this is a tightly forged iron chain,
Which keeps the Enslaved Faith bound by her Church discipline.
By the triple Crown <note>The Papal Tiara.</note> one can measure the great Authority;
She sets her left foot upon the militant Roman Empire,
Which lies here in impotence, trampled by her power,
While Superstition has snatched away that which was Imperial,
To clothe the High Priesthood with those spoils.
In her Retinue, one sees strict Spiritual Discipline;
A Jesuit applies himself to praising to the Bishop,
The Pope's Bull (2) <note>original: "Paussen Bulle"; specifically the bull *Unigenitus*.</note>; yet this tasteless Fruit,
Bears in his pure soul a distaste of horror.
The Cardinal with all the further procession of Bishops,
Stand yet to earnestly consider the Papal Command.
Also this Ecclesiastical Rule steps with her right foot,
Upon Jewish Rabbinism, sunk down here helpless
With Moses’ Book of the Law, as if trampled into the dust.
Now the enjoyment of Statehood appears, and allows itself to be blinded:
The Greek Patriarch swears fealty to the Roman Court (3);
While Monastic Orders bind themselves no less to her.
In the appearance of Piety, the Main Banner of the 
Inquisition-discipline parades here, encompassing both Peace and Punishment;
Wherein this Tribunal seeks, with a perverse flourish 
Of its opportunity, to drag in the innocent.
But when one considers the foreground of the Scene,
It shall reveal to us Purgatory, as an underground place,
Upon which the Ecclesiastical Rule of Rome is built,
Where Souls for a time always reside for purification.
The Reformation, depicted here with the pruning knife in her hand,
Embraces the Tree (4), which she prunes of dead shoots,
And points to the Bible-book, wherein one finds the right understanding
Of true Piety, accurately enclosed.
Around her are placed, the Heroes Luther and Calvin,
Melanchthon and Jan Hus, as true Church Reformers;
Prince Henry (5) <note>Henry VIII of England.</note>, Cranmer, and Martyr <note>Peter Martyr Vermigli.</note>, Bucer, Zwingli (6),
Sincere Zealots and stormers of Church abuses.
It is Menno Simons, who keeps himself busily occupied
With incorporating an elderly maid through Baptism.
But that which one observes in the front of the Frontispiece,
Is Ali, who, to strengthen the Doctrine of Muhammad,
Explains the Quran to the Turk, Tartar, and Moor;
Also in the foreground, the Persian holds in his hands
A Tablet, upon which the Fundamental Rules of that nature
Are written. One sees their annual Offering,
Represented by the Camel (7). But if one turns one's sight,
To the distant background, the Mexicans
And Peruvians appear (8), deprived of the true light,
While they pave the way of cruelty through Temple-service.
The East Indians are depicted with their Gods,
Being no less Wretched and blinded in all their dealings,
For no glow of truth shines upon their Pagoda-worship;
But they wander in darkness through their perverse conduct.

(4) This Tree represents Religion, from which the Reformation has cut away the Abuses and Ceremonies like withered branches. (5) Henry VIII, King of England.

# GENERAL PREFACE

Introductory Treatise on Religious Worship in General. Herein emerges a sufficient idea of the uncommon practices that humans have put into use to serve God, etc. Upon reading this, we find ourselves obliged to confess that—excluding the marks of Revelation which must be recognized in some religions—*they all (a) agree in many matters, having the same principles and fundamental rules in the minds of many people, who generally agree in their positions, maintaining the same advancements and progress on the same footing.* The common people are imitators of one another regarding this point: but however it may be, all humans have certain extravagances that they practice in their religion; nevertheless, they have a Being or Beings as their object, whom they fear or honor, and who are consequently elevated above them. These Beings they call Gods, Guardian Gods, <term>Demons<note>In this context, "Demons" refers to the classical Greek *daimon*, signifying a spirit or lesser deity that acts as an intermediary between gods and humans, rather than the modern concept of an evil entity.</note></term>, etc. Indeed, it is certain that they are regarded as very powerful, since one yields to them in what all nations allow to be called a Spiritual Service.

As for the strange stubbornness noted in this worship, it is undoubtedly born from a false idea one has of the Divinity and His attributes. If all nations could agree to behold God as a single Being, perfectly Supreme through His Essence, Virtues, and His immeasurable absolute Perfection; then **I.** the offices of a great number of vicars of the Divinity, Intercessors or <term>Mediators<note>Religious figures or spirits believed to bridge the gap between the human and the divine.</note></term>, Patron Saints, etc.—whom people believe to be appointed for the salvation of the human race, to be an advocate for them before God, and to distinguish the matters that concern them—would soon be abolished: one would come to God entirely without any detour and by the shortest routes. **II.** One

<summary>This preface explores the universal similarities between different religions, suggesting that despite various "extravagances," all faiths share common psychological foundations. ...one would not find so much refuge in sacrifices and incensing; in feast days and brotherhoods; in the rigors of the body and penances <note>The original Dutch *boetoeffeningen* refers to voluntary acts of self-punishment or asceticism intended to show repentance.</note> to achieve deficient excesses; in vows and the monastic life, etc. One would give these things their true value, and those who—as *Charron* <note>Pierre Charron (1541–1603), a French philosopher and theologian known for his skeptical and Stoic-influenced views on religion and ethics.</note> says—*carve and cut themselves, and impose a painful labor*, would be seen as people who undertake in vain to seek healing herbs—at least when they do not prove an internal purity through their conduct—or like people who are sick of mind, whose bodies one must heal in order to subsequently give to their souls the true Idea of Religion. 

**III.** One would seek within oneself to satisfy the Divinity, and one would find that the love of Virtue and honorability of life are matters alone pleasing to God. It is marvelous that these truths have been known at all times, <margin>(a) Even the pagans have recognized them, and we provide only this beautiful passage from *Ovid* <note>Publius Ovidius Naso, the famous Roman poet.</note> to prove it: "The heavenly powers do not delight in the slaughter of an ox, but in the faith which must be offered, and that without stain." <note>original Latin: *Nec bove mactato caelestia numina gaudent, / Sed quae praestanda est & fine labe fides.*</note></margin> and yet people have treated them so poorly. Consequently, one could much sooner flatter oneself with a hope for a union in religion, if it were to resume its original simplicity; one would then see a thousand-fold ceremonies fall away which men have invented to give themselves authority and prestige, and which they presented to their posterity as purely Spiritual Acts.

As for the second Section of this Treatise, one finds therein an explanation of Jewish ceremonies and a distinction of various Jewish ecclesiastical customs. ...the Writer being an Italian, was not sufficiently experienced in the full scope of the Ceremonies and Customs of the other Jewish Churches <note>The author refers to the differences between Sephardic (often Italian/Iberian) and Ashkenazic (German/Eastern European) Jewish customs.</note>.

We also provide some account therein of *Jansenism* and *Quietism* <note>Two significant theological movements within 17th and 18th-century Catholicism that were eventually condemned as heretical; Jansenism focused on divine grace and original sin, while Quietism emphasized a passive mystical union with God.</note>. Bonanni*, a learned Jesuit who, through his erudition, has brought much glory to his Order—an Order that has made itself very famous through the great men who have arisen from it.

For a long time, we deliberated whether we should limit ourselves to the account of the mournful Ceremonies of the *Inquisition*, regarding the History of this Tribunal, without coming to the investigation of its origin and legal proceedings, or whether we should incorporate into this Work the Historical Memoirs concerning this *Inquisition* to give a clear Idea of a judicial coercion that causes a sense of horror <note>original: *afgryzing*</note> in Jews, Muslims, and so-called Heretics. But, some will say, it is a subject that cannot be considered a part of Christian Doctrine; one cannot record it as a Ceremony or Custom: therefore, would it not be better if it were included under Punishments and Capital crimes? By no means. It is a treatment of Religion; the Judges are, after all, zealous Ecclesiastical Personages for the glory of God; the Clergy, encouraged by the Spirit of Peace, labor for the conversion of...

# GENERAL PREFACE.

...heretics, exercising against them JUSTICE (a) as Judges appointed on God's behalf, and showing them MERCY and PEACE as Ambassadors of Jesus Christ. Undoubtedly, it is in their capacity as Ministers of God and of *Mercy and Peace* that they refrain from spilling the blood of those deserving punishment who fall into their hands; which is why they content themselves only with burning them <note>The author is being deeply ironic here, referring to the "Relaxatio ad curiam secularem"—the practice where the Inquisition handed over "unrepentant" heretics to secular authorities for execution to avoid the Church technically "spilling blood."</note>. The *Inquisition* is of a Holy invention, authorized by the Popes, and is praiseworthily carried out under the governance of the Cardinals. Finally, it is a subject that truly depends on Religion, although some countries, which are otherwise very devout in the Roman Religion, reject and condemn it.

These Historical Memoirs <note>original: "Gedenkstukken"</note> are noteworthy; the Author has collected many interesting matters therein, but he has described them in a writing style of an inconsistent nature. We trust, however, that the Reader will be somewhat forgiving regarding the style in favor of the subject matter. The Treatise that follows contains observations on these Memoirs, whether to improve them or to serve as a supplement. It also refutes those who have made a defense for some of the irregular legal proceedings of this Tribunal, etc.

After this subject has concluded the second Volume, we shall proceed to the third Volume, in which the modern Temple Service, Ceremonies, and Customs of the Idolatrous Heathens <note>In the 18th century, "Heathen" was a standard term for non-Abrahamic religions, including those of Asia and the Americas.</note> will be treated, and concerning the content of that subject, we shall then further inform the Reader for that Volume in a continuation of this Preface.

Besides what has been said here in general, we have deemed it very useful and helpful in the translation, to enable the Reader to make better use of this Work, to [arrange] the subject matter of each Treatise—

...divided into Chapters, with the most important subjects indicated in the margin <margin>subject matters</margin>, so that one might perceive the contained Content more clearly and briefly at a glance.

During the translation, we also felt obliged in many places, for the service of our Countrymen, to incorporate some Observations on various matters—placed between these two text brackets [ ]—for further enlightenment of this Work, adding them to the previous notes from the French edition. Likewise, we encountered some terminology specific to the solemn service of the Roman Church <note>The "Roman Church" refers to the Roman Catholic Church; the translators are contextualizing it for a Dutch Reformed/Protestant audience.</note>, which we feared might appear incomprehensible to the Protestants of our nation; therefore, it has pleased us to briefly explain these in passing, so that the Reader might have a concise Concept of the entire arrangement.

But there is one matter of which we must inform the Reader: namely, that we had intended to translate the inscriptions and explanations on the Plates and Illustrations from French into our Dutch Mother Tongue; however, because this was advised against by the Engravers <term>Plaatsnyders (Engravers)</term>, as the scraping away of the French and the subsequent re-cutting of the Dutch <note>The original text uses "Duits" (German/Germanic), which in this period frequently referred to "Nederduits" or the Dutch language.</note> would weaken the plates too much. In order to avoid damaging this excellent plate-work, we have instead placed the translated explanation of these Illustrations beneath the pages where they are to be bound—excepting some whose explanations would expand too far, which have been placed on a separate half-sheet to be inserted opposite the Illustration or the following depictions.

We would have preferred to maintain this Order consistently: but as the aforementioned difficulty arose, the Treatises on the Religious Duties of the Jews <note>This refers to the section based on the work of Leon Modena regarding Jewish rituals.</note> were already printed; and since the required Plates and Illustrations, as described in French, also necessarily had to be translated, we have been forced to include the Translation of these Illustrations along with the explanation of the...

# FOREWORD

<meta>catchword: the</meta>

It is also asserted that it is characteristic of the Italian nature to keep what they have understood in their minds, so as to knead the matter together, whereas other nations must be more powerfully affected to achieve their intended purpose. Nevertheless, however small this little work may be, it nonetheless contains many matters that Buxtorf <note>original: "Buxtorf" – referring to Johannes Buxtorf the Elder (1564–1629), a celebrated Christian Hebraist whose works on Jewish customs were the standard for Christians at the time.</note> left untouched.

Since our Rabbi <note>This refers to Leon Modena (1571–1648), the author of the original work, a famous scholar and rabbi of Venice.</note> had no other aim than to be understood, he was content to write clearly, neatly, and in a concise style; therefore it is not necessary to be high-flown in a narrative. To be even more precise in the execution, we have sometimes made two or three sections out of his original ones, and in other places expanded them to make the meaning clearer. His writing style is, however, sometimes a bit obscure, so that one must have at least some knowledge of the subject matter of which he treats, or he would otherwise be difficult to understand. This has forced us to rearrange several sections into their natural order to follow the thoughts of the Author, who generally speaks Synagogal Italian <note>Likely referring to the Judeo-Italian dialect or the specific liturgical/scholarly terminology used by Italian Jews of that era.</note>.

Since the Christian religion has its beginning and origin in Judaism, there can be no doubt that the reading of this Book will be advantageous for understanding the New Testament, because of the agreement and connection it has with the Old Testament. Those who wrote the New Testament were, after all, Jews; therefore it is impossible to explain it otherwise than according to the sense of Judaism. Likewise, a portion of our church customs * agree with those of the Jews. The Doctrine is almost the same, and as for Morals, the Ten Commandments are common to them and us. Purgatory itself, which the Protestants do not wish to recognize, is nonetheless explained at the end of this work, as is what we believe regarding Paradise, Hell, the Resurrection, and the Day of Judgment.

The Christian religion also has this in common with the Jewish one: that everyone grounds themselves in the Holy Scripture, as well as in the Tradition of the Church Fathers, and on the customs and accepted usages which we, in our religion, call Church Discipline. What is more, just as our Teachers often say that this arises from *Apostolic Traditions*; so too the Rabbis always have in their mouths: <term>A Law of Moses from Sinai</term> <note>original: "HALACA LE MOSCE MI SINAI" (Halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai)</note>, <gloss>This explanation was given to Moses on Mount Sinai.</gloss> It is true that under the name of Tradition they sometimes serve up some vanities: but this is not so much a flaw of the Tradition as it is of those who possess it.

Regarding the prayers of the Jews, they are very pious, and almost all set on the same footing; although they were composed at various times and places. They are little more than a weaving of scriptural passages that contain God’s praise; and it is likely that Ezra <note>original: "Efdras" – the biblical priest and scribe credited with reconstituting Jewish law and liturgy after the Babylonian exile.</note> was the writer of a portion of these prayer formulas, and that the Scribes who followed him have done nothing but add a few things to them. In the early times of the Church, our ancestors sang hymns of praise to God, as well as Psalms, and read in their assemblies the—

# P R E F A C E

...the Holy Scripture, namely, certain passages from the Law or Prophets, such as corresponded with each day that was celebrated, just as the modern-day Jews still do. The reading of the Gospel has subsequently taken the place of the Law of Moses; but some of the Old Testament and especially the Psalms have nonetheless been retained, as seen in the Introduction of the Mass, which is nothing but an abbreviation of the Psalms, which were perhaps sung in their entirety in the beginning; and they were only brought into that state <note>Likely referring to the shortened, "abbreviated" form of the liturgy.</note> to finish the work sooner.

Let us add here that the first Church Fathers observed the Sabbath no less than the Sunday. Also, one sees how the ancient Church ordinances unanimously forbade fasting on either of these two days. *Celebrate*, says the ancient Book of Ordinances, *which bears the name of Clement <note>referring to the Apostolic Constitutions, traditionally attributed to Clement of Rome</note>, the Sabbath and the Sunday as Feast days; because one day is consecrated in memory of the Creation, and the other in memory of the Resurrection.* Truly, these days were in great esteem for a long time, and Saturday was also a day of assembly for the Christians, just as Sunday is now; indeed, one still sees a remnant of this custom on Holy Saturday, when several chapters of the Law and the Prophets are read in our churches.

One cannot wonder enough at the modesty and inner restraint of the Jews when they go to prayer in the morning. For it is not permitted for them to perform any business, nor to visit anyone, nor to greet anyone, unless they have fulfilled this duty toward God. This is an ancient custom among the Jews, and this must serve us to explain these words that **Jesus Christ** spoke to his disciples when he sent them out to preach the Gospel: *Luke 10 verse 4. Greet no one on the road.*

If one examines the Order of Jewish prayers and their rules well, one will find that they differ little from ours. They have morning, afternoon, and evening prayers. Although they do not use the expressions of "double," "semi-double," and "single" services <note>original: "dubbele, half dubbele en enkele Diensten" — these were the traditional Catholic rankings for feast days in the liturgical calendar</note>, they nonetheless have various services in use. They have common and proper services just like us. They also celebrate their Commemorations, as we shall see in the place where we deal with their Feasts. Finally, just as we have the Roman use, as well as that of the Gallican Church <note>The "Gallican" use refers to the distinct liturgical customs of the Catholic Church in France</note> and others, so they also practice the use of the Spanish, High-German <note>meaning the Ashkenazi tradition</note>, Italian, and other Synagogues.

The description that our Author gives of the **Tephilin** <term>Tephilin: small leather boxes containing Torah verses, worn on the head and arm during prayer; often called phylacteries</term>, which they use in prayers, informs us that these were like the protections <note>original: "Bewaarmiddelen" — a translation of the Greek "phylakterion," implying a protective charm or amulet</note> mentioned in the Gospel, which are generally poorly explained by our commentators. We do not know, among other things, what *P. Amelot* <note>Denis Amelote (1606–1678), a French priest and scholar who translated the New Testament</note> intends to say in his French notes on the New Testament, when he suggests that the **Tephilin** and **Taled** <term>Taled: the prayer shawl, or Tallit, worn by Jewish men</term> are Jewish ornamental garments with which the Father of the Household dresses himself to eat the Paschal Lamb in a more exalted manner. He must have been mistaken in this by following *Genebrard* <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine scholar and Hebraist</note>, who, to maintain this opinion, cites *Orah Haiim* <term>Orah Haiim: the portion of the Shulchan Aruch (Jewish Law Code) dealing with daily life and ritual</term>; nor—

-># P R E F A C E<-

Currently, in the passage he presents from this Book, no mention is made of any ceremonial finery needed for the celebration of Passover; but only of a garment with four strips or fringes, which the Jews were then obliged to wear, and from which they have now excused themselves so as not to be mocked; contenting themselves with wearing beneath their clothing a square piece of fabric with four knotted cords frayed at the ends <note>This refers to the *tallit katan* or *tzitzit*, the fringed garment worn by observant Jews.</note>.

On this false ground, some have established the use of sacred vestments in the Ministry of the mysteries <note>The "mysteries" refers to the sacraments, particularly the Eucharist or Mass.</note>; and even today, some imagine they can display the chasubles <term>Kasuifels: an ornate, sleeveless outer garment worn by a priest when celebrating Mass</term> of certain Apostles. However, the most sensible and learned writers do not consider themselves certain of this, and we are amazed at how Cardinal Bona was so very disturbed by *Nicolaas Alemannius*, because he maintained that the Apostles made no use of sacred garments, and that he considers everything said about them to be embellished and ridiculous. This Cardinal bases his presented opinion on those of *Baronius, Monchi, Stapleton, du Saussay*, and others, who believe that *Jesus Christ* held the Last Supper in sacred and ceremonial robes; whereas Cardinal Bona says only that there were none but the Apostles who ministered the mysteries in sacred garments, but as for *Jesus Christ*, He instituted this Sacrament in nothing but ordinary attire. Nevertheless, it appears that the one is no better grounded than the other, and *Walafrid Strabo* <note>original: "Walfried Strabo," a 9th-century Benedictine monk and theological writer</note> rightly said: *that in the early Church, the Mass was served in nothing but ordinary attire;* not for the reasons given by *Josephus Vicecomes* <note>original: "Joseph de Vicomte," likely referring to the 17th-century liturgical scholar</note>, that at that time the Church was unable to bear the expense of such costly garments as were customary in these ceremonies: but rather because the first Christians, who for the most part had been Jews, ministered the mysteries in the Assemblies with the same garments they had worn in the Synagogues. We also do not doubt that the surplices <term>Koorkleeden: white linen liturgical vestments worn over a cassock</term> worn by our Priests originate from the cloaks used by the Jews, or from the Roman gowns <term>Tabberden: heavy, formal robes or surcoats</term>, or from both together. For it is probable that both, upon leaving their religion to embrace Christianity, did not change their usual style of dress. To this one may add that in ancient times, the Mass was performed with surplices, and that the Eastern peoples <note>Referencing the Eastern Orthodox or Oriental churches</note>, in order to minister the same, still value them today even above our chasubles. But as these surplices were found to be too cumbersome, they were cut off at the bottom and left open at the sides, which was more convenient and less costly. Likewise, the *Alb* <term>Albe: a long white linen liturgical robe</term> originates from the Roman gown, which was shortened and made wider to serve as our choir garments. Thus, at that time, there was no distinction between ceremonial dress and that which was used habitually; for it is only time that has brought about this change. The laity have changed their customs, but the clergy have always retained their manner of dressing. As they then kept their best clothes for ministering the Mysteries, and as the Church gradually became wealthier and subsequently built magnificent Temples, it so happened that they also provided themselves with costly and splendid garments.

# PREFACE

<margin>* 1 Corinthians 10.</margin>The great number of Blessings and Thanksgivings, which the Jews are accustomed to perform at the beginning and end of all their actions, also serve to help us understand several passages of the Apostle Paul, where he speaks of the Praises and Thanksgivings that one must continually offer to God. *If I by grace,* he says, *partake of the food, why am I slandered over that for which I give Thanks? Whether then you eat, or you drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.* <note>The author is quoting 1 Corinthians 10:30-31 to show how Paul’s instructions mirror Jewish daily blessings over food and drink.</note> We do not mean here that he is speaking particularly of the Blessings and Thanksgivings included in the tenth chapter of the first letter to the Corinthians regarding the subject of the *Eucharist* <term>Eucharist: The Christian ceremony commemorating the Last Supper, in which bread and wine are consecrated and consumed</term>, although those are very well explained through the Blessings and Thanksgivings of the Jews in the celebration of their Passover feast. There are many other things of this nature which cannot be well explained except through the usage and custom of the Jews.

In the Regulations of Jewish Prayers, there is one which they perform in public for the Princes and Authorities whose subjects they are. It consists of many Articles, and at the end of each Article, the People say *Amen*. To show their zeal, they recite it while embracing their Book of the Law <note>The Torah scroll.</note>. Nevertheless, it seems that what they pray to God for their Authorities serves only their own advantage and interest, which the Jewish nation might enjoy from it. *May the King of Kings,* they say, *by his mercy preserve our Prince; may he conduct himself so as to do good to all the Israelites, and may Judah be saved under his reign; may Israel be in safety, and may the Redeemer come to Sion.* <note>This refers to the prayer *Hanoten Teshua*, a traditional Jewish prayer for the welfare of the government.</note> We do not know if one could conclude from this prayer that Paul, who had been so well instructed in the Synagogue, took the opportunity from it to exhort the first Christians to pray to God for the Kings and Princes of the Earth. However that may be, one must not condemn this great number of Jewish Blessings for many reasons; since the Christian Churches of the East and West are provided with little less in their liturgical service books. Also, all the Blessings they perform without superstition to the honor of God are always good.

We say without superstition, because the Jews are accused of misusing the name of God and those of the Angels with certain Blessings, in the hope of making themselves more familiar with them through a kind of Magic <note>original: "Toverkunde"</note>, and because this is grounded in an imagination they have that the Patriarchs <note>original: "Artsvaders"</note> had Angels as their guides and instructors. But our Rabbi is so entirely removed from these thoughts that he would never place Magic in agreement with the Bible and Talmud. One even sees in the fifth Article of their faith <note>Referring to Maimonides' Thirteen Principles of Faith, specifically the one stating that prayer should be directed to God alone.</note> that they forbid the Service of Angels, when they say that one must not worship them, nor serve them as mediators or intercessors. Bewaart ons, bewaart ons. Helpt ons en staat ons by." This is an address to guardian angels.</note> Even today, there are Jews so pious that they offer this prayer, leaning upon what is said in Psalm 91: *He shall command his angels to guard you in all your ways.* <note>The source cites Psalm 90, following the numbering found in some older translations, whereas modern English Bibles number this as Psalm 91:11.</note> For the rest, the belief in Guardian Angels was introduced into the Synagogue in the time of our Savior, just as it was introduced and still holds firm in the Roman Church today.

Nevertheless, one must admit that there are Jews who misuse the names of God and the Angels, believing that they can perform supernatural feats, covering this forbidden practice with the fair-sounding name of <term>Kabbalah: A school of Jewish mysticism; here the author views it skeptically as a source of superstition</term> *Kabbalah*, so as to claim they do nothing but follow the traditions of their ancestors. And truly, under this word "Tradition," they convince the simplest among them—and even some Christians who allow themselves to be filled with these *Kabbalistic* dreams—of things that form the foundations of their magic. But what is most wonderful of all is that *Reuchlin* <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering German humanist and scholar who sought to reconcile Kabbalah with Christian theology.</note>, one of the most learned men of the past century, stooped to write on this subject. Even the extravagances of the *Count of Gabalis* <note>A reference to *Le Comte de Gabalis* (1670), a satirical French novel about secret sciences and elemental spirits like sylphs and undines.</note>, which appeared recently, were not unpleasing to the world—if it is true that man is naturally inclined toward superstition. The *Kabbalah*, in our opinion, took its origin from the philosophy of *Pythagoras* and *Plato*, which some Jews mixed with Judaism, spreading many dreams everywhere, produced by idle brains and superstition; as can be seen in the Books of *Adam*, *Enoch*, some of *Solomon*, and many others, in which our author—neither Jew nor Christian—places any faith.

The Jews excel not only in prayer but also in charity; and it seems that in their compassion for the poor, one sees the shining image of the love the first Christians had for their brothers. At that time, they followed what was practiced in the *Synagogues*, a practice and custom which the Jews have maintained, while we have barely preserved the memory of it. We shall make no mention here of their discipline, which is very orderly, as can be seen in the chapter on Excommunication <term>Excommunication: The formal exclusion of a person from the religious community</term> and Penance; but we shall only note in passing that the Jews seek to satisfy God not only through repentance and inner penitence, but also through their outward conduct. For to this end they have their books dealing with penance, just as the Church used to have, and perhaps in imitation of them. It is true that they impose strict punishments on those who have committed great crimes, but this is carried out in secret, as the Sovereigns whose subjects they are would not tolerate it. Likewise, it is true that the Jews are very inclined toward outward rituals in everything; because, as they say, all outward acts serve only to govern the inner self. Consequently, when washing their hands, they think of the purification of their conscience; and by abstaining from unclean animals, they...

<meta>catchword: voor- (for-)</meta>

to expect to commit no crimes, and they regard the doctrine of the outward ritual as an application for the inward spirit. We would not, however, be inclined to approve of the excessive precision of some superstitious people; consisting in this, that when someone rises before sunrise for six consecutive days to better praise God, he then lies in bed longer on the **Sabbath** <note>The Jewish day of rest, from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset.</note>, in order to best observe the rest of that day; which appears to us as a flawed affectation. We also consider it unnecessary to have such scrupulous examiners <note>The author refers to the *shochetim* (ritual slaughterers) or those who inspect meat for kosher status.</note>, such that one might not eat a dove or a chicken without approval, as the suspicion of any defect, of which hardly the slightest blemish was apparent, would be enough to abstain from eating it.

One will, what is more, perceive in this work how they perform their general and private confessions; how they forgive one another, and how they plead for forgiveness, reconciling amongst themselves, just as is prescribed to us in the **Gospel** <note>original: "Euangeli"</note>. But what is remarkable is that they are concerned about having failed in any matter during the past year, and for this reason they observe a hallowed day to remedy this defect <note>A reference to Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement.</note>. We shall mention no less with what circumspection they examine their conscience during illnesses, and also with what zeal they change their name when they find themselves in danger of dying: but we have noted that sometimes a good deal of superstition creeps in. When they see themselves in extreme danger, they take on the names of **LIFE** <note>original: "HAIIM" (Chaim)</note>, and **GOD’S HEALING** <note>original: "RAPHAEL"</note>, and others; and if they return to health, they keep that name for the rest of their lives, attributing their health to the change of name.

Their Teachers do not care for eloquence as much as being instructed in the Holy Scripture and in the debates of the **Rabbis**. They practice primarily in the study of certain books which they call <term>Questions and Answers: Known in Hebrew as *She’elot u-Teshuvot* (Responsa), these are legal decisions given by scholars in response to specific inquiries about Jewish law</term>, and which primarily correspond to the books of the **Casuists** <note>Theologians or scholars who resolve moral problems by applying general principles of ethics or law.</note>. Since it is permitted for anyone to preach, one can sufficiently understand from this why the Lord Jesus and his Apostles, upon entering the **Synagogues**, preached; and how one must understand what Luke says, that Jesus was found sitting in the Temple in the midst of the Teachers, listening to them and questioning them: not that he was there to teach these Teachers: but he had placed himself in the rank of the students to be instructed, as is still the custom of the Jews now, giving in this respect the name of **Schools** to their Synagogues <note>The Yiddish word *Shul*, commonly used for synagogue, literally means "school."</note>. One could bring forward many other matters: but it should be known that we are writing a Preface here and not a Book.

We leave the reader’s observations free regarding what our Author says of Marriage, Divorce, and the degrees of kinship; which can serve to explain various passages of the **New Testament**. And just as the Spanish Jews excelled in the scholarship of the Holy Scripture, those of France were the most skilled in the science of the *Talmud* <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note>. In this era, Paris served as the "Athens of the Jews," and they came from all regions to be instructed in this learning. *Rabbi Salomon Isaak* <note>Known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note>, that great commentator of the *Talmud*, was a Frenchman, and we do not doubt that he gave public lectures on this subject in Paris. He was a native of *Troyes* in Champagne, and he wrote the most distinguished commentaries on the Bible, which the Jews generally value more highly than all others. We are not unaware that others wish to assert that this Rabbi was a native of Lunel in Languedoc, basing this on the name *Jarchi* <note>original: "Jarchi"; a common but mistaken name for Rashi, derived from the Hebrew "Yareach," meaning moon, which corresponds to the French "Lune" in Lunel.</note> which was commonly given to him, meaning "of *Lunel*" in Hebrew: but in my judgment they are mistaken; for the true name of this Jew was not *Jarchi*, as the majority of our writers call him: but *Isabaki*, or *Isaac’s* Son, thus named by the Jews. It is true that *Rabbi Benjamin* <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler.</note> in his *Travels* mentions a certain *Rabbi Salomon* of *Lunel*, whom Constantine L’Empereur <note>original: "Keizer Konstantyn"; referring to Constantijn L'Empereur (1591–1648), a famous Dutch Hebraist and professor at Leiden.</note> believes to be our famous *Rabbi Salomon*: but he failed to notice that he had already passed away before this time. We note in passing, to the credit of the French Jews, that they earned great esteem because they surpassed others in knowledge of the *Talmud*, and especially those of Champagne who made a particular study of it. They are the authors of a large part of what we call *Tosaphot* <note>original: "Tosaphot"; meaning "Additions," these are medieval glosses on the Talmud.</note>, Additions or Explanations of the *Talmud*, as can be seen in the book which bears the name *Juhasin* <note>original: "Juhasin"; the *Sefer Ha-Yuhasin* or "Book of Genealogies" by Abraham Zacuto.</note> or *of the Families*, as well as in *Tsemah David* <note>original: "Tsemah David"; "Sprout of David," a work of Jewish history by David Gans.</note>. Most were from Rheims or Troyes, and they openly taught the *Talmud* there to all the Jews.

One could further add here that although the manuscripts of the Spanish Bibles are to be valued above all others, those written by the Jews of Languedoc and the Spanish borders need not yield to them. The city of Narbonne has been the preeminent place in the world where the Jews made it their work to transcribe the best copies of the Bible, and it is in this sense that one must understand the words of *Rabbi Benjamin* at the beginning of his *Travels*:

> *Narbonne is the Mistress of the Law, and it is from there that the Law goes out to spread itself into all parts of the world. She has distinguished scholars, and those who are Princes, of whom the foremost is Rabbi Kalonymus, son of the Nasi <term>Nasi: a Hebrew title meaning Prince or communal leader</term> or very great Prince Rabbi Theodoros of happy memory, and descended from the line of David, who possesses estates and lands granted to him by the Authorities of this land.*

The best of all those he brought back is a copy written by this Nasi, or Prince *Theodoros*, whom the Jew *Benjamin* mentions. # PREFACE

...at the end of the manuscript it appears, in the year 967 <note>This refers to the year 4967 in the Hebrew calendar, which corresponds to 1207 AD.</note>, corresponding to our dating of the year 1207. We have also seen very beautiful manuscripts of the Bible from Perpignan, which however are not to be compared with those of Narbonne. The copy of the Bible famous among the Jews, which bears the name of *Hillel* <note>The "Hillel Codex" was a famous, highly accurate manuscript of the Hebrew Bible, now lost, which served as a standard for medieval scribes.</note>, and according to which they correct their books as if from an original source, originates from the Kingdom of Leon in Spain, and not from Lyon in France, as others have written. One must nevertheless take note that it is not of such great antiquity as the Jews claim, as we could easily prove by the various readings in this manuscript. For the rest, we believe it would be very difficult today to find manuscripts of the Bible that are more than 600 years old, and we should not trust those that are claimed to be of a much older origin. Although some might be found that they had corrected according to the *Masorah* <term>Masorah: a traditional system of notes and grammatical rules used by Jewish scribes to ensure the biblical text was copied exactly without even a single letter being changed.</term>; just as we have seen some that were nowhere near as old, yet had been "purified" according to the corrections of the *Masorah*.

Since this *Masorah* has gained more respect among the Jews than sheer antiquity, old manuscripts are no longer held in such high regard; because it was believed they were not sufficiently purified or corrected. We could make many remarks here about such manuscripts to distinguish the good from the bad: but this would lead us too far astray, and we believe we have already exceeded the bounds of a Preface for this book concerning the Ceremonies of the Jews. We shall only add that this edition (which served for the translation of this work) is more accurate than the previous one, although a certain person who was asked to proofread the pages, without the author's knowledge, added and removed various things, which was not discovered until the author reviewed his work some time later.

# I N T R O D U C T I O N ,
### TREATING of
## RELIGIOUS VENERATION
->In General.<-

<margin>General excesses regarding external religious duties identified.</margin>
The majority of people would be ignorant of the fact that there is a God, if the respect one is duty-bound to give Him were not accompanied by some outward signs. The less the Supreme Being was known, the more these signs were strange in nature and excessive. Ignorance has even incited religious devotion to the point of inhumanity, and the wise, among an infinite number of imposing pseudo-devout people, have made themselves look ridiculous. Some have believed that to serve God it was required (a) to kill humans in a barbaric and cruel manner <note>A reference to human sacrifice, which Enlightenment-era writers often used to contrast "civilized" religion with "barbarism."</note>. Others (b) believed that one must harden oneself by jumping around, beating the dust of the earth from one's chest; (c) bouncing and swinging over a fire; (d) holding oneself for several hours in a state of ecstasy <note>original: "verrukking," referring to a spiritual trance or "rapture."</note>, etc. People have called the founding of temples and chapels "religious veneration"; likewise the ceremonies of religion, the processions, and the multiplicity of churches. Finally, people have believed that to obtain God's help and the forgiveness of their sins, it was required—if one may say so—to trouble Him with frequently repeated expressions, and to dazzle Him with magnificent ceremonies or unusual gestures, which were accompanied by agonizing and sometimes unbearable

# INTRODUCTORY TREATISE

...supported by strange ceremonies, to compel the Divinity to their favor. We believe, of course, that there is no Christian so superstitiously foolish as to imagine that their prayers have such a power; but possibly there are some among them who imagine they can obtain from God what they entreat of him by the power of using many repetitive words, accompanied by this outward religiosity which constitutes the entire religion of countless peoples.

<margin>
The origin of prayer and what it consisted of.
</margin>
It is not very difficult to trace the origin of prayer. Since the first human sinned, he was compelled to call upon Divine mercy and to request help against the evils he had to fear after his disobedience. But even when he wished to cover his innocence <note>The author likely means "to seek cover for his lost innocence" or to seek atonement.</note>, he could not refrain from calling for help from his Creator and offering Him his vows. This is the origin (a) of the offerings of Abel and Cain, of whose merit and manner we are otherwise ignorant; everything that can be said about it consists only—following the sacred Text—in the fact that Cain was already an evil person at that time. After the death of Abel, (b) and when Seth had come to an age of discernment to worship God, sensible people possibly began to found a kind of Church and to practice a regulated religion; but we are also ignorant of the manner of that worship.

<margin>
And how the true purpose was corrupted, from which superstition arose.
</margin>
All people are inclined to pray to God for the same things; it is not surprising that the examples of their prayers almost coincide, or at least in many matters. They have the same purpose, and their needs are corresponding. But as man has lost the true idea of the Divinity and takes pleasure in attributing physical or weak human qualities to God, so too has he lost the true impressions of prayer. He has added superstition to his religion; he has served God under physical concepts, and no longer having the capacity to behold Him in the spirit—whether through pride, fear, or weakness—he takes pleasure in representing Him to himself through

<column-break/>

images, through statues, etc. He offers Him everything that one can offer to humans to satisfy them, and he has reached such a level of extravagance that he no longer dares to address Him without ceremonies of a brief, easy, and clear manner, which is too easily understood by the common people, and which he himself hardly understands. This is the principle and the origin of so many unusual ceremonies, extravagant religious acts, and an infinite variety of methods introduced into prayers, which can cause nothing but a ridiculous effect when they are not understood. Such was the *Io pean* <note>A ritual cry or hymn of praise, originally used for Apollo.</note> among the ancient Pagans, which they placed in the prayers dedicated to Apollo and which they did not understand, judging it very differently in how they explained these (c) two words.

Among the ancient idolaters, prayers sometimes preceded the sacrifice; sometimes they followed it, and they were also divided into two parts. It is apparent that the first of mankind did not make bloody sacrifices to God and had no temples: they worshipped Him in the open field, or each by himself within his household, without making a noise, without mysteries, and without any human inventions—which subsequently produced the irreligiosity of some and the hypocrisy of others. This practice was very simple; soon they went to serve Him in the woods and built Him chapels there. The silence had an influence on religiosity. They dedicated the tallest trees of the forests to Him and moved on to the hills. Finally, the spiritual service was practiced on the mountains, and as they changed locations, they took care to leave the gods in the places they had vacated. God reproached the Jews for this idolatry. Nevertheless, it is to be noted in the Holy Scripture that the Patriarchs, before the giving of the Law, had acted similarly regarding the true God. After all this, there was no other evil in the practice of this religiosity than the transfer of it to false deities. Piety required silence and detachment, for which the woods and fields served. The mountains and other high places gave an idea of

### RELIGIOUS WORSHIP, etc.

<margin>How the ancient Persians conducted themselves in the matter of Religion.</margin>
...of the majesty of God set above us; and this was, possibly, why according to *Arrian* <note>original: "Arrianus," a Greek historian of the Roman period.</note> (a) *Jupiter* was worshipped on the mountains of Bithynia <note>An ancient region in north-central Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey.</note>; but without dedicating a Temple to him (due to the immensity of God), no more than the Sicyonians <note>Ancient inhabitants of Sicyon in Greece.</note> did to any of their Gods. The Getae and ancient Indians dedicated none to them either; and as for the ancient Persians, it is well enough known that in their invasion of Greece they destroyed all the Temples they found there; understanding that God being infinite, could not be confined, nor locked in a Temple. These Persians did not represent a Supreme Being through statues; they built him no Altar: but they sacrificed to him on high places. It is certain that the Idolatry of these peoples was much purer than that of other Heathens, and above all more free from the trifles of superstitions and the fictions of the Greeks. The learned *Hyde* <note>Thomas Hyde (1636–1703), an English orientalist and author of a major work on ancient Persian religion.</note> goes much further; he believes in his *History of the Ancient Persians* that they for a very long time retained the true religion.

<margin>The multitude of Gods greatly increased under the Romans and what it consisted of.</margin>
The Romans themselves, who subsequently increased their Gods so greatly that they had them for all the necessities of life: for sickness and health; for the kitchen and the hearth; for the table and the bed, etc., without mentioning so many minor Gods they imagined to have the management of their marriages; (b) The Romans, we say, spent 170 years in the service of worshipping the Gods without making any image thereof; and if this were still observed today, says Varro <note>A prolific Roman scholar and writer.</note>, the religiosity shown to them would be purer and holier. It is somewhat evident that Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many religious institutions.</note>, the founder of their religion, had much more righteous ideas of it than other Idolaters; and possibly he unearthed them from the source, which was not yet entirely destroyed. The same Romans of the earliest times did not degenerate—namely, from the custom of worshipping the Gods in the groves, and practicing their religiosity in forests; it was there that they placed the Temple of Diana Aricina and Juno Lacinia; it was there that one saw that of the Goddess

The religiosity having thus retreated into wild and inaccessible places, it must necessarily follow that men, more Religious than others, set aside the care of their lives, are negligent with the work of their hands, become lazy and even feral because of their devotion to the Gods. But this does not suffice; one gives a secret allure to this solitary service, and one adds penances to it. ### DISCURSIVE INTRODUCTION

<margin>
Christians, under the pretext of piety, have transitioned [to this].

...of their *Dervishes* <note>Sufi Muslim ascetics known for their extreme poverty and austerity.</note> among the rocky cliffs and in the forests, just as the most famous travelers recount to us. The Christians themselves conform to this solitary and difficult form of piety. We once had, and still have today, pious hermits who practiced no less severity than the *Brahmins* <note>The highest-ranking social and religious class in India, often associated with asceticism in this period’s literature.</note> of India, and who willingly endure everything that the body can suffer in the strangest, most painful, and cruelest manner. Finally, it is certain that humans of all times have had a great inclination to practice their piety in solitude; undoubtedly believing they would discover there the means to serve the Deity more worthily, with less distraction and more secrecy: and possibly taking pride in putting aside disorders in the company of wild animals which they could not avoid in the presence of men.

<margin>
Strange behavior of some Ancient Idolaters and what it consisted of.
</margin>
Whenever the Ancient Idolaters arrived in any place, they had to offer a kind of outpouring prayer for the local gods. If they wished to travel, they paid their homage to the gods they assumed they would find in the places where their journey lay: *Fauns, Dryads, Napaeae* <note>Nymphs of wooded valleys and glens.</note>, *Boundary-Gods* <note>In Rome, known as Terminus, the protector of property markers.</note>—none were forgotten. Even the respect of the Romans for the gods of their enemies was so great that, before they besieged a city, (a) they sent priests to implore those gods to depart from there, fearing they would not conquer the place if the gods were stronger, or that they would be forced to take these gods captive if they were defeated. In extraordinary needs of the state, individuals sacrificed themselves for the Fatherland, such that the wrath of the gods was appeased by the voluntary death of someone for all the people. Many nations have performed human sacrifices, and in this manner the Ammonites served *Moloch*, the Carthaginians *Saturn*, and the Tauric Scythians *Diana*. This religious practice is still in use today among various American peoples. The Mexicans practiced this until the arrival of the Spaniards in the New World. But less cruel peoples were formerly satisfied with some incising and scourging to appease the angry gods, and one still sees among us remnants of this bloody piety. Penitent Christians scourge, cut, and tear their flesh in their processions,

The practice of building Temples introduced.
</margin>
As humans gradually became more civilized, cities were founded: piety became more zealous and was brought from the fields into the cities. We have said that the Persians believed that the Supreme Being could not be enclosed within the narrow bounds of a Temple: nevertheless, it was now absolutely necessary, for the sake of the convenience of the temple service, to build them in his honor and for religion; it even seemed that the ignited zeal and piety established themselves in this spiritual place. God presided over these assemblies held there. The least enlightened Heathens believed it; and this is what God makes known: *I shall be*, he says, *in the midst of three or four persons gathered in my name*.

<margin>
And how the Greeks and Romans conducted themselves in this.
</margin>
The Greeks and Romans worshipped their gods in Temples. All of Antiquity testifies to it: but under the pretext of religion, unmannerliness soon crept in, and eventually became almost an act of faith in the service of many deities. *Bacchus, Saturn, Adonis, Pan, Flora, Priapus*, and *Venus* were served there in a disorderly and immoral manner. The women in Babylon allowed themselves to be used as harlots in honor of this last deity, whom they honored under the name of *Mylitta*; (a) and the nocturnal mysteries of Ceres were accompanied by infamy. Christianity indeed does not tolerate such abominations: but there are those who still practice certain pleasures, amours, and similar deeds in the churches; meetings held there are all too "respectable," <note>The author implies that church gatherings are often used as social opportunities for courtship rather than worship.</note> and the pious acts of Pilgrimages, modern prayers, etc., are very often intended for matters other than religion.

Ministers established, and what followed from that.
</margin>
However it may be, religious worship being enclosed in Temples, it necessarily required the appointment of Ministers of the Deity. God himself was the institutor of those who were to be served in the true religion. Men instituted the false service. In both, infinite human motives increased. # ON RELIGIOUS WORSHIP, etc.

[...solemnities] were expanded; false worship became full of mysteries and more dogmatic. The priests discovered the secret of preventing people from performing their own religious exercises unless they first consulted them. They made all matters of the heart's inclination depend upon themselves; they managed the subtle intricacies of ritual and even knew how to make themselves masters of the courts of Princes. Finally, they condemned them to the favor of God <note>This likely refers to the idea that the priests controlled access to divine grace.</note>. Such has always been the authority of the Clergy in all religions. * Indeed, the power of the Wizzards, Soothsayers, and Priests among the Greeks and Romans, the Wise Men among the Persians, the Druids among the Gauls, and the Bards among the Celts and Britons is not unknown to us. Today, the world is still governed in nearly the same way. The *Mufti* <note>A Muslim legal expert and advisor on religious law.</note> and the scholars of the Islamic Law are often the driving wheels of the deliberations of the *Divan* <note>The high council or government body of the Ottoman Empire.</note>. The inhabitants of America, Africa, the East Indies, etc., do nothing without consulting their Priests and Clergy. It is unnecessary to provide examples of what goes on among us.

Let us briefly recount everything that men have put into practice to honor the Deity in their religious worship. The Romans greeted the Gods in the morning. One honored them through songs of praise on feast days and other solemn occasions according to this command (the Law of the 12 Tables <note>The earliest attempt by the Romans to create a code of law, c. 450 BCE.</note> explicitly looked to this): that one must honor the Gods who had always been recognized as such, and those men whose merit had placed them in heaven, such as Hercules, Aesculapius, Castor and Pollux, etc. That one should dedicate chapels in honor of virtuous men, to whom Deification was owed. One took refuge in them in times of need: one celebrated days of penance, just as happens today. One arranged (a) barefoot processions, etc. The ancient Germanni or Germans sacrificed every Thursday to their God *Thor*, so that he would ward off the thunder from

<column-break/>

them, as well as hail and lightning. (b) Vows were brought into use to bind the Gods to them to some extent, and to interest them in their affairs through favorable proposals presented to them. (c) The conditions entered into with them on these occasions were placed on the statues in their Temples. When the favor requested from the Gods had been obtained, it was time to fulfill one's vow, and one tore up the condition, which served as a discharge or receipt.

<margin>Long prayers established, and some particulars noted therein.</margin>
Regarding prayers, Jesus Christ forbade his disciples from expanding them through repetitions. It is certain that the repetition of the same thing in prayer is an act neither of zeal nor of respect. Probably these prayers of the Idolaters were long enough; but presumably, the Christians have fallen into this same error. To consider it one's duty to recite the same prayers fifty times in a set period seems to us to have no more effect on God than if, through one's own stubbornness, one intended to present a sequence of fifty copies of the same petition to one's Prince. (d) The Turks have certain religious practices among them which require the repetition of the name of God with a certain speed, which involves more folly than religiousness. The Ancients made much of the number three in their prayers; (e) (We shall give some examples of this here.) They believed that their Gods took pleasure in receiving many titles and various surnames, to thereby make known the extent of their power; and being fearful of giving them any (f) unpleasant name, they were careful to accompany these attributions with a softening expression. But this did not yet comprise the entire solemnity of the prayer. When they did it with a raised voice, a (g) Minister of the Gods proposed it to the people, who did nothing but repeat it with the same words. This is still done today.

# INTRODUCTORY TREATISE

in the Roman and English <note>Referring to the Anglican Church</note> Churches, as also observed among the Turks <note>A common historical term for Muslims within the Ottoman Empire</note>. We shall make no mention here of whispered prayers in public assemblies, nor of (a) those commonplaces usually devoted to this pious custom by the ancients and moderns. Every religion has its own: and it would even be impossible to note everything, at least if one wished to avoid introducing disorder and anarchy into religion.

We have said that the Romans greeted their Gods in the morning. Almost all peoples of the world, even the most savage in nature, have this custom. With the rising of the dawn, the Wise Men of the Persians sang hymns of praise in honor of their gods, and greeted the rising sun—this fire, which they regarded as an eternal Source. The ancient Tartars also began the day by worshipping the sun, and they offered it the first fruits of their food and drink in the morning: but the idolaters who were pious did not limit their devotions to the morning; all hours of the day were suitable for practicing such a duty: likewise the evening hours, like those of the morning, were dedicated to the Gods; without mentioning the many sacrifices, ceremonies, and nightly prayers in use among the Heathens. The Mohammedans pray five times a day, and to be a faithful *Muslim*, he must strictly observe this custom. They display in this devotion such a modest and composed countenance, that no humbler submission can be imagined. The (b) Je-

<column-break/>

ws and (c) Christians also practice their hours for the public use of prayer, and to show honor to the Deity. We shall now note what men have judged necessary to serve God purely, how this is established, and what they have believed the Supreme Being could demand of them on this occasion.

It is well known that the Jewish people have hallowed, and still today hallow, Saturday to be engaged in their devotions with a precision that almost passes into childishness. Besides that, the Jews have established solemn days to maintain the memory of the benefits God has done for them.

Possibly some self-interest has been mixed with it; for the more ignorant a man is, the more the Teacher of the conscience is honored as a leader. Ignorance is a mother who liberally feeds a good number of lazy children. Regarding the religion of the household; (the venerable Oracle of Delphi recommended to the Athenians to follow the customs of their ancestors: see *Cicero, On the Laws* <note>original: "Cicero de Legibus"</note>) one knows people who, of all the editions of the *Psalms of David* set in rhyme by *Clement Marot* and *Theodore Beza*, prefer those in which the words are most perfectly expressed in Old Gaulish <note>original: "oud Gallisch," referring to the archaic French used in early Huguenot psalters</note>, as if hallowed; such that they can sing them in the language of their great-great-grandfathers, and eternalize a holy obscurity in the devotion of their household.

(b) The writer *J. Ross* <note>Alexander Ross (1591–1654), author of "Pansebeia, or a View of All Religions in the World"</note> tells in his *Religions of the World* of many customs that the Jews observe in prayer; for example, he says, that they pray while standing, with their face turned toward the Temple and hands placed on the heart; that while praying they may not belch, nor pass wind, nor let themselves be distracted, even if during their prayer they were in danger of being bitten by a venomous animal, etc. The Jews go three times a day to pray. See *P. Simon* <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), a French priest and influential biblical critic</note> in his *First Treatise on the Ceremonies of the Jews.*

(c) The Roman Catholics have *Canonical hours* for prayer. In some Protestant States, one goes once a day to prayer; in others, it is at the choice of the pious. In short, unhappy is he who prays to God in an improper manner. A good Christian has this as his first subject. The *Calvinists* have investigated all the occasions when prayer should be performed. They pose these questions: for example, whether it is permitted to praise God, sing Psalms, etc., when one is occupied with procreation? or when nature requires one to relieve oneself?

(d) One suspects well that neither God nor His Saints can take pleasure in the devotion of these days, which are spent in nothing but pomp, pleasure, and vanity; as for the clergy in these days, among some Christians, unnecessary church duties are coupled with devotion. Piety is not awakened there except in commonplaces and with great gesturing.

# RELIGIOUS REVERENCE, etc.

<margin>And how one conducted oneself in the practice thereof</margin>
...dedicated to solemn days, upon which they were not permitted to labor. (a) <note>original: "Lex apud Athenienses jubebat, ut Sacra Diis rite fierent, non avocado ad alias curas animo." — The law among the Athenians commanded that sacred rites be performed properly to the Gods, without the mind being distracted by other cares.</note> The Greeks confirmed the holiness of these days by law. It was believed that labor desecrated the Festival, and to prevent such an occurrence, the Romans had a Herald proclaim that everyone must cease their work; for if the Sacrificial Priest (b) <note>original: "A Flaminibus praemittebantur qui denuntiarent opificibus, manus abstinerent ab opere..." — The Flamines (priests) sent ahead messengers to warn the craftsmen to stay their hands from work, lest the rites be polluted if the Priest saw work being done.</note> perceived anyone working during the sacrifice, the ceremony would have been defiled. At such times, all disputes and quarrels were ceased in honor of the Gods; but after the Festival, they were permitted again and legal proceedings resumed their course. The uninitiated were forbidden from laying a hand upon these hallowed ceremonies. (c) <note>The Greek phrase was: "let all the people be favorable"; that of the Romans: "favor with your tongues" (keep a holy silence). Seneca says: "That the rite may be performed properly, with no evil voice interrupting, silence is commanded."</note> A spiritual silence was imposed upon the bystanders; for they feared that, in speaking, some word might slip out that would portend a troublesome outcome. And let it not be thought that this piety was merely superficial. It was a silence of solemn bearing, which perhaps gradually turned into true godliness for some; for it was perceived that during the performance of these mysteries, the people held a true, pious attention, and that custom eventually bound their hearts to religion over time. However that may be, (d) <note>The Imams carefully admonish Muslims to maintain silence and to be attentive in prayer.</note> silence in the Temples and at the Altars, while

<column-break/>

performing Divine Service, has always been regarded as the greatest sign of respect due to God. It is the same with the purity of conscience. A man defiled by crimes can be pleasing to no deity. It was therefore necessary to exclude him from worship (e) <note>original: "PROCUL ESTE PROPHANI" — BEGONE, YE PROFANE. Livy writes: "Every preface to the sacred rites excludes those from the rites whose hands are not pure."</note> with explicit words: and if this was practiced in Heathendom, there is even more powerful reason to confirm this custom in Christianity. The administration of the <term>Sacrament of the Holy Supper|The central Christian rite of sharing bread and wine in memory of Jesus</term> is denied to Christians who lead a shameful life; they are exhorted to repentance and the judgments of God are proclaimed to them: and if, despite this proclamation, they do not repent, they are excommunicated from the Church.

<margin>How the Romans noted Janus and Vesta in their worship of the gods.</margin>
It was through the invocation of † Janus that the Romans began their public devotion. Evidence of this is given in the (f) <note>Martial says to Janus: "The incense asks for you first, the vows salute you." Ovid says: "Janus, to you I first bring incense and wine." A Roman prayer from Livy also proves this: "Janus, Jupiter, Mars Father, Quirinus... I pray to you, venerate you, and seek your favor..."</note> remarks. Many other ceremonies existed which can be looked up in the authors who deal with them. The Romans believed Janus to be their introducer to the Gods, and that he acted as the conveyor of their prayers and their advocate. It was also believed that he was the first institutor of the worship of the Gods, of their Temples and

<meta>catchword: Altars</meta>

---

† [Scholars do not agree on the etymology of the name <term>Janus|A Roman god usually depicted with two faces, presiding over beginnings, gates, and transitions</term>; some derive the word from the Latin verb *Ire* (to go) or from one of the participles *Eundo*, as if one said *Janus*, because this God was the executor of the beginning of all deeds and undertakings. To him was attributed the introduction of prayers made to other Gods; and since the doors of buildings opened the entrance to the inner rooms, they were named after *Janus*, since they were dedicated to him. Vossius says, among other things, that the word *Janus* seems to come from the Hebrew *Jain* (wine).

The origin of this *Janus* is no less in dispute; some maintain that *Janus* signifies both the world and the Sun: others compare him to Ogyges, who built Thebes more than fifteen hundred years before the founding of Rome. There are those, like Ovid, who conflate *Janus* with <term>Noah|The biblical patriarch who survived the Great Flood</term>. They give him the honor of being the beginning of the World, and the only one who beheld the ancient and new World before the flood. Likewise, it is said that Noah, dividing the lands among his sons after the flood, gave Europe to his son Japheth, and that Japheth was called *Janus*, who populated Italy where he invented many things necessary for man's sustenance. Fabius Pictor reports that he taught the Tuscans viticulture, the sowing of grain, and the baking of bread: likewise the building of Temples to the Gods and the erecting of Altars.

To him was also attributed the walling of cities; for Romulus, wishing to build his City, had himself instructed by the Tuscans in all the circumstances that they had learned from *Janus* on this subject. He instituted the first customs of prayers in honor of the Gods; and for this reason, the preparations for sacrifices were attributed to him, and he was invoked first, as being the one who presented the prayers to the Gods. He was given <term>Vesta|The Roman goddess of the hearth and home</term> as a wife, who invented the sacred fire, which was entrusted to the care of certain virgins, who were called *Vestals* after the name of *Vesta*, their founder. *Danet, Dictionary of Roman Antiquities.*]

# INTRODUCTORY TREATISE

<columns>2</columns>

Altars. † *Vesta* brought about the awakening of religious devotion. She was the symbol of religion, the keeper of the sacred fire, the possessor of the mysteries; *the guardian of the innermost things* <note>original Latin: "rerum cultos intimarum"</note>, says Cicero. It was sufficient to end with this Goddess. Nevertheless, the Greeks, on the contrary, began their religious devotion through this *Vesta*, and one can see some evidence of this in (a) the ancient symbols. Thus it is that fire was the first subject of the prayers of the ancient Persians.

<margin>With what exactitude unblemished purity was observed among the religious duties of the nations.</margin>
The negotiation of marriage was kept away from the Altars of the Jews. Many passages of the ancient writers prove it. Likewise, it was in use among the Jews. These people regarded all bodily defilement as punishable, but especially the impurity of women, or those who had contact with them. The religion of the *Brahmans* <note>original: "Brachmannen" — an early European term for Hindus of the Brahmin caste</note> compelled them to observe chastity, which they (according to the reports of travelers) neglected quite enough, such that they are depicted as the greatest hypocrites in the world. It is asserted that the Samaritans do not sleep with their wives during the Sabbath. Also, the Muslims are

<column-break/>

very strict observers of everything concerning the purity of the body. They not only abstain from women during their religious ceremonies, but they even have several *washings* <term>ablutions: ritual cleansings</term>, which they perform more or less depending on how much they have been defiled. If we are to believe Gregory the Great, a man who has had relations with his wife may not enter the Church, so as not to fail in the respect due to God. However, it is to be suspected that Gregory did not find it unbefitting to release the Christians from this on the testimony of their own consciences. The Roman Catholics make their Priests maintain the unmarried state, and the rule of their office directs them to maintain (b) a constant purity. But this abstinence (if we may be permitted to say so) was not the only thing prescribed to them in ancient times. The ancient Egyptian Priests abstained from wine and from (c) women; the Jewish Priests from all strong drink. † [According to Apollodorus and Diodorus Siculus, *Vesta* was the daughter of Saturn and the Goddess Ops; according to Ennius, the wife of Uranus, father of Saturn; and in the opinion of Fabius Pictor, the wife of Janus. Sanchoniathon calls her the Earth. Ovid says that, being born of Saturn and Rhea, she remained always a virgin and barren, just as fire is pure and barren. This Poet adds that the everlasting fire was the true image of *Vesta*. Some derive the name from the Hebrew word אש, *Esch* <note>original: "Esch" — meaning fire</note> which means fire. \* [It is not entirely to be rejected what Vossius says of the origin of the word *Isis*, since he derives it from the Hebrew word *Ir* or *Hir* <note>original: "Ir or Hir" — meaning an Angel or Messenger</note>. By the Greeks, Isis is also called Ceres, because she propagated the grain crop; for which reason she was depicted with a crown of corn ears. The Romans honored her as the Earth under the name of TELLUS and TELLUMO, of which Tellus was feminine and Tellumo masculine, because she represented both a God and a Goddess. It was in Phrygia where she was extraordinarily honored. ### RELIGIOUS REVERENCE, etc.

[released] from the anxieties of life to arise for public worthiness in honor of some Gods, and one submitted to a voluntary poverty: just as that of the Ministers of *Cybele*, the Mother of the Gods, was. They religiously carried (a) the images of the Gods through the streets, and from province to province. These images struck the hearts of the God-fearing Pagans, and generously provided for the Holy Pilgrims of this Goddess that which made the misery of their poverty bearable.

One could discuss various impurities caused by dreams. In the *Frogs* of *Aristophanes*, water is demanded to wash oneself after a distressing dream. A certain number of days were required to regain purity: sometimes ten (b) and sometimes thirty. The Law of the Jews prescribed seven days of purification for a man who was *Seminifluus* <term>Seminifluus: a Latin term for one suffering from a nocturnal emission or seminal discharge</term>, and also for the woman who had her monthly period; thirty-three days if she was in childbed with a boy, and sixty-six for one who bore a daughter. Among the ancient Idolaters, anyone who had committed a murder or any other act of violence was not permitted to approach the Altars without having (c) washed themselves. The Christians command Penance in such cases. Finally, all punishable crimes, of whatever nature they might be—whether their origin consisted in the impurity of the body or the impurity of the soul—were considered displeasing to the Deity and kept one away from the mysteries of Religion. Funeral rites were subject to the same. Among the Jews, those who have touched a dead body are defiled; and the (d) Greeks hung the hair of the deceased at the door of the

<column-break/>

house, so that those entering had to beware of defilement.

The purification of the body, however difficult it was, was nevertheless much lighter than that of the soul. <margin>The use of Holy Water—how and for what it is useful.</margin> The imagination of the soul had to be preserved, and this is what established the use of the *Holy Water* of the Pagans, which the Christian Religion subsequently abolished in order to introduce their own Blessed or Holy Water. The Priests and the people took from this Holy Water when they went into the Temple to sacrifice.

Those among the Christians who have maintained the use of *Blessed or Holy Water* attribute many qualities to it that cause rare miracles. We shall assign one to it which cannot be disputed: this is to remind Christians that they ought not to present themselves before God without having a pure conscience, and that without this, the sprinkling of *Holy Water*, however religiously it is received, (e) can affect nothing but the outward man. Pagan piety, so scrupulous regarding the use of water in religion, did not explicitly determine whether one had to use Spring or Sea water, etc. (f) Thus, one had the freedom to use whatever pleased them best. Sea water was nevertheless highly esteemed in this regard; and in former times, it attracted a great number of the devout to the shores of the Sea. If one found oneself defiled by some offense, one had only to plunge into the Sea and perform one's prayer at the place of purification. However it might be, one had to wash in spring water, and since it was required to wash frequently, the Priests of ancient Egypt took the precaution of building Temples and Chapels on the banks of the Nile.
