In the *Frogs* of *Aristophanes* <note>A famous Greek comedy writer; here referencing a scene regarding ritual washing after a bad omen</note>, water is demanded to wash oneself from a troubling dream. A certain number of days were required to regain purity: sometimes ten (b) and also thirty. The Law of the Jews prescribed seven days of purification for the man who was <term>Seminifluus</term> <note>A Latin term for someone suffering from a seminal discharge</note>, and also for the woman who had had her monthly period; thirty-three if she lay in childbed with a son, and sixty-six for one who bore a daughter.

Among the ancient Idolaters, anyone who had committed a murder or any other act of violence might not approach any Altars without having (c) washed themselves. The Christians command Penance in similar cases. Finally, all punishable crimes, of whatever nature they might be, whether their origin lay in the impurity of the body or the impurity of the soul, were considered displeasing to the Deity and excluded the mysteries of Religion.

Funeral rites were subject to the same. Among the Jews, those who have touched a dead body are defiled; and the (d) Greeks hung the hair of the deceased on the door of the

<column-break/>

house, so that one, upon entering, had to beware of contamination.

The purification of the body, however difficult it was, was nevertheless much lighter than that of the soul. The purity of the imagination had to be preserved, and this is what established the use of the <term>Holy Water</term> <note>original: "Wywater"</note> of the Pagans, which the Christian Religion subsequently abolished to introduce their Blessed or Holy Water. The Priests and the people took this Holy Water when they went into the Temple to sacrifice.

<margin>The use of Holy Water, and for what purpose it is useful.</margin>

Those among the Christians who have maintained the use of *Blessed or Holy Water* attribute many qualities to it, which cause rare miracles. We shall assign one to it which cannot be disputed: This is, to make Christians remember that they should not present themselves before God without having a pure conscience, and that without this, the sprinkling of *Holy Water*, however religiously it is received, (e) can affect only the outward man.

Pagan piety, so scrupulous about the use of water in Religion, did not explicitly determine whether one had to use Spring or Sea water, etc. (f) Thus one had the freedom to use whatever pleased them best. Sea water was nonetheless highly esteemed in this instance; and in former times it lured a large number of the pious to the Shores of the Sea. If one found oneself defiled by any offense, one had nothing to do but to plunge into the Sea and perform one's prayer at the place of purification. Be that as it may, one had to wash in spring water; and since it was required to wash often, the Priests of ancient Egypt took this precaution of building Temples and Chapels on the banks of the Nile. Besides that, they have an explicit reverence for the water of the *Ganges*; but since they always find themselves near these holy waters to wash, the *Brahmins* teach them that all other waters have the same power as the *Ganges water*, if one says while washing: *O Ganges, purify me*.

<margin>Solemn washing: the benefits of washing as observed among the Romans.</margin>The Romans also held great awe for the floods and fountains; for they imagined that these waters were governed by the Gods, who kept their eternal residence there, and they were commanded to wash in them with much circumspection. (a) It must not be cloudy water. In washing, a silence was required, so as not to disturb the rest of the Gods.

These same Romans (b) washed the feet of the newlyweds; this was the symbol of the purity that was recommended to them in marriage. Those who had to offer sacrifices (c) often washed the entire body, and sometimes only the head. As for the practice of washing hands, one was so accustomed to it in religious practice that it is almost unnecessary to speak of it, as it is all too well known. The Examples taken from this custom are found frequently in the holy leaves <note>referring to the Bible</note> and secular Writers. This practice of washing the feet under the pretext of Religion was not entirely common; yet it was nevertheless practiced often. Perhaps Jesus Christ made an allusion to this custom when he washed the feet of his twelve Apost-

<column-break/>

les: although it further appears that the custom of washing the feet of a guest invited to a meal was nothing but common politeness among the Easterners. The Pope and Roman Princes now still practice the Ceremony of washing feet through a Christian humility.

The ablution was not always necessary. One was often satisfied with a sprinkling. This sprinkling was performed with an olive or laurel branch, or indeed with a tool * manufactured for that purpose: but the principal mysteries, as for example those of † *Ceres*, always required the full washing. The consultation of the Oracle of *Trophonius* might not happen, except after having washed many times in the waters of the flood <term>Hercyna</term> <note>A river in Boeotia, Greece, associated with the oracle</note>, and when the consultant stood ready to enter the cave, where the notorious Oracle was given, two Youths, servants of the Priests of this Oracle, washed him once more. Finally, purification by water was formerly of an almost universal use among the Pagans. The Religion of the Jews also required constant washings: and, since one was imperceptibly accustomed to overlook these sacred practices with a regard for superstition accompanying the designated things, which was nothing but an image, the essence of the Religion was lost among them, as Jesus Christ reproaches the Jews for this. Today the same washing is maintained with uncommon care by the Turks and all the Muhammadans; and one can also consider the (d) Baptism of the Christians as a washing.

# RELIGIOUS WORSHIP, etc.

<margin>How covering the head was formerly used in spiritual service, and still is: which is done the opposite way among Christians.</margin> Covering the head was also an essential practice in spiritual service. The Jews still, as in ancient times, cover the head in the Synagogue with a veil <note>original: "sluier"; likely referring to the *tallit* (prayer shawl) or a head covering</note> during their public devotion. The Turks, who profess a religion partially sprouted from Judaism, follow the Jews in this covering of their heads when they pray to God in their Mosques. The Romans, after having washed themselves, covered themselves when they approached their Gods, partly out of respect and partly out of superstition. These signs are voluntary. The dispute is not whether to bind oneself to the subject they represent to us. We shall uncover ourselves to pray to God and to approach sacred things. We shall uncover ourselves when entering the Church; but it is strange that the Reformed Protestants cover the head while the reading of the Bible occurs and while the Minister teaches, despite the fact that they uncover themselves during the singing of Psalms and in prayer. These same Reformed Ministers preach in some places with covered heads. But to return again to the Romans, the custom of covering oneself usually occurred during the service of the Gods when they worshipped them, etc.: they covered themselves when it concerned the evoking of pity, and this practice was observed not only on this occasion, but also in marriage ceremonies, to indicate the modesty of the married bride and her virginal shame, which, gradually ending and being erased, passed from the heart into the face to serve her as an ornament.
In mourning, one covered the face;

<column-break/>

one also covered those condemned to death. It was believed that the custom of covering oneself was anciently instituted to prevent the sight from being distracted during spiritual service, and it was possibly to teach men that they are not worthy to behold the Deity. Nevertheless, one did not cover oneself to sacrifice to certain Gods, such as *Saturn*, (a) *Hercules*, *Ops*, or *Rhea*, etc.: and the Greeks always sacrificed to their Gods without covering their heads.
<margin>As also how garments were solemnly used for the service of purity in the ministry.</margin> The veils with which one covered oneself were usually white. It was the same with white garments intended for the ceremonial practices of religion. Whiteness is the symbol of the purity of the soul and of the state of innocence in which one must be before God. It is also a symbol of joy, but conversely, black represents sadness. One offered white victims to the Gods in thanksgiving offerings, and it was generally believed that one could perform nothing more pleasing to the Supreme Being than to serve him in white: but as for the hellish <note>meaning the gods of the underworld, or chthonic deities</note> Gods, since it was imagined that they were evil, that they delighted in human misfortunes, and that, always dwelling in darkness, they could be nothing but dismal and mournful, so one served them according to their nature; one dressed in black to honor them. The ancient Christians reclothed the baptized in white, and it is well known that this color is sanctified in the spiritual Church service of the Roman Catholics: but the Reformed and the Protestants in general, who have purified their religion of almost all ceremonies, reject (b) this whiteness. # INTRODUCTION, CONCERNING

<margin>[They] have chosen to use black.</margin>
Teachers <note>Ministers or clergy</note> are always dressed in black. They preach in black. One also commonly goes to the Lord's Supper dressed in black, choosing this color for its modesty. 
As for the Turks, they loathe black (a) as being mournful and of a bad omen: but they regard white and green as a hallowed color, this color being the privilege of the descendants of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> to wear. Green is especially forbidden to Christians and Jews: but yellow and (b) black are permitted to them.

The Pagans, to honor their Gods all the more, followed them barefoot when they were carried in procession <note>original: "omgang"</note>. This was constantly practiced for Cybele, the mother of the Gods. The Roman maidens never entered the Temple of Vesta except barefoot, and the custom of going barefoot is still maintained in the processions performed in times of distress. The Jews do likewise when they wish to humble themselves before God, and even more strictly when they add sackcloth and ashes to it. The Cretans did not allow one to enter the Temple of Diana while wearing shoes, and it seems that the religious practitioners of Greece were formerly no less fearful on this subject than the pious Romans: for they followed the procession of Ceres barefoot and with disheveled hair, as can be seen in an instance from Callimachus. The strict Pythagoras commanded his disciples to sacrifice to the Gods and to worship them barefoot: but it is probable that he recommended this to them through this symbol, representing a humility of soul and this simplicity of heart so necessary in spiritual service. Similarly, God, whose insights are infinitely above human ceremonies, commanded (c) Moses and Joshua to take off their shoes.

<margin>Going barefoot: how it was a religious custom, and on which occasions it was used.</margin>
This custom of taking off shoes was in vogue among the Pagans of the most superstitious religions indifferently. The Romans exorcised caterpillars and other vermin that damaged the trees and fields, (d) by means of women who walked barefoot around the trees. Sorcerers took off their shoes in their magical <note>original: "Tover-verkundige"</note>

<column-break/>

ceremonies, and this is what one reads in Ovid, Horace, and Virgil: but let us return again to the custom of removing shoes in honor of the Deity. The ancient Christians practiced it in solemn processions. Examples of this are found in Church Histories. Emperor Theodosius the Younger and the Patriarch Proclus deigned to humble themselves through this custom when they attended the processions held because of earthquakes. Heraclius even more so. He wished to load the Cross upon his shoulders and to carry this Holy Wood during a long procession, although he almost succumbed under the weight of the Imperial ornaments: but finally, valuing the humbling weight of the Cross more than all the Royal dignities, he laid aside his garments and took off his shoes, to complete his journey to Mount Calvary with less difficulty. 

Today, Roman Catholic penitents still commonly perform their processions barefoot. The most pious of the Brothers of Mercy walk in no other way in Portugal and Goa when they perform the great and solemn procession of Holy Thursday. The Capuchins, whose life must be a continual penance, have nothing but soles on their feet to protect them from the prick of thistles and thorns: but there are Christians who wish to testify their humility much further, obliging themselves to climb the twenty-eight steps of the *Santa Scala* <note>Holy Stairs</note> on their knees, to worship the (e) *Sanctum Sanctorum* <note>original: "Sancta Sanctorum"; the Holy of Holies</note>. Is this arduous devotion more exemplary than all others, under the pretext that it, so to speak, abolishes the use of the feet? As for this custom of going barefoot when one must humble oneself before the Deity, the same has been introduced in almost all religions of our times. Wherever signs of spiritual service have been found, a sort of solemn penance has also been found, instituted by men to satisfy the order they believe the Supreme Being may demand of them. The Peruvians observe this custom as the greatest mark of humility, which

<margin>The intentions behind giving the right foot precedence in several instances when approaching the Temple.</margin>
The ancients took care that they first entered the Temple with the right foot. This was also observed when visiting a powerful Lord, and the Romans were seriously attentive to such pedantic details. (d) The great *Augustus*, a wise Prince if ever there was one of high rank, could not tolerate having the shoe of the left foot pulled off before the right, believing the luck or misfortune of his undertaking depended on it. *Vitruvius* expressly commanded (e) that the steps to the Temple must be an odd number, so that by stepping up with the right foot first, one would also enter the Temple with that same foot first. We cannot imagine that God pays heed to these trifles: nonetheless, a dignified man, who is himself held in high regard among Christians, (f) advises that when one builds a Church, the head <note>The apse or altar end</note> should be turned exactly toward the East. This esteemed custom, when it is the result of an inner conversion to God, served to express even more modesty in Divine service. (g) Never is it more commendable than on this occasion, says *Seneca*. A good *Muslim* <note>original: "Muſſulman"</note> must also come to prayer with a downcast face; but, as a masked face seems to agree with virtue, it commonly happens among us that the downcast face is a sign of hypocrisy. What might we think of a numerous crowd of Christians, all going to Church, looking at the Earth, and returning from Church in the same manner? But if the downcast face is a sign of humility, then looking toward Heaven is a trust in God, and therefore one commonly raises the eyes toward Heaven when praying to God with a zealous spirit.

<margin>How the laying of the hand on the head displayed a humble reverence.</margin>
According to the ancients, the forehead, the seat of modesty, was dedicated to the Guardian God: thus, one touched the forehead every time one performed their duties to God. This is still observed today among the East Indians. They join their arms together in worship and bring their hands to the forehead, according to *Tavernier* <note>Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, a famous 17th-century French gem merchant and traveler</note>. In several other places in India, they do almost the same. They often bring their hands to their heads out of awe, and even throw themselves to the earth in the fervor of their religious devotion. This custom is also held in the East in honor of Authorities: but formerly—

Subsequently, both Teachers and Listeners show that they are very satisfied, and so content that they recall this proceeding with praise and affection at the first opportunity.

the pious women maintained a different conduct in this spiritual service. They prayed with unbound locks of hair. It is true that they did not practice this custom except when it was required to entreat the help of the Deity in an extraordinary way; a thing which is still seen today among Christians. We admit that this way of humbling oneself has something heart-stirring about it, and that one cannot see without emotion how the women, with hair loosened, melting in tears, and sighing, beat their breasts. Gregory of Tours <note>original: "Gregorius van Tours"; a 6th-century bishop and historian known for his "History of the Franks."</note> describes in a moving manner the pious procession of a band of penitents, both men and women of his time, who, in order to solemnly humble themselves before God, followed in mourning clothes girded with hair-belts <note>likely cilices or hair-shirts used for penance</note>, with loose-flowing hair, the undergarment of St. Vincent <note>St. Vincent of Saragossa, a martyr whose relics were highly venerated</note>; they thus went to partake in Divine mercy under the pretext of this miraculous garment, in which they placed their trust.

# RELIGIOUS WORSHIP, etc.

Nothing is more offensive, it seems to us, than a pious person who, under the pretext of pleasing God, worships Him in an erected image. The **Banjans** <note>original: "Banjanen"; a historical term used for Hindus, particularly merchants in Western India</note> throw themselves down before their Idols with their hands upon their heads. (a) As for the inclination of the body, or merely of the head, there has always been a use for it in Spiritual Service, and it is a natural sign of respect which one owes to God. The **Roman Catholics**, the **Greeks** <note>referring to the Eastern Orthodox Church</note>, and some other Christians have maintained this in their Spiritual Service.

<margin>And how others carry themselves in prayer.</margin>
The **Reformed** are satisfied with taking off their hats when the Teacher <note>the minister or preacher</note> ends his Sermon, and when they pray, this is done standing without any bowing of the body. (b)

Some perform their prayer kneeling. The Roman Catholics stand up when one sings *O God, come to my assistance* <note>original: "Deus in Adjutorium"; the opening of the Catholic Liturgy of the Hours</note>, at the *My soul magnifies the Lord* <note>original: "Magnificat"; the Canticle of Mary</note>, etc. The people pray while lying on their knees, stand up during the Gospel, and sit down during the exhortation or preaching, etc. The Protestants of the **English Church** <note>the Anglicans</note> also pray kneeling. The order of all Christian Churches is that one should be modest and observe propriety while engaged in serving God. The Preaching must be heard with reverence, and the prayer performed with attention. The most religious among the **Jews** wind the veil <note>the tallit or prayer shawl</note> around the neck, which they wear on their heads in their Synagogue, in order to be more attentive in prayer. # 16 INTRODUCTION, DISCURSIVE

...to demonstrate only one thing here. (a) **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio was a 1st-century BC Roman architect whose works deeply influenced Renaissance building standards.</note> ordered that the arrangement of a Temple should be such (b) that he who went to the Altar to offer a sacrifice must turn toward the side of the East. Also, according to **Vitruvius**, the Altar itself had to be turned toward this quarter of the world. It is suspected that this custom (c) originated from the first idolatry of men who worshipped the sun. This idolatry still reigns (d) among the East Indians and Americans. The Ancient Christians adopted the Pagans' custom of turning toward the East, and one finds a complete proof of this in the writings of **Augustine**. This custom has persisted to our day and is still practiced among the Roman Catholics; but the ancient Jews, by contrast, turned toward the West, so as not to follow the idolatry of the Pagans in this matter. When they set out on a journey, or if they were forced to live outside the district of Jerusalem, they performed their prayers while turning toward that city. But the **Mahometans** <note>A historical term for Muslims.</note> turn toward the South because the tomb of **Mahomet** <note>The Prophet Muhammad.</note> is in **Mecca**.

<margin>Gestures made with the hands and how.</margin>
Nature has given man certain movements through which he, almost imperceptibly, expresses the torment of his heart and the restlessness of his spirit. Such is the use he makes of his hands when, in pressing need, he implores some mercy from God, or wishes to gain the pity of an enemy who opposes him. It would then be very absurd to wish to place these movements in the rank of mere ceremonies. It is almost innate to humans, and yet they have also judged it necessary to mix ceremony with these movements that are so simple, and therefore so emphatically aligned with Nature. Consequently, when the ancient Pagans worshipped the hellish Gods, they let their hands sink down while stretching them out. If they worshipped the Sea-Gods, they stretched them out toward the sea. The **Tur-**

<column-break/>

**ks** <note>Turks/Muslims.</note> lay their hands crosswise upon the chest. Christians, when praying, fold their hands together or join them. Some among them distinguish themselves in prayer by the sign of the cross. Those who are fond of a load of cited passages would find many among the ancients and moderns. We leave this fertile field to them, and we shall only remark that there is nothing to contradict in these customs when they serve solely to bind the spirit to the prayer: but there are (even among Christians) very many pious people who regard the outward signs as the essence of the Spiritual service; and there are many who command their household to fold their hands together or make the sign of the cross, without mentioning a word to them about the attentiveness and the loftiness of prayer.

<margin>Of what use the Altars were in former times.</margin>
The Altar has always been one of the principal instruments of Divine worship. In former times, one performed one's prayers, vows, and (f) oaths before it, and one then laid one's hands upon the Altar. The ancient Jews confessed their crimes to God there: of which this was the ceremony. One laid one's hands between the two horns of the sacrificial animal near the Altar where it was slaughtered, and one showed regret for the crimes of which one acknowledged guilt in this posture. A portion of the Christian Church has maintained the use of the Altar for the ceremonies of the sacred service. Mass is said there, one prays to God there, one invokes the Saints there, and one even places their **Relics** <note>Physical remains or personal effects of a saint preserved for veneration.</note> there. We shall not expand upon the various ceremonial uses of the Altars of the Roman Catholics in this narrative: but <margin>but the abuse of this pointed out.</margin> we only wish to remark that through an abuse which dishonors Christianity, they have become in Italy a (g) refuge for the most wicked **evil-**

---

(a) *Apuleius in his Metamorphoses. Ovid, 4th Book of the Fasti. Valerius Flaccus in the Argonautica.*

(b) <note>original: "Ædes Sacræ Deorum immortalium ad regiones, quas fpectare debent fic erunt conftituendæ, ut .... ædis fignum, quod erit in cella collocatum, fpectet ad vefpertinam coeli Regionem, ut, qui adierint ad aram immolantes, aut facrificia facientes, fpectent ad partem coeli Orientis, & fimulacrum quod erit in æde, & ita vota fufcipientes contueantur ædem & Orientem coeli."</note> "The sacred houses of the immortal gods must be arranged according to the regions they ought to face, so that... the temple's image, which is placed in the inner chamber, faces the western region of the sky, so that those who approach the altar for immolation or sacrifice face the eastern part of the sky, and thus those undertaking vows may behold the temple and the East." **Vitruvius**.

(c) The worship of the Sun was formerly in use among the majority of nations. The Ancients dedicated to it the day of the week which we have sanctified to God, and which has retained the name of **Sunday** <note>original: "Zondag"</note> among the Germans and English.

(d) The Sun is honored in the Kingdoms of Bengal, Gujarat, Deccan, etc. These peoples, while washing and praying, turn their faces toward the rising sun. *Canada, Florida, Peru, etc.* acknowledge the Sun as their God. Pagan *Africa* does likewise.

(e) <note>original: "Cum ad Orationem Stamus, zegt Auguftinus, vertimur ad Orientem, ut admoneatur animus ad naturam excel-fiorem fe convertere &c."</note> "When we stand for prayer," says **Augustine**, "we turn toward the East, that the mind may be admonished to turn itself toward a more excellent nature, etc."

(f) Among Roman Catholics, one still swears upon the Altar, whether by laying the hand on the Gospel, or receiving [the host] from the Priest during the Lord's Supper, etc.

(g) Not only the Altars, but also the Monasteries, serve as places of sanctuary. A murderer, a bankrupt, and other criminals merely flee thither; and if the authorities undertook to oppose this, they would commit a sacrilege, which the Monks and Ministers of the Altars would not leave unpunished. # RELIGIOUS ADORATION, etc.

...serve as a refuge for criminals. It is nonetheless true that this custom is very ancient, and that both Jews and Heathens <note>Non-Christian "Pagans" or Gentiles.</note> have permitted it; but the Jews did not tolerate this except for crimes committed by accident and chance; and the respect one ought to have for the Christian Religion should require the abolition of the evil customs introduced by Ancient Heathenism. To the devotion shown at Altars, the Idolaters added this (a): of embracing the Temple doors and the Statues of the Gods; of weeping and sighing at their pedestals; of tearing out one's hair and promising a better life; and subsequently of flattering the Gods (b), grasping them by the knees, placing small crowns upon their heads, and offering flowers and fruits. These are customs (c) that some Christians have dedicated to God and the Saints: but primarily to the Holy Virgin, whom in many places in Europe they crown, and offer flowers and fruits to gain her favor, honoring her with the noblest names, the most dignified titles, and the most flattering prayers. The Greeks added to these recounted ceremonies those of branches wound with wool, with which they touched the knees of the Gods when they entreated them in their needs. If the fulfillment of the prayer was expected, the Petitioner took the liberty of behaving more familiarly, and touched with his branch the right hand, and even the chin and cheeks of the God to whom he prayed. This custom is also to some extent maintained among Christians in honor of the Saints, and it is well known with what benefit many Believers have touched the sweat-cloths <note>original: "zweed-doeken" or sudaria, cloths used to touch relics or statues to gain a blessing.</note>, linens, etc., of the Statues of the blessed, and how many blessings they...

<margin>The turning of the body; what kind of custom this was.</margin>
In former times, it was also observed to show homage to the Gods by turning around. **Pythagoras** seems to recommend it in his symbols. *By this rotation*, says **Plutarch**, *one intends to follow the movement of the World: but*, he adds, *I believe rather that this command is based on the fact that since Temples faced the East, those entering them turned their backs to the sun, and consequently they were forced to turn to the side, making a half-turn to the right; and then to position themselves before the God, they ended their prayer by completing the turn.* Mr. **Dacier**, who translated these words of **Plutarch**, (d) believes that **Pythagoras**, by this turning, commanded that one worship the immensity of God, who fills the entire Universe. A strange folly of human wit, which always stifles itself under the use of some hidden and obscure ceremonies; it is simplicity that the Father of Light and Truth desires. However it may be; (e) the Romans performed their turn to the right, (f) and the Gauls, on the contrary, to the left. The East Indians observe the same ceremony. They turn themselves to the right side around the Statues of their Gods; and each time they make this turn, they are obliged to bow with their faces to the earth. The Ancient Jews also offered this turning to the right side. One went to the Altar on the right side and returned on the left, as is evident from a command in the *Mishnah*. The ancient Persians had regard for this turning...

### INTRODUCTORY DISCOURSE

...view of the immensity of God, who surrounds everything and contains everything within Himself. This ceremony of turning around is also observed in the Mass, and undoubtedly contributes in the highest degree to the dignity and majesty of this sublime Sacrifice: for it awakens (so it is believed) godliness in the heart, yet much sooner turns the Christian away from the sense of the Spirit, attaching itself to vanity and outward customs, and the pleasure one takes in imagining the apparatus of religion as religion itself.

An entire treatise on this subject could be drafted if one wished to expand upon *Spiritual kisses*, upon the *songs sung in honor of the Deity*, and upon the *sacred dances*: three main points of solemn worship. We shall mention as little of them as possible.

<margin>Kissing as a ceremonial custom and how it is performed.</margin>
(a) One kissed the hand and sometimes even the mouth of the Gods. (b) One kissed their feet and knees. Finally, out of piety, one kissed (c) the Temple doors, the pillars and posts of the gates, (d) the foreign soil upon which one arrived, and what has one not kissed? Since it satisfied the extravagance of superstition to discover any rare object and attach human trust to it. It is by this same superstition that the Turks and other Mahometans <note>An older term for Muslims.</note>, who go on pilgrimage to *Mecca*, kiss the black stone (e) which they call *Hagiar Alafuad* <note>Original: "Hagiar Alafuad," referring to the Hajar al-Aswad or the Black Stone set in the Kaaba.</note>, and the four corners of the *Kaaba*. † The modern Idolatry of the East Indians and Americans (f) <note>Referring to the Indigenous peoples of the Americas.</note> also practices this Spiritual Service, which the

<column-break/>

Roman Catholics have dedicated to the honor of the Cross and the relics of the Saints. They have even dedicated this according to the occasion of the ceremony: at the sprinkling of the Holy Water, the Priest kisses the sprinkler; during the Procession of Palm Branches, the Deacon kisses the Palm branch that he (g) offers to the Priest. It is unnecessary to expand upon this, and to analyze when and how the Priest kissed the Altar, or the kissing performed on the censer, the chalice cover, the chalice, the white Stole, the hand of the Priest, etc. (h) When one cannot kiss the object of worship, one kisses the hand and "throws" the kiss toward the Gods. In Spain and Portugal, this religious act is practiced; commonly, one brings the index finger crosswise to the thumb and kisses the hand, making the sign of the cross in honor of the Image from which they are separated.

<margin>Likewise singing, which accompanies a ceremony;</margin>
Regarding the custom of the Mexicans in Spiritual Worship, it is very ancient and widespread. Perhaps no peoples are found in the world who do not acquit themselves in singing to bring praise to the Supreme Being in their own way; and it seems that the ancient Heathens believed that (i) Music appeased the wrath of the Gods and drew them down to earth: for this reason, Heathen piety was commonly accompanied by harmonious instruments and voices. The first musicians and players, such as *Linus*, *Orpheus*, etc., were regarded as a kind of Prophets, and perhaps they were all simultaneously Priests, Physicians, and Sorcerers, like the Priests of the East Indies,

# RELIGIOUS VENERATION, etc.

However that may be, the Romans, Greeks, and Egyptians were steadfast in observing the use of music in all religious exercises, such as sacrifices and festivities (a) in honor of their Gods. (b) They mixed many absurdities into the praises that formed the substance of the songs, and sometimes the praise of the Gods was a collection of rudeness or filth. People set into verse and sang religiously the most fabulous and ridiculous things to be found in the legends of their heroes and Gods, who were the saints of Heathendom. For the Heathens generally agreed upon the unity of a Supreme Being, and regarded all other Gods as representatives <note>Original: "stedehouders," meaning lieutenants or deputies.</note> of this absolute Being. These Gods each had their own office and their own dwelling, and the hymns sung in their honor were applicable to the skill with which they performed their duties, to the benefits with which they favored their worshippers, to their miracles, etc. The Jews and Christians have likewise dedicated music to religion. The former used for this purpose trumpets, cymbals, and drums, mixed with the voices of the Levites and of the congregation. As for the music of the first Christians,

<column-break/>

it was very simple. They sang the praises of God with a loud voice, as the Protestants do, (c) according to modern custom. In the music of the Roman Catholics, more ceremonies, more art, and more variety are used; but perhaps more pleasantness was required than utility for godliness, considering that these charms do not produce such an effect unless they, so to speak, stifle true religiousness.

<margin>To which dancing was also added, and sometimes excesses were introduced into the dance.</margin>
The (d) modern Heathens, even the most savage, also make use of hymns and music of voices and instruments in honor of their deities. The greatest part of the religion of the Americans <note>A historical reference to the Indigenous peoples of the Americas.</note> consists of dances and songs, with which they believe they appease their Gods and show them true respect. The ancient Syrians <note>Likely referring to the Scythians or ancient Near Eastern peoples, though the text says "Syryen."</note> in the earliest times attributed all the dignity of the people to the poets and musicians; for they were then regarded as interpreters of the Gods, and people of divine inspiration: but this religion is worth little anymore. The Prophets among the Jews were encouraged by the sound of instruments. One sees an example of this in the person (e) of Elisha. (f) Saul, troubled by an evil spirit, found relief through music. # INTRODUCTION, CONCERNING

the supernatural and divine to be noted in these two examples, we shall say that the ancient Heathens were uncommonly struck by them. If one may believe all that Antiquity tells us—namely, the extraordinary medical skill of (a) Xenocrates, Thales, Empedocles, etc.—the violent frenzy of the Soothsayers of Heathendom and the predictions of their Oracles contributed much to this; but deception is commonly esteemed above the Truth.

Although dancing is naturally a consequence of music, it will nonetheless be very difficult to find a true correspondence between Religion and dancing. The Divinity wished to be served with joy; but this joy had to consist of an unbridled spirit and an inner contentment that accompanies such freedom. The majority of men have no conception of this sort of joy and believe that true cheerfulness must consist of dancing and singing. This is the principle which leads the Idolaters to add amusements to Spiritual Service: Thus, one should not be surprised to see debauchery and sacred mysteries paired together. This must naturally follow in a religion where God is made into a man. (b) They danced around the Statues and Altars. (c) They instituted round-dances for the affection of the Gods, and even sent a band of pilgrims annually to the place particularly consecrated to some God, (d) to dance there in his honor. Men, women, children, and old men joined in these Holy dances. In Rome, the Salian Priests of Mars performed these round-dances around the Altars of the Idol, attentively singing his hymns of praise. Finally, these dances were so pleasing to Heathen Antiquity that the Poets made no difficulty of making their (e) Gods dance. No less are the dances esteemed among the Idolaters of both the Indies

<column-break/>

and by most of the modern ones likewise. Dancing makes up a good portion of the religion they perform in honor of their Gods; there are even those who do not cease from dancing and jumping until they fall to the earth from exhaustion. The Brazilians and other wild peoples make their prisoners sing and dance before they are to be sacrificed: this being the pinnacle of inhumanity.

Christianity has had enough difficulty purifying itself from such an unseemly thing—and one as unregulated as dancing is in a Spiritual service. <margin>How the current irregularities of the Roman religion persist.</margin> Travelers who have traversed Europe today know well enough with what abuse Christian Festivals are celebrated in some countries. They do not neglect dancing there, nor mummery, nor the most uncouth amusements of a theatrical performance. The Festivals of the Sacrament and the Passion of Jesus Christ are not exempt from this, and one sometimes observes on these occasions a mixture of Penitents and Jesters <note>Original: "Poetsemakers," meaning buffoons or pranksters.</note> who, in such an extravagant way, undoubtedly believe they are collectively honoring Religion.

<margin>How they adorned the Gods by putting crowns on them.</margin> We shall not forget the Crowns that were placed on the heads of the Gods. It was also a sign of special honor. They primarily crowned the Household Gods, the Protective and other Gods, whom they worshipped in a pressing need: but in general, Heathen Antiquity had no God whom they did not crown by a principle of Religion. They decorated them with flowers, offered them incense, and censed them; and all this was, so to speak, a consequence of religious flatteries performed for their benevolence. Doubts, or rather Religion, brought men to even further absurdity. All the occupations of life depended on certain Deities; it was fitting not to forget the Garden-God, the notorious Priapus, a God venerable for certain qualities. <margin>Extravagance of the women</margin> Women of a less-than-charming nature offered him crowns and flowers: but the zeal—

# RELIGIOUS VENERATION, etc.

the most zealous crowned (a) a part of his body that was certainly the most remarkable. <note>The author refers to the phallus of the god Priapus, a Greco-Roman deity of fertility.</note> As this was particularly the subject of their wit, they believed that by performing this duty they were fulfilling the object of their religion. They were not satisfied with merely crowning the deities; the priests who offered the sacrifices also crowned or wreathed themselves like the gods, and very often the surrounding people crowned themselves during the spiritual ceremony. The crowns offered to the gods (b) were sometimes hung upon the temple doors; furthermore, it was the custom among (c) the Greeks and Romans to crown the deities they sought to win over, acknowledging their sovereignty through such a solemn manner to wrap themselves in their favor. Nevertheless, it was not enough simply to crown them; to make them entirely favorable, it was required to seek the most suitable branches from their own lands to weave these crowns. Thus, the Oak was chosen for *Jupiter*, the Myrtle for *Venus*, the Laurel for *Apollo*, the Pine for *Cybele*, the Poplar for *Hercules*, stalks of Corn for *Ceres*, the Olive tree for *Minerva*, Reeds for the River gods, Fruits for *Pomona*, the Elm for *Pan*, and Hay for poor *Vertumnus*, <note>Vertumnus was the god of seasons and change; the author implies he was seen as a "lesser" or "poorer" deity compared to the Olympians.</note> whose power and dignity held nothing special enough to give him more than this. But as even the least deity had a voice in the heavenly council of the gods, it was therefore necessary to crown him as well,

<column-break/>

so that, when it was his turn to express his opinion, he would give no contrary report against the interests of the worshiper who might have had the rudeness to forget him. For the illustrious *Priapus*, it was well known that it was not enough to wreath his head; he demanded reverence in another place, where he desired that the marks of esteem always be brought, and it fell (d) to the women to carry out this hallowed custom.

We shall not expand further upon these crowns, which have provided so much material for (e) treatises full of learning; we would much rather give a better judgment of the piety of the Roman Catholics, which has purified that which the superstition of the Heathens had dishonored. (f) The images of the immortal Saints have not usurped these crowns like the wretched deities of Heathendom; they have taken what rightfully belongs to them, and the Vicar of Jesus Christ <note>The Pope.</note> has preserved them until the end of ages through the consecration of those who represent these Holy Images.

In this Discourse, this sample shall suffice, serving as an Introduction to the *Spiritual Church Customs of all Peoples of the World*. It was a necessary requirement to give the Reader an idea of many different religious practices, in use across all times, consecrated in all Religions, and finally regarded as the only refuge for the devout who have neither the feeling, nor the courage, nor the strength required to be simple in the worship of the Supreme Being.

It costs much for those who are ignorant of the customs of the World to live with men in a simple and unified manner. With all the ceremonies they practice, they have hardly been able to pass themselves off as people of pleasant company. Let it be permitted for us to compare them to those who bind themselves to all Spiritual exercises as if they were the Essence of Religion. It costs them nothing to speak with God and to entreat him without ceremonies; and if they have the misfortune of achieving nothing with this outward splendor, perhaps it will be difficult to regard them as people of a sensible piety; and with this, we shall end this Introduction.

# EXPLANATION

->Regarding some Monuments of Antiquity, mentioned in the Introduction—which contains the Treatise on Religious Worship—and represented by these Illustrations.<-

I.
The first illustration shows a TEMPLE of POMONA in a Forest or rather an Orchard. *Pomona* was a Forest Goddess of the Heathens. Subsequently, she became the Wife of *Vertumnus*, who was regarded by the Latins as a Harvest-God. It was also believed that he concerned himself with the conditions of buying and selling, and directed or altered the thoughts of men in civil matters. *Vertumnus*, falling in love with *Pomona*, assumed various forms, yet could in no way soften the heart of this Goddess; but by assuming that of a young man, he overcame all his applied labor and inner sighing.

*Pomona*, as the Wife of *Vertumnus*, was recognized as the Goddess who had governance over pleasure gardens or rather over garden fruits. One offered a sacrifice to her. She was depicted as youthful like *Hebe*, Jupiter’s daughter, and crowned with flowers. Her Priest is called by the Romans the *Flamen Pomonalis* <note>original: "Flamen Pomonalis"; a "flamen" was a priest assigned to a specific state deity in ancient Rome</note>, and his dignity corresponded with the power of this Goddess; for he was the least of the known Priests under the name of the *Flamens*.

II.
The various SPRINKLING BRUSHES <note>original: "WYQUISPELS"; also known as aspergilla, used for sprinkling holy water</note> depicted in the Commemorative Medals alongside the Temple of *Pomona* were used for Purificatory Offerings <term>lustration: the ritual cleansing of a person, place, or object through sacrifice or washing</term>. We would stray too far if we wished to recount here even a portion of what relates to this subject, so learnedly described by *Lomeierus* <note>Johannes Lomeier (1633–1699) was a Dutch theologian and author of "De lustrationibus veterum gentilium" (On the Lustrations of the Ancient Heathens)</note>. This spiritual service was by no means permitted to everyone. Since this offering was an established ceremony intended to erase to some extent the crimes of the people, or indeed of a particular household—so that the soul would not feel the vengeance of God, to avert all misfortunes, etc.—it required that the person who performed this purificatory offering be a man of standing, of a venerable age, and of noble birth. Priests (a), Mayors, Virgins, and Youths were often employed in this solemn custom. The Families

<column-break/>

who possessed a hereditary right to certain priesthoods were privileged in matters required for the purificatory offering. This ceremony was necessary when one was about to be admitted to some Mystery of the Religion; when one wished to approach the Gods; before one sacrificed; after one had had dreams of a bad outcome; after certain Funeral Rites; to cleanse oneself from certain contaminations of the body, and especially from those believed to accompany the intimacy of marriage.

The purificatory offerings were performed by means of water, fire, or air. One chose a natural Divine water, just as river and spring water were believed to be, due to the dwelling of the Gods, Wood-Goddesses, or Tutelary Gods. For want of this water, one consecrated ordinary water. To this end (b), one had large water vessels standing at the entrance of the Temples, in which one extinguished the firewood taken from the Altar when one sacrificed. One sprinkled oneself with this water; however, this sacred sprinkling was commonly performed by the priesthood of the Gods.

To complete the purificatory offering by means of the air, one took a winnowing fan and fanned or blew the air for the purification of souls. The moving oscillation caused in the air was also a kind of purification.

The purificatory offering or purification by fire was very common among the ancient Heathens. To carry this out, one used the power of this element, or merely the smoke. It is possible that this purificatory offering laid the foundation for the ordeal by glowing iron used in the eighth century of the Church. The purificatory offerings for which smoke was used were those of some incense. One used for it Sulfur, Resin, Frankincense, Fragrant herbs, Laurel, etc. In marriage purifications, one used water and fire together, and sometimes they were used in funeral processions. Honey could also serve in place of water; and for the atonement of a homicide, one often mixed the water with blood. Eggs were also of some use,

...practice, as they imagined that these, by a shorthand of sorts, encompassed the four elements. Finally, it is unnecessary for us to expand upon the expiatory offerings <note>original: "zoenoffers"; sacrifices made to appease a deity or purify a person</note> performed by means of human blood; or those in which fruit was used; or those (a) in which dogs, cats, and other animals were used. They were often left alive, but they were burdened with the sins of the people. In the work of *Lomejerus* <note>Johannes Lomeier (1636–1699), a Dutch theologian known for his writings on ancient religious rituals</note> one finds many other expiatory offerings noted for People, Cities, Armies, Fields, Fruits, and Animals; we refer the reader to that work.

One should also regard as an expiatory offering the sprinkling performed with a branch of Laurel, Olive, or Rosemary, or with a bundle of Hyssop or other tools made solely for Sprinkling.

After this solemn ritual of Expiatory Offerings and Sprinklings, one regarded oneself as a new man, and one was counted among the number of the Blessed. The ceremonies of reconciliation ended with an *Ilicet* <note>Latin: "Ilicet," meaning "it is permitted to go," used to dismiss a crowd after a ritual</note>, corresponding very well with the blessings with which the Clergy take leave of the people. For *Ilicet* can be expressed by *go in Peace*, or *Pax vobis*, *peace be with you*.

### III.

<margin>(a) Ibid. Chapter 23.</margin>
<margin>(d) See Soler. on the Cap.</margin>
The Sacrifice of HERCULES depicted in one of these commemorative medals reminds us of something concerning this ceremony here. (d) This God deigned to teach two illustrious families <note>original: "Geſlachten"</note> how they ought to serve him. These two families, being the most prominent among the *Aborigines* <note>the earliest inhabitants of Italy</note>, bore the names *Potitii* and *Pinarii*. They sacrificed a young bull to Hercules, because they had arrived too late on a solemnly appointed day of sacrifice. When sacrificing to him at the Altar called the *Ara Maxima* <note>Latin: "The Greatest Altar," located in the Forum Boarium in Rome</note>, (a) the entire assembly had to stand with uncovered heads to show more respect for *Hercules*; for this God was shown with his head covered, and it would have been an act of extreme indignation to be so bold as to cover oneself before him. The Romans, appearing before the *Ara Maxima*, confirmed their promises and concluded conditions with an oath.

### IV.

The PIETY that accompanied the sacrifices, and generally the entire Service, necessarily had to be covered, since one covered the head so as not to turn one's eyes away from the object of attention, and to prevent the wandering of thoughts. The manner in which Piety is shown here veiled before the Altar is much like how Roman women were accustomed to appear when they performed their worship to the Gods. The Emperor *Severus* is also seen in a commemorative medal covered in this way, holding an Olive branch in his hand.

Public Faith <note>original: "Geloof"; referring to the Roman personification Fides</note> is represented in a (b) commemorative medal with the horn of plenty in her hand, and the head wreathed with laurel; it required that one cover oneself with a white veil when sacrificing. This veil was the symbol of sincerity and purity that accompanied Faith, just as the horn of plenty is that of prosperity, which commonly accompanies this Virtue.

The PHRYGIAN CAP was sometimes used here, as depicted in the last of the four commemorative medals under the Temple of *Pomona*: (c) Nevertheless, it is not perfectly certain that it was always made in this manner. ### VI.

ANUBIS, before whom one sees a bowed man lying, was an Egyptian Deity. He was represented in the form or with the head of a dog; and his name sufficiently indicates who he was: for *Anubis* means, according to some Scholars, *one who barks*, and is originally from *Hebrew*. *Hanubé* <note>original: "Hanubé"; likely referring to the Hebrew root 'nabach' (to bark)</note>, a Hebrew word, is a *Participle* (participle) to which the exhaled H is added. This Egyptian Deity and *Mercury* <note>original: "Merkurius"</note> are taken for the same thing. Through the image of the dog, one wished to represent the wisdom of that Idol; for no animal is more intelligent than a dog. The symbol is fitting. The God of Thieves, Merchants, and public Officials required perfect wisdom to acquit himself worthily in his duties. *Anubis* is also represented on some commemorative medals with a Staff of Mercury <note>original: "Merkurius-Staf"; the caduceus</note> in his hand.

The other four commemorative medals, which follow this one of *Anubis*, represent various postures in which the Worshippers find themselves while honoring him.

<margin>The ceremonies and customs of the Jews, and how they are distinguished into three Orders.</margin>
All the ceremonies currently in use among the Jews are not of the same authority, nor are they all observed in the same manner; they are divided into three arrangements. The first of these comprises the Doctrines of the written Law—namely, those contained in the five Books of Moses. reassured by the prophecy, they add these words to him from *Ecclesiastes* <note>The original Dutch text cites *Ecclesiasticus*, but the verse provided is from Ecclesiastes 9:7</note>: (a) *Go, eat your bread with joy, etc.* after which the faster goes to eat.

<margin>Which garments the Jews are forbidden to wear.</margin>
The Jews are forbidden to dress themselves in fabrics woven of flax and wool <note>This prohibition is known as *shaatnez*</note>: (b) *You shall not wear a garment*, says the Lawgiver <note>Referring to Moses</note>, (c) *of mixed fabric, wool and linen together.* For this reason, they do not even sew their woolen clothes with linen thread, nor a linen garment with wool. It is also forbidden for them, both men and women, to dress in the clothing of the opposite sex: (d) *The garment of a man shall not be upon a woman, and a man shall not put on a woman's garment.* Likewise, all feminine actions are forbidden to men, such as all kinds of face-paint for the countenance, and ointments to make hair fall out. The same prohibition is also placed upon women, that they may not perform anything that is characteristic of men.

It is possible that the prohibition against men shaving their beards arose from this, such that the hair from the temples of the head along the cheeks, and even the entire beard, had to remain unshaven; (e) *neither shall you destroy the corners of your beard.*

Regarding their way of dressing, they follow other nations in that regard, though reluctantly, if only to avoid making themselves ridiculous among them. They are not permitted to make tonsures <note>Shaved circles on the crown of the head, associated with Christian monks</note>, nor distinct tufts of hair in the middle of the head, nor anything resembling such things; however, they are generally inclined to go about in long clothes or robes.

<margin>How the women dress.</margin>
The women dress according to the custom of the country, except on their wedding day; they cover the hair of their head with a hair-cap, or some headdress resembling natural hair <note>A wig or *sheitel*</note>, conforming to the fashion of the land for their outward appearance: but they take careful care not to let their own hair be seen.

The men consider it an improper act to uncover the head, as they do not believe it to be a sign of respect; they do not even practice this in their Synagogues. Whenever they see this duty performed for persons of rank among the Christians, they also fulfill it accordingly.

<column-break/>

<margin>The men's clothing described.</margin>
Every garment they wear must have four panels or edges, and on each hangs a band like a tassel, which they call *Zizit* <note>original: *Zizit*, now commonly spelled *Tzitzit*</note>. This band usually consists of eight threads, spun for that purpose, each having five knots, which take up half the length. That which is not knotted but raveled represents, says the Law, (f) *that they*, says the Law, (g) *make fringes on the corners of their garments.*

This command concerns only the men, and not the women, just as there is no command regarding it that is observed by them.

Indeed, this custom is now almost no longer practiced where men wear these four-paneled garments openly, so as not to be mocked by other nations among whom they reside. They satisfy themselves by wearing this only under their clothes, consisting of a piece of fabric that is square, with four bands, which they call (h) *Arban Canfoth* <note>original: *Arban Canfoth*, meaning "Four Corners"</note>, in memory of the commandments of God, since in the same chapter of *Numbers* verse 40, it is said: *that you may remember and perform all my commandments, etc.* <margin>How they cover themselves with a head covering.</margin> But in their hours of prayer which they perform in the Synagogues, they cover themselves with a square woolen head-veil, which has these tassels at the corners, which head covering they call *Taled* <note>original: *Taled*, now commonly spelled *Tallit*</note>, of which we shall make mention in the fifth Chapter.

Also, the men must have on their foreheads that which the Holy Scripture calls *Totafot*, and the Jews call *Teffilin* <note>original: *Teffilin*, also known as Phylacteries</note>, as it is written; (i) *And you shall bind them for a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes:* We shall treat the quality and shape of these in the fifth Chapter. Meanwhile, so as not to be ridiculous to the people in a matter they hold sacred, and which they wear only with great caution, they satisfy themselves with using them during the time of their prayers. They also believe it fitting to wear a belt over their clothing, or something else that makes a separation of the upper part from the other parts of the body <note>This refers to the *gartel*, a belt used to symbolically separate the heart from the lower organs during prayer</note>.

<margin>The caution of the Jews in relieving themselves, noted.</margin>
The Rabbis also have much to say regarding the place of relieving oneself, and how one must behave there, all of which serves nothing but health, honor, and modesty: based on what is noted in *Deuteronomy* (k).

### IV. CHAPTER.
#### ->Concerning PURITY; BLESSINGS; and the Jews' SYNAGOGUES and SCHOOLS.<-

<margin>In what manner the Jews must guard against impurity.</margin>
One reads in *Leviticus* that anyone was unclean who had touched a dead body, a leper, or any vermin, etc. and in this state, they were forbidden from entering the Temple: but since the Temple has been destroyed, the Jews believe that all these commands regarding unclean things have been suspended. Nevertheless, there was a command from *Esdras* <note>Ezra the Scribe</note>, which remained in force for some time thereafter, and stated; that one was unclean if any seed escaped him: and this was based on what is said in the 15th Chapter of *Leviticus*, verse 16; *And if any man's seed of copulation go out from him, then he shall wash all his flesh in water, and be unclean until the even.* But as it was very difficult to pay heed to this, due to the intimacy of marriage, this was further abandoned.
<margin>The Jews' Blessings</margin>
The Rabbis have obli-

<column-break/>

ged the Jews to offer particular blessings and praises to their God, not only in their prayers and whenever they receive some benefit from him; but even in all unforeseen occurrences, and upon every act they perform, whether they eat or drink, or smell some pleasant scent; and finally for every commandment of the Law and decree of the (c) Rabbis. Which they understand of everything new or unusual they see: for they have various blessings for all things; and as the number of them is very great, one cannot cite them all in detail here. However, one can look them up in a great treatise which the Rabbis have made concerning them.
In the morning, as soon as they have risen from bed, they say: *Blessed are you, Lord our God, King of the World, who gives life to the deceased, who enlightens the blind, who spreads the earth upon the wa- ter* <note>original: "Gezegent zyt gy, Heere onze Godt..."</note>

They are daily obliged to speak at least one hundred blessings; and as in the morning the majority are repeated in the Synagogues with their prayers, they call these blessings repeated in the morning <term>MEATH BERACOTH</term>, which means *one hundred blessings*. <note>original: "MEATH BERACOTH"; from the Hebrew *Me'ah Berakhot*</note>

<margin>How the Jews build their Synagogues, and for what use.</margin>
They have their Synagogues, which they call Schools, whether large or small, whether downstairs or upstairs in a house, or if they can, in a separate place; since they have no opportunity to erect Temple structures that are magnificent. At the doors one finds alms-boxes where one can practice charity; this money being subsequently distributed to the poor.

# CHAPTER V.

-> Concerning the PRAYERS of the Jews; their CLOAKS; HEAD-WRAPS, and the PENTATEUCH or five Books of Moses. <-

<margin>When the Jews go to the Synagogue daily to pray.</margin>
Three times a day the community goes to the Synagogues to pray. First, in the morning during the first four hours after sunrise. Second, in the afternoon; the first time of prayer is called (g) Shacharit <note>original: SCIACRID</note>, and the second (h) Mincha. The third, which occurs in the evening and is called (i) Arvit <note>original: HARUID</note>, is performed in various places like the first and second prayer times when it is not a Feast Day; they perform them at the same time around sunset, praying the afternoon and evening prayers together, as it pleases them.

<column-break/>

<margin>What they must do before going to the Synagogue, and their behavior therein.</margin>
They are forbidden to eat or drink, or do anything—even to greet anyone—until they have said their morning prayer; they must also wash their hands before going into the Synagogue. Having entered the Synagogue in the morning, they cover themselves with the (k) *TALED* <note>Prayer shawl</note>, already mentioned (l), and repeat the blessing (m): *Blessed are You, etc.* Some cover their heads with this veil, others wrap it around their necks, to be more attentive in prayer and not to look here or there. Next, the head-wrap is placed—

---

(a) Tree of Life. (b) Pomegranates. (c) Crown of the Law.
(d) The Jews pronounce their prayers in a singing manner. Even when they read a text from the Bible, it is done singing.
(e) The *Cazan* is to the Jews what the reader is to those of the Reformed Religion, and this word *Cazan* is found in St. Epiphanius.
(f) The *Sciamas* or Servant serves much like the Deacon did in the past, and the Syrian Churches still call their Deacons by this name today, although it is commonly understood to refer to all those who perform divine service.
(g) Morning prayers. (h) A certain ninth hour of prayer. (i) Evening prayers.
(k) The word *TALET* or *TALED* as the Italian Jews pronounce it, means in Rabbinic Hebrew a Cloak, or a garment that covers all others.
(l) Chapter III and Numbers 7-9. (m) Numbers 10.

## CHAPTER V.

### Concerning the PRAYERS of the Jews; their CLOAKS; HEAD-WRAPS, and the PENTATEUCH or five Books of Moses.

<margin>When the Jews go daily to the Synagogue to pray.</margin>
Three times a day the Jews go into the Synagogues to pray. First, in the morning during the first four hours after sunrise. Secondly, in the afternoon; the first time of prayer is called (g) MORNING PRAYER <note>original: "SCIACRID"</note>, and the second (h) is called AFTERNOON PRAYER <note>original: "MINCHA"</note>. The third, which takes place in the evening and is called (i) EVENING PRAYER <note>original: "HARUID"</note>, is performed—like the first and second prayer times—in various places when it is not a Feast day; they perform it at the same time around sunset, praying the prayers of the afternoon and evening together, as it pleases them.

<column-break/>

<margin>What they must do before they go to the Synagogue, and their conduct therein.</margin>
It is forbidden for them to eat or drink, or to do anything, even to greet anyone, before they have performed their morning prayer; they must also wash their hands before entering the Synagogue. Having entered the Synagogue in the morning, they cover themselves with the (k) CLOAK <note>original: "TALED"</note>, already mentioned (l), and repeat the blessing, (m) *BLESSED ARE YOU, etc.* Some cover their head with this veil, others wrap it around the neck, in order to be more attentive in prayer and not to look hither or thither. Next, the head-wrap <note>the phylacteries or tefillin</note> is placed.

# HISTORICAL TREATISE

<margin>
Their head-bands and memorials described.
</margin>

(a) **TEFFILIN** (b) <note>These are commonly known as phylacteries—small leather boxes containing scriptural verses worn during prayer.</note>, which have already been mentioned, are described as follows. One writes upon two pieces of parchment, using ink prepared for this purpose and in square letters, these four scriptural passages with great accuracy on each piece. I. (c) *Hear, O Israel*, etc. II. *And it shall come to pass, if ye shall hearken diligently*, etc. III. *Sanctify unto me all the firstborn*. IV. *And it shall be when the Lord shall bring thee in*, etc. These two parchments are rolled up like a small, pointed scroll, which is then placed into leather prepared from a black calfskin; then it is set upon a square and stiff piece of the same leather, from which hangs a leather strap of this same material, a finger's breadth wide and about one and a half cubits long. They place these **TEFFILIN** by winding them around the left arm; after tying a small knot in the shape of the letter **JOD** <note>The Hebrew letter Yod (י), the first letter of the Divine Name.</note>, they wind the leather strap around the arm in a spiral fashion, ending at the tip of the middle finger. This they call **TEFFILA SCEL JAD**, which means the *Teffila of the hand*. As for the other **TEFFILIN**, they write the four mentioned scriptural passages on four separate pieces of parchment; these they join together to make a square, upon which they write the letter **SCIN** <note>The Hebrew letter Shin (ש), representing "Shaddai," or Almighty.</note>; then they place upon it a small square of stiff calf-leather like the other, from which two leather straps emerge, both of the same appearance and length as the first. This square is then placed before the forehead, and with the leather straps wound around the head, a knot is made behind it, resembling the letter **DALET** <note>The Hebrew letter Dalet (ד).</note>. They call this head-band **TEFFILA SCEL ROSCH**, or *Teffila of the Head*. Such are the head-bands which are usually donned only in the morning along with the **TALED** <note>original: "TALED" (Tallit); the fringed prayer shawl.</note>. Nevertheless, it is true that there are very devout individuals who use them during the afternoon prayer; but except for the **Cantor**, there are few who wear the **TALED** during these prayers.

Their manner of singing noted, and how they differ from one another.

Among the Jews, the manner of praying is very different. For, as we have already noted, there is nothing in which they differ so much. The High German Jews <note>The Ashkenazim.</note> sing much louder than the others. Easterners and Spanish Jews <note>The Sephardim.</note> sing in a way resembling the manner of the Turks; and the Italians softly and with ease. These prayers consist of more or fewer words, depending on whether it is a Feast day or an ordinary day. Even in this, they differ among themselves.

Besides this, they repeat a collection of praises to God, which are frequently repeated in all prayers and at all times, namely, (d) **CADIS** <note>The Kaddish prayer.</note>, which means *Holiness*; a blessing to the Creator of light and day, which is called (e) **JOZER**; a portion of Deuteronomy: *Hear, O Israel*, which ends with these words: *And it shall come to pass, if ye shall obey*, etc., and which have already been cited several times; and that of Numbers chapter 15 verse 38: *Speak unto the children of Israel, that they make them fringes*, etc. These three readings are called (f) **CHIRIATSCEMAN** <note>The Keri'at Shema, or "Reading of the Shema."</note>, and they add (g) **VEIAZIU**, etc., to it, along with eighteen blessings of God, called (h) **SCEMONA ESRE** <note>The Shemoneh Esrei, also known as the Amidah or Standing Prayer.</note>, in which they praise Him and request the most necessary things, such as bread, health, a good understanding, freedom, the forgiveness of sins, etc., recited in a low voice; and the **Cazan** then sings them aloud, beginning again with the 145th Psalm, along with some scriptural passages from the Prophets, and especially those from Isaiah 6: *Holy, Holy, Holy, God of Sabaoth*, with the explanation of the same words in Chaldean <note>original: "Chaldeeuſch" (Aramaic).</note>. # ON THE RELIGIOUS DUTIES OF THE JEWS.

Having finished, one concludes with a reading and a thanksgiving to God for what he has revealed for his service, requesting that he allows himself to be honored and worshipped by everyone in the same way. This they call (a) <term>It is our duty to praise</term> <note>original: "HALENU LE SABEAH," the Aleinu prayer, which acknowledges God's sovereignty.</note>, and this is their morning prayer.

<margin>Penitential prayers and when they are prayed.</margin>
On Mondays and Thursdays, one adds certain kinds of confessions and penitential prayers to the prayers after the <term>Eighteen Blessings</term> <note>original: "SCEMONA ESRE," the central standing prayer of the liturgy, also known as the Amidah.</note>; and if someone wishes to fast or practice abstinence, he usually chooses these two days of the week, which they call days of justice: because the ancient Judges, out of mutual respect for Divine justice, held their sessions on these days, both in the large cities and in the villages and surrounding areas, to which everyone traveled.

<margin>Afternoon and Evening prayers accompanied by thanksgivings.</margin>
In the afternoon, one begins the prayers with the 145th Psalm. The <term>Sanctification</term> <note>original: "CADIS," the Kaddish, a prayer hallowing God's name.</note>, the eighteen blessings or <term>Eighteen Blessings</term>, are said with a low voice, then raised, and the <term>Sanctification</term> is said once more; after which one concludes.

In the evening, one repeats a praise to God, who leads the night, who loves Israel, and has given them his commandments; the three readings called <term>The Reading of the Shema</term> <note>original: "CHIRIAD SCEMAN," the central declaration of Jewish faith.</note>; a memorial of the miraculous deliverance from Egypt; and a prayer to obtain undisturbed rest from God during the night. One adds eighteen verses of the Prophets, the 18 blessings of the <term>Eighteen Blessings</term>, though entirely softly, the <term>It is our duty to praise</term>, and the <term>Sanctification</term>, with which the evening prayer ends.

These are the most essential matters that accompany all prayers, and how they are joined together on certain days and solemn festivals, corresponding to the church duties, as we shall describe in their proper place. Each time, these prayers always serve as the foundation for the others, both in terms of order and the nature of the content. Also, there is no difference here, which is otherwise notable among various Jewish nations; since they almost all agree.

<column-break/>

<margin>Into how many readings they divide the books of the Law.</margin>
They have divided the entire <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible, also known as the Five Books of Moses.</note> or five Books of Moses into forty-eight or fifty-two readings, called <term>Portions</term> <note>original: "PARASCIOD," the weekly sections of the Torah scroll.</note>; and one of these is read weekly in the synagogues: so that in one year, whether it consists of twelve or thirteen months (as will be said hereafter), the entire reading is completed. On Mondays and Thursdays, after the penitential prayers are done, one takes from the chest that was spoken of, the (b) <term>Book of the Law</term> <note>original: "SEFER TORA," the hand-written Torah scroll.</note>, and repeating the verse from the 34th Psalm: *O magnify the Lord with me*, etc., and some others, one places it on the small altar or the lectern, where, being unwound and unrolled, one requests three persons to read the beginning of the (c) <term>Portion</term> <note>original: "PARASCIA," the specific weekly reading.</note> that they are currently in. Each reads a few words of it, which are preceded and followed by a blessing. After which the Cantor blesses them, and they each promise to give something, either for the poor, or for the needs of the synagogue, or to the Cantor or (d) <term>Sexton</term> <note>original: "SCIAMAS," the synagogue attendant or beadle.</note>. After this, the <term>Book of the Law</term> is lifted high, being unfurled, and one says to the congregation, showing them the writing of the Book, (e) *Behold the Law which Moses has established*, etc. <note>original: "Ziet de Wet die Moses heeft ingestelt"; quoting Deuteronomy 4:44.</note> The Easterners, nonetheless, are accustomed to doing this before the start of the reading. Then the Book is rolled up again, wound, and placed back in the chest.

<margin>The reading of the five Books of Moses instituted by Ezra.</margin>
This church custom of reading from the <term>Pentateuch</term> or five Books of Moses, and in this manner requesting more or fewer persons to read, is an order instituted by <term>Ezra</term> <note>original: "Esdras," the priest and scribe who led the return from Babylonian exile.</note>, which is observed on all feast and fast days, as we shall mention in its proper place. And since everyone, out of religious devotion, desires to have a part in this act—to fetch the Book from and return it to the storage chest, or in other actions that occur during the prayer hours—it is offered to the highest donor, and the money collected from it is distributed, as has been said, to the poor, or used for the maintenance of the synagogue.

# CHAPTER VI.
## *Of the* PRIESTS *and* LEVITES; *the* GIFTS *given to them, and of the* TITHES.

<margin>How in former times Aaron's descendants were Priests, and what their Priesthood consisted of.</margin>
In former times, there were no Priests and Teachers in the Temple except the descendants of Aaron, as one reads in <term>Exodus</term> <note>original: "Exodus," the second book of the Bible.</note> and elsewhere. These were the ones who offered the sacrifices, performed the offerings, burned the incense, or served the Altar of Incense, and in a word, did everything that was necessary. They also had designated for them not only the portion of the offerings in that same place, but also from all the animals that were slaughtered, from which they were given the shoulder, breast, and jawbones. Furthermore, they had the firstborn of all livestock, and that which was given in exchange for a woman's firstborn <note>The ritual of Pidyon HaBen, or redemption of the firstborn son.</note>; the first sheared sheep’s wool, and the remnants of other animals; the fiftieth part of the harvest and fruits; a piece of dough from every baking of bread; and everything else that is expressed in Holy Scripture.

<margin>What office the Levites held.</margin>
The office of the Levites was to sing in the Temple at certain times. They held the tithe of the harvest, which they gathered in the field; however, one is no longer subject to this feudal right, unless it concerns Jews belonging to Jerusalem and ancient Judea <note>Referring to the halakhic principle that agricultural tithes apply primarily to the Land of Israel.</note>. Everywhere, Jews are forbidden from sowing two kinds of seeds together, such as wheat and barley, nor anything mixed with grape seeds: (c) *You shall not sow your field with various grains*, etc. <note>original quoting Leviticus 19:19.</note> nor to graft any tree, such as Peach trees, Apple, Orange, and other trees; likewise, they may not cultivate grafted trees on their land; but they may indeed eat the fruits of a grafted tree.

### CHAPTER VIII.

### Of the CHARITY of the Jews for the POOR; and for animal CREATURES.

<margin>The Jews' charity toward their poor.</margin>
Although the Jews are subject to scorn and injustice more than other peoples; that few rich are found among them, and that those who are possess nothing that one can call true riches <note>The author adds a footnote here specifying this refers to the "High German" or Ashkenazi Jews.</note>; nevertheless, these few rich come to the aid of the needs of the poor, who are in great number, and support them at all times and on all occasions; such that one cannot deny that the Jews have a great compassion for the poor.

In the large cities, the poor go to the rich and those who are a little inclined toward them on the day before the Sabbath or other high feast days; then everyone gives according to their ability. What is more, the <term>PARNASSIM (communal leaders)</term> (f) or <term>MEMUNIM (overseers)</term>, who are appointed for this, provide them with some money weekly, and especially to the "shamefaced" poor <note>Historically, this refers to people who have fallen on hard times but are too embarrassed to beg publicly.</note>, or widows and the infirm, who cannot come to them. From the money in the charity boxes, and what is received from the synagogue services and ceremonies, as already said in the fourth chapter, a savings chest is made from which to feed the poor.

When it is required to show a general charity, whether to a poor resident or to a stranger;

(d) One could redeem a donkey's foal by giving a lamb to the Priest.

When these charities are collected, they are given to the poor for whom they were intended.
