<margin>
Coming to the aid of urgent Poverty.
</margin>
If the poverty of no one in the city of his residence exceeds his own <note>This suggests that if local resources are exhausted or his needs are particularly high</note>, he approaches the most prominent Rabbis, who provide him with one (a) of their signed certificates, stating: *That the bearer is an honest and needy man, and that one is requested to offer him a helping hand.* On the presentation of this document in places where Jews are found—whether a castle, a farmstead, or any other location—he is sheltered and maintained for one or two days; and upon his departure, he is given some money. In every city through which he travels, he has a new certificate issued to him, or he has the first one countersigned, with which he goes to the Synagogue, to the <term>PARNASSIM (communal leaders)</term>, or to the societies, where those reside who have the means to assist him; and he then receives his necessary maintenance, as has already been described.

(a) <note>original: "Deze ſoorten van Brieven zyn mede lang onder de Chriſtenen in gebruik geweeſt."</note> These types of letters were also long in use among Christians.

<margin>
Alms sent to Jerusalem.
</margin>
From all places where Jews are found, they yearly send alms to Jerusalem for the support of the poor living there, and for those who

<column-break/>

pray for the well-being of the community. They also send something to other places in Judea, such as Joppa, Tiberias, and Hebron, where the graves of the Patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their wives are located. Besides these public alms, each individual gives privately as much as he wishes and is within his means.

<margin>
And to all different peoples.
</margin>
They also believe that it is a good deed to give alms to all kinds of miserable people, even if they are not Jews themselves nor residents of their city: since this is a kindhearted generosity that must extend to everyone without distinction, and of which the Rabbis also make explicit mention.

By the same effect of compassion, they neither plague nor treat any animals poorly, and they take great care not to make them die cruelly; for they regard them as God’s creatures, according to the words of Psalm 145, verse 9:
> *The Lord is good to all, and his mercies are over all his works.*

### CHAPTER I.
->Concerning the **LANGUAGE** of the *Jews*; the **PRONUNCIATION**; the **SCRIPTURE**, and **PREACHING**.<-

<margin>How little experienced the Jews are in Hebrew,</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'W' featuring intricate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
FEw Jews are there who are able to converse perfectly in Hebrew, or in the Holy Tongue, which they (a) call <note>original: "LASCHON HACO-DESCH"</note> the Holy Tongue, in which the twenty-four books of the Old Testament are written. In <term>Chaldean <note>This refers to Aramaic, the language of many Jewish legal and liturgical texts.</note></term>, or the (b) <term>TARGUM (Aramaic paraphrase)</term>, they are likewise no more experienced. Nevertheless, they spoke these languages when they still possessed a national assembly <note>Referring to the period of the Jewish commonwealth or the Sanhedrin.</note>. Thus, they are now only experienced in the language of the land where they were born. Likewise, those of Italy and Germany understand nothing but Italian and High German, and those of the East and the Barbary Coast understand the Turkish and Moorish <note>Arabic</note> speech. They are even so inclined toward these foreign languages that many Jews who came from Germany into Poland,

<column-break/>

Hungary, and Russia, have carried the High German language into these countries and made it hereditary to their children. <margin>and how they have made the local languages of their residence their own.</margin> Those who, after being driven out of Spain, fled to the East or the Levant, also carried the Spanish language there. In Italy, both of these languages are spoken according to the custom of their ancestors. The Jewish people are inclined to remain in the land whose language they understand, satisfying themselves by mixing some broken Hebrew words into the same. The scholars who understand the Scripture a little are very scarce, and there are few besides the Rabbis who know how to produce a coherent discourse in Hebrew with any elegance.

<margin>Diversity of Hebrew pronunciation noted among them.</margin>
As for the pronunciation of Hebrew, it varies greatly among them, such that the High Germans are hardly understood by the Italians and the Easterners. There are none who speak more accurately or more in accordance with the rules of grammar—which they (a) call <term>DICHDOUCH <note>original: "Dikduk", meaning grammar or linguistic precision.</note></term>—than the Italians.
<margin>Scarcity of words in which the Holy Language consists.</margin>
The Holy Language, considered on its own, is very limited and poor in words; for no ancient writings remain other than the 24 Books of the Old Testament, to which one must have recourse if anything needs to be extracted from it. It is true that the Rabbis, who understand enough for general use, make use of <term>Chaldean <note>Aramaic, a sister language to Hebrew used in many legal texts.</note></term>, and even a little Greek and other neighboring languages. They have also invented many words for naming things, which has since been followed from century to century by authors, primarily to make themselves understood in philosophical matters and in other sciences, for which they found it necessary to borrow expressions.
<margin>The Jews' common custom of writing in Rabbinic Hebrew.</margin>
This manner of writing in Rabbinic Hebrew is commonly practiced in authorship, in contracts, in journals, in public business, and further; but for common matters and writings, one mostly uses the local language of one's residence. Nevertheless, there are those who write this in Hebrew letters. The Jews of

<column-break/>

Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.</note> are now the only ones who still express everything in Hebrew.
<margin>What their sermons consist of.</margin>
The sermons are delivered in the local language so as to be understood by everyone; however, the passages of Scripture, as well as the citations from the Rabbis, are presented in Hebrew, which the preacher then explains in the common tongue.
Since preaching is readily permitted, whoever is inclined toward this takes his opportunity while the entire assembly in the synagogue sits in silence. Then he covers himself with his <term>TALED <note>original: "Tallit", a ritual prayer shawl.</note></term>, and even without being covered, leaning against the lectern—of which we have already spoken (b)—he begins with a verse from the reading currently being used, called (c) <term>NOSE <note>original: "Noseh", meaning the subject or theme of the discourse.</note></term>, which he accompanies with a proverb of the Sages called <term>MAAMAR <note>original: "Ma'amar", a saying or discourse.</note></term>. Next, he presents his introduction, drawn from some material related to this reading. After that, he explains the text and cites passages of Scripture and those of Rabbinic authority, each according to his own style, which varies greatly among different peoples. The sermon is delivered on the Sabbath, and most often on major holidays, unless a funeral oration for some prominent head of a household is required, which commonly happens on a day when there is no holiday or other extraordinary occasion.

CONCERNING THE RELIGIOUS DUTIES OF THE JEWS. 39

...is not permitted, one exercises oneself in the tenets of the Sages, Interpreters, or the abridged *Talmud*.

<margin>Their Academies established for this purpose.</margin>
For this purpose, they have High Schools (a) called JESIVOD <note>original: "Yeshivot", meaning places of sitting or study</note>, where the Rabbis and their students gather to debate; but this proceeds in a disorderly manner and with much noise, such that it seems the subject matter being handled causes much labor. They are usually found there after the practice of the morning prayers, except on Fridays, the day before a Feast, on the Sabbath, and on Feast days.

<margin>How all their doctrines are based on the Talmud, and how these formerly could only be passed down by tradition without being recorded.</margin>
Since the foundation of all the teachings, ecclesiastical customs, and traditions of the Jews stems from the *Talmud*, and they derive all their authority from it, it will be necessary to discover its origin and present in order what it contains.

We noted in the first chapter of the first Section that the Jews received the Law of Moses in writing, and from the Rabbis the oral Law, which is the interpretation of the first, along with the collection of all other institutions. As long as the Temple existed, the Jews were not permitted to put any of this second Law into writing, which for that reason was called the *oral Law*; since it was taught only with a living voice through tradition. But about one hundred and twenty (b) years after the destruction of the temple, lived the Rabbi *Judah*, who, because of his Holy life, was called by the Jews RABENU HAKADOSH, or our Holy Master; this Rabbi was very wealthy and a great friend of the Emperor Antoninus the Pious; seeing that due to the scattering of the Jews this Oral Law was neglected, he described all the opinions, institutions, and traditions of the Rabbis up to his time; and this sufficiently in brief <margin>Rabbi Judah, the first writer of the Mishnah, divided into six parts.</margin> in a Book which he (c) called *Mishnah* <note>The Mishnah is the first major written collection of the Jewish oral traditions.</note>. He divided this work into six parts, of which the first deals with Agriculture and seeds, the second with Feast days, the third with

<column-break/>

marriages, and what concerns women; the fourth, with lawsuits and disputes from which damages and interests arise, along with all sorts of civil matters; the fifth, with sacrifices; and the sixth, with purity and impurity. But as this book was very concise and somewhat unintelligible, it caused many arguments, which ran so high that the zeal of two Rabbis who were in Babylon, one called RAVENA and the other RAVASCE, strove to collect all the interpretations, disputes, and additions that had been made regarding the *Mishnah* in their time, to which they added many stories, proverbs, and remarkable sayings that had come to their experience, placing the *Mishnah* as the Text, and the rest as a <margin>By whom the Babylonian Talmud was compiled, as well as that of Jerusalem.</margin> clarification, from which they compiled the Book which is called (d) *Talmud Babeli*, or rather *Gemara*, divided into sixty parts, called (e) MASSAKTOTH <note>original: "Masechtot", meaning tractates or volumes</note>. Some years before, a certain Rabbi *Yochanan* of Jerusalem had made a similar work, which is called TALMUD GERUSALMI, or *Talmud of Jerusalem*. But since this writing was very short and harsh in style, the Babylonians chose the other as more extensive and understandable. Over this latter work, Rabbi Solomon, commonly called (f) RASCI <note>Rashi, the famous medieval commentator</note>, made a commentary, and a High School of Rabbis also added the debates, called (g) TOSSAFOTH <note>meaning "additions" or "supplements"</note>. From this *Babylonian Talmud*, many matters have been drawn, and especially the three Treatises included in the six of which we have spoken, since those concerning Agriculture, sacrifices, and purity and impurity are no longer in use today.

<margin>Where and by whom the Talmud was forbidden.</margin> Since then, there have been Popes who forbade the *Talmud*, and others again who tolerated it; but now it is primarily forbidden in Italy, where it may not be possessed, read, nor seen.

### CHAPTER III.

#### *Concerning the* ELECTION *of* RABBIS, *their* AUTHORITY, *and* EXCOMMUNICATION.

<margin>Whom one elects as Rabbis.</margin>
The Rabbis do not strive for a teaching position, and they consider it a shameful vanity to express a desire for it. Nor does one interview them; rather, when an educated person is seen to be fit to become a Rabbi—namely, one who is more practiced in the oral Law than in all other sciences—he is then declared a Scholar by common vote, and is called <term>CACHAM</term> <note>Hebrew: Hacham, meaning "wise"</note>, or wise man. At the very least, this is the custom of the East, whereas those of Germany and Italy receive this title from the oldest Rabbis, such that they are called by choice or in writing <term>CHAVER DE RAU</term> <note>Hebrew: Chaver le-Rav, meaning "Associate of the Master"</note>, or Master's companion; this title is given to youths who are not yet as experienced in the sciences as their elders. Or they give him the name <term>MORENU</term> <note>Hebrew: "Our Teacher"</note>, or <term>RAU</term> <note>Hebrew: Rav, meaning "Master"</note>, which signifies Teacher or Master.

<margin>And who perform the office of judges in disputes.</margin>
The <term>CACHAM</term>, <term>RAU</term>, or <term>MORENU</term> settles all sorts of disputes, judges concerning forbidden or permitted matters, and likewise all religious topics, involving himself even in civil administration.

<margin>False swearing forbidden to the Jews.</margin>
It is forbidden for Jews to swear in vain, nor to use the name of God without necessity, according to what is expressed in the Ten Commandments and can be read in the fifth chapter of *Deuteronomy*. (a) Lying and falsehood are not tolerated, as is said in *Leviticus* 19 verse 12: *You shall not swear falsely by my name.*

Vows are also rarely approved; but when one makes them, one must fulfill them. A man can release his wife—even if she herself did not wish it—from a vow of abstinence she might have made; however, it is required that this occur within 24 hours of him gaining knowledge of it. They occupy the first seats in the Synagogues and assemblies. They expel the disobedient and can place them under the ban <note>The "Kerkban" refers to *Herem*, the highest ecclesiastical censure in the Jewish community</note>; they are also accorded great respect.

<margin>How excommunication is handled,</margin>
When they place someone under the ban, they curse him openly, after which no Jew may speak to the banished person, nor approach him within a distance of one rod. Access to the Synagogue is forbidden to him, and he is required to sit on the ground barefooted, as if one of his close relatives had passed away <note>This practice imitates the Jewish customs of mourning</note>, until he is released again by one or more Rabbis and blessed anew.

<margin>And what must be observed therein.</margin>

# ON THE RELIGIOUS DUTIES OF THE JEWS. 41

<margin>Deceptive trade of the Jews forbidden.</margin>
The Jews are commanded, both by the Law of Moses and by the Oral Law <note>The "Oral Law" refers to the Talmud and rabbinic traditions believed to have been passed down alongside the written Torah</note>, to be upright and to deceive no one, whether Jew or otherwise. They are to maintain with all people the standards of commerce prescribed in various places of the Scriptures, and especially in *Leviticus* 19, from verse 33 to the end.

There are those who have said and written that the Jews take an oath to deceive a Christian daily, and that they consider this a good deed; but this is an outright slander, spread to make them even more hated than they already are. On the contrary, many Rabbis have written—and our Master <term>Bachii</term> <note>Rabbeinu Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish scholar</note> has a treatise in his book <term>The Jar of Flour</term> <note>original: "CAD ACHEMA" or Kad ha-Kemach</note>, under the letter <term>G</term> for <term>Robbery</term> <note>original: "Ghimel Ghezela" or Gezelah</note>—stating that it is a greater sin to deceive someone who is not a Jew than to deceive a Jew. This is both because the act itself is evil and because the disgrace resulting from it is greater. They also call this act the <term>Desecration of the Name</term> <note>original: "CHILLUL ASCEM" or Hillul Hashem</note>, or *blaspheming the name of God*, which is one of the greatest sins. Therefore, if someone among them is a deceiver, he alone should be blamed as an individual. Truly, there are no observant Jews who practice this, as deception is not tolerated by the Law, nor is it permitted in any way by the Rabbis.

It is, however, quite true that in the lamentable state into which their dispersion has brought them, they are forbidden from owning almost any land, as well as from the principal means of trade to enrich themselves. Because of this, their spirit has been somewhat extinguished, and they have fallen away from the ancient Israelite integrity.

<margin>Why they are inclined toward Usury.</margin>
For the same reason, they are also inclined toward the excess of <term>Usury</term> <note>The practice of lending money at interest</note>, based on what is said in <note>original: (b) Deuteronomy 23:20</note> *To the stranger you shall lend upon usury; but to your brother you shall not lend upon usury.* By "strangers," the Jews can only understand those seven nations—the Hittites, the Amorites, the Jebusites, etc.—whom God himself commanded to be put to the sword. But since the majority

<column-break/>

of the Jews have no other means of livelihood, they imagine that it is permitted to them, acting as brothers by nature.

It is only to the seven nations that one must apply this passage where the Rabbis permit extortion, based on the fact that these nations are so often cursed in Holy Scripture. But it is by no means understood to apply to the nations where the Jews are now tolerated, and where they are treated with compassion by Princes and peoples—especially among Christians—since this would not only be a matter against the written Law, but also against the Law of Nature.

<margin>How they conclude their contracts,</margin>
All contract-dealings of purchase or agreement are considered closed when the parties have touched the garment or the handkerchief of witnesses; which is a type of oath called <term>Acquisition by Cloth</term> <note>original: "KINIAN SUDDAR" or Kinyan Sudar</note>, which means *the acquisition of material*.

<margin>and make them legal.</margin>
Public Notaries hold no authority among them unless they act in the capacity of a scribe. The scribe must be a witness, accompanied by two others; he draws up and legalizes all types of documents, whether they concern commerce, wills, the marriage contract, divorce, or any other type of agreement.

To subsequently make such an act more credible, and to enable it to be used at any time and place, it is validated by three other legal authorities, who are called judges of trade. To ensure that the witnesses are beyond reproach, they must be examined in the presence of the debtor or the opposing party.

<margin>Rabbis hold the position of Judges.</margin>
In all lawsuits and disputes, whatever the matter may be, the most prominent Rabbis among the Jews serve as the Judges; or, the parties may agree to choose "good men" from among their friends.

The Rabbis judge in accordance with what is written in the <term>Breastplate of Judgment</term> <note>original: "CHOSEN HAMISPATH" or Choshen Mishpat</note>, or in the collection of future cases called <term>Questions and Answers</term> <note>original: "SHEELOTH VESCIVUOD" or She'elot u-Tshuvot</note>, mostly drawn

->CHAPTER V.<-
->Of the Forever Forbidden MEAT, and the Jews' conduct in Eating; of their DRINK; of their BREAD BAKING; and how they eat at the table.<-

<margin>Which meat the Jews are forbidden to eat.</margin>
The Jews may not eat the meat of any four-footed beast which does not have cloven hooves and, like cows and sheep, does not chew the cud; rabbits, hares, and pigs are a forbidden food to them. They also eat no fish without scales or fins <note>original: "kraabbeenen", literally "crab-legs," likely referring to the appendages of shellfish or a misinterpretation of fins</note>, nor any birds of prey, nor any creeping creatures, as is clearly enough expressed in Leviticus 11.
For this reason, they eat nothing except that which is cooked or prepared by Jews, and they also use no kitchen utensils from anyone who is not of the Jewish Nation; being fearful of meat that is forbidden to them, as we have noted (a). They will also not allow themselves to be served with the knives of others. They likewise eat no fat <term>suet</term> <note>The forbidden fats known as *Chelev*, which were reserved for altar sacrifices in ancient times</note> of oxen, nor of lambs, nor of goats, as is noted at the end of Leviticus 3. They are also forbidden from eating the thigh muscle <note>The sciatic nerve, or *Gid HaNasheh*</note>, forbidden to them at the end of Genesis 32. For this reason, they carefully cut away the fat and this muscle from all beasts that they eat; and indeed in many places in Italy, and especially in Germany, there are many who do not eat the hindquarters at all, because of the fat and the muscles found there which must be carefully removed, as there are few who know how to remove them accurately (b).
<margin>As also the eating of blood.</margin>
They may eat no blood of four-footed beasts, nor of poultry, nor even of animals in which the slightest blood appears to be. This is perhaps why they are forbidden from eating any land animal or poultry whose throat has not been slit to make the blood flow out.
<column-break/>
<margin>How the circumstances in which the throat-slitting must be done.</margin>
When it is required to slaughter a beast <term>shechita</term> <note>The ritual slaughter of animals for food</note>, this must be carried out by a person who understands the circumstances to be observed therein. For one must observe the proper time and have a sharp, cutting knife that is without any nicks, so that the blood may flow out more quickly without hindrance (c), flowing over the earth, or into sand or ash, with which it is subsequently covered. They may not cut a piece from any living animal, and eat it neither cooked nor raw. They also may not kill a cow and its calf on the same day, nor any sheep or goat along with its young, when they are aware of it.
<margin>and what is observed therein.</margin>
If (d) any beast or poultry of which they may eat has died of itself, or was killed in another manner than described, they are forbidden to taste of it. Likewise, if a thorn or needle were found in poultry that had been opened, or any blemish in four-footed beasts, or those that had a lung disease <note>original: "zongziekte", likely a typo or archaic form of *longziekte* (lung disease); such defects render the animal *treif* or unfit</note>, which is carefully inspected after they are killed; one shall not eat of it, in accordance with the prohibition of Exodus 23 at the end, and other places in Scripture. If any animal had a broken bone in one of its limbs, or if it were mortally wounded, one may not eat of it according to the explanation of the Rabbis.
To better observe the prohibition against eating blood, the meat is laid in salt for about an hour before it is put into the pot, so that the blood is entirely drawn out; without this, they may have no

# ON THE RELIGIOUS DUTIES OF THE JEWS.
F 2

eat no meat unless it is roasted: and as the liver is full of blood, they let it roast on coals before it is boiled.
<margin>How fish is permitted for them to eat.</margin> Regarding the fish that is permitted for them to eat, there is nothing special to observe here; for the eating of their blood is not forbidden to them, nor is it commanded to throw it away when they are dead or defective.
<margin>Forbidden to eat meat and milk dishes at one meal.</margin> One may not, at one and the same meal, eat meat, cheese, or milk dishes, since it is said: (a) *You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk* <note>original: "Gy zult het Geitenbokje niet kooken in zyns moeders melk"</note>. Which they understand to apply to all kinds of animals, and from whatever milk it might be. Likewise, they may by no means prepare meat with anything made of boiled or raw milk; they do not even consume any mixture during the meal, and do not eat meat and subsequently cheese in the same hour: because, as they claim, they are concerned that some meat might remain between the teeth, which would then mix with the cheese.
<margin>Some drink no wine except that which is handled by their own Nation.</margin> For this reason, the kitchen utensils that have served for meat may not serve for any milk dishes, and they even use special knives for them. If by chance one of these two aforementioned things is prepared in a utensil belonging to the other, they not only do not eat them: but even if it is an earthenware vessel, it can no longer be used.
<margin>How the Jews feel about eating cheese.</margin> They eat no cheese unless they have seen it made, being concerned that milk from forbidden animals might be used, or that some part of the skin might be mixed with the rennet <note>original: "ſtreſſel", the curdling agent used in cheesemaking</note>, which could be regarded as meat and cheese together, or that it might have been warmed in a kettle that had served to boil some forbidden meat. They then place a mark on the cheese where the rennet was seen to be made.
The Rabbis have indeed introduced a rule that one may drink no wine unless it has been handled by their own Nation. The Eastern and High-German <note>referring to the Ashkenazi Jewish communities of Central and Eastern Europe</note> Jews observe this strictly; but the Italian Jews do not. They say that when the Rabbis gave this command, they lived among idolaters, with whom they wished to have no social interaction; but that this should not be understood as applying to the peoples among whom they now live, whom the same Rabbis declare not to be such.

->handled by their own Nation.<-
They have many other ceremonies; for example, at the beginning and the end of every feast, whether a wedding or circumcision, etc., in which they are accustomed to repeat some praise with a glass of wine or beer; and every time they drink, they pronounce a blessing before and after. For they hold wine in great value, as it is said: (b) *Wine gladdens the heart of man*, and in another place: (c) *That it gladdens both God and men*.
->Kneading Their Bread.<- When the Jews' bread is kneaded, namely, when a lump of dough is made the size of forty eggs, a small portion of it is taken, from which a cake is made that serves for the firstfruits, as commanded in *Numbers 15, verse 20*: *The firstfruits of your dough, a cake*, etc.
It was customary to give this cake to the Priest, but now it is thrown into the fire, where it is entirely burnt: this being one of the three commandments that must be observed by women, since they commonly knead the bread.
->And what they do before they sit at the table.<- Before the Jews go to sit at the table to eat, they are required to wash their hands; on which the Rabbis are very insistent, no less than regarding their manner of washing themselves in the morning, as has already been said.
After they are seated, they usually repeat the words of the 23rd Psalm: *The Lord is my shepherd, etc.* Then the master of the house takes a bread, and after having blessed it, breaks it, and gives to each of those seated at the table a piece the size of an olive, after which those who are invited eat as much as they please: but for the first time someone drinks, (e) he is obliged to repeat the blessing of which we have spoken.

# HISTORICAL TREATISE
### Page 46

the rest is a burden or load. This precision extends to observing the habits of women, children, and household members, without exception for the animals; as included in the Ten Commandments; (a) *You shall do no work, neither you nor your sons, etc.*

<margin>Trade on this day forbidden.</margin>
It is unlawful for them to speak of trade on this day, and they are commanded to refrain from matters concerning things bought or sold; neither to give nor to receive anything, as is expressed in *Isaiah* 58: *If you turn away your foot from the Sabbath, etc.*

They may handle nothing on this day, nor touch anything that is heavy, nor any craftsman’s tools, unless they are items required for the celebration of the Sabbath. They also may not walk more than a mile outside the City and suburbs; namely, two thousand paces <note>This is the 'Sabbath day's journey' (Tehum Shabbat), a traditional limit on travel distance.</note>.

To ensure that all commercial work and manual labor ceases with even greater care on this day, the Rabbis have added many other prohibitions to these; such as not handling money, nor riding a horse, nor traveling in a boat, nor playing any musical instruments, nor bathing.

<margin>Order regarding Surgeons and Physicians established, and for everything concerning the Sabbath.</margin>
In illnesses and defects that require a Surgeon <note>original: "Wondheelder," referring to a barber-surgeon who performed physical procedures.</note>, the Rabbis are very strict: but regarding Physicians, if the Doctor judges that there is danger, or when a woman is about to give birth, everything is permitted <note>This refers to the principle of *Pikuach Nefesh*, where the preservation of human life overrides almost all Sabbath laws.</note>. They then consider on Friday what may be necessary for the Sabbath, corresponding to what *Moses* says of the Manna: (b) *And it shall come to pass on the sixth day, and they also consider it very well done to go to great expense on this day to celebrate the Feast, as Isaiah 58 verse 13 says; they even believe they honor the Sabbath by humbling themselves, performing something lowly and beneath their station.* <note>Historical accounts often describe scholars or wealthy individuals performing menial tasks like chopping vegetables or sweeping to show personal devotion to the Sabbath preparation.</note>

On Friday, one undertakes no work which cannot be finished before the evening. About an hour before sunset, one places in a warm place, as best as one can, that which has been prepared to eat the following day. After which all labor is ceased, and in some Cities, there is someone appointed who 

<column-break/>

calls this out or gives a signal half an hour before the Sabbath begins, so that everyone may then be free and without labor on that day.

<margin>When the Sabbath begins.</margin>
It is about half an hour before sunset that the Sabbath is set to begin, and consequently, all the commandments must be observed. At that time, the women are obliged to light a lamp in a room, which according to custom has six, or at least four wicks, and must burn for a large part of the night. They also cover a table with a white cloth and set bread upon it, which they cover with another long and narrow linen. This is done, they say, in memory of the Manna which fell in such a manner, being moistened by the dew above and below, for on the Sabbath day it did not rain.

There are those who, to begin the Sabbath well, take white linen, wash their hands and face, and then go to the Synagogue, where they recite the 92nd Psalm: *It is good to praise the Lord, etc.* and the usual prayers, adding the remembrance of the Sabbath with these words from *Genesis*, (c) *Thus the Heavens were finished, etc. And the Lord blessed the seventh day, etc.*

<margin>How the Jews behave upon leaving their Synagogue.</margin>
Upon leaving the Synagogue, everyone returns to his house, and in greeting, they say neither good day nor good evening: but *a good Sabbath.* Furthermore, the Fathers bless their children, the Masters their pupils, to which they add certain other Proverbs in honor of the Sabbath, some before and others after the meal, according to the custom of the Land where they find themselves.

Everyone being seated at the table, the Father of the House, holding a drinking cup of wine in his hand, says these words from *Genesis*, (d) *Thus the Heavens were finished, etc.* after which he thanks God for having commanded the Sabbath, and he blesses the wine; then he drinks of it and also gives a little of it to all those at the Table. After that, he says the 23rd Psalm: *The Lord is my Shepherd, etc.* Having performed this, he blesses the bread and gives some to everyone, after which each makes good cheer this evening as best he can, and also the following day. After the meal, they wash their hands and occupy themselves as has been said regarding the manner of eating. (a) Some recite the 104th Psalm after eating: *Bless the LORD, O my soul*, etc.

<margin>Their conduct on the Sabbath in the Synagogue described.</margin>
On Sabbath mornings, they rise later than usual, and having arrived in the Synagogue, they recite many Psalms and appropriate prayers of praise regarding the Sabbath, interspersing the chanting of the regular prayers. They also bring forth the Pentateuch <note>The Torah, or the first five books of Moses.</note> or the Books of Moses, and seven persons read the entire Portion <note>The weekly Parashah.</note> for that week; subsequently, a passage from the Prophets is read which relates to what was read from the Law. This last reading is called (b) HAFTARAH <note>original: "AFTARA," meaning "conclusion."</note>, and it is customary for a child to read it for practice.

Subsequently, the Reader lifts the Book, which he holds in his arms, on high and gives a blessing to all those present. After that, he gives a solemn blessing for the Prince under whose rule they are gathered, praying to God that He might keep them in peace and joy during their rest; that his undertakings may succeed; that his States may expand; and that he may love their Nation, as it is written: (c) *And seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace you will have peace.* He then recites another prayer, called MUSSAF <note>From the Hebrew for "additional."</note>, which signifies "added." They conclude then with the words of the offering that were spoken in the Temple on the Sabbath day, and this is the end.

<margin>What their sermons consist of.</margin>
Sermons are preached indifferently in the morning or the afternoon in the Synagogues or other places designated for assembly, the subject of which is taken from what was read that day in the Pentateuch or Books of Moses. In these sermons, good morals are taught, and all wrongdoing is condemned, accompanying these with the maxims of the Rabbis, as has already been said. (d)

When evening has come, they return again to the Synagogue, where they add the remembrance of the Sabbath to the usual prayers, and the beginning of the following week's Portion is read by three

<column-break/>

persons from the Books of Moses.

<margin>When the Sabbath ends.</margin>
They have the custom of eating three times during the 24 hours of the Sabbath; the first of these is on Friday after the evening prayer, the other two the following day to honor the Festival. The tablecloth remains on the table throughout this time. When night falls and three medium-sized stars can be seen, the Sabbath is then ended, and one can return to work, provided the evening prayer (which they delay as long as possible) has then begun.

They add to the usual evening prayer a remembrance of what distinguishes the Sabbath from other days of the week, with the 91st Psalm, *He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High*, etc., accompanied by many Scripture passages, blessings, and favorable wishes.

As they also believe (e) that the souls of the damned and those who are in the forecourt of Hell <note>Referring to the belief that souls in Gehenna are granted a respite from punishment during the Sabbath.</note> feel refreshment during the time of the Sabbath, they prolong this time through singing and their prayer.

<margin>Ceremonies with which the Sabbath ends and what they consist of.</margin>
When everyone has returned home, a torch is lit, or a lamp that has at least two wicks. The master of the house, having taken wine in a bowl and spices of a good scent, as well as some Scripture passages from the Prophets, recites them, such as Psalm 116: *I will take the cup of salvation*, etc., and what is said at the end of Esther Chapter 8: *The Jews had light*, etc., and other such sayings to wish for all salvation and prosperity in the coming week; thus he blesses the wine and spices and smells them to begin the week with pleasure. Then he blesses the light of the fire, which has not yet been used, and he examines his hands and nails <note>The light of the Havdalah candle is traditionally reflected off the fingernails to represent the first "work" of the new week: distinguishing between light and shadow.</note>, since they are returning to work. What we have mentioned here has many other meanings in the Books of the Rabbis: but it all boils down to signaling that the Sabbath is finished and separated from the day of labor that follows, and thus they conclude. This entire ceremony is called HAVDALAH <note>original: "HABDALA"</note>, or distinction. At that same time, some pour out wine as a sign of

## II. CHAPTER.

->*Of the* NEW MOON; *the name of the* MONTHS *and intercalated Months.*<-

<margin>How the Jews formerly observed the new Moon; but now use calendars.</margin>
According to the Jews' chronology, the lunar cycle constitutes a Month, and the New Moon the beginning of the Month. 
In the time of the *Sanhedrin* <note>The supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of ancient Jerusalem.</note>, or the Judges of *Jerusalem*, they usually sent out two men to give them a report as soon as the Moon had been discovered, and upon this report, they announced that the Month had begun that day, and they arranged the Festivals thereafter in the prescribed time. But since the destruction of the Temple, this is done by calculation, and they print an Almanac <note>A calendar or Luach.</note> annually, which serves them to know the time of New and Full Moons, the four seasons of the year, the Festivals, and other matters of that nature. They also keep a chronology of the Christians' Festivals, in order to arrange their commerce accordingly.
The New Moon is a Feast Day, designated according to *Numbers* (a), since on that day a new offering was made. 
This Feast sometimes lasts two days, namely, at the end of one and the beginning of the other Month. At that time, it is not forbidden to work or engage in commerce: but the women alone have the custom of abstaining from work, and one makes somewhat better cheer <note>Preparation of more festive food.</note> than is usual.
<margin>Ceremonies regarding the New Moon and what they consist of.</margin>
Mention is made in the prayers of the first Month <note>Likely referring to the first day of the month.</note>, and on this day they read the Psalms from 113 to 118 <note>Known as the Hallel, or songs of praise.</note>. They also bring out the Books of *Moses* <note>The Torah scroll.</note>, in which reading is performed by four persons, and they add the

# On the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

Those living in the surrounding regions celebrate this for eight days, following the ancient custom from the time when, by order of the *Sanhedrin* <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish nation</note>, the New Moon was declared by observation rather than calculation, as we mentioned in the previous chapter. This Feast is commanded in *Exodus* 12 (a), and in many other places of Scripture where it is explicitly described.

The first two and last two days of the Passover are the most solemn; and during that time, one may neither work nor engage in trade, just as on the Sabbath. However, it is permitted to light a fire, to prepare food, and to carry what one needs from one place to another. During the four middle days <note>Known as Chol HaMoed, or the intermediate days of the festival</note>, it is also forbidden to work; however, one may handle money, and these days are distinguished from ordinary workdays only in certain specific matters.

During these eight days, it is forbidden for Jews to eat leavened bread, or to have any leaven in their possession or under their authority; thus, for these eight days, they may eat nothing but unleavened bread (b).

<margin>How carefully the Jews search so that no leaven remains;</margin>
To observe this commandment well, they search with diligent accuracy through the entire house to clear away all things subject to fermentation. They therefore rummage through all corners, chests, and cupboards. Subsequently, having cleaned the house well, white-washed it, and renewed the table and kitchen utensils—or using those only used on this day—they prepare for the feast. If utensils used at other times are made of iron or copper, they must be purified by fire or scoured, so that during these eight days nothing is used that is suspected of containing leaven. From this arises the custom that on the evening before the preparation for the Feast, the Father of the house searches the entire house to see if any more leavened bread remains. On the following day before the feast, the bread is burned at eleven o'clock to signal that the prohibition of leavened bread has begun; and this act is accompanied by words declaring that there is no leaven in his power, or at least that he believes so, and that he has done everything in his power to ensure it.

<margin>And how they prepare and bake their Passover cakes.</margin>
Immediately after this, they are busy preparing unleavened bread, which they call *MATZAH* <note>original: "MAZZA"</note>, and they provide themselves with it

I. PART.

<column-break/>

for eight days during the Feast. They take great care that the flour they use has not been damp or warmed, so that it might not have been subject to fermentation. They make cakes of it that are flat, dense, and of various shapes; and so that they do not rise or sour, they immediately thrust them into the oven to bake, and once taken out, they keep them pure and well-preserved. These cakes they eat in place of bread during this time. Some are prepared with eggs and sugar for delicate palates, as well as for the sick: though also without any leaven, and these are called *MATZAH ASHIRAH* <note>original: "MAZZA ASCIRA", literally "rich matzah"</note>, or rich cakes.

<margin>When the Passover falls to them, and why the firstborn must fast beforehand.</margin>
On the 14th of *NISAN* <note>The first month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, occurring in March–April</note>, being the eve of Passover, the firstborn of the Passover households have the custom of fasting, in memory of the night in which God struck all the firstborn of Egypt.

In the evening they go to prayer, and having come home, they sit at the table, which has been prepared beforehand and well-laid according to each person's means. In place of the ceremony that had to be observed then, as stated in *Exodus* 12:

<margin>Ceremonies that they use during the Passover, and what they consist of.</margin>
> To eat the Lamb with unleavened bread and bitter herbs etc.

they have in a dish, or in a small basket, a piece of a lamb or kid, prepared entirely with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, such as celery, chicory, or lettuce, alongside a small dish containing the sauce; all in memory of the mortar and stone they were forced to make in Egypt; and holding a small drinking cup with wine in hand, they repeat the (c) *HAGGADAH* <note>original: "HAGADA", meaning "The Telling"</note>, containing the misery endured by their ancestors in Egypt, and the wonders God performed for their deliverance. Then they thank God for all these benefits and recite the 113th Psalm and the following ones, called (d) *HALLEL* <note>Psalms of praise</note>, after which they hold the supper. After this meal, they continue to recite the remainder of these Psalms, to sing, and to offer other praises proper for that time, after which they go to sleep; and the following evening, they do the same.

<margin>What is handled in the Synagogue.</margin>
The morning prayers are the same as those they perform on other festivals, except that they add what is proper to this feast, along with the preceding Psalms from 113 to 119. They bring out the *Pentateuch* or five Books of Moses (e) and read the 12th Chapter of Exodus, and the institution of the Passover offerings. After the prayer

<margin>How the Jews count the Feast of Weeks.</margin>
Once the <term>Mussaf<note>The additional prayer service recited on Shabbat and festivals.</note></term> is finished, the Prophets are read, relating to what was read in the Books of Moses—the reading we have called the <term>Haftarah<note>A selection from the books of the Prophets read in the synagogue.</note></term>—just as on the Sabbath. In the afternoon, the memory of the Feast is observed, and the blessing for the authorities of the land is spoken, exactly as on the Sabbath.

The same is practiced on the final two days, except that on the last two evenings, one does not do at the table what was done on the first two.

This feast is concluded with the ceremony of <term>Havdalah<note>A ritual marking the symbolic end of a sacred day.</note></term>, as on the Sabbath, in words only, without the smelling of spices; and upon leaving, one once again eats leavened or raised bread.

From the second night of Passover, they count forty-nine days until the Feast of Weeks, during which a handful of grain from the barley harvest was offered, which they

<column-break/>

<margin>Days of mourning, and why they are observed.</margin>
called an <term>Omer<note>original: "Homer"; a biblical unit of dry measure.</note></term>; and this is what they call (a) "counting the Omer," *and you shall count from the following day, etc.* Every evening after the blessing of the commandment is performed, they say: "today so many days of the Omer are counted."

From the day after Passover until the following 33rd day, they spend the time in mourning, without marrying, without putting on new clothes, without powdering their hair, nor engaging in any outward joy. This is because during this period of 33 days, there was a great mortality among the students of <note>Rabbi Akiva, a famous 1st-century sage.</note> Rabbi Hachiba, a man of great prestige among them. And as the plague stopped on the 33rd day of the Omer after the deaths of many thousands, they call this day (b) **Lag**, which means 33, taking the letters as numbers <note>In Hebrew, the letter L (Lamed) stands for 30 and G (Gimmel) for 3.</note>. This day is celebrated with joy and to some extent as a feast, and once it has passed, all outward melancholy is set aside.

---

### CHAPTER IV.

->On the Jews' Feast of Weeks, or Pentecost.<-

---

<margin>How and when the Jews celebrate their Pentecost festival.</margin>
**The** fiftieth day of the Omer, which is the sixth of the month of Sivan, is celebrated as the feast of **Shavuot** or the Weeks, so named because it falls at the end of the seven weeks counted from Passover, as we have noted. In Scripture, this Feast is also called the Day of Firstfruits, (c) because on this day the firstfruits of the harvest were offered in the Temple. It was also called the Feast of Harvest, because that was when they began to cut the grain. It is distinguished by various names in several places in Scripture. Now it is celebrated for two days. These two days are celebrated like the Passover, meaning that during this time one does not work or trade, any more than on the Sabbath, except that one may light a fire, prepare food to eat, and move what one

<column-break/>

needs from one place to another.

By tradition, they hold that the Law was given on Mount Sinai on that day: (d) Therefore, they have the custom of decorating the synagogues and places of reading, and even their houses, with flowers and roses, woven as crowns and various floral ornaments.

The prayers are suited to the feast, and one reads from the Books of Moses about the offering made on that day, alongside the <term>Haftarah</term> in the Prophets, and the blessing for the Sovereign Authority; and in the afternoon, a sermon is given in praise of the Law.

Once the second day of the feast is ended, the ceremony of the **Havdalah** is performed in the evening, as we described at the conclusion of the Passover, to signify that it has ended.

(a) Leviticus 23, verses 10 and 15. (b) Because L. and G. are 33 in Hebrew.
(c) Deuteronomy 16. Exodus 23. Leviticus 23. Numbers 28. (d) Exodus 19.

ON THE RELIGIOUS DUTIES OF THE JEWS. 51

## CHAPTER V.
### On the Jews' NEW YEAR, and on the month of ELUL.

<margin>Dispute among the Jews regarding the institution of their New Year.</margin>
The <term>Talmudists<note>Scholars and teachers of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism containing legal and ethical discussions.</note></term> are in dispute regarding the time when the world had its beginning. Some maintain that it was in the Spring, namely, in the month of *Nisan*, which corresponds to the month of March; and others in the Autumn, namely, in TISHREI, which is our month of September. One is bound to this latter opinion because the year is started at that time. Nevertheless, it is written in the Holy Scripture, speaking of *Nisan*: <gloss>(a)</gloss> *This Month shall be to you the beginning of months*, and following this manner of counting, one says the first, second, third month, and so on until *Adar*, which was the last and twelfth; but afterwards, this manner of counting months was changed, and the year was started with *Tishrei* or the month of September.

From this originates the festival of <term>ROSH HASHANAH<note>original: "ROSCH HASANA"; literally "Head of the Year."</note></term> or head of the year, which is celebrated during the first two days of *Tishrei*, when one then says what stands expressed in Leviticus; <gloss>(b)</gloss> *In the seventh month, on the first of the month, there shall be a rest for you, etc.* During this festival all work and business is forbidden, as in the two other festivals of which we have spoken.

<margin>Days of Penance introduced among them and why.</margin>
Through tradition they believe that God particularly judges the deeds of the past year on this day, and arranges the events of the year into which one has entered, since they imagine that God on this day—being the first point of the birth of the world—accurately reviews everything that happened in the past year. This is the reason that they begin from the first of the month of ELUL, which precedes this one, to do Penance; and in some places people rise before dawn to say prayers and confessions, and to recite the Penitential Psalms. There are many who from this day begin to fast, do penance, and constantly give alms, until the Day of Atonement, which we shall deal with in the next Chapter, which then lasts forty days; and the <term>Horn<note>The Shofar, a ram's horn used as a musical instrument in Jewish liturgy to call the community to repentance.</note></term> is blown at the start of the month of *Elul*, for reasons to be presented hereafter.

<column-break/>

These acts of piety are observed at least during this week that precedes this feast, and on the day before the Feast, many are busy washing themselves and giving thirty-nine lashes, serving as a discipline, <gloss>(c)</gloss> as it is said: <gloss>(d)</gloss> *With forty stripes he shall cause him to be beaten, and he shall add none* etc. <note>The Scripture commands forty lashes, but the tradition recorded in the Talmud commands no more than thirty-nine. Paul in 2 Corinthians 11 verse 24 informs us that this tradition was the practice of his time.</note> and they call this <gloss>(e)</gloss> <term>MALKUT<note>original: "MALCUTH"; ritual lashes performed as a symbolic act of penance.</note></term>.

<margin>Solemn customs of the New Year in use.</margin>
Having come to the Synagogue on the first evening of the year, they wish each other a good year; to which the same wish is returned in answer. They have the custom on this day to serve honey and leavened bread at the table, and everything that can serve as a good omen, so that the year may be fruitful and favorable.

There are some who go to the Synagogue in the mornings of these two feasts dressed in white, to demonstrate their penance and purity. There are even those among the <term>German Jews<note>original: "Hoogduitsche Jooden"; referring to the Ashkenazi tradition.</note></term> who then put on their burial shrouds; and this in order to mortify their flesh. More prayers are said on this Feast than on others, because of the good year that is wished for, and the reconciliation of sins. The Books of Moses are taken out, and five men read the offering that was performed on that day. The <term>HAFTARAH<note>original: "AF TARA"; a selection from the books of the Prophets read in the synagogue.</note></term> of the Prophets is recited, and they bless the Sovereign Authority.

<margin>Blowing of the Horn and why this happens.</margin>
Subsequently, the Horn is blown thirty times, of which some tones are very soft, and others strong, <gloss>(f)</gloss> corresponding to what is said in *Leviticus* and *Numbers*: *A memorial of the sounding*, etc. They say that this is done to think of God’s judgment, and to dismay the sinners, and to bring them to conversion. They add to it the prayer called <term>MUSSAF<note>An additional service recited on Shabbat and holidays.</note></term>, along with many others arranged for this day: to which the blowing of the Horn is again added, just as before. Having returned home and eaten, they spend the rest of the day hearing Sermons and practicing deeds of piety. These two days are equal in everything, and in the evening when the Feast ends, the <term>HAVDALAH<note>original: "HABDALA"; a ceremony involving wine and blessings that marks the end of a sacred day.</note></term> is performed, as has already been said of the other Feasts.

HISTORICAL TREATISE

the <term>Musaf<note>The "additional" prayer service recited on Shabbat and festivals.</note></term> prayer is finished, the Prophets are read, having regard for what was read in the Books of Moses; this is the reading we have called the <term>Haftarah<note>A series of selections from the books of the Prophets that are read publicly in the synagogue as part of the religious service.</note></term>, just as on the Sabbath. In the afternoon, the commemoration of the Feast is discussed, and the blessing over the <term>Sovereign Powers<note>A prayer for the welfare of the government or ruling monarch, a common practice in Jewish liturgy.</note></term> of the Land is spoken, likewise as on the Sabbath.

The same is practiced on the last two days, except however that on the last two evenings, one does not do at the table what was done on the first two.

One ends this feast with the ceremony of <term>Havdalah<note>A ritual marking the symbolic end of a holy day and the return to the mundane week.</note></term>, as on the Sabbath day, in words alone, without the smelling of spices; and upon leaving, one again eats leavened or fermented bread.

<margin>
How the Jews count the Feast of Weeks.
</margin>
From the second evening of Passover, they count forty-nine days until the Feast of Weeks, where a handful of ears of grain—specifically barley—was offered, which they

<column-break/>

called the <term>Omer<note>An ancient Hebrew unit of dry measure. The "Counting of the Omer" (Sefirat HaOmer) is the 49-day period between Passover and Shavuot.</note></term>; and this is what they call counting the (a) Omer: *and you shall count from the following day, etc.* Every evening after the blessing of the commandment is performed, they say: *today so many days of the Omer are counted.*

<margin>
Days of mourning, and why they are observed.
</margin>
From the day after Passover until the following 33rd day, they spend the time in mourning, without marrying, without putting on new clothes, without powdering the hair, nor performing any outward joy: for the reason that during this time of 33 days, there was a great mortality among the students of <term>Rabbi Akiva<note>original: "Rabbyn Hachiba." A major Jewish scholar of the late 1st and early 2nd centuries. Tradition holds that 24,000 of his students died from a plague during this period.</note></term>, a very prominent man among them. And so, after the death of many thousands, the mortality ceased on the 33rd day of the Omer; they call this day (b) <term>Lag<note>Lag (ל״ג) represents the number 33 in Hebrew numerals (Lamed = 30, Gimel = 3).</note></term>, which signifies 33, taking the letters for the ciphers. This day is celebrated with joy, and in some measure as a feast; and when it has passed, all outward melancholy is set aside.

->*Of the Jews' Feast of Weeks, or Pentecost.*<-

<margin>
How and when the Jews celebrate their Pentecost feast.
</margin>
The fiftieth day of the Omer, which is the sixth of the month of Sivan, is celebrated for the feast of <term>Shavuot<note>original: "Schavuoth"; literally "Weeks."</note></term> or "of the weeks," so named because it falls at the end of the seven weeks counted from Passover, as we have noted. This Feast is also called in the Scripture the Day of Firstfruits, (c) since on this day one offered the firstfruits of the harvest in the Temple. It was also called the Feast of the Harvest, since one then began to cut the grain. It is further distinguished by various names in different places of the Scripture. Now it is celebrated for two days. These two days are celebrated like the Passover feast, namely, that during this time one does not work, and conducts no trade, no more than on the Sabbath, except that one may light a fire, prepare food to eat, and move what one

<column-break/>

has need of from one place to another.

By tradition they hold that the Law was given on Mount Sinai on that day: (d) Therefore they have the custom of decorating the Synagogues and places of reading, even their very houses, with flowers and roses, woven like crowns and various floral ornaments.

The prayers are suited to the feast, and one reads in the Books of Moses of the Offering that was made on that day, alongside the Haftarah in the Prophets, and the blessing for the Sovereign Authority; and in the afternoon a sermon is given in praise of the Law.

The second day of the feast having ended, the ceremony of the Havdalah is performed in the evening, as we have said regarding the conclusion of the Passover feast, to signify that it has ended.

## V. CHAPTER.

->Of the Jews’ NEW YEAR, and of the month of ELUL.<-

<margin>Dispute among the Jews over the establishment of their New Year.</margin>
The <term>Talmudists<note>Scholars of the Talmud, the primary source of Jewish religious law and theology.</note></term> are in dispute regarding the time at which the World had its beginning. Some maintain that it was in the Spring, specifically in the month of <term>Nisan<note>The first month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, occurring in March–April.</note></term>, which corresponds to the month of March; and others in the Autumn, namely, in <term>Tishrei<note>The first month of the Jewish civil year, occurring in September–October.</note></term>, which is our month of September. One is bound to this latter opinion, since the year begins at that time. Nevertheless, it stands written in Holy Scripture, speaking of *Nisan*: <note>original Latin: "Mensis iste vobis principium mensium"</note> *(a) This month shall be unto you the beginning of months*, and following this manner of counting, one says the first, second, third month, and so on until <term>Adar<note>The twelfth month of the Jewish calendar.</note></term>, which was the last and twelfth; but thereafter, this manner of counting months was changed, and the year was started with *Tishrei* or the month of September.

From this comes the feast of <term>Rosh Hashanah<note>Literally "Head of the Year," the Jewish New Year.</note></term>, which is celebrated during the first two days of *Tishrei*, when one says that which is expressed in Leviticus: *(b) In the seventh month, in the first day of the month, shall ye have a sabbath*, etc. During this feast, all work and commerce are forbidden, just as in the two other feasts previously mentioned.

<margin>Days of Penance introduced among them and why.</margin>
By tradition they believe that God judges the deeds of the past year specifically on this day, and ordains the events of the year into which one has entered, since they imagine that God—this day being the first point of the birth of the world—closely inspects everything that happened in the past year. This is the reason why they begin to do penance from the first of the month <term>Elul<note>The month preceding Rosh Hashanah, dedicated to spiritual preparation and repentance.</note></term>, which precedes this one; and in some places, they rise before dawn to offer prayers and confessions, and to recite the Penitential Psalms. There are many who begin to fast from this day forth, doing penance and constantly giving alms until the Day of Atonement (which we shall treat in the following Chapter), which then lasts forty days; and they blow on the Horn at the beginning of the month *Elul*, for reasons to be presented hereafter.

<column-break/>

These devotions are observed at least during the week preceding this feast, and on the day before the Feast, many are busy washing themselves and receiving thirty-nine lashes, departing for a discipline, *(c)* as it is said: *(d) With forty stripes he shall cause him to be beaten, and he shall add none thereto, etc.* and they call this *(e)* <term>Malkut<note>original: "MALCUTH," a ritual of symbolic lashes performed as an act of repentance.</note></term>.

<margin>Solemn customs of the New Year in use.</margin>
Having arrived at the Synagogue on the first evening of the year, they wish each other a good year; to which the same wish is returned in answer. They have the custom on this day of serving honey and leavened bread upon the table, and everything that may serve as a good omen, so that the year may be fruitful and favorable.

There are some who go to the Synagogue on the mornings of these two feasts dressed in white, to signify their penance and purity. There are even those among the High-German <note>Ashkenazi</note> Jews who then put on their burial shroud; and this in order to mortify their flesh. More prayers are said on this Feast than on others, for the sake of the good year that is desired and the reconciliation of sins. The Books of Moses are brought out, and five men read the offering that was performed on that day. They recite the <term>Haftarah<note>original: "AFTARA," a selection from the Prophets read after the Torah portion.</note></term> of the Prophets and bless the Sovereign Power.

<margin>The blowing of the horn and why this occurs.</margin>
Subsequently, they blow thirty times upon the Horn, of which some tones are very soft and others strong, *(f)* corresponding to what is said in *Leviticus* and *Numbers*: *A memorial of blowing of trumpets*, etc. They say that this is done to think of God’s judgment, and to make sinners tremble and bring them to conversion. They add to it the prayer called <term>Musaf<note>The "additional" service for Sabbaths and festivals.</note></term>, along with many others arranged for this day: to which the blowing of the Horn is again added, just as before. Having returned home and eaten, they spend the remainder of the day hearing sermons and practicing acts of piety. These two days are alike in everything, and in the evening when the Feast ends, they perform the <term>Havdalah<note>original: "HABDALA," the ceremony marking the end of a holy day.</note></term>, as has already been said of the other Feasts.

(d) The Scripture commands forty lashes, and the tradition inserted into the *Talmud* commands no more than thirty-nine. Paul in 2 Corinthians 11, verse 24, informs us that this tradition was the custom of his time.
(e) Rod or whip-lash. (f) Leviticus 23, verse 24. Numbers 29, verse 1.
</note>

## VI. CHAPTER.

### Concerning the Jews' CHIPUR, or the DAY OF ATONEMENT.

<margin>How the Jews conduct themselves on the Day of Atonement.</margin>
After these two feast days, people still rise before dawn to attend prayers and do penance until the tenth day of the same month <term>Tishrei<note>The first month of the Jewish civil year, occurring in September–October.</note></term>, which is the Fast of Atonement; and it is called (a) <term>Yom Kippur<note>Hebrew: "Day of Atonement," the most solemn day in the Jewish calendar, focused on repentance and reconciliation.</note></term>, commanded in *Leviticus* 23: *On the tenth day of this seventh month shall be the Day of Atonement*, etc. and during this day all work must be ceased, just as on the Sabbath; and everyone fasts, whoever they may be, without eating or drinking anything.

Formerly, the Jews were accustomed to a certain ceremony on the day before this feast, consisting of striking the head of a living rooster three times and saying each time, "May this be sacrificed for me." This ceremony was called (b) <term>Kapparah<note>Hebrew: "Atonement." A ritual where a person's sins are symbolically transferred to a rooster; though less common today, it was a major folk custom in the past.</note></term>; but it has been abolished in *Italy* and the *East*, since they came to recognize that this was a superstition based on a worthless thing.

<margin>And make a beginning of their fasting, to make themselves worthy and prepared for atonement.</margin>
On this day they eat more heartily, since the following day is a Fasting Day. Some go to bathe and give themselves thirty-nine lashes, called <term>Malkut<note>A symbolic lashing performed as a physical act of penance to stir the heart to repentance.</note></term>. Those who possess another's property, if they are conscientious, return it. One also requests forgiveness from those whom one has offended; and he who has been offended reconciles himself. Alms are distributed, and in general, everything is done that must accompany a sincere practice of penance.

Two or three hours before sunset, one goes to the afternoon prayer and subsequently holds the evening meal, finishing it before sunset. Then some dress themselves in white, putting on their burial clothes <note>Original: "doodkleeden." This refers to the *kittel*, a white linen robe that symbolizes purity and reminds the wearer of their mortality.</note>, and in this state they go barefoot to the Synagogue, which on this evening is illuminated, surrounded by burning lamps and wax candles. Each nation <note>Referring to the different regional Jewish traditions, such as the Sephardic or Ashkenazic customs.</note> performs many

<column-break/>

prayers and confessions to express their penance, which lasts at least three hours; after which one goes home to sleep. There are some who spend the entire night in the Synagogue, praying to God, reciting Psalms, and sleeping little or not at all.

The following day in the early morning, they return to the Synagogue, dressed as on the previous day, and remain there until nightfall, constantly praying, reading Psalms, making confessions, and beseeching God for forgiveness for their committed sins. This prayer is divided into four parts: that of the morning is called <term>Shacharit<note>The standard morning prayer service.</note></term>, and that which follows is (c) <term>Musaf<note>An "additional" prayer service recited on holidays and the Sabbath.</note></term>, in the afternoon, <term>Mincha<note>The afternoon prayer service.</note></term>, and in the evening, (d) <term>Neilah<note>Hebrew: "Closing." The final service of Yom Kippur, symbolizing the closing of the gates of heaven at the end of the day.</note></term>. At the first and third of these timed prayers, the *Pentateuch* or the Books of *Moses* are brought out, and six sections are read in the morning and three in the afternoon. To which the reading of the Prophets or <term>Haftarah<note>Selected readings from the biblical books of the Prophets that accompany the Torah reading.</note></term> is added.

At the *Musaf* one reads of the sacrifice, and one recounts the famous ceremony of the High Priest, who was permitted only on this day of the year to enter the Holy of Holies to offer incense and to cast lots over two goats, one of which was to be for God, and the other for (e) <term>Azazel<note>Commonly known as the "scapegoat." In this context, the author identifies it as the name of a mountain.</note></term>, as one reads in *Leviticus* sixteen.

When evening has come and one sees the stars, one blows on the same Horn <note>The Shofar, or ram's horn, used to signal the conclusion of the fast.</note> upon which one blew at the beginning of the year, to indicate that the Fast is ended. After which they leave the Synagogue, wishing each other a long life. They bless the new Moon, as we have said in the third Chapter, and having returned home, their Fast ends after having said the <term>Havdalah<note>A prayer ceremony that marks the transition from a holy day to the ordinary week.</note></term>, and they go to eat.

<meta>Catchword: VII. CHAPTER.</meta>

---

(a) Day of Atonement. (b) Atonement.
(c) This is a thanksgiving that is added to the morning prayers.
(d) Since this prayer concludes the evening prayer, just as in the Roman Church the Psalms and hymns that are sung after Vespers.
(e) This is the name of the mountain to which the Goat was sent, and the Mountain bore the name of this goat; for *Azazel* is a compound word, meaning a goat that departs.

Concerning the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

## VII. CHAPTER.
### Of the Jews' FEAST OF TABERNACLES.

<margin>Their Feast of Tabernacles, and why it was established.</margin>
On the fifteenth day of the month <term>Tishrei<note>The seventh month of the Hebrew calendar, occurring in September or October.</note></term> is the Feast of Tabernacles, which they call <term>Sukkot<note>Hebrew: "Booths." A week-long harvest festival.</note></term>, in memory of their encampment in the wilderness upon the Exodus from Egypt. Thus it is said in *Leviticus* 23 verse 42: *You shall dwell in booths for seven days, etc.* Everyone then constructs a booth in an open place, covered and enclosed all around with greenery, and decorated inside as best as one can.

<margin>In what manner these huts are made,</margin>
The Rabbis have exerted themselves no less over the form and quality of these huts than over their height and breadth. In these huts the Jews eat and drink, and some sleep in them: but at the very least, one spends the day in them, and at night it is customary to be indoors; and this is practiced for the duration of eight days.

This feast lasts nine days, seven of which are commanded; and one which is celebrated according to ancient custom, as on the Passover feast, of which we spoke in the third Chapter of this Treatise. There is also a day for the assembly, besides the seven days, commanded. (a) *On the eighth day you shall have the assembly, etc.* The first two and the last two days of this feast are celebrated solemnly: but the remaining days are not bound by this, as was said regarding their Passover feast.

Nothing unusual occurs in the prayers of this day, other than what has already been said regarding the subject of the feast. They read the Psalms from the 113th to the 119th, called <term>Hallel<note>Hebrew: "Praise." A sequence of Psalms used as a prayer of thanksgiving.</note></term>. They bring out the Books of Moses and read from them. They read the <term>Haftarah<note>original: "AFTARA." A selection from the biblical Books of the Prophets read after the Torah.</note></term>, and they speak the blessing over the <note>original: "Oppermogentheid." A prayer for the welfare of the sovereign or the state.</note>Sovereignty. Subsequently, they pray the <term>Musaf<note>Hebrew: "Additional." An extra service recited on festivals.</note></term> prayer, or they repeat the memory of the offerings made on this day, as it stands written in *Numbers* 29 verse 13; on the first day thirteen Bulls; the second twelve, the third eleven, thus decreasing daily, totaling seventy Bulls over seven days; and on the eighth day a single Bull.

<margin>and with what they</margin>
They provide themselves for this day with

<column-break/>

<margin>provide themselves to celebrate this feast solemnly.</margin>
a palm branch, three myrtle branches, two willow branches, and (b) a citron branch bound together: and when the <term>Hallel</term> Psalms have been read in the Synagogue, they take in their right hand all these bound branches, except for the citron branch which they hold in the left hand, and approaching one another, they turn and face toward the four quarters of the World, as is said in *Leviticus* 23: *And on the first day you shall take branches of beautiful trees, Palm branches and boughs of leafy trees, with Willows of the brook, and singing certain hymns of praise*, they make a circuit once a day around the small Altar <note>The Bimah or reading platform.</note> which is in the Synagogue, holding these branches in their hand, as well as the citron branches with the fruit; since formerly the same ceremony was performed in the Temple around the Altar.

The seventh day of the Feast, which they call (c) <term>Hoshana Rabbah<note>Hebrew: "The Great Supplication."</note></term>, they use only the willow branch of these branches and make seven circuits, singing the 29th Psalm: *Give unto the Lord, O you sons of the Mighty, etc.* and this day is the most solemn of the Feast, and more so than other Feast days.

The ninth (d) and last day is called <term>Simchat Torah<note>Hebrew: "Rejoicing of the Torah."</note></term>, or joy because of the Law, since they have finished the reading of the Books of Moses, corresponding to the division that has been made for each week, as we have already said here before.

<margin>Bridegroom of the Law chosen.</margin>
And when the year has ended, they choose in every Synagogue two men, whom they call *Bridegrooms of the Law*; of whom one, called (e) <term>Chatan Torah<note>Hebrew: "Bridegroom of the Torah."</note></term>, reads the end, and the other, whom they call (f) <term>Chatan Bereshit<note>Hebrew: "Bridegroom of Genesis."</note></term>, shortly thereafter begins again. Which they accompany with certain signs of joy. The same is observed in all Synagogues, and they spend the remainder of the day in joyful activity.
