## CHAPTER VIII.

->Concerning the Jews' VOLUNTARY AND COMMANDED FASTS.<-

<margin>
Which voluntary and commanded fasts the Jews observe, which are of many kinds.
</margin>

**O**n the seventeenth of <term>Tammuz<note>The fourth month of the Hebrew calendar, falling in June or July.</note></term>, which corresponds to the month of July, the Jews observe a fast day in memory of several misfortunes that occurred on that day in Jerusalem in ancient times; and because it was on that day that Moses, due to the idolatry committed with the Golden Calf, broke the first Tables of the Law.

All fast days, whether they are commanded or voluntary, begin in the evening: and one neither eats nor drinks anything until the following evening, when the stars appear.

In the morning, they add confessions to the prayers and repeat the sorrowful events that occurred on such a day. They bring out the Books of *Moses* and read from *Exodus 32 verse 11*: *And Moses pleaded*, etc. and in the afternoon, during the <term>Mincha<note>The afternoon prayer service.</note></term> prayer, they read in the same manner, and for the <term>Haftarah<note>A series of selections from the books of the Prophets read publicly in the synagogue.</note></term>, they read what *Isaiah 55 verse 6* says: *Seek the Lord while he may be found*, etc.

Some abstain from eating meat and drinking wine from the 17th of *Tammuz* until the 9th of <term>Av<note>The fifth month of the Hebrew calendar, occurring in July or August.</note></term> (which makes three weeks): though this is voluntary; and this is done only because these days were unfortunate for *Israel*.

The 9th of *Av* is a fast day called <term>Tisha B'Av<note>Literally "the Ninth of Av," the primary day of mourning in Judaism.</note></term>. This fast is greater than the others. For it was on that day that Nebuchadnezzar burned the Temple, and on the same day it was later burned by the Emperor Titus. This fast begins the day before, about an hour before sunset, from which time one no longer eats or drinks until the stars are seen the following evening. They spend this time barefoot, or without leather shoes, and without being allowed to wash.

In the evening, after the usual prayer in the Synagogue is finished, they sit upon the ground and read the Lamentations of *Jeremiah*. They do the same the following day, adding many other lamentations, and spend the day in sorrow, as it is forbidden for them to read the Law: but only in *Job*, *Jeremiah*, and other books of mourning.

The Sabbath that follows this fast day is called <term>Nechama<note>Hebrew for "Consolation."</note></term>, or comfort. For reading these words of *Isaiah* for the *Haftarah*, <note>original footnote (c): Chapter 40.</note> *Comfort, comfort my people*, they console themselves with the hope of the restoration of Jerusalem and the Temple.

On the thirteenth <note>This likely refers to the 3rd of Tishrei; the "13th" in the Dutch text is likely a printing error or a reference to a specific local custom, as the Fast of Gedaliah traditionally occurs on the 3rd.</note> of <term>Tishrei<note>The seventh month of the Hebrew calendar.</note></term>, being the first day after the Feast of the New Year, they usually fast from one evening to the next, because on such a day <term>Gedaliah<note>A righteous governor of Judah assassinated after the destruction of the First Temple.</note></term> the son of *Ahikam* was killed, <note>original footnote (d): Jeremiah 41.</note> being a man of extraordinary piety, and who remained alone to defend the remnant of *Israel*. As this day was established as a day of repentance, the opportunity was taken to remember the memory of this righteous man; and this fast was therefore called <term>Tzom Gedaliah<note>Hebrew: "The Fast of Gedaliah."</note></term>.

After this follows the fast of <term>Kippur<note>Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement.</note></term>, or of reconciliation, of which we have spoken before <note>original footnote (f): Chapter 6 in this Treatise.</note> and that it was celebrated on the 10th of *Tishrei*.

They also commonly fast on the 10th of <term>Tevet<note>The tenth month of the Hebrew calendar, occurring in December or January.</note></term>, which corresponds to December, because Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem on that day, and subsequently captured it.

On the 13th of <term>Adar<note>The twelfth month of the Hebrew calendar, occurring in February or March.</note></term> they fast, which is our month of March, and they call this fast <term>Purim<note>Refers here to the Fast of Esther, which precedes the holiday of Purim ("The Festival of Lots").</note></term>. This is done in memory of *Esther*, who fasted in former times, as one reads in her history.

Besides these commanded fast days, there are others in use by some: such as the <term>German Jews<note>The Ashkenazi Jewish community.</note></term>, who, after the Feast of Passover and of Tabernacles, have the custom of fasting for three days, namely, the two following Mondays, and the Thursday that comes between them: and this is based on the fact that the preceding feasts—

# CHAPTER IX.

### *Of the Festival of (b) HANUKKAH, or of LIGHTS, and of PURIM.*

---

<margin>How the Jews celebrate their Festival of Dedication, and why.</margin>
The Scholars of former times instituted a Festival of eight days, which begins on the 25th of <term>Kislev<note>The ninth month of the Hebrew calendar, usually coinciding with December.</note></term>, corresponding with December, and this in memory of the victory achieved by the Maccabees over the Greeks. On the first day, one lights a lamp, two on the second, and so continuing until one has lit eight. This is based on the fact that the enemies had already entered the City and Temple; and having profaned it, they drove out and killed <term>Johanan<note>Referring to the Hasmonean leaders, specifically John Hyrcanus or Mattathias's lineage.</note></term> and his sons. And as they found no pure oil upon their return to light the lamps of the <term>menorah<note>The multi-branched candelabra used in the ancient Temple.</note></term>, but found only a little in a small jar, enough to burn for one night, it burned for eight days through a miracle. Which is why these lamps are lit in memory of this. In this Festival, one also celebrates the undertaking of Judith against Holofernes, although some believe this was not carried out at that time of the year.

During these eight days, one may trade and work: for the most important part consists in the order of lighting these lamps, and since a Song of Praise concerning the victory is added to the prayers, and every morning the 113th Psalm, and subsequently those which are called <term>Hallel<note>original: "HALLEL." A series of Psalms (113–118) recited as a prayer of thanksgiving and praise.</note></term>, along with the 30th, *I will extol thee, O Lord*, etc. There is also a slight difference in what is eaten.

It is called <term>HANUKKAH<note>original: "HANUCA."</note></term>, a word that signifies *training* or *renewal*, since the Temple service, which had been profaned, was renewed.

<margin>As also the Festival</margin>
On the 14th of <term>Adar<note>The twelfth month of the Hebrew calendar, usually coinciding with March or February.</note></term>, or March, (c)

<column-break/>

<margin>of Purim in memory of Esther.</margin>
is the Festival of *Purim*, which is celebrated in memory of *Esther*, who on that day prevented the people of Israel from being entirely rooted out by the conspiracy of Haman, who was therefore condemned to the gallows with all his sons. The name PURIM is given to this Festival, as one reads in the 9th Chapter of *Esther*: *therefore these days shall be called* PURIM, etc. <note>Purim refers to the "lots" cast by Haman to determine the date of the Jews' destruction.</note>

This Festival lasts two days; however, the first day is celebrated solemnly. One fasts the day before, as has been said; but during these two days, one may trade and work. Nevertheless, this does not happen on the first day, though one is not bound to refrain.

<margin>What is then performed in the Synagogue.</margin>
On the first day, one goes to the Synagogue, and after the usual prayers, the memory of this happy deliverance from the hour of death is repeated. And all the Books of *Esther* are read, which are written on parchment and rolled like the Books of Moses. They also call it <term>Megillah<note>original: "MEGHILLA." A Hebrew word meaning scroll.</note></term> or volume. While hearing the name of Haman pronounced during the reading, one strikes their hands to signify his curse. They do the same in the morning prayers. On this day, one reads in the Books of Moses, *Exodus* 17 verse 8: *Then came Amalek*, etc.

<margin>How people send each other gifts and practice mutual joy.</margin>
On this day, great alms are given. Friends and relatives send each other gifts that are edible. Students give them to their Masters, the Head of the Household to his household members, and the great to the small.

## CHAPTER I.
->*The interaction of Jews with* WOMEN *forbidden; their* MARRIAGES, BETROTHAL *and* WEDDING CELEBRATIONS.<-

<margin>How adultery and other unlawful cohabitation of the Jews are strictly forbidden.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'V' decorated with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>Of all the crimes that one might commit with women, the Jews know none greater than sleeping with a married woman, even if she were only betrothed <note>The Dutch "ondertrouwt" refers to the formal engagement or "erusin" period, which in Jewish law carries significant legal weight similar to marriage.</note>. And following this in magnitude is when one has to do with one's own blood relative, according to the prohibitions in *Leviticus* 20. Thus, the children born from such a union are called **Mamzerim**, or Bastards <term>Mamzerim<note>A Hebrew term referring to children born from forbidden relationships, such as incest or adultery, who face specific restrictions in Jewish law regarding whom they may marry.</note></term>, and they cannot be legitimized. (a) *No Bastard shall enter the Congregation of the Lord*. The third rank of these crimes is to have dealings with a woman who is not Jewish (this being based on the prohibition of *Esdras* <note>Esdras is the Latin form of the name Ezra; this refers to the biblical prohibition against intermarriage found in the Book of Ezra.</note>); or with a Jewish woman who acts as a harlot; since neither the Law nor reason allows them to openly tolerate this, as is said in the 17th verse of the same chapter: *There shall be no dishonest Daughter among the Daughters of Israel*, etc.

It is also a sin to have to do with any woman, whoever she may be, even if one were free of all these specific restrictions; for one may know no one but his own wife, since to seduce a maiden and not marry her is considered fornication.

<column-break/>

They are likewise forbidden from having intercourse with a woman who has her monthly period, *Leviticus* 18. Also, *you shall not approach her to uncover her nakedness during her period of uncleanness*, etc., and this applies to his own wife as well as to another, as will be shown hereafter.

<margin>Why the Jews are obliged to marry.</margin>
All Jews are required to marry. The Rabbis have decided that this may occur at eighteen years of age; that those who reach more than twenty years without taking a wife are judged to be living in sin; and this is based on the obligation to procreate children to fulfill God's command given to the first man: (b) *Increase and multiply*, etc. But if one has a son and a daughter, the command is fulfilled. Because by remaining unmarried, one can more easily fall into fornication; therefore, they do not consider it good to live unmarried.

According to what is found in many places in Scripture, it is permitted for the Jews to have many wives. This is in use among them in the East: but among the High Germans <note>The Dutch "Hoogduitsche" refers to Ashkenazi Jews from Central and Eastern Europe.</note> and in the Netherlands, it is not tolerated, except only very rarely in Italy, and only when one, after being married for several years, ha— <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

HISTORICAL TREATISE

# III. CHAPTER.
## Concerning Jewish JEALOUSY and DIVORCE.

<margin>What is to be noted regarding the Jealousy of the Jews.</margin>
In former times, a jealous husband brought his wife before the High Priest, who gave her a certain water to drink, from which she would swell <note>The original Dutch "borst" implies bursting or swelling; this refers to the biblical "Sotah" ritual.</note> if she were guilty; but if she were innocent, she suffered no harm, as is expressed in *Numbers 5*. But now a jealous man is satisfied with forbidding his wife from seeing whatever is offensive to him. However, if it becomes public that she is misbehaving, if strong evidence arises against her, or if he catches her in the act of infidelity, then he is compelled by the Rabbis to divorce his wife. Subsequently, we shall deal with Divorce. Nevertheless, this woman who is divorced from the marriage is permitted to marry whomever she pleases, except for the one who gave cause for the divorce.

Even if a woman should give no reason for complaint about her behavior, the man can still cast her off (a) because she is somewhat distasteful to him. *Deuteronomy 24: When a man shall have taken a wife, and having married her, she shall not please him*, etc. However, if jealousy reached the point of accusing his wife of some offense, one ought not to abandon her. To prevent this privilege from being abused, the Rabbis have established many types of legal procedures that require much time; so that, as often happens, before the drawing up and writing of the Bill of Divorce, one feels regret or reaches a mutual agreement, and the spouses are subsequently seen reunited.

<margin>How he can give his wife a Bill of Divorce.</margin>
The prescribed rules for these Bills of Divorce, which they call (b) <term>Get<note>original: "GHETT"; the formal document required by Jewish law to effect a divorce.</note></term>, and give to the wife, are drawn up by a scribe in the presence of one or more learned Rabbis; and must be written on lined parchment, and extend no more nor less than twelve lines, set in square let-

<column-break/>

ters, accompanied by many minor meticulous details <note>original: "vitteryen"; implying small, precise requirements or scrupulous points of law.</note>, both regarding the letters and the manner of writing, as well as the name and surname of the husband and wife. Furthermore, the Scribe, the Rabbis, and the Witnesses may not be related to the husband, the wife, or to each other: the substance of such a Letter or **GET** consists of these words:

<margin>Contents of the Bill of Divorce.</margin>
> On such a day, month, year, and place, etc: I leave you voluntarily, separate myself from you, and set you free, just as before you were my wife, and permit you to marry whomever you please, etc.

Once the Bill of Divorce is written, the Rabbi examines the man with fine skill to know if what he is undertaking is done voluntarily. Effort is made to have at least ten persons present at this transaction, besides the two witnesses who sign and two other witnesses to the dating.

<margin>How it is delivered to the woman.</margin>
After which the Rabbi commands the woman to open her hands, and for each to approach the other, so that the Bill of Divorce does not fall on the floor; and having questioned everything anew, the man gives her this parchment and says: *Look here, take your divorce. I separate myself from you, and leave you at liberty to marry whom you wish.* The woman receives it and gives it to the Rabbi, who reads it once more, after which she has her freedom. There are many more small circumstances which we pass over so as not to bore the Reader, and which were invented solely to make divorce more difficult.

The Rabbi then commands the woman not to remarry until after three months (c) have passed, so that it may be known if she is pregnant. Upon departing, the husband and wife may no longer stay together alone; and then each may remarry.

# IV. CHAPTER.

### Concerning the Jews' <term>Yibbum|Levirate marriage</term> and their <term>Halizah|The ceremony of the shoe</term>.

<margin>How a widow without children is subject to her deceased husband’s Brother.</margin>
When a man dies without leaving children, whether they were by his wife or another, if he leaves a brother, his widow is in the power of this brother; he may marry her or give her the freedom to marry another, *as is said in Deuteronomy 25: If brothers dwell together, and one of them dies without children, the widow shall not be given to a stranger, but to her husband’s brother.* <note>This practice is known as Levirate marriage, intended to preserve the deceased man's lineage and estate.</note> But if the deceased leaves many wives, his Brother has this power over only one of them; and if the deceased has more than one Brother, the eldest has the privilege therein: but to grant the widow her freedom, one alone has the authority to do so.

This taking of a Brother’s Widow is called <term>Yibbum|Hebrew: Yibbum</term>: for this word signifies *to marry one's sister-in-law*; so that to marry her it is enough that he desires her: but the Rabbis have commanded that such marriages should take place under the usual ceremonies like others. Since all the deceased's goods belong to him, he even takes possession of the marriage dowry that the Woman brought to the deceased, and in a word, she becomes his own wife.

In former times, the one who married his Brother’s Widow was praised much more than the one who set her free: but now that men are more covetous and driven by desire, they prefer beauty and the enjoyment of property over this duty; and there are few who fulfill it, especially among the German <note>Original: "Hoogduitfche," referring to Ashkenazi Jews.</note> and Italian Jews: instead, they set her free.

<margin>But upon refusal he must let himself be unshod by her, and with what ceremony this occurs.</margin>
This kind of freedom they call <term>Halizah|Hebrew: Chalizah</term>, or *removing the shoe*, as is expressed in *Deuteronomy* 25: *But if this man does not wish to take his Brother’s Wife, then his Brother’s Wife shall go up to the Gates before the eyes of the Elders and come unto him, and pull his shoe from his foot, and spit in his face*, and this is performed in this manner: Three Rabbis and two other witnesses choose a place the day before where this ceremony shall be held. The next day, after the conclusion of the morning prayers, everyone follows 

<column-break/>

the Rabbis and witnesses, who, having been seated, cause the Widow and her Brother-in-law to appear before them, who then declare that they are inclined toward their freedom. The presiding Rabbi puts many questions to the man and exhorts him to marry the Widow; yet seeing that he persists in his refusal, after some further questioning, the man receives and puts on a suitable shoe provided by the Rabbis that fits his feet, while the Woman approaches him, and helped by the Rabbi, she says in Hebrew the 7th verse of the mentioned Chapter: *My husband's Brother refuses to raise up the lineage of his Brother in Israel, and refuses to marry me as my brother-in-law, etc.* <note>Original Hebrew: "Ma-en yabami..." translated here into English from the Dutch transcription.</note> which she explains to him. Whereupon the Brother-in-law answers her with the following verse: *I do not wish to take her.* Then the woman stoops down, unbinds and pulls off his shoe, which she throws to the ground, and spits before him, saying with the help of the Rabbi in Hebrew: *So shall it be done unto that man who will not build up his Brother's house, and his name shall be called in Israel, the house of the barefoot.* Thrice she says these words, and the bystanders answer her each time, *the unshod one.*

<margin>And then the woman is released from the marriage bond.</margin>
As soon as the Rabbi tells her that she may marry again, and she requests a document regarding this matter from the Rabbis, it is granted to her. All further circumstances observed on this occasion arise entirely from *Deuteronomy* 25, when one pays close attention to it.

But since in the case of this <term>Yibbum</term> the woman cannot obtain her marriage property, nor may she marry again without this release, there are men who, in order to possess their Sisters-in-law's money, keep this matter dragging on and postpone it indefinitely. Therefore, there are those who, when marrying off their daughter to a man who has Brothers, stipulate that in the event of "unshoeing," they are not obliged to pay anything for the widow to be released. Others obligate the husband, if he becomes ill and the Physician judges there is danger of death, to divorce his wife, so that she might not fall under the power of her Brother-in-law. <note>This refers to a conditional divorce intended to bypass the need for a Halizah ceremony if the husband died childless.</note>

# V. CHAPTER.

->Concerning the CIRCUMCISION of the Jews.<-

<margin>
Ceremonies of the Jews' circumcision and of what nature they are.
</margin>
When a son is born to someone, his friends say, in order to share in his joy: *at a good hour* <note>original: "ter goeder uure"; a traditional congratulation similar to the modern Hebrew "Mazel Tov."</note>. Some have the custom of placing small slips of paper in the four corners of the nursery, with this content: *that Adam and Eve be here: but (a) Lilith stay outside*, alongside the names of three Angels, under the pretext of protecting the child from all sorcery: however, one is not obliged to do this; for it has less the appearance of a command than of superstition.

The Father of the child is required to have his son circumcised on the eighth day, (b) as is said: *at the age of eight days you shall circumcise all that is male*. Which is repeated in *Leviticus 12*; *And on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised*. This may not be done before the eighth day: but, if the child is sick or too weak, it can be postponed until a better opportunity.

The night before the day of circumcision is called the *night-watch* <note>Dutch: "nachtwaak"; a vigil kept to guard the infant.</note>, because no one in the house goes to sleep, in order to tend to the child. In the evening, friends come to visit the Father, and likewise the women visit the mother; which time is spent with joy.

The Godfather has already been chosen to hold the child during the circumcision, and the Godmother to bring him to the Synagogue; and for this, one commonly takes a man and woman from the friends of the Father and Mother. As for the <term>Mohel|Dutch: MOLEL; the ritual circumciser</term>, or the man who performs the circumcision, one chooses whomever they wish, provided he is worthy and capable of performing this service. The title of <term>Mohel|Besnyder</term> is of no small value among the Jews; and if the Father of the child understands this service, he may circumcise his own child.

In the morning, in the Synagogue, or else in the house where one wishes to complete the ceremony, two chairs with silk cushions are placed; one for the Godfather who holds the child and the other, according to the saying of some, for

<column-break/>

the Prophet Elijah, whom they believe invisibly attends all circumcisions: as much out of affection as to see the Law observed. When many people have then gathered, the Circumciser comes with a dish upon which lie the necessary things and tools, such as the knife, the astringent powders, the linen, lint, and rose oil. To this he also adds a bowl of sand, in order to place the severed foreskin therein. Some hymns are then sung while awaiting the Godmother, who carries the child in her arms, accompanied by a retinue of women, though none of them enter through the door of the Synagogue. There she gives the child to the Godfather, upon which all those present cry out: **BARUCH ABA**, *the Father is welcome* <note>original Hebrew: "Baruch Habah," which literally translates to "Blessed is he who comes."</note>.

The Godfather being seated on his chair and taking the child on his lap; the Circumciser then unwinds the swaddling clothes. There are those who make use of a small silver pair of tongs to grasp the foreskin that they wish to cut off. The Circumciser then takes the small knife and says: *Blessed art Thou, Lord, who has commanded us circumcision*. And saying this, he cuts off the thick skin of the foreskin: subsequently, he tears another thinner skin with the nails of his fingers <note>This second step is known as "periah," intended to ensure the full exposure of the glans.</note>. Meanwhile, the Father praises and thanks God for this commandment, and the bystanders wish him well in raising his child until the years of marriage. The Circumciser continues his work and sucks the seeping blood two or three times, and puts it into a bowl of wine <note>This practice is known as "metzitzah."</note>. Afterward, he places dragon’s blood <note>A bright red resin from the Dracaena tree, historically used as a medicine and coagulant.</note>, coral powder, and other blood-stanching remedies upon the incision. To which he adds cloths moistened with rose oil, and swaddles everything well again.

After this performance, he takes a bowl of wine; and after having blessed it, he speaks a blessing over the child, giving it the name according to the Father's desire, with the speaking of the words from *Ezekiel 16: And I said, live in your blood*, etc. while he moistens the lips with the wine in which he has placed the drawn blood. Subsequently, one says the—

One imagines her to be a night-specter, who is the enemy of women in labor and newborn children; and this is what the Latins call *Striges Lamia* <note>original: "Striges Lamia"; refers to screech-owls or mythical child-devouring demons in Roman folklore.</note>.

<margin>When the circumcised child is healed again.</margin>
Usually, the child is healed within twenty-four hours of the circumcision. For this reason, some are accustomed to send sweets and preserves to friends and kinsmen after three days have passed, to rejoice with them over the recovery.

<margin>How one deals with a newborn daughter.</margin>
When a daughter is born, no ceremony is performed: except at the beginning of the Month after the Mother has left her childbed, when the child is brought to the Synagogue; and the Cantor <note>original: "Zanger"; the ritual leader who chants the liturgy.</note> pronounces a blessing over the little daughter, giving her a name according to the Father's wishes. Among the High Germans <note>The Ashkenazi Jewish community.</note>, the Cantor goes to the house, takes the child from the cradle, blesses it, and gives it a name. If a child dies within the eight days before circumcision, there are those who circumcise it with a reed before it is buried.

In the morning, the Father of the child treats the Circumciser <note>The Mohel.</note>, the Godfather, and the Godmother, along with his friends and kinsmen, as best he can. After the meal is finished, blessings and prayers for the child are added, to obtain from the Lord that it may grow up in prosperity and the fear of God.

## VI. CHAPTER.

->Concerning the REDEMPTION OF THE FIRSTBORN, the upbringing and INSTRUCTION OF CHILDREN, and the RESPECT one owes to one's BLOOD RELATIONS and others.<-

<margin>Solemn circumstances of the redemption of the firstborn, and what they consist of.</margin>
If the first child to whom the Mother gives birth is a son, he belongs to the Priest <note>A Kohen, a descendant of the biblical Aaron.</note>, even if the Father has had a child by another woman, as we have already stated (a); and this is according to the commandment which contains: (b) *Sanctify unto me all the firstborn.* And further, *All the firstborn of thy children shalt thou redeem*, etc.

See how this is carried out. When the child has reached thirty days of age, one summons from the descendants of Aaron the one to whom the father is most well-disposed. When several friends have come to his house, the father brings some gold and silver in a drinking bowl or a washbasin, and the child is placed in the arms of the Priest, who says aloud to the mother: *Is this your young son?* to which she answers yes. *Have you*, he continues, *never had any other child, whether male or female, or any miscarriage or premature birth?* to which the answer *no* is given. *This being so*, the Priest adds, *this child belongs to me as the firstborn.* Then he turns to the Father and says: *If you desire it, you must redeem him.* To which the Father responds: *This gold and silver* (c), *is offered to you for that purpose.* *So you wish to redeem him then?* the Priest asks again. *Yes, I do*, the Father answers. *Well*, says the Priest aloud, turning to the bystanders, *this child as firstborn belongs to me, as is said in Numbers 18 verse 16; and those that are to be redeemed from a month old shalt thou redeem, for the money of five Shekels, etc.* but I satisfy myself with this in *exchange:* and having finished these words, he takes approximately as much gold as he desires, more or less, and then gives the child to the father and mother. After which this day is ended with joy. But if the father or mother are of the tribe of the Levites, this redemption of the firstborn is not necessary.

<margin>How the Jews have their children instructed.</margin>
As soon as a child can speak, he is taught to read, and subsequently to translate and explain the Bible into the local language, without instruction in the principles and knowledge of grammar, which they call <term>DIKDUK|Dutch: DICHDUCH; the Hebrew term for grammar</term>: but having reached about ten years of age, he learns the grammar or art of letters if he has the inclination for it. This is in use among very few Jews, for most of them speak, read,

<margin>And what kind of education is given to the youths.</margin>
Next, the youths are made to read certain interpreters of the Bible; such as (a) Rabbi Solomon <note>original: "Rabi Salomon"; referring to Rashi (1040–1105), the most famous medieval Jewish commentator.</note>, and some concise works on temple duties and the customs of the Rabbis, such as (b) our Teacher Moses <note>original: "Rabenu Mosé"; referring to Maimonides.</note> and others. Those youths who possess a good intellect proceed immediately to the *Mishnah* <note>original: "Misnah"; the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions.</note> and to the subject matter contained in the Talmud, which they consider the best foundation for their learning: but there are others who apply themselves to more sciences, as we have said in the second Section, second Chapter.

<margin>When a youth becomes of age, and a daughter becomes marriageable.</margin>
When a youth has reached thirteen years and one day, he is considered of age <note>Literally, "manly" or "of age."</note> and is then obliged to follow the commands of the Law. For this reason, he is then called BAR MITZVAH <note>original: "BARMIZVA"; Hebrew for "Son of the Commandment," marking the transition to religious adulthood.</note>, although others say MINIAN (d). Since this age is declared to be that of majority, he may then act and make decisions on his own, because he is no longer under his guardians, if he has any; for he may perform everything that pleases him, both in temporal as

<column-break/>

well as in spiritual matters. As for daughters, at the age of twelve years and six months, the status of women is attributed to them.

<margin>What duty children owe to their parents.</margin>
Among the Jews, children consider themselves highly obligated to honor father and mother. *Honor thy father and mother* is said in the Ten Commandments; which the Rabbis have explained at length, regarding what is owed in this life and after death.

They also teach how a father should live with his son, especially when he has reached his years of maturity, so as not to give him any reason to fail in the respect due to his father.

Furthermore, they draw this conclusion from this commandment: that one must honor one's elder brother and mother-in-law. They even believe that more respect is due to him who instructs them in Religion <note>A teacher or Rabbi.</note> than to him who was the cause of their life. For the latter gave only being, but the former gave well-being. They also desire that one honors the wise and godly in word and deed, (e) as well as the aged, even if they are not Jews: since, as the Rabbis say, they are the ancient citizens of the world, who having lived through many events, possess more experience: (f) *In the very old is wisdom and power: and in length of days is understanding.* <note>Job 12:12.</note>

opinion are *Rabbanites*, or *Followers of the Sages*. These in turn hate the *Karaites* deathly, and will by no means unite with them or have any fellowship. ### INTERLUDE concerning the beliefs of the KARAITES.

<margin>An investigation into how obscure the origins of Karaism are.</margin>
The time when *Karaism* first arose is difficult enough to point out accurately. Jean Morin <note>original: "P. Morinus"; a 17th-century French Oratorian priest and biblical scholar</note>, who treated this dispute, traces the beginning of this sect to the eighth century \*, immediately after the spread of the Talmud, and believes that this great work was brought to light much later than the Jews imagine. Truly, the birth of *Karaism* did stem from the spread of the *Talmud*: for one does not see that the name *Karaite* was hateful among the Jews before that time, as it has been since. On the contrary, by the word *Carai* one then understood a man perfect in the knowledge of Holy Scripture. The origin of this sect, then, comes from the more enlightened Jews of that century, who opposed many of the fables that were being peddled as the oral traditions of *Moses*, although most had no foundation other than the ambition of their scholars, who wanted their private pronouncements to pass for Oracles spoken on Mount Sinai. Since these Jews did not want to accept these imagined traditions, they made use of what they call *Micra* <note>The Hebrew Bible, or "that which is read"</note> to cast doubt on them, for which reason they received the surname *Karaites*, just as has been seen in our days with the *Protestants* who call themselves *Evangelical* †, because they believe that one must rely on nothing but the Gospel, rejecting all traditions.

<column-break/>

<margin>And how this sect has been viewed as Samaritans.</margin>
The Jews who hold with the *Talmud* regard them as *Samaritans* and *Sadducees*; not that they truly were so, but because they followed such traditions as those groups with which they did not wish to agree. Nevertheless, in the course of time, there were Jews who believed that a *Karaite* was a true *Samaritan* and *Sadducee*. And what strengthened them in this error is that they [the Karaites] only rarely applied themselves to the study of history and chronology. The Author of this Treatise, knowing that the *Karaites* are by no means of the faith of the Samaritans, has, to reconcile this contradiction, introduced a "new sect" of *Karaites*, as if the first ones were merely *Samaritans* and *Sadducees*, and that these current ones had changed their opinion, or at least softened it. But the judgment of our Rabbi is unfounded, as has been shown, and based on the ignorance of the Jews; for the reasons he brings forward to make his opinion acceptable are not capable of being defended.

<margin>Errors regarding the opinions of scholars pointed out, and especially that of Morin.</margin>
Our critics, who have wished to speak of the *Karaites* regarding the faith of the Jewish Books, have fallen into a great error; since the *Rabbanites*, who are their enemies, blame them for almost everything. Jean Morin behaves in the same way, since he possessed a commentary on the Books of *Moses* written by a *Karaite*. And as we have this manuscript in hand, we wish to describe what properly concerns this *Karaism*, and show in what ways the *Karaites* differ from the Jewish Rabbanites or Scholars. We shall begin with the belief they have regarding the Biblical texts, since our Author confuses them with the Samaritans, who accept nothing but the Books of Moses, and we still find many Scholars who believe that the *Karaites* differ very much from the other Jews regarding the Biblical text. Also, we do not know whether a Doctor of the Sorbonne, and Royal Professor of the Hebrew language, well understood what he recently wrote on this subject regarding the *Karaites*. He explains the word

---

\* [It was around the eighth century that this Jewish sect was given the name *Karaites*, to distinguish them from the Rabbanites or Rabbinists; namely, those who shortly thereafter introduced the Rabbis' *Talmud* and attached it to the Biblical books: which traditions, signed by the Rabbis, they refused to accept. The word *Carai* means a man perfect in the knowledge of Holy Scripture; for which reason those who founded their faith on the Bible were called *Karaites*. Some have called them purified Jews, since they professed to maintain their religion unadulterated. Of this Jewish sect, some are found in Constantinople, Cairo, and other places in the East, even in Muscovy, where they have their own synagogues and call themselves the only true maintainers of the Law of Moses, as they likely are. Richard Simon: *Supplement to the Ceremonies of the Jews.* Jovet: *History of Religions.*]

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the Karaite sect, specifically refuting common misconceptions about their rejection of Hebrew vowel points and clarifying their relationship to traditional Jewish scholarship and the Masoretic text.</meta>

# On the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

...word *Caraïm* or *Karaites* <note>From the Hebrew *Qara'im*, meaning "Scripturalists" or "Readers"</note> thus: those who insist that there should be nothing in the Bibles but consonants, and no Points <note>original: "Punten"; referring to the *Nequdot*, or Hebrew vowel marks</note>, because they believe the points are nothing but tradition. And furthermore he adds: *that the Karaites have imperceptibly gained the upper hand among the Jews, mainly among the Talmudists and Allegorists, and that it was thus more easily believed that the Books of the Law, in which the points and dots were found, were unauthentic.* Scarcely a true word is found in the reasoning of the learned Professor, as we shall see in what follows.

<margin>What the Author says regarding the expansion of the Karaites.</margin>
The Author of the *Expansion of the Karaites* of whom we have spoken, carries the name of *Aaron*, son of *Joseph* <note>Aaron ben Joseph the Elder (c. 1260–1320), a famous Karaite physician and philosopher in Constantinople</note>, who lived at the end of the thirteenth Century. He approves of all the Biblical books included in the Jewish canon, and gives them the name of the "twenty-four," just as the other Jews do. To distinguish these from human traditions, he calls some of them "Prophetic," wishing not to equate the word of God with that of men. On this account he rejects the Rabbanites, who wish to pair the fictions of the *Talmud* and the dreams of their ancestors with the sacred Books of the Holy Scripture. He also shows that the *Karaites* do not, as is often said, reject all types of tradition: but only the false and absurd ones, of which he gives some examples in the introduction to his work, where he ridicules the Rabbanites. He cites the "beautiful" explanation that these scholars give for the Serpent mentioned in the beginning of *Genesis*. For the Rabbanites and Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystics</note> say: *that it was as large as a camel, that Samael (a) was higher, and that God himself sat upon the camel and mocked him.* He also reports how the Allegorical and Kabbalistic interpreters among these scholars explain this, whom he vigorously refutes, adding these words: *in this sort of explanation and others like it, they ground themselves on nothing but the authority of their Fathers.* Subsequently, having grown weary of those who thus twist the Word of God, he says: *Unhappy is he who has the impudence to express himself in this way.*

<column-break/>

<margin>and how he makes a distinction between true and false traditions.</margin>
To show that they approve of reasonable and well-founded traditions, he distinguishes certain and constant traditions from those that are false and doubtful; and it seems that the criteria he points out to validate a tradition are the same as those described by *Vincent of Lérins* <note>original: "Vincentius Lerinus"; a 5th-century monk who argued that true Christian doctrine is that which has been believed "everywhere, always, and by all"</note>. He professes not only to accept the Holy Scripture: but furthermore agrees with reason and tradition that has always been constant and not newly invented. He adheres to the Teachings of the Ancestors, insofar as they do not vary and agree with the authentic Scriptures, not being invented out of the stubbornness or instability of the human brain, which the Jews are otherwise accustomed to approving. It is according to this principle that they accept all the Biblical scriptures just as the Rabbanites do; and what is even more wonderful, they accept them with the points <note>vowel marks</note> exactly as they are accepted today: for they have no other copy than that of the *Masoretes*. Thus, if they sometimes read differently, this happens only in the capacity of critical judgment, in which they follow the Rabbis *Judah, Jonas, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi, Abenmelek* and other linguistic and grammatical Rabbanites.

<margin>His remark regarding linguistics.</margin>
Our *Karaite*, who with much attention searches for the literal sense of the text, sometimes cites various readings in order to subsequently choose the most prominent. And in this matter, he agrees with the Rabbanite philologists who follow the same practice. He devotes himself to the smallest linguistic details to bring the literal text into a good sense. But it is unnecessary to cite examples of this here, as it is a habit he employs throughout his entire work.

We shall not occupy ourselves with refuting the opinion of those who believe that the *Karaites* have different *Copies* <note>Manuscripts</note> of the Bible than the common ones. For it is enough to have said that they not only accept the twenty-four Books of the Holy Scripture, as all other Jews do; but even that they use Hebrew copies such as those that currently exist with the points of the *Masoretes*.

The origin of the name comes from the word *Masora*, which means "tradition"; or from *Massora*, which means "to join together."

# HISTORICAL TREATISE

<margin>The accusation against them is declared to be slander.</margin>
...differs in no way from that of other Jews, were it not for the fact that it is purer and more distant from superstition. For they in no way admit the explanations of the *Cabalists* <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, a form of Jewish mysticism</note> nor their allegories, which are without foundation. Furthermore, our *Karaite* clearly expresses his faith regarding the nature of the soul and the quality of the afterlife when he explains these words from *Genesis*: *Let us make man in our image and our likeness.* <note>Genesis 1:26</note> *The spirit of man,* he says, *is derived from exalted things, and his body consists of the nature of lesser things. For his soul,* he adds, *exists like the Angels. And a little later: The world to come is made for the soul of man.* Indeed, these sentiments are entirely contrary to those of the *Sadducees* <note>A Jewish sect of the Second Temple period that denied the resurrection of the dead and the existence of spirits</note>, and they sufficiently prove that all the errors with which the *Karaites* are charged are mere slanders.

<margin>The Karaites reject the Jewish institutions of the Mishnah and the Talmud; and why.</margin>
As for the customs and ceremonies of the *Karaites*, one could compile a broad account of them: but we believe it will suffice to say in general that the *Karaites* reject all the institutions of the *Mishnah* <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note> and the *Talmud* <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, comprising the Mishnah and Gemara</note>, unless they are consistent with Scripture, and unless they can be drawn from it by necessary and firm logical consequence. We shall content ourselves with bringing forward three undeniable examples. The first concerns the command of the *Mezuzot* <note>Small parchment scrolls inscribed with specific Hebrew verses from the Torah</note>, or the parchment which the Jews attach to all the posts of the doors where one is accustomed to go in and out; the second, the *Tefillin* <note>Also known as phylacteries: small black leather boxes containing Torah verses, worn during prayer</note>, or Protectors, of which mention is made even in the New Testament; the third, the prohibition against eating milk with meat. Although the first two seem clearly and explicitly mentioned in *Deuteronomy*, where it is said, speaking of one and the other: (a) *You shall bind them for a sign upon your hand: and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes; and you shall write them upon the posts of your houses and on your gates.* <note>Deuteronomy 6:8-9</note> Our *Karaite* believes

<column-break/>

nevertheless, in the explanation he gives of these words, that it is a figurative way of speaking; and that when God said to write it on the doorposts, He only wished to make it understood that one, whether going in or out, must always have it in his thoughts. By this means, the *Karaites* exclude a great number of ceremonies—not to say superstitions—which the Jewish Rabbinists have invented regarding these *Mezuzot* and *Tefillin*. From this it also arose that even the *Karaites*, seeing the Rabbinists perform their prayers while binding these *Tefillin* to their foreheads—as described in the first Section of this Treatise, the fifth chapter—they could not refrain from mocking them, calling them *bridled donkeys*. Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate)</note> did not treat these *Tefillin* any more favorably: for explaining the words of the Gospel where these *Protectors* <note>original: "Beschermmiddels"; referring to phylacteries</note> are spoken of, he says; *the Pharisees, poorly explaining this passage of Scripture, wrote the Ten Commandments of Moses on parchment, which they rolled up and bound before their foreheads, and they made a kind of wreath around their heads of it, so that it was always before their eyes.*

The third example is taken from the negative command not to eat meat and anything prepared from milk together at the same meal, based on the passage from *Exodus*: *You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk.* <note>Exodus 23:19</note> But our *Karaite* gives no credit to the Traditions that provide an explanation for this passage which deviates from the literal sense; and he believes that this passage of Scripture is explained by that where it is said, speaking of a bird's nest: *You shall not take the mother with the young.* <note>Deuteronomy 22:6</note> And when he presses the Jewish Rabbinists on this, they answer, as has happened to us: *Ameru Hachamenu* <note>Hebrew: "Our Sages have said"</note>; this is what *our Masters or Scholars have decided, to believe-*
<meta>catchword: believe-</meta>

---

will. Since they then found words in the Text that had to be read differently than they were written, and consisted of more or fewer letters than one had to pronounce, they wrote their remarks on the margin of the text, calling these *Kethiv* <note>Hebrew: "Written"; the literal text as it appears in the scroll</note>, the way of writing, and *Qere* <note>Hebrew: "Read"; the pronunciation or word to be used in reading</note>, the way of reading. Likewise, they marked many irregular words with respect to the Vowel Points or Sound-signs. Some believe that they invented these Vowel Points: but it is not probable that before their time the Biblical writings would have been like a body without a soul. Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a prominent Christian Hebraist</note> believes that this Sect of the *Masoretes* <note>Scholars who standardized the Hebrew Bible text and added vowels/accents</note> flourished for one hundred and thirty years, and was destroyed about 330 years before Christ's birth; that the last of these *Masoretes* was Simeon the Just, who, in his High Priestly robes with the High Priest Jaddua, went to meet Alexander the Great when that Prince intended to besiege Jerusalem. But *Louis Cappel* <note>A French Protestant clergyman and Hebrew scholar (1585–1658) who argued vowel points were a later invention</note> asserts that the Masoretes are not the inventors of the Hebrew points, and would not have lived until 400 years after Christ. *Buxtorf, Commentary on the Masorah; Genebrard, Book 2; L. Cappel, Arcanum Punctuationis, etc.*

believing that the interpretation of their Forefathers is of no less dignity than the *Biblical text*; and that God gave this explanation to *Moses* on Mount Sinai.

We do not dwell on the other commandments, which are without number; since they for the most part contain the explanations of the *Rabbinists* <note>Followers of Rabbinic Judaism who adhere to the Talmud</note>, which are not accepted by the *Karaites*. According to the Rabbinic purpose, they do not touch the *Biblical text*, since they take pleasure in inventing new solutions at the slightest opportunity. The *Karaites* consult reason, and explain the Scripture by itself, or what follows by what precedes <note>A method of interpretation using context rather than outside tradition</note>. In a word, they reject everything that the Holy Scripture, sound reason, and a steady tradition do not teach them.

<margin>Yet they agree with them on certain disciplinary duties.</margin>
Nevertheless, because they profess good sense, the *Karaites* sufficiently agree with certain disciplinary customs observed by the *Rabbinists*, although they see well enough that Holy Scripture commands otherwise therein. They follow, for example, their *almanacs* and the calculations of *Rabbi Hillel* <note>Hillel II, traditional creator of the Hebrew calendar</note>; since, being forced to agree on some common usage, they have chosen this over others, just as some *Protestants* make use of improved calendars, although they do not approve of them in every detail.

<margin>As also with circumcision.</margin>
They not only agree with the *Rabbinists* in their manner of circumcision: but they sometimes make use of them to circumcise their children. Nevertheless, Circumcision is indeed indicated in Holy Scripture, but not the specific manner of the act. For example, the Turks <note>Muslims</note> and Jews who both circumcise, nevertheless differ in that the Turks, after having cut off the foreskin, do not touch it further; whereas the Jews in many places tear the edge of the skin that remains after the circumcision with their fingernails. Possibly this happens for the reason that the Jewish circumcision heals much sooner than that of the Turks.

<margin>How they cover themselves with the <term>TALLIT</term>, though it is different in appearance.</margin>
The *Karaites* also make use of the <term>TALLIT</term> <note>A fringed prayer shawl worn during Jewish services</note>, which our author mentioned in the first part of his book. Their <term>TALLIT</term> nevertheless differs a little from that of the *Rabbinists*: for it is cut in a special way, and the cords, which hang like tassels, are also of a distinct shape.

### HISTORICAL TREATISE

<margin>And how Scaliger attempted to maintain correspondence with them.</margin>
They claim to be descended from *Aaron* <note>The brother of Moses and the first High Priest</note>. Their Temple, or formerly their Chapel, is located on Mount *Gerizim*, where they perform their sacrifices. *Joseph Scaliger* <note>A famous 16th-century Dutch scholar of history and chronology</note> wrote of this to the Samaritans of *Egypt* and to the High Priest of this sect, who lived in *Shechem*. Answers were written to him on their behalf regarding all the difficulties that Scaliger had presented to them in his letters. These answers were signed in the year 998 of the Hijra <note>The Islamic calendar</note> of Muhammad, corresponding to the year 1590; however, they never reached Scaliger's hands.

In the first of these answers, written in the name of the Assembly of Israel in Egypt, they testify that they annually celebrate the Passover feast on the fourteenth day of the first month on Mount *Gerizim*, and that he who then held the office of High Priest was named *Eleazar*, and being the son of *Phineas*, was a descendant of *Aaron*. They subsequently resolved the difficulties that Scaliger had proposed to them; but as these are very formally refuted in the answer sent to Scaliger himself under the name of the High Priest *Eleazar* and the Synagogue of Shechem, we shall content ourselves with reporting this latter account; and it will suffice to show what the sect of the *Samaritans* is today: this being the essence of *Eleazar’s* answer sent to Scaliger.

<margin>Wherein the Samaritans actually differ from the Jews, considered.</margin>
It is true that the Samaritans do not consider any books of the Bible credible except the Books of Moses <note>The Pentateuch: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy</note>. They do have the History of Joshua and a few other histories of the Old Covenant; but they differ from ours. They also do not place faith in them as Divinely consecrated books; since the Jewish institution that determined the number of Bible books is from a much later time than their schism, and no less because the majority of those books, they believe, were written to defend the lineage of David and establish him on the throne. Wherefore they speak of *Esdras* <note>Ezra the Scribe</note> as a deceiver who, they say, abolished the true Hebrew letters to use others, which the Jews still use to write the Biblical text. Truly Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin</note> and the most famous philologists <term>Taalzifters</term><note>Literally "language-sifters" or critical scholars</note> of our time are of the opinion that the first Hebrew letters are those of the Samaritans, and that *Ezra*, upon the return from the captivity, made use of letters that are Chaldean <note>The square Aramaic script</note>, of which our Bibles consist. Possibly he used them to further distinguish the Jews from the Samaritans, making it so they had nothing in common. This could also have been done because the people were accustomed to this sort of writing during the captivity, having learned that language. What adds weight to this belief is that one was obliged, in order to understand the Hebrew text, to explain it in Chaldean.

<margin>How the Samaritan Books of Moses differ in letters from those of the Jews;</margin>
The Samaritan Books of Moses do not differ from those of the Jews except in letters. *The Samaritans, says Jerome, have written the Books of Moses in just as many letters as the Jews: since they differ only in shapes and dots.* <note>original: "De Samaritanen, zegt Jeronimus, hebben de Boeken Moses in even zoo veel letteren als de Jooden geschreeven: vermits zy niet dan in figuuren en punten verschillen."</note> In place of "dot," one finds in the Latin of Jerome the word *Apex*, which is a small and thin stroke with which the Jews decorate the top of certain letters, serving them in place of a crown <note>Known as "tagin," these are decorative "tittles" or flourishes used in Torah scrolls</note>. They use this in books that must serve in the Synagogues and in their *Mezouzot* <note>Mezuzah: parchment scrolls containing scripture fixed to doorposts</note>. And it is apparent that it was these small strokes that the Savior intended to speak of when He said: (a) *Not one iota, nor one tittle <note>original: "unus apex"</note>, shall pass from the Law.* For the [vowel] points used

> (a) Matthew.

<column-break/>

<margin>And how this difference is to be compared.</margin>
For the rest, when we say with Jerome that the Samaritan books differ in letters, this must not be taken too strictly: but one must regard them as two copies drawn from the same original script, which each wrote in letters that were their own: but it has been impossible that in the course of time some variant readings did not creep in. Jerome notes some, which others before him also observed. And it is by paying attention to all these circumstances that one can reconcile the disputes arising over this subject. For if one, like those Greeks who recognized the Pope, took a fancy to write common Latin in Greek letters; and if they used them in their daily custom, we do not doubt that in a course of years, some difference would be found between these two copies.

<margin>Besides the Hebrew Books of Moses in Samaritan letters, they also have an Arabic and Syriac translation.</margin>
The Samaritans have not only the Hebrew Books of Moses in Samaritan letters: but also two translations, of which one is written in Arabic, and the other in Syriac or Chaldean, which is called the Samaritan Translation, as if it were a distinct language, although it is nothing but a kind of Syriac or Chaldean, which nonetheless differs from common Syriac. Both these translations are likewise written in Samaritan letters, and they are arranged with the Text in three rows. Mr. *le Jay* <note>Guy Michel Le Jay, who published the Paris Polyglot Bible between 1629 and 1645</note> printed [them], as also in the *Polyglot* of England <note>The London Polyglot Bible, 1657</note>; and the letters of it are existing in the *Exemplar* <note>Copy or manuscript</note> of the Books of Moses, which is preserved in the library of the Fathers of the *Oratory* <note>original: "Oratrium"</note> of Paris near the Louvre. Nonetheless, these printings cannot equal the value and the loftiness of the manuscript. Many of these Samaritan books are still found today in private libraries: but no one has ever investigated more accurately than the Lord of *Peiresc* <note>original: "Pyresk". Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc, a famous French polymath and scholar</note>. For besides these three columns, he has many pieces of particular works in a language sufficiently different from common Syriac, which one [calls] Samaritan...

...can call it; for the rest, if one wishes to rely on *Postel* <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a French polyglot and researcher of Eastern languages</note>, the Samaritans are aware of the literary arts.

Since the Samaritans wrote the text of the Books of Moses without points or vowel letters, it is unknown whether their manner of reading corresponds with that of the Jews, which is now firmly established by the Masoretes <note>Jewish scholars between the 6th and 10th centuries who compiled the Masorah, a system of pronunciation and grammatical guides for the Hebrew Bible</note>. It would, however, be a very extraordinary thing to hear a Samaritan read the text of the Books of Moses, to see if he entirely agreed with the Jewish manner of reading, which we follow accurately since we have no other. One may hope that some traveler experienced in the Hebrew language will one day satisfy our curiosity; then religion itself could gain great benefit from it.

<margin>
How one should generally distinguish the Samaritans from other sectarians.
</margin>
We believe it is not necessary to speak of the Greek translation of the Samaritan Books of Moses, since anyone with even a little knowledge of the Greek Church Fathers knows what it consists of. One must, however, take care not to confuse the main body of the Samaritans with a certain sect whose head is called *Dositheus* or *Dousis*, as he is named by the Arabs. This *Dousis*, according to the account of a Samaritan, wrote the history of his people and mutilated the text of the Books of Moses in many places, for which he was punished by the High Priest. Nevertheless, he had disciples who made use of these corrupted Books of Moses; as one can see in detail in the remarks of *Abraham Echellensis* <note>A Maronite scholar who worked on the Paris Polyglot Bible</note> regarding the Book of *Hebedjesu* (a). Mention is also made in *Photius* <note>Photius I, a 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar</note> of a certain *Dositheus* or *Dosthen*, a great violator of the sacred books, who was a Samaritan in the time of Simon the Sorcerer <note>A figure mentioned in the New Testament (Acts 8:9–24) as a practitioner of magic</note>, and the head of the Samaritan sect called Dositheans.

One of the most learned men of our day has imagined that our Samaritan-Hebrew Books of Moses originate from this *Dositheus*. (b) But this thought has not the slightest shadow of a foundation: for the Samaritan-Hebrew Books of Moses that have been printed in our time are read in all the Synagogues of the Samaritans.

Furthermore, we know that some learned men, particularly regarding...

->Part I. K<-

<column-break/>

...the peoples of the East, have been astonished by the claim that the modern Samaritans have a place of sacrifice on Mount *Garizim* <note>Mount Gerizim, the sacred mountain of the Samaritans near Shechem</note>; since, they say, *Pietro della Valle* <note>An Italian traveler (1586–1652) known for his journeys through the Ottoman Empire and Persia</note>, who visited the Samaritans in this place, does not mention them in his travel description: and that the extraordinary poverty into which they have fallen for many centuries has made them unable to perform their sacrifices. But without it being necessary to examine what *Pietro della Valle* wrote about the Samaritans, and whether the translation of his travel description matches the Italian, or even whether he allowed himself to be properly informed there, it is pointless to bring up counter-arguments about matters that can be very easily explained.

<margin>
and how they still flourished in the time of Scaliger.
</margin>
It is certain that in the time of *Scaliger* <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a foundational figure in modern chronology and historical criticism</note>, the Samaritans of Shechem <note>Sichem</note> had priests, as they requested from him by letter some fine linen for the clothing of their High Priest. Many memoirs regarding the sacrifices of the Samaritans have also been found among the papers of the Lord of *Peyresc* <note>Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637), a French humanist who maintained a massive network of correspondence with scholars and travelers</note>, borrowed from some travelers whom he had encouraged to visit the Samaritans in order to buy some books from them.

The same Samaritans of Shechem recently wrote to some English scholars, whom they called by the name of their dear brother Samaritans of England. In these letters, they assured them they had a High Priest, whom they claimed to be of the lineage of *Phinehas* <note>Phinias; the grandson of Aaron the High Priest</note>, and priests of the tribe of the Levites. In the last of their letters, written in the year 1676, they give them news of the death of their High Priest, and also pray that they might offer help in their misery by sending sacrifices to the Holy Mount *Garizim*, providing them with clothes for their priests, and finally providing gifts and their bounties for the graves of their fathers. *P: Morinus* <note>Jean Morin (1591–1659), a French biblical scholar who defended the antiquity of the Samaritan Pentateuch</note>, who was also informed about the Samaritans, assures that they still sacrificed on Mount *Garizim*, and that their High Priest, who resided in Shechem, extended his jurisdiction over all the other Samaritans, to whom he recommended the Passover and other solemn festivals annually by proclamation.

## CHAPTER II.
### ->Of the Divinations and Sorceries of the Jews; of their<-
### ->New Converts; of the Commandments for Women; and of Slaves.<-

<margin>Among the Jews, all soothsaying and divination is forbidden, along with anything similar.</margin>
The Jews consider it a great crime to place any faith in divination, as well as astrology, geomancy <note>original: "Stipwaarzeggery," a form of divination involving markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand</note>, palmistry, and other enchantments or soothsaying.

But they believe it is an even greater offense to give oneself over to the black arts, sorcery, delusions, the imitation of God, the invocation of angels, or indeed to demons; to seek counsel from the dead to obtain an answer from them; and, in a word, to do anything designated as forbidden in *Deuteronomy* 18.

They are also forbidden from cutting the skin or marking themselves with ink or other dyes, according to *Leviticus* 19: *You shall not make any marks upon you*; and the Rabbis have forbidden many other superstitions that were in use among the Amorites, which they have called (a) <term>Darch Ha-Emori</term> <note>Hebrew: "Darkhei ha-Emori," meaning "The Ways of the Amorite," a general term for pagan customs or superstitious practices not explicitly mentioned in the Torah but prohibited by rabbinic law</note>.

<margin>Their conduct toward those who wish to become Jewish.</margin>
When someone wishes to become Jewish, three Rabbis or men of distinction are obligated to learn accurately from him what thought brought him to this decision, and to pay close attention to whether this occurs for any human motive <note>such as marriage or financial gain</note>. For if it is found to be so, he is rejected, showing him how strictly severe the Law of Moses is, and how the co-religionists of the Jews are now greatly despised and scorned; and that he would do better to remain in the state in which he finds himself. If he then perseveres in his resolve, he is circumcised, and when he is healed, he is bathed entirely in water <note>ritual immersion or Mikvah</note> in the presence of the three Rabbis who questioned him, after which he is declared a Jew like the others.

<column-break/>

<margin>Which commandments women must submit to.</margin>
Everything that is forbidden to men, women are also subject to: but regarding the positive commandments, the Rabbis have decided that women are not obligated to perform those that must be carried out and observed at specific times <note>time-bound commandments</note>, based on the weakness and tenderness of this sex, due to the obedience they owe their husbands, and the servitude of their submission.

There are then three commandments that they are bound to observe: first, to be careful to have no intimacy with their husbands during their monthly times, and not even before they have bathed themselves <note>referring to Niddah and ritual immersion</note>. Secondly, to prepare the bread and make a cake <note>referring to the "Challah" portion</note> that was formerly offered to the Priest, and is now burned. And lastly, to ignite the Sabbath lamp in the evening, to burn through the night before the Sabbath day, as has already been said here before (b).

However, there are women of a more godly conduct than the men, who not only watch over the education of their children, but who exemplarily provide their husbands with the occasion to practice virtue.

<margin>How slaves are treated among the Jews.</margin>
Formerly, among the ancient Jews, there was a great distinction between slaves, as there were Hebrew and Canaanite slaves: but now, except in the East and in the Barbary Coast <note>North Africa</note>, they do not buy any. Those they possess, they allow to serve them, following the customs of the places where they reside; and if these slaves wish to become Jewish, they circumcise them, and once they have been bathed, they are set at liberty.

# ON THE RELIGIOUS DUTIES OF THE JEWS. 75

<margin>The duties of the Jews.</margin> it is called (a) <term>Viddui</term> <note>original: "Viddui," meaning confession</note>. Each letter of the alphabet represents a cardinal sin, or those which are most frequently committed; but when they have the capacity, they reflect upon the consequences and memory of their sins, noting them by their type and circumstance.

They are accustomed to make this Confession on Mondays and Thursdays, and on all Fast Days. They also fast frequently in private for Atonement, as previously described (b), and even more so when they are ill or in significant danger. There are some who make their confession every evening before going to bed and every morning when they rise.

The days appointed for penance begin on the first of the month of <term>Elul</term> <note>the sixth month of the Hebrew calendar, a time of preparation for the High Holy Days</note> and last until the Day of Atonement; but they often practice this custom from the beginning of the year until the Day of Atonement. For those who find their conscience burdened, no times are excluded. If someone finds himself too inexperienced in this, he usually seeks counsel from a Rabbi; or, if he knows how to manage, he takes recourse in books that deal with Penance, and he lives according to what corresponds with his crimes, whether it be abstinence, fasting, discipline, alms, prayers, or other godly works, to satisfy for the committed crime as much as possible.

<margin>How they consider it their duty to visit the sick, and how the sick person behaves during illness.</margin> They consider it a good work to visit the sick and provide them with necessary assistance. When someone finds himself mortally ill, he requests ten persons, more or less as he pleases, among whom a Rabbi is included, and in their presence, he then confesses all his committed crimes, followed by a prayer in which he implores God for his health, or, should it please Him to end his life, he commends his soul to Him, and asks that death be the wiping away of his sin. If he has a burdened mind or something secret to say, he confesses it to the Rabbi. Next, he asks God for forgiveness and also forgives all those who might have offended him. If he has children and members of the household, he gives them his blessing, having called them to his bed; and if he has a father or mother, he takes his leave of them. Should he wish to make his will and order a disposition of his goods, he does so as he sees fit.

There are some who have a public

<column-break/>

prayer said for them in the Synagogue and change their name, to signify thereby the improvement of their life. They then give and promise alms to the Synagogues and the poor.

<margin>The vigil over the sick is carefully observed.</margin> When the sick person is in danger of death or lying at the point of dying, they are not left alone; instead, a vigil is kept day and night. For they believe it is a good work to be present at the separation of body and soul, especially when it is a learned or wealthy man; basing this on Psalm 49, verse 10: *That he shall live forever, and not see corruption*, etc. When the sick person gives up the ghost, the next of kin tears his garment in some place, following the ancient custom.

There are also those who desire that, on such an occasion, all the water found in the house of the deceased and in the neighborhood be thrown out into the street; and it is believed this is an old custom to make it known that someone in the neighborhood has passed away.

<margin>How the corpse of the deceased is handled.</margin> When someone has died, the body is stretched out on the earth wrapped in a sheet, the face is covered, and a burning wax candle is placed at the head. Soon after, linen trousers are made, calling someone to sew them. But the women offer themselves for this task out of love. The corpse is washed with warm water in which chamomile and dried roses have been boiled. Next, they put a shirt and trousers on the corpse; to which many add a kind of fine linen overcoat, the deceased’s <term>Taled</term> <note>original: "TALED," or Tallit, a fringed prayer shawl</note>, or square mantle with hanging cords or bands, and a white cap on the head. Thus prepared, it is laid in a coffin lined with linen, and a sheet is draped over the body. When it is a man of standing, in some places they make his coffin tapered, and if it is a Rabbi, some books are placed upon it. They make the coffin (c) black, and the body is carried outside.

Then everyone gathers to accompany the body: for since the Jews regard it as a good work to bury the dead, they carry the body in turns for a short distance on their shoulders. In some places, those following the body carry burning torches and sing laments. The friends who are in mourning follow the body weeping.

(a) Confession. (b) Third Section, 6th Chapter.
(c) These and many other customs noted by our Rabbi are only in use in certain places. The Jews even adopt some customs of the lands where they reside.

# CHAPTER II.

->Of the Divinations and Sorceries of the Jews; of their NEW<-
->CONVERTS; of the commandments for Women; and of Slaves.<-

<margin>All divination and soothsaying is forbidden among the Jews, as is anything similar to it.</margin>
The Jews consider it a great crime to give belief to any soothsaying, as well as astrology, divination by points <note>original: "stipwaarzeggery," likely referring to geomancy or divining by lots</note>, palmistry, and other enchantments or divinations.

But they believe it to be an even greater transgression to give oneself over to black magic, sorcery, illusions, mimicking the divine, the invocation of angels, or indeed to demons; to seek counsel from the dead in order to receive an response from them; and in a word, to do anything designated as forbidden in <term>Deuteronomy 18</term>.

They are also forbidden from cutting the skin or marking themselves with ink or other dyes, according to <term>Leviticus 19</term>, which says: *You shall not make any marks upon you;* and the Rabbis have forbidden many other superstitions that were in use among the <term>Amorites</term> <note>an ancient people whose pagan customs are frequently cited in Jewish law as practices to be avoided</note>, which they (a) have called <term>Darch Ha-Emori</term> <note>original: "Darch Ha-Emori," meaning "The Ways of the Amorites"</note>.

<margin>Their conduct toward those who wish to become Jewish.</margin>
When someone wishes to become Jewish, three Rabbis or men of distinction are obligated to know precisely from him what thought has brought him to this decision, and to take good care to see if this is done for any human or worldly reason. For if it is found to be so, he is rejected, showing him how strictly the Law of Moses is observed, and how the fellow believers of the Jews are now greatly despised and scorned; and that he would do better to remain in the state in which he finds himself. If he then persists therein, he is circumcised, and when he is healed, he is bathed entirely in water <note>a ritual immersion known as a mikvah</note> in the presence of the three Rabbis who questioned him, after which he is declared a Jew just like the others.

# CHAPTER III.

->On the Jews' Confession and Penance; on Sickness, Death,<-

<margin>The manner of Penance</margin>
The Jews offer their confession in their prayers to God alone.

<column-break/>

<margin>Which commandments women must submit to.</margin>
Everything that is forbidden to men, women are also subject to: but regarding the [positive] commandments, the Rabbis have decided that women are not obligated to perform those which must be strictly executed and observed at specific times <note>these are known as "time-bound positive commandments"</note>, based on the weakness and tenderness of this sex, due to the obedience they owe their husbands, and on the servitude of their submission.

These three commandments, then, are those they are bound to observe: first, to be careful not to have intimacy with their husbands during their monthly cycles, and not even before they have bathed [ritually]. Secondly, to prepare the bread and make a cake <note>referring to the "Challah" portion of dough set aside</note>, which was formerly offered to the Priest and is now burned. And lastly, to light the Sabbath lamp in the evening to burn through the night before the Sabbath day, as has already been said here before (b).

However, there are women of more godly conduct than the men, who not only watch over the education of their children, but who also give exemplary guidance to their husbands in the practice of virtue.

<margin>How slaves are treated among the Jews.</margin>
In former times, there was a great distinction among the ancient Jews between the slaves who were from the Hebrew [and] Canaanite slaves; but now, except in the East and in Barbary <note>the coast of North Africa</note>, they do not purchase them. Those whom they possess, they allow themselves to be served by, and follow the customs of the places where they reside; and if these slaves wish to become Jewish, they circumcise them, and after being bathed, they are set at liberty.
