<sig>K 2</sig>

<margin>The Jews directed [regarding confession].</margin>
...they call it (a) *<term>Viddui</term>* <note>original: "Viddui," the Hebrew term for confession</note>. Each letter [of the alphabet] represents a principal sin, or those most frequently committed; but when they have the capacity, they reflect upon the consequences and memory of their sins, and record them by their types and circumstances.

They are accustomed to make this Confession on Mondays and Thursdays, and on all Fast days. They also frequently fast specifically for Reconciliation, as previously described (b), and even more so when they are sick or in significant danger. There are those who make their confession every evening before going to bed and every morning when they rise.

The days appointed for penance begin with the first of the month of *<term>Elul</term>* <note>the month preceding the High Holy Days, dedicated to repentance</note> and last until the <term>Day of Atonement</term> <note>Yom Kippur</note>, but they often practice this custom from the beginning of the year until the Day of Atonement. For one who finds their conscience burdened, no times are excluded. If someone finds themselves too inexperienced in this, they usually consult with a <term>Rabbi</term>; or if they can manage themselves, they take recourse to the books that treat of Penance, and they live according to what corresponds with their crimes—be it abstinence, fasting, discipline, alms, prayers, or other pious works—in order to satisfy for the committed crime as much as possible.

<margin>How they consider it their duty to visit the sick, and how the sick person conducts themselves in illness.</margin>
They hold it to be a good work to visit the sick and to provide them with the necessary assistance. When someone finds themselves mortally ill, they request ten persons, more or less as they desire, among whom a Rabbi is included; and in their presence, they then confess all their committed crimes, subsequently saying a prayer in which they beseech God for their health, or should it please Him to end their life, they commend their soul to Him, praying that death may be the wiping away of their sin. If they have a burdened mind, or something secret to say, they confess it before the Rabbi. Next, they ask God for forgiveness and likewise forgive all those who might have offended them. If they have children and housemates, they give them their blessing, having had them come before their bed; and if they have a father or mother, they take their leave of them. Should they wish to make their will and order an arrangement of their goods, they do so as they see fit.

There are those who have a public

<column-break/>

prayer said for them in the <term>Synagogue</term>, and change their name to signify the improvement of their life thereby. They then give and promise alms to the Synagogues and the poor.

<margin>What care is carefully observed with the sick.</margin>
When the sick person is in danger of death or lying at the point of dying, they are not left alone; but one watches over them day and night. For they believe it is a good work to attend the separation of body and soul, especially when it is a learned or wealthy man; basing this on Psalm 49, verse 10: *That he shall live continually, and not see corruption,* etc. When the sick person gives up the ghost, the next of kin tears their garment in some place, following the ancient custom.

There are also those who desire that, in such an instance, all the water found in the house of the deceased and in the neighborhood be thrown out into the street; and it is believed this is an old custom to make it known that someone in the neighborhood has passed away.

<margin>How the corpse of the deceased is handled.</margin>
When someone has died, the corpse is stretched out on the earth wrapped in a sheet, the face is covered, and a burning wax candle is placed at the head. Soon after, linen trousers are made, calling someone to sew them. But the women offer themselves for this out of love. The corpse is washed with warm water in which chamomile and dried roses have been boiled. Next, the corpse is dressed in a shirt and trousers; to which many add a kind of fine linen over-coat, the deceased’s *<term>Tallit</term>* <note>original: "TALED," a four-cornered fringed prayer shawl</note>, or square mantle with hanging cords or bands, and a white cap on the head. Thus prepared, it is laid in a coffin lined with linen, and a sheet is covered over the corpse. When it is a man of status, in some places his coffin is made pointed; and if it is a Rabbi, some books are placed upon it. The coffin is made (c) black, and the corpse is carried outside.

Then everyone assembles to accompany the corpse: for since the Jews regard it as a good work to bury the dead, they carry the corpse by turns for a little while on their shoulders. In some places, the followers of the corpse carry burning torches and sing laments. The friends who are in mourning follow the corpse weeping.

---

(a) Confession. (b) Third Section, 6th Chapter.
(c) These and many other customs that our Rabbi notes are only in use in certain places. The Jews even adopt some customs of the countries where they reside.

In this order, the body is led to the Cemetery, which is usually a piece of land set aside for this purpose; they call it <term>Beth Hachaim</term> <note>Hebrew: "House of the Living"</note>, or the *house of the living*, considering the dead to be alive on account of their souls. When the body has been set down, if it is that of a praiseworthy man, someone delivers a eulogy. They also say a prayer for him called <term>Ridduc Addin</term> <note>original: "Ridduc Addin," a phonetic rendering of Tzidduk Ha-Din, meaning "Justification of the Judgment"</note>, or *justice of the judgment*. They begin it with the words from *Deuteronomy 32, verse 4: He is the Rock, whose work is perfect, for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, etc.*

<margin>Funeral rites observed before the burial.</margin>
A small bag of earth or sand is placed under the head of the deceased: after which the coffin is shut, and it is carried to the grave near the place where the deceased's friends are buried. In some places, once the coffin has been brought near the grave, if the deceased is a man, there are ten people who walk around the coffin seven times, and they read a prayer for the soul of the deceased. The closest blood relative of the deceased tears his garment in some place. Then the body is lowered into the grave, and it is covered with earth,

<column-break/>

with everyone throwing a handful of earth or using a shovel to put earth on the coffin until the grave is filled.

They consider it a sin, for both men and women, to tear the skin or to pull out their hair on this occasion, whether they weep or lament for the deceased before or after; as is mentioned in *Deuteronomy 14, verse 1: You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.*

Upon leaving, everyone pulls a handful of grass from the ground two or three times and says, while throwing it behind them, the words of the 72nd Psalm, verse 16: *And they of the city shall flourish like the grass of the earth;* and this is done to signify the resurrection. They wash their hands, sit down and stand up again nine times, and recite the 91st Psalm: *He that dwelleth in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty,* etc. Then they return home. These now are the most general customs of the Jews regarding this subject; and if there are some matters that differ from these, they will be of little importance.

## CHAPTER IV.

->Regarding the Mourning of the Jews, of Prayer, and the remembrance of the deceased. Of Paradise, Hell, and the Outer Court.<- <note>original: "Voorburg," likely referring to Limbo or a transitional state</note>

---

<margin>How the Jews behave in mourning for their deceased relatives.</margin>
**The** closest friends of the deceased—be it father, mother, children, husband or wife, brother or sister—sit upon the earth; and after they have taken off their shoes, they are served bread, wine, and hard-boiled eggs, which they then eat and drink; according to *Proverbs 31, verse 6: Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that be of heavy hearts,* etc. The one who usually says the blessing over the meal is accustomed to add some words of comfort. In the East and many other places, friends and kinsmen are accustomed to send gifts to the next of kin of the deceased for seven days, every morning and evening, from which they make large and costly meals; and they even come to eat with them to comfort them.

As soon as the deceased has been carried out of the house, his sleeping mattress is folded up, and the blankets are rolled up and left on the straw; then a burning lamp is placed at the head of the

<column-break/>

bedstead, which burns without ceasing for seven days.

The closest friends of the deceased, as has been said, remain sitting in the house, not on a chair but on the floor, and eat while sitting thus; except on the Sabbath day, when they go to prayers accompanied by others, and are visited and comforted more by their friends on 그날 than on other days. During these seven days they may do no work, nor conduct any trade. The husband and wife may also not sleep together, and there must be at least ten persons who come to perform the usual prayers with these friends every morning and evening, and who then remain in the house. To this, some add the 49th Psalm: *Hear this, all ye people,* etc. Then they pray for the soul of the deceased. They dress in mourning according to the custom of the country, without being obligated to do so by any commandment.

The seven days having passed, they go out to the Synagogue, where many lamps are then burning. They then pray, and

...they promise alms for the souls of the deceased. This is repeated at the end of the month and of the year. If the deceased is a Rabbi or a Person of distinction, during these days the <term>ESPED</term> <note>original: "E S P E D"; Hebrew: *Hesped*, a funeral oration or eulogy</note> is performed, that is, his funeral oration and praise are spoken.

In some places, the grave is covered with a tombstone, upon which the name of the deceased is carved, along with something in his praise, whether in verse or prose, indicating the day, month, and year of his passing.

<margin>Why the Jews pray for the deceased.</margin>
Since we have said that the Jews pray for the soul of the deceased, we must also state the reason for this here.

<column-break/>

<margin>Praying for every soul; and their views on Paradise, etc.</margin>
They believe that there is a Paradise, called by them (b) <term>GAN HEDEN</term> <note>Hebrew: *Gan Eden*, meaning Garden of Eden</note>, where the blessed partake of glory in the contemplation of God. As for the evildoers, they are tormented there by fire and other means of punishment; there are the damned who must suffer this punishment forever, without any hope of release; but others are there only for a certain time. And this is what is called the Forecourt <note>Dutch: "Voorburg," referring to a temporary state of purgation in Gehenna</note>, which is not separate from hell except by the duration of time.

They hold that all Jews who are not infected with heresy and have not transgressed anything designated by the Rabbis, remain in the Forecourt for no more than a year, and that these constitute the majority. For they believe there are few who remain in Hell forever because of their crimes.

### CHAPTER V.
#### On the TRANSMIGRATION OF SOULS, on the RESURRECTION and on the JUDGMENT; as well as the thirteen ARTICLES OF FAITH.

---

<margin>How some Jews adhere to the opinion of Pythagoras.</margin>
**T**here are Jews who, like *Pythagoras*, believe that the soul moves from one body into another, which they call (d) <term>GILGUL</term> <note>Hebrew: *Gilgul*, the cycle of souls or reincarnation</note>, and they seek to justify this opinion from many places in Scripture, mostly taken from *Ecclesiasticus* <note>The Wisdom of Sirach</note> and *Job*: but this opinion is not universal among them, and whether it be so or not, this is not held among them as heresy.

<margin>But others believe in the resurrection according to their articles of faith.</margin>
They believe in the resurrection of the dead, and this is one of their thirteen articles of faith; that at the end of days the dead shall rise again, and that God will subsequently exercise a general judgment over all people and souls, as written in *Daniel 12, verse 2: And many of them that sleep in the dust shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.*

<margin>What the thirteen articles of faith consist of.</margin>
Having reviewed the Ceremonies and Customs that are still in use among the Jews, there remains the presentation of the thirteen articles of faith

<column-break/>

<margin>of the Jews.</margin>
which contain their entire belief, corresponding with what the Rabbi *Moses* the Egyptian, (e) says in his explanation of the <term>Misnach</term> <note>The Mishnah, the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note>, and the treatise of the *Sanhedrin* Chapter *Helek*. These have been accepted by all Jews without any dispute.

I. That there is a God, Creator of all things, the first origin of all beings, who can exist without any part of the Universe; but that there is nothing in the world that exists without him.

II. That God is one, and indivisible; but of a different unity than all other unities.

III. That God is incorporeal, and that he has no possible bodily quality, and that man can neither understand nor conceive of him.

IV. That God is from all eternity, and that everything that exists, him alone excepted, had a beginning in time.

V. That one must serve and worship none but God; and that one must [serve] no other...

(d) Which means revolution or cycle. As if the souls did nothing but continually cycle from one body into another.
(e) Otherwise called *Maimonides* or *Rambam*; namely, *Rabbi Moses Ben Maimon*, who was the most learned and least superstitious of all Jews.

VI. That there have been, and that there can still be Prophets, fit to receive the inspirations of God.

VII. That Moses was a greater Prophet than all other Prophets, and that the degree of Prophecy with which God honored him was extraordinary, and far above those which He gave to other Prophets. <note>These points refer to the unique status of Moses as the only prophet to have spoken with God "face to face."</note>

IX. That this law (a) is unchangeable, and that one may neither add to nor take away from it.

X. That God knows and governs all our human deeds.

<column-break/>

XII. XIII. That God shall raise the dead again, as has already been said before.

These then are the Fundamentals of the Jewish faith, with which we conclude this account of what they believe and are accustomed to practice.

### First Section.

Since we now seemed to have satisfied the subject of the Manners and Customs of the Jews, according to what *Rabbi Leon of Modena* <note>Leon of Modena (1571–1648) was a famous Venetian rabbi whose work "The History of Jewish Rites" was widely read by Christians to understand Jewish life.</note> has written of it: yet let it be permitted to us, along with the Learned (a)

<column-break/>

Writer of the *History of the Jews*, to say that *Leon of Modena* has skipped several weighty matters. Therefore, it shall be necessary to fulfill this deficiency through the following Treatise.

### CHAPTER I.

### The DISPERSION of the Jews Traced.

<margin>Various opinions regarding the dispersion of the Jews considered.</margin>

There is no Christian Teacher who must not confess that the dispersion of the Jews, since the destruction of the Temple and the City of *Jerusalem* under the reign of *Vespasian* <note>Roman Emperor (69–79 AD) whose forces, led by his son Titus, destroyed the Second Temple in 70 AD.</note>, has such particular marks that it is impossible not to recognize the hand of God in it. This dispersion has become a fertile field of miracles, rarities, and noteworthy things. Christian and Jew harvest from it alike. Each finds wonders there, though in a different manner. The aid of scholarly study has from time to time provided Christian Teachers with the means to awaken in the minds of their listeners the idea of the Jews' rejection. The insults with which this people is everywhere oppressed; the contempt in which they live; the destruction of the essential ceremonies in their Religion; all the ecclesiastical governance of their Church thrown into turmoil; their

<column-break/>

Lineages and Ancestries mixed, and the Sacrifices abolished; these are all matters upon which this lamentable rejection is grounded. The Jews, on the contrary, draw from these inconveniences a subject of glory, and always comfort themselves that (b) their People are the heart of the World’s Nations. *The Heart is the noblest part of the human Body: nevertheless, it must suffer the ailments of the body; it is the heart which the passions consume and grievances torment: but it cannot conform to the infection, because it has, so to speak, an original purity, and it maintains to the end the power to rid itself of the corrupt fluids that spoil the other parts. The fine and tender matter of which the heart consists attracts various discomforts to itself, which it then wards off by the strength of its constitution.* The Jews also say, according to the Prophet

# SECOND HISTORICAL TREATISE

<columns>
2

Amos <note>Referencing Amos 3:2: "You only have I known of all the families of the earth."</note> writes that God knows no one among all the nations of the earth but them, and that He therefore punishes their iniquity. But these iniquities are temporary, since God does not allow them to consume the heart, as they once consumed the Canaanites and others. The Jews suffer through the lawlessness of their neighboring nations, just as the heart suffers from the ailments of the liver, spleen, stomach, etc. It is enough to show here that they have a very different idea of their humiliation than the Christians do.

<margin>And how uncertain the Writers are on this point, is indicated.</margin>

History is uncertain regarding the dispersion of the ten Tribes of Israel whom Shalmaneser <note>Shalmaneser V, King of Assyria (reigned 727–722 BC), who besieged Samaria.</note> carried away to Media: but however it may be, it is certain that since this dispersion, the Jews have become known in many lands. We believe, however, that they did not become well known until after the destruction of the Kingdom of Judah. (a) Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> makes them appear in an innumerable multitude since the times of King Ahasuerus. A certain (b) Eldad <note>Eldad ha-Dani (9th century), a traveler who claimed to be from a Jewish state in East Africa.</note> has written a history of the dispersion, and attempts to heighten its luster with so many fables that they need not yield to the mythology of the ancient Greeks. Benjamin of Tudela <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler from Spain who visited Europe, Asia, and Africa.</note> decorates the subject no less, and gives a description of a great extent of land possessed by his people in absolute power: but which was known to no one but himself. Peritsol <note>Abraham Farissol (c. 1451–1525), a Jewish-Italian geographer.</note>, another notorious writer among the Jews, places them in locations where they have not been able to be found to this day. For example, he posits a community of Rechabites * in the Desert of Khaibar. He has his countrymen reigning in the Desert of Arabia. He has the Jews inhabiting the banks of the Ganges and the borders of Bengal, the Philippines, etc.

<column-break/>

Finally, he places them near a certain Sabbatical River † <note>The Sambation, a mythical river in Jewish legend that flows with stones six days a week and rests on the Sabbath.</note>, in the neighborhood of the states of Prester John <note>A legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in European chronicles from the 12th to the 17th centuries, said to rule over a nation in the Orient.</note>, and this Kingdom of the Jews is situated by this writer in such a way that one might mistake it for the borders of Tibet. If it were true that there was a Jewish state in these regions, one might reasonably believe that they were the remnants of the ten Tribes. William of Rubruck <note>A Flemish Franciscan missionary and explorer.</note>, traveling in Tartary in the year 1246, reports that two days' journey above Derbent, extending toward Great Tartary, (c) a great number of Jews are found in a city called Samaron. He speaks of a stretch of land near the Caspian Sea where it was said the Jews lived as if enclosed. Carpini (d) <note>Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, one of the first Europeans to enter the court of the Great Khan.</note>, who traveled at the same time, also speaks of certain Jewish Tartars whom he calls Brutaches or Bastarken. Others tell us of (e) Naphtalites and Danites living in Great Tartary, and of certain Sadducees on the borders of Tibet.

It is also believed that the Jews of the ten tribes were dispersed in the Kingdom of Kashmir, one of the provinces of the Mughal Empire: but although these thoughts are supported by some evidence, as can be seen in the reports of Bernier (f) <note>François Bernier (1620–1688), a French physician and traveler who spent 12 years in the Mughal court.</note>, one cannot conclude that the Jews had an absolute government there. In a province of China, one also finds Jews (g) <note>Referring to the Kaifeng Jews.</note> who have preserved and maintained a portion of the sacred Books, church customs of their religion, and many traditions: but it seems they have mixed many things into their religion borrowed from the Chinese; such as, among others, the honors they pay to Confucius ‡.

(a) *Antiquities of the Jews, Book 11, Chapter 5.* (b) See *Basnage, History of the Jews, Book 7.* <note>Jacques Basnage (1653–1723), a French Protestant theologian and historian.</note>

# ON THE RELIGIOUS DUTIES OF THE JEWS.

...do. (a) We shall not expand upon the sovereignty of the Jews in certain regions of Ethiopia. If one may believe the reports of this land, this people is very numerous there; and this is what one can see described in the *History of Ethiopia* by Ludolf <note>Hiob Ludolf (1624–1704) was a German orientalist whose work was the primary European source for Ethiopian history and the Ge'ez language.</note>.

It is also imagined that the Jews are to be found in America; but the reasons brought forward as proof are weak (b) enough; nevertheless, not only the Jews but even the Christians hold this opinion. One can see what Mr. Basnage (c) <note>Jacques Basnage (1653–1723) wrote a monumental history of the Jews intended to update the work of Josephus.</note> has said of it. It is true that a contemporary traveler reports (d) that the Indians of the Peruvian coast around PLATA have many Jewish customs, as do the CALCHAQUEN who live between PERU and TUCUMAN; that they have a sort of circumcision and eat no pork. Others have believed they found evidence of Judaism in the religion and customs of Japan. If one may build upon conjectures, why is it not believed that the Christians, and particularly the Roman Catholics, shared a portion of their religion and church practices with the Americans? In the

<column-break/>

continuation of this work, we shall see how possible it would be to maintain, if one wishes to build upon conjectures, that the Mexicans and Peruvians have borrowed many things from Christianity. It is indeed true that all these vain conjectures, based solely on some similarity of customs, could not prove that peoples so utterly distant from Asia would have their origin from the Jews. It is easier, however, to prove that the captive Jews—being hated, despised, and mistreated by their neighboring peoples—found means to spread themselves into Tartary <note>A historical term used by Europeans to describe North and Central Asia, from the Caspian Sea to the Pacific Ocean.</note>, etc., and subsequently established a powerful enough state there to withstand these neighboring peoples. But all these fictional imaginings and boastings (e) must be excused in this people, who formerly (f) believed they were to be rulers of all nations, and who, raised on miracles and prophecies, believed that Nature might never act nor dispose except for them. We shall not expand further upon the dispersion of the Jews, but refer the reader to the History by Mr. Basnage (g).

...one is. In all Chinese cities, one finds a building erected in his honor, and whenever one of the officials of the robe <note>original: *Amptenaren van den Tabbert*; refers to civil magistrates or scholars who wore formal robes.</note> travels through them, he steps out of his palanquin and walks a few steps on foot to honor him in memory. In the facades of these buildings dedicated to Confucius, one sees in large gilded letters such titles of honor: *to the great Teacher; to the eminent one; to the wise King of Letters*, etc. But in all these praises, the Chinese never use the word *Tan*, which is a name of their Idols; by which they wish to signify that this philosopher condemned idolatry. P. Couplet, *Confucius of the Chinese* <note>original: "Confutius Sinarum"; a reference to *Confucius Sinarum Philosophus* (1687) by the Jesuit Philippe Couplet.</note>.]

(a) See Basnage, *History of the Jews*, Book 9, Ch. 38, in which an accurate account of the present state of the Jews, drawn from an Italian writer, is to be found. For the rest, there is reason to believe that the Jews did not migrate from Asia until long after the destruction of Israel's Kingdom. Thereupon they settled in Media, Chaldea, Armenia, etc. They subsequently moved into Europe through Georgia, the Black Sea, and Muscovy <note>An early modern name for the Grand Duchy of Moscow/Russia.</note>. They spread into Tartary, around the northern parts of the Indies, and even to the coast of China. The overthrow of the Kingdom of Judah did no more than finish what the other had begun. They thus settled among foreign nations, preserved their religions and customs there—which they often corrupted and even lost as they moved further from their origin. These changes were very painful for the first Jews; but one must not imagine that it was impossible, eventually, to forget the misfortunes of comfortless Zion. There was only a small number of pious refugees who had made vows never to forget their dear Jerusalem.

(b) It is said that the Americans calculate their time by Moons; that they offer the firstfruits of their crops to their idols; that the majority of American peoples, particularly the Mexicans and Peruvians, had knowledge of the Deluge; that those of Mexico celebrate a great Jubilee feast; that most American peoples use circumcision, etc. But this does not suffice to prove that the Americans are originally Jews. Mankind has involved itself in many similar outcomes without ever sharing their ideas. The method of calculating by Moons is so simple and natural that it is not surprising that nations who had no other rule for counting chose it to determine the passage of time. Circumcision, and the memory the Americans have preserved of the Deluge, etc., prove more likely that they are descended from the Egyptians, or from the Colchian peoples, or from the Assyrians, than from the Jews.

It is difficult, indeed impossible, to prevent the pride that such a high-flown origin—as that of the Jewish religion—allows one to assume.

82 SECOND HISTORICAL DISCOURSE

## CHAPTER II.

->Of the Persecutions which the Jews have suffered since the last Destruction<-
->of Jerusalem, under the Emperor Vespasian.<-

---

<margin>The corrupt nature of the Jews after the Babylonian Captivity, and from what it arose.</margin>
Religions must almost always be subject to oppression during political revolutions. One must have more courage than one might think to profess in good faith a despised religion that has set human passions aside. The destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians dealt Judaism an almost irreparable blow; for although many honest and well-meaning Jews subsequently returned from the Babylonian Captivity, there were nevertheless many among them of a corrupt nature, who carried out what the wickedness of their ancestors had set in motion, and mixed their crimes with those whom the King of Babylon had left behind in Judea; this being a natural result of the intermingling of different peoples. The common man imagines that these ancient captives were all of a holy conduct, and that their only occupation was to sing night and day to the honor and glory of God: but one is mistaken.

<margin>How they give themselves over to trivial traditions.</margin>
The purity of morals and of the spiritual service was gradually erased after the return from the Captivity: but the stubbornness of the Jews became all the more forceful regarding ceremonies and Temple customs. Let us venture to present our thoughts here. For lack of miracles and prophecies, people were not prevented from accepting as religion that which was nothing but the mere husk or something similar; the Jews blindly surrendered themselves to trivial traditions <note>The author uses "beuzelachtige overleveringen" (trifling traditions) to describe the development of the Oral Law and Rabbinic traditions, reflecting a common 18th-century Christian view that these were departures from the "pure" religion of the Prophets.</note> of their scholars, who held to the remnants of the Prophets and to all the outward appearances of the Law, which seemed necessary to them to maintain with splendor a heavy and difficult institution, since miracles no longer provided assistance. Subsequently, the appearance of Judaism was entirely changed, and the Jews took on the mask of hypocrisy. However tedious the ceremonies and the human-imposed exercises seemed, they were much easier than the improvement of the human heart.

<column-break/>

<margin>and by their disorderly conduct bring many calamities upon themselves.</margin>
It is in the midst of this disorder that Heathendom triumphed over the weakening and decline of Judaism under the formidable power of the Romans. It seemed that this disorder (a) extended over the Jewish Church as the time of its destruction approached. This same disorder primarily drove the nation to rebellion, which dragged the destruction of the State in its wake. The Roman Emperors, under whose dominion the Jews were forced to live, treated this people harshly; they had no less to endure after the downfall of their capital. Domitian burdened them with taxes, which he caused to be extorted from them with such severity that those suspected of being Jews (b) were stripped naked to determine if they were circumcised <note>original: "naakt ontkleedde, om te ervaaren of ze besneeden waren." This refers to the *Fiscus Judaicus*, a tax imposed on Jews by Rome; Suetonius records that even the elderly were inspected to ensure the tax was paid.</note>. He included them in the persecution, among the Christians, whom he made to suffer. Their uprising under Emperor Hadrian brought new misfortunes upon them: and if one may believe *Juvenal* (c) <note>Decimus Iunius Iuvenalis, a Roman satirical poet who often wrote disparagingly of foreign customs in Rome.</note>, they were then driven to give themselves over to fortune-telling and soothsaying: but one must not, however, imagine that the entire nation occupied itself with these despicable activities. Besides that, *Juvenal* was not very favorable to the Jews; for there is reason to believe that it was a lowly and common people who busied themselves with this trade. Be that as it may, misery having made them irritable, they rose up under the leadership of *Bar Kochba <note>original: "Barcochebas." Simon bar Kokhba led the final major Jewish revolt against the Roman Empire (132–136 CE).</note>, who gave himself out to be the Messiah, which nevertheless turned out poorly for him; for Emperor Hadrian had a very large number of these rebels killed. He had them sold like beasts and forbade them to remain in Judea.

<margin>Their misery under the yoke of the Romans noted,</margin>
We shall occupy ourselves for a moment with presenting to the reader an idea, although a little expanded, of all the misery endured by the Jewish People since the birth of the Savior of the World in a succession of consecutive centuries.

<margin>and what the Jews had to suffer according to the Christians.</margin>
The Rabbis say that Emperor Antoninus the Pious <note>original: "Antoninus de Godvruchtige"; likely referring to Antoninus Pius, reigned 138–161 AD</note> was not ill-disposed toward Judaism. Severus and his successors were likewise well-disposed toward the Jews. At the very least, it does not appear that they were badly treated by these Pagan Emperors. But the Christians, having become masters of the Roman Empire, did not have so much respect for that nation, which was viewed by them as a sworn enemy of Jesus Christ. It was remembered that they had crucified him, and it was believed that the wrongs done to the Messiah had to be avenged. Constantine made a beginning with laws that were moderate enough: but Constantius showed them less respect, desiring that a Jew who married a Christian woman should be punished with death. The Emperor Theodosius allowed the Jews the free exercise of their religion. This favor seemed so dangerous to Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, the influential Bishop of Milan</note> that he employed every Christian effort to prevent the calamities he so feared. The Feast which the Jews celebrated in memory of the deliverance obtained for them by Queen Esther <note>The holiday of Purim</note> was abolished at the beginning of the fifth century: because the Christians imagined that under the effigy of Haman, Jesus Christ was being mocked, and the Clergy confirmed this abolition. People took pleasure in bringing down the Enemies of the Religion whenever the Teachers merely gave permission for it, and it was imagined then that this was a Christian work. Let us pass to the times of Justinian. This Prince forbade them from eating the Paschal Lamb. He also made them cease their religion in Africa. The favor of a Prince aligns with his aims of authority, (a) when he wishes to labor for their conversion. Subsequently, the Jews were treated well or poorly according to the nature of Justinian's successors; but He-

raclius declared himself entirely their enemy, persecuted them on every occasion, and used force to compel them to embrace Christianity. History informs us how Leo the Isaurian likewise zealously endeavored to convert the Jews and desired that they become Christians.

In the West, the reign of Charlemagne <note>original: "Karel den Grooten"</note>, and subsequently Louis the Pious, was favorable enough to the Jews: but this did not please the notorious Agobard, Bishop of Lyon. This occurred at the time when the Crusaders were gathering near *Toledo* to recover the Holy Land, and they believed that for the honor of Jesus Christ, they must exterminate those who had formerly caused him to suffer the death of the cross. They caused thousands of Spanish Jews to perish, sacrificing them as so many victims—which they believed were pleasing to God—to obtain his blessing. On the other hand, the devout Jews attributed these misfortunes to improper procedures in the manner of making their *Teffilins* <term>Tefillin: small leather boxes containing Torah verses worn during prayer</term>. See the *Mishnah* <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note>. *Vol.* 1. p. 9.

...favorable. <note>original: "goetgunstig"</note> Al-Qadir <note>The Abbasid Caliph Al-Qadir, reigned 991–1031</note> persecuted them most vehemently in order to seize their possessions, which were considerable; this persecution lasted for several years. It was around this same time that Caliph Hakim <note>Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, Fatimid Caliph of Egypt, known for his erratic and sometimes harsh decrees</note>, who ruled in Egypt and set himself up as the head of the religion of the **Druze**, likewise mistreated those who confessed to being Jews.

<margin>A plan to persecute the Jews in Spain by means of a Crusade;</margin>

# ON THE RELIGIOUS DUTIES OF THE JEWS.

<columns>2</columns>

...to gain the unusual necessities of the body. The opportunity was extraordinarily advantageous. The Genoese met the Jews with the Cross in one hand and bread in the other. Bread was given to those who paid homage to the Cross. This was called a "masterpiece" of conversion; for since the human soul is so subject to physical needs, it is generally very difficult to resist when suffering. But when the soul recovers its strength, this suffering is forgotten.

<margin>How the frenzied Shepherds in France raged against them.</margin>
We should not forget the notorious gathering of the Shepherds <note>The Shepherds' Crusade, or *Pastoreaux*, of 1320 was a popular movement led by a defrocked priest and a renegade monk that targeted Jewish communities in France and Spain.</note> in the fourteenth century. This frenzied gang, which had a priest and a monk as its leaders, committed great disorder in France (a) under the reign of Philip the Tall <note>Philip V of France, reigned 1316–1322</note>, murdering the Jews everywhere in an unmerciful manner. These rioters treated them no better in Spain: but finally, the Sovereigns were forced to work toward the extermination of these devastating Shepherds, who brought misfortune with them everywhere, so much so that the Plague also took an interest in their cause to destroy this brood. The Jews were in a piteous state due to the Plague. They were accused of poisoning the waters: but even when they were found innocent, they were nonetheless doomed to convert or be burned. Thousands of Jews who refused to become Christians were sentenced to the fire.

<margin>And the Flagellants in Germany persecuted them.</margin>
The Flagellants <note>The *Geeffelaars* or Flagellants were religious sects who publicly whipped themselves as penance to ward off the Black Death and other perceived divine punishments.</note> likewise distinguished themselves around the middle of the fourteenth century in Germany. These people believed themselves to be more compassionate and godly than other Christians of their time; they were willing to take upon themselves the burden of scourging themselves while naked, using ropes fitted with sharp iron pins, to refresh the souls in Purgatory and erase the sins of men. Before they began this scourging, they publicly read their commission, contained in a Letter that God (as they claimed) had written to them and given to them by an Angel, with an express command to do penance as described. They extended their commission against the Jews, believing they had to kill and burn them to make their penance more meritorious before God.

<margin>Violent persecutions carried out by</margin>
In Italy, the Jews had as their enemy Pope John XXIII <note>The Pisan Pope John XXIII, who reigned during the Great Western Schism (1410–1415).</note>, who strictly persecuted them, and who, as the Vicar of Jesus Christ, Lord of Souls and Sovereign 

<column-break/>

<margin>the Popes against them.</margin>
of the States, commanded that they should be converted to the Christian faith. He wrote to Spain so that they might work toward the conversion of the Jews, and a great number were converted. Whoever refused to walk on the path of truth was burned or forced to flee. Two Popes, namely Pius V and Sixtus V, drove them out of the Papal States, with the exception of Rome and a few other cities. One of the reasons given for tolerating them in Rome was the hope that they would convert through contact with Christians, and that by frequently seeing the Pope, they would become more manageable. This reason is firm, strong, and of weight: but why does the common Father of Christians not also grant this favor to the Heretics? <note>The author here subtly critiques the Catholic Church's relative tolerance of Jews in Rome compared to its treatment of Protestant "heretics."</note>

<margin>Banished from France or doomed to the fire.</margin>
We must admit that the Jews sometimes brought about their own harm, whether through their usury <note>The practice of lending money at high interest, which was one of the few professions legally open to Jews but led to deep social resentment.</note> or through other equally punishable irregularities. These irregularities were curtailed in France during the time of Philip the Fair <note>Philip IV of France, reigned 1285–1314</note>, under whose reign they were so numerous and powerful that Jewish writers claim a greater number of their brothers were driven into exile from France than had left Egypt in the time of Moses. This exile and the loss of their property were not the only misfortunes that befell them: they were also doomed to the fire.

<margin>What they had to endure in England.</margin>
Let us see if they were treated more favorably in England than in other Christian states. Henry III sought to work toward their conversion without violence: but subsequently, the poverty of this King caused him to cast his eye upon the Jews. The King's chief official demanded a large sum of money from them, and upon their refusal, they were accused of murder to find a legal right to their property, of which they were forced to forfeit a third part to obtain peace. They were frequently burdened with taxes under this reign, until finally, at the end of the thirteenth century, they were entirely banished from the realm. The history of England shows with what intensity the Jews in Lincoln and other cities of this Kingdom were plagued from time to time.

It shall now suffice, what we have said here of the persecutions which the Jews have had to endure at the hands of Christians, intended to avenge the death of the Messiah. These persecutions were sometimes based on loathsome crimes with which the malice of certain peoples charged the Jews, and whose reckless zeal punished them with every conceivable cruelty that the fanaticism of hypocrites ever knew how to carry out.

### CHAPTER III.

->*Concerning the Crimes Charged against the Jews.*<-

<margin>
Various loathsome crimes charged against the Jews.
</margin>

The most loathsome crime of all is this: that of having crucified children. They have been frequently accused of this, and some even wish to assert, although without foundation, that they solemnly renew this atrocity annually (a). *Nauclerus* <note>Johannes Nauclerus (1425–1510), a German historian and theologian.</note> tells us that the Jews gathered secretly on Good Friday to sacrifice a child out of hatred for Christianity. Other historians (b) add that the Jews *communicated* <note>The author uses the Christian term for the Eucharist to describe this supposed ritual.</note> with the heart of such a sacrifice. The murder of a youth named *Richard*, which was charged against them, drove them out of France during the reign of Philip the Illustrious <note>Philip II Augustus (reigned 1180–1223).</note>. It is unknown to us what gave rise to these frequent allegations of such a crime, with which the Jews have been accused in all the lands of Christendom, and why the historians of past centuries have depicted them so hatefully. It may be that some Jews were indeed so malicious as to commit a similar evil deed, and possibly this sufficed to charge the entire nation with it time and again,

<column-break/>

and to add the most hateful circumstances to it. However that may be, the Church nevertheless drew great benefit from this imagined sacrificing of children.

Father *Daniel* <note>Gabriel Daniel (1649–1728), a Jesuit historian.</note> seems to give credence (c) to this accusation, saying: *that around Easter they murder Christian children, whom they have kidnapped, and hold the time of their Supper <note>The author refers here to the Passover Seder, which was often misrepresented by contemporary Christian writers.</note> with them, an ungodly sacrifice performed out of hatred against Jesus Christ, etc.* But Father *Daniel* should have taught us what the Supper of the Jews actually was. We shall give the reader a clearer idea of it than what is usually told.

I. Shortly after the murder of the youth *Richard*, the Jews gathered on the banks of the Seine, where they (d) sacrificed another youth after they had scourged him and crowned him with thorns. *Alberic of the Three Fountains* <note>Alberic of Trois-Fontaines, a 13th-century Cistercian chronicler.</note>, a barbaric and disregarded writer, accuses them of this crime more than once.

<margin>
In England they are
</margin>

II. Likewise, the Jews were accused of sorcery (e) and foul misdeeds.

Another *Host*, thrown by a Jew (b) into a kettle of boiling water, gave cause for a miracle no less famous than the one we have spoken of. The accusation was renewed again some years later. The Jews then supposedly used beggars, who threw into the wells and springs a mixture made of nails and the flesh of a hanged thief, etc.

# III. CHAPTER.
## Of the CRIMES charged against the Jews.

<margin>
Several loathsome crimes charged against the Jews.
</margin>
I. THE most loathsome crime of all is this: of having crucified children. They have been frequently accused of this, and some even wish to assert, although without foundation, that they solemnly renew this abomination annually (a). *Nauclerus* <note>Johannes Nauclerus (1425–1510), a German historian and theologian.</note> tells us that the Jews gathered secretly on Good Friday to sacrifice a child out of hatred for Christianity. Other historians (b) add that the Jews *communicated* <note>In this context, it implies a ritualistic consumption, mimicking the Christian Eucharist.</note> with the heart of such a victim. The murder of a youth named *Richard* <note>This refers to Richard of Pontoise, a victim of a 12th-century blood libel in France.</note>, which was charged to them, drove them out of France during the reign of Philip the Illustrious <note>Philip II Augustus (1165–1223).</note>. It is unknown to us what gave rise to these frequent allegations of such a crime, with which the Jews in all countries of Christendom have been accused, and why the historians of past centuries have portrayed them so hatefully. It may be that some Jews were indeed so malicious as to commit a similar evil deed, and possibly this sufficed to charge the entire nation

<column-break/>

with it every time, and to add the most hateful circumstances to it. However it may be, the Church nevertheless drew great benefit from this imagined sacrificing of children.

We shall give the reader a clearer idea of what is told about it.

## CHAPTER IV.

### Of the Deceivers and False Messiahs of the Jews.

Which Deceivers have from time to time set themselves up as Messiahs, and how their trickery was subsequently discovered.

For he promised that both one and the other would be marked on the hand. The Caliphs carried this out. Subsequently, they forced the Jews (a) to wear a patch of yellow cloth on their clothing to distinguish them from the Muslims.

*Motawakel* (b) <note>Al-Mutawakkil (822–861), the tenth Abbasid caliph.</note> desired that the Jews should be distinguished from the Muslims by wearing a leather belt. He barred them from public offices, forbade them from riding on horseback, and would allow them no transport other than donkeys and mules. These orders of *Motawakel* still stand; according to what is asserted, they bring dishonor and shame in their wake. But there was something even more defamatory in the treatment used by the Emperor *Hadrian* to plague the Jews after the uprisings stirred up by the Seducer *Barchochebas* <note>Simon bar Kokhba, leader of the Jewish rebellion against Rome (132–136 AD).</note>; for he had their ears cut off. Some time before this, *Ptolemy Philopator* desired that the shape of an ivy leaf be pressed onto the bodies of the Jews with a hot iron, as this plant was dedicated to *Bacchus*: this was to indicate that they had lost their freedom. This Prince wanted to draw them to his religion through the fear of punishment, a penalty all the more shameful because it was a consequence of slavery.

<margin>How despicably they have been treated in many places.</margin>

In a Council (a) it was decreed that the Jews should wear a Wheel <note>original: "Radt"; a circular badge or 'rota' commonly required in medieval Europe to distinguish Jews from Christians</note> upon their breast. Some other Councils added to this that their tabards and sleeves had to be of a specific length (b); but without pleats. They were required to wear the red hat in Toulouse around the beginning of the twelfth century. The use of the Wheel was confirmed in the fourteenth century, and for women and daughters, the Horn <note>A specific peaked or horned headdress intended to be conspicuous and humiliating</note> was added. Philip the Bold <note>original: "Philips de Onvertraagde"; Duke of Burgundy (1342–1404)</note> also desired that the Jews should wear a horn on their caps; a sorrowful identifying mark indeed. Distinguishing them from the Christians, they were thus put on display for the mockery of the common people. They were also forbidden from bathing in the water that Christians used for bathing. King John <note>John II of France (1319–1364)</note> wanted them to be distinguished by color, commanding them to use red and white (c). A Council of the fourteenth century judged that women, like the men, must wear the red wheel. The horned hat was commanded to be worn by men in various places. The Council of Salzburg confirmed this order in the year 1420. The wheel on the clothing, stitched with yellow threads, was commanded (d) to be worn by the Jews by a Council of Cologne in the year 1442. The women also had to provide themselves with two white threads on their heads. Two Popes (e) <note>Paul IV and Pius V</note> covered the Jews with a yellow hat, and the Jewish women with a veil of the same color. Likewise, they wore such a hat in Avignon; but in Venice, it had to be red; and as it is very common for fashions to change into something that was originally worn out; the Jews in Venice wore the finest scarlet which they lined with black taffeta. High hats, the turban, and violet shoes make up a part of the Jews' clothing in Constantinople and in the East, by which the faithful followers of *Mahomet* or *Ali* <note>Referring to Sunni and Shia Muslims</note> can be distinguished from the unfaithful, both the circumcised and the uncircumcised. Besides this, they are also greatly despised by the Muslims. *Borromeus* <note>Saint Charles Borromeo (1538–1584)</note>, Archbishop of Milan, who by the Roman Church is placed among the number of the

<column-break/>

Saints, forbade the Jews from going out without a hat and a yellow veil, and from leaving their houses three days before Easter to take up residence near the churches. Before him, the Council of Basel (f) introduced a part of these prohibitions. We shall, in ending this chapter, not forget their foul odor <note>original: "quaaden reuk"; a reference to the 'Foetor Judaicus,' a persistent medieval antisemitic myth claiming Jewish people possessed a distinctive, unpleasant smell that vanished only upon baptism</note>, and the blood with which their children are born. These are visible signs of the people's rejection and of the wrath of God, if one may believe certain Christians. It is then rightful to count these marks among the punishments to which the Jews are subject. *Avitus* <note>Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus (c. 450–518), Bishop of Vienne</note>, a Christian poet, has sung that the foul odor of the Jews is driven away by the grace of Baptism.

The residence of the Jews in Augsburg, when their trade requires them to be there, is sold to them for a heavy price; costing them one German guilder for every hour. In Trent, they may not stay longer than three days. Formerly they were allowed to reside there for this long: but subsequently they were denied this, because they had bravely defended Buda against the Emperor's army. Thus they were punished because they were loyal to their Sovereign. Must we not therefore conclude that loyalty is not owed to the unfaithful?

# CHAPTER VI.

## Concerning the SAINTS of the JEWISH CHURCH since Jerusalem’s second destruction; and various MIRACLES performed by them.

**W**e could find a fertile source of curiosities and miracles in the History of *Joseph, son of Gorion* <note>original: "Joseph, Gorions zoon"; referring to the author of the *Josippon*, a 10th-century history of the Jews often confused in the Middle Ages with the Roman-Jewish historian Flavius Josephus</note>, who might be called the Jews’ (a) *Jacobus de Voragine* <note>A 13th-century Archbishop of Genoa and author of the 'Golden Legend', a famous collection of hagiographies of Christian saints</note>: but without dwelling on that, we shall limit ourselves solely to a few remarkable examples.

<margin>What is told of Maimonides’ miracles,</margin>
*Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), also known as Rambam, one of the most influential Torah scholars and physicians of the Middle Ages</note> has been too famous for us not to mention him. This Jewish Scribe owes his birth in the year 1131 to the decision his father took to abandon the unmarried state in which he had previously lived. Nevertheless, *Maimon*, the father of *Moses Maimonides*, dared to decide nothing in this weighty matter without some special revelation. He flattered himself that a command from above might relieve him of his vow, perhaps made a little too rashly. His hope was not in vain. A dream made him understand that it would be permitted for him to marry in the future, with a butcher’s daughter being pointed out to *Maimon* in his sleep. This daughter, having become his wife, became the mother of *Maimonides* and died while giving birth to him. The father, having gained a taste for marriage, soon gave the young *Moses* a stepmother, but one of a wicked nature. He was beaten and treated poorly. He ran away, slept under the roof of a Synagogue, and upon waking, found himself a brilliant man, whereas he had previously been dull and slow of understanding. This miracle was not new. *Hesiod*, a lowly shepherd in *Boeotia* <note>A region in Ancient Greece</note>, had dreamed eighteen

<column-break/>

hundred years before *Maimonides’* birth that he became a poet, and indeed he was one upon waking. Subsequently, the Jew enjoyed the favor of the Egyptian Sultan, which brought the envy of the Muhammadan <note>original: "Mahometaansche"; a historical term for Muslim</note> Physicians upon his neck. They forced him to drink poison, imagining that *Maimonides’* expertise would succumb to the power of the poison. Having survived this danger, he conversely caused ten of these Physicians to burst, forcing them subsequently to undergo what they had brewed for him. He was also accused of plotting against the life of the Sultan. He was ordered to open his veins: but he saved his life by doing this to a vein known to no one but him, and which from then on had not been known to the most capable Anatomists; for since the correct vein was not opened, the hemorrhage held no danger. When he finally passed away and they intended to bury him, a band of highwaymen attacked those following his funeral. They took flight; the corpse of the deceased Scholar was abandoned, which the robbers wanted to throw into the sea: but these villains, not knowing they were dealing with a Saint, were powerless to lift him up.

<margin>and what befell Rabbi Judah before his birth.</margin>
The Rabbi *Judah the Pious* (b) fell into danger of dying before he was born (c). A hay wagon would have crushed her who was pregnant with him, as she found herself trapped between the wagon and a wall. Thereupon God commanded the wall to recede, so that the preg- <note>The text cuts off here due to the catchword 'zwan-' leading to 'zwangere' (pregnant) on the next page.</note>

The Jews honor the memory of their Saints and Martyrs in a *diptych* manner (a) <note>original: "Diptique"; likely referring to the practice of maintaining lists of martyrs to be read during communal prayers, similar to Christian liturgical diptychs</note>. Mention is found of one *Isaac Castro* of *Tartas*, whom the Portuguese burned alive (b) in *Lisbon*, and who endured this sentence with great steadfastness. The Amsterdam Jews regard <margin>Various miracles performed by Jews are recounted here.</margin> him as a Saint. Likewise, one finds notes of a Physician named *Silva*, whom the Spaniards wished to burn: but a violent storm extinguished the fire. This miracle is indeed the most recent. Of another burned in Portugal, the chains fell from his hands and feet, and he was so fortunate as to save himself—or rather, he disappeared through the assistance of an invisible power. *Dom Lopez de Vera*, who became a Jew and was subsequently named *Judah the Faithful*, suffered the sentence of fire with such great steadfastness and lack of softening for his eternal well-being that his judges stood amazed. From these examples one can judge that the steadfastness of those called Martyrs is not always from divine assistance, and that prejudices very often add an astonishing hardening. Let it then not be wondered at that Martyrs are found under all Religions. Shall one say it is madness, impulsiveness, stubbornness, or hypocrisy that works supernatural powers in man and makes him forget self-love? We shall conclude nothing on this, so as not to wrong this well-known saying: *that the cause makes a martyr, but not the punishment* <note>original: "dat de oorzaak een Martelaar maakt, maar niet de straf"; a translation of the Latin legal and theological maxim *Martyrem facit causa, non poena*, often attributed to St. Augustine</note>; but however it may be, Martyrs of Morality are not very common (c), as long as they view their basic rules as a foundation for numerous Religions. Let us present a few more examples of Saints of the Jewish Church and their miracles.

<margin>Jochanan’s conduct is noted, along with other rare occurrences.</margin> *Jochanan* (d) <note>Yochanan ben Zakkai, a primary contributor to the core of the Jewish Oral Law, the Mishnah</note> was of an exemplary pure conduct. He took care to be at least four cubits <note>approx. 6 feet or 2 meters</note> away from a house of prayer when he was forced to relieve himself. He celebrated the feast days with godliness, and to better observe the Sabbath, he drank until he became drunk. How easily the

<column-break/>

irregularity of this godliness is noticed.

When *Judah the Holy* (e) <note>Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century Chief Rabbi and editor of the Mishnah</note> was buried, the day lengthened, and the night delayed until everyone had returned home to light their Sabbath lamp. *The Daughter of the Voice* <note>original: "De Dochter der stemme"; a translation of the Hebrew *Bat Kol*, a divine echo or heavenly voice that provided guidance to the Sages</note> proclaimed that all who had been in the funeral procession would be pardoned, except for one who died in despair. This Daughter of the Voice was commonly a good or evil omen, which one drew from the first words spoken by the first person one heard, or whom one met upon seeking counsel. This word was as awe-inspiring as the Oracle of Divine Providence, and Jews have been seen mad enough to value it higher than those of the Prophets of the Old Testament; and these words were spoken by chance. Thus have the Pagans consulted their fate with the verses of *Homer* and *Virgil*; likewise, superstitious Christians formerly sought to know the outcome of their undertakings in the Bible by opening it at two or three different places by chance.

The Spiritual offices naturally having precedence over all others, it is not difficult to understand how one <margin>How the power of miracles acts upon the human imagination.</margin> presumes that God favors them with certain special gifts of grace. It is enough to be a Priest or Theologian to believe one is the possessor of the secrets of the Supreme Being, and what is more, to imagine it to oneself. From this arise miracle-working deeds attributed to these Spiritual duties. The Tradition-bearers <note>The Sages who passed down the Oral Law</note> were formerly among the number of these privileged ones, since they were the possessors of the *Traditions* <note>The Oral Law or Talmudic traditions</note>, and the care of leaving them to posterity was recommended to them. These Traditions consisted of very many religious linguistic quibbles, yet they were so necessary to the faithful Jews that without them it was impossible for the Law given by God to Moses to pave the way to Heaven for them. It was fair that such a heavy service was accompanied by many uncommon gifts. These excellent guides performed miracles; they had power over the devil; they resisted enchanting works; they foretold or foresaw the death of the sick, etc. We shall—

## CHAPTER VII.

->*Of the Sects of the Jews, such as* SAMARITANS, KARAITES, SADDUCEES, PHARISEES, HALF-JEWS, SABBATARIANS, ESSENES, HERODIANS *and* CHINESE JEWS.<-

There are two sects that the Jews regard as schismatics, heretics, and those worthy of excommunication: namely, the Samaritans and the Karaites.

<margin>Concerning the investigation into the beliefs of the SAMARITANS.</margin>

II. They hate the other Jews with a deadly hatred, and the other Jews do the same to them.
III. Just as the name *Jehovah* (b) is unpronounceable to the Jews, so it is also for the Samaritans, who read *Sema* <note>original: "Sema"; likely the Samaritan pronunciation of the Hebrew "HaShem," meaning "The Name," used to avoid speaking the sacred tetragrammaton</note> in its place.

VI. They deny the substantial reality of the Angels, and explain the Scriptural passages where these spirits are mentioned by the word *Command* or *Power*: *God sent an Angel* (c), by which they wish to indicate that God gave a *Command*. The Angel of God did *such a thing*, namely, the *Power of God* worked, etc. Nevertheless, there are scholars who believe that the Samaritans truly believe in the reality of these spirits.
VII. Their High Priest is the Judge of the people. All things are settled by his decision and before his tribunal. These High Priests claim to have their origin from *Aaron*.

(d) *See the Discourse of Father Simon, which follows hereafter.*

If the new Moon falls on the eleventh of the month of *Adar* (a), they add a month in between, counting 13 months in that year, and the month that follows is the first month of the year. If the month begins on the twelfth of *Adar* or a day after, it is the first month of the year, and they then count twelve months.

# On the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

XII. On the 15th of the same month, they celebrate their **Festival of Tabernacles** <note>original: "Loofhutten Feest"; also known as Sukkot, a harvest festival where booths are built to remember the Israelites' trek through the desert</note>. They set up tents and rejoice for seven days; the eighth day, which is the last of the festival, is spent in praising God.

XIII. They pay close attention to whether the *conjunction* of the Sun and Moon occurs during the night or at midday. If it happens before six o'clock, this day is the first of the month. If it occurs at six o'clock or a little later, the start of the month is postponed to the following day. If the *conjunction* concerns the Moon, the month has 29 days, and 30 if it concerns the Sun. If the new Moon falls on the eleventh of the month of *Adar* (a), they add a month in between, counting 13 months in that year, and the month that follows is the first month of the year. If the month begins on the twelfth of *Adar* or a day after, it is the first month of the year, and they then count twelve months.

XIV. They pour out the water of Separation <note>original: "Onderscheiding"; likely referring to ritual purification rites</note>, so-called, on the thirteenth or fourteenth day, especially if it is defiled by the touch of women. They pour it out on the seventh day for a woman who has suffered a loss. Regarding the childbirth of a son, the days of separation are 41, but for a daughter 80 <note>This refers to the biblical laws of purification found in Leviticus 12</note>.

XV. They believe in a general judgment, which will be a day of vengeance upon the wicked, and a day of peace and reward for the pious.

We have taken a portion of these observations (b) from several letters written by the Samaritans around the year 1690.

<margin>The opinion of the KARAITES and their customs and habits considered in eleven parts.</margin>
As for the *Karaites*, they reside in the East, and even in Poland and Lithuania. The other Jews sometimes mix them with the *Sadducees*; and to make them hateful, they call them (c) *Cutheans* or *Samaritans*, *Epicureans* <note>In Jewish tradition, the term "Apikoros" (Epicurean) is used to describe a heretic or one who denies divine revelation</note>, etc. These *Karaites* are less superstitious than the other Jews.

I. They reject the alleged (d) oral Law <note>The Oral Torah or Talmudic tradition</note> given to Moses on Mount Sinai

<column-break/>

given, and in this regard, they do toward the Jews what the Calvinists do toward the Roman Catholics <note>A common 17th-century comparison: just as Protestants rejected Catholic tradition for "Scripture alone," the Karaites rejected the Talmud for the written Torah alone</note>. This oral Law of Moses is a convenient invention that helps support the yoke of numerous trifles that the Jewish Scholars have commanded within Judaism, and which have been imperceptibly introduced as essential matters belonging to Religion.

II. This has caused their Judaism to be purer. They bind themselves carefully to the original Text of the Holy Scripture and believe (e) that interpretations, however concise they may be, always weaken its power. They demand a blind trust and do not wish to doubt in the least the essence of God nor the divinity of the Law.

III. These latter desire that astronomical calculation be necessary to establish their years accordingly; and the former wish that one must not establish them until after the first appearance of the New Moon. They reject the chronologies and intercalations <note>the insertion of leap days or months into a calendar</note>, since Moses did not introduce them (f). One cannot deny that there is some ridiculous prejudice in the conduct of the Karaites. The ministry of Moses could not prevent a custom, indifferent in itself to religion, from being completed. It is because of this blind authority that they hold this ancient error, and because of the tribute given without judgment to the establishers of certain customs, that many dangerous superstitions must be attributed to them.

and helped carry out the residency with the Powers of the State. The Italian Jews are also regarded as *Benjamites*; yet not as contemptibly as the High German ones. Nevertheless, a Portuguese man will not give his daughter to an Italian Jew.

<margin>Matters noted regarding the Chinese Jews.</margin> The Chinese Jews can be considered a special Sect. According to the report of *Father Gozani* <note>Jean-Paul Gozani was a Jesuit missionary who visited the Jewish community in Kaifeng, China, in the early 1700s</note> they differ in these following points:
->I. Although they have no images, they nevertheless place the *Tablet*, upon which the name of the Emperor is written, in the chair of *Moses*; which would be viewed as a profanation by the European Jews.<-
->II. They use censers with incense to honor the memory of the Holy Patriarchs, etc.<-
->III. They mix many fables and ridiculous stories with the true matters of the Holy Scripture; in which they possibly partly agree with the *Rabbis* of the European Jews. It would be necessary to know if it is in the interpretation or in the text that they also mix these fables?<-
->IV. They honor *Confucius*, and attend the solemn services with the other Chinese which they perform in his honor.<-
->V. In the spring and in the autumn, they perform Funeral Rites for their Ancestors in the manner of other Chinese; and set meat before them, but abstain from pork.<-
->VI. They seem to have no idea of the *Messiah*.<-

### Of the Jews' Confession of Faith; and of specific Articles of Faith,

<margin>Of the thirteen principal Articles of Faith.</margin> The faithful Jews may not alienate themselves from this Confession of Faith, which includes the fundamental Articles of their Religion; (d) which we set down here; and every Jew confesses thus.
I. I believe with perfect confidence, that God, forever blessed, the Creator—

(a) These are the words of *Basnage* <note>Jacques Basnage, a notable historian of the Jews</note>.
(b) This is what we say on the faith of some Jews: but see here what an intelligent and enlightened Writer says of it, in his *Memoirs and observations concerning England* <note>original: "Memoires en observations touchant l'Angleterre"</note> page 267, printed in the year 1693.
"There is a society of men known under the name of Sabbatarians. They profess to expect a thousand-year kingdom... These Sabbatarians are thus named, because they do not wish to transfer the Day of Rest from Saturday to Sunday. They finish the work of Friday evening early, and are very strict in observing the Sabbath. They administer Baptism to adults... Most among them eat no blood, nor pork, nor that which is strangled... Their morals are strict, and all their outward behavior is Pious and Christian." These Sabbatarians are then marked as Jewish Christians in certain points.
(c) Among the Portuguese Jews they are called *Benjamites* or Jews of the tribe of *Benjamin*.

## On the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

...creator and Sustainer of all that is Created; that he has done everything, that he does everything, and that he will do everything, until the end of all ages.
II. I believe, etc. *That God is one*, and that there is nothing to be compared with his unity. He has been, he is, and he shall always be, God alone eternally blessed.
III. I believe, etc. *That God is not physical*; that he is not tangible, and cannot be understood as material; and that nothing exists that is like him.

VIII. I believe, etc. *That God gave the Law to Moses (b) our Master* exactly as we now possess it.
IX. I believe, etc. *That God will never change this Law, nor give any other.*
X. I believe, etc. *That God searches the thoughts of all men, and that he knows all their works.*
XI. I believe, etc. *That God will reward the doers of good and punish the evildoers.*
XII. I believe, etc. *That the Messiah must come, and I shall always and constantly await him*, until he comes.
XIII. I believe, etc. *That God shall raise the dead.* I do not know the time of this resurrection: but it shall nonetheless be, when it is the will of God, eternally blessed. May his memory be glorified into all ages, AMEN!

<margin>Seven Articles upon which the Jews do not agree.</margin>
I. The Jews have much respect for the Angels: but they neither worship them nor serve them as Advocates and Mediators. Nonetheless, they address them (d) on certain occasions. According to *Buxtorf*, there are Jews who attribute great power to the prayer which they call the 72 verses. These verses, recited with zeal, have the power to draw the Angels to oneself and to compel them to provide help to the petitioner. *A. Ross* <note>Alexander Ross (1590–1654), a Scottish writer who published a famous catalog of world religions</note> asserts "that the Jews believe that before their Synagogue there is a good and an evil Angel, to take note of who is the most zealous and attentive in prayer. These Angels take oversight of their houses, and finding everything pure and tidy, they depart with joy, etc." Thus speaks the good man likewise in the translation of his book (e) by *Tomas la Grue*, Master of Liberal Arts and Doctor of Medicine. At the very least, he should have named the author who provided him with such a remarkable detail.
II. They offer prayers to the Saints. A learned German (f) cites this. (g) The pilgrimages of the Jews to the grave of the Prophet Ezekiel and the miracles they promote on the Prophet's account seem to confirm it. *One would not propose these fictions among the Jews, says Bayle, if the invocation of Saints seemed a forbidden thing to them.* (h) <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a famous philosopher and encyclopedist</note>
III. They admit to Purgatory or the Place of Purification, and it is to deliver their friends that they recite the prayer called Cadish <note>Kaddish, the prayer recited for the dead</note> daily for eleven months. (i)
IV. The Congregation prays (k) for the dead. The friends of the deceased gather in the morning and evening, and pray...

### SECOND HISTORICAL TREATISE, etc.

<columns>2</columns>

...to pray (a) for his soul for seven days. They also give Alms (b) and make offerings for the soul of the deceased.

V. The Traditions <term>Overleveringen: This refers to the Oral Law (Torah she-be'al peh), which includes the interpretations and legal discussions later compiled in the Talmud</term>, the absolute necessity of which they acknowledge, are an extensive supplement to the Law they received from Moses. It is possible that these Traditions are the silent expressions found in the 7th, 8th, and 9th Articles of the Creed <note>Referring to the Thirteen Principles of Faith listed on the previous page</note>.

VI. They hold various opinions regarding the Messiah. Some believe that his coming is delayed because of the sins of the people. Jewish Scholars assert that there shall come two Messiahs: one who is poor and wretched <note>This likely refers to Messiah ben Joseph, a figure in Jewish eschatology who suffers and dies in battle</note>, and the other glorified and powerful <note>Messiah ben David, the final redeemer</note>. The latter shall restore them to their former glory; he shall destroy their enemies; and his Kingdom shall be temporal

<column-break/>

in nature. There have been some Scholars who have written that the Messiah had already come long ago, and that he was being expected in vain.

VII. They are not in complete agreement regarding the concepts of Paradise, Hell, and Resurrection. Many Jews flatter themselves with the idea that Paradise will be for them a dwelling place full of pleasure, where the delights of the senses will take place, and where companionship with women—as a primary element of true delight—will be permitted and allowed. We may rest assured that they shape their thoughts according to their desires, and that many people would greatly please themselves in advance if religion guaranteed them this Article.

---

(a) The reason that obliges them to pray in community is that they are certain that God allows himself to be found in a gathering of many persons who pray together. In these private gatherings, there must specifically be no more than ten persons <note>While ten men (a Minyan) are required for communal prayer, the author suggests here that private groups were limited to ten to ensure the main synagogue services remained the primary place of worship</note>. If they exceed the number of ten, the heads of the Synagogue have the right to forbid them, due to the harm they might cause to public assemblies.

(b) These Alms are performed with much pride and haughtiness. The Jews assure us that prayer for the dead exists among them because of the great benefits the Synagogue enjoys through these offerings.
