The Council formerly possessed an almost Supreme Authority. They were attributed infallibility in religious decisions: but scholars constantly disputed this delicate and essential point, which subjected the faith of all believers to 70 Persons. This Council was also attributed the power to judge Kings. But this point was no less disputed than the other. The Council had the right to pass judgment on life and death, and furthermore to explain the Law and to take notice of all Ecclesiastical matters. Gabinius, Governor of Syria on behalf of the Roman Court, granted the Council these privileges around 57 years before the birth of Jesus Christ.

<margin>Where the Sanhedrin met, which is now abolished.</margin>
The Great *Sanhedrin* held its meetings in the Temple at Jerusalem, and received the appealed sentences of the Law Courts of the other Cities of Judea. These lower Courts were called the Little *Sanhedrin*, consisting of 23 persons.

This is all we deem necessary to say on this subject of the Great *Sanhedrin* and the lower Council meetings; since both have come to an end since the destruction of Jerusalem. They have never been seen to revive since this destruction, and one finds nothing in the Histories of our time relevant to it, unless it be a Council held by the Jews in the previous century in Hungary. These Ceremonies and particulars are reported by *Basnage* (a), having been informed of them by an English Jew who said he had attended this presumed Council.

<margin>A Council allegedly held by the Jews in Hungary, and what was discussed therein.</margin>
This *Council*, which was held thirty miles from *Buda* in the plain of *Ageda* <note>The "Council of Ageda" (1650) is a famous narrative, though many modern historians consider the account by Samuel Brett—which Basnage cites—to be a fabrication or highly exaggerated.</note>, was assembled to investigate everything concerning the *Messiah*, and subsequently to give ripe consideration to whether he had come or not. Three hundred Rabbis made up this venerable Assembly. They were encamped under Tents, of which the largest served as the Meeting Hall.

<column-break/>

No one was recognized as a Member of this Assembly unless he spoke Hebrew and showed his genealogical table. A President was chosen, descended from the lineage of Levi. It was he who made the proposals, seated at a table opposite the East Gate, having the Scholars of the assembly sitting around him in a row.

The first day was spent in mutual courtesies and honors; they kissed one another brotherly, and excluded anyone who could not prove his right to a seat. On the second day, a proposal was made with these words: *We must investigate whether the Messiah has come, or whether we must still expect him.* Some Rabbis indicated that they believed he had come: but the denial prevailed, and it was decided that the true cause of this mournful delay must be attributed to the people's ungodliness and crimes. The former were divided between two particular opinions: Some found the marks of the Messiah in *Elias* <note>Elijah</note> and others in Jesus Christ. A certain Rabbi dwelt long on the miracles of the latter: but he was vehemently refuted. The fathers of the Council then consulted in investigating how the Messiah was to come, and it was decided that he was to be expected as a Conqueror, that he would make no change in the Religion, and was to be born of a Virgin.

The Council had already sat for six days when six Clergymen arrived from Rome and appeared before the Assembly; who, after they had attempted to prove the coming of the Messiah, showed the Jews the excellence of the Ceremonies of the Church, the dignity of the Service, the riches and the authority of the visible Head of the Church, who is the Vicar of the Messiah, etc.: but they unanimously rejected all these things as so contrary to the spirit of Judaism, and they pronounced a kind of curse against the *God-Man* <note>original: "Mensch-Godt"; referring to the Christian doctrine of the Incarnation</note>, against the intercession of the Saints, Iconography <note>original: "Beeldendienst"; literally "image service" or "idolatry"</note>, and the invocation of the Virgin.

# Concerning the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

We have presented the History and the Ceremony of this Council thus far: but the authority of the English Writer who has written this History does not seem firm enough to us to take him at his word. Is it indeed probable that such a solemn Assembly as this Council would have been tolerated by the Princes? That the Jews would have been so bold as to express themselves with such disdain against Jesus Christ, etc., and that in the presence of some Clergy come from Rome? That this Assembly would have caused no stir in the world, and that one should consider it of value to have to trust a single man regarding this Article?

<margin>Special Courts.</margin>
After the destruction of the ancient *Sanhedrim* <note>The Sanhedrin was the supreme council and tribunal of the Jews in ancient Israel.</note>, the Jews established special Courts in its place to pass judgment on matters of 

## CHAPTER II.

->Of the JEWISH SYNAGOGUE and its Dedication.<-

---

The Synagogues were established upon the return from the Jewish captivity. One must seek their origin in the dispersion of the Jews, which made them necessary; for a portion of the Jewish people finding themselves too far from Jerusalem, it was impossible for them to accurately perform their duty before God in the Temple of Jerusalem. It then required the establishment and erection of Assemblies or Synagogues in those places where a Prince granted them freedom of conscience. Nevertheless, one can regard these first Synagogues as Temples: the Law was explained there: but it was not permitted for them to offer sacrifices there, and it was always required, as much as was ever possible, to perform their worship in Jerusalem. It was the great flood of salvation, where the small streams were necessitated, sooner or later, to bring their tribute. For in some places they had certain persons of an outstanding holiness beyond the usual, with whom the believers assembled and practiced their piety. These assemblies were true Synagogues, although they did not bear that name. The wealthy sometimes had a Governor of conscience, and it is probable that one should thus regard the Levites 

<column-break/>

<margin>established by the Jews after the destruction of the Sanhedrin, whose members are called *Parnassims*.</margin>
conscience and points of dispute. These Spiritual Courts, which were subsequently called houses of judgment, were an imperfect image of the *Sanhedrim*: however, they still exist today; but with a much more limited authority than formerly. Those whom they call *Parnassim* <note>Parnassim (plural of Parnes) are lay leaders or trustees of a Jewish congregation, responsible for administrative and financial matters.</note> make up these small Courts. These *Parnassim* are secular men chosen for that purpose by a majority of votes. They take care to collect the money of alms and offerings, and distribute it to the poor; they are Directors of the Synagogue; they generally provide for the needs of the Church <note>The author uses the Dutch word 'Kerke' (Church) here to refer to the Jewish religious community or building.</note>, and judge certain disputes, even in matters of religious conflict. Finally, they strike the rebellious and the apostates with the lightning of excommunication: but one rarely finds examples of it.

<margin>How the Jews formerly built their Synagogues.</margin>
In former times, the Jews built their Synagogues outside the cities and surrounded by trees: nowadays they choose an elevated place in the cities where they are granted the practice of Judaism. The building must be higher than the common houses; for, they say, *the House of our God must be exalted*. The interior of the Synagogue has been very well described by *Leon de Modena* <note>Leone di Modena (1571–1648) was a famous Venetian Rabbi and scholar whose work on Jewish rituals was widely read by Christians.</note> in the first Treatise. The Synagogue must be built such that the entrance looks out upon the place of prayer; namely, that if one prays one turns toward the East, and the door is toward the West; this arrangement is made so that the Jews bow toward the Ark (a) when entering the Synagogue.

<margin>The layout of the Synagogue considered.</margin>
The seats are distributed there for money, and this income serves to maintain the Synagogue: but it is not permitted to place oneself between the Reading-place <note>The Bimah or platform where the Torah is read.</note> and the Ark, because those who occupied these places would turn their backs to the Ark in the view of the Teacher; for such a position could only bring dishonor and offense to the believers.

# SECOND HISTORICAL TREATISE

The Jews must religiously observe the respect that is owed to the Synagogue, and refrain from speaking of any business matters there. (a) They are even forbidden from thinking of temporal interests. One must also take great care not to sleep there, nor to cast one's eyes hither and thither, etc. It is required that the Jews maintain a modest disposition and cast away all impure thoughts. We shall subsequently speak more broadly of what true Jews are obliged to do when we describe the ceremonies of prayer.

The Jews call their Synagogue *Beth Hakkenefeth* <gloss>original Hebrew: *Beit Knesset*, meaning "House of Assembly"</gloss>, which signifies a *House for Gathering*.

The Jesuit *Gozzani* <note>Father Jean-Paul Gozzani was a missionary who visited the Jewish community in Kaifeng, China, in the early 18th century.</note> has provided us with an accurate description of the Jews' Synagogue in China. This is his report: "Their Synagogue is oriented toward the West for the same reason that European Jews set theirs toward the East. Both have this regard for the direction of Jerusalem: because this City lies to the East in Europe and to the West in China."

<margin>
A Jewish Synagogue in China described.
</margin>

"Their Synagogue is divided into three sections, corresponding to the Churches of Europe. The first division, and the Most Holy, corresponds somewhat to the *Hechal* <gloss>the Ark or Sanctuary where the Torah scrolls are kept</gloss> of our Jews, and even better with the *Holy of Holies* of the Ancient Temple. It is there that they lock away the Books of Moses' Law. The Head of the Synagogue, whose authority corresponds to the Ancient High Priest, alone has the privilege of entering this holy place. Father *Gozzani* saw twelve Tabernacles made in the manner of Arks for the twelve tribes of Israel, and a thirteenth for Moses, placed upon tables, and each draped with curtains. In each of these Tabernacles were the five Books of Moses locked away, which they called *Kim* <note>original: "Kim". This likely refers to the Chinese word *jing* (经), meaning "classic" or "scripture," used by the Kaifeng Jews to describe the Torah.</note>, written on long parchments and wound upon rolls.
"In the second part of the Chinese Synagogue, according to the report of *Gozzani*, one saw an elevated pulpit, entirely corresponding to the part of the Synagogues where the reading of the Law takes place on the Sabbath and other feast days. This pulpit serves them in the same use as the *Theba* <gloss>the *tevah* or *bimah*, the platform used for reading the Torah</gloss>: but it does not correspond to the Hall

<column-break/>

"which *Gozzani* saw upon exiting this Synagogue, and which constituted the third part of the same. This had little resemblance to the place where the people gather in European Synagogues, and looked more like an outer chamber of the Ancient Temple. Father *Gozzani* saw many censers there with which they possibly burned incense in memory of their most prominent Forefathers.
This description is to be found in the *seventh collection* of the *Edifying and Curious Letters* of certain *Missionaries* <note>The *Lettres édifiantes et curieuses* was a famous 34-volume collection of reports sent by Jesuit missionaries from around the world.</note>.

<margin>
How and when the Jewish Synagogue in Amsterdam was dedicated.
</margin>

As for the dedication of Synagogues, we shall describe the particular ceremony thereof, which must not be confused with the Feast of *Chanuccah* <gloss>Hanukkah, the Festival of Lights</gloss>. We shall elaborate on it when we treat the Feasts of the Jews.
Here we show the dedication (b) of the famous Synagogue of the Portuguese Jews in Amsterdam. This Synagogue, the finest to be found anywhere, was dedicated with all conceivable solemnity on the 10th of the month of *Menahem* <gloss>The Hebrew month of Av</gloss> of the year 5435, corresponding to the second of August 1675. The most prominent among the Jews carried the Law, richly decorated, in a procession, and distinguished themselves on the occasion of the introduction of their sacred Books through piety and extraordinary alms. Their devotion was accompanied by pleasant Music, and several moving Sermons concerning the solemnity of a day that is worthy of being placed among the most memorable that their people have experienced since the destruction of Jerusalem. The Feast lasted eight days, and it is still celebrated annually on the second of August.

<margin>
How and where it was built.
</margin>

This Synagogue is built in the East of the City; it has a length of 150 feet and a width of 100 feet, excluding the courtyard and surrounding walls. The height is seventy feet up to the vaulting. Two galleries for the women are built along the right and left sides of the Synagogue, and five rows of lamps illuminate this building on the Sabbath. The *Hechal* <gloss>the Ark</gloss> and *Theba* <gloss>reading desk</gloss> are made of Rosewood <note>original: "Sakkerdanen hout," referring to Brazilian Rosewood or Jacaranda, a luxury timber.</note>. Four prominent Jews (c) laid the four cornerstones of the Synagogue's foundation.

# III. CHAPTER.
## Concerning the MEETINGS and SCHOOLS of the Jewish Scholars, their RABBIS and Scribes.

<margin>Origins and use of the Jewish Schools.</margin>
The Jews call the Meetings of the Learned *Bathe Hammidrash* <term>Beit Midrash; literally "House of Study"</term>, or *Explanation-Houses*, since the Law is taught there along with its interpretation and Rabbinical expansions. The establishment of these Learned Meetings and Schools is very ancient among the Jews; in former times, the Prophets were the presiding officers: but one should not imagine that the prophetic gifts were obtained there through human exercises (c). We are of the opinion that the Law was explained there, instruction in godliness was given, and the mysteries of religion were unfolded. Possibly, poetry and music were also taught there, which in former times were two essential parts of the Temple service.

The Schools are commonly located near the Synagogue. Instruction is given there in all the subtleties of the *Talmud* <term>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism containing legal and legendary traditions</term>, and they debate fiercely over useless matters. It was permitted to eat and drink in these Schools, although it was forbidden in the Synagogue (d). This is said on the condition that the desire and necessity for study forced them to remain in the Schools for a long time: meanwhile, among the Jews, these schools acquired a higher dignity than the Synagogues.

According to the Rabbis, one must go to School with contentment and diligence, after having washed oneself well, and provided with the (e) *Zizith* <term>Tzitzit; the ritual fringes worn on the corners of garments</term> and prayer. One must even enter with a fierce passion, but depart with regret; for it is there that

## CHAPTER III.
### Concerning the ASSEMBLIES and SCHOOLS of Jewish Scholars, their RABBIS, and Scribes.

<margin>Origins of the use of Jewish Schools.</margin>
The Jews call the *Assemblies* of scholars *Bathe Hammidrasch* <note>original: "Bathe Hammidrasch," from the Hebrew Beit Midrash</note>, or *Houses of Interpretation*, since the *Law* is taught there along with its explanations and Rabbinic expansions. The institution of these Scholarly Assemblies and Schools is very ancient among the Jews; in former times, the Prophets were the presiding officers. However, one should not imagine that the prophetic gifts were acquired there through human exercises (c). We are of the opinion that the Law was explained there, piety was taught, and the mysteries of religion were unfolded. It is possible that poetry and music were also taught there, which in ancient times were two essential parts of the Temple service.

The Schools are commonly located near the Synagogue. There, instruction is given in all the quibbles of the <term>Talmud|The central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara</term>, and they dispute fiercely over useless matters. It was permitted to eat and drink in these Schools, although it was forbidden in the Synagogue (d). This is said on the condition that the desire and necessity for study forced them to remain in the Schools for a long time; meanwhile, among the Jews, these [Schools] attained a higher dignity than the Synagogues.

According to the Rabbis, one had to go to School with contentment and diligence, after having washed oneself well and being provided with the (e) <term>Zizith|The ritual fringes or tassels worn by observant Jews</term> and prayer. SECOND HISTORICAL DISCOURSE

wise, learned, and all other great men can adopt. Currently, these titles are much disparaged, and the names of Rabbi, Scribe, Master, etc., command very little or no respect anymore; instead, they almost serve as a mark of ignorance. <note>The author reflects a period of internal or external critique regarding traditional Jewish leadership titles.</note>

Jewish Scholars are not satisfied with the name of Rabbi; some, however glorious that title may appear to them, subsequently desire to acquire others. In the East, they give themselves the name of *Mir*, or *Mor*, and *Maran*, all three meaning "Lord." In Spain, they adopt the title of *Wise Men*; but it is believed that the scholars who bore this title were of a lower rank than the Rabbis. Finally, the heads of the high Assemblies claim for themselves the titles of "the resting-place," "the refuge," (a) and "the seat" or "the bed of the Law." These qualities are by no means beyond the reach of these Scholars, who pride themselves on being infallible in their decisions. Besides the privilege of lecturing and teaching, the Rabbis also possess the right to *bind and loose*, <term>to bind and loose: a legal authority to declare specific actions or items either forbidden (bound) or permitted (loosed) under religious law</term> namely, to make decisions as to whether a matter must be forbidden or may be permitted. They elect new Scholars and confirm their appointment

<column-break/>

and progress by the laying on of hands. However, they limit the power of these Scholars as they please. One is appointed to explain the Law, or only the disputes concerning the Law; another has only the power to judge among those who debate these disputes. Despite being provided with these fine privileges, they are not always shown the respect that corresponds to the Office of a Scholar among them, for sometimes they are exposed to the contempt of their own people. Nevertheless, the Rabbis easily console themselves regarding the world’s contempt, since they imagine that, by favor of the holiness of their Office, the Gate of Paradise must always stand open for them. Thus, those who are advocates of Religion more easily convince themselves that Heaven is always open to them; they cannot conceive it possible that, after having labored so zealously through the power of teaching for the salvation of the people, they could be excluded by God. To be sure, the example of Moses, who had to forego entry into the Land of Canaan after he had led the Israelites to the borders, is not very favorable to the Rabbis. <note>A subtle theological jab suggesting that even the greatest leader, Moses, was not guaranteed his earthly goal despite his service.</note>

# ON THE RELIGIOUS DUTIES OF THE JEWS.

Knowledge of the **Talmud** <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note>, combined with a certain sharpness in debating and constant activity in the Schools, suffices for the dignity of a **Rabbi**.

The **Cantor** <note>original: *Chazan*</note> must call out loudly for the person who is worthy of becoming a **Rabbi**, and invite him, calling him "**Rabbi [Name], son of such-a-one**," to approach the sacred Books of the Law. However, the young scholar ostensibly <note>original: *quanswys* - a Dutch term suggesting a modest or feigned pretense</note> refuses at the first invitation; he excuses himself citing his own inability and the heavy weight of that burden. After these preliminary formalities, he approaches the Law with a stately step, his face covered with the **Tallit** <note>original: *Taled*; a fringed prayer shawl</note>.

<margin>The dignity of their **Morenu**, and what the duty of the **Rabbis** consists of.</margin> The **Morenu** (this name means "one who teaches") is above the **Rabbi**. He holds the position of President among the **Rabbis**. This dignity, formerly unknown to the Jews, originated in Germany in the fifteenth century.

The duty of the **Rabbis** is to uphold justice; to exhort others to virtue and purity; to resolve doubts and difficulties; to excommunicate <note>original: *in den Ban te slaan*</note> those who live improperly, or those who do not observe the Sabbath and the days of Penance; to perform and dissolve marriages; to explain the Law, and so forth.

Thus, the office of **Rabbi** is diffi-

<column-break/>

-cult to perform well, although it brings in almost no profit. There are but a few, such as those in Cologne and Frankfurt called the **First** or **Great Rabbi**, who draw income from their dignity; even the other **Rabbis** cannot choose a new **Rabbi** without his permission.

The privileges attached to this office are exemption from taxes and duties. If the **Rabbi** engages in trade, he has the right to sell his goods much sooner and more advantageously than others, so that the time he loses with commerce is not detrimental to his studies. He is also helped first in matters of litigation; he is permitted to sit before his Judges, etc. A portion of these privileges are now abolished, as the Jews no longer have absolute authority.

Regarding the **Cantor** <note>original: *Chazan*</note> and the **Beadle** <note>original: *Sciamas* - derived from Shamash, a synagogue sexton</note>, **Rabbi Leon de Modena** * <note>A famous 17th-century Venetian scholar whose works explained Jewish customs to the Christian world.</note> has already given us a report. The duties of the High Priest and Priests are now entirely suspended or abolished, since there is no longer a Temple, nor slaughter, nor offerings. We have nothing to add to what **Leon de Modena** has said of it. The name **Cohen** <note>Priest</note> is now little more than a title of honor.

## CHAPTER V.

### Concerning the Jewish TALLIT or HEAD-COVERING; the TZITZIT or TASSELS; the TEFILLIN or FRONTLETS; and some other customs regarding prayer.

<margin>The origin of the use of the Jewish **Tallit** or head-covering indicated, and the same described with the **Tzitzit**.</margin> The **Tallit** (a) is a white square veil with cords and tassels at each corner.

The Jews cover their heads with it in the Synagogue while they pray, or roll it around the neck. When **Moses** returned from Mount Sinai to the camp of the Israelites, after he had enjoyed the honor of dealing directly with God, the radiance of the Divine Majesty shone from the face of this great Lawgiver, by which the People were blinded. (b) Then **Moses** had to cover his face with a veil; and this is, according to some Scholars, the first origin of the **Tallit**. It is also thought that the **Tallit** was invented to prevent distracting thoughts during prayer, since

<column-break/>

<margin>Their four-cornered garment called **Arba-kanfoth** worn under their clothes, how this consists.</margin> one also sees that the most devout cover themselves with it entirely. Be that as it may, in former times the Jews wore a four-cornered garment. A tassel hung from each corner of the garment, which served to distinguish the Jews. Subsequently, the garment was abolished; the use of the veil passed into the Synagogue; but the four-cornered garment was not expressly forbidden; it was merely changed into a single square of fabric, of which **Rabbi Leon de Modena** gives us a description. A faithful Jew must especially wear this fabric, as it serves as a preservative against temptations and prevents him from sinning. The cords with the tassels hanging from the four corners are called **Tzitzit**.

# SECOND HISTORICAL DISCOURSE

called <term>Zizith</term> <note>Tassels or fringes worn on the corners of garments as a reminder of God's commandments.</note>. Each cord of the *Zizith* has five knots, representing the five Books of *Moses*. When dressing, this cloth must hang down in front and behind, for a righteous Jew must be provided with and surrounded by the commands of the Law, as if by a bulwark. To move on to other precepts; (a) the Jew, while dressing in the morning, must say: *Blessed be God, who has sanctified us through His Law, and commanded us to put on the Zizith.* This blessing must be spoken while looking at the *Zizith*, and finish before it is hung around the body. There are those who kiss them while pronouncing the blessing.

The *Zizith* encompasses the 613 commandments of the Law. (b) Thus the Scholars among the Jews have taken the trouble to count them. As such, it is absolutely necessary to always be covered with the *Zizith* and to observe due attention to it; for a Jew who is meticulous regarding this article observes the 613 commandments at the same time, and the conclusion is clear. We refer the reader to Buxtorf (c), who provides the proofs regarding the power of the *Zizith*, drawn from the Rabbinical writers.

<margin>Description of the Jews' Tefillin or Arm- and Head-bands.</margin> Leon de Modena <note>A famous 17th-century Venetian Rabbi known for explaining Jewish customs to the Christian world.</note> has written accurately about the <term>Tefillin</term> <note>Small leather boxes containing Torah verses, worn on the arm and forehead during weekday morning prayers.</note>, which the Greeks have called *Phylacteries*. It is a very holy matter among the Jews, and one which they wish to trace back to the time of *Moses*, since he says to the People: *You shall bind these words for signs around your hands. They shall be as frontlets between your eyes. You shall write them upon the posts of your gates.*

<margin>And of what use they are.</margin> The *Tefillin* of the arm is placed first, and then that of the head: but conversely, the one for the head is removed first, and then the one for the arm. The ink used to write what is enclosed in the *Tefillin* must be pure and black. The letters must be well distinguished from one another. One must write the scriptural passage starting from the right hand. No crossing out must be tolerated in the writing. In a word, if any defect were found in these *Tefillin*, the prayer of the user would be power-

<column-break/>

-less, and God would not hear him. One generally uses the *Tefillin* upon rising in the morning, since the spirit is then freer and one finds oneself better able to pray without distraction. If by accident the *Tefillin* falls from the arm or the forehead, the Jew to whom this happens and the bystander (if he be a Jew) must fast the entire day. When one must relieve oneself, the *Tefillin* must be placed four cubits away, or, if it cannot be otherwise, one must put them in a lined pouch and place them before the chest directly in front of the heart. Also, one must beware of having them with him at a burial.

These *Tefillin* are forbidden for women, since they are subject to certain weaknesses <note>A reference to ritual impurity laws surrounding menstruation.</note>; besides that, the Scholars have seen fit that they may suffice by saying *amen* to the prayers of their husbands. Jews of an uncommon godliness have sometimes brought their attention to the *Tefillin* even into the wedding bed: a wise and prudent means to sanctify an act where holiness seems to have very little place, and where the most steadfast piety runs the risk of falling into strange distractions of thought.

<margin>The nature of the Mezuzah noted.</margin> The <term>Mezuzah</term> <note>A small scroll of parchment containing Hebrew verses, placed on the doorpost.</note> (d) has been described by Rabbi Leon de Modena. The Synagogue (e) has none, since it is a designated place for public prayer, and where one does not have his habitual residence. The parchment of the *Mezuzah*, on which the scriptural passage is written, must be rolled from the end of the line toward the beginning, so that one reads as one unrolls the parchment; and when one puts it into the wooden tube, one blesses God, who commanded the *Mezuzah* to his people. One must also observe whether it is contaminated. When one moves house, it is the custom to leave it behind in the house from which one departs; for (f) without that, the Devil would surely enter: yet if a Christian comes to live in the house, this precaution is not taken; but then the *Mezuzah* is removed.

Concerning the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

# CHAPTER VI.

->Concerning the BLESSINGS and PRAYERS of the Jews.<-

<margin>Concerning which blessings the Jews employ in prayer.</margin>
The Jews have innumerable blessings that extend over all tangible things; for they may not undertake nor touch anything, whatever it may be, without first lifting their hearts to God and blessing Him. This institution is laudable in itself. It is praiseworthy that the first of all religious duties is that which does not permit a person to do anything without first having blessed the Supreme Being. Nevertheless, this pious exercise unhesitatingly transitions into an unworthy form of religiosity. (a) For example, the "hundred blessings" of the Jews, repeated so often without attention and in haste, resemble those of a schoolboy who longs for the end of his lessons. From what does this abuse arise? Everything that is brought into a system in the practice of religion depends on an order prescribed by the Church <note>The author uses "Kerk" (Church) here to refer generally to organized religious authority or the Synagogue system.</note>, which one subsequently imposes upon oneself willingly. However it may be, one becomes imperceptibly accustomed to the system, and religious devotion becomes a daily task that must be completed. The worst part is that people view this systematic religiosity as an equivalent for their misconduct, and they strongly convince themselves that they are appeasing the wrath of God. This is the zeal of many who are religious by profession; regarding the precepts and the precision with which many dishonorable men conduct themselves to be found in pious gatherings.

<margin>And how far these blessings of theirs extend.</margin>
We say that the blessings of the Jews extend over all tangible things: let us add that they are sometimes marked with the stamp of pride, and that many of these blessings transition into the most trivial nitpicking. A full account of these would indeed be too tedious for the reader:

<column-break/>

but we shall give an example of the former. Among the Jews, one blesses God (b) that He has granted them the grace to be born of the male sex. This blessing is slanderous toward God <note>The author's 18th-century perspective finds the traditional blessing "who has not made me a woman" to be offensive, reflecting the Enlightenment-era debates on the equality of souls.</note>. The female sex is no less pleasing to Him than the male, since He has included the one as well as the other together in His covenant.

The first thing commanded to be done upon waking is to praise and bless God, and one must undertake nothing of importance without having said one's prayer. This was also a command under Heathendom, which (c) *Virgil* did not forget in one of his poems <note>original: "A Iove principium Musæ, Iovis omnia plena," meaning "From Jove is the beginning of the Muse, all things are full of Jove."</note>. One must go together to the Synagogue in the morning with a fiery affection; according to what is said in *Psalm 55, verse 14* <note>The Dutch text cites verse 15, corresponding to verse 14 in many English translations: "We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company."</note>. God attends the Synagogue as soon as the door is opened, and allows Himself to be found in the midst of the assembly, provided it consists of at least ten persons <note>This refers to the <term>Minyan</term>, the quorum of ten adult males required for communal worship.</note>. (d) Upon entering the Synagogue, one recites several verses of the *Psalms*, bows before the <term>Hechal</term> <note>The Ark where the Torah scrolls are kept.</note>, then reads a verse from *Numbers 24* in a soft voice, and finally recites the prayers with (e) the congregation, which are led by the <term>Chazan</term> or Singer <note>The Cantor.</note>.

<margin>How the Jews must conduct themselves while praying in the Synagogue.</margin>
The reading of the <term>Scheman</term> <note>The Shema, the central declaration of Jewish faith.</note> (f) is performed just as *Leon de Modena* reports. After this reading (g), the entire congregation must stand and pray with a soft voice while standing. The *Chazan* usually begins. Then, out of reverence, everyone takes three steps backward, and the *Chazan* begins to sing the "eighteen blessings" (h). These eighteen blessings <note>The <term>Amidah</term> or Standing Prayer.</note> are, as they believe, of great power. No other prayer can be compared to them. (i) One must speak them while standing, with feet joined together, like those of the...

It is also required that it be said: *that their feet stood straight.* After one has recited the eighteen blessings <note>The *Shemoneh Esrei* or *Amidah*, the central prayer of the Jewish liturgy.</note>, one lets the head hang. Subsequently, one raises it a little and prays one's private prayers either sitting or standing. We consider a broader account of the various prayers in use among the Jews to be unnecessary, since one can consult them in *Buxtorf’s Synagogue*. <note>Referencing Johannes Buxtorf’s *Synagoga Judaica* (1603), a famous but often critical Christian study of Jewish customs.</note>

Regarding the posture of the body during prayer, one must, as much as possible, remain standing, even without leaning elsewhere; the head must be covered; the body must be girded to distinguish the heart from the lower parts, which are considered unfit. <note>This refers to the use of a *gartel* or belt to symbolically separate the "higher" spiritual organs from the "lower" physical ones.</note> The face and hands must be well washed before one goes to the Synagogue. While praying, one must be careful not to touch anything that is unclean, and at the very least, the spirit must be composed for an hour for the prayer.

The worshiper must turn toward Jerusalem, having the feet next to each other, the hands on the heart, and the eyes downcast. He must be careful, as much as possible, not to yawn, spit, blow his nose, pass wind (a), etc. Being at home, one may pray aloud to edify one's household; but in the Synagogue, one must perform one's private prayers very softly, so that the praying Jew only has to move his lips; for it is necessary that the congregation be convinced that this worshiper is praying. Two things may be added to note the necessity of this practice. I. A Jew who sees another praying must say *Amen*, and thus helps to bring the prayer before God—

<column-break/>

the piety of the believer encourages the people and is shown before everyone's eyes. This Pharisaic custom pleases the modern Jews most of all.

We shall leave untouched some pedantic disputes that nonetheless concern the manner of praying, for one can consult those in Buxtorf in the 10th Chapter of his *Synagogue*.

<margin>Defamatory accusation that the Jews supposedly pray against Jesus Christ, the Christians, and the apostates of the Jewish religion.</margin>
Regarding the prayers of the Jews against Jesus Christ, the Christians, and the apostates of the Jewish religion, some examples of this can be found in the aforementioned Buxtorf: but if one had no better proof to bring forward than these examples, the accusation would be easily rejected. They are forced attributions, brought forth by the hatred of some religious persons. If it is true that the Jews damn Jesus Christ and the Christians, one must admit that the matter (b) lies locked in great secrecy.

Exiting the Synagogue, one must be careful not to turn one's back to the *Hechal*, <note>original: *Hechal*. The Ark where the Torah scrolls are kept.</note> in which the sacred Books of the Law are enclosed; one must exit with slow steps, since *Job 14, verse 16* says: *You have numbered my steps.* God now counts the steps of those who leave the Synagogue. One must also be careful not to cast one's eyes upon objects that could arouse desire, and not step outside the door of the Synagogue without softly repeating a spontaneous prayer.

<margin>
Vows, and of what nature they are in Religion.
</margin>
Of all matters pertaining to Religion, there are none in which piety is more easily led astray than in Vows. A pious and zealous Clergyman will allow the bread to be taken from entire families under the pretext of enriching a parish church, without involving himself in the injustice of those who dedicate their property to the Church. Monasteries overflow with wealth, which is of no use to the piety of the Monks, while the children of those who bequeathed their inheritance to these Monasteries must beg for alms. One offers God unnecessary people in the World. A Maiden in the bloom of her years, of healthy constitution, who should be encouraged to love her neighbor, is forced to approve of the cloistered life, since she is betrothed to a God whom she does not love, and whom she will not love until she has come of age. How many Youths have been forced to take vows of chastity; although they had an uncommon capacity for procreation, which they are then obliged to suppress, or rather exercise in an irregular manner? Love and grief give birth to many thoughtless vows. Finally, Vows commonly nourish great errors in Religion. We shall add nothing further to what *Leon de Modena* <note>Rabbi Leone da Modena (1571–1648), a famous Venetian scholar who wrote "The History of the Rites, Customs, and Manner of Life of the Present Jews" for a Christian audience.</note> has said regarding the Vows of the Jews.

Penance, of what kind is presented to strangers.
</margin>
The precepts of the Jewish confession are arranged according to the differences of the Countries. Besides this, they have a Great and a Small Confession. These must be recited while standing.

After this confession is made, some Jews scourge themselves. This scourging is called <term>Malcut</term> <note>original: *Malcut* (Malkhut); a ritualized form of symbolic lashing for atonement.</note> (b): but the practice is not universal, nor commanded. The Ceremony of this scourging is as follows: Two religious men perform it alternately upon each other: one of these penitents lies upon the ground with his face turned toward the North,

<column-break/>

and his back toward the South. One may not allow oneself to be scourged stretched out toward the East and West, because God makes His dwelling in those places. <note>The writer likely refers to the direction of the Holy of Holies in the Temple of Jerusalem.</note>

The Penitent then receives thirty-nine lashes with a bullwhip, confessing his sins again during the lashes applied to his back. The Scourger performs his work while reciting the 38th verse of the 78th Psalm, and at every spoken word he gives a lash. (c) The thirteen words of the verse are repeated by the Scourger three times, thus making up the number of thirty-nine. <note>In the Hebrew text, Psalm 78:38 contains exactly thirteen words.</note> The scourged person then stands up and scrupulously pays back the one who scourged him in the same coin. This scourging is based on *Deuteronomy* 25 verse 2. Although forty lashes are mentioned there, one can see in Buxtorf (d) how the Rabbis explain this. <note>The Rabbis interpreted "forty lashes" as "forty minus one" to ensure the biblical limit was never accidentally exceeded.</note>

Fasts, and how they are observed.
</margin>
Similarly, one can find in Buxtorf (e) a detailed account of many special Fast-days that the Jews observe voluntarily. When the Eve of the Fast has arrived for one who has personally made a vow to fast, he offers God a sacrifice of *his blood and the fat of his body*, which this voluntary penance may diminish. The Rabbis, the Scribes of the Law, and all persons who instruct and teach the people are not obliged to these special Fasts, as repeated abstinences exhaust their strength; but they must observe the Fasts imposed by Church duties like others. In particular, it is forbidden to fast on a Festival or the Sabbath, and on the day when the Moon is renewed.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### *Concerning the Jews’* ECCLESIASTICAL DISCIPLINE *and* EXCOMMUNICATION.

<margin>Private punishment for a committed crime and what it consists of.</margin>
The <term>Parnassim<note>community leaders or wardens of a synagogue who managed both administrative and disciplinary affairs</note></term> are responsible for the punishment of those who do not live according to the Law; first in private, and if this private imposition of punishment is not obeyed by the guilty party, they have the right to do so in public. It is then made known on the Sabbath in the assembly of the <term>Synagogue<note>the Jewish house of prayer and communal gathering</note></term>. A man who has had dealings with an unclean woman <note>referring to a woman in a state of ritual impurity, such as during menstruation</note> must be subject to the punishment of scourging and must fast for forty days. A single kiss given to a woman who is unclean, or even a touch, must be atoned for by the man with a forty-day fast, during which time he may drink no wine, nor eat anything warm, except on the Sabbath.

The civil penalty for a committed manslaughter is an exile of three years; according to the rule of the Church, he is scourged in the Synagogue during the exile, and during the scourging he must cry out: *I am a murderer*. During this imposition of penance, one must abstain from wine and meat; the penitent must leave his hair and beard unshaven, wear dirty linen and a torn garment; he must go bareheaded, or at least not cover himself more than once a month; the arm that committed the manslaughter he must carry in a chain fastened around his neck. There are some who even wear a sort of

Those who appear devout with a forced gesture must have much more patience than other people. Their trifling regularity is never without some anxiety. The High German Jews <note>the Ashkenazim</note> especially are fully provided with them. One may not, they say, pour away the water with which one has washed; one must not walk over this water; one may not scratch oneself before washing, etc. They add that the neglect of these observations subjects one to distressing accidents. Washing the face with no less care, and the details of this washing, do not yield in the least to what has already been recounted.

Others lie down before the door of the Synagogue and allow themselves to be trodden underfoot by those who come there to practice their worship. A theft, a blow with the fist, a false witness, etc., is punished with a penance corresponding to the crime. That of adultery is subject to the strictest. For several following days in the depths of winter, one must go and sit in cold water, and if the water is frozen, one must plunge into the broken ice up to the chin, and remain therein as long as it takes to boil an egg hard. If the crime is committed in the summer, the adulterer is stripped naked and exposed to the stings of bees and gnats. These punishments are reduced in proportion to the abominableness of the crime: but if villainies are mixed therein, such as if the adultery was accomplished under a prearranged agreement, etc., the punishment must last a whole year.

->Concerning the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.<-

...shows that the legitimate administration of punishment, although less common than in former times, has not fallen entirely out of use.

<margin>When and how Excommunication was established in former times.</margin>
Excommunication <note>Dutch: *Kerk-ban*, literally "Church-ban," referring here to the Jewish *Herem* or communal exclusion</note> was undoubtedly established by the *Sanhedrin* <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the Jews during the Second Temple period</note> of the Jews under the reign of the Maccabees. It is a result of the investigation of crimes and the punishment of the guilty, which this Court claims for itself. There is reason to believe that this legal punishment is very different from that which is often mentioned in the ancient Law under the name of *Cutting Off* <note>original: *Affnyding*, referring to the biblical penalty of *Karet*, a divine punishment of being "cut off" from one's people</note>. When the Government began to introduce the Traditions, the Jewish clerics spared no effort to assert the authority of the Church and to claim supreme jurisdiction for the decrees of their Scholars. This latter circumstance perhaps contributed as much to the birth of Excommunication as the former. Excommunication appears before the eyes of the pious as a preparation for the fires of hell; and consciences that lean toward fear and superstition feel the punishment more keenly than they would the sword of the Civil Court.

<margin>Greater and lesser Excommunication, and what they consist of.</margin>
The Jews have a greater and a lesser Excommunication. The minor one <note>known as *Niddui*</note> lasts thirty days: but one can sometimes be released from it even as soon as it has been pronounced. One sees an example of this Excommunication in *Basnage* (a) <note>Jacques Basnage (1653–1723), a French Protestant historian who wrote a famous history of the Jews</note>. A man who disregards the respect due to God is cast out of the community and reinstated almost at the same time. To neglect the authority of a Scribe of the Synagogue also merits Excommunication. Finally, crying and public crimes, profanation, apostasy, etc., freethinking, and schism deserve the same punishment.

<margin>On the heavy consequences of Jewish Excommunication.</margin>
According to the opinion of the Rabbis, Excommunication is so piercing and powerful that it penetrates two hundred and forty-eight members in the body of the Excommunicated person <note>In traditional Jewish anatomy, the body was said to consist of 248 limbs or organs, corresponding to the 248 positive commandments of the Torah</note>. One must distance oneself at least a rod's length from him and refuse him all human aid. This severity also applies to those under his authority: for if someone has died in his house, or if a child must be circumcised, no one may come to his aid—O, what an astonishing act of bitter zeal! (b) One does not mourn the death of the Excommunicated, and a stone is thrown upon his grave to indicate that

Such violent and inhumane behavior is approved as a cruel and even more inhumane good. By this, the truth is perfectly justified; *that it is better to fall into God's hand than into the hands of men.*

<margin>A strange ban-curse that extends over animals.</margin>
A ban-curse can also be pronounced over animals.
A custom among the Jews: but one which had not yet
risen to this level of tolerance, attached
to true wisdom, since a dog was struck with the
ban who had the insolence to gnaw on the
shoes of the wise man. The ban-curse
then gnawed at the tail of the dog with
all the intensity of material fire.

<margin>Into what misfortune an excommunicated person falls, of which an example is provided.</margin>
The Dictionary of Bayle <note>Referring to Pierre Bayle's *Dictionnaire Historique et Critique*, a famous 17th-century encyclopedia</note> will provide us with
striking proof of the inconveniences
into which someone falls who is placed
under the Ban. *Acosta* <note>Uriel Acosta (c. 1585–1640), a philosopher in Amsterdam who famously clashed with the Jewish authorities</note> is known
through his own experience that the
lawful punishment of excommunication <note>original: *Kerkban*, literally "Church-ban"</note> is sometimes
more heart-crushing, and almost always of a
more distressing consequence, than that of the
secular arm. The least of it was what he
had to endure from the discourtesy and the bad
treatment of his brothers. Children were incited
to do him every insult publicly on the
street, and in the throwing of stones against
his house. They ran after him screaming,
vomiting out all manner of curses. He was
spat upon when encountered, and young boys
were likewise egged on to do so. Truly,
the power of the excommunication had burst
forth against *Acosta* with astonishing force;
as long as the impenitence of the banned Jew
lasted, one of his brothers was ordered
to prevent the effects of that wretched man.
All these calamities finally forced
him to place himself back under the obedience
of the Church <note>referring to the Synagogue</note>, or at
least to feign a reunion with it.

<margin>A strange Ban-curse that extends to animals.</margin>
A Ban-curse can also be pronounced over animals. This was a custom among the Jews, but one which had not yet climbed to that level of tolerance linked to true wisdom, seeing as a dog was struck with the ban for having the insolence to gnaw the shoes of a wise man. The Ban-curse then gnawed the tail of the dog with all the intensity of a terrible fire.

<margin>The predicament into which an excommunicated person falls, of which an example is provided.</margin>
The Dictionary of Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706) was a French philosopher whose "Dictionaire Historique et Critique" was a cornerstone of the Enlightenment.</note> shall provide us with striking proof of the predicaments into which someone falls who is placed under the Ban. *Acosta* <note>Uriel Acosta (c. 1585–1640), a philosopher born in Portugal to a crypto-Jewish family, who famously struggled with the religious authorities in Amsterdam.</note> is the figure known through his own experience that the lawful punishment of Church-ban <note>original: "Kerkban". Though a Christian term, the author uses it to describe the Jewish Cherem.</note> is sometimes more heart-crushing, and almost always of a more sorrowful consequence, than that of the secular arm. The least of it was what he had to endure from the discourtesy and bad treatment of his brothers. Children were incited to do him every insult publicly in the street, and to throw stones against his house. They ran after him screaming, vomiting all manner of curses. He was spat upon when met, and small boys were likewise goaded to do the same. Truly, the power of the Church-ban burst forth against *Acosta* with wonderful force; as long as the impenitence of the banned Jew lasted, one of his brothers was ordered to prevent the effects of that wretched man <note>likely meaning the brother was tasked with enforcing the social isolation</note>. All these calamities finally forced him to place himself back under the obedience of the Church, or at least to feign reuniting himself with it.

The conditions of his release were laden with an intolerable penance for an honest man. ### CHAPTER IX.
## Of the Jewish SABBATH CELEBRATION and their ceremonies.

<margin>Who holds which Sabbath. Regarding the souls who are persecuted during their Sabbath.</margin>
The Sabbath is a Divine institution; to violate it is to undermine the very foundations of the Jewish religion. The Jews are not content with the primary elements that God promised them—those who precisely observe the religious holiness of this day—but their Scholars <note>referring to the Rabbis and Talmudic authorities</note> have added uncommonly many others to it. The Sabbath prayer, which one performs on Friday evening, grants a release to the souls who are in the Vestibule of Hell <note>original: "Voorburg der Helle," referring to Gehenna, where souls undergo purification</note>. This release lasts for the entire following Saturday; during these twenty-four hours, they hasten to draw water for their cooling. For this reason, the Scholars have forbidden scooping the water from the cisterns down to the very last drop, so that the souls would not suffer a lack thereof. On the Sabbath day, the damned souls have permission to change places. This day is brought forward <gloss>a</gloss> a little early, in order to soften the punishment of the Vestibule in the meantime. We shall not recount further the many other advantages that both the living and the dead derive from the Sabbath celebration.

<margin>Why it is the work [of women] to light the Sabbath lamp.</margin>
The Sabbath, we say, begins on Friday evening, half an hour before sunset, at which time even the very poorest Jew must light his Sabbath lamp, even if he must beg for the necessary oil for its maintenance. The Women must light these lamps, because Eve, by giving her husband the occasion to sin, *extinguished the first light of the world*; that is to say, to speak non-metaphorically, that she caused the death of man.

<column-break/>

<margin>What a customary Sabbath prayer is, and the manner of preparation.</margin>
...[it is customa]ry, even if he himself had a great number of servants in his service. One prepares oneself <note>The text describes the ritual of "cutting" or "trimming" in preparation for the Sabbath</note> for the Sabbath prayer, which is carried out in this manner. One begins with the left hand, trims the nail of the pinky and subsequently of the middle finger; then one moves to the index finger, thereafter to the third or the one next to the pinky, and finally the thumb. On the right hand, one begins with the second or middle finger, and subsequently trims the nail of the pinky, etc. The clippings of the nails must not be thrown away, nor trodden underfoot: but one must bury them in the earth or burn them. At the meal which is held on Friday evening, when the Sabbath begins, the Father or the Master of the house blesses the Bread, and he gazes with attention at the Sabbath Lights. This observation is, according to a very clever scholar, a reason to strengthen a person’s failing eyesight; he holds the bread high in his hands when he pronounces God's name. One places two Breads on the table in memory of the double portion of manna <note>the miraculous food provided to the Israelites in the desert</note> which was gathered on Fridays. It is commanded to possess a joyful spirit on the Sabbath day; but above all, one must not forget the poor and the oppressed; nor the marital duty. It is even a matter of weight to acquit oneself properly <gloss>c</gloss> on the Sabbath night, being greatly benefited thereby, such that a man who refuses to fulfill the marital duty to his wife at that time would be considered senseless. We shall point out these advantages. The Scholars have declared that the work of marriage, when observed with zeal on the Sabbath day, is very honorable before God.

<gloss>c</gloss> Buxtorf, *Jewish Synagogue*, Chapter 15.

is [praiseworthy], and rewarded as such; for it testifies to the desire one has to please God, taking full delight in it. Those who are so fortunate as to see this <term>Sabbath labor<note>A reference to marital relations, which in Jewish tradition are considered a holy duty particularly appropriate for Friday night.</note></term> crowned with some fruit, hold themselves assured that they shall bring into the world a chosen one of the Jewish faith, a child of grace, a disciple perfected in wisdom, and that this shall certainly come to pass: but it is necessary (a) that heart and soul lift themselves up to God, and maintain themselves in that elevation, while the marital tribute is mutually offered.

<margin>An imagined Pharisaical pride with which the Jews are possessed.</margin>
The prayers and blessings of the Sabbath are more numerous than those of the weekday. One must admit that they are generally good and edifying, were it not that a considerable amount of <term>Pharisaical pride<note>The author displays a common 18th-century Christian bias here, interpreting Jewish prayers of gratitude for being "chosen" as a sign of arrogance.</note></term> crept in among them. The Jews thank God that He, setting them apart from other nations, preserves and has chosen them to the exclusion of all others. Their prayers are commonly accompanied by this distinction, and certain humiliations they imagine they perform before God, they view as being of far greater value than the rest of mankind.

<margin>The Law being lifted and shown to the people, the reading is begun.</margin>
The greatest solemnity of the Sabbath is (b) that the Law is shown to the people. The <term>Chazan<note>original: "Chazan" — The Cantor or worship leader.</note></term> (c) performs this duty and says to the assembly: *See the Law, which Moses has set before the children of Israel, the Law of God is perfect etc.* After having shown it, he lays it upon the lectern and calls seven persons (d) from the congregation to perform the reading of that day. The <term>Cohen<note>original: "Cohen" — A descendant of the priestly line of Aaron.</note></term> or Priest reads first, followed by a <term>Levite<note>original: "Liviet" — A member of the Hebrew tribe of Levi who assisted the priests.</note></term>, and subsequently the others have their turn. (e) An eighth person reads several scriptural passages drawn from the Prophets, and this reading is called <term>HAPHTARA<note>original: "HAPHTARA" — The Haftarah, a series of selections from the books of the Prophets.</note></term>. Everyone is admitted to this reading, except for women. After the reading, the Cantor lifts the Book of the Law again and gives the blessing to the people. The Book of the Law is then locked away, and the prayers are repeated.

<margin>The nature of the Jews' sermons.</margin>
Sermons are given on the Sabbath and other feast days. The sermons are delivered in the common tongue: but citations from the Bible and the scholars of the Law are given in Hebrew. These sermons are sometimes burdened with needless ci-

<column-break/>

tations; likewise accompanied by many obscure ideas, and much noise and movement, to express a difficult entanglement full of conjectures, which often serve to show the ability of the Teacher and the value of his sermon. All of this must be attributed to the unrefined manner of study that the Rabbis have chosen for themselves.

<margin>Their funeral commemorations and for what reason they are used.</margin>
On the Sabbath day (f) they also offer a sort of funeral commemoration, or rather a prayer for the dead. At that time, offerings and acts of charity are performed. Wise and pious Jews have assured us that this custom is purely political and was introduced among them for no other reason than to derive benefit from the idle pride of rich and prominent Jews, who are inclined to show themselves charitable on these occasions, this being a snare with which superstitions are subsequently fastened tight.

After the evening prayers, the blessing is pronounced once more, and the Jews thank God together. Everything that subsequently concerns religious practice must be distinguished between the Sabbath day and the following week, and is called <term>HABDALLA<note>original: "HABDALLA" — Havdalah, a ceremony marking the symbolic end of the Sabbath.</note></term>. Although *Leon de Modena* has described this Havdalah here previously, (g) we shall nonetheless describe it once more according to Buxtorf, who reports on the customs maintained by the <term>High-German Jews<note>original: "Hoogduitfche Jooden" — Referring to Ashkenazi Jews.</note></term>. <margin>The Jewish Havdalah, which is described in its particulars.</margin> The father of the house performs this ceremony standing, and does so in the presence of his family and household. A torch or lamp is lit, and an incense burner is placed before him. The most precious perfumes are used for the *Havdalah*. The father of the house then takes a glass full of beer or wine in his right hand and says aloud: *God is my savior, I will fear nothing etc. All salvation comes from God; I will take the Cup of Salvation etc.* <note>original: "Godt is myne behouder... Heilkelk" — References to Psalm 116.</note> Then he blesses the wine, and at the beginning of the blessing, he pours a little of it out in front of him. The blessing being done, he takes the glass in his left hand and the incense in his right. He blesses the incense, smells it, and then lets those standing by smell it: after which he takes the glass back in his right hand, and approaching the torch, examines his nails <note>original: "nagels" — It is a tradition during Havdalah to look at the reflection of the flame in one's fingernails to make use of the light.</note>

Having said this and repeated the Blessing, he pours out a little wine, drinks a few drops of it, and then hands the glass over to the company.

The Jews trace the reason for this ceremony back to the separation that God made between light and darkness, and because God commanded them, in *Leviticus* 10 verse 10, *to separate that which is Holy from the unholy*. Finally, this ceremony represents the distinction that God has made between them and other peoples—

The ceremony called <term>Havdalah<note>A Hebrew word meaning "separation." It is a ritual performed at the end of the Sabbath to mark the transition back into the secular week.</note></term> serves to drive away the foul air of hell, the door of which stands open at that time to let the damned souls back in. As for the nails, they are viewed as an image of fertility, since they grow very quickly, or as an idea of strength. Various other reasons given for this inspection of the nails are even more trivial than the first two. The pouring out of the blessed wine represents the abundance one promises oneself through one's labor. Some Jews rub their eyes with it, believing it to be a primary remedy for strengthening the sight. Others use it as Roman Catholics use blessed or holy water, and test their houses, beds, cradles, and small children with it, likewise everything that might be exposed to the Devil's contempt.

<margin>Ceremonies of the New Moon and how they observe them.</margin>
This <term>Feast<note>The celebration of the New Moon, or Rosh Chodesh.</note></term> exempts women from labor: but as for the men, they are permitted to follow their professions as usual. (c) The Jews believe that the <term>New Moon</term> is primarily the Feast of the women, and this in remembrance because they generously gave their jewelry to serve the splendor of God's service. This deed, so praiseworthy for a sex that values nothing more highly than finery, was performed on the New Moon in the month of March.

Some Jews must fast on the day before this feast, and implore God that the <term>New Moon</term> may be profitable to them.

<margin>How the Month of Elul serves as a preparation of penance for the Jews.</margin>
The Month of <term>Elul<note>The twelfth month of the Jewish civil year, roughly corresponding to August or September.</note></term> corresponds with August. The most religious among them spend it in acts of penance. They reflect on all their past conduct and make a firm resolution to live better in the future. This practice of penance serves as a preparation for the upcoming New Year. (a) The Italian Jews rise before dawn during the entire month of Elul to recite their prayers and perform their confession and penance before God: but the <term>High German Jews<note>original: "Hoogduitsche," referring to Ashkenazi Jews from Central and Eastern Europe.</note></term> are content to do this four days before the New Year. As soon as one has entered the Month of Elul, the <term>horn<note>The Shofar, a musical instrument made from a ram's horn.</note></term> is blown in the evening and the morning in the Synagogue.
<margin>What their horn-blowing signifies.</margin>
Two reasons are given for this custom. Moses (b) climbed Mount Sinai a second time on the morning of the first day of Elul to receive the new Tables of the Law from God’s hand, and did not return until the 10th of <term>Tishrei<note>original: "Tisri," the first month of the Jewish civil year.</note></term>, the day on which the Day of Atonement is celebrated. He then commanded, they say, that the horn should be blown in the camp of the Israelites while he climbed the mountain, so that people would no longer say: *we do not know what has happened to Moses* etc. The

## XI. CHAPTER.

### Concerning the Jews' NEW YEAR FESTIVAL; their KIPPUR or DAY OF ATONEMENT.

<margin>How the New Year is inaugurated by the blowing of the horn;</margin>
On the first day of the year, the horn is blown to inform the Jews that they must listen with attention and humility to the judgment which God will pronounce over sinners, and to thank Him for His mercy and the assistance granted to them during the past year. This Festival lasts two days: the congregation must then pray aloud and with a humbler countenance than usual. In Germany, the Jews send their children to the <term>Chief Rabbi<note>original: "Groot Rabbyn."</note></term> to receive his blessing, and

<column-break/>

sound of the horn awakens the fear of God’s judgments in the heart of the sinner and moves it to penance. It is also believed (c) that the sound of the horn deafens the Devil and makes him forget that the New Year is approaching, which leaves him unable to oppose the Jews in the Judgment. In the meantime, the horn-blowing is omitted on the day before the New Year, and the Festival of the Moon <note>Rosh Chodesh, the celebration of the New Month.</note> is no longer celebrated in Tishrei, it being the first month of the year: or at least it is postponed until after the Day of Atonement.

<margin>In what the penance of the Month of Elul consists.</margin>
The acts of penance for the Month of Elul consist of immersing oneself in cold water, confessing one's crimes, striking the breast with powerful fist-blows while in the water, and undergoing the <term>discipline<note>original: "tucht," referring to the ritual of Malkut, or symbolic lashes.</note></term> (d). Those who take true care for the circumcision of their hearts and give themselves over entirely to the severity of their penance, coupled with alms-giving, recite all the prayers while fasting on the day before the New Year. (e) The penitents flatter themselves that God agrees with them to forgive at least a large portion of their crimes. It is not believed among the Jews, as it is among Protestant Christians, that despite all repentance and regret one is still an *unprofitable servant*: but on the contrary, they imagine that their acts of repentance are highly meritorious.

When one sits down at the table with the master of the house, he takes a piece of bread and dips it in honey, saying: *may this year be sweet and fruitful*; which all those sitting at the table likewise do. One also does not neglect to serve a sheep’s head (f) at this meal, and if one believes the Rabbis (who are excellent judges on this occasion), one should eat fennel, garlic, and some other similar things on this day of the year.

### SECOND HISTORICAL TREATISE

<columns>

The Horn-blower (a) must stand at the place where the Law is read. The Synagogue must do likewise. This Horn is made of a Ram’s horn, so that it may be a memorial of the Ram of Isaac <note>Referring to the biblical story of the Binding of Isaac, where a ram was sacrificed in his place</note>. It is somewhat more curved, giving as the reason that it represents the posture of a humbling human being. The time for this horn-blowing is from sunrise to sunset.

<margin>How and why the first ten days of the year are days of penance.</margin>
The ancient Jews formerly laid their crimes upon a goat, which they sent to the Wilderness: but the contemporary Jews (b) now lay them upon the fish; for after the ritual meal they go to the bank of the water and shake out their clothes there. This custom they derive from a passage of Scripture from the Prophet *Micah* (c).

The first ten days of the Year are intended for the exercise of penance, and through a sincere conversion to submit oneself before God. As the Jews believe, the Supreme Being examines the actions of men during the first nine days, and pronounces the sentence of punishment on the tenth day. One fasts, one prays often, one is mournful, and one lets their extraordinary piety be seen, so that on the day of <term>Kippur<note>original: "CHIPUR," referring to Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement</note></term> one may be inscribed in the Book of Life, and crossed out in the Book of the Dead, since one cannot be recorded without repentance.

<margin>Strange custom of the Jews formerly in use among them.</margin>
The Jews have had the <term>Kapparot<note>original: "CAPARA," an atonement ritual where the sins of a person are symbolically transferred to a fowl</note></term> in use for a long time. This ceremony was performed the day before the Fast Day of Atonement (d). The men chose a rooster, and the women a hen (pregnant women a rooster and a hen). The Father of the Household, having the rooster in hand, recited some passages from the *Psalms* and from the Book of *Job*; after which he struck his head three times against that of the rooster, saying at each blow: *This rooster shall be exchanged for me, he shall wipe out my sins, he shall die the death, and I shall enjoy life.* This ceremony was repeated three times, as it represented the wiping out of his crimes, likewise those of his family and of his household members, and this in imitation of the practice (e) of the ancient High Priest. After these three given blows, he squeezed the throat of the rooster and strangled him, in order

<column-break/>

to show the Sinner how he is guilty of death. Subsequently, he threw the animal with force against the floor: this was intended to signify that the Sinner deserved to be stoned. Finally, the rooster was roasted, so that the Sinner would do right and understand that he was worthy of being roasted by the eternal fire. The animal's entrails were thrown upon the roof of the House. Two reasons could justify this remarkable custom. I. They imagined that sin comes from the heart and the other entrails. It then required leaving such a cursed thing to the Birds of Heaven: and for this same reason, the Egyptians formerly threw the entrails of their corpses into the Nile. II. It could also be that they wanted to imitate the custom that their Ancestors formerly had under the ancient Law, of sending a Goat burdened with the people's iniquity to the Wilderness. It was also observed that the rooster had to be white; therefore it was believed to be more fitting for the burden of crimes; for it was assumed that a rooster of another color was already sufficiently burdened. After killing the rooster, one went to pray to God at the graves and gave the value in money of the killed animal to the poor. Formerly they were given the rooster itself: but the poor, subsequently noting the quality of this meat burdened with iniquities, refused (f) to accept it.

One also prepares for the ritual washing customary on the Day of Atonement; one prepares the wax light or the candles for that day, and everyone brings theirs to the Synagogue. (g) In Germany <note>Referring to the Ashkenazi tradition</note> every man has one: but the women have none. Elsewhere the women are also provided with one. Some religious people come with two, of which one enlightens the body and the other the soul. One usually reconciles with all one's enemies; one even visits them to make peace with them, and requests forgiveness from those whom one has insulted. If the offered Reconciliation is refused, one declares the refusal of the refuser before three witnesses, and one appears three times upon the summons, after which the conscience of the Penitent is [cleared] by the

### SECOND HISTORICAL TREATISE

the Shofar Blower <note>original: "Hoornblazer"</note> (a) must stand upright at the place where the Law <note>The Torah</note> is read. The Congregation must likewise do so. This Horn is made from a ram's horn, so that it may be a memorial of the Ram of Isaac. It is somewhat curved, giving as a reason that it represents the form of a humble man. The time for this horn-blowing is from sunrise until sunset.

The ancient Jews formerly laid their crimes upon a goat, which they sent into the Wilderness; but the modern Jews (b) now lay them upon the fish; for after the meal has been held, they go to the water’s edge and shake out their clothes there. They derive this custom from a passage of Scripture from the Prophet *Micah* (c).

<margin>How and why the Jews observe the first ten days of the year as days of penance.</margin>
The first ten days of the Year are designated for the exercise of penance, and for submitting oneself before God through a sincere conversion. As the Jews believe, the Supreme Being examines the deeds of men during the first nine days, and pronounces the sentence of punishment on the tenth day. One fasts, one prays often, one is mournful, and one allows their extraordinary piety to be shown, so that on the day of CHIPUR <note>Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement</note> one may be inscribed in the Book of Life, and erased from the Book of the Dead, since one cannot be recorded without repentance.

<margin>How the Jews reconcile themselves regarding their offenses.</margin>
...relieved of the burden of enmity. This behavior is very well-suited to ensuring peace and union. No matter how great an offense may be, one does not always have the boldness to refuse the Reconciliation that is requested with such emphasis; but is it truly sincere? And does one not still feel entitled to resentment over the dishonor?

# CHAPTER XII.
## Of the FEAST of ATONEMENT or YOM KIPPUR <note>original: "Chipur"</note>.

<margin>Concerning the solemn penance that accompanies the Jews' Feast of Atonement.</margin>
In Leviticus 16 and 23, verse 17, this Feast is spoken of. At the beginning of this Feast, people gather in the Synagogue; everyone lights their candle there; prayers and hymns are raised with a lofty and mournful voice. One must not withhold from the Jews the credit they deserve: they observe everything with extraordinary diligence—what one might call the "husk" or outward form of penance <note>The author uses "Schorsse" (shell/bark) to describe the visible, external rituals of the fast</note>—and as imitation carries much weight on this occasion, it is rare that the observer does not, in turn, feel a genuine stirring regarding their own sins when seeing all the outward signs (b) of repentance united in the person of a Jew. He strives to complete his penance and solemnly condemns himself before God through a long series of enumerations of his sins. This confession is arranged according to the order of the alphabet <note>Referring to the *Viduy*, a confessional prayer where sins are listed in an alphabetical acrostic</note>. Every crime has its letter and presents itself more easily to the meditation of the sinner.

The women also light candles at home and draw good or bad omens from them, according to whether the light burns brightly or dimly.

The Jews explain the "affliction of the soul," of which *Leviticus* 23 speaks, as the total deprivation of that which pleases the body and delights the spirit: but for children who have not yet reached eleven years of age, for pregnant 

<meta>PART I.</meta>

<column-break/>

The right of postponement is then retained until the tenth day of the following year. Whatever the case may be, two things favor this behavior; namely, the practical effect it produces on the people's conscience, and the improvement by which it curbs the pride of others. (a)

women, for those who have recently given birth, for nursing women, for the sick and the elderly, exceptions have been established.

<margin>All scandalous Jews and those living in disorder invited to the Feast of Atonement.</margin>
On the first evening of the Feast, those who lead a scandalous and disordered life are tolerated in the Assembly, and they are even invited there, since they must be counted among the believers, just as *Galbanum* <note>A bitter-smelling resin used in the sacred incense of the Temple; the metaphor suggests that the prayers of the community are only complete when they include the "bitter" sinners</note> (c) is included among a good perfume. Two Rabbis, placing themselves one to the left and the other to the right of the Singer <term>Cantor or Chazzan</term>, make this solemn invitation and declare to the Assembly that they may pray with these sinners. Subsequently, the Singer opens the HECHAL <term>the Ark where the Torah scrolls are kept</term> and sings a very long prayer, which the Assembly follows softly. This prayer nullifies the vows, the oaths, and the thoughtless resolutions of the preceding year, insofar as they were made voluntarily and to oneself.

<margin>How some Penitents spend day and night in their penance.</margin>
Some Penitents spend the entire night and sometimes the following day standing, without changing their place, being constantly occupied in prayer and meditation: but those who spend the night at home must find themselves back in the Synagogue the following day at the rising of the dawn and continue their penance. At the end of the day, the Rabbi stretches out his hands toward the people and gives them the (d) Blessing...

(b) These signs are soiled and worn clothes, mourning garments, or shrouds <note>original: "dood kleeden"</note>; a sad and dejected countenance; a rough beard; downcast eyes, which shows a languishing penance and a tendency even toward weeping; a mournful silence; a Holy intensity that urges the penitent to push through the crowd of the godly to be the first in the Synagogue; a very powerful inwardness while one reviews the list of one's sins, as if one were losing the use of one's senses.
