...blessing of Moses. The people receive this with great humility, covering their faces with their hands, as they believe that God remains behind the Rabbi, and that man should not be so bold as to behold Him. Likewise, the hand of God covered the face of Moses when this Lawgiver (a) humbled himself before Him on account of the sins of Israel. It is likely that the true origin of this custom comes from here.

<column-break/>

A Jew who perfectly fulfills the duty of penance when the Synagogue is charged before YOM KIPPUR <note>original: "CHIPUR"</note> is regarded as a blameless man, standing above the reach of ordinary devotees; for the Divine voice assures him (b) that he may henceforth eat his bread with joy, and that God accepts his good works. This is purely Pharisaic <note>The author refers to the theological traditions of the Pharisees regarding merit and law</note>: yet one must exclude some persons of a more rigorous piety, who desire that one's repentance be shown in such an edifying manner that Divine mercy is never left unaddressed for more than twenty-four hours before the return <note>referring to the cycle of daily repentance</note>.

# CHAPTER XIII.

## Concerning the Jewish PASSOVER and PENTECOST FEASTS.

---

<margin>
How 
accurately 
the 
Jews 
search 
for 
leaven.
</margin>

The Jews celebrate the Feast of Passover very religiously. At least thirty days in advance, they provide themselves with the necessary grain for the unleavened bread <note>Matzah</note>, and the care taken for the selection and preservation of this grain is quite extraordinary. (c) For example, it is not loaded onto the back of a horse without a saddle to be brought to the mill, for fear that the grain might ferment <note>literally "broeyen" or "stew" in its own heat</note> due to the warmth. The sacks in which the grain is to be kept from one Passover to the next must be unstitched, washed, and resewn. The search for leaven <note>the ritual of Bedikat Chametz</note> is very meticulous *, and the anxieties regarding it cause no small amount of investigation for Jews of a tender conscience. (d) The sun does not shine brightly enough to illuminate the cracks and holes of the house where, by chance, some crumbs of leavened bread might lie hidden: one also makes use of (e) a candle, and when the Father of the household mistrusts his own sight as being too weak, he uses spectacles to better search the cracks and crevices of the walls. Still distrusting such a meticulous search—having searched everywhere by night, day, and sunlight, and even with spectacles on his nose—

<column-break/>

he then prays to God that it may please Him to fulfill the deficiency of the search, *that all leavened bread that might be in the house, whether he has found it or not, shall become as the dust of the earth and be annihilated.* <note>This is the formal declaration of "Bitul Chametz," nullifying any missed leaven</note>

The Sabbath before Passover (f) is called the Great Sabbath <note>Shabbat HaGadol</note>. A sermon is then preached about the Paschal Lamb. At least two days before Passover, one cleans or replaces certain kitchen utensils. The Jews are no less concerned about the mixture for the Unleavened Bread than they are about the search for leaven and the preparation of the grain. The water which is to serve for preparing the dough of the unleavened bread is inspected and kept with all possible care. He who draws or scoops the water will do well (g) to then lift his heart to God and offer his prayer at a moderate volume <note>literally "half-height"</note>, for then the water will be all the better. The master of the house or the Father of the household will do well to participate to some extent in the handling of the Unleavened Bread: if he can or will put his own hands to the dough, let him at least perform it as a spiritual labor; let him give free reign (h) to the small pieces of dough that are separated from the whole...

<margin>The form of these unleavened Breads and how they are prepared.</margin>
The kneader of the dough takes a piece of it to make a cake which he burns. This cake, under the Old Testament, was the right of the High Priest. <note>original: "koek die hy verbrand." This refers to the "Hafrashat Challah," the mitzvah of separating a portion of dough.</note> One must also take great care not to knead in a place shone upon by the Sun, and that the dough is moved constantly so that it does not begin to ferment. The Unleavened breads are flat, commonly round, bland in taste, and full of holes; but the wealthy Jews, and gourmets who do not wish to surrender themselves to this, mix eggs and sugar into this *miserable food and bread of tears*. <note>The author refers to "Matzah Ashirah" (rich matzah), which is generally restricted during Passover except under specific circumstances.</note>

One solemnly burns all the Leaven which has been found in the careful search, and one even burns the vessels which served for that purpose. This practice is grounded in a Scriptural passage from Exodus 12, verse 10.

<margin>Of what the Table-dish for the Passover consists,</margin>
The Table at which one sits to keep the Passover is prepared and covered by the women. The Father of the household sits there with his children and household members. On this table one finds Unleavened Breads; a covered dish in which are three cakes of mystery <note>Likely referring to the three Matzot representing the Priests, Levites, and Israelites.</note>, one for the High Priest, the other for the Levites, and the third for the people: as also the shoulder bone of a Lamb, or at least a part of the bone. (a) When the shoulder serves entirely for this ceremony, a hard-boiled egg is placed with it. One adds a table-dish representing a brick upon which their Forefathers formerly had to labor in Egypt. This is a thickish dough, prepared from Apples, Almonds, Nuts, Figs etc., which they let cook in wine and prepare with broken Cinnamon to represent the straw which was included in the mixture of the bricks. <note>This is "Charoset," a sweet paste symbolizing the mortar used by Israelite slaves.</note> Another dish was provided with Lettuce, a certain herb, Cress, wild Chicory, and Parsley, serving for the bitter herbs, with which the vinegar was also placed.

<margin>and by which Ceremonial observation</margin>
One must (b) sit down at the table with a gesture of haste. After the consecration of the Passover, a glass of wine is poured for all the company; it is even given to the

<column-break/>

<margin>one is required to pay attention.</margin>
children in the cradle. One washes the hands before and after the consecration. The House-father must be seated at the table in an armchair, leaning with the left elbow on the table, as the guests also do. It is a sort of freedom which they assume, to point out that obtained by their Fathers, departing from Egypt. The glass of wine being empty, everyone dips a little of the aforementioned bitter herbs into the vinegar, while the Master of the house says a prayer corresponding to the circumstance of this ceremonial custom. Subsequently, he breaks the cake of the Levites into two pieces, hides one of these pieces under his napkin, to signify how the Israelites formerly had to manage, hiding their unleavened bread in haste; he then takes the other piece, and holding it aloft with the shoulder of the Lamb, says to his Household, who must also set their hands to these table-dishes: *see the bread of misery and oppression, which our Fathers ate in Egypt: let him who is hungry come and eat. This is the sacrifice of the Passover lamb, etc.* <note>The author is describing the "Ha Lachma Anya" and the "Afikoman."</note> One then sets the Lamb's shoulder back on the table, another cup is poured to drink: but the basket or dish with cakes is set aside. (c) This shoulder represents, say the Jews, the Mighty arm of the Lord, who delivered them from the oppression of the Egyptians.

The Father of the household, after this Ceremony, has a Hymn of Praise sung; being a Godly narrative of the miraculous deliverance of their Forefathers. A young child begins the song, and it is also (d) charged to ask some questions about the Ceremonies of Passover, which the House-father then explains, giving the reason for every mystery. When one has come to the place in the song where the ten plagues are spoken of that came over Egypt, they let a little wine be spilled from the glass with the finger. This signifies as if they would say, *that these plagues be turned away from us*. Then they raise their voice, which they had previously let be heard more softly, empty their glass, and continue their song. The master of the house then washes his hands once more, as he is fearful that they might have become soiled since he has been at the table.

He leaves the other cakes whole, since on *this night of tears and worries* <note>original: "nacht van traanen en bekommernisse." This refers to the symbolic "bread of affliction" (Matzah) eaten to remember the hardships of slavery in Egypt.</note>, one had to be satisfied with a piece of bread. This bread and the bitter herbs must then be eaten with the prepared dough <note>The "prepared dough" refers to Charoset, a sweet paste made of fruits and nuts intended to resemble the mortar used by Israelite slaves.</note>, after which one partakes of the Lamb (a). The meal being nearly finished, the Father of the household takes half of the cake which he had hidden under the napkin, eats a little of it, and breaks the remainder into small pieces for his family. The Rabbis have carefully established these ties, so well-suited to keep the people in wonder and reverence.

<margin>
How the Jews differ among themselves from ancient custom in the celebration of Passover.
</margin>
Several differences are found regarding the celebration of Passover between the ancient and modern Jews. (d) I. Formerly, the Lamb was eaten roasted; since the destruction of the sacrifices, which could not be offered to God except within Jerusalem, one part was roasted and the other part boiled, or rather a small portion of the Lamb was used, which sufficed because the sacrifice could not be fully completed. II. The lack of the sacrifice now obliges them to abolish certain Hymns of praise that referred to the Paschal lamb. III. The dispersion of the Jews also obliges them to pray to God for the restoration of Jerusalem, the Temple, and the sacrifices, and that he might henceforth deliver them as he once delivered their forefathers from Egyptian slavery. IV. Modern Jews end their meal with the unleavened bread, whereas formerly it was ended with the Lamb. V. One now omits eating the Paschal lamb with loins girded, taking a staff, and removing one's shoes, which was the custom under the ancient Law; however, the reverence they owe to this religious ceremony remains. They keep the head bowed during the meal, and

<column-break/>

those Jews who are exceptionally pious put nothing into their mouths without reverently thinking of the mystery of the matter.
The Jews call the fifty days counted from Passover to Pentecost the *Omer* days <note>The source uses "Homer," an older transliteration of "Omer," a biblical measure of grain.</note>; the reason for this name *Omer* is found in *Leviticus* 23, verse 10 and following.
On the day of Pentecost, one reads of the offerings, as well as the History of *Ruth*, since much is said there regarding the harvest. One treats oneself to delicacies in which milk is used, which they take as a symbol of the Law because of its sweetness and whiteness; and as the Jews boast as much as they can of speaking and sensory images of the most remarkable events at the origin of their religion, they do not neglect to serve on the table during the Feast of Pentecost a fairly thick cake, which they call *the Cake of Sinai*. This cake reminds them again of the Mountain upon which God once gave the Law.

<margin>
What the Jews must observe on their Feast of Pentecost.
</margin>
This is now the most important thing to be said regarding this Feast, based on what *Leon de Modena* <note>Leon de Modena (1571–1648) was a famous Venetian rabbi whose work "The History of Jewish Rites" was a primary source for European scholars.</note> has written of it. Formerly it was called *the Harvest Feast*, since the first grains and first fruits of the land were then offered. This was indeed the purpose of this ceremony: but this could have no place in Europe, where the harvest comes much later than Pentecost. This name was specific to the Land of Canaan, in Arabia, and around the *Red Sea*. Certain institutions, even the most religious ones, have in their origin been dependent on times, places, and some other circumstances. These being of such a sort, they had to be imperceptibly abolished: nonetheless, people practice them very faithfully, even when they have become entirely useless. One sees those which have become ridiculous through their uselessness: yet they wish to maintain them unto the world's great age.
The German Jews <note>Referring to the Ashkenazi Jewish community.</note> decorate their candelabras, lamps, pulpit, and <term>Hechal</term> <note>Hebrew for the "Ark" or "Holy Place" where the Torah scrolls are kept.</note> with fragrant flowers and herbs on Pentecost. The Portuguese Jews <note>Referring to the Sephardic Jewish community.</note> also did this formerly, and in Italy, it is still in use among them.

He leaves the other cakes whole, *since on this night of tears and worries, one must be satisfied with a piece of bread.* This bread and the bitter herbs must then be eaten with the prepared dough <note>Charoset, a sweet paste symbolizing mortar.</note>, after which one partakes of the Lamb (a). When the meal is nearly finished, the Father of the House takes half of the cake which he had hidden under the napkin, eats a little of it, and breaks the rest into small pieces for his family. (b) After this, it is not permitted to eat anything more: but one drinks a third and a fourth cup of wine. Upon the fourth drink, the Master takes the glass and prays to God, *that He might pour out His wrath upon the nations that do not know Him.* (c) These four times that one pours a drink are four mysteries. The Rabbis have carefully handed down these traditions, so suited to keep the people in wonder and reverence.

<margin>How the Jews differ from ancient usage in celebrating the Passover.</margin>
Several differences are found regarding the celebration of Passover between the ancient and modern Jews. (d) I. Formerly, the Lamb was eaten roasted; since the destruction of the sacrifices, which could only be offered to God within Jerusalem, one part was roasted and the other part boiled, or a small portion of the Lamb was used, which sufficed because the sacrifice could not be fully completed. II. The lack of the sacrifice now necessitates them to abolish certain Hymns of praise that referred to the Passover Lamb. III. The dispersion of the Jews also obliges them to pray to God for the restoration of Jerusalem, the Temple, and the sacrifices, and that He might deliver them henceforth, just as He formerly delivered their ancestors from Egyptian slavery. IV. The modern Jews end their meal with the unleavened bread, whereas formerly it ended with the Lamb. V. They now omit eating the Passover Lamb while girding their loins, taking a staff, and removing their shoes—which was the custom under the ancient Law; however, they still observe the humility and attentiveness due to this religious ceremony. They keep their heads bowed during the meal, and

<column-break/>

those Jews who are exceptionally pious put nothing into their mouths without thinking with reverence on the mystery of the matter.

The Jews call the fifty days counted from Passover to Pentecost <term>Omer days<note>Original: "Homers dagen." Refers to the "Counting of the Omer."</note></term>; the reason for this name *Omer* is found in *Leviticus 23:10* and following.

On the day of Pentecost, the section on sacrifices is read, as well as the History of Ruth, since much is said there concerning the harvest. One treats oneself to delicacies in which milk is used, which they take as the symbol of the Law because of its sweetness and whiteness; and as the Jews boast as much as they can about evocative and sensible representations of the most remarkable things that happened at the origin of their religion, they do not neglect to serve on the table during the feast of Pentecost a fairly thick cake, which they call the <term>Cake of Sinai</term>. This cake reminds them again of the Mountain upon which God formerly gave the Law.

This was indeed the purpose of this ceremony: but this could have no place in *Europe*, where the harvest comes much later than Pentecost. The Portuguese Jews <note>Sephardic Jews.</note> also did this formerly, and in Italy it is still in use among them.

## CHAPTER XIV.

### Concerning the Festival of Booths or the Festival of Tabernacles.

<margin>The significance of the Festival of Booths.</margin>
This festival is the symbol of the Israelites' journey and the hardships they endured in the wilderness after the passage through the Red Sea. It commemorates the care of God's Providence, which preserved them for forty years in barren and fearsome plains without permanent housing, constantly exposed to the elements, yet without ever succumbing to all these hardships.

<margin>Where and how the Jews make their tents for the Festival of Booths.</margin>
The Jews spend this festival in tents <note>The Hebrew term for such a booth is a "Sukkah."</note> which they build at the entrance or behind their houses, in courtyards or in gardens. The tent (a) must be no more than twenty cubits <note>original: "elleboogen"</note> in size, nor less than ten spans high. They are erected as much as possible in a well-situated, pleasant, and especially non-foul-smelling place. Wealthy Jews decorate the interior of these tents with carpets, as well as leafy branches and fruits, such as lemons and oranges, etc., and sometimes with branches of non-fruiting trees, pumpkins, or even externally with green reeds. The booths are covered on top with green foliage, yet in a way that provides shade without being completely enclosed. One must also ensure that this greenery does not wither. Finally, they must not be erected under a roof or under the branches of a tree.

<margin>Which ceremonial customs are practiced in the synagogue, and what these mean to them.</margin>
During this festival (b) one appears in the synagogue with a palm branch, three branches of myrtle, and two of willow, all bound together, which are carried in the right hand; in the left hand, one carries a small citron branch <note>The Etrog or citron fruit.</note> with its fruit. The congregants follow one another, turning and facing first to the East, then to the South, then to the West, and finally to the North. There is a hidden meaning in each of these distinct branches. The palm branch, which produces an unsavory fruit, is the image of hypocrites; the myrtle, which is barren although it has a pleasant scent, is the symbol of those who do good works under the Law; the willow represents the godless, and the citron branch represents the righteous. A small circuit is made around the lectern or pulpit with these branches in hand. In ancient times, this was done in Jerusalem around the Altar.

The seventh day is the greatest festival day <note>Known as Hoshana Rabbah.</note>. On this day, the myrtle, palm, and citron branches are set aside, and only the willow branch is kept. Seven times (c) one circles the lectern or pulpit. The prayers are recited more hastily than usual, the reason for which is given (d) as a reminder that during the wanderings in the wilderness, they were forced to hasten their divine service. Seven scrolls of the Law are removed from the <term>HECHAL<note>original: "HECHAL." The Ark or chest where the Torah scrolls are kept.</note></term>. The lectern is decorated with flowers; and because this day and the following—which is the eighth day of the festival—are days of rejoicing for the synagogue, the people are quite exuberant, which surprises those who do not understand the mysteries of Jewish ceremonies. People move about, tripping back and forth, reciting prayers with great speed and noise, and they beat the willow branches upon the benches.

<margin>Why the activity appears strange to a spectator who does not understand the symbolism.</margin>
The human wit, always inclined to judge negatively that which offends it and whose mystery it remains ignorant of, has enough work to do to avoid taking a side against such religious actions where, it seems, no dignity is to be found. The cool sense of modern piety fits very poorly with these foreign religious duties; people unaccustomed to observing symbols and mysteries are bold enough to ask those who take pleasure in serving God in this way, how it can be permitted to treat divine service such that the ceremonies appear ridiculous and the behavior in worship so unseemly. The seven circuits made around the pulpit, it is said, are done in memory of the circuit Joshua made around the walls of Jericho.

The opening of the Festival of Booths or Tents is performed by the household with blessings, followed by the evening meal. One takes delight...

> (d) See Basnage, *History of the Jews*, Book 6, Chapter 17.

## CHAPTER XIV.

### Concerning the Feast of Booths or the Feast of TABERNACLES.

<margin>The significance of the Feast of Booths.</margin>
This Feast is the symbol of the Israelites' journey and hardships in the Wilderness after the passage of the Red Sea, and of the care of God's Providence, who preserved them during forty years in barren and dreadful plains, without housing, constantly exposed to the inconveniences of the air; yet without ever succumbing to all these hardships.

<margin>Where and how the Jews make their Tents for the Feast of Booths.</margin>
The Jews spend this Feast in Tents <note>Sukkot</note>, which they build in front of the entrance or behind their houses, in the courtyard or in gardens. The Tent (a) must not be more than twenty cubits <note>approx. 30 feet</note> in size, nor less than ten spans high. They are erected as much as possible in a well-situated, pleasant, and especially not foul-smelling place. The wealthy Jews decorate these tents internally with carpets, likewise with leafy tree branches and fruits, such as Lemons and Oranges, etc., and sometimes also with branches of infertile trees, of Pumpkins, or even externally solely with green reeds. The Booths are covered from above with green foliage, but without creating a solid shade <note>The roof must be made of organic material (S'chach) and allow the stars to be seen</note>. One must also ensure that this greenery does not wither. Finally, they may not be erected under a roof nor under trees.

<margin>Which Ceremonial customs are then practiced in the Synagogue, and what this signifies among them.</margin>
During this Feast (b) one appears in the Synagogue with a palm branch, three of myrtle, and two of willow, all bound together, which one carries in the right hand, and in the left a Citron branch <note>Original: *Sitroentakje*; referring to the Etrog</note> with its fruit. They follow one another; turning and facing first to the East, then to the South, then to the West, and finally to the North. There is a mystery in each of these distinct branches. The Palm branch, which produces an unsavory fruit, is the Image of the Hypocrites; the Myrtle, which is barren although of a pleasant scent, is the symbol of those who do good works under the Law; The Willow represents the Godless, and the Citron branch the Righteous. One makes a small circuit around the lectern or pulpit with these

<column-break/>

branches in hand. Formerly, this was done in Jerusalem around the Altar.

<margin>How the activity appears strange to an observer, since they do not understand the symbolism.</margin>
The seventh day <note>Hoshana Rabbah</note> is the greatest Feast day. One then sets aside the Myrtle, Palm, and Citron branches, retaining only the Willow branch. Seven times (c) they go around the lectern or pulpit. The prayers are performed more hastily than usual, for which the reason is given (d) that during the wandering in the Wilderness they were forced to hasten with Divine service. They take seven Books of the Law from the HECHAL <note>the Ark or cabinet where the Torah scrolls are kept</note>. The lectern is decorated with flowers; and because this day and the following, which is the eighth of the Feast, are days of rejoicing for the Synagogue, one is then as if unrestrained, which astonishes those who do not understand the mysteries of the Jewish Ceremonies. They move, they trip back and forth, reciting the prayers with much speed and noise, and they beat the willow branches on the benches. The human wit, always inclined to judge negatively of what strikes it and of which it remains ignorant of the mystery, has enough work to free itself from taking a side against such Religious actions where, so it seems, not the least dignity is found. The cool sense of piety fits very poorly with these strange Religious duties, and people, unaccustomed to regarding the symbols and mysteries, are shameless enough to ask those who take pleasure in serving God in such a way, how it is permitted to handle the Divine service thus, such that its Ceremonies appear ridiculous, by behaving so unbecomingly in Religion. The seven circuits made around the pulpit, it is said, occur in memory of the circuit that *Joshua* made around the walls of *Jericho*.

### CHAPTER XV.

->Concerning the FEAST of the LAW, the FEAST of LIGHTS called in Hebrew HANUKKAH <note>original: "CHANUCCAH"</note> or DEDICATION, and the FEAST of PURIM.<-

<margin>
The Feast of the Law, when and by whom it was instituted.
</margin>
This Feast occurs on the ninth day of the [Feast of] Booths or Tabernacles; (a) it is of the institution of the Rabbis, and is celebrated on the 23rd of September. The Jews rejoice then, because God shows them the grace of reading through and observing the Law. It is well known that the reading of the sacred Books of Moses is divided into 52 readings (b) <note>These are the weekly Torah portions, or *Parashot*</note> and that one is read on every Sabbath; thus the last reading falls on the ninth day of the *Feast of Booths*, or on the following Sabbath.

In the evening, when the ninth day begins, all the scrolls of the Law (c) are taken out of the Ark and they are carried in procession around the pulpit. The Cantor <term>Zanger</term> <note>The Hebrew term is *Chazzan*</note> has precedence in this procession. The following morning, the same ceremony is performed again, and these Books are then brought back with ceremony into the HECHAL, (d) <term>Hechal</term> <note>The Holy Ark where Torah scrolls are kept</note> except for three that are kept back. In the first Book, the end is read, in the second the beginning of the Law, and in the third that which according to *Numbers 29* contains the offerings. This is what *Buxtorf* <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629) was a famous Hebraist and scholar of Jewish customs</note> tells us about it: but generally one is satisfied with reading the end and the beginning of the Law in two distinct Books. The two persons chosen to read these two places of the Law are called Bridegrooms <note>Specifically *Chatan Torah* (Groom of the Law) and *Chatan Bereshit* (Groom of the Beginning)</note>. This reading takes place amidst the noise of the people's acclamations, and the Rabbis imagine that this (e) is a wonderful preservative against the Devil's slanders.

<margin>
How those are named who are chosen for the reading of the beginning and end of the Law.
</margin>
<margin>
And with what ceremony.
</margin>
On the day of this Ceremony, the ecclesiastical Offices <note>Synagogue honors or *Mitzvot*</note> are distributed, especially those concerning the Law. They

<column-break/>

<margin>
Duties performed, as well as the offices distributed.
</margin>
are sold to the highest bidder, and the money is spent on the maintenance of the poor and the Synagogue. *Buxtorf*, who gives us this account as he saw it in the High German <note>Ashkenazi</note> Synagogues, also tells us what these Offices are.

I. The duty to light the lamps of the Synagogue.

II. That of distributing the wine for the public sanctification <term>Kiddush</term> of the Sabbath and other solemn days, for the benefit of the poor who have no means to provide it for themselves.

III. That of rolling the scrolls of the Law open and closed.

IV. This one to lift the Books of the Law and thus, held aloft, to show them to the Congregation <term>Hagbah</term>.

V. That of touching the wood and the cords used to roll and fasten the Book of the Law. This Wood is called the *Tree of Life* <term>Etz Chayim</term>, and the young men are willing to observe this duty, since they flatter themselves that the touching of this Wood lengthens their lives, preserves their health, and makes them wise and understanding.

VI. This one to read something from the Law on solemn days.

VII. That when someone is appointed in the place of those who do not behave well in any of the aforementioned duties.

The Sabbath following this Feast is called the *Sabbath of the Beginning* (f) <note>Shabbat Bereshit</note>.

<margin>
The Feast of Lights, why so established.
</margin>
The origin of the Feast of Lights has been shown to us by Leon de Modena (g) <note>A famous 17th-century Venetian Rabbi</note>. It is not enough to light the lamps in the Synagogue in the designated order.

# XV. CHAPTER.

->Regarding the FEAST of the LAW, the FEAST of LIGHTS (called CHANUCCAH or DEDICATION in Hebrew), and the FEAST of PURIM.<-

---

<margin>The Feast of the Law: when and by whom it was established.</margin>
**T**his Feast falls on the ninth day of the Tents or Booths; (a) it is an institution of the Rabbis and is celebrated on the 23rd of September. The Jews rejoice at this time, because God has granted them the grace to read through and contemplate the Law. It is well known that the reading of the sacred Books of Moses is divided into 52 readings (b) and that one is read every Sabbath: thus, the final reading falls on the ninth day of the Feast of Booths, or on the following Sabbath.

In the evening, when the ninth day begins, all the Books of the Law (c) are taken out of the Ark and carried in a procession around the pulpit <note>original: "preekplaats," referring to the Bimah or central platform</note>. The Singer <note>the Cantor or Chazzan</note> has precedence in this procession. The next morning, the same ceremony is performed again, and these Books are subsequently returned with great state to the <term>HECHAL</term> <note>original: "HECHAL," the Hebrew term for the Holy Ark where Torah scrolls are kept</note>, (d) except for three which are held back.

<margin>What those chosen to read the beginning and end of the Law are called.</margin>
In the first Book, the end is read; in the second, the beginning of the Law; and in the third, that which concerns the offerings according to Numbers 29. This is what Buxtorf tells us of it: but generally, people are satisfied with reading the end and the beginning of the Law from two distinct Books. The two persons chosen to read these two portions of the Law are called <term>Bridegrooms</term> <note>These titles are Chatan Torah (Bridegroom of the Law) and Chatan Bereshit (Bridegroom of the Beginning)</note>. This reading takes place amidst the sound of the people’s cheers, and the Rabbis believe that this (e) is a miraculous preservative against the Devil’s slanders.

<margin>And with what solemnity</margin>
On the day of this Solemnity, the Ecclesiastical Offices are distributed, especially those concerning the Law. They are

<column-break/>

sold to the highest bidder, and the money is spent on the maintenance of the poor and the Synagogue. Buxtorf, who gives us this account as he saw it in the High-German <note>Ashkenazi</note> Synagogues, also tells us what these Offices are.

<margin>performed, as well as the rings distributed.</margin>
I. The office of lighting the lamps of the Synagogue.
II. That of distributing the wine for the public sanctification <note>Kiddush</note> of the Sabbath and other solemn days, for the benefit of the poor who have no means to provide it for themselves.
III. That of unrolling and rolling up the Books of the Law.
IV. This one: to lift up the Books of the Law and thus, while raised, to show them to the Congregation <note>The ritual of Hagbah</note>.
V. That of touching the wood and the cords used to roll, unroll, and fasten the Book of the Law. This Wood is called the <term>Tree of Life</term> <note>Hebrew: Etz Chaim. These are the wooden rollers of the Torah scroll</note>, and the youths are eager to undertake this office, as they flatter themselves that touching this Wood lengthens their lives, preserves their health, and makes them wise and understanding.
VI. That of reading something from the Law on solemn days.
VII. That of being appointed in place of someone who does not behave well in any of the aforementioned offices.

The Sabbath following this Feast is called the <term>Sabbath of the Beginning</term> (f).

<margin>The Feast of Lights, why it is so called.</margin>
The origin of the Feast of Lights has been shown to us by Leon de Modena (g). One is not content merely to light the lamps in the Synagogue in the designated order.

The <term>MEZUZAH<note>A small parchment scroll containing Hebrew verses from the Torah, fixed to the doorpost of a Jewish home.</note></term> must be on the right side, as has already been said, so that one passes between two commandments (b). On this Feast, the memory of the *Dedication of the Tabernacle* is also celebrated, and the reading from *Numbers 7* is performed.

There are also several special prayers for this Feast; among others, there is one to bless God, *who has commanded the lighting of the Lamps in these days of Solemnity.* This Feast lasts eight days, because in the time of the Maccabees—those famous deliverers of the Jews—circumcision, which had to occur on the eighth day, had been abolished or suspended by the enemies of Judaism.

<margin>The origin of the name "Purim," by whom it was established against Haman, and what this Feast signifies.</margin> The word PURIM, from which this Feast of Purim takes its name, is a Persian word and means *Lot*. It is the plural of *Pur*. Thus the Jews name the two days of this Solemnity, because *Haman*, their enemy, had cast the lot (c) to exterminate them on these days.

The Fast held on the day before PURIM is an institution of the Rabbis: but it is probable that the Feast itself was introduced by a Prophet (d) who was a contemporary of *Haman*. However that may be, the *Purim* is in some sense the "Shrove Tuesday" <note>The author compares the revelry of Purim to the Christian Carnival or Vastenavond (Shrove Tuesday) celebrations common in Europe.</note> of the Jews; they also celebrate it at the same time as the Christian Shrove Tuesday: But with this distinction, that the Jews spend it with penance and mourning instead of joy.

<margin>The Feast of Purim described.</margin> The Fast must last three days, and the most religious observe it very strictly. The Jews in general spend it as a day of bodily affliction. "In the morning one " gives the poor something with which " they can rejoice in the evening; one " sometimes sends them dishes from one's own table, so that they might be " better satisfied; one takes a collection of the " half-Shekel, which was formerly paid for the " Temple, and it is distributed to " those who go on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, where they desire to be buried, in order to be " spared from a long journey on the day of Resurrection, and to find themselves so much closer to the Valley " of *Josaphat*. <note>Also known as the Valley of Jehoshaphat; according to tradition, this is the site of the final judgment.</note>

<column-break/>

" In the evening one goes to the Synagogue, " to hear the reading of the Book of Esther, " which the <term>Chazzan<note>The Cantor or leader of the synagogue service.</note></term> explains before the Assembly. The reader may " sit during this reading, whereas " otherwise, when reading the Law, he must " stand. After having unrolled this scroll, " he must say three prayers, to " thank God that they are called to this " Solemnity, since He delivered them from " *Haman's* snares, and spared their " lives until the day of this Feast. Joy is so strongly attached to this PURIM, that one could not be a sincere Jew if one did not give free rein to one's pleasure. One would indeed believe that strange efforts must be exerted to pass, in almost a single moment, from a strict penance to such an extravagant joy, which has no moderation at all, thus stepping from one act to the other without interval. ## CHAPTER XVI.

### Concerning the FAST DAYS of the Jews commanded to them by the SYNAGOGUE.

<margin>
The significance of the commanded Fast Days.
</margin>
Leon de Modena (c) has dealt with the commanded Fast Days; however, this one of the 17th of <term>Tamuz<note>The fourth month of the Hebrew calendar, falling in June or July.</note></term>, which corresponds with the month of June, involves many matters—such as the Tablets of the broken Law, the idolatry of the Golden Calf, the cessation of the daily sacrifice that had to be performed, and the desecration of the Temple by the idolatry of <term>Manasseh<note>A king of Judah who, according to the Bible, re-introduced pagan altars into the Temple.</note></term>—which are then part of the subjects of their mourning.

<margin>
How strictly the Fast Days regarding the Destruction of the Temple are established.
</margin>
The fast that they impose upon themselves regarding the destruction of both Temples is very remarkable. The meal that precedes it must be accompanied by moderation and modesty. A single dish on the table shall suffice for those who, with a sincere heart, bewail the destruction of Jerusalem. One shall reject everything that can flatter the palate as improprieties. One shall eat little and drink even less. The <term>High German Jews<note>original: "Hoogduitsche Jooden"; this refers to the Ashkenazi Jewish community.</note></term> then eat (d) legumes and eggs, since they represent the image of mourning and sadness. In former times, people were satisfied with dry bread dipped in water, with a little salt. This mournful meal took place while sitting on the earth near the hearth, dressed in a sack, sometimes sprinkled with ashes: but always weeping and sighing. A jug filled with water served to quench the thirst of the penitent and to strengthen the powers weakened by the mourning ritual. Silence was broken only by sighs; they sat barefoot; and to increase the misery, one sometimes mixed

They are arranged almost like (b) those hanging on a gallows.

During this fast, one spent the night (e) with the most intolerable discomforts. One had to sleep on a hard bed, having a low bolster, the feathers unswung, and the sheets had to be hard and coarse. Some took a stone for a pillow. The following day, one did not read from the Law books, because this gladdens the heart. The day following this Fast Day is also a day of mourning, such that one abstains from meat and wine, although not all the ceremonies of the first day are required. Nevertheless, great signs of sadness and dejection are shown. On the day before this solemn day, one must come into the Synagogue without shoes; one sits down upon the ground; one reads the <term>Lamentations of Jeremiah<note>A biblical book consisting of five poems mourning the destruction of Jerusalem.</note></term> by a dimmer light than usual, and at every verse which begins with a Hebrew word corresponding to *How* <note>original: "Hoe"; in Hebrew, the book of Lamentations is called "Eichah," meaning "How," which is the first word of the text.</note>, one raises the voice in a moving manner. Finally, those who celebrate the memory of the destruction of the Temple most religiously must carefully employ everything that can awaken a mournful heart in them.
Leon de Modena also mentions other Fast Days recommended by the Synagogue. But besides these, some are celebrated that are not generally accepted. The Calendar which will follow this explanation expresses the names of these Fast Days and some other Feasts.

# CHAPTER XVII.

## The Monday and Thursday RELIGIOUS DUTY of the Jews.

<margin>To which religious duties the Jews are bound on Mondays and Thursdays.</margin>
Regarding this religious practice, Buxtorf (a) gives us this description. One of the ten enactments that *Ezra* <note>original: "Esdras"; the priest and scribe who led the Judean exiles back from Babylon.</note> gave the Jews upon their return from the Babylonian captivity was, according to the account of the *Talmud*, to read something from the *Law* <note>The Torah, or the first five books of the Bible.</note> publicly in the Synagogue on *Mondays* and *Thursdays*, and to perform this reading in a certain manner and with all due godliness regarding the loftiness of the subject. Another of these commandments dictates that legal matters must be judged or decided on *Mondays* and *Thursdays*. It is said that *Moses* climbed Mount Sinai for the second time on a *Thursday*, and returned the following Monday with the new Tablets of the Law. The Pharisee (b) had undoubtedly chosen these days to fast twice a week. There are also special prayers for Monday and Thursday.

<margin>Reading of the Law.</margin>
Several remarkable ceremonies accompany the display and reading of the Law. Buxtorf provides us with a description that corresponds with what is practiced in the High German Synagogue <note>original: "Hoogduitsche Synagoge"; referring to the Ashkenazi Jewish community.</note>. The Book of the Law has two handles for lifting it, so that one does not touch the Book itself, which could sometimes be defiled by soiled hands. These wooden sticks or handles are called the *Tree of Life* <note>original: "Hout des levens"; in Hebrew, "Etz Chaim."</note>. *Leon de Modena* speaks very precisely of the scrupulous care the Jews take in the choice of the parchment upon which the Law is written; of the ink, the lettering, and the manner of writing; of the Ark in which it is kept, etc. We shall therefore say no more about it.

<margin>The Book of the Law described with its accompanying ornaments.</margin>
The Book of the Law is wrapped in a type of bandage or wide ribbon, stitched with a needle. Every child brings his own to the Synagogue. Commonly, the name of the child and his friends, his age, and the day of his birth are embroidered on this ribbon. The father of the child hands the ribbon over to the person entrusted with the care of the *Tree of Life*, and he gives it to the Jew who is commissioned to roll and unroll the Law. He winds it in such a way in these ribbons that the letters stitched upon them

<column-break/>

face toward the Law, and if possible, they should even touch it. Besides that, the Book of the Law is dressed in a very magnificent silk covering. A silver plate is fixed to the covering by means of a small silver chain. This plate is hollow, containing other much smaller plates upon which are engraved the names of the Festivals and other Holy Days that require the reading of the Law. On the large plate are engraved the words, *the Crown of the Law*, or these, *Holiness to the Lord*.

<margin>and how it is handled.</margin>
When the <term>Chazan<note>A cantor or worship leader who chants the liturgy.</note></term> takes the sacred Book of the Law out of the Ark, the congregation says: *Let God arise and His enemies be scattered*; and when he closes the Ark again, he speaks a blessing corresponding to the action, and the congregation responds with another. When the Law is carried to the pulpit or lectern, the most godly approach to kiss it, as do those who are within reach; others at least try to touch it with their hand.

The Law is placed on a silk cloth spread over the lectern; after which the <term>Seghen<note>An official or deputy who assists in the synagogue service.</note></term> loosens the bands, opens the Book, and commands the *Chazan* to begin the reading of the Law.

After the ending of the reading, the "lifter" <note>The person performing the "Hagbah" ritual.</note> takes the opened Law, lifts it as high as he can, and turns it—thus opened and lifted—toward the four winds. Then the congregation says: *Behold the Law that Moses gave to the children of Israel.*

This religious duty being performed, those who have purchased the privilege of rolling the Law and grasping the *Tree of Life* approach to carry out their work. Everyone also approaches to kiss it and at least touch the sacred Wood. Two fingers have the honor of this touch, which are immediately placed upon the eyes; for this touch gives the fingers the power to strengthen the eye and to cure the defects of the eyes. This Wood also strengthens the health, cures illnesses, and benefits pregnant women in their labor who behold it.

# Regarding the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

The Civil Year begins in the month of *Tisri* <note>Tishrei</note>, which is September, and the Ecclesiastical Year <note>the religious or church year</note> in *Nisan*, corresponding with the month of March.

<margin>How the Jews count the months in a Civil Year.</margin>
Since *Basnage* <note>Jacques Basnage (1653–1723), the French historian previously mentioned.</note> saw fit to include abolished and little-known Festivals in this Year and Month Indicator, we shall follow him in that regard.

These are as follows:

### I. FIRST CIVIL MONTH, VII. SEVENTH ECCLESIASTICAL MONTH, the Month of TISRI or September.

<margin>The Month of Tisri, and what one must observe within it.</margin>
**Days. I.** The beginning of the Year. The Feast of Trumpets. See *Leviticus* XXIII, verse 24 and *Numbers* XXIX, verse 1 <note>The original text cites verse 17, but the command for the Feast of Trumpets is found in Numbers 29:1.</note>.
The Trumpet <note>The Shofar</note> is blown for many reasons: I. Because *Isaac* having lain upon the Altar, a Ram was offered in his place, caught by its horns in a thicket. II. Because when *Moses* returned to Mount *Sinai* to request new Tables of the Law from God, the Trumpet was blown in the Camp of *Israel* to prevent the People from falling back into Idolatry. It is believed the Trumpet should be blown daily—namely, in the evening and the morning—from the 1st of *August* <note>The month of Elul</note> until the 28th, after the ending of prayers, in memory of *Moses'* ascent.

There is great concern regarding the Trumpets one should use, and the manner in which one must blow. It is required that it be a Ram’s Horn; one from an ox or calf is not lawful. It must be curved rather than straight. Even if one had stolen it, it would still be fit for use, because the command to blow the Trumpet and the prohibition against stealing are two distinct commandments. However, if the Horn has served in any act of Idolatry, it must be rejected. It is not permitted to enrich the same with gold or any other precious decoration. If there is a cross-crack in it, it does no harm; but if the crack runs lengthwise along the Horn, it is unusable. One must blow upon it as strongly as one can. Even women are permitted to blow the Trumpet.

<column-break/>

**Days.** On the first day of the Year one rises early; one goes to the Synagogue; many prayers are recited there; subsequently, the Books of the Law <note>The Torah scrolls</note> are taken from the chest. Five Persons—namely, a Priest <note>Kohen</note>, a Levite, and three Israelites—are chosen to read the Law on this day. One of the five reads a passage from the Prophets: namely, *Samuel* I and II up to the tenth verse <note>Referring to the story of Hannah in 1 Samuel 1-2.</note>. Subsequently, he is commanded to blow the Trumpet, and taking the Horn, he pronouses these words:

> *Blessed are you our Lord and God, King of the World, who has sanctified us through your Law, and commanded us to hear the sound of the Trumpet. Blessed are you, my God, who has given us life, who sustains us, and who has allowed us to exist until this day.* (d)

Then the Horn is blown; but there are three manners of blowing which must be accurately fulfilled and observed, blowing thrice in a particular way, which are called *Tischbrath*, *Taschiath*, and *Tarath* <note>original: *Tifchbrath*, *Tafchiath*, *Tarath*; these are phonetic renderings of the Shofar sounds: Tekiah, Shevarim, and Teruah.</note>.

When one has blown, this prayer is repeated: *Remember the Covenant of Abraham and the sacrifice of Isaac.* The custom of the Spanish Jews <note>The Sephardic community</note> is slightly different; for they begin with these words: *Blessed is the People that know the joyful sound* <note>original: "Gelukzalig is het Volk 't welk weet 't geen tot vernoeging dient"; a translation of Psalm 89:15.</note>. They then implore God to remember the Covenant established with their Forefathers. Then they begin to blow the Horn; a prayer is recited, composed by Rabbi *Amnon*, beginning: *Give strength to the holiness*, etc. <note>The prayer *Unetanneh Tokef*, traditionally attributed to Rabbi Amnon of Mainz.</note>. Then they begin to blow again. The prayers called the Trumpet Prayers are repeated, because the word שופרות, *Sciopparoth* <note>original: שופרות (*Shofrot*); the "Trumpets" section of the Rosh Hashanah service.</note> is frequently mentioned therein; and having recited the prayers, one ends with the blowing of the horn.

# SECOND HISTORICAL DISCOURSE

`Days.` [III.] Those who had remained after the conquest by Nebuchadnezzar <note>The King of Babylon who destroyed the first Temple</note>. Many of these Jews were killed along with Gedaliah through the treachery of Ishmael. (a)
On the same day, another Festival was established during the time of the Hasmoneans <note>The Jewish dynasty following the Maccabean revolt</note> to celebrate the memory of a miracle that God performed during the time of the persecution.
Legal cases were argued through writings, and the debtors were required to place God’s name in their <term>Promissory notes</term> <note>original: 'Handſchriften'; legal documents acknowledging debt</note>: *On such a Day, and Year of John the High Priest and Servant of God* <note>Referring to the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus</note>. The Judges then ordered that one should pay their debts the following day and tear up the notes, which was carried out; but they stood amazed, seeing that the name of God in them had been erased <note>By divine intervention, to prevent the holy name from being discarded with the paper</note>. They judged the notes to be of no further value and that a Festival should be celebrated in memory of this miracle. (b)
V. Is a Day of Fasting because of the death of twenty Israelites and that of Akiba, son of Joseph, who had been imprisoned.
VII. Is a Day of Fasting, because of the Idolatry of the golden Calf and the burden given by God to have the people perish in the Desert by hunger and the sword.
X. Is a Day of Atonement <note>Yom Kippur</note>. We have previously explained how this is celebrated.
XV. Is the <term>Feast of Tabernacles</term> <note>Sukkot</note>. We have also indicated its origin.
XX. Is the eight-day Feast of Tabernacles.
XXIII. Is the Rejoicing of the Law, <note>Simchat Torah</note> שמחת תורה. By this, one understands the blessings that Moses gave to the people before his death: therefore, one reads the last two Chapters of *Deuteronomy* and the first of *Joshua*. One also reads the Book of *Ecclesiastes*.

They built a new Altar, purified the Courtyard and the contaminated places, and offered sacrifices with much solemnity and joy. (c)
XXV. Is a day of joy, in memory of the Jews returning from the Babylonian captivity and taking back various places that the Cutheans <note>Samaritans</note> had occupied in their absence. (d)
XXVII. Is a day of joy, since *Rabbi Jochanan*, son of *Zakkai*, defended himself against the Sadducees and triumphed over these Heretics, who wanted to eat from that which was offered to God, whereas it was to be consumed upon the Altar. *Leviticus XXIII. verse 15.*

# Concerning the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

<margin>(a)</margin>
XXI. Is the day of Mount Gerizim. The Rabbis recount that the Samaritans <note>A group related to the Jews but practicing a rival form of the religion centered on Mount Gerizim</note> sent a delegation to *Alexander the Great* when he arrived in Judea, to request his permission to destroy the Temple in Jerusalem; and to carry out their plan, they obtained from him the purchase of a portion of Mount Moriah <note>The site of the Jewish Temple</note>. But *Simon the Just*, then High Priest, went to meet that Prince. Alexander, marveling at the dignity and majesty of the High Priest, soon rejected the proposal of the delegates, since *Simon* requested him to prevent the Samaritans from destroying their Temple. To this, *Alexander* replied, *“They are in your hands”*; and thereupon they pierced the heels of the Samaritan envoys, tied them to the tails of their horses, and dragged them over stones and thorns as far as Mount Gerizim, which they then tilled, and where they were forced to sow weeds—just as the Samaritans had intended to do on Moriah. Therefore, they established a Feast Day in this memory.

XXIV. Is the *Feast of Dedication* <note>Hanukkah</note>; when the Altar, which had been profaned by *Antiochus* <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king</note>, was purified. (b) This Feast is very solemn and lasts eight days; (a) it is also called the *Feast of Lights*.
Some have added to this day the Feast of *Judith*, because of the addition attached to her history in the common Latin translation <note>The Vulgate</note>, namely: *“The feast of this victory is placed by the Hebrews in the number of their holy days, and this day has been celebrated by the Jews from that time until now.”* Sigonius and Tornielli <note>Carlo Sigonio and Agostino Tornielli, 16th-century historians</note> have incorporated this into the chronologies they compiled for the Jewish Feasts. But the words of the common Latin

<column-break/>

translation are not found in the Greek; thus it is an addition inserted by some deceivers, obscuring the honor of *Judith*, or rather the truth of the history. This Feast is not found in the calendars compiled by the Jews, nor even in those of *Selden* <note>John Selden, a noted 17th-century English jurist and scholar</note>, who is more accurate than the others. *Sigonius* compiled his through his own invention.

<margin>What the Jews had to observe in the month of Teveth.</margin>

The Jews imagine that the Law was profaned by this translation, although it was carried out by Jews; and they claim that God, to show his displeasure, allowed a thick darkness to come over the Earth, which lasted for three days. But the Jews called <term>Hellenists</term> <note>Greek-speaking Jews living outside of Judea</note>, and those of the Diaspora, hold this translation in great esteem, as it was absolutely necessary for them, as it also was for the Early Fathers of the Christian Church, since they did not understand Hebrew.

These *Sadducees* were so inexperienced that they could not derive a single proof for their rulings from the Law. ### V. The Month of *Shevat*; or January full, 30 Days.

<margin>
Fast and Feast days observed by the Jews in the Month of Shevat.
</margin>
II. Is a Feast day, on account of the death of *Alexander Jannaeus* <note>A Hasmonean King of Judea known for his conflict with the Pharisees</note>. He was an enemy of the Israelites, namely the *Pharisees*. Having fallen ill, he had the seventy members removed from the *Sanhedrin* and imprisoned. He ordered the Jailer that, if he should die, he should kill all the imprisoned Israelites. The King died, but the Queen <note>Salome Alexandra</note> took his ring, sent it to the prison, and informed the Jailer that the King had had a dream which compelled him to set the Israelites free, and that this ring was the mark and Seal of his will. Soon after, the prisoners were released, and only then was the King's death proclaimed, which the Queen had kept hidden until her plan was carried out.

VIII. Is a Fast, because on this day the righteous of Israel died who lived in the time of *Joshua*. (b)

XXII. The Ceremony of Circumcision has, according to God’s pleasure, become a sign of the Covenant established with the Jews. It is the image of the purification of the heart, without which the service performed for the Supreme Being could not exist. Before we provide a description of this Ceremony, we shall look at what occurs during the labor of pregnant women up to their delivery, and subsequently the Circumcision. During labor, and especially when there is danger, (b) a Rabbi is called and requested to perform the reading of some Psalms and a prayer for the woman in labor. The joy is extraordinary when a little boy is born; but more moderate if it is a daughter. The Father is congratulated, vows are made, toasts are drunk to the health of the newborn, and subsequently everything is prepared for the initiation into Judaism on the eighth day, (c) by means of Circumcision. On the day before, the joy is doubled. One goes to visit the woman in childbed, who is then in a state to endure the bustling joyful activity of the company. All the guests must have reached at least thirteen years of age. On the appointed day, the Circumciser is summoned. Women are not permitted to undertake this procedure, as they lack the sign of Judaism; and the only way one could allow them to perform this cutting of the foreskin would be if there were no men available to complete the execution: and even then, one would have to be entirely certain of her skill and experience.

# On the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

As shown in the illustration above. Since *Leon de Modena* <note>original: "Leon de Modena" (1571–1648), a famous Venetian Rabbi whose work on Jewish customs was widely read by Christians.</note> has described this explicitly enough, there is almost nothing left for us to add.

When the wound of the circumcision is cleansed and dressed, the father thanks God and prays for Him to bless the child. Likewise, the entire company adds their own blessings; after which the Circumciser also offers a prayer for the newly circumcised boy, having washed his hands and taken a drink of wine, etc., just as *Leon de Modena* (a) has explained. The circumcision of a sick child is postponed until they are healed: for just as one cannot be a Jew without Circumcision, so too one cannot be a perfect Christian without Baptism. If a child dies without Circumcision, the devout Jews nevertheless cut away the foreskin of the deceased before burial and give him a name, so that his friends may recognize him again at the resurrection.

In some countries, the entire assembly must stand during the ceremony of Circumcision, except for the *Peter* <note>The "Peter" or "Peiterman" refers to the Sandek, the person who holds the baby during the ritual, similar to a godfather.</note> who alone remains seated.

There is some difference in the Blessing given to newly circumcised children born out of wedlock; for it is believed they are unworthy of a portion of the Blessings usually pronounced over those born in wedlock.

There are sometimes children who are born as if already circumcised; nevertheless, they are given a slight incision to draw at least a little blood from the required part.

It is the same with this ceremony as with all others. They gradually acquire an absolute authority, which almost degenerates into cruelty, and which eventually takes the place of virtue and religion.

## CHAPTER XXI.

### Concerning the Bath of Women for their PURIFICATION; the REDEMPTION of the FIRSTBORN, and the UPBRINGING of CHILDREN.

<margin>
The caution taken with the purification of women in the Bath.
</margin>

*Leon de Modena* (b) has dealt with the purification of women. We shall, however, provide some examples of the anxious precautions they must take, so that the Bath which is to purify them is not in vain. (c) It is required that the bathwater flows entirely over her whole body, and it will be even better if it penetrates to the internal parts. They must occasionally open their mouths, stretch out their arms, open their hands and fingers, and lift and lower their breasts, so that no impurity remains hidden elsewhere. If any accident should happen to her in the bath, care must be taken that nothing is touched without washed hands. Also, the bathing woman must have another woman with her as a witness to the proper conduct of the Bath. This washing is accompanied by appropriate Blessings; however, those of the High German <note>Ashkenazi Jews</note> differ slightly from the Portuguese <note>Sephardic Jews</note>.

The above illustration is shown. Since *Leon de Modena* <note>Rabbi Leon of Modena (1571–1648) was a famous Venetian scholar whose work on Jewish customs was widely read by Christians.</note> has described this explicitly enough, there is almost nothing left for us to add to it.

When the wound of the <term>circumcision</term> <note>original: "befnydenis"</note> is cleansed and bandaged, the Father thanks God and prays for Him to bless the child. Likewise, the entire company adds their own blessings; after which the <term>Circumciser</term> <note>original: "Befnyder," commonly known as the Mohel.</note> also offers a prayer for the young circumcised boy, after having washed his hands and taken a drink of wine, etc., exactly as *Leon de Modena* (a) has explained. The circumcision of a sick child is postponed until recovery: since one cannot be a Jew without circumcision, just as one cannot be a full Christian without Baptism. If the child should die without circumcision, the pious Jews nevertheless cut away the foreskin of the deceased before burial and give him a name, so that his friends may approach him again at the resurrection.

In some countries, the entire assembly must stand during the ceremony of circumcision, except for the <term>Godfather</term> <note>original: "Peter," referring to the Sandek, who holds the child.</note> who alone is seated.

There is some difference in the blessing given to newly circumcised illegitimate children; for it is believed they are unworthy of a portion of the blessings that are usually pronounced over those born of legitimate marriages.

There are sometimes children who are born already circumcised; nevertheless, they are given a slight incision to let at least a little blood flow from the required part.

It is the same with this ceremony as with all others. They gradually acquire an absolute authority, which almost degenerates into harshness, and which finally takes the place of virtue and religion.

->Concerning the Ritual Bath of Women for their PURIFICATION; the REDEMPTION of the FIRSTBORN, and the EDUCATION of CHILDREN.<-

<margin>
How carefully one proceeds with the purification of women in the Bath.
</margin>
*Leon de Modena* has dealt with the purification of women. (b) We shall, however, provide some examples of the anxious precautions they must take, so that the <term>Bath</term> <note>Referring to the Mikvah, the ritual immersion pool.</note> which is to cleanse them is not in vain. (c) It is required that the bathwater flows entirely over her whole body, and it will be even better if it penetrates to the internal parts. They must occasionally open their mouths, stretch out their arms, open their hands and fingers, and lift and lower their breasts, so that no impurity remains hidden elsewhere. If any accident should happen to her in the bath, care must be taken that nothing is touched without washed hands. Also, the bathing woman must have another woman with her as a witness to the proper conduct of the Bath. This washing is accompanied by appropriate blessings; however, those of the <term>High Germans</term> <note>Ashkenazi Jews.</note> differ slightly from those of the <term>Portuguese</term> <note>Sephardic Jews.</note>.

## XXII. CHAPTER.

->*Concerning the BETROTHAL of the Jews in general.*<-

<margin>Polygamy not allowed among European Jews: but certainly in the East.</margin>
The Law of the Christians now obliges the Jew to have no more than a single lawful wife. In the East, where Mohammedanism favors <term>polygamy</term> <note>original: "veelwyvery"</note>, he may have many, and sleep with them without fear, without dreading that he might be reproached for performing his marital duty to others. It is indeed true that in European regions, the husband does not always fulfill his duty to the one who has the right to demand it: but it is Religion that rebukes such evasions. Polygamy gives rise to great misfortunes, and it is difficult to understand how Jewish households are not disturbed by this disorder. One would perhaps find much work in forcing the women into a great submission, not to say a kind of slavery. However it may be, it is certain that women have little to say in countries where polygamy reigns.

<margin>How the betrothal is confirmed among them.</margin>
The marriage promises are confirmed in the presence of some witnesses. The future Groom says to the future Bride: *That you are my Bride*; while he places a ring on her finger: but this custom is not universal. Sometimes

<column-break/>

<margin>becomes of age,</margin>
for previously he sinned for the account of his Father. The reaching of majority is declared in the presence of ten Jews. The Father gives an account of the care he has carried for his Son up to this point, and ends with a declaration that he relieves himself of all the injustices of the youth <note>This refers to the *Baruch she-petarani* blessing, where a father thanks God for being released from legal responsibility for his son's actions.</note>. The witnesses confirm the Declaration; after which the Father then offers a prayer.

<margin>and may marry.</margin>
Having reached eighteen years, the one of majority may marry, as it is not considered proper after twenty years. These eighteen years are sometimes moved forward for those in whom *strength does not wait for the count of these years*, and for whom one is fearful of untimely irregularities <note>A euphemistic reference to early sexual maturity or the risk of "sinful" behavior.</note>. Although this precaution may be fitting, one cannot be certain that it always turns out well.

several months and even years pass before the marriage is completed. Meanwhile, one visits the future Bride with the maintenance of courtship. This is a pre-joy expected with much patience, which is as yet unknown in the beginnings of marriage. However brave a warrior may be, he may nevertheless not scale the fortress except on the day his General appoints. The day that the Rabbis arrange for the marriage is commonly Wednesday or Friday for virgins, or Thursday for widows. Let us follow *Leon de Modena* <note>A famous 17th-century Rabbi of Venice.</note>. It is required that this day, if possible, be during the New Moon.

During the betrothal, the marriage portion of the betrothed is arranged, and the day is chosen to escort her to the wedding house (b). A document is drawn up whereby the Groom promises to give a sum of money for usufruct, and binds all his goods, even his very cloak; yet these cannot be claimed until after the Groom's death. This kind of marriage portion is the same for all daughters, whether rich or poor, and the Rabbis have set the value of it at fifty <term>Rijksdaalders</term> <note>original: "Ryksdaalders," a common silver coin in early modern Europe.</note>.

<margin>Acts of Joy preceding the Wedding.</margin>
When the marriage portion and the usufruct have been mutually agreed upon, and consent to the marriage contract has been given, a short blessing is pronounced. The disorder and irregularity are then tolerated and even serve as a joyful day for the wedding ceremonies.

### XXIII. CHAPTER.

->Concerning the MARRIAGES and WEDDINGS of the Jews.<-

---

<margin>The details with which the marriage of the Jews is accompanied,</margin>
This accompanying print illustration <note>Referring to an engraving included in the original manuscript or book.</note>, consisting of two depictions, shows the marriage of the High German <note>Ashkenazi</note> and that of the Portuguese <note>Sephardic</note> Jews. But to the description by <term>Leon de Modena</term> <note>A Venetian Rabbi (1571–1648) known for his scholarly explanations of Jewish rituals for a non-Jewish audience.</note> regarding these ceremonies and what occurs at weddings, we shall add some further details: The glass which is broken by being thrown down with force, and the ash which is scattered on the bridegroom in some places, represent, according to some, the destruction of Jerusalem: but it is considered with more reason that both these actions represent the fragility of life and the instability of riches.

On the wedding day, the bridegroom and bride dress themselves as sumptuously as their means allow. The bride is led with ceremony by the women and daughters of her friends to the wedding house. Her head is bare and her hair is unwound; she is placed between two elderly women; others hang ornaments upon it, comb it, arrange it, and curl it, and cover her face.

<column-break/>

The eight days (b) before the wedding are days of joy. There is laughter, singing, and dancing; people are, as it were, abandoned to joy and set all sorrow aside. It is also difficult at such a time to find perfect contentment, just as at other times it is easy to encounter subjects of melancholy; for the future spouses remain indoors during these eight days. This is what Buxtorf says.

On the day before the wedding, the betrothed bride goes into the bath <note>The Mikveh, or ritual immersion bath.</note>, according to all the required observations already noted regarding the purification of women; being accompanied by other women.

The future bridegroom (c) sends a Wedding Belt to the future bride; she does the same for him: but that of the bride is wrought with gold, while that of the bridegroom is wrought with silver. We hesitate to express the secret meaning of the gold and silver of these Belts in our mother tongue: but we prefer to share it with the reader in the Latin wording of Buxtorf (d). <note>original: "Mihi causam quaerenti respondit Judaeus argento semen virile, utpote album, innui, auro vero semen, muliebre, &c." — Translation: "When I asked for the reason, a Jew replied to me that by the silver, the male seed, being white, is hinted at, but by the gold, the female seed, etc."</note>

<term>Ontschoeijng: Referring to the rite of Halizah, where a widow is released from the obligation of marrying her deceased husband's brother by ceremonially removing his shoe.</term>

After Marriage, we let Divorce follow. This practice would be used quite frequently if civil laws did not impose order upon it, without which few people would be so religious and honest as to carry their sorrow patiently until the end of their lives, and the flaws one discovers after having had a few months of companionship.

<margin>What marital irregularities cause Divorce.</margin>
Adultery and fornication are the primary reasons that cause Divorce, and almost the only legal ones. In former times, these crimes were punished much more severely than now, and yet they crept in under the Law quite fre-

<margin>How the wedding table is prepared.</margin>
At the wedding feast, poultry is served, sanctified by seven blessings. The first dish served to the Bride is a hen with an egg. After the Bride is served, the wedding guests fall upon the remainder of this poultry. The hen is very significant; it predicts the Bride’s future fertility, and that she will give birth with no less ease than this hen lays her eggs. The meal is followed by the usual wedding joy. Meanwhile, the companions lead the newly married couple to their room, and it is there that the final scene of the wedding play is performed.

After the Bride has transitioned from her virginal state to that of a Woman, the young man leaves her untouched for a set number of days.

We will not involve ourselves in presenting the internal workings of the new household, nor in the account of all marital duties. There are scholars who instruct the Jews precisely on this subject. It is up to the man to fulfill the debt of his duty; and as for the woman, her first objective shall be to produce chosen ones in the Jewish faith.

## Concerning the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

We shall subsequently in this work, when we deal with *Civil Customs*, provide a description of the execution of punishment for **Adulterers**, etc. For this will be a subject of no less importance in this book.

<margin>Of what power the dread bitter water once was, and when it became powerless.</margin>
The Jews now find themselves deprived of the miracle of the **bitter waters** <note>The "bitter waters" refers to the Sotah ritual from the Book of Numbers, an ordeal used to determine if a wife had been unfaithful.</note>. It is a great loss for revengeful, jealous husbands, who would gladly see those who dishonor the brow of a spouse burst asunder. Their wives are no longer exposed to the deadly swelling caused by these disaster-inducing waters. They can now step out of bounds in all safety. The shame that **Divorce** brings in its wake is not powerful enough to prevent people from loving. It is believed that after the cessation of the miracle of the bitter waters, which possibly occurred during the time of the Jewish captivity, divorces came into use because no means of proof could be found anymore to expose the love affairs of Jewish women. They, no longer subject to the effects of a miracle so sorrowful for them, gave free rein to their affairs, and the men were forced to content themselves with divorce. This granted divorce then became more common. A single suspicion gave birth to it, and the women consented all the sooner to this decision by their husbands (a) <note>original: "Jofeph. L. 15. C. 9." referring to Flavius Josephus, Book 15, Chapter 9.</note>.

<margin>How their divorce is impermissible under the laws of Christian Powers.</margin>
In the course of time, the Jews have been obliged to live under the laws of Christian powers, which is why they cannot leave their wives so easily. Stronger reasons than before are required, and the Rabbis themselves increase the obstacles to make the divorce less easy to execute.

<margin>With what particulars this divorce is accompanied.</margin>
We would have nothing to add to what *Leon of Modena* <note>Leon of Modena (1571–1648) was a scholar and rabbi in Venice known for his work "The History of Jewish Rites."</note> has written regarding divorce, if we did not intend to describe this ceremony as it is observed by the **High German Jews** <note>Ashkenazi Jews.</note>. (b) <note>original: "Buxtorf Syn. Jud. C. 46." referring to Johannes Buxtorf’s *Synagoga Judaica*.</note> The divorce is performed in this manner at the door of the Synagogue. The Rabbi who presides over this solemn custom places himself at the entrance, turning his face toward the East. Besides the parties involved in the dispute, two other Rabbis, a Scribe, and two witnesses are present, the eldest of these

<column-break/>

witnesses placing himself at the right hand and the youngest at the left hand of the aforementioned Rabbi. The Scribe, alongside the man and woman, stands directly across from the President, and the two other Rabbis position themselves on either side. The presiding Rabbi then asks the man if he is of the mind to divorce, etc. After he has answered all the questions put to him, the President and the witnesses read the **Letter of Divorce** <term>Get: the formal document used in Jewish law to effect a divorce</term>, which bears the signatures of the witnesses. Subsequently, the Rabbi addresses the Scribe and asks him if he is the writer of that letter, if he wrote it on parchment with the consent of the future divorcees, with his own pen and ink, etc.; after which he addresses the two witnesses, puts the same questions to them, and asks more broadly if they signed it and how. The woman, who has her face covered, is also questioned. Upon the consent to this divorce, she is told to open both her hands. The palms must be bent forward, and if she has rings on her fingers, she must remove them. The Rabbi folds the Letter of Divorce, gives it to the man, with orders to keep it until he commands him to deliver it into the hands of the woman he wishes to leave. After some further circumstances, the man gives the writing to the woman, who shortly thereafter closes her hands and, at the command of the President, puts the Letter of Divorce in her pocket or hides it in her clothing. Not long after, the Rabbi demands the letter back, reads it once more, and asks again what was said before by the witnesses and the Scribe. This caution of the Rabbi is not to be blamed; perhaps he is still seeking to bring the parties to other thoughts: but rarely does any repentance follow. For when things have gone this far, hesitation has little place. If, after this questioning, no change of mind occurs, the Rabbi pronounces the divorce, cuts the letter crosswise, and forbids the divorcer or divorcee from remarrying for three months. Sometimes the President keeps the Letter of Divorce with him without cutting it.

We shall only add a few questions (c) <note>original: "Idem. C. 41." referring to Buxtorf.</note> that the presiding—
