## CHAPTER XXV.

->*Concerning the conduct of* TRAVELING JEWS; *as also of the* SICK *and* DYING, *with the* CEREMONIES *of their* FUNERAL PROCESSIONS.<-

---

<margin>
How the Jews conduct themselves while traveling.
</margin>

If we observe the conduct of a traveling Jew; (b) he must, at a certain distance from his place of departure, and turned toward that direction, perform his prayer, repeating some scriptural passages that pertain to his journey. Superstition creeps in here not a little. There is a prescription to acquire the assistance of the Angels, namely: *May the Angel* MICHAEL <note>original: "MICHAËL"</note> *be at my right hand; may* NEMUEL <note>original: "NEMUËL"</note> *precede me; may* SHATSIEL <note>original: "SCHAATSIËL"</note> *follow me, and may the Divine Majesty rest upon my head*, etc. Those traveling by sea are also provided with a prescription.

<margin>
What conduct is observed regarding the sick, and how he confesses his sins.
</margin>

We then proceed to describe a journey of the highest importance, more significant than any made in this world: which is that of eternity. Someone being dangerously ill must, from the beginning of his sickness, contemplate that the time approaches in which one must lay down life: he must also, well-comforted and with steadfastness, behold the dissolution of his being. This is like an annihilation for those who possess the pleasures of life.

The sick Jew, believing his illness to be dangerous, confesses his sins with a humble spirit in the presence of ten witnesses. It is unnecessary in this state to hide anything in his heart. The confes-

<column-break/>

Then the widow approaches at the word of the Rabbi, removes the shoe from her brother-in-law with her right hand, shows it to the bystanders, subsequently throws it away with some indignation, and finally spits upon the feet of the unshod man, who is then heartily laughed at; for the spectators raise a great shout, and nothing is heard but a doubling of the cries of the mockers to his shame.

In the *Talmud* <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> (a) it is asked how a woman who had no right hand could perform the ceremony of unshoeing. To which the answer is given: that she could pull off the shoe with her teeth.

The prescription (c) for this confession is arranged according to the order of the alphabet; undoubtedly to assist the contemplation of the ignorant or the hypocritical <note>The "Ashamnu" is a standard Jewish confession of sins organized as an acrostic following the Hebrew alphabet.</note>. An intelligent person prays to God with a better aim than the common man, and he confesses his sins with greater awareness of repentance. One prays to God for the sick in the Synagogue, just as the Christians do in their churches. They nevertheless change the name of the sick person to deceive the devil, and to show evidence that they have renounced their sins <note>This custom, "Shinui Hashem," is based on the belief that a new name creates a new identity, thereby confusing the Angel of Death or averting a divine decree.</note>. They make vows, give alms, and piously take heed of themselves to regain their health through holy focus on God, or to implore His mercy and attain eternal salvation in the next world.

In Venice (d) the Rabbi goes to visit the sick, has him recite the 20th, 38th, and 90th Psalms, to which he adds a long prayer to implore divine mercy for the sick, and in general for all who are oppressed. After which he proclaims forgiveness.

...as a duty or an inherent quality of Judaism; this use is very old and depends more on the tenderness one feels for the dying than on custom. The Pagans received the last sigh (a) <note>The author cites Virgil’s *Aeneid* and the poet Statius, describing the ancient Greco-Roman custom where a relative would catch the final breath of a dying loved one with their mouth to preserve their spirit.</note> of dying ones who were dear and worthy to them.

<margin>
Clothing torn in mourning and how.
</margin>
One tears one's clothing in some places when the dying person gives up the ghost: which is a remnant of the ancient custom of the Israelites. The tear is usually (b) <note>Footnote (b) explains that the tear is made from top to bottom. In the Netherlands, it was a small slit near a buttonhole, sewn up after seven or eight days. In Germany, widows were expected to tear their house-garments.</note> made on the front left side, and must continue for about the length of an eighth of an ell <note>An "ell" was a historical unit of measurement; an eighth of an ell would be roughly 3 to 4 inches.</note>: but if the mourning is for the death of a father or mother, one tears the clothing on the right side, whereas one is otherwise satisfied in a common mourning to tear the outer garment on the left side. Further details on this subject can be found by the reader in the Treatise by Leon de Modena. <note>Leon de Modena (1571–1648) was a famous Venetian rabbi whose work "The History of Jewish Rites" was widely read by Christians to understand Jewish life.</note>

<margin>
How one treats the corpse.
</margin>
After one has closed the eyes and mouth of the deceased, one wraps the corpse in some linen, covers the face, (c) folds the thumb into the hand, and binds it with one of the cords of his <term>Tallit<note>The original text uses "Taled." A Tallit is a fringed prayer shawl worn by Jewish men.</note></term>; for with this veil the deceased travels to the other world. The thumb bent into the hand forms an image of <term>Shaddai<note>Original: "Schaddai." One of the names of God in Hebrew, meaning "Almighty."</note></term>, one of the names attributed to God. The Jews, it is said, have this custom to protect the corpse from the claws of the Devil. The open hand of the deceased proves that he has left behind the goods of the world. The corpse must also be washed; this washing signifies that death, through sincere repentance, is a cleansing of the impurities of life; and who is otherwise capable of receiving a new life from the hand of God? Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf was a 17th-century Christian Hebraist who wrote "Synagoga Judaica," a detailed study of Jewish customs.</note> says (d) that one mixes an egg with wine and rubs the head of the deceased with it. Some perform this anointing in the house of the deceased, others in the <term>House of the Living<note>Original: "Huis der levendigen." A traditional Jewish euphemism for a cemetery, reflecting a belief in the afterlife.</note></term>, for thus the Hebrews call their burial places, and not without reason. It is added that after the washing, all the openings of the corpse are stopped.

Some godly people are buried with the garment that served them on the day of <term>Yom Kippur<note>Original: "Chippur." The Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year.</note></term>. However it may be, one places in the coffin a fine white linen, along with some earth which they call Holy, and a stone under the head, or perhaps a bag of earth, as Leon de Modena says. If anyone has neglected to reconcile with the deceased during his life, (e) he must, if he is not hardened of heart, touch his big toe and thus ask for forgiveness; so that the deceased does not accuse him before the Judgment Seat of God.

Buxtorf, who describes this ceremony according to the custom of the High German Jews <note>Refers to the Ashkenazi Jewish community.</note>, says that when the corpse is brought out of the house of death, a brick (f) <note>Original: "tichelsteen" or "testa" in Latin, meaning a shard of pottery or a tile.</note> or a piece of a broken pot is simultaneously thrown into the street; indicating that by removing the deceased's corpse from the house, all sadness is driven away.

<margin>
And with what solemn custom the corpse is buried.
</margin>
When one has arrived at the grave, a blessing is pronounced, or rather a kind of speech is made to the dead. (g) Saying:
> Blessed be God, who created you, etc. O dead! in whatever number you are, and He shall give you a day of life among them, etc.

After the blessing and the eulogy for the deceased, if he is worthy of it, a prayer is said called the <term>Justice of the Judgment<note>Original: "Gerechtigheit van 't oordeel." Referring to the Tzidduk HaDin prayer, which affirms God's justice in taking a life.</note></term>.

The coffin being closed, the friends and blood relatives of the deceased—ten of the most capable and chosen persons—go seven times around the coffin, praying to God for the soul of the deceased. This is practiced in Holland as shown in the accompanying illustration, which depicts this ceremony and was drawn from life. ### On the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

...as a duty or an inherent quality of Judaism; the use of this is very ancient and depends more on the tenderness felt for the dying than on custom. The Heathens received the last breath (a) <note>original: "laatste zucht"; a reference to the Roman custom of *ore legere*, catching the final breath of a loved one with a kiss</note> of the dying who were dear and worthy to them.

<margin>Clothing torn in mourning and how.</margin>
In some places, one tears their garment when the dying person gives up the ghost: which is a remnant of the ancient custom of the Israelites. The tear is commonly (b) made on the left side in the front, and must continue for about the length of an eighth of an ell <note>approximately 9 centimeters or 3.5 inches</note>: but if the mourning is for the death of a father or mother, one tears their garment on the right side, whereas otherwise, in common mourning, it is sufficient to tear the outer garment on the left side. The reader can find further details on this subject in the Treatise by Leon de Modena <note>referring to the 17th-century rabbi Leone Modena, author of "History of Jewish Rites"</note>.

<margin>How the corpse is treated.</margin>
After the eyes and mouth of the deceased have been closed, the body is wound in some linen, the face is covered, (c) the thumb is folded into the hand, and it is tied with one of the cords of his *Taled* <note>original: *Taled*, known today as a *Tallit* or prayer shawl</note>; for with this veil the deceased travels to the other world. The thumb bent into the hand forms an image of *Schaddai* <note>El Shaddai, a Hebrew name for God often translated as 'Almighty'</note>, one of the names attributed to God. The Jews, it is said, have this custom to protect the corpse from the claws of the Devil. The open hand of the deceased proves that he has left behind the world's goods. The corpse must also be washed; this washing signifies that death, through sincere repentance, is a cleansing of the impurities of life; and who else is capable of receiving a new life from the hand of God? Buxtorf says (d) <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a prominent 17th-century Christian Hebraist</note> that an egg is mixed with wine and the head of the deceased is rubbed with it. Some perform this anointing in the house of the deceased, others in the *House of the Living*, for thus the Hebrews call their Burial Grounds, and not without reason. It is added that after the washing, all the openings of the corpse are stopped.

SECOND HISTORICAL TREATISE

The image is shown being covered with earth. Hardly any mourning is observed for those who have made themselves unworthy, nor for those who die while under **Excommunication**. Far be it from anyone to lament them; (a) because

<column-break/>

# CHAPTER XXVI.

->How the Jews OBSERVE MOURNING, and their MEMORIALS<-
->for the Dead.<-

<margin>
How the
surviving
relatives
must behave
during the
first thirty
days of
mourning.
</margin>
The food that the Jews consume during mourning may rightly be called the *bread of affliction*, when they take their meal during the time of the primary mourning days; one then recalls the painful grief that weighs upon their heart through mournful actions and words. They eat seated upon the floor and unshod <note>without shoes, a traditional sign of humility and grief</note>. Constant consolations are offered to them, which might perhaps be called bitter, since their burdensome seclusion serves only to sustain the grief. One must weep and maintain a sorrowful countenance for the first three days. At the very least, one must act in this manner, even if the heart has no part in it. During the following seven days, one still laments: but the grief gradually wears away. Meanwhile, ten people come every evening and morning to pray with the bereaved to comfort him, to praise the deceased—all according to the occasion—and to pray to God for his soul. After the seven days of mourning end, the mourner goes to the Synagogue to pray, has several lamps (b) lit, and gives alms to the poor on behalf of the deceased. Meanwhile, thirty days pass without the mourner being permitted to wash, groom himself, or have his beard shorn. Soiled and dusty clothes, and an unsightly

<column-break/>

neglect of the nails, the beard, and the hair, are visible and repellent signs of the thirty-day mourning, which makes the Jew look so haggard as if he had risen from the grave. Otherwise, they end the mourning according to the customs of the country where they reside; but an essential matter in this mourning is the **KADDISH** <note>original: "CADISH"; a prayer recited by mourners that praises God and is believed to assist the soul of the deceased</note>, a prayer which the son must recite daily for eleven months to soften the state of his Father’s soul, which must suffer during this time in the Courtyard of the Souls (c).

<margin>
What the
memorial
of the
deceased is
after their
death.
</margin>
Regarding the memory of the Dead, the remembrance and the esteem owed to the departed faithful have introduced these commemorations. The sight of graves, skeletons, and the apparatus of burial teach us how little reliance can be placed on man. It is because of this honor, mixed with fear and piety, which to some extent allows the virtues of the deceased to penetrate the hearts of the living and seeks to maintain forever the memory of those already consumed by worms, that religious Jews occasionally pour out prayers at the graves of their kin and friends. Those who have a true esteem for their deceased Father and Mother observe the anniversary of their death every year through an annual fast.

# CHAPTER XXVII.

### Concerning some CUSTOMS of the JEWS in their DAILY LIVES, in which RELIGION has some PART.

We will only mention these customs in passing, those which depend solely on religion, so as not to mix worldly affairs with ecclesiastical matters. Judaism binds the one with the other much more closely than other religions do. This attachment can be attributed to the passion that the Jews have for their tradition, which has sanctified many different matters equally, and to the quality they ascribe to the People, of being chosen by God from among all other nations. For this reason, they feel obliged to distinguish themselves from others through special customs, to which they have attached connections with and to religion.

<margin>How the Jews must observe certain special customs in their daily activities.</margin>
One may not let a single day pass without reading from the Book of the Law. Their activities may not be undertaken without first having prayed to God for His blessing, and that He may turn all evil thoughts away from them. It is well known with what care the Jews are concerned not to eat anything that the Law has declared unclean for them. Some religious Jews extend their scrupulousness even further. They believe that in order not to defile oneself with what one eats, one must normally relieve oneself once a day. <note>A reference to maintaining ritual and physical purity in connection to consumption.</note> The washing of hands is also a matter of the utmost importance. (a) A certain Rabbi has declared that there is no difference between eating bread without having washed hands and the crime of defiling oneself through fornication with a woman.

The High German Jews <note>The Ashkenazim</note> (b) place salt and bread on the table. The bread, if possible, must be uncut; they make a cut in it, which however does not go all the way through, after which they lay it on the table with both hands and bless it: and the guests say *Amen*. They rub their bread with salt, and while eating, observe the silence of a Carthusian Monk <note>The Carthusians are a Catholic religious order known for their vow of silence; the author uses this as a comparison for the solemnity of the Jewish meal.</note>. They distribute the blessed bread to those

<column-break/>

who are at the table with them. If wine is poured, it is blessed just like the bread, taking it in the right hand, and lifting it up, one speaks the blessing over it. If another drink is used, it is also sanctified in the same way, unless it is plain water. The Master of the house ends this ceremony with the recitation of the 23rd *Psalm*. After which the meal truly begins.

The salt then represents the ancient sacrifices. To apply this spiritually: meat is tasteless without salt, and to prove it, a passage of Scripture from *Job 6, verse 6* is cited. See how the worldly is supported by the spiritual. The ceremony that requires cutting the bread without the cut going all the way through is likewise supported by a text from *Psalm 10, verse 3*. The father of the household takes the bread in his hands in memory (c) of the ten commandments of the grains; for every finger must represent a commandment. <note>In Jewish tradition, there are ten agricultural commandments related to bread, or ten words in the blessing over bread; authors like Buxtorf linked these to the ten fingers of the hands during the blessing.</note>

<margin>Their behavior when they eat.</margin>
At the table, modesty is recommended; moderation and sobriety have no lesser place. (d) The bread must be carefully stored in a clean place. One must talk little at the table and speak only sensibly, since, according to the judgment of the Rabbis, the Prophet *Elijah* and the Guardian Angel of every guest attend every meal. They depart and make room for evil angels when one speaks of nothing but absurd things. It is not only improper to throw meat bones and fish bones on the floor; but this must primarily be done out of fear of offending invisible beings. The same knife may not be used to cut meat and that which is prepared with milk. <note>A reference to the laws of Kashrut (Kosher), which prohibit the mixing of meat and dairy products.</note> Everything that is edible and whatever one touches, toward which one's appetite may be inclined, must be blessed. When clearing the table, something is always left over for the poor.

(d) If one may believe the Talmud, an Angel has the goodness to humble himself to serve by guarding the bread. See Buxtorf, Chapter 12.

### CHAPTER I.
### The first FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLE of RELIGION, about which the Jews do not differ from the Christians. Investigation into this PRINCIPLE.

<margin>How the Jews establish their traditions, added to the Divine Law, as the foundation of their religion.</margin>
The Jews agree with most Christians in this: that their religion rests simultaneously on the word of God and Tradition. One can even say that they recognize but a single principle of their Faith, to which they give the name of Revelation, or the word of God revealed to men. For whether this word was written or unwritten, it is nevertheless the same, since it is indubitable that it comes from God. † For this reason, the Jews find no difficulty in equating their Traditions with the Law of Moses, saying that this written Law is a body without a soul, and a torch without light, if one were to separate it from the Oral Law or the Traditions. Under penalty of <term>excommunication</term> <note>The original text uses 'Kerkban,' referring to the 'Herem,' the highest formal censure and exclusion from the Jewish community.</note>, they are obliged to believe that God inspired in Moses everything contained in the Books of Moses down to the smallest syllables; and what is more, that God also gave to Moses on Mount Sinai the explanation of this Law;

<column-break/>

which Explanation they believe has been preserved among them without change, from the time of Moses until they were finally forced to commit it to writing.

Moses (a) wrote several copies of the Law with his own hands before his death, and gave one to each tribe of Israel; enclosing another copy in the Ark besides these. He subsequently communicated the interpretation of this Law orally to the <term>Sanhedrim</term> <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish nation, consisting of seventy-one sages.</note> of his time. Joshua taught this interpretation after the death of Moses—having received it from the hand of God through this Lawgiver—to the ancient Jews, his contemporaries; and those who succeeded him as Heads of the Sanhedrim did likewise in respect to others; such that, if one wishes to rely on the Jews, their Religion would still be entirely pure and intact today. But, although their principle concerning the traditions might be true in general, it is nevertheless convicted of falsehood if one examines it in detail

<meta>catchword: the</meta>

---

† [It should be noted that this is stated by P. Simon as a Roman Catholic writer.] <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712) was a French priest and scholar who argued that because the Bible is complex, tradition and Church authority are necessary for its interpretation—a view he here projects onto Jewish scholarship.</note>
(a) See Rambam <note>Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon, known as Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> in his Preface to the Book *Yad Hachazakah* <note>original: "Jad. Hazeka," meaning 'The Strong Hand,' Maimonides' massive code of Jewish Law.</note>.

The author compares this reliance on tradition to Roman Catholic doctrine, while citing Maimonides as a primary source for this historical lineage.</summary>

amongst those who investigate, not only because the Prophets and our Savior condemned many of their traditions: but furthermore because their Scribes do not agree among themselves regarding the true successions of those who have preserved these traditions, of which one finds several Registers composed by different writers. This alone can surely make their Faith suspect and less worthy of esteem.

<margin>Which P. Simon, as a Roman Catholic writer, intends to relate to the Roman Traditions.</margin>
One cannot deny that, in order to maintain a religion in its purity, the principle of accepting Traditions in general is not absolutely necessary, as the author of the book *Cozri* <note>The *Kuzari*, a famous 12th-century work by Judah Halevi defending Judaism.</note> says with many persuasive reasons; he clearly indicates that various opinions of Philosophers and Heretics regarding religion derive their origin from their unstable principles, insofar as they are not grounded in any true Tradition. As for the Jewish Traditions that our Savior rejected, he contested no others than certain false Traditions that the Jewish Scribes had attached to the ancients; and when this all-wise Teacher directs us to the written Law, saying, *Search the Scriptures* <note>original Latin: "Scrutamini Scripturas"</note>, one must not imagine that he intended to lead us to the simple text of the Scripture: but rather to that same text as explained by the Scribes who had succeeded Moses. They sit, he says, speaking of these Scribes, on *Moses' seat; observe and do whatever they tell you, etc.* And this corresponds with these words of the law:
> ,, (b) Whenever you
> ,, shall have any difficulty
> ,, regarding the interpretation
> ,, of the Law, you shall present
> ,, yourselves to the Priests and
> ,, to the persons who have been
> ,, given to you as Judges.

If one looks with emphasis at the testimonies of the Old Testament which the Apostles used to legitimize their Doctrine, one will find that they brought them forth only according to the sense that was then accepted. Irenaeus, Tertullian, and other early Fathers of the Church took refuge in this same Tradition in their disputes against Heretics, and in the succession of Bishops in the principal Churches, especially that of Rome, which they recognized as having been established by Peter and Paul.

<column-break/>

Likewise, we see how many of those who attended the Council of Trent <note>A 16th-century ecumenical council of the Roman Catholic Church that defined doctrine in response to the Protestant Reformation.</note> made no difficulty in equating true traditions with the Holy Scripture and viewing them as a revealed word. (c) *As much the traditions as the scriptures are words of God and first principles of faith, with an accidental difference between them: that the latter remain written in books, and the former only in the hearts.* <note>original Italian: "Tonto le tradizioni quanto le scritture son parole di Dio e primi Principii della fede, con accidental differenza trà loro, che quelle rimanessero scritte ancora né libri, e queste solamente né cuori."</note> This expression is entirely consistent with that which the Jews use when they speak of their traditions; and just as Tertullian once said that no one but the Church possessed the true Holy Scripture—*Holy Scripture is the proper possession of the Catholic Church* <note>original Latin: "Scriptura Sacra Ecclesiae Catholicae possessio est propria"</note>—the Jews likewise say that no one but the Synagogue possesses it, and that other nations possess nothing but the letters, but not the Spirit.

But to tell the truth, the number of Traditions is now so great among the Jews that Moses' entire lifetime would not have been enough to receive them from God on Mount Sinai, where he received them, according to their supposition, within the time of forty days that he spent on this Mountain. It is then not a defect in the Tradition itself, but rather in the men who have been its possessors; and for this reason, one must not always place faith in this fundamental principle of the Jews: <margin>How one has sometimes erred in the matter of Traditions.</margin> A LAW GIVEN TO MOSES AT SINAI <note>original Hebrew: "HALAKAH LE MOSCE MI SINAI," referring to oral laws believed to have been given to Moses that were not recorded in the written Torah.</note>; it is a decree which Moses received on Mount Sinai—just as little as in this other principle of our Divines, which is the Apostolic Tradition—since it is certain that neither one nor the other is infallible. Since the first centuries of Christianity, learned men have been found who have given the name of Apostolic Tradition to opinions that were their own private views, and which even ran contrary to orthodoxy. If the Jews could prove that a matter had been believed among them for all time, and especially since Moses, one could not doubt the truth of this Tradition. (d) Vincent of Lérins prescribed this rule to the Roman Church, in which he proposes believing that which has been believed everywhere, for all time, and by everyone: *Let us hold to that which has been believed everywhere, always, and by all.* <note>original Latin: "Id teneamus quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est."</note> Thus the Fathers of the Tren-

<margin>(a) Council of Trent, Session 4.</margin>
...the Council of Trent attempts to make us accept as true traditions those which were immediately received from the Apostles of our Savior, (a) or even from the Apostles to whom the Holy Spirit had revealed them, and which subsequently came down to us without corruption.

<margin>(b) Abrabanel in his Preface to *Nahalat Avot* <note>original: "Nahalot Avoth," a commentary on the Ethics of the Fathers.</note>.</margin>
For the rest, although the Jews show an uncommon zeal for the Traditions which they believe they possess from their ancestors, and which they stubbornly defend—to such an extent that they believe death is deserved by anyone who opposes them—nevertheless, there has never been agreement among their writers regarding from whom they received them: as can be sufficiently proven when one compares the books that deal with the subject; for example, the explanations made regarding the book which has (b) *Pirkei Avot* or *Chapters of the Fathers* <note>A compilation of ethical teachings and maxims from the Rabbis of the Mishnaic period.</note> as its title. Isaac Abrabanel <note>A famous Portuguese Jewish statesman and theologian (1437–1508).</note> exerted all his power to justify this supposed and uncorrupted Tradition: but he was unable to demonstrate its internal consistency. There is dispute regarding *Rabbi Moses* <note>Moses Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note>, who also wrote on the same subject regarding the compilation. *Rabbi Joseph Hagon* <note>Likely referring to Saadia Gaon or another "Gaon," the heads of the Babylonian academies.</note>, and *Rabbi David Ganz*, the author of the *Yuchasin* or *Book of Genealogies*, and other Jews who have dealt with the same dispute, also do not agree with one another: so that the majority, in order to validate the connection of the writers of their Tradition, are forced to make their scholars live for many centuries, the better to join the broken parts together. The Jews have had this advantage over other peoples, even over the Greeks, that they have unhesitatingly laid this burden upon everyone. Their books are full of embellished histories, and it is a wonder that Christians are still found who give credence to their fables,

<column-break/>

especially when they speak of their Tradition.

<margin>(c) In his great Book of the Commandments of the Law <note>The *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* (SeMaG) by Moses ben Jacob of Coucy.</note>.</margin>
<margin>And how they have attempted to make the continuity indisputable.</margin>
In general, however, they agree that from *Joshua*, the successor of *Moses*, until *Rabbi Judah*, surnamed the Holy <note>Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century rabbi who redacted the Mishnah.</note>, who collected all the Traditions and was the first to commit them to writing; therein one finds first a rank of Ancients who received the explanation of the Law from *Joshua*, then come the Prophets in order, of whom *Samuel* was the first, and after the Prophets follows the Great Assembly or Synagogue <note>The *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah*, the governing body of Jews during the early Second Temple period.</note> which was held under *Ezra*, and which also consisted in part of Prophets. *Rabbi Moses of Coucy*, (c) a learned Jew, in order to complete this chain of Tradition and to show at the same time that it had not been broken during the Babylonian captivity, cites certain excellent men of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin who had been carried captive to Babylon; and he even asserts that these men had established the famous Academy of *Nehardea* <note>original: "Nahar dea," one of the most important centers of Jewish learning on the Euphrates.</note> on the Euphrates, which was subsequently maintained so that the Tradition was taught to those who returned with Zerubbabel and *Ezra* from Babylon to Jerusalem, where they also established an Academy in imitation of the one in Babylon, which remained in existence there, even though all the Jews did not return to Jerusalem. Finally, this Tradition was preserved from the time of *Ezra*, who was the head of the Assembly commonly called the Great Assembly, until the time of this *Rabbi Judah* of whom we have spoken, who convened at the end of the second century under the reign of the Emperor *Commodus*, or as others maintain, under *Antoninus the Pious*. Now, that the Tradition of the Jews has been subject to no change, we see no reason to be obliged to believe this without proof being given, any more than one can give them credence in many other matters.

### THIRD HISTORICAL TREATISE

<margin>
The components of the Jewish Faith consist of thirteen distinct Articles.
</margin>

According to *Maimonides* (a), who organized these Articles in order: the first point involves the existence of God; the second, His unity; the third, His spirituality and His distinction from anything that can be imagined as having a physical body; the fourth concerns His eternity, which can correspond to nothing but Himself; the fifth, the service of worship which is owed to no one but Him; the sixth pertains to Prophecy, namely, that there have been Prophets among the Hebrews and that there may yet be more among them; the seventh specifically includes the Prophecy of Moses, which was uniquely housed within him and communicated far beyond the reach of the prophecy given to other Prophets; the eighth determines that the Law did not originate from Moses, but that God inspired it to him entirely, as well as the explanation of that same Law; the ninth, that this Law is unchangeable, and that one may neither add to nor take away from it; the tenth establishes the providence of God and the care He takes for His creatures; the eleventh teaches that God will reward those who observe the commands of the Law and will punish those who violate His commandments; the twelfth, that a Messiah shall come, and though he tarries in his coming, one must nevertheless not doubt it, nor prescribe a specific time in which he must arrive; and finally, the thirteenth involves the resurrection of the dead. These thirteen Articles, upon which the Jewish religion is grounded, separate them from all other peoples, as they claim for themselves to be the sole confidants of God and His true children to whom the inheritance is promised; and they view those who deny these Articles as abominable people who deserve death. It is for this reason that the Jews would be much to be feared if they held sovereign power; for although they outwardly testify that Christians should not be included under the name of "abominable people" since they believe in the unity of God as well as the Jews, they nevertheless do not hesitate to place Christians in the same rank as idolaters because of the mystery of the Trinity, viewing them as if they truly increased the Divinity by multiplying the Persons <note>The author reflects a common 17th/18th-century Christian anxiety regarding Jewish views of the Trinity, which many Jewish theologians viewed as a violation of absolute monotheism.</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>
And how, however, some do not agree with their opinion here, from which four [points] are drawn.
</margin>

Although the Jews generally adhere to the opinion of *Rabbi Moses* <note>Referring to Moses Maimonides.</note> regarding these thirteen Articles of their religion, there are nonetheless some scholars among them who do not follow them in every part; such as (b) *Rabbi Hasdai* <note>Hasdai Crescas (c. 1340–1410), a Spanish-Jewish philosopher.</note>, *Rabbi Joseph Albo* <note>A 15th-century Jewish philosopher known for his work on the fundamentals of Judaism.</note>, and *Don Isaac Abrabanel*, among others. Their doubt deserves to be presented here, as it can serve to clarify the Christian religion. They say, firstly, that the Article which establishes the service of a single God is difficult enough to understand, as it simultaneously forbids one from taking recourse to any other, nor to any Mediator or advocate; yet the Jews offer their prayers to Angels when they call upon them in their need.

Secondly, regarding the Article of the unchangeability of the Law, this seems to contradict what God Himself has observed since the beginning of the world, having immediately given specific commandments and forbidden the eating of [certain] flesh <note>The author may be referring to the transition from the Noahide laws to the Mosaic Law.</note>. From this, it appears that one cannot reasonably say there can be no Law but one which is in no way subject to change. Nor can one say that nothing may be added or taken away, although it is certain that *Solomon* and others added things; but this prohibition was only made in a specific sense, which can add nothing to nor diminish anything from the Law in its particular authority.

Thirdly, the Article mentioning the coming of the Messiah seems not to be grounded, since *Rabbi Hillel* was of the opinion that the Jews should no longer expect their Messiah, as he had, according to his view, already come in the time of *Hezekiah* <note>A reference to a famous Talmudic statement by Rabbi Hillel (not the Elder) in Sanhedrin 99a.</note>. Nonetheless, this scribe was no less zealous for the fellowship with other Jews.

Fourthly, there appear to be many other matters that deserve to be placed among the number of the fundamental rules of the Jewish faith, such as a great number of God’s attributes, of which *Rabbi Moses* made no mention in the place where he deals with the principal Articles of the religion; and furthermore, the Creation of the world; man’s free will; and the Faith which one must [place in the miracles...]

### Concerning the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

...must have included; the immortality of the soul; prayer; the utility of penance, and many other points that the Jews are obligated to believe: from which it appears that they have many more Articles of Faith than *Rabbi Moses* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the influential Sephardic philosopher</note> has set forth. The same Rabbi also noted others in a different place. One can nonetheless say that he only sought to cite those which were the most prominent and most fundamental; and it is in nearly the same manner that *Isaac Abrabanel* <note>A Portuguese Jewish statesman and philosopher who defended Maimonides</note> has excused him in that regard.

<margin>Allegorical fables introduced.</margin>
For the rest, let us observe how the Jews have, at various times, employed means to explain their theology. The majority of the Ancients had recourse to certain allegories and fables, with which they filled their books to such an extent that one possessed a kind of mythology among them no less than among the Heathens: and which, as we believe, gave more occasion to keep the Ancient Jews in ignorance, through certain institutions that forbade them the reading of the Philosophers and other non-sacred books. Some among them, however, did not fail to apply themselves to the *Platonic Philosophy*, of which they made a mixture with their fancies; and from which a great part of their Kabbalistic wisdom has sprung.

<margin>How they applied themselves to Platonic Philosophy.</margin>
One must also attribute to this same school of *Platonic Philosophy* many expressions found in their ancient allegorical books, which do not deviate far from the expressions used by Christians to explain the mystery of the Trinity.

<margin>How the Jews gradually surrendered themselves to the arts and sciences of the Arabs.</margin>
But since the Arabs spread the philosophy of *Aristotle* throughout many regions, especially Logic and Metaphysics; some inquisitive Jews surrendered themselves to it, and even translated the books of this philosophy from Arabic into *Rabbinic Hebrew*. It seems that since that time, the theology of the Jews changed entirely regarding the manner of explanation, which caused great unrest among them, primarily among those who devoted themselves entirely to the reading of ancient books and held to the traditions of their forefathers, such that they were offended to see their theology supplemented with Metaphysics, and that reasoning held more place than authority. *Rabbi Moses*, having made public his book called *Moreh Nevukim* <note>The Guide for the Perplexed</note>, was accused by other scribes of debasing religion with the introduction of philosophy, as can be seen in the letters of the principal Rabbis of this time, and even in those written by *Rabbi Moses* himself. In the meantime, the Jews gradually became accustomed to this sort of ingenuity and finally found a taste for the book of this Rabbi.

<column-break/>

<margin>What opinion they held regarding the Angels.</margin>
Regarding the other Articles of the Jewish faith, it is certain that they also recognized the Angels, whose names and duties they believe they know, and for which purposes they are used. These names, however, are for the most part invented by their Kabbalistic theologians, who have given them names according to the various effects attributed to them. Therefore, one must distinguish what pertains to their faith concerning Angels from what they do not believe. (a) They believe that lesser entities are subject to the Supreme Powers, and that, for example, there is no kingdom which does not depend on some Angel, with the exception nonetheless of that of the Hebrews, which depends immediately upon God, without any Mediator being necessary. It is in this sense that the fifth Article of their faith is explained, in the manner brought forward by *Rabbi Moses*, where it is said that one must worship and serve no other but God alone, in which no Mediator nor Advocate may have a place.

<margin>How they led the simple-minded astray.</margin>
One must not always take literally what the Jewish scholars relate of the Angels in their writings; for they are often nothing but allegories and spiritual allusions, invented for amusement by men who delight in leading the credulity of the simple folk astray: besides which, they sometimes introduce these apparent names to untie some difficulty, just as the Poets of old used the names of their Gods in similar instances. These same scribes are the ones who invented the art of their *Cabbala* <note>Kabbalah, the Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation</note>, which is a fictitious science without any foundation: for the Jews who devote themselves to it are for the most part imaginative Sages, so strongly taken with their visions that they believe...

One must not always take literally what the Jewish Scholars relate of the Angels in their writings, for they are often nothing but allegories and spiritual allusions, invented for amusement by men who delight in misleading the gullibility of the simple folk: besides which, they sometimes introduce these apparent names to untie some difficulty, just as the Poets of old used the names of their Gods in similar instances. # THIRD HISTORICAL TREATISE

<margin>In what the learning of the Kabbalists consisted.</margin>
...to be able to perform miracles by means of this art.

They divide the *Kabbalah* into speculative and practical *Kabbalah* <note>original: "oeffenende Cabbala," often known as *Kabbalah Ma'asit*.</note>; and it is this latter kind that serves to perform supposed miracles, by pronouncing certain names of God and of Angels, or certain verses of the Psalms which they have arranged according to their science. The Polish Jews, and those of other Northern regions especially, are so superstitious in this regard that if they find someone among them sentenced to death, he takes recourse to this practical *Kabbalah*: but we do not see that it performs any service for them, unless it is contained in the histories they have written concerning the wonders of practical *Kabbalah*.

<margin>And to what extent it is relevant.</margin>
It sometimes happens to them by accident that judges, who are not knowledgeable enough about the vanity of this science, condemn them as sorcerers. Truly, the fantasies of the magical arts, which we read of in the books of *Agrippa* <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous German polymath and occult writer.</note> and some other modern coarse writers—who are commonly believed to have been great sorcerers—are all drawn from the Jewish *Kabbalah*, to which other fictions have been added to more easily mislead simple folk.

<margin>Qualities attributed to the Angels by the Jews, and in what they consist.</margin>
To better unfold the belief of the Jews concerning the service of Angels—to whom they attribute no service other than as Mediators and Advocates—it is observed that not everything appears to agree with their Books: for one finds prayers in them which are presented to Angels for their assistance. *Joshua* greeted an Angel; the Jews themselves recognize the Angel *Michael* as their head and Guardian Angel; and they are so accustomed to attributing everything to their Angels, especially when they follow the manner of speaking used by the Kabbalistic scholars, that they recognize them as the executors of the majority of their affairs. There are none but those of the sect of the Sadducees who deny the reality of Angels, as if everything indicated in the Books of *Moses* consisted of nothing but mere metaphors: but our Savior himself condemned this sect, and approved the common belief of the Jews regarding the reality of Angels; which was subsequently confirmed by the Apostles and accepted by the Church.

<margin>What the Jews feel regarding the future</margin>
Finally, these same Jews also believe that there is a Hell, a Purgatory <note>literally "Voorburg der Helle" or "Forecourt of Hell."</note>, and a Paradise: and although these three Articles of their faith are difficult to

It matters very little whether their Purgatory is a specific place rather than a part of Hell, as the Eastern Christians also hold: it is enough that they confess there is a Paradise, where the souls of the Blessed partake in glory, and a Hell where the souls of the damned are tormented by fire and other punishments; and that nonetheless, some are doomed to these punishments for a time and others forever. But it is strange from whence the Rabbis derive the idea that Jews who were not heretical, or who had not sinned against certain fundamental points of the Law, stayed no longer than one year in this Purgatory. Thus, not only were minor sins wiped away in this Purgatory, but even the most abominable ones, for which one had to remain there longer; which the Jews regard as a special privilege granted to them, because, they say, they are true children of God. It is for this reason especially that God has prepared another world for them, from which they exclude all other peoples, at least if they do not believe in the unity of God and in certain other basic articles contained in their Books; for one must not imagine that the Jews absolutely damn all other peoples because they do not accept their Law. This unity of Religion over the entire Earth is, according to their view, deferred until the coming of the Messiah, in which they entirely agree (though in another sense) with us Christians.

### CHAPTER III.

### Of the Ethics of the JEWS compared with those of the CHRISTIANS.

<margin>How the Ethics of the Jews relate to their Religion.</margin>
The Jews have no other foundation for their ethics than the Law of the Ten Commandments, for which the Christians are indebted to them. The love of God, above all the creatures of the world, is recommended to them by their scribes <note>original: "Schriftge-leerden," referring to rabbis or teachers of the law</note> no less than to us, unless it be that they add to the majority of their observations something peculiar to them, which seems linked to it, or rather superstitious: which, however, is not a defect of the Law, but of their scribes. One misjudges the Jews, so we believe, when one accuses them of recognizing no other holiness than that which consists in the ceremonies of the Law; as, for example, if they believe their sins to have been wiped out after they have washed their body. On the contrary, they are convinced that all these external ceremonies were only introduced to lead them to internal holiness. Their fasting and their other outward bodily mortifications must be accompanied by the internal, and they also believe that besides outward and ceremonial penance, one must have, so to speak, a true remorse for sins, and a sincere repentance of one's sins, if one wishes to satisfy God’s justice. It is unnecessary to bring proof of this belief among the Jews here, as the majority of their books dealing with ethics and the practice of penance <note>original: "Boetöeffening"</note> are filled with these customs. What we find necessary to note is that we should not reproach them too freely, as is commonly done, by saying that they are entirely bound to the letter of the Law without being able to grasp the inherent spirit. They testify to us the contrary: that to follow the sense and spirit of the Law, it was not necessary to look away entirely from the letter, which serves as a precursor to the internal aspect of that same Law.

<margin>and how they have improved it.</margin>

When the Savior says to His disciples (a) that He gives them a new Commandment, speaking of love; He does nothing other than renew for them the ancient commandment, which had been made powerless by the false interpretations of the scribes. Love for one's enemies is thus recommended in the Law as well as in the New Testament: but it was necessary that our Savior renewed it, since this commandment was no longer maintained among the Jews, and for this reason He says to His disciples: *A new commandment I give unto you, that ye love one another.* To indicate how highly they should regard love for their neighbors. Their scribes testify (b) that the world is founded on three fundamental principles, which are the Law, Prayer, and Charity <note>original: "Barmhartigheid"</note>. One can, however, say that they are much more bound to the ceremonies of their Law, which rests on good works, and this causes a great number of commandments to which they are enslaved, which nonetheless for the most part contain only the external.

<margin>Hypocrisy of some European Jews noted.</margin>
The pitiable state in which they found themselves for so many centuries contributed not a little to making them more apostate; especially those who lived in Europe in secret and as if unknown, some of whom believed it was enough for a Jew to possess his religion in his heart, without it being necessary to make an outward confession. On that ground, many made no difficulty in outwardly embracing the Christian religion, while keeping Judaism in their hearts. A great number of such Christians, who are truly Jews, are perhaps still found in Spain, where the severity of the Inquisition that reigns in that region will never be able to prevent it, since no people are found who feel so bound to their religion as the Jews. # Concerning the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

(a) For this reason, the most learned Rabbis believe that the words of the Law <note>The Torah</note> where the unity of God is spoken of do not express a particular and separate commandment, but rather serve as a preface to all the Ten Commandments.

Other Jews (b) believe, through a similar cleverness in the *Kabbalah* <note>The Jewish mystical tradition</note>, that these 613 commandments of the Law are all included in the words of the Ten Commandments, which they say contain 613 letters. And since 620 are actually found, some have brought the doctrines or commandments to the number of 620 <note>This relates to the 613 commandments plus the 7 Noahide laws, or the numerical value of the word 'Keter' (Crown)</note>; but it is unnecessary for us to dwell on these kinds of subtleties, which have their origin in the philosophy of Pythagoras and Plato. It is not these [Jewish ideas] that one finds in similar remarks about numbers in the works of the early Church Fathers who devoted themselves to Platonic philosophy; however, they did not attach the same faith to these hidden numbers as the learned Jews did, having invented an art which they call, as we have said, the *Gematric* or Geometrical *Kabbalah* <note>Gematria: a system where letters of the alphabet are assigned numerical values</note>.

What is more, they divide these 613 precepts into 248 affirmative and 365 negative. The 248 affirmative commandments, the Rabbis say, correspond to the same number of limbs found in a human being according to their view; and since we are assured in *Ecclesiastes* (c) that keeping the commandments of God is the whole duty of man <note>Eccl. 12:13</note>, they add that all parts of the human being are nourished by these commandments, as if every part corresponded to every commandment. As for the 365 negative commandments, they correspond to the 365 days of the Solar Year, since we are obligated not only to fulfill the Law of God with all our limbs—to speak according to the thoughts of the Jews, namely, with all our strength—

<column-break/>

but also all the days of our lives. If these numbers were invented for no other reason than to remind us of the obligation we owe to love God from the bottom of our hearts, we could not accuse the Jews of superstition; and furthermore, the dreams of the ancient Heretics, which were based on a similar principle, might not seem so ridiculous to us as when they are explained literally. Of this sort is it that *Basilides* * understood the great secret under the word *Abraxas* †, which was a word expressly invented to represent the number 365 according to the letters of the Greek alphabet, and to simultaneously designate the 365 days of the year. We could thus, by this means, explain many other hidden fictions of the ancient ‡ *Gnostics*, who sometimes agree with the Jewish scholars on this subject; but it would lead us too far from our path.

There is yet another *Division* of the Commandments of the Law according to the three distinct names which Moses used to express these same commandments; these are: MITSVOTH, Commandments, HUKIM, Statutes, and MISPATIM, Judgments. Those are called MITSVOTH or Commandments whose reason is indicated with clear words in the text of the Law. For example, the reasons why the Jews are obligated to keep Passover and observe the Sabbath are clearly contained in the Books of Moses. The *Statutes* on the contrary, which in Hebrew are called HUKIM <note>Original: Hukim (statutes/decrees)</note>, include words that are not explained or expressed in the Law: God willed that these reasons remain hidden from the Jews. <margin>Why the Jews are inclined toward usury <note>The practice of lending money at interest</note>.</margin>
One must attribute the misery of their state and the usury they practice daily to this: they are not permitted, as Christians are, to possess lands in freedom, nor are they allowed to hold much immovable property. Consequently, they are forced to spend and make use of their money through other means. They trade with it just as others trade with merchandise; and perhaps this would not be blameworthy if their Law did not expressly forbid this conduct. However, they limit this prohibition, believing that it extends only to their brothers and co-religionists. Therefore, they allow themselves that freedom [with others], not only aiming for profit but refusing to receive any interest under any pretext when it is offered by a fellow Jew. Far from the Law not extending over usury regarding those who are needy (and consequently in need of our assistance), they consider it no less usurious to give money to the rich for profit than to give it to the poor.

The 248 affirmative commandments, say the Rabbis, correspond with as many limbs as one finds in the human body, according to their opinion; and since we are assured in *Ecclesiastes* (c) that *to keep the commandments of God is the whole man* <note>original: "de geboden Godts te onderhouden den geheelen menſch is." See Eccl. 12:13</note>. They add that all the parts of man are nourished by these commandments, as if every part corresponded to every commandment. As for the 365 negative commandments, they correspond to the 365 days of the Solar Year, since we are not only obliged to fulfill the Law of God with all our limbs—to speak according to the thoughts of the Jews—namely, with all our pow-

<column-break/>

-ers: but also all the days of our lives. If these numbers were not invented except to remind us of the obligation we owe to love God from the bottom of our hearts, we could not accuse the Jews of any superstition on that account; and even more, the fantasies of the ancient Heretics, which were based on a similar principle, would perhaps not seem so ridiculous to us as when they are explained literally. It is of this kind that *Basilides* <note>An early Gnostic religious teacher in Alexandria</note> \* understood the great secret under the word *Abraxas* †, which was a word expressly invented to represent the number 365 according to the letters of the Greek alphabet, and to simultaneously indicate the 365 days of the year. We could thus by this means explain many other hidden fictions of the ancient ‡ *Gnostics*, who sometimes agree with the Jewish scholars on this subject: but it would lead us too far off the path.

Yet another Division of the Commandments of the Law exists according to the three distinct names which Moses used to express these same commandments; these are: *Mitsvoth* <note>Mitzvot</note>, *Commandments*; *Hukim* <note>Chukim</note>, *Statutes*; and *Mispatim* <note>Mishpatim</note>, *Judgments*. Those are called *Mitsvoth* or *Commandments* of which the reason is indicated with clear words in the text of the Law. For example, the reasons why the Jews are obliged to keep Passover and observe the Sabbath are clearly contained in the Books of Moses. The *Statutes* on the contrary, which in Hebrew are called *Hukim*, include words that are not understood in the Law nor stand expressed: God willed that this reason remain hidden from the Jews. Finally, there are the judgments that Moses calls *Mispatim*, Precepts of Reason, as the Jewish scholars call them, and when they in the Law

# THIRD HISTORICAL TREATISE

[If they] were not expressed in the Law, reason would require it.

Besides these commandments included in the Law of Moses, the Jews recognize others, which they call the Precepts of the <term>Hacamim</term> <note>Hebrew: Chakhamim, meaning "Wise Men" or scholars</note>, or the Learned. They attribute these likewise to Moses, as he had the power to make new institutions according to the circumstances of the time. This power is even based on the words of God, who commanded them to submit to the Elders of the <term>Sanhedrim</term> <note>The supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of ancient Israel</note> to resolve all difficulties that might arise regarding the Law. Moses first made many institutions of this nature, decided in the Assemblies of his time. Joshua did the same after him, and subsequently all others who

<column-break/>

succeeded him in his office. Therefore, the Jews believe they are no less bound in conscience to obey everything decided by the scholars of the Sanhedrim than the commandments of the Law, although the institutions of the former were of less value than those of Moses. The reason given for this is clear: they believed that these members of the Council were guided by God's Spirit and therefore had to be infallible in their decisions. Under the name of *Wise Men* or Scholars, they included not only the Elders of their Sanhedrim or Ecclesiastical Assembly, but also the Prophets who lived among them at various times, and who likely had the right to sit in their Assemblies.

## CHAPTER V.

-> Concerning the great ECCLESIASTICAL ASSEMBLY or the JEWISH SANHEDRIM; the PLACE where it was held. Various EXPLANATIONS of this MATTER, regarding what is observed among CHRISTIANS. <-

<margin>
What the Sanhedrim formerly consisted of.
</margin>
**T**he great Ecclesiastical Assembly, or the Sanhedrim of the Jews, has its origin in Moses, as already noted. It consisted of 71 Elders, among whom one was the Head or President of the Assembly; and it is this person (a) whom the Jews today still call <term>Hannasci</term> <note>Hebrew: Ha-Nasi, meaning "The Prince" or President</note>, or *Prince*. Besides this president, there was a second or Deputy, to whom they gave the title of <term>Ab</term> <note>Hebrew for "Father"</note>, Father of the assembly. All the other members were called Elders or Councilors. Their arrangement was as follows: they sat together in the shape of a half-circle, in the middle of which the <term>Nasci</term> or president of the assembly placed himself, and at his right side the second president was seated. The others took their places according to their rank beside the <term>Nasci</term>. Some add a third Elder, to whom they gave only the name of <term>Hacam</term>, or *Wise Man*, who sat to the left of the President; so that the Deputy to the <term>Nasci</term> and this <term>Hacam</term> were like two Associate Councilors. It is necessary that we notice the order of this seating, since we shall subsequently pass from their Church-

<column-break/>

assemblies to their Synagogue, and then to the Churches or first assemblies of the Christians, as will appear hereafter.

<margin>
And where it had to assemble.
</margin>
This great Sanhedrim could only be held in Jerusalem, in a place called <term>Liscat Hagazit</term> <note>Hebrew: Lishkat HaGazit, the "Chamber of Hewn Stone"</note>, which bordered the Temple, or rather was a part of it; in the same way that [Christian] Councils commonly meet in Churches. This <term>Liscat Hagazit</term> was almost the same as what was formerly called in *Trullo* <note>Latin: "In the dome"</note> * in Constantinople. The Talmudists called this place the Great Court of Justice. The most important matters and those of the utmost consequence were judged there; and this is the sense one must give to these words of the Evangelist Luke, (b) that no Prophet dies outside of Jerusalem. When there was any case for which Tradition gave no decision, or at least was not clear enough, every Councilor had a deciding as well as a consultative vote.

This consisted, according to the Jewish opinion, of 120 of the most prominent men, in which the <term>Nasci</term> <note>Hebrew: *Nasi*, meaning "Prince" or "President"</note> or Head was the chairman. They added, furthermore, that in this assembly were found the prophets *Haggai*, *Zechariah*, *Malachi*, and some other great men of God's inspiration, such as *Daniel*, *Nehemiah*, *Mordecai*, *Zerubbabel*, *Azariah*, *Mishael*, and *Hananiah*. Although one should not give credit to everything the Jews claim specifically regarding this Great Assembly, we must nevertheless conclude that the prophets and other excellent men were admitted alongside the Elders or Councilors.

<margin>
And of what power this Great Assembly was.
</margin>
There was no greater assembly in the common state of the Hebrews than this *Sanhedrim*, which had the power, being the absolute master, to declare what it judged most appropriate for times and occasions. (a) And it is in this sense that <term>Rabbi Moses</term> <note>Moses Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> gives it the name of *Foundation of the Oral Law* and the support of true learning. Likewise, those who refused to submit were regarded as rebels and excommunicated. This is undoubtedly what the Son of God alludes to when He pronounces this judgment against those who will not submit to the decision of the Church: (b) *If he also refuses to listen to the congregation, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.*

<margin>
Roman Councils compared to the Jewish Synagogue and among one another.
</margin>
If we, in truth, compare the ecclesiastical laws in the assemblies or Councils with those of the Jewish Synagogue, we shall find little difference between the one and the other. Firstly, our Savior, in the establishment of His Law (being the absolute Lawgiver, of whom Moses was but a declarer and a figure), had no subordinate authority to that of Moses. And just as Moses left his power to Joshua and other Elders of his time, regarding the interpretation of the Law; so our Savior left it to Peter to succeed him, so that he might be the *Nasci* or Head of His Church; and Paul

<column-break/>

calls some of the Apostles by the name of pillars: (c) *James*, and *Cephas* <note>The Aramaic name for Peter</note>, and *John* who were esteemed to be *Pillars*. The Roman Catholics also attribute to their Councils a certain infallibility, which they recognize in their Church, just as the Jews imagined that infallibility reigned in their Great Ecclesiastical Assembly or the *Sanhedrim*. In this, (*) the Apostles and Elders followed them, in which *Peter*, as *Nasci* or Prince, was the chairman (being by divine right the Head of the Church) when they wrote to their brothers in *Antioch*, *Syria*, and *Cilicia* regarding what they had decided in the Assembly. (d) *For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us*, indicating by these words that this was truly their inspiration.

<margin>
And how the Papacy benefits through this.
</margin>
The Roman Bishop, who (as is believed) is the true successor of Peter, also has a place as *Nasci* or Head of the Church in this Assembly. One must, however, not limit this infallibility to the city of Rome, as the Jews did to Jerusalem. Nor is it true that the Pope with his clergy, as the sole advisor, represents the ancient *Sanhedrim*, of which he, the successor of Peter, is the <term>Hannasci</term> <note>The Prince/The Head</note>, or Prince. And it is in this sense that the Church Fathers, speaking of the Bishop of Rome, have always given him the privilege over other bishops (*). Furthermore, just as the Elders in the Jewish *Sanhedrim* had all the decision-making votes, it is the same in the Councils; the Bishops also have, along with the Pope, who is the *Nasci* or Chairman, a decisive vote. The reason why the same authority is not given to the Roman Church Assembly under the New Law as the *Sanhedrim* of Jerusalem formerly had under the Old Law arises because the religion that the Messiah was to proclaim was not a religion limited to a certain place on earth, as the Jewish religion was limited; a principle in which the Jews, however, agree with us. <margin>And what order was maintained therein.</margin> These Students, who were called <term>Talmide Hacamim</term> <note>original: *TALMIDE HACAMIM*; Hebrew for "Students of the Sages."</note> or *Students of the Sages*, were divided into three different ranks. For Paul says that he was "educated at the feet of Gamaliel," by which he meant to show that he had been the Student of that Scribe, seated at his feet among the other Students. The author of the commentary on the Epistles of Paul, which some attribute to *Ambrose*, explains with few words and accuracy all that we have noted regarding the Synagogues of the Jews. (a) *This is the tradition of the Synagogue,* he says, *that the elders sit in chairs of dignity, those next on benches, and the latest on the floor upon mats.* <note>original Latin: "Hæc traditio Synagogæ est... ut sedentes disputent seniores dignitate in Cathedris, sequentes in subselliis, novissimi in pavimento super mattas."</note>

If our Painters had understood this layout of the Synagogue, they would have been careful not to depict our Savior in the midst of the Scribes and in a high pulpit, as if at the age of twelve he had been the Head of a Synagogue; basing this on the words of Luke: (b) *And it came to pass, after three days, they found him in the Temple, sitting in the midst of the Teachers, hearing them, and questioning them.* He was seated on one of the benches among the other Students, and had the freedom to present his points of dispute as a Student, for as much as these places were the true Schools for being instructed in the Law, and they simultaneously learned their Traditions as they still observe them today. Likewise, they distinguished two kinds of Schools, one of which was called <term>Beth Ha-Mikra</term> <note>original: *BETH HAMMIKRA*; Hebrew for "House of Reading."</note>, *the house or place of reading*, because the Text of the Law was specifically read there: and the other bore the name <term>Beth Ha-Midrash</term> <note>original: *BETH HAMIDRAS*; Hebrew for "House of Investigation" or "Study."</note>, *place of interpretation or investigation*; and through these, the Jews intended to preserve both Laws

that Moses had received on Mount Sinai, namely the Written Law—to wit, the five Books of Moses—and the Oral Law, which contains their Traditions. But our Savior showed on many occasions that under the name of Tradition, they had corrupted the Law through false interpretations.

### 164 THIRD HISTORICAL TREATISE

...held office, [they took] the name of *Presbyteri*, Elders, or Priests. The Chairman or Bishop, who was the Head of these Elders, usually maintained the status of Elder; and for this reason, in the New Testament, the name of Bishop is sometimes mixed with that of Priest or Elder. Those who are ignorant of this beginning or the origin of the name Priest have not well understood that in the beginning of Christianity there was no distinction between Bishop and Priest.

<margin>Origin of the name of the Cathedrals according to the thoughts of the Roman Catholics, and when churches were first built.</margin>
For the same reason, the Council of the first Christian assemblies was called *Presbyterium*, or the Council of the Elders. The Bishop was Chairman as Head and first Elder, seated in the midst of the other Elders, just as was said before regarding the Assemblies of the Jews. *Let them praise him in the seat of the elders*, <note>original Latin: "In Cathedra Seniorum laudent eum" (Psalm 107:32)</note> says the Royal Prophet. The Priests or Elders who sat beside him each had their own seat of judgment, which is why they were called *Assessors of the Bishops* <note>original Latin: "Assessores Episcoporum"</note> by the Early Fathers of the Church. Nothing of weight was carried out that had not been previously deliberated in this Council, where the Bishop and the other Elders or Priests constituted the body of this assembly; for at that time the jurisdiction which is now called "Episcopal" did not depend on the Bishop alone, but on all the Elders of whom the Bishop was the Chairman. This was also the custom in Rome for several centuries.

It is also probable that the name Cathedral <note>original Dutch: "Hoofdt-Kerk," literally "Head-Church." The term "Cathedral" comes from "Cathedra," referring to the Bishop's seat.</note> had its origin from this ancient manner of seating in the first Churches or Christian Assemblies: from which has arisen the fact that the Feasts of St. Peter’s Chair in Rome and Antioch are still celebrated, as two Cities where the Blessed Apostle is said to have been the Chairman in a convened and closed Church Council. Note, however, that by the word Cathedral, we do not speak of the Head-Churches nor of the Temples such as they are today or are understood. This word Church originally meant nothing but an Assembly, and it is certain that the Chris-

<column-break/>

-tians before Constantine had no freedom to build temples or churches for their assemblies. Nothing is more ridiculous than what we find noted by some writers, and especially the Spanish ones, regarding the antiquity of their Cathedrals, imagining them to have been founded since the times of the Apostles, as if a Cathedral in this time had been anything other than the Chair <note>original Dutch: "Stoel," referring to the *Cathedra* or seat of authority.</note> of a Bishop accompanied by a number of Elders. Nevertheless, if we give credit to the new Breviary <note>original Dutch: "Getyboek," a book of hours or liturgical prayers.</note> of the Carmelites, there would have been a Church built on Mount Carmel in honor of the Holy Virgin by the Prophets who succeeded Elijah, who visited the Virgin, and whom she subsequently visited in return. Trifles, truly!

<margin>Who held authority over the Schools.</margin>
This similarity of Institutions between the Church and the Synagogue is even more apparent if one considers the ancient customs of the Church. There was, for example, formerly a custom that the Bishops held supreme authority over the Schools, and one cannot doubt that since the Jewish Synagogues were Schools where the Law was taught, or that the Schools were built near the Synagogues, the Bishop and Elders or Priests likewise took care of the Schools of the Christians. The same was done from the first centuries in the City of Alexandria. We still see a remnant of this custom in most Dom-churches or Cathedrals, where there are some officials to whom the care of the schools is entrusted. For example, in Paris this care is recommended to the Cantor <note>original Dutch: "Voorzanger," the lead singer or precentor.</note>, and in Rouen to the one who holds the dignity of Chancellor. The Council of Trent <note>A major 16th-century ecumenical council of the Catholic Church that prompted the Counter-Reformation.</note> intended to restore the use of these schools under the name of Seminaries <note>original Dutch: "Queekſchoolen," literally "nursery schools" or "breeding schools."</note>, which differ greatly from the Seminaries that the majority of the Bishops of France daily establish in their dioceses. The intention of the Fathers of the Council was not that one should only be instructed there in some ceremonies for the administration of the Sacraments for those ordained to the priesthood: but that these Seminaries should serve as true Schools, in which the youth would be practiced in knowledge almost from their childhood, to subsequently find themselves capable in the service of the Church.

### CHAPTER VII.

*A closer look at the SIMILARITY between the CHURCH and SYNAGOGUE; and which OFFICES were held in the SYNAGOGUES.*

<margin>How legal disputes in the beginning of the first Christians were brought before the Bishop and Elders.</margin>
The Church had this in common with the Synagogues: that in the beginning, Christians recognized no other judges to settle disputes arising among them than the Court of the Bishop and the Elders. It is for this reason that Paul forbids the Believers, whom he calls Saints (just as the Jews also call themselves by that name), to take recourse to any judges other than the Elders of the Assembly, to whom he gives the name of Sages, which was a name the Jews gave to their Scribes. (a) *Is there no CHACHAM <note>original: "HAGAM", a Hebrew term for a wise man or scholar</note> or Sage among you*, says the Apostle, *who can judge the disputes of his brothers? Is there not a Wise Man among you who can judge between his brother? <note>original Latin: "Sic non est inter vos Sapiens qui possit judicare inter fratrem suum?"</note>* These, we believe, have not well understood Paul's meaning who have translated this as: *Is there no wise man among you?* for the name "Sage" in this place is a title of Office, and signifies a *Chacham* of the Assembly, namely, an Elder or Scribe.

<margin>The laying on of hands brought into use for the confirmation of established Offices.</margin>
It is enough to judge from this that the Church, in its practice of appointing its Ministers, followed the Synagogue with the laying on of hands; and the Jews still call this laying on of hands *SEMICHA* <note>original: "S E M I C A"</note>. To make someone a Doctor or Elder, and the laying on of hands upon someone, are synonymous terms among them. Moses is the first institutor of this ceremony. He laid hands on Joshua, who was to succeed him, and on the other Elders of the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme council or court of the ancient Israelites</note>, who were immediately filled with the Holy Spirit. In imitation of Moses, the heads of the Church assemblies who followed Moses and Joshua laid hands on those who were chosen as Elders of the Sanhedrin. Jewish scholars note, however, that it was not strictly necessary to go to the *Nasi* <note>original: "Nasci", meaning the Prince or President</note> of the Sanhedrin: but that an Elder upon whom hands had once been laid had the right to do the same to others, who had to be at least three in number, just as from the beginning of the Church it was determined that there had to be at least three Bishops to carry out the Ordination of a Bishop. (a) I. Epistle to the Corinthians 6. verse 5.

<column-break/>

sides the laying on of hands, it was subsequently found good to add certain words to indicate the action being performed; for example: *I lay my hands upon you*, or *let the hand be laid upon you*. This is entirely consistent with the way in which Ordination and other Sacraments of the Roman Church are administered.

<margin>What the Office of Deacons was in former times.</margin>
There was also in the Temple, and subsequently in the Synagogues, a Minister who entirely represented the Deacons of the Church. He was called the *SHAMMASH* <note>original: "S C I A M A S", the sexton or assistant</note> or Minister of the Temple, and even the Syrians still use the word *SHAMMASH* to signify their Deacons and other lesser Ministers. The Jews usually call him *CHAZAN* <note>The Chazan, or Cantor, originally had more administrative duties similar to a beadle</note>, because his office is to oversee everything that happens in the Synagogue, and primarily the reading of the Law. It is for this reason that Deacons in the Church must not only provide for the needs of the Assembly: but they are further charged with the Reading of the Gospel; which is still strictly observed among Roman Catholics.

We do not find in the Books of the New Testament that the Apostles chose other Ministers in the Assemblies than those already noted; namely Bishops, Priests, and Deacons: nevertheless, one must understand all other lesser Ministers under the name of Deacons; since strictly speaking, the word for Deacon in Greek signifies all kinds of Ministers. The Syrian Churches often use a single word to express the lesser Ministers through "Deacons"; which the Jews also observe in the word *Chazan*, sometimes signifying the Porter of the Synagogue. The Levites performed this service in the Temple; they had to open the doors and also play flutes <note>original: "fluiten", likely referring to musical accompaniment or signaling</note>, and what is more, they went to the pulpit to sing while the offerings were being made.
