occupied these positions, the name of *Presbyteri* <note>original: "Presbyteri", from the Greek for "Elders"</note>, Elders, or Priests. The Chairman or Bishop, who was the Head of these Elders, mostly took on the character of an Elder; and for this reason, in the New Testament, the name of Bishop is sometimes mixed with that of Priest or Elder. Those who are ignorant of this beginning or origin of the name Priest have not well understood that in the beginning of Christianity, there was no distinction between Bishop and Priest.

<margin>Origin of the name of the Cathedrals according to the thoughts of the Roman Catholics, and when churches were first built.</margin>
For the same reason, the council meeting of the first Christian assemblies was called a *Presbyterium* <note>original: "Presbyterium", a council of elders</note>, or Council of the Elders. The Bishop was Chairman as Head and first Elder, seated in the midst of the other Elders, just as was said before regarding the Meetings of the Jews. *In the seat of the Elders let them praise him* <note>original Latin: "In Cathedra Seniorum laudent eum", from Psalm 107:32</note>, says the Royal Prophet [King David]. The Priests or Elders, who sat beside him, each had their own Seat of Judgment, which is why they were called *Assessores Episcoporum* <note>original Latin: "Asfesfores Epifcoporum", meaning assistants or co-judges to the Bishop</note> by the Early Fathers of the Church. Nothing significant was carried out which had not been previously deliberated in this Assembly, where the Bishop and the other Elders or Priests made up the Body of this Assembly; for at that time, the jurisdiction which is now called the Episcopal did not depend on the Bishop alone, but on all the Elders of whom the Bishop was Chairman. This practice also continued in Rome for several centuries.

It is likewise probable that the name of Cathedral <note>original Dutch: "Hoofdt-Kerk", literally "Head-Church"</note> had its origin in this ancient manner of seating in the early Churches or Christian Assemblies: from which has arisen the fact that we still celebrate the Feasts of St. Peter’s Chair at Rome and Antioch, as two cities where the Blessed Apostle is said to have been the Chairman in a formal and closed Church assembly. One should note, however, that by the word "Cathedral," we do not speak of the Great Churches nor of the Temples as they are currently known or understood. This word "Church" <note>original Dutch: "Kerk"</note> in its origin meant nothing other than an Assembly, and it is certain that the Chris-

tians before Constantine had no freedom to build Temples or Churches for their assemblies. Nevertheless, if we give credit to the new Breviary <note>original Dutch: "Getyboek", a book of daily prayers</note> of the Carmelites, there was supposedly a church built on Mount Carmel in honor of the Holy Virgin by the prophets who were successors of Elijah, who visited the Virgin, and whom she subsequently visited in return. Trifles, truly!

<margin>Who formerly held authority over the schools.</margin>
This similarity of institutions between the Church and the Synagogue is even more apparent if one considers the ancient customs of the Church. ## CHAPTER VIII.

->Remarks on the PRAYERS of the JEWS, and the Similarity of their PRAYERS with those of the CHRISTIANS.<-

<margin>
The prayers of the Jews considered in comparison with those of the Christians.
</margin>

The Jews have a great number of Prayers, which consist of various kinds. Although they were always obligated to pray to God, it nonetheless appears that while they were busy with the offering of Sacrifices in the Temple, they did not yet have the same fixed and established prayers that they now practice in their Synagogues. The prayers currently in use among them can in some measure be called the fulfillment of their Ancient Sacrifices; therefore, they also give to their Synagogue the name of "little Temple." Just as two specific Sacrifices were made daily in the Temple of Jerusalem, one in the morning and one in the evening, so the Jews have also instituted a morning and evening prayer to satisfy the requirements of these two sacrifices. In addition to these ordinary sacrifices that were offered daily, when a Feast day occurred, a sacrifice for the solemnity of the Feast was added; for this reason, they also perform a new prayer on such a Feast day, called <term>Musaph<gloss>From the Hebrew word for "additional," this refers to the extra service performed on the Sabbath and festivals to represent the additional offerings mandated in the Temple.</gloss></term>, which means *Addition*. What is more, one finds that they not only perform this morning and evening prayer to represent the two sacrifices that were made at that time; but that they also have a night-prayer, which they practice to fulfill the remainder of the evening sacrifice.

Christians also have, just as the Jews have their established prayers, and although they are obligated to pray to God without ceasing, according to the recommendation of the Apostle (a), nonetheless there are specific hours to pray in common, and this common prayer is all the more powerful and pleasing to God. It is true that our Sa-

<column-break/>

vior <note>Dutch: "Heilandt"</note> especially recommended Prayer in secret: but one must not therefore think that public prayers are condemned, since he himself attended them with the Jews. He only wished to condemn the great posturing of some Jewish Scribes, who prayed to God in public specifically to be seen by men.

<margin>
What manner of praying Christ has prescribed;
</margin>

Nonetheless (b) it seems as if our Savior absolutely wanted to reject the long prayers that the Jews did in their Synagogues, when he forbids his Disciples to perform such prayers after the manner of the Heathens, who believed that they were heard sooner through persistent praying. He himself prescribed for them the nature of their prayer, rejecting all other prayers that seemed to him too lacking in intimacy, and desired that one should pray: *Our Father, you who are in the Heavens*, etc. One answers to this that there is no evidence at all that our Savior wished to entirely condemn the prayers that the Jews commonly performed in their Synagogues, but only those of certain Scribes who daily invented new prayers. These were, so we believe, the new prayers that he rejected, and to withdraw his Disciples from them entirely, he determined a manner of praying for them in particular, without however preventing them from attending the Prayers of the Synagogues.

This same defect is also found among some Christians, and it has been necessary that the Councils formerly forbade the use of certain prayers, which had been introduced into the ministry of the Church, and were composed according to each person's thoughts. One must

<margin>And what names were given to different prayers.</margin>
For the rest, the Jews have various ways of praying, which they express through distinct words. It even appears that Paul intended to express all these different names in his Letter to Timothy (a) when he recommends that the faithful perform supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings in public. <margin>How Augustine attempted to distinguish them.</margin>
Augustine, who did not have access to the custom-book of the Jews, exerted all his effort to distinguish the various prayers expressed in the Latin Translation of the New Testament by these words: *Obsecrationes* (entreaties), *Prayers*, *Orationes* (orations), *Postulationes* (petitions), and *Gratiarum actiones* (thanksgivings). <margin>The objective that both Jews and Christians have in their prayers.</margin>

<margin>In what order the prayers were established.</margin>
The order of their prayers was that one began with praising God, and subsequently requested the things one needed. ### CHAPTER IX.

->Concerning the BLESSINGS in use among the JEWS; and the SIMILARITY these BLESSINGS have with those of the CHRISTIAN CHURCH.<-

<margin>How the Jews practiced Blessings compared with those of the Christian Church, and what they consisted of.</margin>
The command among the Jews to bless God is not only recommended by their Scribes: but it is also charged by a commandment in the Law, where it is said, (b) *when you have eaten, you shall bless the Lord your God, and praise Him for such a fruitful land given to you.* (c) Also, no one is unfit for prayer, since one can bless God at all times: but as the Rabbis are very clever in their interpretations of the Law, <term>Rabbi Moses</term> <note>Refers to Moses Maimonides, also known as Rambam (1138–1204)</note> believes that the words of the Law do not strictly refer to the blessing until after one has eaten and finished his meal, as these words are found in the text: *When you have eaten and are satisfied.* Nevertheless, the Scribes desire that one should bless God before and after the meal, which they have also extended to many other matters.

<margin>Blessing over the Bread and the Wine, how observed when Christ held the Last Supper.</margin>
The same practice of blessing food and drink passed from the Synagogue to the first Assemblies of the Christians; *whether you eat*, says Paul, (d) *or drink, or do anything else; do it to the glory of God.* These types of blessings are also called thanksgivings or praises; and it is in this sense that this passage must be understood: If I

<column-break/>

partake in the thanksgivings, *why am I slandered for that which I give thanks for?* Our Savior also observed these blessings accurately when He blessed the five loaves in the wilderness. (e) The blessing He pronounced separately over the bread and over the wine, when He celebrated the last Passover with His Apostles, is accompanied by the same circumstances that are still found in the Jewish ritual books. Therefore, we shall mainly occupy ourselves with this, and at the same time show in what way our Savior followed the Jewish Custom when He spoke these words over the bread which He blessed: *this is my Body*, etc.

<margin>Agreement that the Evangelists brought to this subject;</margin>
First, it should be noted that the person who pronounced the <term>BERACA</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Berakhah*, a formula of blessing or benediction</note>, or blessing over the Bread and the Wine, was commonly someone among the Jews who was judged to be the most prominent and capable of the company; thus our Savior did likewise among His Disciples as Master and Theologian. *Luke*, who describes this history more accurately than the Evangelists *Matthew* and *Mark*, mentions two drinking cups over which our Savior pronounced the blessing, since properly the Jews, when they celebrated the Passover Feast, immediately began with the blessing of the Chalice, which they poured full of Wine...

They took four Drinking-cups during this meal, but blessed only the first and the last; a custom which most Jews still maintain, except for the High German Jews <note>Refers to the Ashkenazi Jewish community</note> who pronounce the blessing over every cup.

However these various customs currently observed among the Jews may be, it nonetheless appears that our Savior followed what was customary at that time, and which Luke describes as it was then observed—whereas the other Evangelists speak only in general terms, noting this action in its entirety. One could not easily say whether Luke, in this place, used a common expression of the Hebrews (who often repeat the same thing), or whether by these two distinct Cups he intended specifically to point out two different Passover Feasts observed by the Savior with his Apostles. This would suggest he first observed the Ceremony of the Passover according to the ancient Law, and subsequently provided the opportunity to distinguish that of the Passover of the New Law. But this does not seem to fit the Gospel text at all, as it is more likely to say that our Savior held the Passover Feast just as the Jews did then. For this reason, the Evangelists even call the Wine that was in the Cup the "fruit of the vine," corresponding to what is still read in the Jews' Book of Church Customs <note>The Siddur or Haggadah</note> with these words:
> Blessed be the Lord our God, King of the World, who has created the Fruit of the Vine. <note>original: "BORE PERI HAGGEPHEN"</note>

<margin>Relating to a continuation of the Jewish custom.</margin>
It is more acceptable that our Savior, after he had blessed and broken the bread according to the Jewish custom, likewise followed the Jews in these—though different—words: *this is my Body*, just as they do when they eat the unleavened bread and say in the Chaldean or Syrian language <note>The author refers to Aramaic</note>:
> THIS IS THE BREAD OF AFFLICTION WHICH OUR FATHERS ATE IN THE LAND OF EGYPT. <note>original: "HA LAHMA VANIA DI ACALOU ABHATANA BE AREA MISRAIM"</note>

Nevertheless, there are some who pronounce these words in their mother tongue, and others are content to repeat them in a language understood by all those attending this Ceremony. The Divine Savior made it known to his Disciples that it was no longer a matter of eating the bread of affliction which their Ancestors had eaten when departing from Egypt; but that He, being the Institutor of a new Covenant, gave them his Body and Blood in place of this Bread. *Take, he says, and eat, that is my Body*; and after having pronounced the blessing over the Wine that was in the Cup, he handed them the sanctified Wine—as the Jews speak—which truly (according to the view of the Roman Catholics) was changed into his blood, and said to them: *Drink all of it; for what I reach to you is my blood, the blood of the new Covenant*; alluding to the words that Moses spoke to confirm the Covenant which God established with the Israelites in the Old Testament.
> *This is the Blood of the Covenant, which the Lord has made with us* (a). <note>original Latin: "Hic est Sanguis foederis quod Dominus pepigit vobiscum."</note>

# CHAPTER X.
## On the FEASTS of the JEWS, and the CORRESPONDENCE with those of the CHRISTIANS.

<margin>
How Christians have some similarity with certain Jewish Feasts in their ceremony, but differ immensely in the essence of their meaning.
</margin>
As the Christian Religion does not
differ in essence from that of the Jews,
since they both strive toward one end,
it must not seem strange to us that the
Christians, in their own way, observe a
portion of the Jewish Feasts. "In their
own way" we say, insofar as they
observe nothing but what is purely
ceremonial. The Christian Passover [Easter],
for example, is entirely different from
the Feast of the Jews, which was nothing
but a precursor. This is what Paul
indicates to the Corinthians, exhorting
them to celebrate the Passover (c) with
*unleavened bread of truth and sincerity*;
and he shows them at the same time
that they have no other Passover Lamb
than <term>JESUS CHRISTUS<note>Jesus Christ</note></term> (d). One sings,

Jews. And just as they make mention

*History of the Passover*, on this night in
which <term>JESUS CHRISTUS</term> triumphed

grace of God that befell them this
night, that they were delivered from

sin and the tyranny of the Devil, of

The Christians celebrate, moreover,
the Pentecost feast; but in a different

Moses on stone tablets.

Besides these great Feasts which

...fasting <note>The text begins mid-sentence, referring to the Jewish prohibition against fasting on the Sabbath.</note> was forbidden, since one was required to show joy and not sadness on the Feast day. The [Christian] Scriptures and their followers, however, were never bound to the Jewish Temple-duties in the celebration of the Sabbath: but rather to the true reason for its institution, which was the Creation of the World. And since this reason had no bearing on the old Ceremonies of the Law, they believed no less than the Jews that they were obliged to show respect for this day, according to what is indicated in the ancient Books of institutions attributed to *Clemens* <note>Referring to the *Apostolic Constitutions*, a 4th-century collection of Christian discipline once attributed to Clement of Rome.</note>: *That one should celebrate the Sabbath and Sunday as a feast day, since the first is dedicated to the memory of creation, and the other to the memory of the Resurrection.*

Now, there remains for us a trace in the Latin Church of this ancient ceremony in the Service of the Saturday before Easter and Pentecost, which one might call the two great Eves of the Christian Religion, just as among the Jews the Saturday of Passover is called <term>SABBAT GADOL</term> <note>Hebrew: *Shabbat HaGadol*, or the "Great Sabbath," the Saturday immediately preceding Passover.</note>, or *Great Saturday*. The Service of these two days in the Roman Church is performed in the same way as it was formerly on all days of Assembly. Something was read from the Law and the Prophets, in imitation of what is still observed today in the Synagogues. For example, the reading performed on Holy Saturday began with these words from *Genesis*: *In the beginning God created Heaven and earth*, to show that on this day one celebrated the memory of the Creation. Subsequently, one read in *Exodus* where the victory of the Israelites over the army of *Pharaoh* is spoken of, during the passage through the Red Sea.

We pass over other scriptural passages in silence that are read regarding the Service of that day, as no one is ignorant of them; what nevertheless deserves to be taken into consideration is the appropriation the Church makes of them, applying these readings to itself, as if all that occurred in the Old Testament was nothing but a figure of the mystery that has been fulfilled in the New Testament. In the Prayer which she joins to the words of *Genesis*, where the Creation of the World is spoken of, she makes

<column-break/>

mention of man's Re-creation, namely, of his Salvation. *O God*, she says, *you have made your power manifest in creating man, and you have shown it even more in redeeming him*: (a) In the other prayer which she joins to the words of Exodus, where the passage through the Red Sea is spoken of, she likewise joins the Truth to the Figure <note>In theology, a "figure" or "type" is an Old Testament event seen as a symbolic precursor to a New Testament reality.</note>, as in the first Prayer, beseeching God that it may please him likewise to save all peoples through the water of Baptism, just as he delivered the Hebrew People from Egyptian slavery.

One could appropriately note the same things in the Service of the Saturday that precedes the day of Pentecost; then a reading of the Law and the Prophets is done, just as on the Saturday Eve of Easter; and since on this day the Jews received the Law, (b) one reads the words of *Exodus* where it is spoken how God gave this Law on Mount Sinai.

It is true that in the course of time much change has occurred in the Ecclesiastical Service, and that even in the beginning there was not this great correspondence that we now observe: but this in no way prevents the fact that, in general, the entire Church has always agreed to perform the reading of the Law, Psalms, and even of the Prophets on days of Assembly, along with some other Books of the Old Testament, as the variety of the Feasts required: to which subsequently the reading of the Gospel and Paul's Epistles was added.

If there has been some variation, it was nonetheless of little importance, and the customs of the Synagogues are also no less different, according to the distinction of Countries, than the various customs of the Ecclesiastical Service are. The Church and Synagogue agree regarding the common prayers, and the daily prayers which are now called <term>Vierdagen</term> <note>Literally "Four-days," likely referring to the ember days or quarterly seasonal fasts/prayers.</note>, and if they contain any specifics, they are adapted to the Feast days. The Synagogue truly has this Privilege above the Christian Church, that it is the Oldest and the first to which God communicated his word. Paul says, (c) speaking of the Jews: *That unto them were committed the oracles of God.* <note>original: "Dat hun de woorden Godts zyn toevertrouwt."</note>

It seems that the religion of the Jews could no longer remain whole after the destruction of Jerusalem, since this city was the place of the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of ancient Jerusalem.</note> or the Great Assembly, to whose decisions all Jews were obliged to submit. Therefore, the Rabbis apply themselves primarily to showing in the Histories that they—notwithstanding the lamentable state in which their People saw themselves brought through so many exiles in various Kingdoms—nevertheless in no way lost their Tradition, since they suppose certain famous High and Low Schools in which they always taught this Tradition. <margin>known as Patriarchs.</margin>

Mention is made of these Heads under the name of Patriarchs in the Imperial Laws. They sent authorized representatives called SELIHIM <note>original: "Selihim," from the Hebrew for messengers or envoys</note> or Apostles, throughout the entire extent of their jurisdiction. They also had their Priests or Elders to settle disputes arising in matters of religion. The Emperors permitted this type of judiciary among the Jews, and even honored their Patriarchs and ministers with many privileges; but when this Jewish administration in these Princes' states began to be feared for its troublesome consequences, it was found necessary to abolish it entirely. Nevertheless, they still have in many places some Heads or Superiors of their civil government: but without letting it be publicly known, nor are they allowed to punish their rebels, being fearful that such might come to the knowledge of the Authorities, under whom they are obliged to obey.

By this means they have at least preserved a part of their educational practice: but as it was impossible to preserve such a large number of Traditions as they had among them, they judged it necessary to put them in writing, even though they previously gave no instruction in them except orally. And since one can object to them that it was not quite possible for all these Traditions to have been preserved during so many centuries, and even during a general upheaval of their states, they take refuge in assuming certain societies of Sages or Scribes, who each gave instruction in his own time, from *Moses* down to those who first put them into writing. Some even add, and among others *Rabbi Moses* <note>Likely referring to Maimonides, known as Moses ben Maimon</note>, that every Head of the *Sanhedrin* <note>The supreme council of the Jews</note> kept private copies of these Traditions, which he nevertheless shared only orally. Those who heard them from the mouths of the Heads stored this teaching in their memories for their private use.

<margin>The first collection of Jewish Tradition attributed to Rabbi Judah.</margin>
Therefore, *Rabbi Judah*, to whom the first collection of these Traditions is commonly attributed, did nothing more than gather all the different Memoirs that were available in his time, and which he sought out accurately. This Rabbi, who was the *Nasi* <note>original: "Nafci," meaning Prince or President of the council</note> or Prince of the *Sanhedrin*, lived in the second Century, under the Antonines, Roman Emperors: but the Jewish

<margin>...calls the Mishnah.</margin>
Historians do not agree among themselves regarding the time in which he completed this collection, which was generally accepted by all the Jews and taught unanimously. This collection has served the Jews as a rule for all matters of religion ever since that time, and they gave it the name MISHNAH <note>original: "Misnah"</note>, to wit, *Repetition*, or rather an explanation of the written Law. The style is indeed pure, but very fragmented; and because the Heads of the Assemblies had for the most part brought forward different pronouncements on the same cases, *Rabbi Judah* reports them all; which has added an obscurity to his work: for he does not always note the opinion that one ought to follow. Some Jews have, however, improved this obscurity, marking with small outlines over the names of the Jewish Scholars whose conclusion has established the Law; and furthermore, there are printings of the MISHNAYOT <note>The plural form of Mishnah</note>, where the pronouncement to which one must adhere is indicated.

The book called MISHNAH, already mentioned, which currently forms the text of the *Talmud*, being described too concisely and not being able to satisfy all the disputes that arose daily concerning the Law, the Rabbis who succeeded *Rabbi Judah* added small declarations or explanations to it, some of which were called TOSIPHETOT <note>original: "Tosiphetot," commonly known as the Tosefta</note>, *Additions*, to serve as a completion, and others bore the title of BARAYEROT <note>original: "Barajerot," commonly known as Baraitot</note>, to wit: *Explanations outside the text*. But these small explanations were still not sufficient to settle all the disputes arising over the Law, such that it was necessary to create much larger explanations of the *Mishnah*, which they ordered to be given the name GEMARA <note>original: "Guemara"</note> or Perfection; and it is actually this *Gemara* that the Jews now call the *Talmud*.

<margin>Rabbi Johanan considered the Compiler of the Babylonian Talmud; and what it contains;</margin>
As they, as we have already noted, had two main Schools in which the *Mishnah* was taught, they also had two separate *Talmuds*. The first was that of Jerusalem, of which *Rabbi Johanan*, Head or *Nasi* of the Palestinian School, was considered to be the Compiler. The exact time when he lived is unknown; for the Jews disagree with each other on this: some assert that he lived around the end of the third century, and others around the end of the fourth. [The Jews] preferred this book <note>The Babylonian Talmud</note> over all others, wherefore they called its author the Prince of Commentators. This Rabbi *Solomon* is commonly called *Jarchi* <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105)</note>, and is the famous author of *Delira* <note>original: "Delira"; likely referring to the *Postillae* of Nicholas of Lyra, a Christian scholar whose work was so closely based on Rashi's that their names were often linked in early modern scholarship</note>. To say much of many other Rabbis here would be unnecessary, who likewise composed or summarized explanations of the *Talmud*; those who wish to devote themselves to this study should especially choose the excellent abridgments that Rabbi *Moses, son of Maimon* <note>Maimonides, author of the Mishneh Torah</note> compiled in a pure and intelligible style.

One could add to this writer another Rabbi *Moses*, nicknamed after his birthplace *Coucy* <note>Moses of Coucy, 13th-century author of the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol*</note>, who in a particular work explained everything concerning the 613 doctrines or commandments of the Jews. <margin>The Jewish traditions are of an ancient authority,</margin>
<margin>and when they were introduced.</margin>
It cannot be denied that the traditions found in the *Talmud* are for the most part very ancient, since the first Fathers of the Church made mention of them, not only generally under the name of *Deuteroses* <note>original Greek: "Deuteroses," meaning "Second Law," used by Church Fathers to refer to the Mishnah</note>, which is the same book as the *MISHNAYOT*: but they even reported on some of them in the same way as one still reads in the Jewish books today. One need only consult the works of *Origen*, *Epiphanius*, *Jerome*, and above all this last one, who will provide a great number of them, especially in his commentaries on the Prophets. It is probable that the Jews invented the majority of these traditions when they no longer had a definite Oracle to consult for advice, and that some time after the return from Babylon to Jerusalem, their scholars wished to make themselves prominent through their new interpretations of the Law.

<margin>The sects of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and how they opposed one another,</margin>
These new interpretations divided them into various sects, which subsequently took pleasure in brewing mutual estrangements as much as possible, as usually happens in such circumstances. The Pharisees, who maintained the Law alongside the traditions of their ancestors, increased their number in order to oppose more strongly and powerfully the opinion of the Sadducees, who, on the contrary, would tolerate none of them. These two sects did not observe the middle way, which was to maintain only those traditions necessary to explain the obscure passages of the Law and to uphold civil discipline and good order in their State. This was the cause by which our Savior <note>Jesus Christ</note> was compelled to oppose not only the Sadducees, who overturned the most important part of the Jewish religion by rejecting all traditions: but also the Pharisees, who made the religion of their fathers ridiculous, multiplying these traditions through their subtleties which departed entirely from the text of the Law.

<margin>and how many fables have crept into all these introduced traditions.</margin>
In our opinion, this is the origin of all the fables and idle maxims that are now to be found in the books of the *Talmud*. The Pharisees finally became the dominant sect among the Jews at the time of their dispersion, and the Patriarchs and heads of the principal schools spread this teaching of theirs in all the lands where Jews resided. There were only a small number of scholars who caused a schism, and having deliberately set themselves against this great number of traditions, could not tolerate that so many dreams were paired with the text of the Law. Consequently, they were given the name *Karaites* <note>from the Hebrew "Bnei Mikra," meaning "Followers of Scripture"</note>, that is, men bound to the text of the Scripture, although they truly rejected only those traditions they believed to be unfounded; and they still read the books of the *Talmud* today, following them in the majority of matters connected to the institutions.

<margin>The vast number of their traditions caused them to be committed to writing.</margin>
Although the Jews believe that their traditions would never have been set in writing had it not been for disastrous times, this would nevertheless have been difficult to carry out because there were such a great number of them. They have not even been careful to collect the most important ones that are considered lost, including those pertaining to their sacrifices. What is more, they are also ignorant of the names of a great number of animals that the Law forbade them to eat, and notwithstanding this, they still dare to boast that they have kept the Law of Moses unmaimed, alongside the Explanation received from God on Mount Sinai. But if one investigates how little care they have taken over all these various collections, as the Jews have done with their institutions at different times, one will find nothing uncommon in it that does not also appear in other religions, which their ceremonies...

# THIRD HISTORICAL TREATISE

[The Jews] possess these [traits] and in other Books in which their institution is contained, without it being necessary that the author of the laws was present. It appears then all the more that these Collections were made by the Heads of their most renowned Schools, and that they subsequently, for the convenience found therein, distributed them among all their people. Afterward, the Scholars invented the idea, in order to give them more authority, that the decrees contained in these Books were delivered to Moses alongside the Text of the Law: but they add so many fantasies and ridiculous inventions as having originated from Mount Sinai, that this alone would be enough to prevent any belief being given even to things of some probability.

<margin>How the conditions [of the countries]</margin>
Besides these Institutions contained in the

<column-break/>

<margin>led the countries of the Jews to adopt different Customs.</margin>
Talmud, and which all Jews find themselves obliged to obey, they also have certain practices that differ according to the conditions of the Countries in which they reside. They call these local practices *MINHAGIM* <note>original: "MINHAGIM"; plural of *minhag*, meaning traditional customs that have the force of law</note> or *Customs*; and to better observe them, they have also written special Books. One can observe this for oneself when reading their Prayer Books, where no small difference is found, whether regarding the matters themselves. The Rabbis have also set down certain *DINIM* <note>original: "DINIM"; plural of *din*, meaning legal rulings or judgments</note>, or *Judgments* in writing, which can be grouped with the Customs, since the Jews differ in this, and because these *Dinim* contain only probable reasons why a Ceremony should be performed in one way rather than another.

### CHAPTER XIII.

->Concerning the BOOKS used in the SYNAGOGUES, and the principal Religious Exercises of the JEWS.<-

---

<margin>The extraordinary accuracy of the Jews in the Writing and preparation of their Book of the Law is pointed out.</margin>
We have already noted, when dealing with the prayers of the Jews, that they have various Books in which all these prayers are collected. Each follows his own particular customs in this, which however does not prevent them from agreeing with the essence of prayers in general. Besides these Prayer-Books which they call *SEDER TEPHILLOT* <note>original: "SEDER TEPHILLOT", literally "Order of Prayers," the standard prayer book or Siddur</note> or *order of the Prayers*, they have yet another Book called *MAHAZOR* <note>original: "MAHAZOR", meaning "cycle"; a prayer book used for the annual cycle of festivals</note>, which contains not only their Annual Exercises but likewise the Poems or Songs sung in the Synagogues on certain Sabbath days, as well as on other Feasts; and these Poems are very difficult to understand, because the style is broken and confused. We shall not speak here of the *SEFER TORA* <note>original: "SEFER TORA", meaning "Book of the Law," specifically the Torah scroll</note>, or the *Book of the Law*, of which there are always many *Copies* or *Transcripts* in every Synagogue, written in a truly unique manner, and even accompanied by an accuracy not without superstition. The Parchment, for example, on which the Law is written, if prepared by a Christian, or a Heretical Jew, or a Samaritan, would be invalid, and might never be used for this purpose. Thus it is strictly required that it be

<column-break/>

prepared by a devout Jew, and also in a certain form, both regarding the height of the Scroll-book as well as the divided page and the determination of every line. They observe the ancient custom of Writing, their Books consisting of long rolls, and we would find nothing to say regarding their accuracy in view of the Divisions of small pages or columns, in which they write the Books intended for Synagogue use, were it not that a superstitious reason accompanied it: whereas otherwise one clearly sees that all these Divisions were invented only to make their Books appear more beautiful and regular.

It is the same with the ink that must be used in the Writing of these Books. This is made in a special way, the ingredients of which are designated by the Rabbis. They desire nothing for decoration to be used in it, whether gold, nor silver, nor any red, green or other colors; if a *Sefer Tora*, or Book of the Law written for the use of any Synagogue, had a single Letter in it that was of a different color than their ordained ink, this *Sefer Tora* would be rejected as unlawful, and might never serve any purpose in any Synagogue.

# ON THE RELIGIOUS DUTIES OF THE JEWS.

<margin>Ancient custom of writing Hebrew Books without Vowel points.</margin>
The same order is observed by them regarding some small Books, which they also read in their Synagogues on certain days of the year. They have, for example, the Book of *Esther*, which they call *Megillach Hester* <note>original: "Megillach Hester"; the Scroll of Esther, read during the festival of Purim</note>, the Book or Part of *Esther*, written on a scroll, just as the Book of the Law is written. What is most worthy of note in these Books dedicated to the use of the Synagogues is that one sees the Hebrew Letters without any of those Vowel points <note>original: "Vokaalstippen"; these are the marks (niqqud) added to Hebrew text to indicate vowel sounds, which are usually omitted in sacred scrolls</note> found in printed Hebrew Bibles, which determine the manner of reading. They have, it seems, kept the ancient way of writing Books from before these Vowel points were invented. One finds there no grammatical marks—upon which the Jews are now very precise in marking out in other Bible books not intended for Synagogue use—to distinguish meanings and matters. They have no other dots or lines than those linguistic marks which also serve to raise or lower the voice in reading, or rather when they chant the words of the Law. Because of this, they must practice for a long time beforehand to read accurately in the Synagogues, where one finds no books with points, question marks, or lines, as are found in their other copies of Scripture, whether they be printed or written.

<margin>How the Jews are set upon the study of their Law books.</margin>
As for the primary study of the Jews, they believe themselves above all obligated to apply themselves to the study of the Law and their Traditions contained in the *Talmud*. Their Synagogues serve them as Schools, and one rarely encounters a Jew who is not skilled enough to read the Law books, or who does not know a portion of them by heart; what is more, many also understand passages from the *Mishnah*, a book which contains the text of the *Talmud*. For as soon, they say, *as a child has reached five years of age, one must lead them to the reading of the Text of the Law, and at the age of fourteen years, to learn to understand the* MISHNAH.

<margin>and the instruction of their Children</margin>
Their manner of instructing Children differs from that of Christians; for they learn the Hebrew and a bit of the

<column-break/>

<margin>instruction.</margin>
Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> language without paying attention to any rules of Grammar, which they never learn. It is also a rare thing to find a Jew who can give instruction to another in what he understands of the Bible and *Talmud*, since all the knowledge he has of it rests on nothing but long-term usage.

When they have reached the age of thirteen, they learn the Commandments, which are very great in number; for then they finally have a more powerful desire to apply themselves to the study of the *Gemara* <note>the component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary</note> or the *Talmud*, putting this into practice around the age of fifteen years. But there are few Jews who understand these perfectly and can give an account of them, although they are taught openly among them, at least in places where they are granted the freedom of their Religion.

In our Schools, there is nothing that can be compared to their passion for disputation when they come to investigate any part of the *Talmud*; since they always have arguments for and against, resting on the authority of their Fathers, and they carry out their dispute so passionately against one another that one would almost think they were entirely mad.
->*A people raging in their reasoning and a mind nourished by chimeras.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Gens ratione furens & mentem pasta chimeris"</note>

<margin>Yet they by no means make any work of other Learning.</margin>
As the Jews rarely apply themselves to general Learning—since they have Ordinances by which the reading of Philosophical writings is forbidden to them—they almost never exercise their intellect in that way. This is why they are so strongly tied to their Religion, and from their childhood possessed of so many prejudices that it is almost impossible to be rid of them. Although their *Talmud* is filled with stories that have no appearance of truth, and consist of mere entertaining tales, they nevertheless have such a respect for this Book as if it were delivered by God to their Ancestors; so that the Jews in general are very simple. However, we do not include here those who are clever enough, yet like the others find themselves forced to hold this Book as a rule of their Faith. For otherwise, they would be accused of impiety and heresy.
->*They speak with the many, but think with the few.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Loquuntur cum multis; sed sapiunt cum paucis"</note>

<header>THIRD HISTORICAL DISCOURSE</header>

## CHAPTER XIV.

->On the BOOKS which are now held in esteem by the JEWS; and whether they can be of any use to CHRISTIANS.<-

<margin>
Which Jewish Writings Christians can benefit from; distinguished from others that can be of no service.
</margin>
Several catalogs of Jewish books have already been published in the past under the title of *Rabbinical Library* <note>original: "Rabbynsche Bibliotheek"; likely referring to bibliographical works such as those by Giulio Bartolocci</note>. We could point out many others here that have not been mentioned; but we believe it will be more useful to consider the use one can make of them, rather than merely contenting ourselves with listing their names. We admit that there is almost no science for which one cannot find some book written in Rabbinic Hebrew: but to tell the truth, very few are found to be accurate; for as far as the arts and sciences are concerned, the Jews have done little else than copy Arabic books, which they have translated according to their own fashion. For this reason, in our judgment, little reliance can be placed on the books of the Jews except regarding their religion: and even this must be done with good judgment, at least if one does not wish to approve of them along with all their fantasies <note>original: "dromeryen"; literally "dreamings" or "delusions," reflecting the author's skeptical view of non-literal Rabbinic traditions</note>.

To make this distinction with a kind of critical discernment, one should consider the religion of the Jews in itself, according to the relationship it has with the Christian religion. If one wishes to view it in the first way, it is clear that books dealing solely with Judaism can be of little use to Christians. For example, of what use is it to a Christian to know how a Jew prepares his tent or hut to celebrate his *Feast of Tabernacles* <note>original: "Loofhutten-Feest"; the holiday of Sukkot</note>? It is enough to know what this feast consists of, which can properly be learned from the Biblical text or the commentaries, if further instruction is required. It is the same with all the other feasts of the Jews, in which the Rabbis are uncommonly well-trained. And as the greatest part of the *Mishnah* <note>original: "Mifnah"; the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note> and *Gemara* <note>original: "Guemara"; the component of the Talmud comprising Rabbinical analysis and commentary on the Mishnah</note> contain almost nothing other than this kind of intricacy, these books can be of little use to Christians, except for certain treatises in which one finds some ceremonies and customs

<column-break/>

that have some relationship to those of the Christians, and from which one could draw some light for the explanation of certain scriptural passages of the New Testament. We will then content ourselves with the shortened *Talmud* compiled by *Rabbi Moses* <note>original: "Rabbi Moses"; referring to Moses Maimonides and his work, the Mishneh Torah</note>, without concerning ourselves with the *Mishnah* or *Talmud*, which we leave to the Jews, since they cannot be read without making the Jews look ridiculous and convicting them of the delusion they hold regarding the traditions of their ancestors. It will even be enough to consult the work of *Rabbi Moses*, which is nonetheless not entirely purged of all these fantasies, although some have asserted that he was the only one among the Jews who did not occupy himself with fantasies: *Among the Jews, Rabbi Moses alone knows not how to rave* <note>original: "Solus inter Judaeos nescit delirare R. Moses"</note>. It is true that one finds fewer of them noted in his work than in other Rabbis: but one cannot say that he was entirely estranged from them; otherwise, he could not have been a sincere Jew. However, one will find many scriptural passages explained by the ancient Jewish scholars in the *Talmud*: but very few are interpreted according to the letter. Every scholar takes pleasure in demonstrating his wit through allegories and childish allusions that in no way correspond to their subject. If they do approach the literal sense somewhat, it nonetheless happens in the Jewish manner and in regard to their ceremonies; therefore, these books can bring no benefit except to the Jews, to explain the Scriptures, or rather to make them more stubborn in the prejudices of their religion.

<margin>
Which Jewish Books are pointed out to Christians for the explanation of their sacred writings.
</margin>
They have other books from which Christians can draw great benefit for the explanation of the Old Testament. Such are all the interpretations they have compiled according to the letter of the Bible, though these are few in number. For the majority, especially the ancients, have been more inclined to attach themselves to the allegorical sense than to explain their texts; and thus these famous explanations, which are called *ZOHAR* <note>The Zohar is the foundational work in the literature of Jewish mysticism known as Kabbalah</note>, and for which the Jews have such a great reverence

<summary>This page evaluates the usefulness of Jewish Rabbinical literature for Christian scholars, specifically criticizing the Talmud for its "fantasies" while acknowledging the value of literal commentaries and the work of Maimonides.</summary>
<keywords>Jewish literature, Rabbinical Library, Maimonides, Talmud, Mishnah, Gemara, Sukkot, Zohar, biblical interpretation</keywords>

<header>On the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.</header>

...importance, likewise the **Midrashim** <note>original: "MEDRAS-CIM"; these are ancient rabbinic commentaries that use storytelling and allegory to explain the Bible</note>, and other metaphorical explanations, are of little use to anyone but the Jews. The collection of Rabbinic commentaries placed in the Great Bible of Venice <note>referring to the *Mikraot Gedolot*, or Rabbinic Bible, first printed by Daniel Bomberg</note>, of which there are several editions, and subsequently in those of Basel, can be very helpful for understanding the literal sense of the text; to these one can add the explanations of *Isaac Abarbanel* <note>original: "Isaak Abrabanel"; a 15th-century statesman and philosopher</note> on the primary parts of the Scripture. We could cite other Jewish writers who have explained the text of the Old Testament in a literal manner, but this last commentator, namely *Abarbanel*, encompasses everything within himself.

As far as their theology is concerned, in our judgment, one need only read the works of those who have explained the primary articles of their religion. To select from the great number of these books found among them, we give preference to **SEPHER IKKARIM**, or the *Book of Principles* <note>original: "SEPHER IKKARIM"; a work by Joseph Albo defining the fundamental beliefs of Judaism</note>, written by *Joseph Albo*, a Spanish Jew. We add to this some other Rabbis who investigated the principles of Rabbi *Moses* <note>Moses Maimonides, the most influential medieval Jewish philosopher</note> on this subject, including *Isaac Abarbanel*, whom we have already mentioned, and Rabbi *Hasdai* <note>Hasdai Crescas</note>. One must especially examine the reasons they bring forward to show that, since God is not subject to change, the Law once given by Him must likewise not be subject to change. They believe this proves that Christians should not have entirely abolished the ceremonies of the Law of *Moses*. However, the objections they pose to themselves on this subject, which they cannot solve, are clear proofs of the falseness of their principle. Furthermore, it would also be necessary to read some other Rabbis who wrote on the principles of the Jewish religion before Rabbi *Moses*, among others the book of *Saadia Gaon* which is called **SEPHER EMUNOTH**, or the *Book of Beliefs* <note>original: "SEPHER EMUNOTH"; typically titled *The Book of Beliefs and Opinions*. The Dutch text incorrectly refers to it as the "Book of Creation" here, though it corrects this later</note>. For although this work was composed at a time when the Jews were more inclined toward the "dreamings" <note>original: "dromeryen"; the author's skeptical term for non-literal Talmudic legends</note> of the *Talmud* than to the explanation of their theology, and though this writer is not always precise, this does not prevent one from learning—by comparing his views with those of Rabbi *Moses*—that the theology of these *Geonim* <note>original: "Gueonim" or "Vitmuntenden"; the "Excellencies" who headed the Babylonian academies</note> cannot be entirely reconciled with that of the Jews of today.

<column-break/>

These Jewish theologians do not only deal with what pertains to their own Doctrine; they also sometimes undertake to refute the Christian Faith. Thus, their books can provide us with some enlightenment on the matters of dispute, which are handled more thoroughly and primarily by Rabbi *Lipman* in a work he published under the title **SEPHER NITSAHON**, or the *Book of Victory* <note>original: "SEPHER NITSAHON"; a famous polemical work by Yom-Tov Lipmann Mühlhausen intended to defend Judaism against Christian critiques</note>.

<margin>Their Kabbalistic books are generally useless to Christians, and why.</margin>
We will not dwell on noting the best books of those who have dealt with theology according to the principles of the **Kabbalah** <note>original: "Cabbala"; the Jewish mystical and esoteric tradition</note>, as they are of an absurd nature. However, it is almost unbelievable how much the Jews value them, especially in the East, where they devote themselves to speculative Kabbalah. The rational treatment of this science seems to be based on certain explanations of the attributes or properties of God—for example, His Unity and His Eternity. But on this subject, they build nothing that is not taken from Platonic Philosophy, to which they have added other subtleties to reconcile the principles of that Philosophy with their Law. They regard as the foundation of this theology a small book bearing the title **SEPHER JETSIRA**, or *Book of Creation* <note>original: "SEPHER JETSIRA"; an ancient mystical text often attributed to the patriarch Abraham</note>, which some among them attribute to the Patriarch Abraham, as if it contained the entire theology of the ancient Patriarchs, although in truth it contains nothing grounded. But the Jews who have since worked upon this foundation—whether in composing commentaries on this little work or in publishing entire books of their Kabbalistic theology—have produced rare "revelations" of the wondrous secrets of this supposed Divine science. These are accompanied by such an impression of authority that even some Christians are found who believe in all the supposed mysteries of the Jewish Kabbalah. In the register of Jewish books believed to have belonged to *Giovanni Pico*, Count of Mirandola <note>original: "Ian Pic, Grave van Mirandola"; a famous Renaissance philosopher who sought to synthesize Kabbalah with Christianity</note>, one sees a great number of these books. We do not doubt that the Jews, who had a greater desire to enrich themselves than the library of this young gentleman, slipped some forged works into his hands.

For the rest, those who do not mind the loss of time and wish to practice the principles of this Kabbalistic science need only apply themselves to the work of

### THIRD HISTORICAL TREATISE

*Rabbi Moses Cordovero* <note>a leading 16th-century mystic in Safed</note>, who summarized everything under the title **PARDES RIMOINIM**, or the *Garden of Pomegranates* <note>original: "PARDES RIMOINIM"</note>. If one is not satisfied with this abridgment and wishes to understand this science fundamentally, one may read the following books, namely: **MAPPETAH HAKKABALA**, or the *Key of the Kabbalah*; **SUD SUDOT**, or the *Secret of Secrets*; **SEPHER BAHIR**, or the *Excellent Book* <note>often called the "Book of Brightness," one of the earliest Kabbalistic texts</note>; and **SEPHER HAPPELIA**, or the *Book of Wonders*. We shall make no mention of "practical" *Kabbalah* <note>the use of mystical names and rituals to affect the physical world</note>, although those who practice this presumed art openly testify that they know its true effects through many proven experiences, taking pleasure in deceiving those who are willing to take them at their word.

We shall only say this of this "practical" *Kabbalah*: that the books they have compiled regarding the influence of the stars, combined with certain images from which their talismans arose, as well as the power of their letters and many other such things, have no other foundation than the superstition of the Kabbalistic scholars, who apply themselves to geomancy <note>original: "Stipwaarzeggery"; divination by dots or lines</note>, palmistry <note>original: "Handkykkunde"</note>, and physiognomy <note>original: "voorhoofdkykery"; judging character from the forehead or face</note>.

The Jews are also provided with many Philosophical books translated into Rabbinic Hebrew, such as the works of *Aristotle* and the commentaries of *Averroes* <note>the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd</note>, along with many other Arabic writers who wrote on logic, physics, and metaphysics. However, these strictly followed the principles of *Aristotle*, or rather the Arabic philosophers who wrote about *Aristotle*. And so, their philosophical books are only useful to their own nation, unless through them one could discover certain Arabic writers whose works are rarely found and must be sought among the Jews who translated them. Even the printed books of *Averroes* themselves were translated from Rabbinic Hebrew and not from the original Arabic. Furthermore, they possess some works under the name of *Aristotle* that we do not have in Greek; but these works were likely fabricated by the Arabs and subsequently translated into Rabbinic Hebrew. The Jews in Italy are also provided with some philosophical books translated from Latin; but we do not advise using these translations to learn the philosophy of *Aristotle*, as we can read them in Greek or at least in Latin,

Truly, there are enough Jewish writers to establish an entire library who have also written on mathematics and medicine; but the majority of their works are nothing more than translations made from Arabic books. For example, regarding mathematicians, they have translated the *Almagest* of *Ptolemy* <note>an influential 2nd-century mathematical and astronomical treatise</note> and the *Abridged Almagest* from Arabic. One finds, moreover, the works of *Al-Farghani* <note>original: "Alphragan"; a 9th-century astronomer</note> and many others of this nature in Rabbinic Hebrew. However, they are not only translators, but also authors in imitation of the Greeks and Arabs, producing books on arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and astrology. *Ibn Ezra* <note>original: "Aben-Efra"; a polymath and biblical commentator</note>, one of the most learned interpreters of Scripture, is the only one among them who wrote on all parts of mathematics, and even a treatise on the measurement of stellar altitude, which is titled **SEPHER ASTROLAB LE ABEN ESRA** <note>The Book of the Astrolabe by Ibn Ezra</note>. *Rabbi Mordechai ben Comtino* has written on the same subject and called his book **SEPHER TIKKON CELI HANNECHOSET**, which is to say: *Of the construction of the copper instrument* <note>referring to the brass astrolabe</note>. This Rabbi also wrote on geometric and astronomical matters.

<margin>
How
they have

their

according
to mathe-

</margin>
For a long time, the Jews have followed the methods of mathematicians in their calendar <note>original: "Tydwyzer"</note>, since they no longer calculate their time from the first day of the moon's appearance, or when it begins to appear, because they have found themselves obliged to consult astronomical tables to arrange their feast days. One can read here the book of *Rabbi Isaac ben Joseph*, which is called **JESUD OLAM**, or *Foundation of the World*, and the astronomical tables of *Immanuel ben Jacob Baal Ha-Kenafeim* <note>original: "baal Haceenaphaim"; the name means "Master of the Wings," referring to his astronomical tables</note>; to which one can add the Hebrew calendar that *Münster* <note>Sebastian Münster, a famous 16th-century Christian Hebraist</note> had printed.

Regarding books on medicine, which also exist in great numbers among the Jews, most must be viewed as translations they made from Arabic writers, and even from some Christian writers. The principal works they translated from Arabic are by *Hippocrates* and *Galen*. In addition to these, they have translated into Rabbinic Hebrew nearly all the books of medicine written in Arabic, of which very few have been printed, and rarely in Arabic; but yet...

There have even been Jews who possessed an accurate knowledge of the Greek and Arabic languages, enabling them to translate the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates <note>an ancient Greek medical text</note> alongside the commentary of Galen <note>a prominent Roman physician</note> from Greek and Arabic: at least, this translation from Greek into Arabic is attributed to a certain Rabbi Hanan ben Isaak <margin><gloss>made proficient.</gloss> and it is said that Rabbi Nathan subsequently translated this from Arabic into Rabbinic Hebrew, adding his own observations.</margin> Finally, we shall not recount the various works of surgery in use among them, nor the many books dealing with medicinal herbs; for it is likely that no advantage is to be gained from them by Christians on this subject.

### XV. CHAPTER.
#### REFLECTIONS concerning some other JEWISH BOOKS written in RABBINIC HEBREW.

<margin>How the Jews are inexperienced in Rhetoric and Poetry.</margin>
**R**hetoric and poetry are little used by the Rabbis: consequently, they have few orators and poets among them, as the Rabbinic Hebrew language is very sparse. For this reason, their teachers never practice the art of eloquence. They apply themselves more to ethics, which they nonetheless treat in a different manner than Christians, since they add a great number of commandments to which they believe they are bound, and from which many cases of conscience subsequently arise, drawing conclusions with all possible subtlety. Since they subject themselves entirely to the authority of their ancestors, they usually consult their *Talmud* regarding all difficulties, and very often the authors who have written books under the title of **SCEELOT VETESCHUVOT** or *Questions and Answers* <note>original: "She'elot u-Teshuvot"; a body of legal decisions and responsa</note>, in which they very easily find the resolutions for their cases.

As for their poets, it is known that poetry among the Jews is not very ancient, at least as it is practiced today, and which they have turned into an art over several centuries in imitation of the Arabs. Formerly, we read an abridgment of the entire Philosophy composed in such types of verses by Rabbi Abraham ben Mesullam. They also have several hymns in honor of some of their festivals in their service-books called *Mahaza* <note>original: "Machzor"; a prayer book used by Jews for the High Holy Days</note>, as we have already noted here before. Most Jews place some verses at the beginning of their works, and some even go so far as to compose their entire arguments in verse. But they cannot, however, be called poets, even though they make verses. Yet, there is no nation that has written as many fables as the Jews, and which was more inclined to them at a time when there were no poets among them.

<margin>Likewise in History and Chronology.</margin>
They also have historians and chronologists among them, but few in number, and also not accurate in their treatises; therefore, they are even less accurate when they report the histories of other nations, whose books they have copied without judgment, and one finds them to be unfaithful in their translations as well. For example, how many fables does one not find in the book of *Josippus*, or *Ben-Gorion* <note>original: "Josippon"; a 10th-century history of the Jews often wrongly attributed to the 1st-century historian Flavius Josephus</note>, who is nonetheless taken for the true Josephus? It is enough that a Jew undertakes to write a history for false assumptions to be fully believed. When we speak of the historical work of *Ben-Gorion* or the false *Josephus*, we do not mean to include under this name a concise abridgment published by *Munsterus* <note>Sebastian Münster, a 16th-century Christian scholar</note>, nor another more extensive edition with a Latin translation brought to light by him: but the edition from *Konstantinolen* <note>Constantinople</note>, which the same *Munsterus* did not have printed in full, in which many things are missing at the beginning, the end, and throughout the work.

Their books of chronology, which are printed under the title of **SEDER OLAM RABBA**, or the *Great Chronology* <note>original: "Great Order of the World"</note>, and **SEDER OLAM ZUTA**, the *Abridged Chronology* <note>original: "Small Order of the World"</note>, contain very few matters, no less than their **SEPHER HAKKABA-** <note>original: "Sefer Ha-Kabbalah" or Book of Tradition by Abraham ibn Daud</note>

# THIRD HISTORICAL TREATISE

<columns>
BALA <note>Likely referring to the *Sefer ha-Qabbalah* or Book of Tradition</note>, or *Book of Tradition*, which is one of their oldest histories. *Rabbi Ghedalias* <note>Gedaliah ibn Yahya ben Joseph (1515–1587)</note> has inserted infinitely many dreams and fictional historical chronologies into his work, to which he gives the title **SCALSCELAT HAKKABALA** <note>Hebrew: *Shalshelet Ha-Kabbalah*</note>, or *Chain of Tradition*; for the aim of the Jews in their histories seems to be to prove the succession of their scholars and schools, in order to more powerfully combat the teachings of the *Karaites* <note>A Jewish sect that follows the written Torah alone and rejects the "Oral Law" or Talmudic tradition</note>, who refuse to approve a great number of Jewish traditions that thus appear to be unfounded. *Rabbi David Ganz* <note>A 16th-century mathematician and historian</note> likewise had no other reason than this to set up a complete chronology that extends to our time, although in the second part he reaches further into the chronology of other nations: but besides the fact that the Jews are generally very ignorant of Christian history, they also err all the more when they translate Christian writers: for this reason, we cannot derive as much benefit from their books on this subject as we can elsewhere. The book called **JUHASIN** <note>Hebrew: *Sefer Yuḥasin* or "Book of Lineages" by Abraham Zacuto</note>, or the *Book of Genealogies*, is nothing other than a collection from various writers, since the Jews have little skill in making a good selection. Nor are they more fortunate when they concern themselves with describing the histories of the Christians and other nations, which they shorten without any judgment; this is clearly evident in a shortened history they have left us in Hebrew of the French Kings and Ottoman Emperors; although very few matters regarding the latter are noted. The title of that history is expressed in these words: **SEPHER DIBRE HAJAMIM LE MALCHE TSORPHAT U MALCHE BETH OTTOMAN HATTURG** <note>The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of France and the Kings of the Ottoman Turkish House, by Joseph ben Joshua ha-Kohen</note>, and seems at once to give a great idea of its execution: but in itself, this history amounts to little of substance. Nevertheless, since the Jews sometimes undertake many travels and are also knowledgeable in various languages, they could certainly compile a good history if they had the desire to devote their industry to it. One of the best Jewish writers we have, in our judgment, is *Rabbi Azarias* <note>Azariah dei Rossi (c. 1511–1578), a famous Italian-Jewish physician and scholar</note>, an Italian, who nevertheless did not write a specific history: but only cited some historical matters in a book that bears the title **MEORENAIM** <note>Hebrew: *Me'or Einayim*</note> or *Light of the Eyes*. He frequently quotes Christian writers,

<column-break/>

which shows that he has read them more than any other Jew.

<margin>Their ignorance in linguistic sciences</margin>
As for linguistics <note>or philology</note>, there is no doubt that the Jews are as little experienced in it as they are in history and all other sciences. They neglected it for a very long time and, around the ninth century, turned to it on the occasion of some Arabic linguists, following their example. They could soon have made a great stride through their cleverness in linguistics: but to tell the truth, one could easily do without a good portion of the Jewish linguists, especially those who have incorporated their books most recently.

<margin>However, the most experienced among them are indicated.</margin>
Their most famous linguists are: *Rabbi Judah, Rabbi Jonah, Rabbi Aben Ezra, Moses* and *David Kimchi* <note>A family of influential Hebrew grammarians and biblicists</note>; both of the first two wrote in Arabic, and their works were subsequently translated into Rabbinic Hebrew: but as we believe, never printed. The linguistic works written by *Aben Ezra* <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167)</note>, a Spanish Jew, are highly esteemed and are found incorporated into a collection of other linguists printed in Venice. Nevertheless, people have turned almost exclusively to the linguistics of *Rabbi David Kimchi*, since his work is more useful and described more accurately than those of all the other Jews. For this reason, his Hebrew dictionary is considered of higher value than all the others, as it is almost the only one used. However, if anyone is eager to understand the Hebrew language thoroughly, let him read the linguistic works of *Rabbi Elias Levita* <note>A 15th-century scholar who taught Hebrew to prominent Christians during the Reformation</note>, which are provided with a good number of useful and dignified observations, and are absolutely necessary to understand the sacred text.

<margin>Rabbinic Hebrew is not based on linguistic rules, but on common usage.</margin>
We shall not deal here with Rabbinic Hebrew, namely the language in which the Jews have written for several centuries, since it has no linguistic rules and varies according to the diversity of the writers. The foundation of Rabbinic Hebrew is indeed truthfully descended from Biblical Hebrew, which every writer has imitated as well as he possibly could: the Spanish Jews have mixed Spanish words into it; the French, French words, and all the others likewise. Nevertheless, it is enough to understand Biblical Hebrew thoroughly to proceed to the reading of the best Rabbis who have explained the letters of the Holy Scripture;

This dictionary is divided into two columns for the convenience of the user, of which the first indicates the Hebrew Biblical words with their meanings in Latin and Italian; and in the second stand the words described in Rabbinic Hebrew, to which words he has given the name of foreign *idioms*, to distinguish them from pure Hebrew. All this he has accompanied with an explanation, written first in Rabbinic Hebrew, and subsequently in Latin and Italian; therefore, by means of this dictionary, one can learn the Rabbinic language as easily as with the great Talmudic and Rabbinic Dictionary of **Buxtorf** <note>Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, a famous Christian Hebraist whose *Lexicon Chaldaicum, Talmudicum et Rabbinicum* was a standard scholarly tool</note>, although this latter expands further.

## CHAPTER XVI.

->Of the usefulness of the HEBREW LANGUAGE; and whether it is necessary for a THEOLOGIAN. Reasons for doubt on this subject.<-

<margin>
How some Church Fathers judged it necessary that one ought to have some knowledge of the Hebrew language.
</margin>
If we rely on the authority of **Jerome** and **Augustine**, it is impossible to have a perfect knowledge of the Sacred Books, which confirm the most important part of our Religion, especially if one is ignorant in the Greek and Hebrew languages, such that it is necessary that one has access to the original languages to resolve the difficulties that might arise. I speak, says **Augustine** to those who understand the Latin language and have need to understand the knowledge of Hebrew and Greek (a) so that they can satisfy themselves in their doubt in the Original language more than in the Latin Translation. *Men of the Latin tongue, whom we have now undertaken to instruct, have need of two other languages for the knowledge of the Scriptures, namely Hebrew and Greek, so that they may have recourse to the preceding copies if the infinite variety of Latin interpreters has brought about any doubt.* <note>original: "Latinae quidem linguae homines... varietas."</note> When there is a dispute to settle a civil matter, one does not behave solely according to the copies of the legal documents brought forward for defense: but one wants to inspect the original documents; and on the contrary, one acts differently in matters of Religion; the majority of Theologians often neglect the Original Text, and content themselves only with the Translations which are sometimes defective or obscure.

<column-break/>

<margin>
What a broad sentiment the Writer of the Latin Translation has, which is nonetheless insufficient.
</margin>
We confess that one can say in favor of our century, that it has become unnecessary to take recourse to the Original Text, (b) since the **Council of Trent** <note>The 16th-century ecumenical council of the Catholic Church that addressed the Reformation</note> declared the Latin Translation <note>The Vulgate</note> to be inherently Authoritative; and what is more, the great number of Translations that have been made into various languages from the Biblical text fulfill to some extent the lack of the Original Book. To which one may add, that many Learned and capable men in the knowledge of the Oriental Languages have explained everything which appears most difficult in the Style of Holy Scripture. This is, in my judgment, all that one can primarily bring forward as an excuse for some Theologians who neglect the study of the Hebrew Language, and who are on the one hand obligated, if this is not entirely unnecessary, at least on the other hand, to easily fulfill this deficiency through other means that are much shorter and less difficult.

But without it being necessary at this place to express the mind of the Fathers of the Council of Trent, when they declared the ancient Latin Translation authoritative; one can give no more authority to the common Translation than was formerly given in the first Centuries of the Church to the Greek of the seventy Translators <note>The Septuagint</note>, who were believed

<header>THIRD HISTORICAL DISSERTATION.</header>

...[the Septuagint was believed] to have been of a Prophetic inspiration, until the times of Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"; St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Vulgate</note>, who was the first to begin to doubt them. However, notwithstanding these doubts, they were forced, regarding the Explanation of the Holy Scripture, to take refuge in other Greek Translations that were made from the original Hebrew. If they had been able to consult the original themselves, they would undoubtedly have done so, since they held such great respect for the extraordinary labor of Origen <note>original: "Origenes"; an early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD)</note>, who arranged these ancient Greek Translations in several columns, alongside that of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint</note> which was placed in the middle of all the others. One cannot read the Interpretations of the Greek Church Fathers regarding the Old Testament without frequently finding the names of Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and some ancient Translators, and even of the Samaritans, who also translated the Books of Moses for their own use.

<margin>Difficulties found in the translations, and how they were addressed.</margin>
We now also have, one might say, the same resources to explain the difficulties that arise in the common Translation, and even much greater ones, since the Latins do not lack good Latin translations made from the Original. But it is nonetheless characteristic that one needs to understand the Hebrew Language so that one can judge which of all these translations should be chosen, as Augustine <note>original: "Augustinus"; St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD)</note> wisely noted in the words cited above. What is more, how many ambiguous words and difficult expressions are there that obscure the meaning unless one checks them in the Original. Also, the various Traditions cannot be of great service in clearing up all these difficulties; and although in the time of Augustine there was also a Latin Translation which was given the name of ancient and common <note>The "Vetus Latina" or Old Latin versions used before Jerome's Vulgate</note>, they nevertheless did not fail to approve a large number of other Translations, which were difficult to count. "An infinite variety of Latin Interpreters," <note>original: "Latinorum Interpretum, infinita varietas"</note> he says. But with the help of all this, he desires that one understands the Hebrew Language to be able to look into the Original. "That one should recur to the preceding copies," <note>original: "Ut ad exemplaria præcedentia recurratur"</note> as this Theologian says. It is very difficult to precisely understand the power of Hebrew words solely by means of Traditions, even if they are precise and faithful, although every language has its own particular char-

<column-break/>

acteristics, and these often cannot be transferred into another language. It would not be difficult to bring forward examples of this; but we would be led too far astray by it, and what is more, we trust that there is no one who is not convinced of this truth through experience.

<margin>Why practice in the Hebrew Language is necessary;</margin>
We only add to this that the practice of the Hebrew language sharpens the mind to accurately perceive and consider the style of Holy Scripture, as is easily noticed when one compares the explanations of Jerome and the Old Testament with those of other Church Fathers who lived in his time and after him. How many unnecessary questions are found in the Books of some Theologians who have not consulted the Original of the Text. Some of the most prominent among them exert themselves greatly to know whether man is born with a single original sin, or with many, because of the words one reads in the printing of the common Translation: "I was conceived in iniquities and in sins my mother conceived me" <note>original: "In iniquitatibus conceptus sum & in peccatis concepit me mater mea"; Psalm 51:5 (Vulgate 50:7). The plural "iniquities" led to theological debates that do not exist in the Hebrew singular.</note>; but the Hebrew Text, in which one reads, "In iniquity and in sin," <note>original: "In iniquitate & in peccato"</note> gives no reason at all for this question.

<margin>Of which examples are given.</margin>
This would be the place to bring forward some examples of successful discoveries that have been made in the Scripture, primarily in our century, obtained through knowledge of the Hebrew Language: but it would be unnecessary to expand further on this subject, which has been sufficiently explained. Cardinal Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a Catholic cardinal and philosopher who sought literal interpretations of the Bible</note> was so passionately taken with the necessity of understanding the Hebrew Language thoroughly and explaining the Books of the Old Testament that, having already reached an age that made this practice too difficult for him, he took refuge in those most practiced in this language, whether they were Jews or Christians, to make his Interpretations written on these Books more concise. Therefore, it is better to give oneself over to the practice of Hebrew more timely, at an age in which one is stronger in practicing one's memory than in using one's judgment.
