## XVII. CHAPTER.

### *Of the easy* METHOD OF TEACHING *to practice the* HEBREW LANGUAGE *in a short time.*

<margin>Means designated to learn the Hebrew Language in a short time and easily.</margin>
We dare to say that there is no language that one can learn more easily and in less time than Hebrew; not only because it comprises a very small number of words contained in the books of the Old Testament, but also because few rules of grammar are necessary to learn this language. Therefore, one would do well to choose the simplest and shortest of all literary books; and for example, the small abridgment by *Schickardus*, entitled *Schickard's Clock* <note>original: "Horologium Schickardi"; a popular 17th-century Hebrew textbook by Wilhelm Schickard</note>, and the compendium of Hebrew grammar by *Buxtorf* <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a celebrated Hebraist</note>. (b) We propose these abridgments to the beginning student because nothing necessary, which he needs to know, has been omitted. On the contrary, as the Jews have split hairs too much over grammar, one cannot expect these concise abridgments from them, unless that which is perfectly necessary is explained in all its extensiveness and purity, so as not to fall into obscurity; "I strive to be brief, and I become obscure." <note>original: "Brevis eſſe laboro, obſcurus fio"; a quote from Horace's Ars Poetica regarding the difficulty of being concise without becoming confusing.</note>

Firstly, regarding the manner of reading Hebrew, one must not concern oneself with the pronunciation of certain letters, since no fixed standard is held among the Jews, who pronounce the Hebrew

<column-break/>

language differently according to the variety of countries. If one wished to choose a certain pronunciation, however, we would prefer that of the Spaniards <note>The Sephardic pronunciation</note> above all other Jews, since it is simpler and comes closer to the pronunciation of the ancient Jews. But let it be enough to present this observation only in general here, to serve as our instruction, if one wishes to follow it, when one desires to obtain a perfect knowledge of the language. For in the beginning, one must simply accustom oneself to the pronunciation of the chosen grammarians.

Secondly, as the Jews make use of certain dots or points for vowel letters or vowels, and which they distinguish into long and short, one shall especially note what the long and what the short vowels consist of, since by this means one bypasses many rules of grammar as unnecessary, which make the language difficult and heavy. It suffices, for example, without meddling much with everything that the grammarians have said of the <term>DAGESH</term> <note>A dot placed in a Hebrew letter to modify its sound or indicate doubling</note>, <term>SHEVA</term> <note>A diacritic representing a very short vowel sound</note>, and some other grammatical hair-splitting, that one knows that in the Hebrew language one never expresses oneself with short syllables,

but only through long vowels; and that one then doubles the letter that follows the short syllable; for this reason, one finds a dot called a *Dagesh* <note>A diacritic mark in the Hebrew writing system used to indicate a "doubled" or stronger consonant sound</note> marked there: or if a *Sheva* <note>A Hebrew vowel sign representing a very short 'e' sound or a vocal silence</note> follows, one does not rest on the point of this *Sheva*. See here, for example, how one pronounces the word *Dibber* with a double 'B', since there is a short vowel under the 'D', which consequently pulls the other letter toward it, so as not to rest on a short vowel. It is the same with the *Sheva* after a short syllable; and for this reason, linguists say that one does not pronounce it then: but only after the long vowel. However, so as not to occupy ourselves with all this "letter-sifting" of linguistics, which does nothing but burden the memory and weigh down the intellect: it is nonetheless enough to know that the pronunciation always rests on a long vowel and never on a short one.

As for the Nouns, whether they are substantive or adjective, these are not difficult to understand in the Hebrew language: but with the Verbs it is quite different, as very many conjugations are in use. In the beginning, it is enough to learn those only in passing: so that, when one proceeds to the unfolding of any Book of the Bible, one can then look up the conjugations. By which means one then learns them in a short time and without any trouble; and what is more, one progresses significantly in this linguistic knowledge during that same time.

It is unbelievable how much one progresses in a language by the unfolding of some authors, as soon as one understands the slightest sketch of the linguistics, and almost as soon as one can merely read it. To what purpose does it serve, for example, that one reads an entire book of grammar, and subsequently learns exactly the genders, inflections, and other such matters? As is customary in the Latin Schools, where one spends several years without often knowing what is required for the interpretation of authors: would one not do better to instruct the youth in the general rules of grammar in a shortened form, and subsequently lead them to the unfolding of the authors? They could learn the rules and the use of these rules at the same time; which would make them more experienced than simply drumming the instruction of linguistic rules into them without having them practice their use. For eventually, after much time

<column-break/>

loss, one is obliged to come to it anyway, and one remembers nothing of all these linguistic rules except that which one makes applicable to oneself in the interpretation of the authors.

He who wishes to apply himself to the practice of the Hebrew language will do well to follow our proposed method, and should relieve himself as much as possible from reading the Hebrew books of their grammar, which for the most part are burdened with almost infinite linguistic rules. It is better that they read those when they have progressed somewhat further in the knowledge of this language. For then all these rules will appear more understandable to them: but in the beginning, one must always keep this fundamental rule before one's eyes: *Much practice, few rules* <note>original: "Usus multus, praeceptiones pauca"</note>. To more easily master this usage through reading, one could read all books indiscriminately; but it is best to begin with the Biblical History books, since those are easier to understand than the others, and there is even some choice to be made among these History books.

<margin>In which Hebrew Books one must then practice, to obtain a thorough knowledge of this language.</margin>
It is Moses who wrote the purest among the Hebrews, primarily in *Genesis*; and what can be of great service to the student in learning Hebrew is that in the first chapters of *Genesis*, he will find the same words and expressions frequently repeated, and by this means one remembers them without any effort. Although there are many words in these first chapters of *Genesis* that are repeated, nonetheless one finds enough distinct words expressed there. One will then see oneself greatly advanced in the Hebrew language in a short time, especially concerning the Biblical History books, since the style there is simple. But with the other books, it is not so, as they are of an abbreviated and figurative style: therefore, it will be good and fitting that one maintain some order in the reading.

We believe that one can do no better than to read the Psalms before *Ecclesiastes*, Proverbs, and the Song of Solomon. These last three books are written in a very compressed style, and one cannot understand them well unless something is added to them. And since the Psalms hold somewhat of a middle way between the History books and these mentioned, one will gradually become accustomed to the compressed style. After this, one can proceed to the Prophets, who nonetheless

### CHAPTER XVIII.

#### Of the LITURGY or *Mass* of the *CHRISTIANS* in all regions of the then-known *WORLD*.

<margin>
Reasoning concerning the Mass in the East, called the Liturgy.
</margin>

Although we have previously pointed out the origin of some ceremonies which are observed among Christians in relation to those of the Jews, and especially that which pertains to the prayers and service of the Church; nevertheless, we cannot fail to insert here a complete discourse on the *Mass*, which the Christians of the East call *Liturgy*, and which is the principal service of the Roman Church: so that one may become more thoroughly acquainted with the difference in ceremonies used in various Churches. </margin>

See here, for example, how one pronounces the word **DIBBER** <note>Hebrew for "speak"</note> with a double B, since there is a short vowel under the D, which consequently draws the other letter toward it, so as not to rest on a short vowel. It is the same with the **SHEVA** after a short syllable; and for this reason the linguists say that one does not pronounce it then: but only after the long vowel. However, so as not to delay ourselves with all this linguistic hair-splitting <note>original: "letterziftery", literally "letter-sifting"</note>, which does nothing but burden the memory and weigh down the mind: it is nevertheless enough to know that the pronunciation always rests on a long vowel and never on a short one.

As for the Nouns, whether they be substantive or adjective, these are not difficult to understand in the Hebrew language: but with the Verbs it is quite different, of which very many conjugations <note>original: "tydvoegingen"</note> are in use. In the very beginning it is enough to learn those only in passing: so that, when one proceeds to the interpreting of any Book of the Bible, one can then look up the conjugations. By which means one then learns them in a short time and without any trouble; and what is more, one makes remarkable progress in this linguistic knowledge during that same time.

It is unbelievable how much one progresses in a language by the interpreting of some writers, as soon as one understands the slightest sketch of the grammar, and almost when one can merely read it. What purpose does it serve, for example, to read an entire book of grammar, and subsequently learn accurately the genders, declensions, and other such matters? as is customary in the Latin Schools, where one spends several years without often knowing what is required for the interpreting of the writers: would one not do better to instruct the youth in the general rules of grammar in brief, and subsequently lead them to the interpreting of the writers? They could learn the rules and the use of these rules at the same time; which would make them more experienced than merely drilling the instruction in language rules into them without having them practice their use. For finally, after much time

loss, one is obliged to come to it, and one retains nothing of all these language rules except that which one applies to oneself in explaining the writers.

Those who then wish to apply themselves to the practice of the Hebrew language, will do well to follow our proposed manner, and to unburden themselves as much as possible from reading the Hebrew books of their grammar, which for the most part are burdened with almost infinite language rules. It is better that they read those when they have progressed a bit more in the knowledge of this language. For then all these rules will appear more understandable to them: but in the beginning one must always keep this fundamental rule before one's eyes: *Much practice, few rules* <note>original Latin: "Usus multus, praeceptiones paucae"</note>. To more easily master this usage through reading, one may read all books indiscriminately; but it is best to begin with the Biblical History books, since those are easier to understand than the others; and there is even still some choice to be made among these History books.

<margin>In which Hebrew books one must then practice, to acquire a thorough knowledge of that language.</margin>
It is Moses who wrote most purely among the Hebrews, primarily in *Genesis*; and what can be of great service to the student in learning Hebrew, is that in the first chapters of *Genesis* he finds the same words and expressions frequently repeated, and by this means one remembers them without any effort. Although there are many words in these first chapters of *Genesis* that are repeated, nonetheless one finds enough distinct words expressed there. One will then subsequently see oneself greatly progressed in the Hebrew language in a short time, especially concerning the Biblical History books, since the style there is simple. But with the other books it is not so, being of a fragmented and figurative style: therefore it will be good and proper that one also maintain some order in the reading.

We believe that one can do no better than to read the Psalms before *Ecclesiastes*, the Proverbs, and the *Song of Solomon*. These last three books are written in a very compressed style, and one cannot understand them well unless one adds something to them. And since the Psalms hold somewhat of a middle ground between the History books and these aforementioned ones, one will gradually accustom oneself to the compressed style. After this one can proceed to the Prophets, who yet...

...then this bread, and it was distributed only to those who attended the ceremony, where the Priest or Elder was the Presider, just as among the Jews the Father of the household or the most capable of the company blessed the bread and then the wine in the chalice, after he had partaken of both, and distributed the rest to those who were with him at the table.

There is no doubt that our Savior, in keeping the Passover with his Disciples as described by the Evangelists, made use of the customs of the Jews when he Blessed or Sanctified the Bread and the Wine, which were observed at that time in the celebration of the Passover feast. He made use of Prayers, Blessings, and Thanksgivings just as they did in the Ritual use of the Paschal lamb, which they called the Sanctification or Dedication of the Passover feast. Therefore, the Savior commanded them always to observe this Ceremony in his memory, just as the Jews celebrated the Passover feast in memory of their exodus from Egypt. And what makes these two Ceremonies even more similar is that the Passover feast of the Jews is the representation of what occurred in the exodus from Egypt, when they were entirely delivered from their slavery. Likewise, the Service of the Liturgy among the Christians included the principal Ministrations of their Religion, especially of the Death and Resurrection of our Savior, who has delivered them from the slavery of sin. This is what one can observe in all the works of the Greek Writers who have written about the Liturgy.

Besides the prayers, praises, blessings, and thanksgivings, in which the Liturgy properly consists, one reads the Gospel and the Epistle, which formerly was accompanied by something from the Prophets and Psalms, of which some marks still remain in the Mass; because it has been shortened for some time, they have not kept anything but certain verses of the Psalms which they

<column-break/>

formerly sang or recited in their entirety. What is currently called an **Antiphon** <note>original: "Antienna"</note> originates from the ancient custom of singing the entire Psalm, whereas now this Antiphon consists of but one verse. The word Antiphon has its origin in the Greek *Antiphona*, since they sang these Psalms alternately in the Assembly. For this reason, also, one finds certain verses of the Prophets and of other Biblical Books in the Mass, since the Abridgers of the Mass have kept only a part of a long discourse. This is clearly evident in the **Antiphon** * which is called the Offertory of the Mass, and according to custom consists of only a verse or two from some Psalm: whereas in the beginning the entire Psalm was sung while the People made their offerings.

One must nevertheless note that the reading of the Books of the New Testament, of the Gospel, the Apostolic Letters, and even the singing of the Psalms, are no singular things attached solely to the Service of the Mass: but every time the first Christians assembled, they never neglected to perform this reading, as is evident from the Letters of Paul and from the Works of the Church Fathers. One cannot doubt, as has been said elsewhere, that this custom came forth from the Synagogues of the Jews, where the reading of the Law and of some Scriptural passages of the Prophets was performed with care. It is also apparent that the custom of reading the Epistle and Gospel at the lectern likewise has its origin in what occurred in these Synagogues, where the Reader performed his reading on a slightly elevated place made in the manner of a Lectern. Finally, through a little attention to the ancient manner of practicing the Liturgy, as it is found in the writings of Justin Martyr and other early Church Fathers, one will discover that the principal part of the customs comes from those observed in the Synagogues of the Jews, and which the Apostles maintained in the first Christian Assemblies. # On the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

...has introduced some changes to it, and such varies according to the diversity of places; which nevertheless does not prevent all the various *Liturgies* <note>The set forms of public worship, particularly the Eucharist</note> that are spread throughout the whole world from agreeing in essence and in that which constitutes the principal foundation of the *Liturgy*. Let us now proceed to the investigation of this distinction of the Masses or *Liturgies*.

<margin>
How the Liturgies can be divided into Eastern and Western.
</margin>

One can generally divide the *Liturgies* into Eastern and Western. Under the name of Eastern *Liturgies* one can include the *Liturgies* of the Greeks and Melchites <note>See the footnote below for a definition of this group</note>, being the origin of all others of the East; those of the Chaldeans or Syrians, which are the Nestorians, Jacobites, and Maronites; those of the Copts or Egyptian Christians, and those of the Ethiopians; those of the Armenians, written in Old Armenian; those of the Iberians or Georgians and Mingrelians written in their national tongue; those of the Albanians, Slavonians, and Muscovites <note>Russians</note>, to which one can add the Circassians and other Tartar Christians. From this, the great extent of the Christian peoples can be sufficiently judged, who currently still follow the Eastern Church customs in the essence of their *Liturgies*.

<margin>
and in what this distinction consists.
</margin>

These different Church customs among the Christians of the East and West regarding the *Liturgy* consist primarily in a certain Prayer, which the Easterners call the "Invocation of the Holy Spirit," and in which, as they believe, the Sanctification of the Bread and the Wine partly consists, and not in these words alone: *This is my Body* <note>original: "Dit is myn Lichaam"</note> etc. This prayer or this invocation is found with nearly the same wording in the *Liturgies* of all the peoples already mentioned; whereas hardly one of the Latin Masses, in use by the Western Church, contains anything of it. Under the name of Latin Masses, we also include the Churches that have incorporated their Church customs with those of Rome. A portion of the Slavonians, for example, who live along the borders of Dalmatia, have translated the Roman Church service into Slavonic, and compared their *Liturgy* with it. Furthermore, the Greeks who belong under the Latin Bishops have also introduced some changes in the ancient *Liturgies*. Likewise, one can say of the *Litur-*

<column-break/>

-gies of the Maronites, and of a portion of the Nestorians and Armenians, that they have also changed their *Liturgies* to come closer to the Mass of the Latins: but it is very difficult to discover these changes by comparing them with the other *Liturgies* of the same peoples, and to distinguish everything that belongs to the custom of the Western Church.

<margin>
In which language the first Writer and composer would have written the Liturgy, and how they were practiced in the early Church.
</margin>

As for the first Writer and inventor of the *Liturgy* and the language in which it was first written, much has been said on this subject, though not accompanied by any appearance of truth. It is provable that everything we have of the *Liturgy* owes its origin to the Greeks; for they are Greek expressions and they seem also to have been translated from the Greek. Therefore, one must not imagine that the Apostles used the *Liturgy* as it is now provided with wording and phrases, since those were out of use in the first centuries of the Church. But from the observation we make here, that all the *Liturgies* seem translated from the Greek, one can draw this conclusion: that the Greek Churches were the first to have composed the *Liturgies*, after which those of the other Christian peoples were subsequently arranged. It is even very probable that the Apostles, in the first Assemblies, allowed the *Liturgy* to take place in Greek, since the Greek Language was then more widespread in the Empire, and many understood it in Rome; besides that in the first Churches founded by the Apostles, the majority spoke Greek; and this is the reason why they never wrote to the Believers, even those who were in Rome, except in this language.

One can also add to this, that in the first Christian Assemblies the reading of the New Testament took place in Greek, before each nation had translated it into its own language, and we also believe that the Psalms were sung or recited in the same Language, especially in this time when the Greek translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament</note> was read in most Synagogues.

# THIRD HISTORICAL DISCOURSE

...neighboring places probably read the Bible in Hebrew in their Synagogues: but this primarily proves nothing other than that some of the first Christians conducted the Liturgy <note>The prescribed form of public worship</note> in the Chaldean or Syriac <note>A dialect of Aramaic used by various Eastern Christian churches</note> language, and that the reading of the Prophets and recitation of the Psalms in their assemblies was done in Hebrew. This is, however, the opposite case if one compares it with all the other places where the Greek language was in use. What is more, the Liturgies had not yet been written in either Syriac or Hebrew at that time, as some writers have imagined. Nothing is more groundless than the fancy of these writers that Peter and some other Apostles performed the Mass <note>The central rite of the Eucharist</note> in Hebrew: for the Hebrew language had not been in use among the Jews for a long time. It is Paul who tells us that in the first Christian assemblies, the Liturgy and other prayers were performed in a language understood by those who attended the assembly; (a) and this same point is confirmed by Cardinal Bona <note>Giovanni Bona, a 17th-century Italian cardinal and historian of the liturgy</note>, who assures us that the Apostles performed the prayers of the Liturgy in the language of the country where they resided.

Yet one must not conclude with this Cardinal, however, that the Apostles were truly the first founders of all the Liturgies that have spread into all languages and Churches: for it is certain that the Liturgies in the Chaldean and Syriac languages—for example, those of the Nestorians, Jacobites, and Maronites <note>Three distinct Eastern Christian traditions with ancient roots</note>—are not the same Liturgies that the Apostles could have practiced in those languages in the lands neighboring Jerusalem; for the Syriac of these Liturgies differs from the Syriac that the Apostles spoke in their time and in their country. Furthermore, as has already been shown, these Syriac Liturgies are translated from the Greek. This fact must also be observed in other Liturgies.

<margin>The use of the Liturgy was first introduced several centuries after the times of the Apostles.</margin>
Under the pretext that the Apostles practiced the Liturgy in the language of the Churches they founded, it does not follow that they were truly the founders of them, even though those Liturgies now bear their names in the Eastern Churches. It is enough to consider these Liturgies to be convinced that they could not have been brought into use until several centuries after the Apostles. The Greeks have had three—

<column-break/>

—three which bore the names of James, Basil, and John Chrysostom: but in common use, they employ only the latter two. If one earnestly investigates the reason why they attributed these names to these three Liturgies, one will find no other than that which they draw from an uncertain tradition, and one cannot give it credit, since learned Greeks do not agree among themselves on this. It is known that this opinion rests on the authority of Proclus <note>Proclus of Constantinople, an 5th-century archbishop</note>, who assures us that James was the first founder of the Greek Liturgy, and that this Liturgy having increased much over time, (a) *Chrysostom* and *Basil* found it necessary to shorten it, from which their Liturgies have taken their names. But we do not now possess the book of Proclus where this is reported; rather, this is drawn only from some remnant, of which one is not certain that it truly belongs to him. The writer (b) who had some works of Proclus, Archbishop of Constantinople, printed in Rome in Greek and Latin, speaking of this remaining fragment, contents himself by saying that the scribe who transcribed the Greek Liturgy only made an extract from a letter or the treatise of Proclus and placed it at the head of these Liturgies to give them more authority, and that he reports the words of Proclus in his own manner, and not from the text itself.

It seems nonetheless that one must regard this piece by Proclus as being his, or at least that what is reported does not rest solely on the testimony of a scribe who wanted to give some authority to the Liturgies he brought to light. For the Greek Bishops gathered in the sixth Council, which was called *in Trullo* <note>The Quinisext Council of 692, named for the domed hall (*trullus*) of the imperial palace in Constantinople</note>, (c) attribute to James the Liturgy which we possess under his name; and most Greek writers who have lived since then do the same, not only regarding this Liturgy, but also regarding the two others which they truly believe to be by Chrysostom and Basil. To which we answer, that the Fathers of this Council followed the common opinion on this matter, which rested on nothing but a popular tradition, without any foundation.

(a) *Book 1, Liturgy, Chapter 5.* (b) *Proclus, book on the Tradition of the Divine Liturgy.*
(c) *Vincent Ricard.* (d) *Canon 32.*

### On the RELIGIOUS DUTIES of the JEWS.

This is true to the extent that *Theodore Balsamon* <note>A prominent 12th-century Eastern Orthodox canonist and Bishop</note>, who was asked via letters whether the Liturgies read (a) in the churches of Jerusalem and Alexandria under the names of James and Mark were truly theirs, gave this answer: *That neither the Holy Scripture nor any Council had attributed to Mark the LITURGY that bore his name; that there was nothing but the thirty-second decree of the General Council IN TRULLO <note>A church council held in 692 AD, named after the domed hall where it convened</note>, which attributed to James the LITURGY believed to be possessed under his name: but that the eighty-fifth Decree of the Apostles, and the fifty-ninth of the Laodicean Synod <note>A regional church council held around 363-364 AD</note>, in the list they made of the Books of Holy Scripture written by the Apostles and which were to be used in the Church, made not a single mention of the LITURGIES of James and Mark.* One could bring forward many other similar proofs to show that neither James nor any of the other Apostles were the writers or founders of the Liturgies that currently bear their names. Would *Eusebius* and *Jerome*, who wrote such accurate registers of the ancient Church writers, have skipped over these Liturgies attributed to the Apostles if any had been in use in their time?

<margin>How Leo Allatius and Cardinal Bona were mistaken in their opinion on the founders of the Liturgies</margin>
We are surprised that *Leo Allatius* <note>A 17th-century Greek scholar and librarian at the Vatican</note> and Cardinal *Bona* believed that the liturgy bearing the name of James—which is the origin of all other Liturgies—was truly his, and that it was merely expanded over time: but the proofs they provide are by no means sufficient. This is why there is more reason to say that neither James, nor Mark, nor Peter, nor any other Apostle, are the founders of the Liturgies issued under their names; these names were used to give authority to the Liturgies that were introduced now and then in various Churches, and which have no other founders than the custom which has always existed in every Church since the time of the Apostles, to pray to God and give thanks as described previously.

<margin>Uncertainty regarding the Liturgy attributed to Chrysostom and Basil.</margin>
As for the Liturgies attributed to *Chrysostom* and *Basil* <note>Two influential 4th-century Church Fathers</note>, one cannot be sufficiently certain that they were the founders of them, since the Church of Constantinople and other Greek Churches already had their Liturgies long before. It may be that these two Ancient Fathers brought some improvement to the ancient Liturgies: but one has

<column-break/>

no certain and clear proof of it. Finally, one also finds in the constitutions bearing the name of *Clement* <note>Clement of Rome, an early Pope</note> a kind of ancient *Liturgy*, but it does not appear to be by him, nor to have originated from these constitutions.

<margin>Various Liturgies brought to light from time to time.</margin>
Now that we have dealt with the Greek Liturgies and their origin, it is almost unnecessary to mention those of the other Eastern Churches, which have done nothing else but translate these Greek Liturgies into their own language and put them into use under various names to give them greater authority. One finds a much larger number of Liturgies written in Chaldean or Syriac <note>Chaldean and Syriac refer to dialects of Aramaic used by Eastern Christians</note> than there are in Greek. The Jacobites <note>Members of the Syriac Orthodox Church</note> alone have more than forty different ones under various names. The Maronites <note>An Eastern Catholic Church in Lebanon</note>, who had their Missal <note>A book containing the texts for the Mass</note> printed in Rome in the year 1592, use no more than twelve Liturgies, although they have a much larger number in common with the Jacobites. Because of this, it is possible that in the printing of this Missal no attention was paid to any corrections; for one finds the *Liturgy* of a certain *Barfufan* <note>A 13th-century Jacobite writer</note>, a notorious Jacobite, inserted there. The Chaldeans, who have a *Liturgy* of James written in their language and translated from the Greek, are of the opinion that this Liturgy is the origin of all others, and that it was truly written by James whose name it bears: but it is unbelievable, as they can provide no arguments for it. They base their claim solely on a folk tradition, without investigating whether it was handed to them as true or false. The Missal of the Nestorians <note>Followers of the Church of the East</note>, of which we have held a copy in our hands, does not contain such a large number. Those who take the trouble to see more in this Missal, which is used by the Nestorians near Babylon, have assigned the name of *Nestorius* to it, and it is much longer than the others. If it is true that *Nestorius* composed a specific Liturgy, it would undoubtedly have been written in Greek. Likewise is the opinion of *Ebed Jesu* <note>Abdisho bar Berika, a 14th-century Syriac scholar</note> in his Register of Eastern Books, where he notes that the Liturgy of *Nestorius* was translated from Greek into Chaldean or Syriac by *Thomas* and *Maraba*. The same Nestorians have two other Liturgies in their Missal, one of which is attributed to the twelve Apostles, and is distinct from the one under the same name in the Missal of the Ma-

Therefore, one must be careful when reading the *Liturgies* <note>The prescribed forms for public worship and the celebration of the Eucharist</note> they have had printed, and especially have recourse to good manuscripts, upon which one can truly build.

Besides these *Liturgies*, they have others under the names of John the Evangelist, James, John Chrysostom, Cyril, Gregory, the blessed Apostles, and some whose authors are not indicated. Thus it is that the Ethiopians flatter themselves to possess very ancient *Liturgies*, as if they were in truth composed by those whose names they bear: but one should note here that the Ethiopian Church has for a long time depended on that of the Copts <note>The native Egyptian Christians</note> who are in Egypt, from whom they received the primary part of these Service-Books.

<margin>Coptic Liturgies: how they have existed.</margin>
These Copts likewise have specific *Liturgies* in the Coptic language, which they no longer use in their worship, since few among them understand this language, given that they currently speak Arabic. This language, according to the opinion of the Jesuit Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a celebrated German Jesuit scholar and polymath</note>, was a mother tongue and independent of all other languages, but is now greatly corrupted by Greek, from which it kept its letters and adopted many words that are entirely Greek. In the *Library of the Ancients*, one finds three of their *Liturgies* attributed to Basil, Gregory, and Cyril, translated into Latin from an Arabic version by a Maronite <note>A member of an Eastern Catholic Church centered in Lebanon</note> from Mount Lebanon. But whether the translator did not have a good copy of these *Liturgies*, or whether he did not well understand the Arabic from which he translated; it has become clear that he made errors in his Latin translation. Furthermore, it should be noted that since the Coptic language is known to very few people anymore, the Copts usually add an Arabic translation to these *Liturgies* written in Coptic in order to understand them, even though the *Liturgy* is performed in the Coptic language.

Victorius Scialac, a Maronite and the author of the Latin translation of this Coptic *Liturgy*, notes that the last Coptic *Liturgies*, since the union of the Coptic Church with the Roman Church under Clement VIII,

<margin>Armenian Liturgies noted.</margin>
We believe that one may also place among the *Liturgies* of the Eastern Church those used by the Armenians, since they have incorporated into their Mass the prayer which is called the invocation of the Holy Spirit <note>Also known as the Epiclesis, the part of the liturgy where the priest asks God to send the Holy Spirit to sanctify the bread and wine</note>. In Rome (a), this Mass has been printed in the Armenian language with the Latin translation: but the Roman supervisors <note>The censors or ecclesiastical authorities</note> have changed some passages in it, without it being necessary. Nevertheless, the extract of the Armenian Mass at the end of the first volume of *The Perpetuity of the Faith* <note>Original title: *Eeuwigduurentheit des Geloofs*, likely referring to the work by Arnauld and Nicole regarding the Eucharist</note> does not agree with this change, although the Armenian Patriarch who sent this extract was in communion with the Latins, and was himself staying in Rome at that time. Bishop *Uscan*, who also gave an extract of the Armenian *Liturgy* to the author of the book *The Perpetuity*, seems to have had more respect for the corrections of the supervisors of Rome; for after he had published his extract in agreement with this change, he contents himself with saying that there are others who read entirely differently in their *Liturgies*, as if this diversity came from different copies, and was not caused by the judges of Rome. Besides the Armenian *Liturgies* written in the Armenian language, we remember formerly having had in our hands a written book which contained many Syriac *Liturgies* for the use of the Jacobites <note>A West Syrian Christian sect</note>, among which was also one written in the Syriac language for the use of the Armenians. After having examined it in detail, it seemed to be nothing other than a shortening of the Greek *Liturgy* attributed to James: which corresponded unusually well with what some ancient historians report of certain Armenians, who formerly knew how to use the Syriac language as well as the Armenian.

The Armenians, as can be seen in the history by Galanus <note>Clemente Galano, a 17th-century missionary and historian of the Armenian Church</note>, attribute the authorship of their *Liturgy* and the institution of their other prayers to one of their Patriarchs named John, who some time after the...

## CHAPTER XIX.

### Concerning the different Masses used in the WESTERN CHURCH.

<margin>How various Masses were introduced into the Western Churches.</margin>
Most authors who have written about the Latin Mass believe that Peter was its institutor, and that it only underwent some changes over time. However, the great variety of Masses that have arisen from time to time in all the Churches of the West—and even in Italy itself—is clear proof that Peter left no set form for any specific Mass, neither in the Church of Rome nor in that of Antioch, of which city he is said to have been Bishop as well as of Rome. Would it be possible that neither Eusebius nor Jerome, who make mention of the Apostle's letters, would have made no mention of this Mass of Peter if he had left one behind? Thus, the opinion of those who make him the institutor of the Latin Mass is based more on uncertain tradition than on sound reason.

The Popes (a) complained for some time about the excessive variety of services appearing in most Churches that owed their faith to the Church of Rome. Italy (says Pope Innocent I in one of his letters), Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the surrounding islands must align themselves with the Roman Church to maintain their worship, since Rome is the Mother Church of all other Churches. All these peoples, he adds, must harmoniously maintain what Peter instituted in the Church of Rome and what has always been

<column-break/>

languages that only the learned understand: namely, Greek, Latin, and Chaldean <note>original: "Chaldeeuwfche," referring here to Aramaic or Syriac</note> or Syriac. But he failed to notice that the Egyptian Copts practice the Liturgy in Old Coptic, which is understood by almost no one; and that the Ethiopians celebrate in Old Ethiopic <note>Ge'ez</note>, which differs greatly from the common tongue. What is more, the Armenian language in which the Armenian Liturgies are written is not entirely the same as the language Armenians speak today. Let us now proceed to the Liturgies or Masses of the Western Church.

But it does not appear that Gregory the Great <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604), known for his administrative and liturgical reforms</note>, who was nonetheless one of the most zealous defenders of the Roman See, concerned himself much with introducing uniformity of service in the Churches that had received their faith from Rome. He wrote (b) to Augustine <note>Augustine of Canterbury, the first Archbishop of Canterbury</note>, who was then in England to establish the Christian faith, that he left him the freedom to follow the customs of Rome, or those of the Gauls, or of other Churches, since indeed the diversity of services and ceremonies could bring no harm to the foundation of religion.

This uniformity that we now observe in the Latin Mass and other church services has not always existed. Charlemagne <note>original: "Karel de Groote"</note>, to favor the Popes, exerted all his efforts to restore the various church services that differed in some Churches from those of Rome. His successors likewise neglected nothing to introduce the Roman service into all places of their domain. But despite all these efforts, and although the Popes were not negligent on their part, it is nonetheless incredible how much resistance the Churches showed when one attempted to make them subject to the customs of Rome. Every nation brought its reasons for not complying, as if one were attempting to kick away the religion of their ancestors.

We shall content ourselves only with showing that the Roman Mass formerly extended little further than Rome, and that even within Rome some change occurred, seeing that the present Mass—which is believed to be according to the ancient Roman Church usage—is by no means the ancient Roman Mass in its entirety, but only one that has been shortened.

<margin>
How the Church of Milan differed from that of Rome in the Church service.
</margin>
To begin with Italy: the Church of Milan had a Mass and a Church service entirely different from that of Rome, a part of which has remained in existence until now. This is commonly called the Church service according to the usage of *Ambrosius* <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), the Bishop of Milan</note>, to distinguish it from that of the Roman Church service. Some writers who have written about this Ambrosian Mass also note wherein the difference with Rome consisted. *Walafridus Strabo* <note>A 9th-century Benedictine monk and theological writer</note> was of the opinion that *Ambrosius* was the institutor of it, and that he arranged it in a particular way, both for his Milanese Church and for all the others of his Diocese. But it is probable that even before *Ambrosius*, the Church of Milan had a different Church service from that of Rome, no less than the other Italian Churches, which were more easily persuaded to adopt the Roman Church service than this one of Milan, which held its ground under the name of *Ambrosius*.

<margin>
And what a difference was found within Rome regarding the use of Masses.
</margin>
In Rome itself one found a great variety of Church services, as *Peter Abelard* <note>A medieval French scholastic philosopher and theologian (1079–1142)</note> has noted. Only, says this writer, (a) <note>original: "Abæl. in Epist. Apol. Adv. Bern." referring to Abelard's Apologetic Epistle against Bernard of Clairvaux</note> was it the Church of the Lateran that preserved the ancient Church service of Rome in its entirety; all the other churches differed from one another. *Radulf of Tongeren* <note>Radulphus van Rivo (c. 1345–1403), a liturgical scholar</note> has also remarked, speaking of the Roman Church service, (b) <note>original: "Radulfus van Tongeren"</note> that there were two kinds in Rome, a long and a short; and that the latter, which was shortened, was practiced in the Papal Chapel, while the other remained specifically for the Roman Service. He subsequently adds that the officials of the Pope changed and shortened this Church service as they saw fit, and as best agreed with the convenience of the Pope and Cardinals, and that the Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note> adopted this shortened service in order to agree therein with the Court of Rome.

<column-break/>

They intended, so it seemed, to fulfill by this the rule that their Patriarch <note>St. Francis of Assisi</note> had left them, to follow the Roman Order. Finally, the same writer notes that Pope *Nicholas III* <note>Pope from 1277 to 1280</note> entirely abolished this ancient Roman Church service, in which the true Service of Rome consisted, in order to give authority to that of the Friars Minor; for this reason, new Missals <note>Books containing the texts for the Mass</note> and other Church service books were instituted in place of the ancient ones, which are presently called the Roman Service; whereas it appears that one should rather call it the Service of the Franciscans.

<margin>
What kind of usage the Gauls had adopted.
</margin>
The Gauls <note>Referring to the inhabitants of ancient France</note> also had their particular Church service, of which some letters of *Jerome* and of various Popes make mention; and it was primarily in that place that *Charlemagne* and his successors put all their power to work to introduce the Roman Service there. Pope *Adrian* sent to the aforementioned *Charlemagne* the book which is commonly called the *Sacramentary* <note>original: "Sacramentarium," a book of liturgical prayers and directions</note> of *Gregory*, for which the Emperor had requested, in order to introduce the Mass and other Church services according to the Roman usage. *Pepin* <note>Pepin the Short, father of Charlemagne</note> had also previously labored powerfully toward the same undertaking. The Abbot *Hilduin* (c) <note>original: "Abbas Hilduinus," an advisor to Louis the Pious</note> gives to *Dionysius*, whom he calls the Areopagite, an account of the origin of the Mass that was in use in France before it was incorporated into the Roman Church service: but without it being necessary to trace this origin, it is beyond dispute that in this part of Gaul, which is now called France, there was formerly a kind of particular Mass differing from that of Rome; and the same Abbot *Hilduin*, writing to the Emperor *Louis*, makes mention of certain very old Missals for the use of the Gallican Church, which were used before the Roman Church custom was introduced into this Church.

The Mass which *Matthias Flacius Illyricus* <note>A Lutheran reformer (1520–1575)</note> had printed in the year 1557 at Strasbourg has been considered by many writers to be the Mass of the Gallican Church; but Cardinal *Bona* <note>Giovanni Bona (1609–1674), a Cistercian cardinal and scholar of liturgy</note> has intended to show the contrary through many reasons, and to show that this Mass had completely deviated from what the ancient writers attributed to the Mass that was peculiar to the French Churches. He believed, moreover, that the Mass which was formerly called the Gallican originated from the Mass which

<margin>Which Masses were practiced in Spain.</margin>
One cannot doubt that there would have been a particular Mass in Spain, and in all the places that were formerly under the rule of the Goths; seeing that this Mass is still in existence now. Although Gregory VII introduced the Roman Mass in almost all of Spain, he could nonetheless not prevent some Churches in Spain from retaining the ancient one, and among others those of Toledo and Salamanca, where it is still in use today. The Spaniards showed a great zeal for the maintenance of their ancient Church customs, and likewise a powerful steadfastness in rejecting the Roman Church service. The Aragonese were the first who accepted the same under Pope Alexander II, who sent a Cardinal as Legate to Spain for that purpose. (a) *Sancho* <note>original: "Sanctus"</note>, King of Aragon, when he had become King of Navarre through the intervention of Pope Gregory VII, brought about so much that it was also accepted in Navarre, just as the Mass and other Church services according to the Roman usage had already been introduced in Aragon: which also sufficiently appears from the Letters written by Gregory VII to King Sancho and other Spanish Kings.

Alfonso <note>Alfonso VI of Castile (1040–1109)</note>, King of Castile, was not easily moved by the powerful solicitations of this Pope. The Castilian People also refused to accept the Roman Mass: and the King himself would never have consented to it, if the Queen—who was of French descent, where the Roman Church custom had already taken hold—had not persuaded him through powerful solicitations. The Spaniards lack neither Histories nor Miracles to assert the value of their ancient Gothic Mass: but as these Histories smell of Fables to us, we judge it unnecessary to recount them here.

It only remains to be noted that this Spanish Mass is the same as that found in the printed edition of the *Library of the Church Fathers* under the name *Missa Mosarabum* <note>The Mozarabic Mass</note>; it is so named because the Arabs formerly ruled over Spain. The Region which we now call England already had its Services and various Church customs long before Gregory sent Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Canterbury, sent in 597 AD</note> there to convert these Peoples. For Augustine was not the first who preached the Gospel to the English, as such was already known when this Land was known under the name of Britain. Augustine introduced Christianity there only in a certain region, a large part of this Island having already embraced the same long before. *Let them do this in your churches,* <note>original: "Hoc in Ecclesiis tuis faciant..."</note> says Jerome in one of his Letters, *as is done in Rome, or as in the East, in Italy, in Cyprus, in Africa, in Illyricum, in Spain, and in Britain.* All the Churches in general acknowledged the Roman Church as their Mother, yet they did not agree with her in the Mass or other Church services. The Bishops of the most prominent Churches took the liberty of increasing or decreasing the Church service according to their own discretion, and sometimes without the authority of any Council. No heed was paid to the decrees of Charlemagne and his successors, who had established the uniformity of the Church service in their States, because everything was gradually changed again. The Clergy, especially, who usually imagine themselves to be more than the common mass of men, also wished to distinguish themselves through a particular Service: which went so far that finally Pope Sixtus V was forced to call a Congregation in Rome called *De' riti* <note>The Congregation of Rites, established in 1588</note>, to have these new Church services investigated, which were increasing daily, in order to prevent their growth in the future. Since then, one has been obliged henceforth to request approval from this Congregation of *Rites* to give authority to their new Church services.

We shall content ourselves only with showing that the Roman Mass formerly extended little further than Rome, and that even within Rome some change has occurred, since the present Mass, which is believed to be according to the ancient Roman Church usage, is by no means the ancient Roman Mass in its entirety, but only one that has been shortened.

<margin>How the Church of Milan differed from that of Rome in its liturgy.</margin>
To begin with Italy: the Church of Milan had a Mass and a liturgy <note>The Dutch "Kerkdienst" refers here to the "Divine Office" or the general order of worship</note> entirely different from those of Rome, a part of which has remained in existence until now. It is commonly called the liturgy according to the usage of **Ambrose** <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), the Bishop of Milan</note>, to distinguish it from that of the Roman liturgy. Some writers who have written about this **Ambrosian** Mass also note wherein the difference with Rome consisted. **Walafrid Strabo** <note>A 9th-century monk and liturgical scholar</note> believed that **Ambrose** was the institutor of it, and that he arranged it in a particular way, both for his Church of Milan and for all the others of his Diocese. But it is probable that even before **Ambrose**, the Church of Milan had a liturgy differing from that of Rome, and no less so than the other Italian Churches, which were more easily persuaded to adopt the Roman liturgy than those of Milan, which held their ground under the name of **Ambrose**.

<margin>And what a difference was found within Rome regarding the use of the Masses.</margin>
In Rome itself, one found a great variety of liturgies, as **Peter Abelard** <note>A famous 12th-century philosopher and theologian</note> has recorded. According to this writer, (a) <note>original: "Abæl. in Epist. Apol. Adv. Bern." — Abelard in the Apologetic Letter against Bernard</note> only the Church of the Lateran preserved the ancient liturgy of Rome in its entirety; all the other churches differed from one another. **Radulf of Tongeren** <note>Radulphus Tangrensis (c. 1360–1403), a liturgical reformer</note> also noted, speaking of the Roman liturgy, (b) <note>original: "Radulfus van Tongeren"</note> that there were two kinds in Rome, a long one and a short one; and that the latter, which was shortened, was practiced in the Papal Chapel, while the other properly remained for the Roman Service. He subsequently adds that the officials of the Pope changed and shortened this liturgy as they saw fit, and as best suited the convenience of the Pope and Cardinals, and that the **Friars Minor** <note>The Franciscans, a mendicant religious order founded by St. Francis of Assisi</note> adopted this shortened service to conform therein with the Court of Rome.

<column-break/>

They seemed, by this, to intend to fulfill the rule left to them by their Patriarch <note>Meaning St. Francis, the founder of their "house" or order</note> to follow the Roman Order. Finally, the same writer notes that **Pope Nicholas III** <note>Reigned 1277–1280</note> entirely abolished this ancient Roman liturgy, in which the true service of Rome consisted, in order to give authority to that of the **Friars Minor**; for this reason, new Missals and other liturgical books were introduced in place of the ancient ones, which are presently called the Roman Service; though it seems one ought rather to call it the Service of the **Franciscans**.

<margin>What kind of usage the Gauls had adopted.</margin>
The Gauls <note>Referring to the inhabitants of Roman Gaul, largely modern-day France</note> also had their particular liturgy, of which some letters of **Jerome** and of various Popes make mention; and it was primarily in that place that **Charlemagne** and his successors put all their power to work to introduce the Roman Service there. **Pope Adrian** sent to the aforementioned **Charles** the book commonly called the **Sacramentary of Gregory** <note>A book containing the priest's parts of the Mass, attributed to Pope Gregory the Great</note>, which the Emperor had requested in order to introduce the Mass and other liturgies according to the Roman usage. **Pepin** <note>Pepin the Short (714–768), father of Charlemagne</note> had also previously worked vigorously toward the same intention. The Abbot **Hilduin** (c) <note>original: "Abbas Hilduinus"</note> gives an account to **Dionysius**, whom he calls the **Areopagite** <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius, whom medieval scholars often confused with a judge converted by St. Paul</note>, regarding the origin of the Mass that was in use in France before it was incorporated into the Roman liturgy: but without it being necessary to trace this origin, it is beyond dispute that in this part of Gaul, which is now called France, there was formerly a kind of particular Mass differing from that of Rome; and the same Abbot **Hilduin**, writing to the Emperor **Louis** <note>Louis the Pious (778–840)</note>, mentions certain very ancient Missals for the use of the **Gallican** Church, which were used before the Roman Church custom was introduced into this Church.

The Mass which **Matthias Flacius Illyricus** <note>A Lutheran reformer and historian (1520–1575)</note> had printed in the year 1557 in **Strasbourg** was considered by many writers to be the Mass of the **Gallican** Church; but Cardinal **Bona** <note>Giovanni Bona (1609–1674), a Cistercian cardinal and scholar of liturgy</note> believed he could show the opposite through many reasons, and show that this Mass had entirely departed from what the ancient writers attributed to the Mass that was peculiar to the French Churches. He believed, moreover, that the Mass formerly called the **Gallican** originated from the Mass that...

<margin>Which Masses were practiced in Spain.</margin>
One cannot doubt that there would have been a particular Mass in Spain, and in all the places that were formerly under the domain of the Goths; since this Mass is still in existence now. Although Gregory VII introduced the Roman Mass in almost all of Spain, he nevertheless could not prevent some Churches in Spain from keeping the ancient one, and among others those of Toledo and Salamanca, where it is still in use today. The Spaniards showed a great zeal for the maintenance of their ancient Church customs, and likewise a powerful steadfastness in rejecting the Roman Church service. The Aragonese were the first who accepted the same under Pope Alexander II, who sent a Cardinal as Legate to Spain for that purpose. <margin>(a)</margin> *Sancius* <note>Sancho Ramirez (c. 1042–1094), King of Aragon and later Navarre</note> King of Aragon, when he had become King of Navarre through the efforts of Pope *Gregory* VII, brought it about that it was also accepted in Navarre, just as the Mass and other Church services according to the Roman usage had already been introduced in Aragon: which is also sufficiently evident from the Letters written by *Gregory* VII to King *Sancius* and other Spanish Kings.

Alfonso <note>Alfonso VI of León and Castile (1040–1109)</note> King of Castile did not easily allow himself to be moved by the powerful solicitations of this Pope. The Castilian People also refused to accept the Roman Mass: and the King himself would never have consented to it, if the Queen, who was of French descent—where the Roman Church custom had taken hold—had not persuaded him through powerful solicitations. The Spaniards lack neither Histories nor Miracles to validate their ancient Gothic Mass: but as these Histories smell of Fables to us, we judge it unnecessary to recount them here. It only remains to be noted that this Spanish Mass is the same one to be found in the printing of the Library of the Fathers under the name *Missa Mosarabum* <note>The Mozarabic Mass, a liturgy developed in the Iberian Peninsula</note>, and that it is so named because the Arabs formerly ruled Spain. The Christians of this Land were then called Mozarabs, that is to say; mixed Arabs <note>From the Arabic "musta'rib," meaning "to become like an Arab," referring to Christians living under Muslim rule who adopted Arabic culture</note>.

The region which we now call England already had its Services and various Church customs long before *Gregory* <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> sent *Augustine* <note>Augustine of Canterbury, the "Apostle to the English"</note> there to convert these peoples. For *Augustine* was not the first who proclaimed the Gospel to the English, as such was known when this Land was called Britain. *Augustine* only introduced Christianity there in a certain region, a large part of this Island having already embraced the same long before.

> *Let them do this in their Churches,*
says *Jerome* <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> in one of his Letters, *which is done in Rome, or which is done in the East, in Italy, in Cyprus, in Africa, in Illyricum, in Spain, and in Britain.* <note>original: "Hoc in Ecclesiis suis faciant, quod Romæ, sive quod in Oriente, quod in Italiâ, quod in Cypro, quod in Africâ, quod in Illyrico, quod in Hispaniâ, quod in Britanniâ."</note>

All the Churches in general recognized the Roman Church as their Mother, yet they did not agree with her in the Mass nor in other Church services. The Bishops of the principal Churches assumed the freedom to increase or decrease the Church service according to their own discretion, and sometimes without the authority of any Council. No heed was paid to the decrees of Charlemagne and of his successors on the throne, who had established the uniformity of the Church service in their States, since something in it was gradually changed again. The Clergy, especially, who usually imagine themselves to be more than the common mass of men, also wanted to distinguish themselves through a particular Service: which went so far that finally Pope Sixtus V was forced to call a Gathering in Rome called <term>De' riti<note>The Congregation of Rites, established in 1588 to standardize liturgy and oversee the canonization process</note></term>, to have these new Church services examined, which were increasing daily, in order to prevent their growth in the future. Since then, one has been obliged to seek the approval of this Gathering of *Rites* henceforth, to give authority to their new Church services.

...prayer which one calls the Invocation of the Holy Spirit <note>Also known as the *Epiclesis*, this is the part of the liturgy where the priest invokes the Holy Spirit to bless the offerings.</note>, have incorporated, and which is not found in the Latin Mass; [at least not in the same place where] the words of the prayer were to be found: <note>original: "Quam oblationem tu Deus in omnibus quæsumus benedictam, adscriptam, ratam, rationabilem, acceptamque facere digneris, ut nobis corpus & sanguis fiat dilectissimi Filii tui Domini nostri Jesu Christi." — Translation: "Which offering, O God, we beseech you, to make in all things blessed, approved, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable, that it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ."</note> It seems to us that this Prayer is the same as what the Christians of the East call the Invocation of the Holy Spirit. All the difference consists in this: that in the Mass of the Eastern peoples, it follows some time after the spoken words: *This is my body*, and subsequently; but in the Latin Mass it precedes them, and this corresponds

<column-break/>

better with the common opinion, which is most widely accepted in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the medieval Scholastic theologians who defined the precise "form" and "matter" of the sacraments.</note>, whereby the Sanctification <note>The Consecration, or the moment the bread and wine are believed to be transformed.</note> primarily consists in these words which we have expressed; whereas otherwise the Eastern Peoples believe that they are not spoken except as a History, of what occurred when our Savior held the last Passover <note>The Last Supper.</note> with his Apostles. For this reason, they subsequently present their prayer to the Holy Spirit again, so that he might change the Bread and the Wine into the Body and Blood of the Lord. [Although this was expressed thus by the Greeks in the Council of Florence <note>A 15th-century ecumenical council that attempted to resolve the differences between the Western and Eastern Churches.</note>, who profess to believe that these words: *This is my body*, effect this Sanctification.]

# PREFACE
### TO THE
# R E A D E R.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting a scholar or religious figure seated in a study with a landscape and town visible through a window.</image-desc>

IN this second part of the first volume of this work on religious duties, church customs, etc., we present to the reader a description of all the ceremonies in use by the Roman Church. In general, they are magnificent (a) and full of mysteries. There are none for which a <term>Mystagogic writer <note>original: "Mystagogisch Schryver"; a writer who interprets and explains the inner meanings of religious mysteries and rituals.</note></term> (b) does not prove the reason and necessity, through books that he believes (c) to be of equal authority with those of the Apostolic Books. Nevertheless, these are not in use in the same way in all countries of the Roman religion. In Italy, for example, there are some in use that are unknown or ignored in France and other countries. We have collected all of these as accurately as possible; if, despite our diligence, some have been overlooked, may the reader please know that these ceremonies are found to be almost without number. So much so that the priests themselves, unable to contain the vastness of all the Christian ceremony books, are forced to take refuge in these books to guide themselves according to the rules contained therein. Ultimately, due to all the circumstances that accompany Roman church customs, this would make for a very difficult description.

When one allows that the ceremonies contain a mystery, one must necessarily present them to Christians as outward religious acts. We shall describe them with all the respect they deserve. We shall refrain from profaning things that have become holy and venerable through consecration, and to which the people have long been bound in their religion. Furthermore, one must have for them all the respect that one owes to elderly men; one must accommodate their weaknesses, which are subject to advanced years. The difference one finds in them, however, is that the great antiquity of these church customs is still uncommonly powerful. It has remained constant for many centuries; it has inherited a powerful establishment from good hands, and yet a small moderate force would be enough (d) to deprive it of all necessary maintenance of its first existence.

Nonetheless, it is required that these ceremonies (e) be shown to the people—

---

(a) Through their splendor, many Indians <note>The author uses "Indians" to refer broadly to the people of the East Indies.</note> converted to Christianity when the Portuguese established themselves in the East Indies. These pagans were very satisfied to find statues and other images in the Christian churches, accompanied by a service that did not seem entirely objectionable to them; and many saints were then baptized with the names of *Brahma*, *Rama*, and *Vishnu*. <note>original: "Brama, Ram en Wixnou"</note>
(b) We call those Mystagogic writers who describe church customs and ceremonies and have given us the key to them.
(c) *Casalius* <note>Johannes Baptista Casalius (1578–1648), an Italian antiquarian who wrote on Roman and Egyptian rituals.</note> and some other Mystagogic writers often cite the institutions that we possess under the name of St. Clement and some other writers, whose authority among scholars is very suspect. Nonetheless, it is certain that Roman ceremonies are generally very old, and

<column-break/>

that this is the primary proof one can give of their origin.
(d) One cannot deny that Roman Christianity has enriched itself with the discarded garments of Judaism and Heathenism. Their primary writers also admit it; and among others *Du Choul* <note>Guillaume du Choul (ca. 1496–1560), a French antiquary.</note> who admits the correspondence of Christian church customs with those of the Romans and Egyptians at the end of his work *The Religion of the Ancient Romans*. <note>original: "la Religion des Anciens Romains"</note> *Casalius* does the same in his book on the ceremonies of the Egyptians, Romans, and Christians.
(e) The common people have neither the time, nor the means, nor the necessary knowledge to judge their faith. Religion has been inherited by them, as it were, through birth and upbringing. In such a state, the visual and the tangible act most powerfully upon them, and that which comes with a display of splendor—

# PREFACE

exists; and let us suppose that Religion without these ceremonies would seem to be but a lean and meager body. This idea is too simple: but does the People not have loftier thoughts on this subject? Such a Religion is indeed a magnificent building, to which very common and lowly parts are attached that in no way correspond to the excellent structure. But what a sense of sublimity accompanies it, which is entirely beyond the reach of mediocre minds, artfully devised and of such excellent workmanship that one must be ingenious enough just to understand it! Men of judgment have bound themselves to it no less than the common man. Happy are the people who lift up their minds to contemplate the sublime and the hidden things of Religion, and release their souls from the needless and self-interested things that are entirely material! But few take heed of this; for some would certainly decide to abolish these materialities, which others nevertheless wish to have maintained.

Of all the parts that make up this our great Work, the most prominent is that which one could charge with the crime of compilation; which in the Learned World <note>The "Learned World" refers to the *Respublica literaria* or Republic of Letters, the international community of scholars in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note> is regarded as no less than a robbery. We confess this crime all the more frankly. We have often found ourselves forced to follow the expansiveness of certain Writers, and that without any caution or concealment. The matters were submitted to our approval; necessity gave us cause, and we have made use of them. Let the Reader please take note that in the matter of Religious Church Duties, it is of the utmost importance to keep oneself beyond reproach by describing them as the Original Authors did. Far be it from us to claim any glory for ourselves on this subject; we even renounce the original right over the Remarks with which we have accompanied the description. Such a display of clever, successful, and tasteful flourish, we leave to others. One robs a discarded and almost forgotten Writer with impunity, without anyone deigning to repay him what was stolen: and how would a Writer not be subject to such an injustice? In our days, people do not hesitate to rob the most illustrious Writers (a) before the eyes of the Learned World. We remain silent about the clever thievery which stealthily passes off another’s thoughts as its own as much as possible; and to say everything in a word, the majority of Books present themselves in a garment turned inside-out, and the most capable <term>patchers <note>original: "t'zamenflanssers"; those who hastily assemble or "patch together" books from various sources.</note></term> (b) know how to stitch them together so skillfully that they are regarded as new Works by even the most accurate connoisseurs.

## CHAPTER I.

### The Concept of the **CHRISTIAN RELIGION**
->*in general.*<-

<margin>
How custom and prejudice are two sustaining qualities of Religion.
</margin>

It is characteristic of humans to exalt the value and virtues of that which they embrace: but one must not always hold this behavior within the experience of one's reason. It is often owed to custom and prejudice. It would be unnecessary to expand upon this here; but it will suffice to say that nothing is more common than this behavior in matters of Religion. One is even indulgent toward people who observe this custom, and one forgives it, out of self-love, to those who defend the interests of their Religion under the banner of prejudice. We ask of the atheists <note>original: "Ongodisten," literally 'un-godlists'</note> and free-thinkers <note>original: "Vrygeesten," a term for 17th- and 18th-century intellectuals who rejected dogma</note> the same tolerance, and all those who might wish to accuse us of some partiality regarding the Christian Religion. If they cannot bring themselves to do so for the sake of the excellence of its morality and the wonders of its origin, then we implore them to tolerate us for the sake of their own self-love.

<margin>
That reasoning produces an obscurity rather than a
</margin>

If one considers the Christian Religion regarding its fundamental principles, one must confess that it is obscure and difficult to grasp, and that its mysteries do not satisfy the reach of reason. It must undoubtedly owe a portion of its obscurity to the cleverness <note>original: "schranderheden," implying intellectual subtleties or intricacies</note> that certain converted philosophers introduced into Christianity during the first centuries of the Church. These philosophers, having become teachers of the Church, wished to explain the mysteries of Christianity through reasonings

<column-break/>

<margin>
clarification in the mysteries of Religion.
</margin>

borrowed from Platonism <note>The philosophy of Plato, which early Church Fathers like Augustine used to help frame Christian theology</note> and other pagan philosophers. Their successors added new obscurities through their explanations, beyond those they already found; and human passions imperceptibly mingling with these systems, people have held to neither one nor the other, whereby the religion of Christians has become an unfathomable mystery. This was undoubtedly the origin of a multitude of sects and heresies in the Christian Religion, all of which claim for themselves the purity of the privileged principles; likewise the signs of Divine inspiration; a right of supremacy; the true knowledge of the path leading toward Heaven; and among which none is found that can prevent the actions of others (at least through indirect means).

<margin>
How the moral—
</margin>

The excellence of its morality <term>Zedekunde: The study of ethics, virtue, and moral conduct</term> proves the divinity of the Christian religion.

religion. It consists not in the vain contemplation of Philosophy, nor in constant outward gestures: but in a steady practice, which expects no reward from men, and neither seeks nor desires to make those appear wonderful whose brilliance shines in their eyes. This practice, grounded in the commands of God, follows the conduct held by the Founder while he was here on Earth. If those who do not believe in Jesus Christ would, with accurate observation, compare his Laws with those of the greatest Lawgivers of Antiquity, and compare his life with that of the most eminent Philosophers, we believe they would by no means view him as a famous Seducer, but at the very least as a Divine Man and as one who worked everything through supernatural powers. Yet we are certain that these enemies of the Christian Religion—known under the name of Free-thinkers <note>original: "Vrygeesten," referring to the 18th-century "esprits forts" who challenged religious dogma</note> or Libertines, and who consider themselves honored to be so named—are encouraged by the same spirit as those who would wish to establish an anarchic state and overturn the laws of government. These are they who wish to recognize no Power, and treat both good and wicked Princes alike as Tyrants. They would treat *Lycurgus* or *Solon* <note>Famous ancient Greek lawgivers from Sparta and Athens respectively</note> no better than JESUS CHRIST and *Moses*, if the Laws of these Heathen Lawgivers seemed as formidable as those of the Founders of Judaism and Christianity.

<margin>And in what practice this religion consists, to arrive at its true purpose.</margin>
The Christian Religion (a) consists, through practice, in the most precise and perfect succession possible to grasp the infinite perfections of the Supreme Being. It is from this fountainhead that true Virtue must spring: the power it holds over the passions, and the satisfaction one finds in defending with all one's might the Laws that God has established in the World, insofar as evildoers seek to overthrow them and, through their disorders, confuse the boundaries of good and evil. We believe, and not without reason, that God takes pleasure in seeing that one follows Him as much as possible in His perfections, and that one observes His Laws. This principle leads us naturally to punishment and reward: and since

<margin>How ethics is inherent to Religion, yet not entirely sufficient.</margin>
both one and the other are but imperfectly distributed in this World—since men themselves often disappoint virtue while rewarding the offense—one must take recourse in the judgments of the Divine Being. Reason alone makes us understand that everything which resists the infinite perfections of the Supreme Being, and everything which seeks to overturn the Laws of Divine Justice, deserves to be punished in proportion to the crime, provided that reason is not corrupted by passions and a bad example. From this arises the fact that natural religion no longer suffices, and it is required to fulfill this through a revelation, which teaches us that the Pious shall enjoy a reward proportioned to the excellence of their virtue, and the Godless the punishment required by the loathsomeness of their crime. We find this revelation in the Christian Religion. Its principle and origin, the life of the Founder, the weakness and inability of those who propagated it through means they were not powerful enough to invent, the testimonies which even its Enemies have confirmed: all this convinces us. Ethics <note>original: "Zedekunde"</note> prescribes nothing which is not consistent with Divine perfections and does not tend toward the well-being of man; its Precepts agree with the Ideas of unblemished natural religion, and its Laws have no other objective than the preservation of the human race. To win people over, it uses only motives worthy of the Wisdom of God. It is true that this Ethics is accompanied by some uncommon Doctrines which the natural light of reason does not comprehend: but to attempt to understand this—or at least let it be permitted for us to approach with our weak reasoning—let us pay attention to this first simplicity, which would safeguard the weight of the matter in dispute, under which it subsequently groaned. If, with this precaution, difficulties still arise, we are ignorant as to why they are not resolved: expecting that a serious investigation in the demonstration is enough to show that the marks of Christianity perfectly match the attributes of the Divine Ma-
