### CHAPTER II.

#### THE CONCEPT of the CHRISTIAN RELIGION
->according to the Principles of the ROMAN CHURCH.<-

<margin>The Roman religion considered in general, and how the life within it is to be.</margin>
Now that we have given a general Concept of Christianity here, it is required to pass on to the particulars. We shall then make a beginning with those of the Religion of the Roman Catholics, whom the Protestants have left for reasons that would require an endless investigation. To search into its credibility is not within our scope: but however it may be, order obliges us to regard it at least as the firstborn of Christianity, without concerning ourselves with the pretensions of other Sects. There is even a reason to be brought forward in favor of the Roman Catholics. This is that their Religion is, in a sense, uniquely dominant, or subject to the power (if one may call it so) of a single person, who keeps it in such a separation, maintaining the unity of the Church to the exclusion of the Salvation of other Christians. It still seems to understand the church as a Political Body. We shall focus on the following fundamental articles of the Christian Religion (a) in general, as well as (b) specifically, the Roman Catholics in the Theology of the Roman Church, and to which they add the principal additions or practices of which they make so much account.

<margin>Wherein the Roman Faith agrees with the Protestants.</margin>
The Roman Catholics believe all the Fundamental Articles of the Christian Religion. They worship one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. They confess that one must trust in *God (b) alone*, through his Son, made flesh, crucified and risen again. They subscribe with the same certainty to the other articles of the Apostles' Creed.

<column-break/>

that a very large number of additions—of which, according to their [the Protestants'] view, some are contrary to the Articles of this Creed—greatly weaken the main points. They also believe that one must, with much patience, tolerantly observe a great number of practices that turn the Spirit away from Christianity. The Roman Catholics answer to this that no one has yet the power to conclude why these practices are evil, nor to prove irrefutably that all the alleged additions complained of are substantial Additions, and what is more, contrary to the Articles of the Creed. The differences have so powerfully increased the <gloss>mutual</gloss> prejudices that it is almost impossible to conclude anything on the subject of the additions; (c) and as far as the practices are concerned, it is added that they generally contain no matter of an Article of Faith, and even vary (d) according to the national character of the people.

<margin>How Bossuet presents the Roman Catholics in the purest manner.</margin>
We shall not involve ourselves in the investigation of this matter. It will be enough to present the Faith of the Roman Catholics in its purest form. Mr. Bossuet <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704), a famous French bishop and theologian known for his eloquent defense of Catholicism.</note> shows it to us in his explanation of the Catholic Church, provided with the most credible approvals, and in accordance with the decrees of the Council of Trent <note>A 16th-century ecumenical council that defined the doctrines of the Catholic Church in response to the Protestant Reformation.</note>.

I. "To make a beginning (he says) with the worship that one owes to God; the Catholic Church teaches that it primarily consists in believing that He is the Creator and Lord of all things, and we attribute to Him all our power of our soul through Faith, through Hope, and through Love, as to Him who alone can make us happy through the communication of infinite goods that are His own."

II. "Hope, and through Love, as to Him who alone can make us happy through the communication of infinite goods that are His own." <note>This second point repeats the conclusion of the first, likely a transcription or printing error.</note>

Part I.

(a) *Nothing is there in our Faith (it is said in the Acts of the General Assembly of the Clergy, held in France in the Year 1682) which can wound a sincere mind, provided that one does not take for our faith the abuses of some individuals, or errors which are falsely attributed to the Church and have neither been accepted nor received authority.*
(b) *Bossuet. Exposition of the Catholic Doctrine, page 3. Brussels Edition, 1695.* <note>original: "Expos. de la Doctr. Cath."</note>
(c) *They answer many other matters, which are almost impossible to bring forward without taking sides.*
*This Subject has produced a great number of writings on both sides, which generally have nothing Christian about them but the name.*
(d) *For example, many practices in use in Rome are in no way to be tolerated in France.*

# THE RELIGION of the ROMAN CHURCH.
Dd 3

32. The **Law** <note>original: *Lex*</note> was given by God to man to teach him through its commands what he owes, and to warn him against the evil things that result from it.
33. After the Fall, no man was able to fully satisfy it, and the **Law** could not deliver him from sin.
34. In the utmost corruption of man, God, out of the movement of His own goodness and generosity, turned the world toward its **Salvation** through the promise of the LORD JESUS CHRIST.
<margin>How the satisfaction of J. Christ is a satisfaction, etc.</margin>
35. Catholics unanimously teach that JESUS CHRIST, as both God and Man, is alone capable through the **Merits** of his death and his love, of offering God a sufficient satisfaction for our sins. Having satisfied abundantly, he could apply this infinite satisfaction to us in two ways: either by granting us a **full pardon** without withholding any punishment, or by exchanging a much greater punishment for a lesser and short, or a temporal and lesser punishment. Since the first is more perfect and more consistent with his goodness, this is practiced in **Baptism**; but we believe that he makes use of the second in the forgiveness granted to the baptized who have fallen back into sin, being compelled in some measure by the ingratitude of those who have misused his first gifts; therefore they must suffer some **temporal punishment**, even though the eternal punishment is forgiven them.
36. One must not conclude, however, that JESUS CHRIST did not satisfy for us entirely; but on the contrary, that having obtained an absolute right over us through the value he paid for our **Salvation**, he grants us forgiveness under such a condition, under such a **Law**, and with such a provision as is pleasing to him.
37. We would be unjust and ungrate—
<margin>(a) Continuation Session 25. Dec. On Indulgences.</margin>
<column-break/>
32. [that] it is our duty to work out our Salvation through the movement of our will joined with the grace of God, which is a help to us: but this is a primary principle which the **free will** cannot carry out unless it is moved and raised up by the **Holy Spirit**, as it is led to eternal Salvation, etc.
33. VI. We openly confess that we are acceptable before God only in and through JESUS CHRIST; and we do not understand how any other thoughts can be attributed to us. We build all hope of our **Salvation** in him alone; as we daily express these words before God in the **Offering** <note>Refers to the Sacrifice of the Mass</note>: *Vouchsafe, O God, to grant to us sinners, your servants, we who hope in your manifold mercies, some part and fellowship with your blessed Apostles and Martyrs, into whose number we pray you to receive us, not considering our merit, but pardoning us by grace in the name of JESUS CHRIST our Lord.* <note>This is an English translation of the Latin prayer *Nobis quoque peccatoribus* from the Roman Canon of the Mass.</note>
34. Catholics unanimously teach that JESUS CHRIST, as both God and Man, is alone capable through the infinite dignity of his person, of offering God a sufficient satisfaction for our sins. Having satisfied abundantly, he could apply this infinite satisfaction to us in two ways: either by granting us a **full pardon** without withholding any punishment, or by exchanging a much greater punishment for a lesser and short, or a temporal and lesser punishment. Since the first is more perfect and more consistent with his goodness, this is practiced in **Baptism**; but we believe that he makes use of the second in the forgiveness granted to the baptized who have fallen back into sin, being compelled in some measure by the ingratitude of those who have misused his first gifts; therefore they must suffer some **temporal punishment**, even though the eternal punishment is forgiven them.
35. One must not conclude, however, that JESUS CHRIST did not satisfy for us entirely; but on the contrary, that having obtained an absolute right over us through the value he paid for our **Salvation**, he grants us forgiveness under such a condition, under such a **Law**, and with such a provision as is pleasing to him.
36. We would be unjust and ungrateful toward the Savior if we undertook to dispute with him the infinity of his merits, and that under the pretext that in forgiving us the sin of Adam, he did not at the same time relieve us of all its consequences, still leaving us subject to death and so many physical and spiritual weaknesses which this sin caused us. It is enough that JESUS CHRIST once paid the price by which we shall once and for all be delivered from all the evils with which we are afflicted; it is for us to receive with humility and gratitude the portion of the benefit, noting the progression with which it pleases him to carry out our redemption, according to the order that his wisdom has established for our well-being, and to present a clearer proclamation of his goodness and justice.
37. For a similar reason, it should not seem strange to us if He, who showed such great indulgence in Baptism, should be more severe toward us after we have violated its holy promises. It is just and even beneficial for us that God, in forgiving us the sin and the eternal punishment we deserved, demands some **temporal punishment** from us to keep us in our duty; fearing that we, too hastily casting off the bonds of righteousness, might give ourselves over to a presumptuous confidence, abusing an all-too-easy forgiveness.
38. It is then to satisfy this obligation that we are subject to certain difficult works, which we must fulfill in the spirit of humility and penance; and it is the necessity of these satisfactory works that compelled the ancient Church to impose punishments on penitents, which are called **Canonical** <note>original: *Regelmatig*, referring to the penitential canons or rules of the early Church</note>.
39. When she then imposes difficult and laborious works on sinners, and they endure them with humility, it is called **satisfaction**; and when consideration is given to the zeal of the penitents, or to other good works which she—
40. prescribes for them; and it is the necessity of these satisfactory works that compelled the ancient Church to impose punishments on penitents, which are called **Canonical**.
41. When she then imposes difficult and laborious works on sinners, and they endure them with humility, it is called **satisfaction**; and when consideration is given to the zeal of the penitents, or to other good works she prescribes for them, she mitigates something of the punishment that is owed, and this is called an **Indulgence**.

One must only note (b), that according to the teaching of the Council of Trent, the sick person is refreshed more in the soul than in the body, and thus the spiritual good is always the primary subject of the new Law; so it is also that we must absolutely expect it from this holy anointing, even though we be in good health: whereas the refreshment of the sick is only granted to us with respect to our eternal salvation, according to the hidden dispositions of Divine Providence, and the various degrees of preparation and of the faith which is found in the Believers.

" When one (c) shall note that JESUS CHRIST gave a new form to Marriage, bringing this holy union (d) into two persons unalterably and indissolubly united; and when one shall see that this inseparable union is the sign of His eternal union with His Church, one will have no difficulty in understanding that the Marriage of the Believers is accompanied by the Holy Spirit and by grace; and one will praise the Divine goodness, because it has pleased Him thus to sanctify the origin of our birth.

" The Laying on of Hands which the Ministers (e) <note>Here referring to the clergy receiving Holy Orders.</note> receive as a holy thing, being accompanied with a present power of the Holy Spirit, and of an outpouring (f) full of grace, must also be placed among the number of the Sacraments.

<margin>In what manner</margin>
" IX. The essential (g) presence

<column-break/>

<margin>one proves the presence of Christ in the Sacrament of the [Lord's] Supper.</margin>
" of the Body and Blood of our Lord in the Sacrament of the Holy Supper <note>original: *Avondtmaals* — the Eucharist</note>, is well-founded by the words of the institution, which we understand according to the letter, and one must no more ask us why we bind ourselves to the proper sense, than one asks a traveler why he follows the common road. We find nothing in the words which JESUS CHRIST uses regarding the institution of this mystery that obliges us to take them in a figurative sense, and we consider that this reason suffices to confine us to the proper sense. But we are even more powerfully bound to it, when we pay heed to this hidden meaning of the Son of God, which I shall explain as simply as possible, and that through principles which I do not believe anyone will be able to dispute with me.

" I say then that these words (a) of the Savior, *take, eat, this is my Body given for you* etc. show us that just as the ancient Jews did not only unite themselves in the Spirit through the offering of the sacrifices that were offered for them: but that they truly ate the sacrificed flesh, which was for them a sign of the part which they had in this offering: likewise JESUS CHRIST has made Himself a sacrifice for us, so that the actual communion of this adorable flesh was a continual testimony to each of us in particular, that He became flesh for us and offered Himself for us.

" God had forbidden the Jews (b) from eating the sin offering <note>original: *zeegenoffer* — literally "blessing sacrifice," but referring here to the sacrificial offerings for sin described in Leviticus.</note> which was offered for their sins, to make known that the true wiping away of misdeeds did not occur in the law, nor was accomplished through the blood of animals: all the people lay under this prohibition, without being able to truly participate in the forgiveness of sins. But by a contrary reason it is that the Body of our Savior, the true offered sacrifice of atonement for sin, is eaten by the believers, to show them through this eating that the forgiveness of sins was fulfilled in the New Testament.

agrees with the Gospel of Jesus Christ: but that the Pope alone, as one possessing power, issues decrees, is something the Church cannot allow him, except insofar as his decrees (a) coincide with that which Jesus Christ teaches us. Whenever, however, the Pope deviates from the true meaning of the Scripture, it is impossible to regard him as the <term>Vicar of Jesus Christ</term> <note>original: "Stedehouder". The representative of Christ on Earth.</note>. The Church then possesses the right to strip him of the authority which she had entrusted to him on behalf of the Savior of the World. It is therefore no longer required of one to obey the Pope in such cases, and it is to the (b) <term>See of St. Peter</term> <note>The institutional office of the papacy, as opposed to the individual person holding it.</note> that the Believer must submit, until it is occupied by a legitimate Pope.

### CHAPTER III.
#### In which the DOCTRINE of the JANSENISTS consists.

<margin>The origin of the Jansenists noted.</margin>
That which we have already brought forward compels us to speak of those who are called *Jansenists*. They owe their birth to *Jansenius*, † a Professor of Theology at the University of Louvain and Bishop of Ypres. The unrestrained Doctrine of some Fathers (c) from the Society of the Jesuits concerning *Predestination* and Grace found so much favor in the Schools of Theology that two Universities (d) found themselves necessitated to censure and condemn them in the Year 1640. This Doctrine was then reported to the Holy See, yet in spite of this accusation, it made no small progress. *Jansenius* wished to <margin>Jansenius accused of five erroneous propositions;</margin> *defend* the *Faith* of the Church and the Grace of Jesus Christ. He set Augustine against the new doctrines and wrote a Book (e) on Grace in which one found the entire content of that great Teacher's doctrine. This Book was contested by the Jesuits, who accused *Jansenius* of five dangerous and <term>Calvinistic Heresies</term> <note>The Jesuits accused Jansenius of following the teachings of John Calvin, particularly regarding the lack of human free will in salvation.</note>. (f) Namely:

<margin>Which consist of these points.</margin>
I. That Jesus Christ did not suffer nor die except for those who are redeemed.
II. That man cannot resist Grace—

---

(a) This is what was determined at the appeal for a Council by that portion of the Clergy of the <term>Gallican Church</term> <note>The French Catholic Church, which sought a degree of independence from Papal control.</note> who opposed the *Constitution* <note>Referring to the papal bull *Unigenitus* (1713), which condemned Jansenism.</note> of Clement XI.
(b) Those who have opposed the *Constitution* claim that one must distinguish between the Pope and this See. The Protestants joke about this distinction and ask what is meant by this "See." One further asks whether a subject who is disobedient to his King—because he commands things contrary to himself or the State—could be exempted from the crime of <term>Lese-majesty</term> <note>original: "gequeste Majesteit". High treason or an offense against the dignity of the monarch.</note> by saying that although he was disobedient to the King, he nevertheless submitted to the commands of his Throne; namely, according to the legal, rightful, and proper authority of the Monarch; but this authority is an essential duty when the Throne stands vacant.
† [A Man of great Learning, born in the year 1585 in the Village of Abcoude, located near Leerdam in Holland. His father was named Jan Ottye, a blacksmith by trade, and his mother was named Lyntje Gysberts; they called this son of theirs Cornelis Janszen, who, having moved on to study, was called *Cornelius Jansenius* according to the Latin naming convention. He laid the first foundation of his Learning in Utrecht; but sent from there to Louvain, he practiced *Philosophy* under the Jesuits in such a manner that after two years he became a *Magister* <note>Master's degree</note> in this study. Subsequently applying himself with all zeal to Theology, he traveled to France, in which Kingdom he remained for twelve years. During that time, he maintained a close friendship with *Johannes Vergerius*; but *Vergerius* becoming Bishop of Tours caused *Jansenius*, missing his friendship, to return to Louvain. Because he was more inclined toward Theology than Philosophy, he was elevated to Doctor in the year 1617, shortly thereafter appointed as Professor, and twice sent on behalf of the Academy to King Philip IV in Spain, who in the year 1635 elevated him to Bishop of Ypres; but in the following year, the Plague snatched him away from this world.
His Learning and modesty could not, however, prevent the Jesuits from looking upon him with an envious eye. The famous Book, over which so much unrest was stirred among the Roman Catholics, he had recommended to his friend *Libertus Fromondus*, who brought it to light in the Year 1640, whereupon the well-known movements against the Jansenists broke out openly, since in the same Book the teachings of the Jesuits were contested in no small measure; therefore, being offended by this, they denounced the Jansenists as heretics in public writings, even though the doctrine of Jansenius gained a large following at that time. Nevertheless, the Jesuits brought it about that five Main Points drawn from Jansenius were condemned by Pope Urban VIII in the year 1641, subsequently by Innocent X in the year 1653, and finally by Alexander VII in 1657. *Melchior Leydekker, Arnold's History of the Church and Heretics, Bayle, etc.*]
(c) *P. Molina and Father Leonard Lessius.* (d) *Those of Louvain and Douai.*
(e) *Augustinus. See History of Jansenism. Vol. I. p. 4. printed 1700.* This Book was already written before the Year 1636, since a privilege had been granted for it since the Year 1639; but it did not come to light until the Year 1640, dedicated to the Cardinal-Infante.
(f) This is drawn from the aforementioned *History of Jansenism. Vol. I. page 20.*

# HISTORICAL TREATISE on the CHRISTIAN

<note>original: "HISTORISCHE VERHANDELING over den CHRISTELYKEN". The header is incomplete as it continues from the previous page's title.</note>

III. That one can in no way cooperate with Grace and good works, and that we have no share in their merit.

IV. That after the fall of Adam, one no longer finds oneself in any state of indifferent freedom to conduct oneself according to our will toward one thing or another.

V. That the sins we commit are neither free nor voluntary except in their cause, which is the Sin of Adam. Only this [original sin] was free; all other crimes are produced by necessity and compulsion, since the weight of concupiscence <term>concupiscence: in this context, a theological term for the innate human tendency toward worldly desires and sin as a result of the Fall of Man</term> overcomes the will.

<margin>What is mutually disputed, and what follows from it.</margin>

The *Augustinus*, from which these Propositions were supposedly drawn, brought forth several writings (a) on the Subject of Grace; but the literary battle did not turn out as the Molinists <note>Molinists: Followers of the Jesuit Luis de Molina, who emphasized human free will's role in salvation, in contrast to the Jansenist focus on predestination.</note> wished. They soon approached the Pope to cast suspicion on and blacken the name of the "New *Augustinus*," who was finally entirely condemned by a Bull (b) from Pope Urban VIII. The Jansenists claimed that this Bull had been drafted by someone (c) entirely devoted to the Jesuits. Meanwhile, the disputes over the teachings of *Jansenius* caused much disorder in the Netherlands, as the theologians—encouraged by a zeal that their imagined orthodoxy inspired in them—did not neglect (d) to immensely exaggerate the subjects they produced.

<margin>Writings on the other—</margin>

*Jansenius*, hiding under the name of *Patritius*, wrote some years before against the official of Car-

<column-break/>

<margin>—side published,</margin>
dinal de Richelieu, a work bearing the name of the *French Mars* (e) <note>original Latin: "Mars Gallicus"</note>. The preachers and teachers devoted to the Cardinal were supported by the Jesuits and acquitted themselves (f) wonderfully bravely against the Jansenist doctrine.

After the death of Urban VIII, the matter of *Jansenism* was brought back to the table, and in such a way that seemed to favor the party: but the cunning of the Molinists nevertheless held the field against *Jansenius*. It would be unnecessary to enter into an investigation of everything that occurred regarding this Article and an endless number of polemical writings. Archduke Leopold, in the year 1648, put forth his utmost efforts to condemn the Jansenists in the Netherlands, and the Molinists decided that the best means to stem the following was (g) to exclude those who adhered to the Jansenist sect from all dignities, offices, and services. This means was powerful enough to test ambitious persons who could not resolve to believe truths harmful to their temporal welfare, however excellent they might otherwise be. The decree was followed by a formula or Confession of Faith (h) which those who wished to be admitted into offices had to swear. One can see this in the *History of Jansenism*, which we cite in the notes, and read in the same book on what footing *Jansenius* and the Bull were then treated in Spain.

The most amusing thing that occurred in these disputes—which, despite the weightiness of the subject and the gravity of the theologians, finally made both parties ridiculous—consisted in the titles with which the mutual writings were adorned. The names of *Shield* and other such did not seem to express the purpose of this kind of work enough.

(b) This Bull was issued on March 6, 1642, and posted only in Rome on June 19, 1643. The Jansenists spread rumors that this Bull was false, or at least wanted it seen as suspicious because of many contradictions found in the transcript of this Bull, and because it openly condemned the teachings of *Augustine*. This Bull was also not received more favorably in France. It was even refuted there by powerful observations, which at the time caused no less spite for the Court of Rome than the Observations made in our days regarding the *Constitution Unigenitus* <note>Unigenitus: A 1713 papal bull condemning Jansenist propositions that caused a massive political and religious rift in France.</note>.

A teacher (this was Fromond) took the name of (a) Vincent the Gentle <note>original: "Vincentii Lenis"; "Lenis" meaning mild or gentle</note> to provide a theriac <term>theriac: historically a medicinal ointment or "universal antidote," here used metaphorically as a spiritual remedy</term> against the views of the Molinists. Another took the name (b) Torch of Augustine. The Jesuit Veron created the Muzzle of the Jansenists. Some theologians of his order wanted to (c) extinguish the Torch of Augustine; but Fromond felt obliged to provide the (d) Snuffer for this Torch. Let us look away from these writings and their authors to come to the Letter signed by 68 French Bishops, through which they obtained from Pope Innocent X the investigation and the condemnation (e) of the five notorious Propositions, regarding which, as they believed, it was very dangerous to dispute, namely:

<margin>
Five specific propositions of the Jansenists, in which they were found and attributed to them.
</margin>

### I.

Some commandments of God are impossible for the righteous, even when they wish to observe them and strive to fulfill them according to their present capacity. They also lack the Grace that makes the same possible.

### II.

One never resists internal Grace in the state of fallen nature.

### III.

To be worthy or unworthy in the state of fallen nature, it is not necessary for man to have a freedom that is separated from necessity; it is enough that he has a freedom unhindered by coercion.

### IV.

The Semi-Pelagians <note>Semi-Pelagians: A group that believed human will could initiate the first step toward salvation, a view condemned as heresy by the Church which insisted on the necessity of God's Grace</note> admitted the necessity

<column-break/>

of an internal prevenient Grace <term>prevenient Grace: the theological concept of divine grace that precedes human decision</term> for every action, even for the beginning of Faith; and they were heretics because they wanted this Grace to be such that man's will could resist or obey it.

### V.

It is a Semi-Pelagian view to say that JESUS CHRIST died or that he shed his blood for all men without exception.

The Jansenists believed that the Molinists only pursued the disapproval of these Articles in order to make the blame fall upon Augustine and the doctrine of efficacious Grace. However that may be, the signed Letter under the name of the French Clergy was sent in the year 1650 to Pope Innocent X, and this Letter brought forth new writings, of which we shall not give an account here. In this same year of 1650, the Bull of Pope Urban VIII against the Jansenists was published in Poland.

At that time, (f) other Roman Catholic powers were requested to write to the Pope to unanimously request from him the disapproval of the five Propositions attributed to Jansenius.

When the Bull of Pope Urban VIII was published in the Roman Catholic Netherlands, the proclamation did not satisfy the Roman Court because of the condition contained therein: that it would be (g) without prejudice to the Rights and Privileges of the Land. In the year 1652, the Pope called a meeting of Cardinals to investigate the matter of Grace. This meeting or Congregation, which supposedly <note>original: "quanswys"; implying a pretense or a deceptive appearance</note> would judge in favor of the Jansenists, nonetheless subsequently (h) did not turn out favorably for them, although

On the other hand, Pope Innocent X was by no means favorable to the Jesuits (a): but the interest that His Holiness took in *Jansenism*, alongside condemning the alleged propositions of *Jansenius*, had no other principle (b) than to strengthen his authority and his infallibility. Finally, Jansenius was completely condemned by a Bull from the Pope granted on May 31, 1653; which contained the statement that *His Holiness, after having devoutly implored the assistance of the Holy Spirit for some favor of His grace, condemned the five notorious Propositions, without any explanation to support the sense in which His Holiness condemned them.* This Bull was posted and proclaimed on June 9 in Rome, and accepted in France. The Bull (c) did not pass without scrutiny from the Jansenists, however: but it was finally accepted, and the conduct held by those (d) who pushed for its adoption was not entirely orderly. After the proclamation in Paris, the pulpits thundered with the ringing of the alarm bell that many parish priests pulled against the heresy of *Jansenism*. Without coming to an investigation of the truth or falsity of the condemned Propositions, one can say that the fire of these clergymen was quite scandalous. All of this caused the disturbances (e) and bitterness to increase. The year 1656 (f) brought forth the notorious *Provincial Letters*

Pressure was forcefully applied regarding the signing of the document <note>This refers to the "Formulary," a statement of faith that all clergy and nuns were required to sign to condemn Jansenism.</note>, and the severity of the Archbishop of Paris (a) on this occasion went completely beyond all bounds. The wrath of this Prelate was kindled against the Daughters <note>The "Daughters" refers to the nuns of the Port-Royal convent, who were the intellectual and spiritual heart of the Jansenist movement.</note> of this persuasion, because they would not speak otherwise than they thought, nor believe that the five Propositions <note>The five theological points extracted from Jansenius’s book *Augustinus* and condemned by the Pope.</note> were to be found in a Latin Book which these innocent Daughters had never read, and were also not able to understand. In the Year 1665, Pope Alexander VII struck Jansenism with a new Bull <note>A formal decree issued by a Pope.</note>, and, wishing to uproot it entirely, demanded the signing of a document of his own making. It was generally signed, though by some (b) purely and simply, and by others, with a distinction regarding the legal nature of the dispute.

<column-break/>

Finally, in the Year 1668, a peace (c) was reached by Pope Clement IX between the parties, which greatly rejoiced the French who were of a truly Christian modesty: but the outcome has shown that it should rather have been viewed as an armistice; and it became clear that it is incomparably easier to win over the Princes of this century than ecclesiastical personages. The War began anew everywhere when Pope Clement XI, in the Year 1713, issued the Bull (d) against 101 Propositions extracted from the New Testament by Father Quesnel. This Bull destroyed, according to the opinion of the Jansenists, all Christian Morality: at the very least, one can be certain that it was less suited to maintain it in its purity.

## CHAPTER IV.

->*The Fundamental Doctrine of the QUIETISTS Examined.*<-

<margin>The Fanaticism of the Quietists and their opinions displayed.</margin>
The sect of the *Quietists* was viewed as extremely harmful to the Christian Religion. Their Fanaticism <term>Geestdryvery: a term used for "enthusiasm" or religious fervor that was seen as excessive or irrational.</term> extended to a contempt for the Majesty that accompanied Religion, and for the nature proper to the Holy Spirit; as well as making the lifting of the heart to God into a mechanical (e) State. This Fanaticism has already appeared in various centuries (f). The Montanists,

<sig>Ff</sig>
<meta>VOLUME I. Catchword: as</meta>

---

(a) After he had armed himself with Excommunication against the Clergy of P.R. <note>P.R. stands for Port-Royal, the Jansenist stronghold.</note>, he subjected them to very harsh and disdainful treatment. *See the History of Jansenism* printed in the year 1700.
(b) Which happened with so much ignorance on the part of some, that Mandates were seen in which Jansenism was called the Heresy of Cornelius Jansenius, surnamed *Augustinus*. See the aforementioned History of Jansenism, Part 3, page 204.
(c) The Peace of Clement IX.
(d) The Constitution called *Unigenitus* <note>original: "Unigenitus," meaning "The Only-Begotten."</note>. It was dated September 8, 1713.
(e) The first principle of the *Quietists* is that the soul must release itself from contemplation, and attach the use of its will to an internal abstraction, as well as to the meditation which they call an acquired knowledge. The body must be in a perfect stillness while the soul enjoys these spiritual gifts.
(f) The first origin of the Mystics must be sought in the Song of Solomon. This does not prevent one from recognizing this Book as Divine. We only mean to suggest that now and then the so-called "born-again" have deceived themselves with these Ideas and Metaphors. It is from this that they have drawn from the Word the betrothal and the Spiritual Marriage of the soul with Jesus Christ, the chaste consummation of this Marriage, and the Dowry of the married soul. Since the first centuries of Christianity, these Ideas and *Mystical* expressions were already found among the Fathers of the Church, and possibly they had borrowed them from Plato and other Pagan Philosophers. Bayle, in his *Critical Dictionary* under the article on Plotinus, calls the *Quietists* "Platonic Script-robbers" <note>Meaning they plagiarized or misinterpreted scripture through a Platonic lens.</note>. "The objective," he says, "toward which Plotinus directed his thoughts, was to unite himself with the great God. He achieved it through an *inexpressible power*; and this was the uniting means of our Quietists." The sectarians of Foe <note>Referring to Buddhism/Buddha.</note> teach a sort of *Quietism* in China, and desire that those who seek true happiness should give themselves over to contemplation and reflection in such a way that they frustrate the use of their understanding. One can consult the Remarks of Bayle on the articles of Spinoza and Taulerus on this subject. Arnold has collected many Mystical Ideas in his book, the *History of Mystical Theology*, to confirm the antiquity and excellence of this Theology. Although he takes great pains to run through all the centuries to show the progress it has made up to our times; it is nevertheless certain that it was not brought into a System until the writings of John of the Cross: but after him, the Mystical Doctrine expanded into Religion with enough passion until the time of Molinos, a Spanish Priest, who was condemned in Rome in the Year 1687 under the Papacy of Innocent XI. One can read about these drivers of *Mystical* Theology in the Latin book of our aforementioned Arnold and see the register of their Works there.

# CHAPTER IV.
## The Fundamental Doctrine of the QUIETISTS Examined.

<margin>The spiritual fanaticism of the Quietists and their</margin>
The Sect of the *Quietists* was regarded as extremely harmful to the Christian Religion. Their spiritual fanaticism <term>Geestdryvery: a period term for radical spiritual enthusiasm often viewed as irrational or dangerous</term> extended to a contempt for the Majesty that accompanied Religion, and

One can read about these drivers of *Mystic* Theology in the Latin book of our aforementioned Arnold and see there the Register of their Works.

as well as the Gnostics <note>A group of early Christian sects that emphasized secret knowledge (gnosis) as the path to salvation.</note>, (a) etc., undoubtedly held with these *Mystics*. One can judge the unusual teachings of the Quietists (b) by their particular, stubborn, and extravagant manner of speaking.
The Quietists hold as principles (c) that once one has surrendered oneself to God, this act exists forever; without it being necessary to repeat or renew it. All one has to do is not take back from God what we have given Him, by acting against His Divine pleasure; provided this does not happen, the essence and perseverance of the surrender to God and of one’s conformity with the will of God lasts forever. The minor failures that one commits without thinking do not erase the reality of the agreement: even the most abstract occupations do not interrupt the act of persevering love; and (d) should it happen that one no longer thought of God at all, it would not be necessary to renew the gift of oneself, which has always existed, (just as a marriage between husband and wife continues to exist, even though they are separated from each other and have had no correspondence for a long time. This marriage, we say, nevertheless exists, provided that no adultery or any other unfaithfulness causes the separation.) One must surely admit that this principle of

<column-break/>

tranquility of mind and contemplation (which, so they say, is accompanied by a perfect submission to God) can introduce a looseness of morals. From which follows the annihilation of acts of faith, as declared in the Articles of Faith of the Apostles <note>The Apostles' Creed</note>, and the petitions contained in the Lord’s Prayer, etc.
All this creates little obligation anymore for the Quietists; since, according to what we have said of their opinion, there is no contemplation except in a single, continuous, and general action. It is an act of faith to be mindful of **Jesus Christ**, and one remembers Him truly by observing the Articles of Faith, or when one reads the writings of the Evangelists: but all this, in the judgment of the Quietists, is of no use. “A soul,” they say, “without having thought of **Jesus Christ** in any way for a period of twenty years, finds that all the power of it is gradually imprinted, although the soul in its objective has no distinct focus on **Jesus Christ**.” Such is the loftiness of this contemplative state. It is not unhelpful to read how Lord *Bossuet* <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704), a prominent French bishop and theologian who fiercely opposed Quietism.</note> refutes this *abolition of acts of faith* in his *Instruction on the States of Prayer* <note>original: "Instruction sur les états d'Oraison"</note>.

The Doctrine of the *Quietists* excludes all deliberation <note>The term "deliberation" (overlegging) here refers to active, conscious reflection or the use of reason during prayer.</note>, and that of *Molinos* (d) is formal in this regard. If one draws from these principles the consequences that can naturally be drawn, it will be found that it is such a conception as the *Quietists* have of God.
It follows then from the foundations of *Quietism* that those actions performed without deliberation must be uncommonly pleasing to God, since the discovered or confusedly discovered actions are the most perfect: but how could one lose oneself through such actions and annihilate oneself in God, since God is the Supreme Reason? Can one please Him without deliberation of action? And if, as a consequence of the reason God has given to man, virtuous works are produced—which by their nature work the opposite effect and better follow the infinite Wisdom of God—can one then love Virtue without deliberation? The **Passive Prayers** (a) of the *Mystics*, known by the name of *Quietists*, do not request any mediation; (this is the established principle, and it is almost unnecessary to repeat it): It is simply a passive contemplation. It can always prepare itself and never dismisses thoughts; for the way of seeking God is so easy and natural (let us add, so involuntary and, according to their opinion, so invisible) that neither the air one breathes nor continuous respiration is lighter. *If one noticed in our wandering brothers (b) a drive to simply believe and pray, one would, instead of much disputing, gently lead them back to God;* thus expresses a *Mystic* cited by Monsieur Bossuet <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704) was a powerful French bishop and theologian who was a staunch opponent of Quietism.</note>, and consequently, he is incompetent in matters of dispute and in reasoning to convert heretics.

<margin>How the Quietists understand the Love of God.</margin>
The soul (c) truly in love with her God soon finds herself in an ignited fire of temptations. She never believes with greater strength than when she is thus oppressed and tormented. Her doubt and fear to know whether she believes or does not believe, whether she has granted or refused her consent, are the tenderest effects of her love, etc. This love requires (according to the opinion of the *Quietists*) that one (d) renounce his neighbor, until God pulls the believer (*Quietist*) out of the state (of rest) in which he is. „ We leave „ this care recommended to him, continues „ *Molinos* <note>Miguel de Molinos (1628–1696) was the Spanish mystic who founded Quietism; his "Spiritual Guide" was later condemned by the Church.</note>, and remain in rest, unburdened of „ everything, entirely surrendering his pleasures. That one is not idle in that regard, etc.

« Divine love purifies the soul when God works in her (e) a passive preparation, exposing her to the fire of adversity and internal torment, etc. One then feels a suffering dryness <term>Spiritual dryness (aridity): a state described by mystics where one feels a total lack of emotional or spiritual comfort, feeling abandoned by God.</term> of darkness, anxieties, contradictions, internal abandonments, etc. The heart is then so constricted and so full of bitterness that one cannot lift it up to God, nor perform a single act of faith, hope, or love. Nevertheless, it is the love of God that works this disorder: but, according to the *Quietists*, this happens only to make the heart of the *Mystic* more capable. Molinos calls this described state the first Spiritual martyrdom. The second (f) spiritual martyrdom, being more useful and meritorious, is only for those who have already advanced to perfection and high contemplation. This consists in a *fire of Divine love*, in which the soul finds herself wrapped and consumed by the pains of love: then the absence of her lover <note>The "lover" here refers to God, as Quietists often used the romantic language of the Song of Solomon.</note> torments her; then the gentle yet heavy burden of the *Divine presence* makes her faint. This is what one calls sighing, suffering, and dying of love. From this arises for the soul a simultaneously hidden and spiritual pregnancy (g) of an *internal salvation*, which finally is brought forth externally in infused *contemplation* <note>original: "ingeflorie befpiegeling," likely a corruption of the Latin "contemplatio infusa," referring to knowledge given directly by God rather than gained through human effort.</note>. Thus it is that *Molinos* names the state in which God raises the soul to a perfect rest, without her being aware of the penetrating inwardness of His light. We believe that this is enough to give the reader an idea of the Love of God (h) according to the principles of the *Quietists*: but we shall see in the remarks (i) what a similarity there is—

### RELIGION of the ROMAN CHURCH. ###

...between their sentiments and those of the (a) *Beghards* <note>The Beghards were a lay religious group from the Middle Ages often accused of heresy for emphasizing a state of "perfection" that allegedly made them exempt from moral laws.</note> is.

<margin>How the sentiment of Molinos was introduced, and what arose from it.</margin>
We must now let our thoughts turn to the person of *Molinos* <note>Miguel de Molinos (1628–1696) was a Spanish priest and the leading figure of the Quietist movement.</note>, and how much favor his sentiments received. This Priest, a Spaniard by birth and sprung from a distinguished lineage, was of a stern and melancholy disposition. It is believed that he always spoke with contempt (b) of the external exercises of the Church and the religious practices of the common people. In the year 1675, he published his (c) *Guida Spirituelle* (*Spiritual Guide*) with the approval of five theologians. In this Book, one finds some excellent passages, although it is otherwise generally filled with various adorned whims and absurdities, and contains very strange ideas, as is evident from the passages already pointed out. The French translation might well have been more accurate. The approval of the five theologians leads us to believe that they either had not read or understood this book, or that they glanced through it (d) too loosely. This *Spiritual Guide* brought the Author into great esteem, which was strengthened by many persons (e) very eminent in the Church; among whom were some Frenchmen who intended to use him to reunite the Roman Catholics with the Protestants. *Pope Innocent XI* showed clearly enough that he protected him, and from then on the Religion—

<insert>
—turned, and that the desire to sin is destroyed, etc. *Molinos* says something more specific in his 3rd Book of his *Spiritual Guide*, Chapter 2, Number 7. Nevertheless, he seems to contradict himself a little later; for he adds that the enlightened Souls are no less convinced of it by their misery and failings, etc. On the other hand, one of the Propositions of *Molinos* condemned by the Bull of *Innocent XI* is this: *that a Soul having passed into Spiritual Death can no longer will anything other than what God wills, since it no longer has a will and that it has been taken from it by God.* In all this, one finds many contradictions. II. *The Beghards* maintain that in the state of perfection, one must neither fast nor pray. The consequence is necessary: if one is perfect, why then humble oneself before God? The inner communion with God in the midst of the tranquility described to us by the *Quietists* necessarily describes the Spirit of bodily mortification <note>In this context, mortification refers to the subduing of physical desires through self-denial or discipline.</note>. III. *The Beghards* imagine they are not subject to human and Ecclesiastical Laws. It seems also that *Quietism* posits a sort of independence. It is difficult to be a good upholder of the *Quietists'* principles. IV. As for the absolute Salvation of this life, the mutual principles are of a clear nature. One has only to read the descriptions that *Molinos* gives of absolute Salvation and inner Peace, calling this inner solitude, etc. V. *The Beghards* assert that one must not look upon the display of the Body of JESUS CHRIST <note>This refers to the elevation of the Host during the Eucharist.</note>; nor perform acts of honor before it: believing that the state of contemplation does not allow them to let their thoughts turn to the mystery of the Sacrament of the *Eucharist*, nor to the suffering of the humanity of JESUS CHRIST. The prohibition of Acts of Faith serves at least as a touchstone of this Teaching, and on this matter, one can consult Monsieur *Bossuet* in the 2nd Book of his *Instruction*. VI. *The Beghards* say that it only belongs to the imperfect man to exercise the effects of Virtue; but that the perfect Soul is exempted from this. This Proposition has every possible resemblance to the prohibition of all actions. The 37th Proposition condemned by Pope Innocent XI entails that one must banish Virtue.
</insert>

In order not to detain the Reader any longer with the Explanation of the resemblance between the followers of *Molinos* and the *Beghards*, called *Quietists*, it is required that we bring forward a few more passages that express the character of the latter. We shall cite the following from a High German writer <note>original: "Hoogduitsch Schryver"</note> brought forward by Monsieur *Bossuet*. "They do not work," says *Taulerus* <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), a famous German Dominican mystic.</note>, "except as the tool regards the Craftsman; likewise they regard the Divine operation, performing nothing at all. They imagine that the work of God would be hindered by their action. The commitment to a vain rest causes them to cease the effects of the Virtues. In this tranquility, they neither praise nor pray to God (since they regard the praises of God and the Prayers offered to Him as intervening works). *Molinos* has said, according to the 19th of the condemned Propositions, that for one who loves God as reason dictates, this understanding and conception is not the love of God. A Soul that would rid itself of the desire to love God proved that it loved him in its own way; which is as much as feeding our own choice." Finally, the contemporary writers of the *Beghards* found in them the annihilation and the passivity of the modern *Quietists*, likewise their abandonment or cessation of desire, thanksgivings, and virtues.

---

(a) Besides the extravagant sentiments attributed to the *Beghards* and *Quietists*, many dangerous signs have been given to both. One must admit that the prohibition of Virtuous Works is a natural consequence. However Spiritual a man might become, he is nonetheless always dependent on the objects that surround him, and consequently, he cannot sustain himself in mere contemplation. He would always find himself possessed by the deep musings of unrefined souls, who rid themselves of the burden of the senses, and who, in the filth and rudeness of claiming such things for themselves, would become capable [of anything]. The difficult spiritualities of the *Mystics* cannot, sooner or later, save them from a shameful fall. Nevertheless, it is good here to distinguish the contemplation from the practice; since the Founders do not always foresee the consequences of their principles that might be drawn from them, nor the weak joints that introduce an irregularity of morals.
(b) According to an Extract of an English Letter to be found in the Collection of papers regarding *Quietism*, printed in the year 1688.
(c) *Ibid.* (d) The first approval says that the style of this Book is understandable even in the obscurest matter; that the Author in no way deviates from the Holy Scripture, etc. The second and third say roughly the same. The fourth expands further and is also more sensibly composed; and the Writer, who was a Jesuit, only approves the book *as far as he can judge of it*, because of the continuous suspension in which *Molinos* maintains the understanding. The Society <note>The Society of Jesus, or Jesuits.</note> was not satisfied with this estimation, and a resolution was taken that the Author should no longer be spoken of. The fifth contained a confusion matching the Dignity of the Capuchin who gave it.
(e) See the extract of the Letter cited above in the Collection, etc.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Quietist movement, shifting from the general reception of Miguel de Molinos’s "Spiritual Guide" to the specific theological and political backlash it faced in Rome and France. ### HISTORICAL TREATISE on the CHRISTIAN ###

<margin>
The Doctrine of Molinos attacked, and with what consequence.
</margin>
The helpfulness of the Molinos-followers was not a little fruitful among the Romans. Many pious people of both sexes discarded their Rosaries and Prayer Beads <note>Small beads used by Catholics to count a sequence of prayers; Quietists argued that such physical tools were unnecessary for true spiritual connection.</note>; silent prayer took the upper hand, and the Jesuits' confessants became more scrutinizing than usual. This, it is said, gave the first cause for the rising troubles for *Molinos*. People wrote against his new heresy, and Father *Segneri* <note>Paolo Segneri (1624–1694), a famous Jesuit preacher who became one of the most vocal opponents of Quietism.</note> excelled the most in this. He vehemently attacked the Proposition regarding God and *Jesus Christ*. He (a) claimed it involved making the faithful despise the Savior's humanity. The *Inquisition* <note>The Roman Inquisition was a system of tribunals responsible for prosecuting individuals accused of religious crimes like heresy.</note> finally involved itself in the handling of these disputes: but *Molinos* triumphed over his enemies then. They further targeted his Office, and invented new accusations; they also investigated whether *Molinos* was of Jewish or Moorish descent <note>At the time, "purity of blood" was often used in Spain and Italy to discredit religious figures, suggesting their lineage might incline them toward non-Christian beliefs.</note>. Nevertheless, *Quietism* grew so powerfully that Mr. *Burnet* <note>Gilbert Burnet, a Scottish bishop and historian, whose travel letters from Italy provided Protestant readers with a window into Roman religious life.</note> in his *Italian Journey* counted twenty thousand of this sect in Naples. This spiritual propagation brought new troubles upon *Molinos's* head. If one may believe the author of the cited letter, quite a bit of politics was involved. It was suggested to the Most Christian King <note>A title traditionally held by the King of France, here referring to Louis XIV.</note> that *Molinos*, being a Spaniard, would bring those of his sect into the interests of his own King, and that therefore all the *Quietists* would become sworn enemies of France. Such, it is said, was the pretext used to encourage the zeal of the French King, who charged Cardinal *d’Estrées*, his envoy in Rome, to persecute *Molinos* and his disciples. They began to oppose him with an accusation (b) that he maintained forbidden correspondence and criminal understandings. They subsequently showed His Holiness that it did not befit the universal Father of all Christians

<column-break/>

not to nurture heresy in the Vatican, while the eldest Son of the Church <note>Another title for the King of France, emphasizing his role as a protector of the Catholic faith.</note> worked toward its destruction. Finally, *Molinos* was taken prisoner in the year 1685, and some time thereafter many clergy and laypeople were also thrown into prison, suspected because they were inclined toward *Contemplation* and *inward Prayer*. It is certain that if this sect had been tolerated any longer, a distressing confusion would have been perceived in the religious practice of the Church: especially if Pope Innocent XI, who (c) was regarded as a favorer of *Quietism*, had dared to declare himself openly as its Protector. After this first vain attempt, a circular (d) was sent to all the Prelates of Italy and the whole of Christendom, to inform them that it had been discovered how, in many places of their Dioceses, societies of *Quietists* resided who taught detestable errors. These Prelates were urged to work toward the dispersal of these assemblies, and to choose capable theologians, as well as to ensure that the established path was strictly followed; but as the voice of the Church was not powerful enough to carry out this work unless strengthened by civil punishment, these Prelates were charged to prosecute the *Quietists* before the secular judge. It was then time to provide for this; for inward Prayer had already brought the Rosary into contempt; and what is more, many pious people developed an aversion to Images, to which was added that some no longer counted their prayers. Finally, *Molinos* was condemned and escaped the fire <note>Execution by burning at the stake.</note> only through a public confession, and possibly, by appearance, of his errors: but he was (e) kept in a prison from which he did not emerge until (f) death. One shall see in Remark (g) a portion of the ceremony of his abjuration, just as we

### First Division.
### CHAPTER I.
#### Concerning the AUTHORITY of the CHURCH, and the HEAD placed over it.

<margin>
What power is attributed to the Church.
</margin>

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'D'</image-desc>
The Church (a) is one, visible, Holy, and Catholic or Universal. She is the work of God, who founded her upon unshakeable grounds and gave her the power to open the Heavens to the Faithful and to close them to Heretics and Unbelievers. She also possesses the power to forgive sins and to hurl the lightning bolt of Excommunication against those who are disobedient to her, and so forth. This Church is either Triumphant or Militant. The Triumphant Church (b) is *the excellent Society of the Blessed Spirits and of all the Saints, who, having triumphed over the Flesh and the Devil in this world, enjoy eternal Salvation in perfect certainty.* The Militant Church is the assembly of all the Faithful who, being on Earth, are obligated during their lives to

<column-break/>

<margin>
Which must be governed by a visible Head.
</margin>

fight against the World, the Flesh, and the Devil. JESUS CHRIST immediately governs that part of the Church in Heaven which is Triumphant; but as for the Militant Church, since it required a visible Head, one has been established who is regarded by Catholics (c) as the sole and absolute Guardian of the Faith and the perpetual Governor of the Faith of the Believers. He is the one whose Authority is defended in those States that have adhered to the Catholic Faith, and he governs through a vast multitude of people who are kept in his service. He is also the one charged with distributing Spiritual Weapons (d) to all the Faithful of the world, even elevating some to the highest dignity of Heaven (e) after they have held a place in the Triumphant Church for some time, and giving others (f) Testimonials to eventually reach that state. It is he who has given the Church the power, which she received from JESUS CHRIST, to use the keys to open Heaven. It is he who forgives sins; who, through her absolution, has the right to grant freedom regarding what was forbidden; who draws indulgences from her Treasuries and employs them to restore to the Spiritual life those who were dead in their Sins. It is he who initiates <note>In the sense of restoring or re-consecrating.</note> those whose crimes deserved indignation, through imposed taxes (a), whenever he deems it necessary. And in a word, it is he who watches over the Curse and Excommunication against Heretics, rebels, and those disobedient to JESUS CHRIST. He grants Grace to those who show respect to his Fatherly authority, and who, because they love him with an unconditional love, finds in them, like a good Father, the endurance for all the weaknesses of the Flesh.

### CHAPTER II.

->Concerning the Privileges which the POPE assumes.<-

<margin>How the Emperor formerly acknowledged the Pope's authority.</margin>
This visible Head is called the Pope. The Roman Catholics are not in agreement on this point. Some among them subject him to the General Council <note>A reference to Conciliarism, the belief that a general council of the Church has greater authority than the Pope.</note>. We shall speak of this shortly. In any case, it has been since his time that, through the *gifts* of the Pope, the Stewardship of JESUS CHRIST on Earth was crowned. Formerly, the Emperor went to Rome to receive the Imperial Crown from the hands of His Holiness, and to bind himself (b) by the Trinity, by the Head of the Cross, and by the *Relics of the Saints*, to protect the Church and its Head with all his power. Before his arrival in Rome, he took an oath, of which the *Book of Ceremonies of the Roman Emperors* has left us the image (c). He finally arrived there after the Church and its Head had absolutely secured their rights. The Clergy went to meet him in ceremonial robes and gave him the Cross to kiss. The Pope received him sitting upon a Throne, erected before the first covered gallery of the great Hall of the Apostles. It was there (d) that His Imperial Majesty, kneeling, uncovered his head as soon as he saw the Vicar of JESUS CHRIST. Then, approaching the Emperor, he remained continually with one knee upon the earth. Finally, he kissed His Holiness's feet, (e) through...

<margin>How far the power of the Pope extends.</margin>
He has the power to use the Sword of the Apostle Paul to punish in an Apostolic manner those who despise his decrees when he gives judgment on the Christian Faith: He must (e) place the golden Crown on the Head of His Majesty, who is the first Prince of Christendom: He (f) does not rise from his Papal Throne, and does not uncover his head for anyone. It is true, however, that in respect to His Imperial Majesty, he grants him the Grace of rising a little for his sake, when he is allowed to give the kiss of Peace, after homage has already been granted at the feet of the Holy Father. However, the Pope sometimes greets the Princes who have the honor of being received in audience by him with a small tilt of the head: but as for His Holiness, (g) he is not then dressed in his Papal garments, and although he humbles himself with this courtesy, (h) he is nonetheless not obliged to do so. RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH. 235

## III. CHAPTER.
### Of the COUNCIL, and of what it consists.

<margin>The nature and the power of a Council stated.</margin>
The Council (a) is an Assembly that declares if something is undertaken against the Faith, which has several times been uncommonly harmful to them. As a witness to this Truth, the Councils held at Pisa, Constance, and Basel serve as examples.
<column-break/>
The Council (a) is an Assembly that represents all parts of the body of the universal Church. The name "Council" is also given to provincial or national assemblies of the Clergy, which nonetheless represent only a portion of the Church. The Council consists of Ecclesiastical Plenipotentiaries <note>Delegates with full power to act on behalf of their home regions.</note> of the ruling States of Christendom, representing their nation, and even of (b) other Prelates, Theologians, etc., of the particular churches, gathered together in a public place, with the right to work unhindered on the improvement of Morals and Theology, alongside the restoration of Ecclesiastical discipline, etc. *This* Assembly has the power to pass judgment over Prelates, Cardinals, and even the Pope. The Council can also depose one or the other when the interests of Religion are at stake. Finally, this Assembly can, through its (c) Sovereignty, curb the unlawful undertakings of the Popes, which they impose regarding the Matters of Faith of the Church, and which [the Council] labels as Schismatics and Heretics

<margin>With what a solemn session</margin>
Regarding the Ceremonies of the calling of the Council: since it is thought that there has been no [such] Assembly since the one at Trent, we shall describe them in order according to what *Fra Paolo* <note>Paolo Sarpi (1552–1623), a Venetian historian known for his critical history of the Council of Trent.</note> reported in the history of this last one. He says that there was not the slightest quarrel or hindrance regarding the rank and presidency of the Prelates, etc., as if they had only (d) Civil matters to handle; that the Fathers of the Council requested that the place of the session be hung with tapestries, without there being a fear that the Council might

<sig>Gg 2</sig>

(a) It should be understood here that this refers to what is called an <term>Ecumenical<note>Meaning "universal" or "world-wide," referring to a council representing the entire Christian world.</note></term> or general Assembly.
(b) One must make a distinction between the Fathers of the Council and the Theologians, Envoys, etc.; for example: in January of the Year 1546, there were *at Trent* <note>original: "trente Trente," likely a typo or repetition for "at Trent."</note> 43 Fathers and besides these, 20 Theologians. Subsequently, there were about 60 Fathers. In the third session, there were more than 200. These Fathers, properly speaking, constituted the Council. It is not for us to investigate whether those who sat should be given [authority], or whether this Council was free or not free, etc. The Council of Constance was also a General Council; since, as Mr. *Lenfant* <note>Jacques Lenfant (1661–1728), a Protestant historian of the Church councils.</note> says in the Preface to his History, "there were thirty Cardinals, forty Patriarchs, twenty Archbishops, about one hundred and fifty Bishops, more than one hundred Abbots, fourteen Auditors of the Rota, more than one hundred and fifty other Prelates, likewise as many Generals of the Order as Priors, sent from various places, and more than two hundred Theologians." It seems to us that a Council can to some extent claim the title of General when all Christian Powers are invited to send their Plenipotentiaries, so that they might unanimously examine Doctrine and Morals without being hindered in their investigation.
(c) The <term>Ultramontane<note>original: "Overalpfche," literally "from over the Alps," referring to those in Italy or those favoring strong Papal authority.</note></term> peoples, who are more faithful Servants of the Pope than the remaining Christians, believe that the Council has no more authority than his Holiness pleases to give it: They want the Pope alone to have the right to call it, and they try to convince themselves that the Decrees of the Pope have the authority of a General Council. *Cevali* <note>original: "Cefalius," likely referring to Giacomo Cevali.</note>, a Roman Prelate and consequently a traitor <note>Likely used here in the sense of a partisan or advocate.</note> for the Papists, tries in his Latin book on the *Ceremonies of the Ancient Christians* <note>original: "Plechtigheeden der aloude Chriftenen"</note> to prove that the Emperors never had the right to call Councils without the authority of the Pope. Here there is no lack of Italian shameful acts with which he tries to refute the *Impious Calvin*, (as he calls him), who maintains the opposite. See the following Remark.
(d) In the early times of the Church, people gathered without any ceremony, since the Holy Spirit alone ruled their Assembly, and love in all parts encompassed the human aim. True Scholars, or those most influential through the prestige of the Assembly, managed or handled Matters, proposed and adopted Opinions. When the Church became entirely more secure and Religion found itself protected under Secular Power, difficulties arose in Doctrine and Church discipline that caused general unrest, brought about by the Pride of the Clergy, which forced the Princes and Authorities to concern themselves with these Assemblies. They called them by right of Civil Government and as their Head. They attended these Assemblies, established their rules, made proposals, and even gave their judgment over the various [disputes] arising among them, granting the Assembly the settlement of the main disputes that were the subject of the meeting. All this is shown by the Acts of many Councils. One wished to show no preceding matters, nor ceremonies, and one came immediately to the point. See, *Fra Paolo* History of the Council of Trent, Book 2.

->How the Spiritual Jurisdiction of the POPE Extends.<-

We shall, so to speak, make a distinction between the Pope as the head of the Church and Bishop, and the Pope as a worldly Prince. After subsequently giving an idea of the ceremonies of the Conclave and its intrigues <note>The Dutch "kuiperyen" refers to the political maneuvering and secret deals often associated with papal elections.</note>, which the Cardinals employ to elevate an eligible person to the Papacy (in which it is evident how the Holy Spirit maintains silence), we shall then speak of the ceremonies of adoration, of the Pope’s coronation, of the taking possession, etc. Subsequently, we shall proceed to the ceremonial customs which the Vicar of JESUS CHRIST observes, and causes to be observed as the first Prince of the Church. We shall further defer all else to the Civil Ceremonies. This man, whom the sacred Society elevates to the Papal dignity, occupies, as the successor of St. Peter (b), *the most exalted place of power and fortune to which ingenuity can bring a man in the Ecclesiastical state.*

## CHAPTER VI.

->Concerning the PREPARATIONS for the ENTRY of the CARDINALS into the CONCLAVE to elect a POPE; How he is elected, and what intrigues take place in the Election.<-

<margin>How one behaves upon the vacancy of the Papal see.</margin>
While the See stands vacant, and the Conclave is being held, four Cardinals of different orders divide the administration of affairs. These four Cardinals are Deans, or the first Cardinal Bishop, the first Cardinal Priest, the first Cardinal Deacon, and the Cardinal Camerlengo <note>The chamberlain of the Papal court</note>. The first three concern themselves with matters of State and Justice. The Cardinal Camerlengo, after having broken the Seal (c) which served to seal the deceased Pope’s Bulls and other dispatched writings, has money struck under his own stamp (d) with the inscription of the vacant See.

---

(a) Or the first annual incomes of vacant offices, called *Annates* <note>original: "Annates"</note>.
(b) *These Annates* or incomes, these pious works etc. are proofs of the childlike obedience which Princes owe to the Pope and of the Supremacy which he arrogates over them. As the successor of JESUS CHRIST, his Holiness provides from this tribute the necessities for the Church Militant and to nourish his splendor and the appearance of Piety in the Faithful. It is from these tributes that he draws great sums of money, serving to strengthen his Spiritual Troops. For, how could he, without these tributes, find the means of existence for so many Generals and Army Commanders who war against the hellish Powers, and lead the Church against the Enemy with such intrepidity? How could he reward such infinite stratagems of war which are thus devised in the hope of gain? If the Vicar of JESUS CHRIST were poor like St. Peter, if in imitation of J.C. [Jesus Christ] he refused to accept temporal incomes and honors etc. All this is told to us in good faith and with an Ecclesiastical countenance that befits the Christian Religion and eternal bliss: but, if one disarms those who serve in the armies of the Church of all worldly interests, of honorable offices, money-scraping, the right to make war, to live on discretion and to levy contributions; then nothing would remain for the Prelates but the comfort of the Holy Spirit, and one would then see the building of their Religion fall into ruins. Now that we have established the right of Supremacy which the Pope has obtained in the Church, it will not be unserviceable to present to the Reader as a consequence, the twelve means that serve to defend this right, and are like twelve pillars of this Sovereignty. *The new Gospel of Cardinal Pallavicino* <note>Sforza Pallavicino (1607–1667), a Cardinal and historian known for defending the Council of Trent</note> *provides us with these twelve means.*
I. The first annual incomes, of which we have already spoken, show that the Pope is the only Patriarch, that he has the right to receive those from all the Churches of Christendom on account of the Tithes which the Bishops are indebted, etc. The Pope does not receive these incomes, except regarding the temporalities which are attached to spiritual grace.
II. and III. The gift-wages, Ecclesiastical incomes and Abbeys, the temporal advantages of which attract a great number of Christians to the service of the Church of God.
IV. and V. The multiplicity of these Ecclesiastical incomes and the power of an absolute administration.
VI. and VII. The appeal of higher causes and suspension of cases.
VIII. The frequent Jubilees and Indulgences.
IX. The dispensations granted by means of money, of which mention has already been made.
X. The exemptions of Chapters: a means which establishes an excellent distinction between the Bishop and Pope, and immediately subjects the Chapter to its lawful Head.
XI. The privileges and exemptions of the Religions, which Cardinal *Pallavicino* ingeniously compares with the full authority which the Roman Generals received from their Republic when they waged war in remote Provinces on behalf of the Council.
XII. The Inquisition.
(c) He breaks, in the presence of three Cardinals, the seal of the Church which is called the *Fisherman's Ring* <note>original: "Visschers Ring"</note>, and the Under-Chancellor does likewise with the seal of the Chancery, in the presence of the principal officers of the same. The Fisherman's Ring has an engraving of the image of St. Peter, holding a plumb line and a fishhook in the water; it is used for the Briefs that are dispatched with the seal of red wax. The seal of the Bulls has the image of St. Peter and Paul with a cross on one side and a bust with the name of the reigning Pope on the other side. After the death of the Pope, this bust and the name are scraped away, without touching the rest of the seal. This is done only to Bulls that have an impression of Lead.
