<meta>This page continues the historical discussion of the Papacy, shifting from the symbols of power to the practical—and often political—realities of the Papal election process (the Conclave). It provides a detailed breakdown of the voting ballot used in the "Scrutiny" method.</meta>

# HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

Those who hold the reins of state use every trick of the trade to arrange everything to their liking when a Pope must be elected. One never even waits for the death of this primary Head of the Church to put into motion the schemes and clever ruses appropriate for elevating a respected Papal Candidate to the throne of the
<column-break/>
Papacy. And although the College of Cardinals unanimously calls upon the Holy Spirit for aid in guiding them to the election of the Vicar <note>original: "Stedehouder"</note> of JESUS CHRIST, their Eminences nevertheless do everything in their human power to ensure that the Holy Spirit does not (a) interfere with the election.

<margin>(a) It is likely that in the early days of the Church, the Roman Clergy performed the election of the Pope. It is even believed that the people’s consent had a place in this election. Subsequently, Odoacer, King of the Heruli, ordained that the election should not occur without his consent. Theodoric, the Gothic King in Italy, also wished to feed his right to have a hand in this election: but the law that Odoacer had made on this subject was abolished in the year 502 for the benefit of Pope Symmachus; which, however, did not prevent Theodoric from declaring Felix IV as Pope in the year 526. The succeeding Kings followed the example of their ancestors, reserving for themselves the right of confirming the one who had been elected, and no one could take possession of the Papacy unless he was pleasing to the Prince. The Emperors of the East, after they had restored their authority in Italy, retained for some time the right of approval and confirmation of the election performed by the Clergy: but the Popes, under the favor of Louis the Pious <note>original: "Lodewyk den Zachtmoedigen"</note>, Lothair I, and Louis III, cast off this sort of yoke, allowing the elections to happen according to their own choice. In the tenth century, the election and deposition of Popes stood at the discretion of the Roman Lords and Princes of Italy; which necessitated the Emperors to set themselves up as mediators of these elections, and this right was subsequently contested between the Emperors and Popes for nearly a century. Finally, the power to elect Popes was left to the Cardinals, without the Council, the Emperor, or the people having any part in it; and since the election of Pope Celestine II, who in the year 1143 came to the Papacy unconditionally from the Roman People and the Emperor's high officials, they have assumed possession of this right. Honorius III, elected Pope in the year 1216, describes that the election had to be done in a Conclave. Gregory X, occupying the Papal Seat in the year 1271, established—in a General Council held at Lyons—the procedure, laws, and customs of the election in such an order that elections must occur in three ways: by *Scrutiny*, by *Compromise* <note>original: "verblyf," likely referring to the delegated method of *compromissum*</note>, and by *Inspiration* <note>original: "ingeeving"</note>.</margin>

We shall explain the words of these different manners of electing the Pope a little, drawing our *Remarks* from the *History of the Conclave*; from the report of the *Chevalier Carraci*; from the *Remarks of Condorcet* (a small book printed in the year 1676); from *Calesius* in his *book Tapreri*, and from what is called the *Remarks on the Roman Court*. The Election by *Scrutiny* <note>A formal vote by secret ballot.</note> may presently be the only one in use for a long time; it is a procedure that seems most essential to declare the election of the Pope legitimate. Nevertheless, the *Scrutiny* is but a ceremony, since the mutually divided Cardinals are united on the choice of the Pope beforehand. This union is a result of the finest statecraft, and usually follows after their *Eminences*, through many *Scrutinies*, are able to discover the general inclination of the Sacred College. Then, if the voting for one of the candidates comes close to the required number, it often happens that the associates of the other conspiring Cardinals allow themselves to follow the stream, and thus join in the making and electing of the Pope, fearing to bring his enmity upon their heads through a fruitless opposition, and thereby causing their dignity to suffer a blow. Such, then, is the secret negotiation to which the People attribute the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

The *Scrutiny* consists of taking the Votes and examining the balloting, which is done through printed slips of paper placed by the Cardinals in a chalice standing on the Altar of the Chapel where they are gathered to elect a Pope. The preparation of these Slips is entrusted to the *Masters of Ceremonies*, who place them in two silver dishes positioned at both ends of a long table standing to the side of the Altar. Each slip is a span long and half as wide. They are divided by straight lines into eight equal parts; each slip, taken lengthwise, has 400 verses <note>likely referring to line-spacing or decorative marks</note> from the side being written on, as well as those used for the fold when the slip is closed. In the first part, one sees these words: _Ego Cardinalis_ <note>I, Cardinal...</note>, though separated a little from each other to leave room for the name. The second space is blank and unprinted. The Cardinal signs his name and his titles there. The third space has two circles at opposite ends. This is the place for the *Seal* which the Cardinal giving his vote has had made for this purpose: for on this occasion, he does not use his usual coat of arms. The fourth space contains the words _Eligo_ <note>I elect</note> etc., as seen in the adjacent Image. * The fifth serves to write the first name and the titles of the eligible Cardinal. The sixth is, like the third, the place for the Seal. The seventh space remains white, and the eighth is filled by a chosen Scripture passage of the Cardinal whose name the slip carries. The cover of each slip is also divided into eight equal parts, almost entirely filled with scrollwork so that one can neither see nor read the writing from the other side. An illustration of this is also seen here. Before the *Scrutiny*, a small bag is placed with ballot balls <note>original: "keurbatjes"</note> on which the names of all the Cardinals are printed, in order to draw three Scrutineers <note>original: "opzamaelaars"</note>, three Infirmarians <note>original: "Krankbezorgers," those who collect votes from sick cardinals</note>, and three Revisers <note>original: "Overzieners"</note>.

The Cardinals hide the letters of their usual handwriting as much as possible. They write what we have said on these *Scrutiny* slips themselves, or if they cannot change their letters well, they have them written by an unknown hand so that it is not discovered for whom they give their Vote. They fold these slips with all possible dexterity, so that it may not be known from whose hands they came.

One must place this invocation in the rank of those Ceremonies which assist the people in the Priesthood <note>the clerical hierarchy</note> to maintain the appearance of a dignity established by God, and which takes place ten days after the death of the Pope when the men enter the Conclave (a). [Then] this note arrives. Subsequently, they hide the note in their hand and then take their places: after which the *Scrutiny* <note>the formal voting process</note> begins in this manner. Each Cardinal takes between the thumb and forefinger of his right hand the ballot which he has written and folded, and holding it up so that it can be seen by the other members of the Sacred College, they swear before the high Altar and cast it into a certain Chalice. The group of *Infirmarians* <term>Krankbezorgers: officials appointed to collect votes from Cardinals too ill to leave their cells</term>, who after this chalice have their footstool placed in the middle of the Chapel, request the *Cardinals* of the *Church* who are there, [to confirm] the ballots that are in there, and then those of the entire College of *Cardinals* who may be sick; which proceeds thus: they offer these *Cardinals* the prepared *Scrutiny* ballots that are in the Chapel, and then receive a small opening <note>likely referring to a portable ballot box</note>, into which the sick man puts his ballot, and it remains closed; they carry the box to the Chapel, open it in the presence of other *Cardinals*, and subsequently place the ballots in the Chalice, just as was said.
Before one begins the *Scrutiny*, the Sacristan, who is always of the Augustinian order, says the Mass of the Holy Spirit. The Collectors of the *Scrutiny* remain by the high Altar to take care of the opening and the conducting of the *Scrutiny*, and to ensure that the *Scrutiny* proceeds in order. The last *Scrutiny* Collector then takes these ballots one after another, and having shown them to the *Cardinals*, places them in another Chalice. If he finds more or fewer ballots than there are *Cardinals*, he burns all those that are in both chalices, and each *Cardinal* rewrites his ballot again until the *Scrutiny* is recognized—if the number of ballots corresponds with the number of *Cardinals*, the *Scrutiny* is then made known. The Heads of the three Orders of *Cardinals* <note>Cardinal-Bishops, Cardinal-Priests, and Cardinal-Deacons</note> proceed to the high Altar, take the Chalice in which the ballots are, and set them on the table already mentioned. Subsequently, they step back, and the three Collectors of the *Scrutiny* go to sit at this table, their faces turned toward the *Cardinals*. The first Collector turns the chalice over on the table, opens the ballots at the place where the Vote is written, and views the name of the *Cardinal* who is chosen. As he opens them, he gives them into the hands of the second Collector, who also views the name, and he gives them to the third *Scrutiny* Collector, who reads the name aloud. Meanwhile, the *Cardinals* record the names of each on a sheet of paper, upon which the names of all the *Cardinals* are printed. Those who are named are taken from the *Cardinals* who are in the Council, and because the *Scrutiny* is not [finished] by the *Cardinals* of the Pope, so one gives ten must, as said, two days after the death of the Pope, and so are those who are in the Council...

<column-break/>

->PART I.<-
->Hh<-

Prelates then deliver a Latin oration <note>original: "Latynsche redenvoering"</note>, in which he exhorts the *Cardinals* to choose a worthy Person to once again occupy the seat of the Prince of the Apostles <note>referring to Saint Peter, the first Pope</note>. Subsequently, the *Cardinals* then go in procession into the *Conclave*, and such is in pairs according to their rank, accompanied...
All these ballots are threaded together by the last Collector, so that none of them may be scattered, and these threaded ballots lie exposed to the eye, until the last Collector [reads] each ballot, which the three Overseers inspect. When the Election is then found to be legal, all these ballots are burned. It is, however, permitted at that time to unfold them once, and one sometimes finds some bad faith among them. If the number of Votes does not satisfy the requirement, these ballots are kept to seek the Election of the Pope through the *Accessus* <note>original: "Accessus"</note> or the *Accession* <note>original: "Overkomt"</note>. In passing, it should be noted that the *Cardinals* seldom complete the *Scrutiny* without this *Accession*, and that it is almost unheard of for the Pope to be elected by the first [vote] alone. The *Accession* then serves to immediately improve [the tally]. One gives one's Vote through additional ballots upon which one writes "I accede to the Lord [Name]" <note>original: "Accedo Domino"</note> etc., when one adds his Vote to someone, or one stays with his first item. With the *Accession*, one acts exactly as with the *Scrutiny*, except that one does not repeat one's oath. The Collectors examine the ballots of the *Accession* just as they do those of the *Scrutiny*, and the *Cardinals* likewise note the Votes that are cast for the eligible Members.
The use of the *Accession* has its origin in the ancient manner of deliberating in the Senate of Rome and among others, where each Senator who was in the election, and so to speak, the election, as when he [made] the election. Since they do not move from their places, saying "I accede to the opinion" <note>original: "Accedo ad Sententiam"</note> etc.
After the *Cardinal* Overseers have very accurately examined the Votes of the *Accession*, and it is found that the Election of the Pope is entirely legal, three Apostolic Protonotaries are summoned to the Chapel where the Election was held, who draw up the Certificate of the Election regarding the investigation of the ballots and other documents, which the Collectors of the *Scrutiny* and the Overseers have handed over to them. All the *Cardinals* who attended the *Conclave* sign and seal this Certificate, after which the three Collectors, in the presence of all the *Cardinals*, burn the ballots of the *Scrutiny* and the *Accession*.
A Pope is also elected by *Compromise* <note>original: "Compromis"</note> or *Delegation* <note>original: "Verblyf"</note>, when the *Cardinals* cannot agree on the Election, [they] surrender themselves through this delegation to *Cardinals* of proven integrity, and recognize as Pope him whom they, by virtue of this power surrendered to them, shall choose.
The Election by *Inspiration* <note>original: "Inspiratie"</note> or *Divine Prompting* <note>original: "Ingeeeving"</note> is in some ways irregular. Some *Cardinals* of various...

...then this note comes. *Subsequently, they hide the note in their hand and then take their places: after which the **Scrutiny** <note>original: 'Scrutin'; the formal voting process</note> begins in this manner. Each **Cardinal** takes between the thumb and forefinger of the right hand the note which he has written and folded, and holding it aloft so that it can be seen by the other members of the **Sacred College**, he carries it before the high **Altar**. He kneels on the first step of the footstool, performs a silent prayer, soon thereafter climbs the remaining steps of the **Altar**, and takes the **oath**: subsequently, he lays his note upon the cover which covers the **Chalice**, and lets the note slide from the cover into the **Chalice**, subsequently blessing himself as he returns to his place. The <term>Infirmarians<note>original: 'Krankbezorgers'; officials appointed to collect the ballots of Cardinals who are too ill to leave their cells</note></term> attend to this for the **Cardinals** who are sick; which proceeds thus: they offer these **Cardinals** the prepared **Scrutiny** notes alongside a box that has only a small opening, into which the sick man puts his note, and it remains closed until the box is opened again. The **Infirmarians** bring the box to the **Chapel**, open it in the presence of other **Cardinals**, and subsequently place the notes in the **Chalice**, just as has been described.

Before one begins with the **Scrutiny**, the **Sacristan**, who is always of the **Augustinian** order, says the **Mass** of the **Holy Spirit**. The **Scrutineers** of the **Scrutiny** remain by the high **Altar** to take care of the mixing and opening of the notes that are in the **Chalice**, and to ensure that the **Scrutiny** occurs in good order. The last **Scrutiny Scrutineer** then takes these notes one after another, and having shown them to the **Cardinals**, places them in another **Chalice**. If he finds more or fewer notes than there are **Cardinals**, he burns them all in both **Chalices**, and each **Cardinal** rewrites his note again until the **Scrutiny** succeeds. If the number of notes corresponds with the number of **Cardinals**, the **Scrutiny** is made known as follows. The Heads of the three **Orders** of **Cardinals** proceed to the high **Altar**, take the **Chalice** where the notes are, and set them on the table already mentioned. Subsequently, they step back again, and the three **Scrutineers** of the **Scrutiny** go to sit at this table, their faces turned toward the **Cardinals**. The first... is, and inspects the name of the **Cardinal** who is being chosen. As he opens them, he presents a sheet of paper upon which those of all the **Cardinals** [have] the names of each... who have chosen the Pope, and they then give the **first** who... no number must be at least, as has been said, two-thirds of the whole.*

<column-break/>

All these notes are threaded together by the last **Scrutineer**, so that none are scattered, and these threaded notes lie open to the eye until the last **Scrutineer** places them in the empty **Chalice**. After the ending of the **Scrutiny**, one counts the notes once more, which the three **Overseers** inspect. When the **Election** is then found to be legal, one burns all these notes. It is, however, then permitted for those to discover the **Votes**, and one **sometimes** finds some unfaithfulness therein. If the number of **Votes** does not satisfy the requirement, these notes are kept to seek the **Election** of the **Pope** through the **Accessus** or the **Transfer** <note>original: 'Overkomst'; referring to the *Accessus*, a procedure where a cardinal could change his vote to another candidate</note>. In passing, it should be noted that the **Scrutiny** is seldom completed without this **Accessus**, and that it is almost unheard of for the **Pope** to be elected by the first alone. The **Accessus** serves then to immediately improve [the count]. One gives his **Vote** through another **Accessus** by which one also writes "I accede to Lord..." <note>original: 'Accessus Domino'; the formal Latin opening for changing a vote</note> etc., when one [changes] his **Vote**, or one holds to his first **Item**. With the **Accessus**, one acts exactly as with the **Scrutiny**, except that one does not repeat the **Oath** again. The **Scrutineers** examine the notes of the **Accessus** just as one does those of the **Scrutiny**, and the **Cardinals** likewise record the **Votes** that have been cast for the eligible **Members**.

After the **Cardinal Overseers** have more accurately examined the **Votes** of the **Accessus**, and it is done, three **Apostolic Protonotaries** come, who [prepare] the **Writing** of the **Election** regarding the examination of the notes and other documents, which the **Scrutineers** of the **Scrutiny** and the **Overseers** hand over to them, after which the three **Scrutineers** in the presence of all the **Cardinals** burn the notes of the **Scrutiny** and the **Accessus**. One also elects a **Pope** by **Compromise** or **Submission**, when the **Cardinals** cannot agree on the **Election**, surrendering themselves through this **Submission** to **Cardinals** of proven integrity, and recognizing... divisions and those who have decided to venture everything, make a stir of acclamation as if prompted by **Inspiration**, saying, *such a one is Pope*. They venture this choice when they believe they have gained enough **Votes** <note>original: 'Remmen'; likely a typo for 'Stemmen'</note> to carry out their interest. The **Adoration** or **Worship** is not different from the **Inspiration**. It occurs when two-thirds of the **Conclave** have agreed to recognize someone from among them as **Head of the Church** through **Adoration**. The **Election** by **Compromise**, **Inspiration**, or **Accessus** remains.

As soon as a **Pope** is elected, his **Household** and the **People** have the habit of plundering the **Cell** of his stay in the **Conclave**, and this looting extends over the **Palace** of the **Cardinal** elevated to the **Papacy**.

# HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

<margin>Observations on the behavior of the Cardinals in the Conclave.</margin>
Surrounded by Swiss Bodyguards and an immense crowd of people, while the choir masters sing the *Come, Creator Spirit* <note>original: 'Veni Creator'</note>. Having entered the **Conclave**, the **Cardinals** take possession of the Cells assigned to them by drawing lots; after which they go together to the **Pauline Chapel** (a), where the reading of the **Bulls** <note>official papal decrees</note> concerning the election of the **Pope** takes place. The **Dean** of the Sacred College exhorts this distinguished Assembly to confirm them. The reading and exhortation being finished, the **Cardinals** have the freedom to go and eat together, though on the condition that they must be back in the **Conclave** by three o'clock at night. The **Master of Ceremonies** informs them that they should not allow themselves to be locked in the **Conclave** if they do not intend to remain there for its duration, as the **Bulls** expressly command. Whoever then leaves may not enter again. The **Governor** and **Marshal** of the **Conclave** place their soldiers in order—whom we shall describe later in a more appropriate place—for the security of the Election. The **Ambassadors** of the **Powers**, and all who have an interest in the election of the future **Pope**, have permission to remain in the **Conclave** for the first twenty-four hours (b), and it is then that, without any regard for the **Holy Spirit**, the <term>intrigue<note>original: 'kuiperye'; refers to the political maneuvering and secret deals between factions</note></term> (c) begins, and such negotiations whose secrets are difficult to fathom. After those who do not belong to the **Conclave** have departed, the doors are closed, and after they are sealed, guards are placed at all entrances. The **Cardinal Dean** and **Cardinal Chamberlain** conduct a search throughout the **Conclave** to see if everything is properly closed, and a Certificate of this is drawn up by the hand of an **Apostolic Protonotary**.

<column-break/>

<margin>Which offices are held in the Conclave.</margin>
At that time, no one is in the **Conclave** except the **Cardinals** and two <term>Conclavists<note>personal assistants who live in the Conclave to serve the Cardinals</note></term> for each **Cardinal**, one ecclesiastical person and one layman. Sometimes a third is granted to **Cardinal Princes** and to old or infirm **Cardinals**. The other persons and servants appointed for the service of the **Conclave** are the **Sacristan**, the **Under-Sacristan**, a **Secretary** and **Under-Secretary**, a **Jesuit** as **Confessor**, two <term>Physicians<note>original: 'Artisten'; here meaning doctors of medicine</note></term>, one **Surgeon**, two **Barbers**, an **Apothecary** and his assistants, five **Masters of Ceremonies**, an **Architect**, a **Carpenter**, and six laborers or servants to do the heaviest work.
<margin>What a Conclave of Cardinals is like for enjoying income.</margin>
<margin>Which offices are in the Ecclesiastical State.</margin>
Although (d) the office of **Conclavist** is very heavy (e) and uncomfortable, it is sought after because of the advantages it gives. The **Conclavist** can renounce a certain sum of income he holds over privileges, and this sum is regulated by the privilege which the elected **Pope** grants to the one making the transfer. The office also carries the right of **Citizenship** in whichever city one chooses in the **Ecclesiastical State**. Besides that, the **Pope** after his election has a sum of money counted out to the **Conclavist**: but these advantages are nevertheless minor compared to other benefits that the status of **Conclavist** brings. They serve as means to know what is going on in the **Conclave**, and with "Italian ingenuity," to skillfully sound out the inclinations of the **Cardinals**. Sometimes a **Conclavist** acts as a secret Agent for the State Ministers of the Great **Powers**. Nevertheless, the officials of the **Conclave** take an oath not to reveal the secrets.

(b) Until three o'clock at night. For at that time, the **Master of Ceremonies** rings the bell. Everyone must then depart, except those necessary for the service of the **Conclave**, and then the entrance is walled up.
(c) As soon as a **Pope** is elected, the **Cardinals** let their thoughts turn to a successor. The plans are drawn and the foundations for them laid during the actual Papacy. If someone has his eye on the **Papal Throne**, he must carefully hide his thoughts from his simple labor until he reaches the Cardinalate. If the Reader is eager to know what makes an eligible candidate, and how one must behave to be recognized as such, he should read the *Portrait of the Conclave* printed in the year 1676; the account of the *Roman Court by Cursario* and the *History of the Conclave*; or if he desires, the *Tableau of the Roman Court by Aimon*, who copied the aforementioned writers word for word.

The **Conclavist** must fetch food and drink twice a day; he must serve his Master at the table, and take care that everything is kept clean." "He must also serve himself, to say nothing of other inconveniences tied to such a narrow confinement. Since one sees the daylight only through half-walled windows," "and where the warm air, due to the length of time, strongly attacks the constitution of the body."

RELIGIOUS DUTIES etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH.

# CHAPTER VII.

->Of the Order observed in ROME while the CONCLAVE is held.<-

<margin>
How the Governance of Rome was conducted during the Sitting of the Conclave.
</margin>
To prevent all disorder (a) that might occur during the vacancy of the See <note>The period known as 'sede vacante' when there is no sitting Pope.</note>, the Governor forbids anyone who does not belong to the Guard to carry weapons, both by day and by night. Heavy penalties are set against the violators of the Laws. Three Cardinals are chosen, as already stated, who are called the Heads of the Order of the Sacred College <note>original: 'Sacro Collegio'</note>*, to take care for the well-being of the City; and the Governor is obliged to be accountable to them. These three Cardinals manage judicial matters and common revenues: and in a word, everything that concerns the business of the State.

The Secular and Regular Clergy of Rome must make a daily Procession to St. Peter's Church, to implore God for assistance in the Election of his Vicar. They must go around the Vatican, singing (b) *Come, Creator Spirit* <note>original: 'Veni Creator'</note>.

<margin>
How and when the Cardinals go to the Chapel of the Scrutiny.
</margin>
When the Conclave is closed, the last Master of Ceremonies goes through the entire Conclave three times in an hour, and rings once with a bell at six o'clock in the morning and twice after the midday meal, to invite the Cardinals to the (c) *Chapel of the Lord* <note>original: 'Capellam Domini'</note>. When the Cardinals hear the last ringing, they go out of their cells followed by their <term>Conclavists<note>The personal assistants and secretaries permitted to stay with the Cardinals inside the locked quarters.</note></term>; of whom one brings the inkstand to the Chapel of the <term>Scrutiny<note>original: 'Scrutin'; the formal voting process by written ballot.</note></term>, and the other carries the surplice and the cap of his Master. The Cardinal puts on this surplice at the entrance of the Chapel; however, this garment has no resemblance to that which he uses in other ceremonies. It is a kind of <term>armosine<note>A type of light, plain-woven silk fabric.</note></term> mantle with a long tail, resembling a monk's choir robe, and which is fastened with a breast-hook.

<column-break/>

<margin>
The Chapel and the apparatus described.
</margin>
We shall describe this Chapel (d) to satisfy the reader's curiosity. In this Chapel, one sees the Last Judgment by *Michelangelo*. (*Nodot* places it in the Pauline Chapel.) The floor and the stalls where the Cardinals take their places are covered on both sides with green cloth. The Dean of the Cardinals sits on the left side of the entrance, and the first Deacon opposite him on the right side. We have already said that a long table stands before the Altar, and that on this table one sees two dishes or basins, in which the printed slips for the *Scrutiny* and <term>Accession<note>original: 'Accessus'; a procedure where a Cardinal could change his vote to support a candidate who had received votes in the Scrutiny, to hasten the election.</note></term> are. Likewise, in the center of the table one sees two chalices for the slips; a bag in which the last of the Cardinal Deacons puts the lottery balls to draw the lot for the Scrutiny's Collectors, the Attendants to the Sick, and the Overseers; and the Plate of the oath that the Cardinals must take before placing the slip in the chalice.

HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

<margin>...usually held in the Vatican.</margin>considering the Cardinals enclosed therein, who are maintained at the expense of the <term>Apostolic Chamber<note>The central financial board of the Papal administration, responsible for the Pope’s temporal properties and the expenses of the Holy See during an interregnum.</note></term>. * The Conclave is not tied to any specific location, and history provides us with examples (a) of how it has been held in various places. The ecclesiastical institutions allow the Cardinals to choose the location of the Conclave: nonetheless, it is always held in the Palace of St. Peter or the Vatican, due to the size of the building and the convenience of water, open spaces, and galleries, which can contain the great number of servants who must come and go twice a day for the service of the Cardinals. The size of the site for this Palace and the proximity to St. Peter's Church, where these ceremonies must take place, obliges the Cardinals to choose the Vatican to hold the Conclave.

The Conclave is an assembly of cells (b) small in scope, made of fir wood at the expense of the Apostolic Chamber; in which the Cardinals take up their residence while they work on the election of a Pope. Each cell has a partitioned area for the <term>Conclavists<note>The personal assistants, secretaries, or doctors allowed to remain with a Cardinal inside the locked Conclave.</note></term>. They are numbered and drawn by lot, as we have already stated. In the galleries and the halls of the Vatican, they are all placed in a row: but in such a way that a narrow space separates them from one another. The Cardinals who were favorites of the deceased Pope decorate them at their own expense with violet-colored fabrics, and the others with green 

<column-break/>

serge. The chairs, the table, and the bed are decorated with the same fabric. Each Cardinal has his coat of arms placed above the door of his cell. Between the cells and windows is a long gallery to provide daylight to the entire Conclave. The cells receive it through the glass windows that are to the side of the gallery. † The depiction of such a cell is shown to the reader in the plate indicated below.

<margin>And guarding by day and night</margin>The Swiss Guards who protect the door of the Vatican keep a good watch there from the outside day and night, and block off the passage of the galleries that open onto St. Peter’s Square with planks. A guard is placed at this barricade. On the Square, a military guard is maintained under the command of the General of the Church, who is usually supported by the College of Cardinals. He has his residence in the Vatican, next to the Prelate who is the Governor of the Conclave. At the Castel Sant' Angelo is another military guard, whose soldiers are raised by the Marshal of the Church (c), who furthermore places sentries around the Conclave, and especially at the gate by the (d) seven towers, through which the food is brought in to the Cardinals.

One may never speak to the Cardinals, nor to any others enclosed in the Conclave, except at set times and hours, and even then only loudly in Italian or Latin.

Before the food for the service of the Conclave is allowed through, the Prelate—

(a) The Conclave for Clement V was held at Perugia. *See History of the Conclave.*
(b) They measure ten feet square.
(c) This office belongs to the <term>Savelli family<note>A noble Roman family who held the hereditary title of Marshal of the Holy Roman Church and Guardian of the Conclave.</note></term>, through a <term>Bulla<note>An official papal decree or charter, named after the lead seal (bulla) attached to it.</note></term> granted to them by the Popes because the family is very ancient. While the See is vacant, the Marshal of the Church must keep watch day and night at the main gate of the Conclave.
(d) Let it be noted here that there is one main gate of the Conclave that is not opened except to let out Cardinals or their Conclavists when they become ill in the Conclave. The gate and the towers are provided with two locks, one on the inside and one on the outside. The outside keys are kept by the Prelate appointed as Governor of the Conclave, and those on the inside are under the care of the Masters of Ceremonies. The outside keys of the main gate are in the power of Prince Savelli, and those on the inside are in the hands of the Cardinal <term>Camerlengo<note>The Chamberlain of the Holy Roman Church, who acts as the administrator of the property and revenues of the Holy See during a vacancy.</note></term>, who also guards those of a small window, which is only opened for the audience that the Cardinals grant to the Heads of the Orders. There are also outside keys for this window, which are kept by Prince Savelli. Finally, as if all these external and internal locks did not provide enough security, an additional padlock is clamped on the inside of the main gate, of which the first Master of Ceremonies has the key.

# HISTORICAL TREATISE on the...
<note>The title continues from the previous page, likely "Historical Treatise on the Election of the Pope."</note>

<margin>Commonly held in the Vatican.</margin>
...considered as containing the Cardinals confined within, who are maintained at the expense of the <term>Apostolic Chamber</term> <note>The financial administration of the Holy See</note>. * The Conclave is not tied to any specific location, and history provides us with examples (a) of how it has been held in various places. Ecclesiastical institutions allow the Cardinals to choose the location of the Conclave; nevertheless, it is always held in the Palace of St. Peter or the Vatican because of the size of the building and the convenience of water, open spaces, and galleries, which can accommodate the large number of servants who come and go twice a day to serve the Cardinals. The size of the grounds for this Palace and the proximity to St. Peter’s Church, where these ceremonies must take place, obliges the Cardinals to choose the Vatican to hold the Conclave.

The Conclave is a collection of cells (b) small in design, made of pine wood at the expense of the Apostolic Chamber, in which the Cardinals take up residence while they work on the election of a Pope. Each cell has a partition for the <term>Conclavists</term> <note>The personal assistants or aides allowed to enter the enclosure with the Cardinals</note>. They are numbered and drawn by lot, as we have already stated. In the galleries and halls of the Vatican, they are all placed in a row: but in such a way that a single gap separates them from one another. The Cardinals who were favorites of the deceased Pope decorate them at their own expense with violet-colored fabrics, and the others with green <term>serge</term> <note>A durable wool fabric</note>. The chairs, the table, and the bed are decorated with the same fabric. Each Cardinal has his coat of arms placed above the door of his cell. Between the cells and windows is a long gallery to provide daylight to the entire Conclave. The cells receive light through the glass windows that are on the side of the gallery. † The image of such a cell is shown to the reader in the plate indicated below.

<margin>And occupied by day and night watches.</margin>
The Swiss Guards who guard the door of the Vatican keep a good watch there day and night from the outside, and board up with planks the passage of the galleries that lead out to St. Peter’s Square. A guard is placed at this barricade. In the Square, a military guard is kept under the command of the General of the Church, who is usually maintained by the College of Cardinals. He resides in the Vatican, next to the prelate who is the Governor of the Conclave. Near the Castle of St. Angelo is another military guard, whose soldiers are raised by the <term>Marshal of the Church</term> (c), who additionally places sentries around the Conclave, and especially at the gate by the (d) seven towers, through which food is brought in to the Cardinals.

One may never speak to the Cardinals, nor to any others enclosed in the Conclave, except at set times and hours, and even then only loudly in Italian or Latin <note>The text specifies these as the only permitted languages for communication to ensure transparency and prevent secret plotting</note>.

The keys from the outside are under the custody of the prelate appointed to be Governor of the Conclave, and those from the inside under that of the Masters of Ceremonies. The outside keys of the main gate are in the power of Prince Savelli, and those from the inside in the hands of the Cardinal <term>Camerlengo</term> <note>The Chamberlain, who administers the church during the vacancy</note>, who also keeps those of a small window, which is opened only for the audiences that the Cardinals grant to the Heads of the Orders. There are also outside keys for this window, which are under the custody of Prince Savelli. Finally, as if all these outside and inside locks did not provide enough security, an additional heavy padlock is bolted from the inside to the main gate, of which the first Master of Ceremonies has the key.

->RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH.<-

let the guard stationed at the Towers <note>original: "Torens"; these refer to the *ruote* or "turning-boxes" used to pass items into the secluded Conclave area</note> examine the same carefully, and take good heed that one does not, under this pretext, allow letters from Sovereigns or any other persons interested in the Election of the Papacy to slip through.

<margin>And with what ceremony it is delivered into the Conclave.</margin>
(a) "Daily at noon and around the evening, the Officials of each Cardinal come to the Square of St. Peter in their Master's carriages; having stepped out, they ask the Housemaster of the Conclave for their Master's meal, or they go to fetch it if he keeps his own private kitchen, and then carry the food to the Towers (b) of the Conclave in this Order. First, two of the Cardinal's grooms walk ahead, each carrying a wooden violet-colored staff with their Master's Coat of Arms. The Chamber Servant of the Cardinal follows with a Silver Staff in his hand, and the Noblemen follow in pairs with uncovered heads. After them appears the (c) Housemaster <note>original: "Hofmeester"; here referring to the *Scalco* or Chief Steward</note> with a napkin over his shoulder, accompanied by the Cup-bearer and the Carver. The grooms who follow him carry the Cardinal's Food and Drink with a hand-pole, from which hangs a large Kettle containing various Pots, Platters, Dishes, etc. Other grooms carry large baskets with wine bottles, Bread, Fruit, etc. Coming to the Tower, they call out the name of their Master the Cardinal in a loud voice, so that his Chamber-servant, being inside the Conclave, may come to receive the Food and Drink and have it brought by Laborers to the Cardinal’s cell. All this
<column-break/>
food is strictly inspected by the Prelate, who keeps watch outside the Conclave with the Maintainers of the Roman People <note>original: "Handhavers van 't Roomsche Volk"; officials responsible for city security during the vacancy of the Holy See</note>, to prevent any letters from slipping through. They may open everything as a precaution against fraud. The bottles and jars must be made of glass or crystal, without any covering, so that one may see what is inside: but this inspection is now not so strictly carried out, since all the precautions one can take do not prevent the Cardinals from finding a means to carry out their cunning and to know what is happening outside. There are those who, by means of a certain mixture, know how to hide several lines of writing drawn upon the skin of a capon <note>A castrated rooster, often served at feasts</note> without the inspectors noticing it: indeed, sometimes even the dishes and the food sent to the Cardinals serve as hieroglyphs or symbols <note>original: "Beeldschriften of Zinnebeelden"</note> that let them understand what is desired.
When the dishes have all been brought in, a precursor of the Pope, dressed in a Violet Coat and with a Silver Staff in his hands, closes the Tower-gate in the presence of the Prelate who also supervises the closing, and seals the lock with his signet ring; while the Master of Ceremonies does the same from the inside. As for the Prelates appointed to attend to this observation, they are sent from the college for that purpose; such as an Auditor of the Rota <note>A judge of the highest ecclesiastical court</note>, or a Clerk of the Chamber, a Protonotary, a Referendary, etc. They are subordinate to the Governor of the Conclave."

<margin>The kissing of the Pope's foot is an old custom.</margin>
As for the custom of kissing the Pope's feet, it is certainly very ancient. *Baronius* <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607) was an influential Italian Cardinal and church historian.</note> believes he finds an example of it (b) as far back as the year 204. It is subsequently found that the Emperor *Justin* I, Pepin King of France, Frederick *Barbarossa*, etc., have kissed the Pope's feet. Nevertheless, the exact time when this custom took hold is not known. Now we shall see how this refers solely to JESUS CHRIST, although it is generally regarded as a testimony of reverence that Christians bear toward his Vicar. I. One must then take note that His Holiness's Slipper is decorated with a cross, which is the symbol of the crucified JESUS CHRIST. To prevent the superstitious abuse of the People, who often subject themselves to a blind reverence, (c) the Successors of St. Peter, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, desire that their shoes and soles carry this cross on the upper leather; therefore, one does not kiss the Pope's feet: but the Cross of the crucified JESUS
<margin>How this foot-kissing is understood.</margin>

<column-break/>

CHRIST, and this is a clear proof that His Holiness (d) is the Servant of the Servants of JESUS CHRIST. II. Even if the Cross were not on the upper leather of the slipper, the excellence of the dignity would confirm the homage; and III. this is further confirmed by the Holiness of the absolute Papacy. One must then kiss his feet, just as one (e) kisses the Cross and the holy Images.

<margin>As also the adoration.</margin>
Adoration <note>In this context, "adoration" refers to *proskynesis* or deep veneration, rather than the worship reserved for God alone.</note> is relative to God. It is not for the Pope: but for JESUS CHRIST, just as (Mary and Magdalene) (f) threw themselves at his feet and adored him. We believe, however, without intending to offend the dignity of the Pope or the respect owed to the Holy See, that a part of the honor shown to the Pope derived its origin from that which was given to the (g) ancient Roman Emperors, whether they were regarded as High Priests—namely, Heads of the Religion of the Romans—or viewed as the Supreme Powers of the State: But we add at the same time that this honor is now considered rightful and necessary. Pope *Innocent III* said: *(h) that the Church, being the Bride of JESUS CHRIST and having Him in marriage, has brought him a perfect power over the Temporal and Spiritual; that the Mitre is the mark of the Spiritual, that the Crown is that of the Temporal, and that both signify to Christians that he is the King of Kings and Lord of Lords.*
<margin>How such honoring of the Pope is consistent with that shown to the Roman Emperors.</margin>

(a) Stephen II, elected Pope <note>reigned 752–757</note>, is the first who was carried on shoulders to the Church after his election. The Nobles of ancient Rome let themselves be carried in a sort of carrying-chair (*Lectica*) by their slaves. It is possible that the custom of carrying the Pope on shoulders was gradually introduced in Rome after the destruction of Heathenism. As for Stephen II, it appears from what Platina says that the dignity of this Pope was consistent with the honor of being carried on shoulders.
(b) <note>original: "Pedigna ad Caium Papam se contulit, ad pedesque procidens eos ex more exosculata est."</note> "Pedigna betook herself to Pope Caius, and falling at his feet, kissed them according to custom."

As a sign of spiritual things she bestowed the Mitre upon me; as a sign of temporalities she gave me the Crown; the Mitre for the Priesthood, the Crown for the kingdom: constituting me the Vicar of Him who has written upon his garment and his thigh, King of Kings and Lord of Lords."

<margin>*</margin>[Acolytes is an Ecclesiastical Word, derived from the Greek <term>ἀκόλουθος</term> <note>akolouthos</note>, which means
"follower"; because the Acolytes are like Ecclesiastical Servants who must follow the Bishop, who
light the wax candles, who carry the same, etc. But to derive this word from an older usage: The
Greeks gave this name to those who were unyielding in their decisions. For this reason the
Stoics were called Acolytes, since nothing could draw them away from their opinion. Since the Chris-
tian Church, this name has been consecrated, assigned to those who gave themselves over to the Ser-
vice of God. Anciently, youths yearned for this Ecclesiastical office, accompanying and serving the Bish-
ops: whether to follow them or to be witnesses of their conduct. This activity of following the Bish-
ops was assigned to the Acolytes; but today the ministry of the Acolytes is very different from
the first Institution. An Acolyte is the first and foremost of the four Mi-
nor Orders observed in the Church; whose work is to light the wax candles, as has already been said, to
carry the incense pot, to provide the wine and water for the Sacrifice and to perform other Altar services.
*Furetière* <note>Antoine Furetière (1619–1688), a French scholar and lexicographer.</note>.]

<margin>(a)</margin>Or in the chair in which he is carried. <note>original: *Nella Sedia gestatoria, nella quale era stato portato:*</note> "In the carrying chair, in which he had been carried:" thus
*Lunadoro* <note>Girolamo Lunadoro, author of a famous 17th-century guide to the Roman Court.</note> expresses himself.

<margin>†</margin>[The *Pallium* is a Priestly garment, specific to Popes, Patriarchs, and Bishops, which they wear over
their Priestly Vestment as a sign of jurisdiction. It is made band-wise to the width of three fingers,
hanging down over the shoulders like straps in front and behind, with small round lead plates
at the ends covered by black silk, and marked with four red crosses. It is made of white wool,
shorn from two lambs that the Clergy of St. Agnes offer annually on her Feast Day, while
the *Agnus Dei* <note>The "Lamb of God" prayer in the Mass.</note> is sung during the Mass. They are received by two Canons of the Church of
St. John Lateran, who deliver them to the Apostolic Sub-Deacons, who
care for their grazing and shearing. None but they may prepare these *Palliums*, placing
them subsequently upon the Bodies of St. Peter and Paul at the High Altar of their Church, before
which prayers are said the entire night. Some believe that Pope Linus introduced this custom, as
Eusebius of Caesarea says; and that, just as the Ephod was the sign of authority for the Priests in the Synagogue,
the *Pallium* likewise served this for the Christian Priests. Others are of the opinion that one finds
no mention of it until the Year 336. Still others believe that it was Constantine the Great
who granted this to Pope Sylvester, from whom this custom passed to the Patriarchs and Archbishops.

Formerly the Pope sent the *Pallium* to some Bishops under his subject Dioceses; the first of the
Bishops of France who received it was Vigilius, Archbishop of Arles, so that he would excel above the other
Bishops, on whose behalf Childebert II wrote to Pope Gregory, as Pas-
quier says. Some Archbishops have decorated their Coats of Arms with the *Pallium* like an Order's ribbon,
as it is a special mark of their dignity. Among the Greeks, all Bishops wore the
*Pallium*. In several ancient titles, a *Pallium* is spoken of which was a garment strewn with
crosses in rows; and Tertullian testifies that it was a garment of the Christians, which the Hea-
thens called the *Toga*. *Furetière*.]

<margin>(b)</margin>This is expressed in Latin as follows; <note>original: *Accipe pallium sanctam plenitudinem Pontificalis officii ad honorem omnipotentis Dei & gloriosissimae Virginis Mariae ejus matris & Beatorum Apostolorum Petri & Pauli & Sanctae Romanae Ecclesiae.*</note> "Receive the pallium, the holy fullness of the Pontifical office, to the honor of almighty God and the most glorious Virgin Mary his mother and the Blessed Apostles Peter and Paul and the Holy Roman Church."

<margin>(c)</margin><note>original: *Col Pallio indosso*</note> "With the Pallium on."

### RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc., of the ROMAN CHURCH.

<margin>
The Pope performs the Service of the Mass.
</margin>
...goes without a mitre to the Altar, sings or reads the *Introit* <note>original: *Introito*</note> and the *Lord have mercy* <note>original: *Kyrie eleison*</note>, etc. Having begun the *Glory to God in the highest* <note>original: *Gloria in excelsis*</note>, he returns to his place until the Prayer of the Mass is completed. At that time, the first Cardinal Deacon enters the Confession <note>original: *Biechtkamer*. This refers to the *Confessio*, the sunken area in front of the high altar where the relics of the Apostle are kept.</note> (a) of St. Peter. He is followed (b) by the Apostolic Subdeacons, as well as the Auditors of the Rota <note>Judges of the high papal court.</note>, the Consistorial Advocates, etc. All of these walk in pairs according to rank, wearing white surplices and violet ermines over the surplice. The Cardinal Deacon says softly (c) *Hear us, O Christ* <note>original: *Exaudi Christe*</note>, to which the clergy then answer him; (d) *To our Lord the Pope, decreed by God as High Priest* <note>original: *Domino nostro à Deo decreto Summo Pontifici & Papæ*</note> etc. The *Hear us* and the rest is repeated three times, as is the *Savior of the World* <note>original: *Salvator Mundi*</note>, which the same Cardinal then adds, and to which the clergy answer (e) *help thou him* <note>original: *tu illum adjuva*</note>. This is followed by the Litany of the Saints; the Latin Epistle follows the Litany, and the Greek follows the Latin: one being sung by the Greek Subdeacon and the other by the Latin. The Choir Masters who are in the choir sing the Gradual; a Cardinal Deacon sings the Gospel in Latin, another in Greek, and the Mass ends with ceremonies which we shall treat hereafter: but it must be known that His Holiness, after the Mass, places himself again in (f) his chair, without taking off the ornaments that served during the solemnity. Then the Cardinal Archpriest of St. Peter comes, accompanied by two Ca-

<column-break/>

-nons, and offers His Holiness a white damask purse, in which there are 25 *Julii* <note>A silver coin named after Pope Julius II.</note> of old currency, in recognition (g) of his having sung the *Mass* very well (h). His Holiness then gives this money to the Cardinal Deacons who sang the two Gospels, and these give it to their *Caudatarii* or train-bearers.

<margin>
Is carried to the Place of Blessing.
</margin>
Finally, the Pope is carried to the Place of Blessing, accompanied by his Cardinals and Prelates. The canopy under which he is carried is held up by the Conservators of the People and the *Caporioni* or ward masters: two grooms of the Pope, dressed in red, each hold at the side of the Holy Father's portable chair a fan made of peacock tails <note>term: *flabella*</note>. The Cardinals and Prelates stand upright, while the first two Cardinal Deacons, acting as assistants, help His Holiness onto the Throne, which the Sacred College had erected the day before in the middle of the room. As soon as the Pope is seated, the choir sings the *Anthem* (i), *A golden crown upon the head* <note>original: *Corona aurea super caput*</note> etc. with the responses to this chant; after which the Dean (k) recites the prayer of the coronation.

<margin>
And the triple crown put on.
</margin>
The second Cardinal Deacon removes the Pope's mitre, and the first places the triple crown (l) upon his head, saying to him: (m) *receive this Tiara adorned with three crowns, and forget not, while wearing it, that you are the Father of Princes and Kings, the Ruler of the World, and on Earth the Vicar of Jesus Christ our Savior*, etc. In-

---

(a) This is the place where the relics of the Martyrs rest, which is beneath the Altar.
(b) See *Lunadoro*.
(c) *Hear us, O Christ*.
(d) *Our Lord the Pope, High Priest appointed by God*.
(e) *Savior of the World, stand by him*.
(f) *Sella gestatoria* <note>The ceremonial portable throne.</note>. *Lunadoro*.
(g) This is called the *Presbyterium* in the Latin Church.
(h) *For the well-sung mass* <note>original: *Pro bene cantata missa*</note>.
(i) *The golden crown shall be placed on his head* etc.
(k) *God is prayed to, that he may grant the Pope grace to govern the Church with edification, as Father of Kings and governor of the Faithful, over whom God has set him*, etc.
(l) This is a cone-shaped cap adorned with three crowns, glittering with gemstones, and of an inestimable value. That with which Pope Paul II was crowned, although set with precious stones, did not exceed the value of the triple crown of Clement VIII, which was estimated at five hundred thousand pieces of gold. As for that of Paul II, he was the first of the Popes who judged that one should decorate his triple crown with stones. The successors of St. Peter were thereafter very eager to raise the value of the same even higher with precious jewels, to decorate the Papal cap therewith. That of Martin V was provided with five and a half pounds of pearls, and weighed besides that, fifteen pounds in gold. That of Paul V was of even higher value. Nothing is more just than this, says P. *Bonnanni*, who serves us these details in his book *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* <note>original: *Hierach. Eccl.*</note>, since the Pope governs Christ’s Kingdom as his Vicar and Vice-Regent: this Kingdom now incomparably surpasses all the Kingdoms of the world. The High Priest of the Jews wore upon his head treasures that corresponded with the Divine Majesty. The Pope represents the same for the Savior of the World, and nothing is better expressed here than by valuable things. The Priests of the Heathen deities also wore costly crowns: it would then be unjust to refuse a similar apparatus to the one who is the first Priest of the Christian Religion. Let us not forget to say, that the two bands <note>The *lappets* or *infulae* hanging from the back of the tiara.</note> of the Papal cap represent the two different interpretations of Holy Scripture, one according to the mystical and the other according to the literal sense.
(m) *Receive the Tiara adorned with three crowns and know that you are the Father of Princes and Kings, the Ruler of the World, the Vicar on Earth of our Savior Jesus Christ* <note>original: *Accipe Tiaram tribus coronis ornatam & scias te esse Patrem Principum & Regum, Rectorem Orbis, in Terra Vicarium Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi*</note> &c.

## CHAPTER XII.

->*The TAKING POSSESSION by the POPE, and with what CEREMONY this is conducted at the CHURCH of ST. JOHN LATERAN.*<-

<margin>With what a magnificent pageant the Pope takes possession of St. John Lateran.</margin>After the Pope is crowned, he must go to take possession of his Supremacy in his Head Church at St. John Lateran, the first of the mother churches (b) of the Ecclesiastical State and the entire extent of Christendom <note>St. John Lateran is the official cathedral of the Bishop of Rome, outranking even St. Peter's Basilica in ecclesiastical status.</note>. This Solemn Taking of Possession <note>Known in Italian as the "Possesso."</note> occurs a few days after the Coronation, in the most solemn and magnificent manner imaginable. (c) It appears from the *Roman Ceremonial* that this formerly took place on the same day as the Coronation, which was commonly observed in the following order:

(a) Before the led horses <note>original: "Tel-Paerden"</note>, the *Roman Ceremonial* places a hand-horse, twelve Papal Couriers <note>original: "Cursores Papæ"</note> dressed in red, walking in pairs, each carrying a red banner. After them follow the Banner-bearers of the Roman Districts <note>original: "Vexilliferi Capitum Regionum"</note> also dressed in red. These Banner-bearers are followed by the Banner-bearer of the Roman People, those of the Teutonic Order, those of the Pope, those of the Church, and finally those of St. John of Jerusalem <note>The Knights Hospitaller.</note>.
(b) For the Titled Nobles, the *Master of the Chamber* <note>original: "Maestro di Camera"</note>, corresponding with the adjacent illustration titled: THE POPE GOES IN A SOLEMN PROCESSION to take possession of his PAPACY in the Church of ST. JOHN LATERAN, the Head Church of all Churches of Christendom under the Supreme Authority of the POPE. The external Chamberlains, etc. go, after which he places the four Chamberlains who carry the four Papal hats. The *Roman Ceremonial* has them follow the twelve led horses. The *Abbreviators* etc. follow in the *Master of the Chamber* after these four Chamberlains who carry the four Hats.
(c) They carry the same on certain staves covered with red velvet, says the *Master of the Chamber*, as the *Roman Ceremonial* also does.
(d) This is presented to us quite differently in the *Account of the Court* <note>original: "Relatione della Corte"</note>, etc.
(e) Dressed in a large cloak and a wide-brimmed hat <note>original Italian: "Vestito con mantellone e capello largo"</note>, that is, with the priestly overcoat, and on the head a broad-rimmed hat.
(f) A triple-barred Cross <note>original: "drie kruisselings Kruis"</note>, which is a sign of the Pope's Spiritual Jurisdiction over the entire globe. It is believed that Pope Sylvester I was the very first to have this cross carried openly before him. This custom, however, was not followed until Leo IV, who reintroduced it. The Cardinal Deacon who announces the election of a new Pope to the people shows them the cross at that time.
(g) After the Sub-Deacon and those accompanying him, the *Roman Ceremonial* has twelve men follow on foot, dressed in red, each carrying a burning wax candle before the Holy Sacrament. Two others on horseback, also dressed in red, immediately follow the Sacrament, each having a silver lantern in hand. The Holy Sacrament is carried on the back of a white led horse, and the horse has a bell attached. Fourteen Roman citizens carry the Canopy in turns. The Sacristan follows, seated on horseback, with a white staff in his hand, etc. We shall give a broader account of this procession when we describe how the Holy Sacrament is carried when His Holiness travels elsewhere.

(a) The Pope is not always carried in a litter. According to the *Roman Ceremonial*, he is seated on a white pacing horse, with eight noblemen carrying the *Baldachin* <note>a ceremonial canopy</note>. A King, or even the Emperor himself, if he attends this ceremony, is obliged to hold the stirrup for His Holiness and lead the horse by the bridle. See *Ceremon. L. 1.* If the Pope is carried in a litter, the Emperor must be one of the carriers: but only for a moment, as he is immediately relieved. The eight noblemen who carry the canopy are also relieved by eight Roman citizens until they reach St. John Lateran.

(e) While the procession moves forward, money is thrown in some places among the people to push back the crowding a little; <note>original: "ad pressuram imovendam"</note> ("to remove the pressure"), says the *Roman Ceremonial*.
(f) See the *Tableau of the Roman Court*.

After the cross is kissed, the mitre is placed on the Pontiff, and the crown is given into the hands of the auditor. > *...it might seem more like he is lying down; to whom the Cardinals soon approach and honorably lift him up, saying: He raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dung, that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory. <note>original Latin: "suscite de pulvere egenum & de stercore erigit pauperem..." — a reference to 1 Samuel 2:8 and Psalm 113:7</note> Rising, the Pope takes from the lap of the Chamberlain assisting him as much money as a fist can hold, where however there is absolutely no silver or gold, and scatters it among the people, saying: Silver and gold have I none, but what I have, I give to you. <note>original Latin: "Argentum & aurum non est mihi..." — Acts 3:6</note> ---- with the Canons preceding and singing, "We Praise Thee, O God." <note>original Latin: "Te Deum Laudamus"</note> The Pope with the Cardinals enters the Church and, kneeling before the high altar on a faldstool <term>faldstool: a portable folding chair used by high-ranking clergy</term> without a mitre, prays for a short while. Then rising, he blesses the people saying, "Blessed be the name of the Lord" etc. Then ascending with the mitre to the high seat, sitting he receives the Lateran Canons for the kissing of the foot. Then ---- he ascends to the Lateran Palace through the gate which is in the Church, and when he has arrived in ---- the Hall of the Council, the Pope sits in the seat prepared for him by the stone table at the head of the hall which is called the "Measure of Christ" and ----- the praises being finished, the Pope proceeds to the Chapel of Saint Sylvester. There, before the door of the chapel, are two perforated porphyry <term>porphyry: a very hard, purple-red stone used since Roman times for imperial monuments</term> seats --- the Pope sits upon the first --- The Prior of the Church approaches and, with bended knee, gives the Pope the staff into his hands, a sign of correction and rule, and the Keys of the Basilica and palace, as a sign of the power of closing and opening, of binding and loosing. The Pope then rises ---- and sits in the other porphyry seat on the other side, and there returns the staff and keys to the same Prior, and by him is girded over the mantle while sitting with a certain red silk belt, with a silk and red purse, in which are twelve precious stones with musk. Then the Pope, girded and sitting, takes silver coins from the lap of the Chamberlain ----- and scattering them over the people says: "He has distributed, he has given to the poor, his righteousness endures forever and ever." <note>original Latin: "Dispersit, dedit pauperibus..." — Psalm 112:9</note> Then the Pope is led to the Holy of Holies, where he prays kneeling on a faldstool without a mitre. Then rising with the mitre, he returns to the Chapel of Saint Sylvester. There he sits upon the seat prepared for him; then he puts aside the mitre, gloves, pallium <term>pallium: a narrow band of white wool worn over the shoulders</term>, and mantle, and takes up the cope and simple mitre, and sitting he gives the Presbyterium <note>a traditional distribution of money to the clergy</note> in this manner: to the Cardinals, two gold coins and two silver groats. The Cardinals come and bow their heads low before the Pope, and hold out an open mitre, in which the Pope puts the money. Having received the money, they kiss the Pope's hand. ---- Other Prelates kneel before the Pope and receive in a mitre one gold coin and one groat, and kiss the Pope's right knee. Yet other Prelates and officials receive as much in their hand and kiss the foot, etc.*

This extract from the Ceremonial contains many particulars that may now perhaps be abolished or changed, since the author of the account of the Roman Court and its Ceremonies, already cited by us, says nothing of it. Therefore, for the service of our countrymen, we translate the most remarkable particulars of this Ceremony, to present them in our language to the curious reader. The first Canon (Archpriest) of St. John Lateran offers His Holiness the Cross to kiss. The Cardinal Deacon, after having lifted the Princely Hat from the Pope, brings it to His Holiness's mouth; having kissed the Cross, the Mitre is placed back on him. The Sovereignty (this is the Papal Crown) is placed in the hands of an Auditor. Then His Holiness is led to a Gate on the left side, which the Ceremonial calls *Stercoraria* <note>meaning "of the dung-heap," a reference to the humility required of the Pope</note>. He is made to sit there in a chair, and in such a way as if he were half lying and sleeping. Some Cardinals then approach, lift the Pope up again, and say: *He lifts him from the dust who is needy, and the poor from contempt, to be placed with the Princes on the Throne of glory.* The Pope, who is this needy poor man, having straightened himself up, throws a handful of money among the People, in which however there is no silver or gold, saying: *I have neither Silver nor Gold, but what I have, I give to you.* We would not dare to say that this application is quite fitting; for it could be contested with reason. Then His Holiness goes into the Church, preceded by the Canons and accompanied by the Cardinals; he blesses the people and receives the canons at the foot-kiss. After this the Pope is carried to the Palace of St. John Lateran. His Holiness having arrived in the hall of the Council, the Praise etc. is sung. From there one goes to the Chapel of St. Sylvester and finds before the Door of the Chapel two perforated* seats. Here the Holy Father goes to sit; when he is seated in the first seat, he is handed the Keys and a Rod <term>Dutch: "Plak" — a ferule or rod used for discipline</term>, as a sign of his authority and masterly discipline; seated in the second he hands the Rod and the Keys over to the first Canon, or Archpriest, who girds the Pope with a silk belt to which a Purse with twelve precious stones is attached (which undoubtedly represent the 12 Apostles) and some musk. The Chamberlain attending this ceremony gives the Pope some pieces of money which he throws among the people, saying: *he has scattered his goods, his righteousness endures into all eternity.* From there the Pope goes into the Holy of Holies to offer his prayer. Then having returned to St. Sylvester's Church, he distributes some commemorative medals and other gold and silver pieces to the Cardinals, Prelates and lesser Clergy, who then show His Holiness their homage, each according to his rank.

(a) The Pope is kneeling, *But our Lord [the Pope] is kneeling. Relaz. della Corte &c.* cited before. <note>original Italian: "Ma lo nostro signore inginocchione"</note>
(b) The gold Key indicates the absolute power of forgiveness, and the silver that of striking with the Ban <term>excommunication</term>. *Casal de Veter. Chr. rit.* The reason he gives is that silver is less in power than gold. Stately reasoning.
(c) And also sprinkles himself. ibid.
* Called *Stercoraria*.

### XIII. CHAPTER.

->*Of the* PAPAL STATE VESTMENTS, *and of what they consist.*<-

<margin>In what the Papal Solemn attire consists.</margin>
**A**s soon as the Pope is elected (a), they put on him the choir dress of white linen, and adorn him with red cloth slippers, on which a gold cross is stitched, a priest's cape * <note>original: "Prieſterſkap"</note> of red velvet, a red silk girdle with gold hooks, a choir-gown † <note>original: "Koor-rok"</note> and a red bonnet. Subsequently one gives him (b) the priestly head-covering, ‡ the alb ¶ of white linen whose edges consist of red silk ribbon, and the stole § decorated with pearls. If the Pope is a priest or bishop, they hang this stole around his neck; but if he is nothing but a deacon, he must have it on the left shoulder; and if he is a sub-deacon, one gives him none.

If the New Pope (c) is not enrolled in any order, they must confer it upon him; if he were only a deacon, and desired to be established as a priest, they confer the priesthood upon him, and subsequently consecrate him as a bishop (d). ,,This ,,Solemnity is performed in the Chapel of Sixtus ,,by the Cardinal Dean, who ,,is always Bishop of Ostia, and to whom

<column-break/>

,,it has for some time belonged, to consecrate the ,,Pope.

<margin>The Pope's ordinary attire described.</margin>
When his Holiness is in his private and usual attire, (e) he wears a choir dress of white silk, an outer garment of fine linen, a cape of red velvet or deep-red satin. In winter the Pope covers his head with a lined bonnet, and in summer with a satin cape. During Lent, Advent, and fast days, the Pope wears a white wool choir dress with a cape of red cloth: but from Holy Saturday until the following Saturday he wears a white damask cape.

<margin>And in which he performs Mass and dresses at certain times.</margin>
His Papal vestments are of two kinds. When he performs the Mass, he is, besides the choir dress, provided with an outer gown, the priestly head-covering, the white linen alb, the stole, the maniple ¶, the mass-vestment or chasuble, ‡ the mitre, the gloves etc. All these garments correspond with the excellence and dignity of the Vicar <note>original: "Stedehouder"</note> of JESUS CHRIST and the Successor of St. Peter: but the color

<meta>catchword: color-</meta>

---

(a) *See Relazione etc. Table of the Roman Court. Cerim. Eccl. Rom. etc. cited here before.*
* [*Called Mozetta*; it is a piece of fabric just like the clerical garment of the Franciscans, hanging down roundly over the shoulders and before the breast.]
† [*Called Rochet*, being a Bishop's or Abbot's linen choir-garment with narrow sleeves, like those of an alb, commonly well starched and decorated with lace.]
(b) *Cerim. Eccl. Rom. L. I*
‡ [*Called Amice*, a blessed square piece of linen which the clergy cover on the head when they dress with the alb. The priests, deacons, sub-deacons and acolytes serve at the altar with it.]
¶ [The *Alb* is a white linen garment which hangs down to the feet, with which the priests, deacons and sub-deacons are clothed under their choir-garment, and likewise the clerks who serve the altar.]
§ [The *Stole* is a Bishop's garment to represent the supremacy of the Church. The priests also wear it over the *alb* to sing the Mass. It is a broad fabric band set with three crosses, which hangs from the neck to the feet. The stole was among the ancient heathens a tunic and a more feminine than masculine dress, which nevertheless the kings also used. The use of the stole was introduced into the Church at the same time as the alb. *Furetière*.]
(c) *Cerim. Eccles. Rom. ibid. L. I.* (d) *Table of the Roman Court.*
(e) *Relaz. della Corte di Roma &c. di Lunadoro.*
¶ [The *Maniple* is of a clerical use which the ministers, as priest, deacon, and sub-deacon, carry on the left arm. It is a small band three or four fingers wide, just like a small stole, and of the same fabric as the chasuble.]
‡ [*Chasuble* is an ecclesiastical ornament, which the priest pulls over his alb, when he shall perform the Mass. The chasubles of the ancients were entirely round, and tucked up to the shoulders, whereas they are now split at the sides. *Furetière*.]

His Holiness celebrates (a) in red the Feast of Pentecost <note>original: "Pinxter Feeft"</note> and that of the Martyrs; in white the Easter Feast and all the Feasts of the Holy Virgins; in violet the Lenten season, Advent, and everything pertaining to fasting; in black on Good Friday and in Masses for the dead. # XIV. CHAPTER.

## *Of the* ORDER *and* CEREMONIES *which are observed when the* POPE *holds* CONSISTORY; *according to the Roman Ceremonial of the Year 1516.*

---

<margin>
The arrangements and order in the Consistory described, and in what rank one takes their place.
</margin>
This Ceremonial (d) gives us the following account of how the Pope holds Consistory to receive Sovereigns and their Envoys; to consecrate a Saint <note>canonization</note>; to treat of weighty matters, whether Spiritual or Secular; for the elevation of Cardinals, etc. When this Consistory is to be held, the Papal Throne is erected in the Great Hall of the Apostolic Palace, which is nearly square and about twelve palms (e) wide. One ascends it by three steps. The Pope is seated in a Chair covered with cloth of gold or some other similar fabric, under a canopy (f) of the same fabric, to correspond with the excellence of the Seat. The elevated place is (g) covered with red cloth. The Cardinal-Bishops and Cardinal-Priests place themselves on the right side (h) be-

<column-break/>

low the Throne: the Deacons on the left side, such that they all have their faces turned toward the Pope. Between the seats of the Cardinal-Bishops and Priests next to those of the Deacons, there is a sufficiently large space (i) to have free access.

When the Pope is to hold a public Consistory, he goes there mitered and dressed in the Priestly vestments: the Alb, Stole, and the red Chasuble <note>original: "Kafuifel"</note>, preceded by the Cross and the Cardinals. This state procession having arrived in the Hall of the Consistory, the Pope places himself on his Throne, and the Cardinals subsequently having seated themselves in their Chairs—after first having shown their mutual reverence to His Holiness, as the Archbishops, Bishops, Protonotaries, and other Prelates also do—they seat themselves on the steps of the Throne (k); on

---

> (a) One symbolizes by red the fiery tongues spoken of when the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles, and the blood of the Martyrs of JESUS CHRIST; by white the joy that the Resurrection of our Savior awakens in the hearts of the believers, and the purity of the holy Virgins whose Feast is celebrated; by Violet the pale color of those who fast, observing the Vigils and the abstinence of Lent as the Church has instituted them; by black the mourning that the death of JESUS CHRIST works in the hearts of Christians, etc. It is of no small weight to be ignorant of these things, which, being neglected, leave a great unworthiness in the devotion of some godly people.
> (b) *See Tableau of the Roman Court.* (c) Idem. ibid.
> (d) *Roman Eccles. Ceremonial* <note>original Latin: "Cerimon Eccles. Rom."</note> Book 1. Section 9. Chapter 1.
> (e) A palm is an Italian measure of eight inches or thereabouts.
> (f) "Above the head shall hang a golden cloth." <note>original Latin: "Supra caput pendebit aureus pannus."</note> ibid.
> (g) "The whole floor... shall be covered with scarlet cloth." <note>original Latin: "Planum totum... cooperium erit panno coccineo."</note> ibid.

RELIGIOUS DUTIES etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH. 259.
Kk 2

On lower steps sit the Sub-Deacons, the Auditors, the Clerks of the Chamber, and the Acolytes or Sacristans <note>original: "Kofters"</note> with their wide woolen robes; below on the ground (a) <note>Latin: "Super terram inter sedilia Cardinalium" — On the ground between the seats of the Cardinals.</note> between the Chairs of the Cardinals, the Ecclesiastical Officials (b) <note>Latin: "Curiales togati" — Gowned officials of the Curia.</note> of the Papal Court take their places. The Chamberlains and Private Secretaries are also seated on the ground, between the Prelates and Ecclesiastical Officials. The nephews of the reigning Pope, if there are any, and several other Roman Princes remain on either side of the Papal Throne; for which reason they are also called Princes of the Throne. The Ambassadors and officials of other Princes are placed on the right side of the Throne, between the steps and the wall. In this way, the Nobles of the first rank and other noblemen are also placed on the left side next to the officials (c) <note>Latin: "Familiares" — Members of the household.</note> of the Pope's Household. The Consistorial Advocates remain behind the Cardinal Deacons, and the Procurators of the Princes with the Fiscal Procurator stay behind the Cardinal Bishops; the Fiscal holds his rank after the other Procurators. The entrance to the area leading to the Throne is occupied by the Pope's Bodyguard. The Master of the Sacred Hospice remains between the Bodyguard and the end of the row of Cardinal Priests. The Clerks of Ceremonies are placed at the beginning of the Deacons' seating, to be more ready to carry out the Pope's commands. When His Holiness holds a Consistory regarding legal matters, the Advocate places himself behind the Cardinal Priests opposite the Pope. After he has explained his case, he lays his petition (d) <note>Latin: "Cedulam suae Supplicationis inter sedentes in terram curiales projicit" — He casts the scroll of his petition among the officials sitting on the ground.</note> down with the Ecclesiastical Officials, who take it up and place it in the hands of the Vice-Chancellor. When the Consistory is then finished, the oldest Cardinal Deacons step forward to escort the Pope, and this Apostolic Assembly returns in the same order as it had come.

Throne has no steps: it consists of nothing more than a kind of footstool (e) without elevation, except only to appear slightly larger. When the Ecclesiastical Council consults on matters of State or Church, everyone (h) must leave, except the Cardinals, and when the votes are taken (i), he who has given his vote must stand up.
