HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

after the Messengers <note>original: "Lopers"</note> have made this known to the Sacred Society, they notify the Consistory once more by a proclamation at the door of the Apostolic Chancery. By a Decree of the Congregation of Rites <note>original: "Vergadering der Kerkgewoontens"</note> of February 16, 1630, the Post-messengers are forbidden to announce the Consistories, Chapels, and Church Assemblies, etc., to anyone other than the Cardinals.

<margin>As also the semi-secret history and what is treated therein.</margin>
Besides the Public and Secret Consistory, a semi-secret one is also held. In the Secret Consistory, Dioceses are proposed, the qualifications of Bishops are considered, the Pallium <note>A woolen vestment bestowed by the Pope upon archbishops</note> is granted, and the mouths of the Cardinals are closed and opened <note>A ritual where the Pope symbolically restricts and then grants a new Cardinal the right to speak in meetings</note>, etc. This Consistory is held every fourteen days on Mondays. But the semi-secret Consistory usually meets for matters that primarily involve the Ecclesiastical state, such as disputes His Holiness might have with the secular Powers. In such cases, only the persons interested in the matters of dispute are admitted to this Consistory to speak, either themselves or through their officials. Counsel is also taken there regarding the Canonization of deceased Saints, etc.

The Pope (a) appears in the secret Consistories wearing the choir robe of white silk, the surplice, the Mozzetta or priestly hood, the Stole, and the Bonnet of red velvet stitched with silver, or of deep red satin likewise embroidered, if it is in the Summer, and slippers of red cloth, as we have already described.

After the Consistory is closed, and the Cardinals have had an audience with the Pope, they must (b) wear the choir robe over the outer garment, so that they are entirely covered by it. If a Cardinal enters when the Consistory has already begun, (c) he shows a humble

<column-break/>

reverence for the Pope as soon as he has reached the middle of the Meeting Hall, after which he greets all the Cardinals of the Consistory, beginning on the right side, while they stand as he greets them.

<margin>What reasons for appropriation Bonanni gives regarding Papal splendor.</margin>
We must not forget to present here the reason cited by a (d) notorious Theologian of the Roman Church, brought forward by *P. Bonanni* <note>Filippo Bonanni (1638–1725), a Jesuit scholar and scientist</note>, to justify the magnificent decorations and clothing that distinguish the Vicar of JESUS CHRIST from the rest of mankind. This is because, just as God made himself known to men through the Incarnation, so the Popes let themselves be known through their vestments. From this, one must necessarily conclude that the Papal Supremacy must dress in a special manner, and that his clothes must be magnificent and of great luster; therefore, it is required that the People be inwardly convinced by splendor and worldly decorations that he who wears them is the true Prince of the Church and the Successor of St. Peter. For, as *P. Bonanni* (e) says well, following the Apostle Paul: *the natural man <note>original: "dierlyke mensch," referring to 1 Corinthians 2:14</note> does not understand the things that are of the Spirit of God; but he knows the invisible things through those which are visible.* We are furthermore obliged to consider that if the Pope is regarded as (f) *King of Kings, Lord of all Lords, and only Prince of Christians*; if one sees that his (g) authority extends further than that of the mightiest Emperors, and that he restrains the Faithful by his decrees, one can no longer doubt that the Pope must be distinguished from the people just as the greatest Monarchs are distinguished from theirs. One must be a Jansenist <note>A follower of a Catholic theological movement often opposed to Papal centralization</note>, or at least a Calvinist, not to agree with this proposition.

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc., of the ROMAN CHURCH.

<margin>Breviary Service is.</margin>
holy readings (a) instituted by the Church, to be read daily at certain hours by the Clergy. To this Service the name of *Canonical Church Prayers* has been given, as it is ordained by the institution of the Church, which has prescribed not only the hours to practice them, but all the circumstances that one must observe. Nevertheless, they are not the same in all Churches. This Service is also called the *Breviary Service*, due to an old word which some believe was instituted when the Service was shortened <note>The word "Breviary" comes from the Latin *breviarium*, meaning an abridgment or summary</note>: since it was formerly much longer.

The Clergy, appointed for the edification of Christians, find their first obligation is to join in reciting from their *Breviary* or *Books of Hours* <note>original: "Getyboeken"</note>, namely, to pray to God for the Church, to religiously chant the Divine Services to awaken the zeal of piety in the souls of Christians and to give spiritual comforts to those entrusted to them. If they are occupied in these Holy duties, it follows necessarily that they do not give themselves over to the cleverness of politics and State affairs, which draw man away from God and turn him into an unrestrained Courtier. The *Breviary book* does not accord with the pleasant Courtesies that the Clergy often wish to possess as part of their amusements when they devote themselves to the young ladies <note>original: "Juffers" — a critique of worldly priests who preferred social climbing to prayer</note>.

The Service must, according to the Order of the ancient Church, be performed while standing: one only kneels on days of penance. Those who have described the Ceremonies of the Church say (b) that kneeling signifies sadness and dejection: but standing signifies joy and the lifting of the Spirit to God. This posture also indicates the resurrection, which is the subject of the Christian faith.

<margin>How the Service of Hours is conducted.</margin>
The Service (c) consists of seven hours, counting *Matins* <note>original: "Vroegmetten"</note> (d) and *Lauds* <note>original: "het Lof"</note> (e) as one, and eight hours in division. In the first Centuries of the Church, there were only six divisions, which for the day were *Terce*, *Sext*, and *None* <note>original: "Derde, Zesde, en Negende"</note> (f), and for the night

<column-break/>

the Evening Prayers, those of midnight, and those of the morning. Now they have been divided into seven or eight. *Matins* for the night, *Lauds* for the break of day, *Prime* <note>original: "Eerste"</note>, *Terce*, *Sext*, *None* for the Day, *Vespers* for the Evening, and *Compline* <note>original: "Lofzangen"</note> (*) for the coming of Night. Those who have written about these Church customs maintain that *Matins* represent what occurred in the Night of our Savior's passion, and that *Lauds* or Thanksgiving is ordained in honor of the *Resurrection* of Jesus Christ. *Prime* is for reflecting on the indignant mistreatment that the Savior suffered in the house of Caiaphas. The Service of *Terce* is primarily instituted to thank God for the Sanctification of the Church by the Holy Spirit. *Sext* honors the crucifixion of our Savior. *None* is because of the mystery of His Death, which occurred at this hour. *Vespers* honor His coming, which according to the chant of the Church, shall happen *at the Evening of the World* <note>A poetic reference to the Second Coming of Christ</note>. The hour of *Compline* is instituted to implore God for His protection during the night, just as one prayed for it at the First hour before the day. The true hour to pray Matins is at night. The Thanksgiving or Lauds, which has been practically incorporated into Matins, is said with the rising of the Dawn.

These two Services have taken the common name of Matins, which are performed at the end of the night. The hour of *Prime* is as soon as the Sun rises, why it is called the *First*, since the ancients calculated the Day from Sunrise and divided it into twelve hours, which were unequal according to whether the Days were found to be longer or shorter; likewise, *Terce* was the third hour of the Day, and corresponded with the ninth hour of the equinoxes; *Sext* was at the sixth hour of the Day and always at noon; *None*, at the ninth hour, or about three o'clock in the afternoon; *Vespers* was in the Evening and *Compline* after Sunset. On this

Sext, Chapter 10 of the same Book, and None, Chapter 3. Vespers or Evening service in the Savior's Last Supper, etc. The Canonical hours must certainly have originated from Judaism. The Pagans also had their Morning services. The Egyptians went to greet their Gods in the morning. They had first, second, and third tide-hours, which we call first, third, and sixth, etc. *Du Choul on the Religion of the Ancients.*

# HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

at the designated time, one then observed the Services (a).

<margin>And who is obligated to observe them.</margin>
Not only were the Clergy who belonged to the sacred Orders <note>Refers to those ordained as deacons, priests, or bishops</note> found to be bound; but likewise (b) the Monks and Nuns, along with all those who held any Offices, were obliged to observe this Service. All who were negligent in this committed a mortal sin, and were required to pay back the income from their Ecclesiastical Offices <term>benefice: a position in the church that provided an income</term>, unless they held other positions independent of these Ecclesiastical Offices, or unless (c) excusable obstacles justified the omission of these Evangelical works. However, a clever Priest understands the limits of his duty very well and extricates himself from mortal sin through detours of which pious souls are ignorant.

This Service must take place in the Church before the Holy Sacrament, or in a place of prayer, or elsewhere suitable for that purpose.

<column-break/>

Attention—or the total dedication of heart and soul—is highly necessary to accompany this Service, so that the practitioner cannot be accused of honoring God only with his lips. Thus, it is the honor of a Priest or Clergyman, almost like a Law, to perform this Service at the appointed hours to fulfill his post and not to grow weary in his prayers; therefore, he should show with attentiveness what his duty requires before God and the World. The books that treat this subject must discuss the attention that must accompany the reading or the recitation of the prescribed *Book of Hours* <note>original: "Getyboek"; a book containing the prayers for specific times of the day</note>. They explain the various types of attention one can have during the recitation, and many other things necessary for Parish Priests and Clergy, who often find opportunities to employ them as little as they can.

### CHAPTER XVI.

->On the use of CEREMONIES in the PAPAL CHAPEL.<-

<margin>How it is customary to hold Mass annually in the Papal Chapels, and by whom.</margin>
Forty (d) Papal Chapels <note>Refers to the formal liturgical gatherings or "stations" where the Pope or his representatives celebrate Mass</note> are usually held each year to say Mass, of which the Pope has the custom of observing three himself. Thirty are sung by the Cardinals, and seven by the Archbishops and Assistant Bishops. It is (e) on Easter Sunday, Pentecost, and Christmas Day that the Pope performs the Mass, provided he is not prevented by any illness. The other thirty-seven Chapel Masses are performed in his presence on Feast Days, as designated in the *Pontifical* <note>A liturgical book containing the rites performed by bishops or the Pope</note>. It would be

<column-break/>

unnecessary and superfluous to present a Register of them here.

"There are five Matins <note>original: "Vroegmetten"; the earliest prayer service of the daily cycle, often held in the middle of the night or at dawn</note> sung in the Papal Chapel: namely, the day before the birth of our Savior <note>Christmas Eve</note>, the three days of Holy Week which are called the *Dark Matins* <note>original: "donkere Metten"; also known as Tenebrae, characterized by the gradual extinguishing of candles</note>, and the second day of November, which is appointed for the Service of all the deceased <note>All Souls' Day</note>. The Cardinals take turns singing the lessons of the Matins on Christmas Night; but the others are sung by Music Masters.

"...the Pope and Cardinals attend the first Vespers <note>Evening prayers</note> in the Chapel; but the second Vespers are never sung in the presence of the Pope. There are ten occasions indicated in the *Pontifical* <note>A liturgical book containing the orders for rites performed by bishops</note> that he is accustomed to attend. All these 'Chapels' (a) are commonly held in the Apostolic Palace, and in the *Pauline* Chapel when the Pope is at *Montecavallo* <note>The Quirinal Palace</note>; likewise in the *Sistine* Chapel when he resides in the Vatican, except on Easter Sunday and the Feast of St. Peter, when he goes to the Church of this Saint <note>St. Peter's Basilica</note>, as well as on the day of the Assumption of Mary, when he is carried in magnificent procession to *Maria Maggiore*, and on other occasions when he departs from the Vatican and *Montecavallo* to visit certain churches or great halls in Rome.

When the Pope goes to 'hold Chapel,' he is carried in an armchair to the bedchamber where the vestments are kept; but once dressed, he steps into another chair, (b) carried on the shoulders of twelve of his grooms <term>palfreniers: papal footmen or grooms</term>, wearing red coats that hang down to their heels. When he goes to St. Peter’s, the canopy is carried by the Knights of St. Peter, while two other palfreniers, dressed in the same way, walk before him, each (c) carrying a large fan of peacock feathers <term>flabellum: a ceremonial fan made of feathers</term> at the end of two poles, which are attached to the armrests of the carrying-chair. Thus, the Pope, seated in this chair, appears to have two wings at his shoulders, which are constantly moved by means of the two poles as he passes through. This entire apparatus is covered with flowered fabric and decorated with gold embroidery.

On the Sundays of Advent and Lent, the Pope goes to his Chapel on foot as a demonstration of penance. On the third Sunday of Advent <note>Gaudete Sunday</note> and the fourth of Lent <note>Laetare Sunday</note>, he allows himself to be carried, as these days are set aside for a privileged expression of joy.

When the Pope goes on foot from the Sistine Chapel to the Pauline Chapel, carrying the Sacrament during the 'Forty Hours' <note>A period of continuous prayer before the Blessed Sacrament</note>—on the first Sunday of Advent and on the Thursday before Easter, for the tomb—the two eldest Cardinal-Deacons support his arms. A personage of great distinction, (d) if such a one be present, carries the train of his choir robe behind him; and two Apostolic Protonotaries <note>High-ranking papal legal officers</note> hold up the edges and fringes from the front.

When the Pope himself celebrates the Mass, the Cardinals dress themselves in ornaments of white damask trimmed with gold lace, with this distinction: the Cardinal-Bishops wear the rochet <note>original: "Koorkleedt"; a white vestment resembling a surplice</note> (e), the Cardinal-Priests wear the chasuble <note>The outermost vestment worn for Mass</note>, and the Cardinal-Deacons wear the tunicle <note>A vestment worn over the alb</note> with the mitre of white damask, just like all the other Cardinals. The Bishops also wear rochets: but while those of the Cardinals are white, those of the Bishops consist of precious silk fabrics, multi-colored and embroidered with gold; however, their mitres are made only of white linen. This Divine Institution has fortunately been passed down to us. The Apostle James recommended the use of fans in his Liturgy, to be found among the *Constitutions of St. Clement*. It is true that few readers are unaware that these *Constitutions* are attributed to this Clement: but be that as it may, one must know that since the Seraphim covered themselves with their wings before the face of God seated on the Throne, so it can be sufficiently granted to the Pope—who is a 'Sub-God' <note>This term reflects an archaic, highly elevated view of the Papacy</note>—to faintly imitate this divinity, allowing himself to be fanned with peacock feathers; thus his dignity stands out before the eyes of the Christian people. We have here made use of Suarez’s own expressions. We must also not forget to say that he assures us that the song, or rather the scream, of the peacock drives away snakes. The peacock is an image of Jesus Christ and the snake that of the Devil.

> It is doubted whether St. Peter and his successors until Sylvester I had the custom of having the Cross carried before them. 

We also doubt it, and assume with reason that this Apostle and his first successors paid no heed to Ceremonies; if they did use any, however, it could only have happened in secret, since they lived under Princes who were sworn enemies of Christianity. How; would they not have taken it as a sort of contempt against their religion if the Cross had been carried in public? Furthermore, it is clear that the Apostles and their disciples applied themselves solely to the institution of the Church. Those who later thought of Ceremonies already took pleasure in them.

One will find, he says, that Clement I introduced many customs, and among others ordered that whenever the *Supreme Pontiffs or their legates went out representing their office, they should have the banner of the Cross before them*; from which one could conclude that this custom was introduced about 70 years after Peter. If one must follow these thoughts, it appears from this that one would have to believe that the Popes who sat before Clement did not [carry the cross] in public...

HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

The Confessors <note>original: "Biechtvaders"; likely referring to the Penitentiaries of St. Peter's</note> etc., who otherwise must follow the Cross, go after the Pope. III. The Cardinals follow immediately after the cross, and so forth.

When his Holiness goes to hold Chapel in other Churches, the procession does not differ from what we have already described. One proceeds in the same order from the Robing Room to the Church, where first of all one offers one's heart to God before the consecrated body of JESUS CHRIST <note>The Eucharist</note> which is upon the Altar.

One likewise follows the same order when the Head of the militant Church <term>Militant Church: a traditional term for the Christian Church on earth, seen as engaging in spiritual warfare</term> presents himself as an example of humility in the Chapel of Sixtus <note>The Sistine Chapel</note>, allowing himself to be carried there in a sedan chair: for if he goes there on foot on other days, it is a day specifically set apart for a more prominent return to God, as occurs during Lent etc., or when, as has already been mentioned, his Holiness then performs penance. The Pope then walks leaning upon two Cardinals. A *Protonotary* <term>Protonotary: a high-ranking official of the Papal court</term> holds up the fringes of the choir robe from the front, and if a Prince is present, he must carry the train of this sacred garment.

# CHAPTER XVIII.
## The PAPAL CHAPEL described according to P. BONANNI, and the Order in which it is held.

<margin>The internal arrangement of the Papal Chapel described, and the order in which it is held.</margin>
We have drawn this description from the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* (a) or Church Governance by the Reverend Father *Bonanni* <note>Filippo Bonanni (1638–1725), a Jesuit scholar and scientist</note>, and added to it an illustration of the Chapel arrangement engraved in copper in Rome. The numbers indicate the rank held by those who are obliged to attend, whether due to their Dignity or their Office: but before we proceed to that, it will be necessary to give the Reader a concept of this sacred Assembly, and how the Chapel is internally composed of the following parts.

I. The place (b) where the Throne stands is elevated, where his Holiness places himself before the Altar and to the side of the Gospel.

II. The Seats of the Cardinals which are placed around the Altar and the Throne; as well as those of the Envoys and Prelates.

III. The square space (c), which extends before the steps of the *Presbyterium* <term>Presbyterium: the part of the church reserved for the officiating clergy</term>, and is enclosed by the aforementioned seats. This space is intended for the Clergy and Officials (d) of the Pope. The Palatines find no place there.

IV. There is a (e) partition which separates this sacred Court from the people. One places there approximately four, six, or seven lights, according to the requirements of the solemn day.

V. The vestibule is between the square (*Septum*) beneath the steps of the *Presbyterium*. Here the (f) Chamberlains and Lawyers remain.

VI. The aisle runs from the door all the way to the Altar.

VII. The Choir is intended for the Music.

VIII. The Oratory, where the Altar is located. There stands a chair (g) for the Celebrant.

<margin>What spiritual meaning one may derive from the use of the</margin>
The Altar is provided with seven Candlesticks (h) with wax candles: a hidden number which is confirmed by solid reasons. The use of lights was by the...

(a) This description is to be found in Chapter 126 of his Book.
(b) <note>Latin: "suggestum sive Thalamus locus elevatus ubi sedes Pontificis ampla, Solium sive Thronum dicta &c."</note> A raised platform or chamber, an elevated place where the large seat of the Pontiff, called the Seat or Throne, etc. [is located].
(c) *Septum* <note>Enclosure or partition</note>. (d) *Togati Curiales* <note>Gowned officials of the court</note>. (e) *Cancelli* <note>Lattice-work or screens</note>. (f) *Cubicularii Togati* <note>Gowned Chamberlains</note>.
(g) *Faldistorium*, or an armchair <note>A faldstool or folding chair used by a bishop</note>. It is said that this portable seat, which belongs to the ministry of the Bishop, represents his dignity and his power along with the respect owed to him. We owe this precise investigation to the learned *Casalius* <note>Giovanni Battista Casali (1578–1648), an Italian antiquarian</note>, who wrote on the ecclesiastical customs of the Christian Church. It is also he who discovered the independence of the Church in the image of the Episcopal chair. He informs us that this chair has no backrest nor support, and from this he concludes that this chair represents the Church, having no visible support. To wit, that according to the opinion of this Prelate, it in no way depends upon men, and that it must acknowledge absolutely nothing but the authority of JESUS CHRIST, Lord of the World, who subsequently handed over his temporal Kingdom to St. Peter and his Successors.
(h) The Lamps and Wax Candles, which illuminate the Religious mysteries, have often provided oil and wax for various miracles, as *Casalius* testifies in his book on the church customs of the ancient Church. Demons were driven out by them, the dead raised, and the sick healed. This Prelate also assures us that the light of the wax candles is the symbol of the light of the Gospel, which dispels the darkness of unbelief and ignorance. Father *Bonanni*, who provides us with the material for this description, cites a passage from Macri from which one can conclude that the seven Candlesticks indicate to the Bishop that he must be adorned with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; and this thought is, in his opinion, all the more justified as the Church Fathers held the same regarding the Mosaic Candlestick <note>The Menorah</note>.

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH.

instituted by the Apostles, who had borrowed it from the Jews, as Cardinal *Baronius* <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607) was an influential Italian cardinal and church historian.</note> remarks. One must have at least two candlesticks on the Altar: but when one has four, they represent the four Evangelists, who enlighten the Church through their teaching; it was for this reason that ancient writings gave the form of the four beasts of Ezekiel <note>Referring to the four "living creatures" in the vision of Ezekiel 1:5-10, traditionally associated with the Evangelists Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.</note> at the feet of the candlesticks, which served to light their Spiritual Ceremonies. On certain solemn days, six lights are placed on the High Altar of some Churches. This is done in imitation of the six branches of the Mosaic candlestick mentioned in the 25th chapter of *Exodus*. A Bishop performing his service with the greatest magnificence has seven wax candles to light him. The Cross (a) must be placed before the middle wax candles, yet higher than the candles: but with regard to the Altar in the Papal Chapel, although there are already seven wax candles on this Altar, seven Acolytes <term>Acolytes: altar servers who assist the priest and carry candles in procession</term> precede the Cross and the Deacon (b) who is to sing the Gospel, each holding a wax candle in his hand. When the Pope sings the Mass, seven others are added, and in the Vespers, six.

<margin>Regarding the use of the Cross on Altars, as observed.</margin>
Regarding the Cross which is set before the wax candles, it is of an ancient custom and brought down to us from the times of the Apostles through Tradition, according to the opinion of *P. Bonanni*, so that the Priest performing the service of the mystery of the Mass *may always have the suffering of* JESUS CHRIST *before his eyes, of which the Cross and the offering of the Mass are the images.* It is Cardinal *Bona* who expresses himself thus. This is a proof which must convince us that the Cross is an essential part of the spiritual service offered on the Altar, and it worked the miracle which *P. Gretzer* (c) recounts here in memory: *A Spanish Priest was to perform the Mass for a person of rank; but having forgotten the Cross, he did not dare to complete his service. An Angel, seeing the Holy and Godly Father distressed, sought a Cross for a long time and placed it on the Altar in the sight of all the people standing about.* This Cross is now carefully preserved and

<column-break/>

remains for the faithful a venerable subject of wonder.
Pope (d) *Innocent III* was advised to place the Cross directly in the middle before the seven candlesticks, to give Christians the idea of following Christ between the Jews and Heathens, whom he has united in the same Church.
The Papal Throne, indicated by the second numeral, stands to the side of the Gospel <note>The "Gospel side" is the left side of the altar as viewed by the congregation.</note>. This place is not only attached to the absolute Papacy, but also to the Bishop (e), when the Altar stands near the wall of the Chapel where he performs the service.
The Militant (f) <term>Militant Church: the Christian church on earth, struggling against sin and spiritual enemies</term> Church is the living image of the Triumphant Church <term>Triumphant Church: the church in heaven, having achieved victory through Christ</term>. In the latter, JESUS CHRIST is seated on a Throne and the Elders are placed on seats less elevated than the Throne of Jesus Christ. In the militant Church, the Head of the universal Church and the Bishop (who represents the head of the Church in his Diocese) must occupy the first place. Others occupy places of lower rank, which are around the Altar and the Episcopal Seat, each according to the office he holds in the Ecclesiastical government. St. Peter's Chair, which has miraculously endured (g) through time and is so carefully preserved in the great Hall of the Vatican, will undoubtedly maintain the idea of how he was seated in the Church until the end of the ages.

<margin>In which the mysteries of this ceremony are indicated.</margin>
If one may believe the Mystagoguists <term>Mystagoguists: writers who interpret the hidden or symbolic meanings of religious rites</term>, there is no Church custom which does not contain a mystery within itself. They believe that a good Catholic can, with the eyes of Faith, discover an infinity of essential truths that are invisible to the eyes of the carnal Man <note>original: "dierlyken Mensch," literally "animalistic man," referring to one without spiritual insight</note>. These mysteries shine through everywhere in that which relates to the Ecclesiastical government. We are assured that this government carries out nothing without reasons drawn from the purest part of Christianity, and justifies those spiritual aims which men of meager judgment might perhaps view as human caprice: it is with such precision that the

# HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

colors of the Seats according to the solemn nature of the Day.

<margin>How and why the Papal Seats must be elevated.</margin>
The custom (a) of covering the Papal Throne and the Episcopal Seats with precious dyed fabrics (b) is very ancient. *Baronius* <note>Cardinal Cesare Baronius, as noted previously, was a key historian of church traditions.</note> finds this already introduced in the first centuries of the Church. It also appears that since the times of *Augustine*, the Prelates placed themselves in Chairs that were meant to excel above others, and which were undoubtedly also more comfortable and stately. However it may be, it is certain that the Governors of the Church sat higher than others, so that they could oversee the Congregation and also be seen by them. This arrangement is so natural that it is unnecessary to dwell longer upon it; yet we still observe among the ancient Christians how the Papal Throne has always been more elevated than the other Chairs, and that it does not occupy the same place in his Holiness's Chapel today as it did in the early Christian Churches. It was once in the middle of the semi-circle of the apse, as was the Altar, such that the Pope had his eye on both the Altar and the people. The Seats of the Clergy were arranged on either side; as is evident in the Churches of *St. Clement* and *Nereus* <note>The basilicas of San Clemente and Santi Nereo e Achilleo in Rome, famous for their well-preserved early medieval layouts.</note>, where the Seat of the Bishop is elevated three steps above the other Chairs that surround it.

Let us say one more thing regarding the Papal Seat. We have seen how it was covered with precious silk fabrics, and we shall add that when it was made of marble, it was adorned with carved sculpture. On Good Friday, all its magnificent coverings are removed from the Pope’s Chair; for on that day, his Holiness attends the Pious Service in a garment of mourning and penance, namely, in a coarse red woolen choir robe <note>In the Roman rite, red is the color of the Passion and martyrs, here used to show the Pope's humility as he mourns the death of Christ.</note>: laying aside to some extent the highly esteemed dignity of Jesus Christ’s Vicariate, to mourn in all humility the death of the Savior of the World.

The (c) Canopy is also found in use among the ancients. It enhances

<column-break/>

the splendor of the Pope's Majesty. This Canopy is nearly as large as the one erected above the Altar.

The third numerical figure indicates the benches placed on either side of the Chapel, serving for the Cardinals who attend the Ceremonies of the Chapel, wearing red or violet choir robes according to the Service of that Day.

The Chairs, covered with carpets and elevated by steps, are indicated by the numbers 4. Here it is that the Train-bearers of the Cardinals sit, wearing violet choir robes, when their Eminences put on the Mitre.

For this Papal Chapel (b), there are also two Clerks, formerly called *Bell-Clerks*. The reason for this name is unknown, as the use of bells was of no use in this Chapel; all that can be guessed is that they were perhaps called so because they pulled the hand-bell to give the signal to the Music Masters who, at the same

<column-break/>

time, had to sing in the Service, just as was done for the clergy of St. Peter's Church. They might also have been named thus because, when His Holiness travels with the Holy Sacrament, they sound this hand-bell. This is found in an old book of Church customs from Avignon. Be that as it may, when the Clerks accompany the Host <note>original: "het Hoogwaardige," a Dutch reverential term for the Eucharist</note> during a journey of the Pope, they must be dressed in red; but in the Chapel, they arrive in violet with surplices. One of these Clerks must necessarily be a Priest, so that, having dismounted from his horse, he may subsequently carry the Holy Sacrament to the Altar whenever it is required to perform the service during the Pope's journey.

Likewise, they are also charged with accompanying the horse with a lantern in hand; decorating the altar; lighting the wax candles; covering the Altar tables (c); preparing the seat for the Celebrant †; arranging the benches; providing the cushions; dressing the assistants; managing the censer; and handing the water and wine as required for serving the Mass, etc.

<margin>What service the Clerks are to perform.</margin>
We believe that the reader, upon reading this description, will not form a biased judgment against the careful regularity observed in all the spiritual exercises we describe here; yet we can tell him that the piety of many people would appear entirely confused if even the smallest of the Church customs usually observed during their pious actions were omitted. For example, there may be some whose devotion is satisfied by the change of colors in the vestments with which the Celebrant performs the Service. One can lift the heart to God more easily when red takes the place of violet. The magnificent display of the Vicar of JESUS CHRIST—who during His stay on Earth was the humblest of all men—strikes some others. An Altar adorned with its decorations; a Priest in his solemn robes and finery, and all

HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

...further ceremonies serving to [prepare] the Mass or Priest, and to say with contempt, prepare us for the greatest of all the mysteries. One becomes so accustomed to this that one does not even think of the mysteries, if the Priest is solemnly dressed, or if any Ceremonies are forgotten. If the practice of turning and winding like a *Dervish* <note>A member of a Muslim religious order, known for devotional practices like the "whirling" dance.</note>, or those who measure the land with their bodies for several miles, as certain Faquirs † of the Mughal <note>Refers to the Mughal Empire in India.</note> do out of religious devotion, had been introduced into the Christian Religion for several centuries, it is to be suspected that one could get used to it. It is He himself who offers himself through the Priest's hands. # EXPLANATION
## Of the four following
# ILLUSTRATIONS,

->Showing<-

->The **CEREMONIES** of the **LOW MASSES**,<-
->in thirty-five **Representations**, alongside<-
->The **CORRESPONDENCE** with the **PASSION** of the **LORD JESUS CHRIST**.<-

I. Jesus Christ goes to the Mount of Olives; this represents when the PRIEST goes to the ALTAR.
II. J. C. offers his prayer in the Garden of Gethsemane; this represents the START of the PRIEST'S MASS.
III. J. C., throwing himself down, sweats blood while being in anguish; this represents the PRIEST'S CONFESSION <note>original: "BELYDENIS"; refers to the *Confiteor*, where the priest acknowledges his sins at the start of the service.</note>.
IV. J. C. betrayed by Judas; then the PRIEST kisses the ALTAR.
V. J. C. captured and bound; then the PRIEST goes to the side of the EPISTLE <note>The right side of the altar from the viewpoint of the congregation.</note>.
VI. J. C. led to Annas; represents the INTRODUCTION <note>original: "INLEIDING"; refers to the *Introit*, the opening chant or prayer of the Mass.</note> of the Mass.
VII. Peter denies J. C. three times; then the PRIEST says the Lord, have mercy <note>original: "KYRIE ELYSON".</note>.
VIII. J. C. looking at Peter, who weeps for his sins; then the PRIEST turns toward the people and says: THE LORD BE WITH YOU <note>original: "DOMINUS VOBISCUM".</note>.
IX. J. C. accused before Pilate; the PRIEST reads the EPISTLE.
X. J. C. accused before Herod; then the PRIEST bows before the center of the ALTAR, and softly says Cleanse my heart <note>original: "MUNDA COR"; a prayer for purification before proclaiming the Gospel.</note>. &c.
XI. J. C. sent from Herod to Pilate; the PRIEST reads the GOSPEL.
XII. J. C. stripped to be scourged; then the PRIEST uncovers the CHALICE.
XIII. J. C. bound and scourged; the PRIEST performs the OFFERING of the HOST.
XIV. J. C. crowned with thorns; the PRIEST covers the CHALICE after he has made the offering.
XV. Pilate, washing his hands, declares J. C. innocent; the PRIEST washes his hands.
XVI. J. C. covered with a purple robe; then the PRIEST turns toward the people and says, PRAY, BROTHERS <note>original: "ORATE FRATRES"; a call for the congregation's prayers before the Secret prayer.</note>.
XVII. J. C. condemned to be crucified; the PRIEST says the PREFACE <note>original: "VOORREDE"; the introductory prayer to the Canon of the Mass.</note>.
XVIII. J. C. carrying his Cross to die the death of the cross and make us live; then the PRIEST joins his hands together to pray for the FAITHFUL who are alive.
XIX. St. Veronica reaches the veil <note>original: "Zweedtdoek", literally "sweat-cloth"; referring to the veil used to wipe Christ's face.</note> to J. C.; the PRIEST covers the HOST and CHALICE with his hands.
XX. J. C. nailed to the Cross; the PRIEST makes the sign of the CROSS over the HOST and the CHALICE.
XXI. J. C. raised up on the Cross; the PRIEST adores the HOST before the ELEVATION.
XXII. The blood of J. C. flows along the Cross; the PRIEST elevates the CHALICE.
XXIII. J. C. prays for his enemies; the PRIEST says the REMEMBRANCE <note>original: "MOMENTO"; specifically the *Memento etiam*, the prayer for the deceased.</note> for the deceased faithful.
XXIV. J. C. promises Paradise to the converted thief; then the PRIEST says, TO US ALSO, SINNERS <note>original: "NOBIS QUOQUE PECCATORIBUS"; a prayer for the priest and the congregation to share in the fellowship of the saints.</note>.
XXV. J. C. hands John over to his Mother; the PRIEST says the OUR FATHER <note>original: "PATERNOSTER".</note> &c.
XXVI. J. C. offers up his soul to God the Father; then the PRIEST breaks the HOST into two pieces.
XXVII. J. C. descended into Hell; the PRIEST places a small part of the HOST into the CHALICE.
XXVIII. J. C. having given up the ghost, people strike their breasts while returning; the PRIEST, striking his breast, says three times the LAMB OF GOD <note>original: "AGNUS DEI".</note> etc.
XXIX. The Body of J. C. placed in a new tomb; then the PRIEST receives COMMUNION.
XXX. The anointing of J. C.'s Body; the PRIEST performs the ABLUTION <note>original: "AFWASSCHING"; the ritual rinsing of the chalice and the priest's fingers.</note>.
XXXI. The resurrection of Jesus Christ; the PRIEST having received communion, one proceeds to the POST-COMMUNION.
XXXII. J. C. appears to his Mother and before his Disciples; the PRIEST turns toward the Assembly and says THE LORD BE WITH YOU <note>original: "DOMINUS VOBISCUM".</note>.
XXXIII. J. C. visits and instructs his Disciples for 40 days; the PRIEST says the final PRAYERS.
XXXIV. J. C. ascends into Heaven etc.; the PRIEST turns toward the people, and says, THE MASS IS ENDED <note>original: "ITA MISSA EST", literally "Go, it is the dismissal".</note>.
XXXV. J. C. sends the Holy Spirit to his Apostles; then the PRIEST gives the BLESSING to the Assembly.

On Sundays before the solemn Mass, the Holy Water is blessed and a Procession is held. The believers must then attend the Mass with a pure conscience, and to show them the necessity of this inner purity, they sprinkle their bodies with a Water which has been sanctified for this purpose by a solemn Blessing. The Procession or "Carrying-Around" is a preparation of the hearts of the assembly of the Faithful for the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass. The Priest and Clergy make this preparation through singing and the display of the Cross, which is carried before the Clergy while they solemnly make a circuit around the Church, or the nearest adjacent places belonging to it.

<margin>Considering what the Mass consists of,</margin>
The Mass consists of two principal parts. (†) The one which extends from the beginning until the Offertory, formerly called the *Mass of the Catechumens* <term>Catechumens: From the Greek, meaning "those being instructed," referring to new converts not yet baptized</term> or New Converts; and the other which extends from the Offertory until the end, and is called the *Mass of the Faithful*. Everyone was permitted to be present until the Offertory, as this first part included the reading of the Holy Scripture and the preaching of the Gospel, from which one wished 

<column-break/>

to exclude no one. But after the preaching, no one was permitted to remain except the Faithful who were in a state to participate in the Offertory, and the *Catechumens* were made to leave; likewise the possessed and the penitents, who were not only withheld from the Holy Meal or the *Communion*, but even from the sight of the mysteries. This was why the Deacon (a) cried out loudly: *The Holy things are for the Holy; let the unholy depart.* <note>original: "De Heilige dingen zyn voor Heiligen; dat de onheiligen vertrekken," translating the Latin "Sancta Sanctis; recedant profani."</note>

<margin>And shown through the following Illustrations.</margin>
These following thirty-five Illustrations will show the Reader the various actions of the Priest performing the Mass. Devotion has found in all these actions—which the Church places among the mysteries of the Faith and which are very necessary for the Faithful—a complete allegory of the suffering of our Lord JESUS CHRIST. We shall now explain the mysteries and the symbolic meanings thereof.

### I. Illustration.

The believer, while the Priest goes to the Altar, must turn his thoughts to God, viewing this Action as the Image of the departure of JESUS CHRIST with His Apostles to the † Mount of Olives. JESUS CHRIST prepared Himself there for the Sacrifice for the sins of the human race: likewise, the Priest, going to the Altar, prepares himself for the Offering of Blessing or the sacrifice of the Host <term>Host: From the Latin 'hostia', meaning a sacrificial victim</term>, which is the sanctified body of JESUS CHRIST.

### II. Illustration.

Before the Priest begins the Mass, he says his prayer. The believers must likewise pray from the heart with him, letting their thoughts dwell on the internal sorrow of the Savior of the human race when He said His prayer in the Mount of Olives and perceived Himself to be forsaken by God. The Priest, standing below the Altar, must remember how mankind, through the sin of Adam, was as if cast out, driven from Paradise, and estranged from the presence of God.

### III. Illustration.

In Gethsemane or the Mount of Olives, JE-

# HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing the description of the Priest's initial prayers.</note> JESUS CHRIST knelt down, sweating blood just before his passion, because of the most shameful and cruel death of all punishments. In this state, he confessed before God his Father the iniquities of the human race. This, we are told, is the concept that the confession of the Priest before the Altar impresses upon the faithful. The confession is a result of the reflections that the Priest has made while standing at the foot of the Altar. He implores God for the forgiveness of his own crimes and for those of the whole People. He considers that the action he is about to perform requires a heart not only purified of mortal sins, but even of venial <note>minor or pardonable</note> sins: so that the People, along with the Priest, are obliged to make the confession of sins.

## IV. Representation.

Next, the Priest approaches the Altar and kisses it; which is a sign of his reconciliation with God, and through him, of the reconciliation of the faithful. However, this representation does not prevent the faithful from imagining another matter; namely, the kiss which the Priest gives to the Altar represents to him the kiss of the Traitor Judas; a beneficial kiss, since he delivers JESUS CHRIST over to his executioners, and by this means the wretched Traitor, without knowing it, brings about our Salvation.

## V. Representation.

After the Priest has kissed the Altar, and while the beginning (a) of the Mass is being sung, he incenses the Altar to offer up to God the prayers of the faithful, represented by the incense. The allegory is also applicable to the movement of the Priest to the side of the Altar.

<column-break/>

turning to the Epistle *; but one must be careful not to force this allegory; since the faithful, through the power of meditation, can imagine in the actions of the Priest how JESUS CHRIST was captured and bound, to be delivered over to his Enemies.

## VI. Representation.

JESUS CHRIST is led to the High Priest of the Jews; the beginning of this history of our Lord's passion is added here. This is called the *Introit*, † the introduction or beginning of the Mass. This changes daily to correspond with the mystery or the Feast being celebrated. The *Kyrie Eleison* (b) <note>original: "Kyrie Eleison" — Greek for "Lord, have mercy"</note> is a Greek Prayer following the *Introit* or beginning; these two words mean *Lord have mercy on us*. The *Kyrie Eleison* is addressed three times to each of the three Persons of the Trinity, to indicate how greatly we need the mercy of God. Fervent piety can find a rightful connection between the Beginning of the Mass and the entrance of JESUS CHRIST when he was led before Annas <note>a high priest in the New Testament</note>.

## VII. Representation.

As for the three-fold denial of Peter being applicable to the *Kyrie Eleison*, this is more perfect. The Priest invokes the mercy of the Supreme Being for Himself and for the Assembly of the faithful. The devout find from this that this concept represents to them the weeping of Peter. To sin against God is to not recognize Him and to deny Him. One must then repent just like this Apostle.

(a) It is believed that Pope Celestine was the first to have the Psalms sung as *Antiphons* <note>short chants</note>. Gregory the Great subsequently brought these *Antiphons* to their specific use for the *Introit* <note>entrance</note>, the *Response*, the offertory, the *Communion*, etc. These were collected into a book called the *Antiphonal*. See *Bona* <note>likely Giovanni Bona, a 17th-century liturgical scholar</note>.

* [On the right side of the officiating Priest lies the Epistle, a book from which a portion of the Mass is sung by the Subdeacon, a little before the Gospel.]

† [*Introitus* <note>original: "Introitus" — entrance</note> is the name given to the beginning or introduction of the Mass, or the first specific Prayer of the Feast, which the Priest says when he approaches the Altar. In the Missal, there are various *Introits* according to the days of the annual feasts. *Requiem aeternam* <note>original: "Requiem aeternam" — Eternal rest</note> is the *Introit* of a Funeral Mass. *Quasi modo* <note>original: "Quasi modo" — As if [newborn babes]</note> is that of the Sunday after Easter. *Reminiscere* <note>Remember</note>, *Oculi* <note>Eyes</note>, *Judica* <note>Judge</note>, *Laetare* <note>Rejoice</note> are *Introits* that give their names to the Sundays in Lent. *Furetiere* <note>likely referring to the lexicographer Antoine Furetière</note>.]

(b) This *Kyrie Eleison* which, as said, means *Lord have mercy on us*, is not inappropriate for man when he takes refuge in God. Moreover, this rule is common in all Jewish, Pagan, and Christian prayers: but the Christian Church has especially consecrated it in her service. The custom has made such an impression that the Christian People believe, when saying *Lord have mercy on us* in Greek, that this prayer would have more power than in the common language. However, we do not dare to assert it; but it is always remarkable that the Latins were advised to use this single rule in Greek, without anyone knowing a sufficient reason for it. Therefore, it is true that this custom is very old.

### VIII. Illustration.

After the Beginning and the *Lord have mercy* <note>original: "Kyrie Eleison"</note>, the Priest turns around, signifying that the Lord is about to reveal Himself to the Faithful. The Choir then sings *Glory in the highest* <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis"</note> etc. This is also called the Hymn of the Angels, as it begins with the words (a) that the Angels sang at the birth of JESUS CHRIST. This Hymn expresses the esteem that the Church holds for the infinite Majesty of God, etc. However, it is not sung on days of penance nor in Masses for the dead. The Priest kisses the Altar out of this respect, and does so every time he turns toward the People. He greets the Assembly, saying *The Lord be with you* <note>original: "Dominus Vobiscum"</note>. The Priest, when speaking these words, must look upon the Assembly of the Faithful with a pleasant countenance, and thereby move their hearts so that they may show their penitence. Likewise, just as the Lord looked upon Peter with a compassionate eye and made His Apostle feel these tender words inwardly: *the Lord be with you*. To which the Assembly responds, saying, *And with your spirit* <note>original: "Cum Spiritu tuo"</note>. The Priest and the People thus greet each other back and forth during the Mass to demonstrate the unity that must exist between them in the celebration of the Mysteries. Whereupon the Priest turns back to the Altar and says the *Collect* <note>original: "Collecta"</note>, which is a general summary of the prayers for what the Church requests from God in the Service of that day.

<column-break/>

### IX. Illustration.

The Priest reads the *Epistle* <term>Epistle: A reading usually taken from the letters of the Apostles in the New Testament</term>, and this action is compared to the accusation brought against JESUS CHRIST before Pilate. This reading is called the *Epistle* because it is often taken from some passage of the Letters of the Apostles. The Devil, the Flesh, and the World strive to rise up against JESUS CHRIST: but the heart of the Christian wishes to surrender itself to Him. This is relative to what can be found in these two Discourses. The imagination of a Christian, guided by the meditation of a religious Soul, can discover much more than we are able to express.

### X. Illustration.

After the Epistle, one sings the (b) *Gradual* <note>A chant sung between the readings</note> \*, so named (c) because of the *Rood loft* <note>original: "Jubé"</note> † or singing gallery where it is sung, as is still the custom in many Churches. This is a preparation for the reading of the Gospel. One adds the *Hallelujah* <note>original: "Halleluja"</note> ‡ to it: but from *Septuagesima* <note>The third Sunday before Lent</note> § until Easter, which is a time of mourning, one sings verses from some Psalms in place of the *Hallelujah*; and since these are sung with a mournful tone and a lingering voice, this is called the *Tract* <note>original: "Trait"</note> ¶. Meanwhile, the Deacon offers incense to the Priest, which he blesses, saying: (d) *may God bless you in whose honor you shall burn*. Then the Priest kneels or bows before the Altar, offering a quiet Prayer which begins with the words *cleanse my heart* <note>original: "munda cor"</note>, etc.

---

(a) The continuation of this Hymn is attributed to Pope Telesphorus, who lived in the year 150 after Christ. Others attribute it to Pope Symmachus, who lived three hundred and fifty years later. It is certain that its original author is unknown.
(b) The *Gradual* came into use during the time of Pope Honorius around the year 633. Others consider it to be much older.
\* [*Gradual* is a word from the Breviary or Prayer Book, consisting of a certain verse sung after the Epistle, which in former times was sung on the steps of the Altar. Anastasius maintains that Pope Celestine was the first institutor of the Graduals. The fifteen Psalms that the Hebrews sang on the fifteen Temple steps were also called by this name. Others believe this name originates from the raising of the voice, which occurred in steps and ascending tones. *Furetière*.]
(c) See the Explanation of the Ceremonies of the Mass.
† [Formerly there was an elevated place in the Churches, separated from the Choir and the nave of the Church, which was called the *Jubé* (Rood loft), where the Gospel of the solemn Masses was sung. It is a Latin word meaning *Command* or *Bid*; and it is taken from the Breviary: *Bid, Lord, a blessing* <note>original: "Jubé Domine, benedicere"</note>, because formerly the lessons of Matins were sung on the *Jubé*. *Thiers on Rood lofts*.]
‡ [*Hallelujah* is a Hebrew word, expressed as הללו יה, and means *praise the Lord* <note>original: "laudate Dominum"</note>; it is sung in the Churches as a well-known word. In the early times of the Church, it was also used as a battle cry. It was first in use in the Church of Jerusalem, from where *Damasus* brought it to Rome. *Schmidius Lex. Eccles. p. 31.*]
§ [The Sunday called *Septuagesima* is so named because it comes 70 days before Easter. It is believed that Pope Telesphorus brought this name into use, so that one might gradually prepare for the upcoming Fast. The *Hallelujah* was not sung then: but in its place, *Praise to you, O Lord* <note>original: "Laus tibi Domine &c."</note>, which has the same meaning. *Schmidius Lex Eccl. Part. 3. P. 37.*]
¶ [*Tract* is a word from the Prayer Book, meaning a verse that the choir singers sing after the Epistle on various feast days, and especially on Holy Saturday. It is a slow and mournful song, representing the tears of the Saints and sighs brought forth as a sign of penance. *Furetière*.] 
(d) *May you be blessed by Him in whose honor you shall be burned* <note>original: "Ab illo benedicaris in cujus honore cremaberis"</note>.

## XI. Illustration.

The Priest reads the **Gospel** <note>original: "Euangeli"</note> here, representing how JESUS CHRIST was sent from Herod to Pilate. The *Explanation of the Solemnities of the Mass* <note>This likely refers to a specific contemporary devotional book</note> teaches us this allegorical lesson. The Gospel book is moved from the right side to the left side of the Altar, which represents the preaching offered to the **Gentiles** <note>original: "Heidenen"</note> after the Jews refused to hear it. JESUS CHRIST, despised and scorned by Herod (who is the symbol of the Jews), is brought before Pilate, who represents the symbol of the Gentiles. It is true that on this occasion Pilate grants JESUS CHRIST no hearing, or that he hears him with barely any attention: but the allegorical lesson, while corresponding with the comparisons, is only fitting in certain parts.

## XII. Illustration.

It is solely for this reason that one will find much justice in the comparison of the parts of the Preaching with the covered **Chalice** <note>The cup used for the wine in the Mass</note>, corresponding to the feelings of the Savior. The Christian who sees the Chalice being covered must imagine how JESUS CHRIST was stripped to be scourged: but the comparison must be understood through opposites. The action of the Priest is exceedingly magnificent, and it gives an impression of esteem. The scourging stirred up the Jews and Romans against JESUS CHRIST, because it was contemptuous and shameful.

## XIII. Illustration.

<margin>(a) We shall speak of it more broadly hereafter.</margin>
After the reading of the Gospel, the Priest stands up. We leave untouched the Sermon (a) which follows the reading, and the incensing of the Gospel, which the Priest kisses and the Choir must join in, when the Priest says: *behold here the Holy Law*, etc. <note>original: "zie hier de Heilige Wet"</note> to which the Choir responds: *I believe it from the heart and confess it with the mouth*; to which the Priest then adds: *that your sins may be blotted out by the word of the Gospel.* <note>The original text includes these Dutch translations of the Latin liturgical responses.</note>
<column-break/>
blotted out by the word of the Gospel. Also, the *Creed* <note>original: "Credo"</note> is commonly sung after the Sermon, etc. This Article of Faith being ended, and the Priest having kissed the Altar, he turns toward the people and greets them a second time with the words already mentioned <note>Referring to "Dominus Vobiscum" or "The Lord be with you"</note>, which is followed by the offertory part, and the Priest then performs the Offering of the **Host** <note>The unleavened bread or wafer</note>, which has some correspondence with the scourging. In the beginning, this represents the suffering of JESUS CHRIST, and now it is the Preface to the Offering of the Mass.

## XIV. Illustration.

The Priest lifts the Chalice to offer it according to the prescribed ritual in the Law (of the Jews). Subsequently, he covers the Chalice. JESUS CHRIST, crowned with thorns, represents that He went to be lifted up as a sacrifice offered to God for the salvation of the human race. It is well enough known that the sacrificial victims of the heathens were crowned before they were offered to the false gods.

## XV. Illustration.

When the Priest has blessed the Bread and the Wine and offered them to God, he then blesses the incense and incenses the Bread and the Wine. He prays to God that the scent of this Offering may be more pleasing to Him than the smoke of the Sacrifices offered to Him under the ancient Law. The incensing of the Bread and the Wine is then followed by the Altar. Finally, the Priest washes his hands to follow the example of JESUS CHRIST, who washed the feet of His Apostles, or rather to let Christians know that to celebrate the mysteries of the Mass, it is not enough to have no defiled will regarding the commission of known crimes: but that one must likewise purify oneself of the slightest stains. On this matter, various other circumstances could be brought forward: but we shall content ourselves with asserting that one finds in it a representation of the act of Pilate, who, washing his hands, declared JESUS CHRIST innocent.

### XVII. Representation.

At the end of this *Secret*, which one must regard as the treasury in which the Priest encloses the Prayers that the Faithful have offered, he raises his voice and says *(a) through all ages, that is, forever and ever, etc.* <note>original: "per omnia secula"</note> After which the Priest *(b)* exhorts the people to be attentive, as the time of the *Consecration* <term>Consecration: the moment in the Mass when the bread and wine are believed to become the body and blood of Christ</term> approaches. The words of the Priest then cause the Lord of Heaven and Earth to descend upon the Altar, *(c)* and the people respond that they are in that disposition which the Priest requests. The Priest exhorts the people *(d)* to thank God for this disposition; to which they respond again *(e)* that it is right and just. Subsequently, the Priest offers his Prayer to God the Father. This is what is called the *(f)* Intro-

### XVIII. Section.

That which now follows the Introduction of the Mass is called the *Canon (g)*. One begins with these words: *Te igitur Clementissime Pater, &c. We beseech you, most merciful Father.* <note>original: "Te igitur Clementissime Pater"</note> In this part of the Mass, one celebrates the memory of the living, just as is indicated in the remarks. One also prays to God for the preservation of their Souls, for the hope of their Salvation, etc. This part of the Mass is attributed to **JESUS CHRISTUS** who carries his Cross, and goes to his death to gain life for us.

### XIX. Representation.

After this commemoration, the Priest covers the Host and the Chalice with his hands; a custom that is followed just as the elevation of the Jewish and Pagan Priests, who formerly laid their hands upon the Animals they were to sacrifice, and subsequently raised a portion of the Sacrifice. This Laying on of Hands indicates the union of the Sacrificing Priest with the Bread of the Mass, which he offers. The Priest testifies here that he offers himself to God as much as is possible for him, for the Salvation of mankind. The People must follow the zeal of the Priest and pray to God that it may please Him to accept this testimony. Finally, it is indicated that the Laying on of Hands by the Priest upon the Host and the Chalice gives the Believer the idea

(a) *To these words* through all ages, etc. <note>original: "per omnia &c."</note> *the People respond*, Amen; *and to* The Lord be with you <note>original: "Dominus vobiscum"</note>, *they say* and with your spirit <note>original: "et cum Spiritu tuo"</note>.
(b) *Lift up your hearts.* <note>original: "Sursum corda"</note> The Ministers of Heathenism formerly used these two words in their Spiritual Ceremonies, *hoc age*, that is, *do this*, or *pay attention to it*. Whoever performs the office of a Preacher, in whatever religion it may be, will conduct himself in pronouncing these rules in such a way that he can touch the people's hearts most tenderly. He will coordinate his eyes, his countenance, and his voice so that he may thereby earn the respect and attention of his Hearers.

## XX. Section.

The Priest makes the signs of the Cross over the Altar-bread and the Chalice, and pronounces the words with which **JESUS CHRIST** instituted the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper to perform the <term>Consecration</term> <note>Consecration: The solemn moment in the Mass when the bread and wine are believed to be changed by divine power into the actual body and blood of Christ.</note>. It is then (b) that the Savior, upon this pronouncement during the Supper, changes the substance of Bread and Wine into that of his Body and Blood, and through his Almightiness works this inexpressible change. This part of the Mass is then the true Representation of **JESUS CHRIST'S** sacrifice on the Cross.

## XXI. Section.

The consecrated Host is adored by the Priest; its elevation, so that it may be adored by the People, perfectly represents the Savior erected on the Cross. He is always worthy of adoration, but especially during the time of his passion.

## XXII. Representation.

The Priest, having consecrated the Chalice, proclaims the words of **JESUS CHRIST**: *This is the Chalice of my blood, etc.* Subsequently, he lifts it high so that the blood of the Savior may be adored by the People, and entreats God through

<column-break/>

his prayers for the fruits of the Sacrifice which he offers.

## XXIII. Representation.

Through the power of this Sacrifice, the Priest commends to God the souls of all the Faithful who are in Purgatory, and especially those for whom he has a particular obligation to remember. This prayer of the Priest relates to that which **JESUS CHRIST** performed on the Cross for his Enemies. The comparison is a little forced, unless the Faithful, out of humility, place themselves in the rank of his enemies—those who daily crucify him through their sins—or if they do not regard themselves as dying in their crimes, seeing no hope of escape from the flames of Purgatory except through the power of the Sacrifice offered for them by the Priest as they suffer in that purifying fire.

## XXIV. Representation.

Subsequently, the Priest raises his voice and strikes his breast; he entreats for himself and the People for Divine mercy, that through the intercession of the Saints, he and the Assembly may have some part in His Kingdom, just as the converted Thief requested of **JESUS CHRIST** on the Cross.

Lord JESUS CHRIST
to save the soul, etc. After the Priest has received <term>Communion</term> <note>The act of consuming the consecrated bread and wine.</note>, he distributes it to the People. One attributes the Communion of the Priest to the grave of our consecrated Lord, who died, was buried, and descended into Hell to earn life for us. During the Communion of the Priest and the People, the Choir sings the <term>Antiphon</term> <note>A short chant or sentence sung before or after a psalm.</note> which is called the Communion.

### XXX. Symbolic Representation.
After this Communion, the Priest takes some of the Wine (a) in the Chalice to perform what is called the <term>Ablution</term> <note>Dutch: Afwaſſing; the ritual washing of the chalice and the priest’s fingers.</note>, and says a short prayer in which he asks God that this Communion—which appears to the senses as a temporary remedy—may serve as an eternal remedy in the heart of the Believer. Subsequently, for a second Ablution, he has water and wine poured in, and pairs this action with another short prayer (b), after which he greets the Congregation. These Ablutions symbolically represent the washing and embalming of the Body of our Lord, who died on the Cross and was offered by the Priest. It is from this Body that the spiritual balm flows, which works the healing of the soul of the faithful Communicant.

### XXXI. Symbolic Representation.
The Priest sings the <term>Post-Communion</term> <note>The final prayer of the Mass after the distribution of the bread and wine.</note>. This is a prayer through which he beseeches God to be allowed to enjoy the fruits of the Sacrament. The fruits of this Communion, which has represented the death of **JESUS CHRIST** to us, are the glorious Resurrection of the reborn Believer; and the Post-Communion must here be the Symbolic Representation of the Resurrection of the Savior.

### XXXII. Symbolic Representation.
The action of the Priest, who turns toward the Congregation and greets the People,
<column-break/>
is a pleasant representation of the appearance of **JESUS CHRIST** to his Mother and Disciples. The Priest is an ambassador of **JESUS CHRIST** and proclaims Peace to their souls, from the one who died—if one may call it such—and awakens him daily through the hand of the Priest for true Christians.

### XXXIII. Symbolic Representation.
The final Prayers and the beginning of the <term>Gospel of John</term> <note>A tradition in the Tridentine Mass where the first fourteen verses of the Gospel of John are read at the end.</note>, which the Priest reads and recites after the Sacrifice of the Mass, are soul-saving instructions that remind the heart of the Christian of those things which the resurrected **JESUS CHRIST** gave to his Disciples during the forty days.

### XXXIV. Symbolic Representation.
We have considered the Sacrifice of **JESUS CHRIST** through the hand of the Priest as the Symbolic Representation of his Resurrection: but now one sees that of his Ascension. The Congregation of the Believers is given their dismissal by these words: *Ite Missa est* <note>original: "Ite Missa est"; translated as "Go, the Mass is ended."</note>, to wit: (c) Go, for the Mass is finished. To which one answers: *We thank God* <note>original: "Wy danken Godt," translating the Latin "Deo Gratias."</note>. It is **JESUS CHRIST** who, through his glorious Ascension, has received the eternal reward for the Sacrifice, just as he offered himself on the Cross as Priest and Victim. The Sacrifice of the Savior on the Cross was a true Mass consisting of all its parts, and this appears clearly in the explanations we have given of it.

### XXXV. Symbolic Representation.
Finally, the Congregation receives the Blessing from the Priest (d) or from the Bishop, if he is present. This

(a) The wine of purification.
(b) He washes his hands and mouth, cleanses the Chalice, and folds the Linens and the Altar cloth, the use of which we shall explain when we deal with the Vessels and the sacred Linens.
(c) As for the Ceremonies of the Service of the *Ite*, the Priests gave the Congregation dismissal through a nearly identical custom which was called *the sending forth of the People*. See <term>Polydore Virgil</term> <note>A 16th-century Italian humanist and historian.</note>, *The Ministers of the Protestants*, after having given the Blessing of Moses, such as one finds it in Numbers, they dismiss the People with these words: *Go in peace, and may the Honor of Peace be with you all, etc.*
(d) This Blessing must be given with eyes raised toward Heaven, after having kissed the Altar. The arms must be stretched out, and subsequently brought gently back before the chest, so that the hands join together in a pleasant manner before the Congregation of the faithful. The extension of the arms and the joining of the hands are both accompanied by a hidden meaning, and signify the Love with which the Priest is imbued toward God and his spiritual brothers. While pronouncing the Blessing, he must turn his head toward the Crucifix with a pleasant inclination. *These rules are described by the Italian mystagogues* <note>Dutch: "Mylagolugotten," likely referring to writers on the hidden meanings of liturgy (mystagogy).</note>. See *Piscara, Bauldry* and others.

<header>RELIGIOUS DUTIES etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH.</header>

<meta>Catchword: Fruit-</meta>

The Blessing is a perfect image of that observation where the *Savior overshadowed his Apostles*, sending them his Holy Spirit.

Now it is necessary to consider the arrangement of the places for those who attend the Mass. The Sanctuary, otherwise called the *Presbyterium* <note>original: "Presbyterium"; the area around the altar reserved for the clergy.</note>, belongs to the Mass priest and his assistants. The Choir is for the Clergy in choir dress; the upper part of the Church is for the men and the lower part for the women.

<margin>The conduct of the Congregation during the Mass and throughout the services.</margin>

The Congregation must *kneel* from the beginning of the Mass until the *Lord, have mercy* <note>original: "Kyrie"</note>; stand while the sprinkling of the *Holy Water* occurs; kneel during the Prayer that follows; stand again at the *Glory to God in the highest* <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis"</note>, and kneel during the prayers. From the beginning of the Epistle until the Gospel, one may sit: but during the reading of the Gospel one must stand. During the Exhortation one sits, and kneels while praying. The Congregation stands while the Priest says the first words of the *Creed* <note>original: "Credo"</note>, and subsequently sits; kneels again and bows when one sings *And was incarnate* <note>original: "Incarnatus est"</note> etc. Subsequently, one may sit again until the end of the *Creed*: but one stands up again until the Priest has said *Let us pray* <note>original: "Oremus"</note>. The People then sit again until the Introduction <note>The Preface of the Mass.</note> and during the Introduction they must stand. At the *Holy, Holy, Holy* <note>original: "Sanctus"</note> one kneels again until the *Communion* has placed the Sacrament in the *Ciborium* <note>original: "Silborie"; the vessel used to hold the consecrated bread.</note>; one stands again until the Priest says *The Lord be with you* <note>original: "Dominus vobiscum"</note>; then kneels and remains standing during the last Gospel. This is the fruit that one can enjoy from these various postures, which the Church must observe during the Mass. For kneeling indicates the humiliation and penance of the Believer, and standing upright signifies the confidence with which we address ourselves with our prayers to God, and the courage with which we must carry out his will: All this signifies the constancy—

<margin>What is forbidden during attendance of the Mass.</margin>

During the Mass it is forbidden to speak or argue, to look hither and thither, and to behave improperly. The Female Sex must avoid testing the power of her charms, and instead show a modest face and countenance in the presence of the Supreme Being. As for the men, they must be armed with a Christian Modesty, and ward off all frivolous amorous glances. Their eyes must be *unfamiliar with the ways of the neighborhood* <note>A poetic way of saying they should not be looking at the people around them.</note>, nor even know that *there are young Women in the Congregation of the Faithful*, also they must *refrain from looking at them*. Likewise, magnificent clothes, a bare bosom, fiery glances and a lovely face must not distract the Christian from Spiritual service:

<column-break/>

<margin>How to proceed in the Mass.</margin>

The Priest's Modesty is no less praiseworthy, and is recommended to him. A young Priest, of a pleasant and healthy stature, and who is favored with the gifts of nature; whose civil and pleasant voice lets itself be heard; who shows a soft and refined piety; who casts his eyes Heavenward with a quite polite humility; who distributes the *Communion* with a white and plump hand ostentatiously; who, accompanied by a tender loveliness, gives the Blessing to the People; and yet testifies through eloquent gestures that he thinks of nothing but his own well-being; such a priest retains few souls and also has much trouble retaining his own.

<margin>Here, why the service is done in a language unknown to the People.</margin>

The advantages of the Mass are communicable to public and general prayer, the mutual union of all believers, the mutual edification and building up shared with one another, and the submission and togetherness that one publicly demonstrates to the Church. One must not object as a defect to the practice, introduced for a long time, of performing the Mass in the Latin language, which is now understood by only the smallest part of the Congregation. On the contrary, an advantage arises from this which the Jews as well as the Roman Catholics understand; it consists in the consistency of the Service, and the grace of following along through the ability of the Parish Priest of the place. The Jews perform their Worship in *Hebrew*, although that language is unknown to many Jews: but they nevertheless have recourse to the Translations in the common tongue, by which means the Jew can accurately follow the Rabbi. The Roman *Hours* <note>original: "Getijden"; prayer books containing the liturgy for specific times of day.</note> in the common tongue are of identical use to the Roman Catholics; without speaking of the practical Piety, an uncommon Guide for the greatest part of men, and of this Godly—

It concludes by defending the use of Latin in the liturgy by comparing it to the Jewish use of Hebrew, noting that vernacular translations allow the faithful to follow along.</summary>

# CHAPTER XX.

->On various principal Masses; the HIGH MASS, SOLEMN MASS, and PONTIFICAL MASS.<-

We shall speak of the Masses of Holy Week when it is required to explain the Ceremonies of Easter; and of certain particulars of the first Pontifical Mass <note>The Mass celebrated by a Bishop</note> when we treat of the Bishop’s *Consecration*. We undertake here only to describe what is particularly noteworthy in the *Solemn Mass*, in certain *Papal Masses*, and in the *Mass for the Dead* <note>Known as a Requiem Mass</note>. Many other Masses (b) which contain almost nothing special other than the name of the Mass, we shall leave untouched.

<column-break/>

<margin>How one behaves when the Bishop is to perform the Solemn Mass.</margin>
When a Solemn Mass (c) is to be performed \*, the Bishop (d), if he is to perform it himself, is led to the Church by the Canons and other Ministers of the Church, all magnificently dressed; but if the Bishop's Palace is far removed from the Church, the Chapter <note>The governing body of the cathedral</note>, which awaits the Bishop before the gate, then approaches and goes to meet the Prelate as soon as they see him arriving. When the Lord Bishop then approaches the Church, the bells are rung to make his arrival known to the People; and in the...
