(a) One finds a verse by an old Poet cited by Bayle in volume 5 of his *Questions of a Provincial*.
> The little child, as soon as he is up,
> Is made to say his *Our Father* and *Hail Mary* <note>original: "Pater-Noster, Ave"</note>.
> Likewise the *Apostles' Creed* <note>original: "Credo"</note>.
> And after he has said his prayers,
> The said child, by customary form,
> Asks a maidservant for bread.

->That is:<-

> As soon as the Child has risen from his bed,
> Having read his *Our Father* and *Mary’s greeting* <note>The Hail Mary</note>,
> Having recited the Holy *Creed* of the Apostles,
> And laid down the Rosary with its beads,
> He demands his Breakfast, as is the custom, and wishes to eat;
> Not that the Mother, but the Maid might have forgotten it.

(b) Such as the Mass of Our Lady of the Snows, celebrated on the 5th of August; the Masses of the Saints; that of St. Margaret, patroness of women in labor; that of the Feast of St. John the Baptist, when three Masses are performed because of the triple mystery found in the life of this Saint. These three mysteries are his Baptism, his life as a Nazarite, and his status as the Forerunner of JESUS CHRIST. Such also is the Mass of the Holy Innocents, from which is omitted the *Glory to God in the highest* <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis"</note> and the *Hallelujah*. It is a day of mourning, and the Altar must be draped in violet. See *Casalius, On Rites, etc.* It is more than a century since some Saints in France were deprived of their Masses by the authority of Pope Pius V and Pope Clement VIII, as these Popes purified the Missal. They were deprived of, for example, St. Rigobert, St. William, St. Mauris, St. Bonet, etc., only to put Italian Saints in their place. As for ordinary Masses, there are some special ones performed for the soul of a believer, serving to release them from Purgatory, or at least to bring them some relief. A Christian who cares for his Salvation must not be negligent in this. He must, through his Will, provide the Parish Priest with the necessary means to be freed from the eternal punishment he might have deserved. In Spain, Portugal, and Italy, it often happens that the souls of the faithful are the primary heirs of the goods they leave behind in this World. A dying man often requests twenty or thirty thousand Masses for his soul, and charges the Priest in whom he has the most trust to apply these required means for him in the next World as soon as he has departed. There are also common Masses requested for lost things, for the healing of people and even of beasts, likewise for travelers, for thanking God, etc. These Masses, and those of which we have already spoken, carry the common name of *Votive Masses*. A distinction is also made between a *High* and a *Low Mass*. The Mass performed at Sea is called a *Dry Mass* <note>original: "drooge Mis"</note>, because the Chalice is not used, from which the Consecrated Wine might spill due to the movement of the ship. See *Durandus, Rationale & Cassander, On Liturgical Matters.*
(c) There are many kinds of Solemn Masses: such as Canonical, Papal, and those performed for the Pope, likewise for Cardinals, for the Bishop, those of Christmastide, those of Holy Week, etc. It shall suffice to treat the Bishop's Mass, leaving the others untouched.
(d) This description is drawn from *Pescara, Baudry,* and the *Ceremonial of Bishops*.

\* See the accompanying Illustration of the SOLEMN or HIGH MASS.

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc., of the ROMAN CHURCH.
N n

<meta>PART I. at bottom of first column block; catchword "of" at bottom right.</meta>

Having arrived at the Church, the organ is heard. The Master of Ceremonies gives the <term>aspergillum<note>original: "Wyquast"; a brush or perforated container used for sprinkling holy water</note></term> to the most senior of the Chapter members, who offers it to the Bishop after he has kissed this aspergillum and the consecrated hand of the Prelate. The Bishop sprinkles himself with the aspergillum in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; after which he sprinkles the Canons, etc., and then performs his prayer before the Altar of the Holy Sacrament on a footstool placed there for this pious exercise. Likewise, he must fulfill his duty before the High Altar. From there, the Bishop goes to the sacristy or <term>vestry<note>original: "Gerskamer"</note></term> to receive the Mass vestments corresponding to the solemnity of the Mass, which occurs in the following manner.

The Sub-Deacon fetches from the credence cupboard the Episcopal <term>sandals<note>original: "Voetzoolen of Pantoffels"; liturgical slippers worn by a bishop during High Mass</note></term> and stockings; kneeling, he removes the Bishop's shoes, surrounded by seven or eight acolytes, all kneeling like the Deacon, who hand the Prelate's choir robe just as the ceremonial stockings were given to his Excellency, all in a proper order. Two acolytes (a) take, after the hands are washed, the consecrated ornaments and give them to the assisting Deacons to reclothe the Bishop, after he has also washed his hands. The Deacon greets the Bishop, removes his choir robe, puts on the priestly headgear, and the Prelate kisses the cross of this garment: then he is given the alb, the girdle, the pectoral cross, the stoles, and the <term>cope<note>original: "Pluviaal"; a long, ornate semicircular cloak worn in processions</note></term>. He kisses the crosses of these garments one after another, and expresses an uncommon rever-

**PART I.**

<column-break/>

-ence for them, because of what is owed to the Cross of JESUS CHRIST. The assisting Deacons must also religiously kiss these consecrated garments. When the Bishop is seated, the <term>mitre<note>the traditional, pointed headpiece of a bishop</note></term> is placed upon him; a Priest gives him the Pastoral Ring. The Deacon hands him the right and the Sub-deacon the left glove. Each of them kisses the glove and the hand he has the honor to serve. Many things of little importance we shall leave untouched for the <term>mystagogical Christians<note>those who study the hidden or symbolic meanings of religious rituals</note></term>, as it will be of more importance to show the Reader how a pouring-out prayer has been applied to each piece of the Episcopal vestments, and how the religiousness of all these ceremonies is supported and reinforced by the singing of the service of the (b) third of the <term>Canonical hours<note>the specific times of day set aside for prayer; "the third" refers to Terce</note></term>.

The Bishop being clothed in his ceremonial vestments (c), the Clergy place themselves around him. Two Canon Deacons join his side, provided with Mass vestments, and after them another Deacon and Sub-Deacon. The censer-bearer appears with the censer, and the Priest with the incense boat. The Bishop takes some of the incense from this boat, puts it into the censer and gives his blessing over it. Subsequently, he bows before the Cross which stands on the Altar of the sacristy, and goes in procession to the Altar where he will perform the Mass. The censer-bearer goes ahead, followed by two candle-bearers with burning wax candles, walking beside the cross-bearer. All the Clergy follow; the Sub-deacon who is to sing the Epistle carries the closed Gospel Book before his chest, in which the <term>maniple<note>a small ornamental strip of silk worn on the left arm</note></term> is placed.

---

(a) The Deacons, acolytes, etc., must also be clothed in their ceremonial vestments. This remark will suffice for all the ceremonies that we shall subsequently describe.

(b) We shall provide an explanation of this when we deal with the Canonical hours.

(c) All the ceremonial vestments of the Bishop and his ministers each contain a mystery. The stole represents the yoke of the Gospel. The Bishop is unshod, just as God said to Moses, "take off your shoes," etc. A powerful proof is brought by the ceremony of this unshoding when one says: "O how beautiful are the feet of those who preach Peace!" The <term>chasuble<note>original: "Misgewaadt"</note></term>, which has the shape of a cross, signifies to the Deacons that one must be crucified to the world. The alb represents the purity of the priest's soul. The Episcopal Ring signifies the spiritual marriage of the Bishop with the Church. To extend the comparison further, we could say that the Bishop often conducts himself toward her as some men deal with their wives when they leave them for their mistresses. The gloves he has on his hands indicate to him his good works, of which he must not be ignorant, or which he must govern spiritually; the girdle, that he must be girded with righteousness and virtue; the sandals, that he must henceforth walk in the ways of the Lord; the two horns of the mitre signify the Old and New Testaments; the Bishop’s staff, fatherly discipline and authority; the choir robe, stretched out in width, expands the Episcopal power. The cope, which was formerly a traveling garment and a garment of fatigue <note>original: "vermoeitheit"; likely referring to its origins as a rain cloak for travel</note> from which it seems to have derived its name, represents the misery of this life exposed to temptations and human uncertainties. Thus a Bishop, sighing for some time under the weight of many difficult duties, becomes, every time he puts on the cope, a true image of a Christian whose life is exposed to all temptations. We have drawn these corresponding metaphors from the most prominent <term>mystagogues<note>interpreters of sacred mysteries</note></term>, such as Cafelius and others.

->HISTORICAL TREATISE on the<-

<term>Presbyterium<note>original: "Presbiterium"; here referring to the area of the sanctuary where the clergy sit, or sometimes the clergy house itself</note></term> † (a) to extinguish them, if no Communion is distributed to the Faithful.

<margin>
How the kiss of Peace is performed.
</margin>

After the *Lamb of God* <note>original: "Agnus Dei"</note>, the Assistant Priest <note>original: "Noodhelpende Priester"</note> places himself to the right side of the Bishop, alongside a Deacon on the left side. This Assistant Priest kneels while the <term>Celebrant<note>The priest or bishop officiating the Mass</note></term> says a short prayer, but soon stands up again, and they both kiss the Altar. The Celebrant gives the Peace to the Priest, who offers him his left cheek (b) to receive the kiss of Peace. After they have thus greeted each other with a Holy kiss, the Assistant Priest goes to the Choir to share the Peace he has received, and begins his pious generosity with the most prominent members of the

<column-break/>

Assembly. As for the <term>Laity<note>original: "Waereltlyken"; those who are not ordained clergy</note></term>, they are allowed to kiss what is called the <term>instrument of peace<note>original: "werktuig van Vrede"; a small tablet or plaque called a 'pax-board' or 'osculatorium' passed around for the faithful to kiss</note></term>, and this is even always practiced in less solemn Masses instead of kissing directly. Everything else that follows until the end does not differ from what is observed in common Masses.

We believe this description can give a general idea of the Masses called Solemn Masses. The illustration inserted between pages 280 and 281 will sufficiently reveal the splendor of this ceremony to the reader's eye. It depicts a High Mass celebrated in the <term>Cathedral of Paris<note>referring to Notre Dame de Paris</note></term>.

## CHAPTER XXI.

### How the POPE celebrates a SOLEMN Mass.

---

<margin>
Which ceremonies are observed at a Papal Mass.
</margin>

We shall not attempt to provide a description of everything that must be observed in the Pope's Chapel, from the moment he enters to practice his devotion until he departs again from this sacred place. This account might perhaps bore the reader, as it matters little to him to know (c) what a Cardinal Deacon must do to remove his Holiness's <term>Mitre<note>A tall, peaked ceremonial hat worn by bishops and the Pope</note></term> from the left side; what an <term>Auditor of the Rota<note>original: "Auditeur de Rota"; a high-ranking official in the Vatican's central court</note></term> must do to receive it; another Cardinal Deacon to lift the <term>Biretta<note>original: "Bonnet"; a square cap</note></term>, and that while his Holiness prays, he is to his right; that the Cardinal performing the Mass approaches to make the confession, and that when one of these two Deacons steps back, the Pope then begins the confession; that upon the reception or the granted Indulgence, the Celebrant steps back a little to receive the <term>maniple<note>original: "Manipul"; an ornamental band worn over the left arm</note></term> from the Sub-Deacon of the Chapel, and that the Cardinal Deacon who had stepped back a little approaches again, ending the Confession with his Holiness. Subsequently, the other Cardinal Deacon returns the Biretta to him, which he had taken with the Mitre. The Deacons

The Pope having then taken his seat, the Cardinals come to pay him their homage. They rise from their seats and, with trailing choir robes, first go to greet the Altar, which is the Throne of **JESUS CHRIST**; then they greet his <term>Vicar<note>original: "Stedehouder"; the Pope's title as Christ's representative on Earth</note></term>, and kiss his hand. Stepping back two paces, they again make a greeting before the visible Head of the Church. Next, they greet their colleagues, as well as the Ambassadors and Princes. Having returned to their places, they remain standing with uncovered heads until the other Cardinals have completed the same ceremonies: but, when the common <term>Prelates<note>High-ranking members of the clergy</note></term> pay their homage in turn, the Cardinals sit and cover their heads. These Prelates—which include Archbishops, and <term>Assistant Bishops<note>original: "Noodhelpende Bisschoppen"; literally "succoring bishops," referring to Bishops Assistant at the Pontifical Throne</note></term>, as well as the Confessors of his Holiness, etc.—only come to pay their homage when the Pope is officiating the service. The Archbishops and Assistant Bishops kiss his Holiness’s knee, and the Confessors kiss his foot.

These, then, are some parts of the Ceremonial of the Apostolic Court: but the most solemn of all consist in its religious observances. (a) *See Sestini.*
(b) The Pope having consecrated the Altar according to Custom, it should be noted that he is the only one who administers the Communion at his Throne. The <term>Mystagogues<note>Writers who interpret the symbolic or mystical meanings of religious rites</note></term> give many reasons for a custom that is very rare, and perhaps has no other basis than the caprice or the pride of some Pope of former times. We shall not present all these reasons. One of them is remarkable enough. The Altar, says *Roccha*, represents the Room where **J[esus] C[hrist]** held the Last Supper and instituted the unbloody Sacrifice of his body: but the Throne of the Pope represents the Cross of the Savior, and the *Communion* of the Pope represents the bloody Sacrifice of the Savior. One must have a very powerful imagination to find that the Pope seated on his Throne, laden with his Papal ornaments and with the burden of a magnificent Dignity, represents Jesus Christ, seated beneath the Cross, heaped with contempt and overwhelmed with a fading humility.
(c) The Mystagogues say that this posture of the Pope, who receives the *Communion* thus turning toward the People, represents the painful state of **JESUS CHRIST** on the Cross.
(d) The Pope receives the Host on the left side, and the <term>tube<note>original: "pypje"; the *fistula*, a golden straw used by the Pope to consume the consecrated wine to prevent spilling</note></term> which he holds in the Chalice on the right side, because, so it is claimed, **JESUS CHRIST** being crucified was pierced on the right side. The Cardinal-Deacon and Cardinal-Sub-Deacon, who receive the *Communion* with the Pope, and like him partake in the two species <note>original: "twee gedaantens"; referring to both the bread and the wine</note>, represent the twelve Apostles to whom **JESUS CHRIST** gave the Last Supper. It is also worth noting here that the privilege of receiving *Communion* under both species is granted to some Supreme Sovereigns, such as the Emperor and the King of France. At their Coronation and at their death, his most Christian Majesty always receives the *Communion* under both species.

The other solemn Masses also have something special. It shall suffice to describe the most remarkable parts of the Great Mass of Christmas, when the Pope performs the Service. After his Holiness has been helped into his attire by the Cardinal Deacons with all the Papal Ceremonial Vestments—of which the most prominent are then the white Cope <note>original: "Pluviaal"</note> and the precious Mitre—he gives his blessing over the Incense, which the Thurifer <note>original: "Wierookvatdrager"</note> brings to him. Subsequently, the Spiritual Head of the Church proceeds to the Church, preceded by the Roman Prelates and others, who all have white Mitres on their heads. (b) The Thurifer and seven Acolytes, each with a wax candle in hand, go before the Cross-bearer, and this Thurifer is preceded by a Clerk of the Chamber, who carries a raised sword with a cap <note>original: "bonnet"</note>, possibly signifying the irresis-

<column-break/>

tible power of the Papal sword, which the Vicar of JESUS CHRIST has inherited from the Apostle Paul, and this to protect Christians from the Devil’s slavery, obtained through a right from the Son of God, whose birth is being celebrated. Perhaps they wish to represent to us, through a symbolic image, the Church of God, or more properly speaking, that of the Clergy under the governance of St. Peter. Of the further retinue who make up and accompany this Holy Procession we shall make no mention, since it consists of the same figures as occurs on other occasions: but if the Emperor or any other Sovereign were to find himself in Rome at that time, he would be obliged to carry the train of the Pope’s mantle, as we have already noted in other Ceremonies; and two Cardinals then also hold up the two end-flaps of the mantle. The Pope walks not a little haughtily under a Canopy <note>original: "Verhemelzel"</note> carried by eight noblemen of the foremost Nobility, and even if King’s Sons had the honor of being in this solemn Procession, they would find no place except by the first Cardinal Priest.

His Holiness, having entered the Church, goes to the Chapel, changes garments there, and sits down. The Cardinals come to greet him and kiss the border of his Cope on the right side. The other Prelates come in order, kissing his right knee after having knelt three times. The two Deacons who assist the Pope—one being a Latin and the other a Greek <note>Reflecting the dual heritage of the early Church</note>—remain near the Altar. ## Papal Throne

"comes to the Papal Throne, where the Pope’s **Sacristan** <term>the official in charge of the sacred vessels and vestments</term> gives him a small gold pipe, one end of which he holds in the Chalice held by the Deacon, while the Pope then takes the other end with his hand, bowing his head slightly to place his lips to it, and (a) thus sucks a portion of the consecrated Wine, leaving the remainder to the Deacon, who carries the Chalice back to the Altar. Having arrived there, he also sucks another portion of the remaining Wine in the Chalice using the same pipe, and leaves a few drops for his Sub-Deacon, who consumes them without the pipe, and subsequently drinks what is poured for him to rinse the Chalice, which he then wipes clean with a cloth. Meanwhile, the Pope gives the kiss of Peace to the Deacon, and the Communion in the form of the Bread to the other Cardinals, Envoys, Princes, and Prelates, and sometimes to private individuals who wish to receive it from his hand; after which he returns to the Altar and concludes the Mass with the customary ceremonies.

We have already spoken of the purse containing 25 *Giulii* <note>original: "Julyën oude munt"; these were silver coins named after Pope Julius II</note> given to the Pope *for having sung the Mass well* <note>original Latin: "pro bene cantata Missa"</note>.

The other solemn Masses also have unique features. It will suffice to describe the most remarkable aspects of the Great Mass of Christmas Day, when the Pope performs the Service. After his Holiness has been helped into his robes by the Cardinal Deacons with all the Papal ceremonial garments—of which the most prominent are then the white **Cope** <note>original: "Pluviaal"</note> and the precious **Mitre**—he gives his blessing over the incense brought to him by the thurifer. Then, the Spiritual Head of the Church proceeds to the Church, preceded by the Roman Prelates and others, all wearing white mitres on their heads. (b) The thurifer and seven acolytes, each with a wax candle in hand, walk before the cross-bearer; this thurifer is preceded by a Clerk of the Chamber, who carries a raised sword topped with a cap, possibly signifying the irresist-

<column-break/>

-ible power of the Papal sword, which the **Vicar of JESUS CHRIST** has inherited from the Apostle Paul, intended to protect Christians from the Devil’s slavery through a right obtained from the Son of God, whose birth is being celebrated. Perhaps they wish to represent to us, through a symbolic image, the Church of God—or more properly speaking, that of the clergy—under the governance of St. Peter. Of the further retinue that makes up and accompanies this Holy Procession, we shall make no mention, as it consists of the same figures as on other occasions. However, if the Emperor or any other Sovereign were present in Rome at that time, he would be required to carry the train of the Pope's mantle, as we have already noted in other ceremonies; and two Cardinals then also hold up the two side-flaps of the mantle. The Pope walks quite majestically under a canopy carried by eight noblemen from the highest nobility, and even if the sons of Kings had the honor of being in this solemn procession, they would find no place except beside the first Cardinal Priest.

Having arrived in the Church, his Holiness goes to the Chapel, changes his vestments there, and sits down. The Cardinals come to greet him and kiss the border of his cope on the right side. The other Prelates come in order, kissing his right knee after having knelt three times. The two Deacons who assist the Pope—one being Latin and the other Greek—remain near the Altar. ### HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

<margin>And with what solemnity this is accompanied.</margin>
Having arrived, the Sub-Deacon takes the Cross after he, like the Deacon, has laid aside his *Maniple*, <note>original: "Manipul," a narrow strip of silk or cloth worn over the left arm, originally used as a handkerchief but becoming a purely ornamental vestment</note> and they go together to the place where the illuminated chapel <note>original: "brandende Kapel," referring to a *chapelle ardente* or a catafalque surrounded by many burning candles</note> is, or the representation of it, just as one would go to bury the body of the Deceased. The Incense-bearer and the Minister of Holy Water go first; the Sub-Deacon follows them carrying the Cross between two candle-bearers, then those of the Choir, each having a yellow wax candle in their hands. The Officiating Bishop is the last, having the Deacon at his left side, and being alone covered <note>wearing a head covering</note>, unless it be in the exit of the Church, in which case the entire Clergy covers themselves just as their Superior does.

<margin>How the Absolution is provided to the deceased.</margin>
Having arrived in the illuminated chapel, where the Officiating Bishop gives the Deceased the *Absolution*, <note>a series of prayers for the deliverance of the soul from purgatory</note> the Incense-bearer and the Acolyte who carries the Holy Water place themselves at the part of the chapel that looks a little to the side of the Epistle side <note>the right side of the altar when facing it</note> on the Altar, and behind the Bishop, who has the Deacon on his right side. The Sub-Deacon who carries the Cross and the two candle-bearers take their place opposite here and at the head of the body, a little to the side of the Gospel side <note>the left side of the altar</note>. When they have all placed themselves, the Officiating Bishop uncovers his head, and receiving the Ritual Book <note>original: "Kerkgewoonte Boek," likely the Roman Ritual or Pontifical</note> from the hand of the Deacon, he begins the Absolution of the deceased, reading the Prayer, of which the first words are: *Enter not into judgment, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Non intres in judicium &c."</note>. We leave untouched some responses that follow this Prayer, such as *Deliver us, O Lord* <note>original Latin: "Libera nos Domine"</note> and some others, to come to the blessing of the incense, after which the Bishop, walking around the funeral representation, <note>original: "Lyk-vertooning," referring to the coffin or the effigy representing the deceased</note> sprinkles some Holy Water there, incensing it on both sides, accompanied by many genuflections and bows of the head. Having performed the great work of the *Absolution*, the Officiating Bishop says the *Our Father, etc.* <note>original: "Pater, enz."</note>. After that, he turns toward the Cross and says some verses and prayers to be found in the Ritual Books. Finally, the Bishop gives the sign of the Cross over the funeral representation and says the *Rest* <note>*</note> over the Deceased, to which the Choir responds: *May he rest in peace* <note>original Latin: "Requiescat in pace"</note>. It is nevertheless certain that the Deceased does not immediately, after his departure from this World, rest, and that he in his

<column-break/>

journey from here to Heaven must at least walk through Purgatory, <note>original: "Vagevuur"</note> even if he had the good fortune to make this journey without taking any residence there. Thus it is that we believe we must explain the rest that these Men of God acquire for the Souls, and that they acquire for themselves through the income connected to these Funeral Masses. <note>original: "Lykmisfen"</note> After the ceremony of the *Absolution*, the Bishop and his retinue depart in the same order as they arrived.

An excess of religiosity sometimes produces fearful people, who have many *Absolutions* performed for the Deceased who were their relatives. It seems that the departed Deceased finds himself not much better for some time, unless five or six other *Absolutions* accompany him; but on the other hand, if the Clergy has more trouble from it, they do not find themselves the worse for it. The *Ceremonial of Bishops* <note>original: "Ceremoniaal der Bisschoppen," the *Caeremoniale Episcoporum*</note> mentions the Acquittal or *Absolution* performed by many Prelates, and describes it as such.

<margin>And with what Solemnity this occurs.</margin>
Four Prelates occupy the four sides of the burning or illuminated chapel. The first and youngest places himself on the right side at the feet of the Deceased; the second on the left side of the head; the third on the left side at the feet; the fourth on the right side of the head. The Officiating Bishop is seated on his Episcopal Throne, as has already been said, having behind him the Incense-bearer and the Minister of Holy Water. The Deceased, being thus surrounded by five Prelates, is no longer exposed to the Hellish plagues, which do not dare to seize him in this state. The Officiating Bishop gives him the first *Absolution*, saying *Enter not, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Non intres &c."</note> After him, the first of the four Prelates, who are placed at the four corners, sprinkles and incenses the funeral representation three times at each of its corners, going around the same. Subsequently, having said some Scriptural passages while the *Rest* <note>Requiem</note> is being sung, the Ministers go with the second Prelate who stands up to do his circuit. He sprinkles and incenses just as the first has done, prays and recites some Scriptural passages, and then everyone returns to his place. While one expects the third Prelate to give his *Absolution*, the *Responsory* <note>†</note> begins.

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH.

Finally, the fourth Prelate gives his blessing, and the Choir sings *Deliver me, O Lord* <note>original Latin: "Libera me Domine," a responsory from the Office of the Dead</note>. Then the Officiating Bishop comes to sprinkle and incense the Funeral Display <note>original: "Lyk-Vertooning," referring here to the catafalque</note> just as the others did; he performs the prayer of the *Absolution*, to which the Choir answers *Amen*; he pronounces the *Requiem* <note>Rest</note>, and *May they rest in peace* <note>original Latin: "Requiescant in pace"</note> is sung in music, if there are many deceased persons to be absolved.

The *Ceremonial* <note>the book of rites</note> adds that these four or five absolutions are not customary except in the first funeral processions of a deceased person. They are performed only once a (a) year, and every (b) nine days.

When there is no (c) Funeral Display present, the Acolytes spread a black cloth in the middle before the Altar: The officiating Bishop, who has the Incense-bearer and the Minister of Holy Water at his side, turns toward this cloth, and taking the Aspergillum <note>holy water sprinkler</note> from the hand of the first Deacon, he sprinkles this

<column-break/>

cloth three times, after which he also incenses the same three times.

<margin>How the Pope and his Cardinals attend Requiem Masses.</margin>
When the Pope and his Cardinals attend Requiem Masses in Rome, their *Eminences* are dressed in violet; the Cardinal Grand Penitentiary <note>original: "Opperbiechtvader"</note> then sings the Mass. His Holiness then incenses only the Offering portion of the Mass. The Pope sings the Funeral Prayer over the (d) *Catafalco* or the grand tomb. The first Cardinal-Priest gives the Censer and the Holy Water to His Holiness. Their *Eminences* show obedience to the Head of the Church. After the Mass, the Cardinals escort His Holiness back to St. Peter’s and perform their devotions before the Holy Sacrament. From there, the Sacred Society goes to visit the Tombs of the Popes, and some prayers are poured out there for the love of them. (e)

We deliberately pass over many observations regarding the ceremonies that precede and accompany the funeral processions.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

->The nature of the DEVOTION shown to the Cross, etc.<-

We shall now pass on to the ceremonies of the Cross, which is of absolute use in all Church duties of
<sig>Oo 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

---

<note>[This has been called a Responsory, because after a Chorister has sung, the entire Choir answers. Rabanus says that Responsories were invented by the Italians long before Antiphons. *Furetière.*]</note>

(a) The ancient Greeks, being convinced by their tradition and by reason that man was not entirely perishable in the grave, but that the noblest part withstood the corruption of matter, therefore celebrated the memory of their Heroes annually, and this ceremony took place around the graves of these illustrious deceased. Since the first centuries, the Christians followed this example, which was subsequently taken much further. All human institutions have a pure and simple beginning. The annual funeral services of the Greeks, preserving the memory of the famous deceased, gave the living the opportunity to follow them, so that they, like them, might earn an immortal name. The purpose of the annual funeral services of the Christians was to encourage people to practice religion holily, and to show that those who died in God live in him and must always live in the memory of the Church. The death of the believer whose memory was celebrated annually was described to the Christians; one prayed to God to obtain a similar passing; after which an offering was given for the needs of the Church. When one became convinced <unclear>service</unclear> that this offering relieved the soul of the deceased of many crying sins, everyone wanted to be helpful to their deceased. Fathers offered for their children, children for their parents, and wives for their husbands. The Priests of these Christians, finding their interest in this, encouraged these religious people to give generous offerings, by which they were benefited not a little: for they then began to enter into obligations for the souls of the Faithful. It is believed that praying for the dead, which was in use among the Heathens, crept into the Church around the end of the second century, and histories inform us that people prayed publicly for the soul of the Emperor Constantine the Great. The writers of the first centuries of the Church also inform us that it sometimes happened that souls returned from the other world requesting assistance from the living. Some Protestants believe that Requiem Masses were not introduced until the sixth century.

(b) The nine-day funeral service of the Christians has some reference to the nine-day service of Heathendom. The Romans mourned their dead for nine days, performed propitiatory sacrifices during this time, and held funeral meals called *Novendial Feasts* <note>original Latin: "Canæ Novendiales"</note>. The entire ceremony was accompanied by Vows and Prayers for the Deceased. Offerings were also made to the *Manes* <note>the spirits of the ancestors</note> or subterranean Gods on the grave of the deceased, and there was no doubt that this religious work brought relief to the souls. The service performed for the deceased was called *Inferiæ* <note>sacrifices to the underworld spirits</note>; whether it was done annually for the deceased or immediately followed their passing.

(c) *Bauldry Manuale Cerem.* (d) This was the name given to the Funeral Display.
(e) *See Relation della Corte di Roma by Lunadoro.*

# HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

<margin>And with what solemnity this is accompanied.</margin>
Having arrived, the Subdeacon takes the Cross after he, like the Deacon, has laid aside his *maniple* <note>a liturgical vestment worn on the left arm</note>; and they go together to the place where the burning chapel <note>original: "brandende Kapel," referring to a catafalque surrounded by candles</note> is, or the representation thereof, just as one went to bury the body of the Deceased. The Incense-bearer and the Minister of Holy Water go first; the Subdeacon follows them carrying the Cross between two candle-bearers, followed by those of the Choir, each holding a yellow wax candle in their hands. The Officiating Bishop is the last, having the Deacon at his left side, and being alone covered <note>wearing a head covering</note>, unless it is in the departure from the Church, in which case the entire Clergy covers themselves like their Head.

<margin>How the Absolution is delivered to the deceased.</margin>
Having arrived in the burning chapel, where the Officiating Bishop gives the Deceased the *Absolution*, the Incense-bearer and the Acolyte holding the Holy Water place themselves at the part of the chapel that faces a little to the side of the Epistle on the Altar, and behind the Bishop, who has the Deacon at his right side. The Subdeacon who carries the Cross and the two candle-bearers take their place opposite here and at the head of the body, a little to the side of the Gospel. When they have all taken their places, the Officiating Bishop uncovers his head, and receiving the Ritual Book <note>original: "Kerkgewoonte Boek"</note> from the hand of the Deacon, he begins the Absolution of the deceased, reading the Prayer, of which the first words are: *Enter not into judgment with us, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Non intres in judicium &c."</note> We leave untouched some responses that follow this Prayer, such as *Deliver us, O Lord* <note>original Latin: "Libera nos Domine"</note> and some others, to come to the blessing of the incense, after which the Bishop, walking around the funeral display <note>original: "Lyk vertooning"</note>, sprinkles some Holy Water there, incensing it on both sides, accompanied by many bows of the knees and head. Having performed the great work of the *Absolution*, the Officiating Bishop says the *Our Father, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Pater, enz."</note> Thereafter he turns toward the Cross and says some verses and prayers to be found in the Ritual Books. Finally, the Bishop gives the sign of the Cross over the funeral display, and says the *Rest* <note>original Latin: "Requiem"</note> for the Deceased, to which the Choir answers: *May he rest in peace* <note>original Latin: "Requiescat in pace"</note>. It is nonetheless certain that the Deceased does not immediately rest after his departure from this World, and that he, in his

<column-break/>

journey from here to Heaven, must at least walk through Purgatory <note>original: "Vagevuur"</note>, even if he had the fortune to make this journey without taking any stay there. Thus it is that we believe we must explain the "rest" that these Men of God <note>referring to the clergy</note> acquire for the Souls, and that they acquire for themselves through the income attached to these Requiem Masses. After the ceremony of the *Absolution*, the Bishop and his entourage depart in the same order as they came.

An excess of religiosity sometimes produces fearful people, who have many and various *Absolutions* performed for the Deceased who were their kin. It seems that the departed Deceased finds himself not much better for some time, unless five or six other *Absolutions* accompany him; but on the other hand, if the Clergy has more trouble from it, they do not find themselves the worse for it <note>a satirical jab at the fees paid for multiple services</note>. The *Ceremonial of Bishops* mentions the acquittal or *Absolution* resumed by many Prelates, and describes it thusly.

<margin>And with what Solemnity this occurs.</margin>
Four Prelates occupy the four sides of the burning or illuminated chapel. The first and youngest places himself at the right side at the Deceased's feet; the second at the left side of the head; the third at the left side at the feet; the fourth at the right side of the head. The Officiating Bishop is seated on his Episcopal Throne, as has already been said, having behind him the Incense-bearer and the Minister of Holy Water. The Deceased, thus surrounded by five Prelates, is no longer exposed to the plagues of Hell, which do not dare to seize him in this state. The Officiating Bishop gives him the first *Absolution*, saying *Enter not, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Non intres &c."</note> After him, the first of the four Prelates, who are placed at the four corners, sprinkles and incenses the funeral display thrice at each of its corners, walking around it. Subsequently, having said some passages of Scripture while the *Rest* <note>original: "Requiem"</note> is sung, the Ministers go with the second Prelate who stands up to make his circuit. He sprinkles and incenses just as the first has done, prays and recites some Scripture passages, and then everyone returns to their place. While one awaits the third Prelate to give his *Absolution*, one begins the *Responsory* <note>original: "Repons"</note> †

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH.

Finally, the fourth Prelate gives his blessing, and the Choir sings *Deliver me, O Lord* <note>original Latin: "Libera me Domine"</note> etc. Then the Officiating Bishop comes to sprinkle and incense the funeral representation <note>original: "Lyk-Vertooning," referring to the catafalque or effigy of the deceased</note> just as the others did; he performs the prayer of the *Absolution*, to which the Choir responds *Amen*; he pronounces the *Rest* <note>original Latin: "Requiem"</note>, and *May they rest in peace* <note>original Latin: "Requiescant in pace"</note> is sung in music, if there are many deceased to be absolved.

The *Ceremonial* <note>a liturgical book governing rites</note> adds that these four or five absolutions are not customary except in the first funeral processions of a deceased person. They are performed only once a (a) year, and every (b) nine days.

When there is no (c) funeral representation, the Acolytes spread a black cloth in the middle before the Altar: The officiating Bishop, who has at his side the Incense-bearer and the Minister of Holy Water, turns toward this cloth, and taking the aspergillum <note>holy water sprinkler</note> from the hand of the first Deacon, he thrice sprinkles this

<column-break/>

<margin>How the Popes and Cardinals attended the Funeral Masses.</margin>
cloth, after which he also incenses it three times.

When the Pope and his Cardinals attend the Funeral Masses in Rome, their *Eminences* are dressed in violet; the Cardinal Grand Penitentiary then sings the Mass. His Holiness then incenses only the Offering-part of the Mass. The Pope sings the funeral prayer over the *Catafalco* (d) or the grand tomb. The first Cardinal-Priest gives the Censer and the aspergillum to his Holiness. Their *Eminences* show obedience to the Head of the Church. After the Mass, the Cardinals escort his Holiness back to St. Peter’s, and perform their devotions before the Holy Sacrament. From there, the Sacred Society goes to visit the tomb of the Popes, and a few prayers are poured out there for love of them. (e)

## CHAPTER XXIII.

->What kind of DEVOTION one shows to the Cross, etc.<-

**W**e shall now pass on to the Ceremonies of the Cross, which is of absolute use in all Church duties of the
<sig>Oo 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

---

<gloss>[...has sung. This has been called a Response, since when a Choir has sung it, the entire Choir answers. Rabanus says that the Responses were invented by the Italians long before the Antiphons. *Furetière.*]</gloss>

(a) The ancient Greeks, being convinced by their tradition and by reason that man was not entirely perishable in the grave, but that the noblest part resisted the corruption of matter, therefore celebrated annually the memory of their Heroes, and this ceremony took place around the graves of these illustrious deceased. Since the first centuries, the Christians followed this example, which was subsequently taken much further. All human institutions have a pure and simple beginning. The annual funeral services of the Greeks, preserving the memory of the famous deceased, gave the living the opportunity to follow them, so that they, like them, might acquire an immortal name. The purpose of the annual funeral services of the Christians was to encourage people to practice religion holily, and to show that those who have died in God, live in him and must always live in the memory of the Church. One described to the Christians the death of the believer whose memory was celebrated annually: one prayed to God to obtain a similar passing; after which an offering was given for the needs of the Church. When it became useful to believe that this offering relieved the soul of the deceased of many crying sins <note>original: "krytende misdaaden," referring to grievous sins</note>, everyone wanted to be helpful to their deceased. Fathers offered for their children, children for their parents, and wives for their husbands. The Priests of these Christians, finding their interest herein, encouraged these religious people to give liberal offerings, by which they were not a little benefited: for they then began to enter into obligations for the souls of the Faithful. It is believed that praying for the dead, in use among the Heathens, entered the Church around the end of the second century, and Histories inform us that one prayed publicly for the soul of the Emperor Constantine the Great. The writers of the first centuries of the Church also inform us that it sometimes happened that souls returned from the other world requesting assistance from the living. Some Protestants believe that Funeral Masses were not introduced until the sixth century.

(b) The nine-day funeral service of the Christians has some regard for the nine-day service of Heathendom. The Romans mourned their dead for nine days, performed propitiatory sacrifices during this time, and held funeral meals which were called *Cœnæ Novendiales* <note>nine-day suppers</note>. The entire ceremony was accompanied by vows and prayers for the deceased. Offerings were also made to the *Manes* <note>spirits of the dead</note> or subterranean Gods on the grave of the deceased, and it was not doubted whether this religious work brought relief to the souls. The service performed for the deceased was called *Inferiæ* <note>sacrifices to the underworld</note>; whether it was performed annually for the deceased, or followed immediately upon his passing.

(c) *Bauldry, Manual of Ceremonies.* (d) Thus the funeral representation was called.
(e) *See Relation of the Court of Rome by Lunadoro.*

(a) The ancient Greeks, being convinced by their tradition and by reason that man was not entirely perishable in the grave, but that the noblest part withstood the corruption of matter, therefore celebrated annually the memory of their Heroes, and this ceremony took place around the graves of these illustrious deceased. ### HISTORICAL TREATISE ON THE
<margin>
What esteem the Christians of old had for the Cross and the signs of the cross.
</margin>
[is] the Roman Catholic religion. We have already spoken of the custom of carrying the Cross before the Pope.

It is noteworthy (a) that among the ancient Egyptians, the letter *Tau*, which represents a type of Cross, signified the future life. They depicted their God *Serapis* with this letter on his chest. Is this not a remarkable symbol of the pectoral cross <term>a cross worn on the chest by high-ranking clergy</term> of the Church’s Prelates? One of the religious duties of Paganism was to bring the hand to the mouth to kiss it, making a shape of the Cross with the forefinger and thumb. The Cross has been honored by Christians since the first centuries of the Church; they traced it on their foreheads to show the Pagans that they considered it an honor to be disciples of a Crucified God. To distinguish themselves even better from the idolaters, they made the sign of the Cross so that they would be recognized among the Unbelievers and unite together under the Banner of the Gospel. They prayed to God, joining their hands together or stretching them toward Heaven in the shape of a cross. They imagined that from then on the Devil had a (b) powerful terror of this sign, and that nothing was more fit to banish him to Hell. It is possible that in this respect, many metaphors accompanied the expressions of the Christians of these first centuries; but however it may be, one cannot deny that the devotion to the Cross increased uncommonly following these first thoughts.

<margin>
Helena, the Finder of the Wood of the Cross, noted.
</margin>
Already at the beginning of the fourth century, this devotion was increased by the discovery of the Cross, which Helena, Emperor Constantine’s mother, found during her journey through the Holy Land. The son, no less religious than his mother, introduced the shape of the Cross into his standards <note>the military banners known as the Labarum</note>. However, it is believed that this did not take hold in the churches until the beginning of the fifth century, although it had been seen for some time depicted on coins, banners, (c) shields, helmets, and on the crowns of Emperors. At the end of the seventh

<column-break/>

century, the sixth General Council held at Constantinople commanded that **JESUS CHRISTUS** should be depicted in a human form upon the Cross, to present the death and suffering of the Savior more vividly to Christians; but symbolic depictions had already been in use for several centuries. Christ was often depicted in the form of a Lamb (d) at the foot of a Cross; the Holy Spirit was added (e) under the form of a Dove. Sometimes a Crown was painted above the Cross to indicate to the believer that the Crown of Eternity is the value and reward for his suffering before the Cross of **JESUS CHRISTUS**. A Stag was also sometimes depicted at the foot of the Sacred Wood, since the stag is the enemy of the Serpent and a symbol of **JESUS CHRISTUS**, who is the Devil's enemy. All these symbolic depictions disappeared upon the appearance of the Savior's image in human form on the Cross by a decree of the sixth General Council; and this is the first origin of crucifixes.

<margin>
Where it is believed the Wood of the Cross, the Inscription, and the Nails of the Cross are possessed, noted.
</margin>
It is believed (f) that the Cross of **JESUS CHRISTUS** was made of oak. We have already said that Empress Helena was the fortunate discoverer of it. Likewise, she found (g) the Inscription <note>original: "Opschrift," referring to the Titulus Crucis or the 'INRI' sign</note> of this Holy Wood. Pope Sergius discovered around the year 690 another remarkable portion of the Cross, which is carefully preserved in Rome. It was in the year 1492 that the Inscription was found again in a church of the same city that was being rebuilt; it had been hidden in a wall, after which it had fallen into oblivion due to the misfortunes of the times. Pope Alexander VI granted a Bull <term>a formal papal decree</term> concerning this in the year 1496, promising an annual forgiveness of sins <note>an indulgence</note> to the pious who visited the church where the Inscription was found every year on the last Sunday of January. (h) Nevertheless, among the Benedictine clergy in Toulouse, a significant portion was seen of

(a) See *Caelius Rhodiginus, Ancient Readings, Book 10, Chapter 8.*
(b) *St. Jerome, On the Nativity: "The Devil trembles at this sign," etc.* <note>original: "Hoc signum Diabolus contremiscit"</note> Cardinal Bona, in his book *Divine Psalmodies, Chapter 16*, took the trouble to gather all the powers of the sign of the Cross. The Cross is, he says, the seal of our Lord; it is as useful to Christians as Circumcision was to the Jews. It is the ladder upon which one climbs to Paradise. It gives us life, delivers us from death, leads to virtue, prevents the temptation of the faithful, moderates passions, opens Heaven, preserves cities, strengthens and confirms friendship, etc. *Moses* struck the rock twice, making the sign of the Cross. *Severus*, a Christian poet, sang in his pastoral songs that a shepherd protected his sheep from the wolf's jaws by marking their foreheads with the Cross. *Prudentius*, another Christian poet, measured out the power of this Divine Wood no less extensively.

<margin>How the Cross was found, and with what a miracle</margin>
Let us not forget to mention that much Wood of the true Cross is to be found in the States of Christendom. The Heretics <note>The author likely refers to Protestant reformers like John Calvin, who famously mocked the proliferation of "True Cross" fragments by saying there was enough wood to fill a large ship.</note> mock this salutary abundance, and believe that from all this Wood, carpenters would find enough material to be able to make various works from it. We have stopped their mouths by bringing forward the reasons to justify the reverence held for the two Inscriptions and for so many Cross-nails, which are still recognized under the name of such.

We have already spoken of the *Finding* of the Holy *Cross*. It was Helena <note>Saint Helena (c. 246–330 AD), mother of Constantine the Great, traditionally credited with finding the relics of the Passion.</note> who found this Divine Wood, besides the Nails and the Inscription, which happened thusly. <margin>
the Finding of the Cross and Exaltation of the Cross celebrated, And by what occurrence the Feast of the Recovery of the Cross was instituted.
</margin>
The *Exaltation of the Cross* <note>original: "Kruisverheffing"</note> is celebrated on the 14th of September. Under the reign of Heraclius <note>Byzantine Emperor, r. 610–641</note>, Chosroes <note>Kosroes II</note>, King of Persia, plundered the City of Jerusalem and carried away that portion of the True Cross which the Empress Helena had left in this City in memory of the Savior, and sent this Sacred Wood to Persia, which his soldiers called the *God of the Christians*. After several battles, in which the King of Persia was continually defeated, the Emperor Heraclius was so fortunate as to find the Wood of the Cross again. The Prince himself escorted it to Jerusalem; he laid aside his imperial ornaments to humble himself before the Cross, and seeing himself hindered by his Imperial garments under the burden of the same, he took them off. He then laid it upon his shoulders to bring it with all the more pomp and state to Calvary, from where it had been carried away. Miracles confirmed this memorable day, and subsequently the Feast of the *Exaltation of the Cross* was instituted, which is still celebrated today under the name of the *Exaltation of the Cross*. Nonetheless, a feast of the same name was celebrated long before, which is believed to have been instituted since the times of Emperor Constantine. However it may be, the recovery of the Cross nonetheless did not compensate the Christians for the loss of the East, which Muhammadanism <note>original: "Mahometanendom"</note> overran with a wonderful speed during the reign of Emperor Heraclius.

Poitiers boasts of possessing a portion of the True Wood of the Cross. Radegund <note>A Frankish queen and saint</note>, consort of Clotarius King of France, provided this Heavenly gift for the Cathedral of all Poitou: Paris also possesses another portion of the True Cross, and one celebrates (a) the feast on the first Sunday of August in honor of this possession under the name of the *Reception of the Holy Cross.*

<margin>
How the finding of the Cross and the recovery of the Cross are celebrated,
</margin>

The *Exaltation of the Cross* <note>The feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, celebrated on September 14th, commemorates both the finding of the True Cross by Saint Helena and its later recovery from the Persians.</note> is celebrated on the 14th of September. Under the reign of Heraclius <note>Byzantine Emperor from 610 to 641 AD.</note>, Chosroes <note>Khosrow II, the last great king of the Sasanian Empire of Persia.</note>, King of Persia, plundered the City of Jerusalem and carried away that portion of the True Cross which the Empress Helena had left in this city in memory of the Savior. He sent this Sacred Wood to Persia, which his soldiers called the *God of the Christians*.

<margin>
And by what chance the Feast of the recovery of the Cross was established.
</margin>

After several battles in which the King of Persia was continually defeated, the Emperor Heraclius was fortunate enough to find the wood of the Cross again. The Prince personally escorted it to Jerusalem; he set aside his imperial ornaments to humble himself before the Cross, and finding himself hindered by his imperial robes under its weight, he took them off. He then placed it upon his shoulders to bring it with greater pomp and state to Calvary, from whence it had been carried away. Miracles confirmed this memorable day, and subsequently, the Feast of the *Exaltation of the Cross* was established, which is still celebrated today under that name. Nevertheless, a feast of the same name had been celebrated long before, which is believed to have been established since the time of Emperor Constantine. However that may be, the recovery of the Cross did not compensate the Christians for the loss of the East, which Muhammadanism <note>An archaic term for Islam; the author is referring to the rapid expansion of the Rashidun Caliphate during the 7th century.</note> overran with wonderful speed during the reign of Emperor Heraclius.

Poitiers boasts of possessing a portion of the true wood of the Cross. Radegund, consort of Clotarius <note>Chlothar I, King of the Franks.</note>, King of France, provided this Heavenly gift for the Cathedral of all Poitou. Paris also possesses another portion of the True Cross, and the feast is celebrated (a) on the first Sunday of August in honor of this possession under the name of the *Reception of the Holy Cross*.

### RELIGIOUS DUTIES etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH.

and an antiphon <note>original: *Antiönna*</note> follows the litanies. He sprinkles the Cross with holy water, then incenses it, and after the incensing, burning candles are placed on the top of the Cross and on both arms. If the Cross is so high that it cannot be reached, (a) a ladder is placed against it. Psalms and prayers then form the conclusion. The consecration of all Crosses in public places, at crossroads, or along common highways ends in the same manner. We shall postpone the *Adoration* of the Cross until the Easter Festivals, when it is shown to the people on Holy Saturday.

<column-break/>

<margin>The ceremony performed for the blessing of the Crosses.</margin>
As for the small, newly made Crosses intended to be carried in processions, or those placed in churches, chapels, on altars, or in private houses: when a priest is to bless some with the permission of his Bishop, he places them on the altar on the Epistle side <note>The right side of the altar when facing it, where the Epistles are traditionally read.</note> upon a cushion. Having ordered a wax candle to be lit, he provides himself with a surplice and a stole <note>original: *Stool*</note> matching the liturgical color of the day. Furthermore, if possible, he is assisted by a clerk in a surplice who carries the holy water vessel and the aspergillum <note>original: *Wyquast*; a brush or branch used for sprinkling holy water</note>. Making the sign of the Cross, he recites the prayers corresponding to the subject, etc. (b) However, it should still be noted that the prayer used to bless a stone or metal Cross differs from the blessing performed over a Cross made of wood. After the prayers, the priest kneels before the Cross to adore it; and subsequently, he shall kiss it, as the clergy present shall also do.

The Cross must always be on the altar. It is carried before the Patriarch and the Archbishop, just as it is for the Pope, with the crucifix turned toward the prelate. The cross-bearer must be dressed in clerical attire.

Prelates wear a pectoral cross <note>original: *Borstkruis*</note> which hangs from a small chain or silk ribbon around their neck. There are always (c) some relics enclosed within this pectoral cross, or a piece

<column-break/>

of the True Cross. The pectoral cross serves as a replacement for the ancient ornaments of the breastplate of the Jewish High Priest. The use of this Cross is believed to have been instituted around the end of the eighth or the beginning of the ninth century. The Patriarch of Constantinople sent a gold reliquary in the year 811 to Pope Leo III, in which lay a small piece of the wood of the Cross. This sacred object was called in Greek an *Encolpium* <note>original: *Encolpium*</note>, which signifies something worn on the breast or bosom.

<margin>When the use of Crosses was introduced.</margin>
This custom possibly originates from the early Christians, who, out of devotion to the Cross of JESUS CHRIST, wore the image on their breast, which served as a subject of remembrance for them on various occasions. For they cut, for example, their bread in the shape of a cross, and this custom lasted a long time in the Church; but, without attributing it solely to the esteem the early Christians had for the Cross of JESUS CHRIST, might it not have been a remnant of the ancient Romans' custom of cutting their bread, which gave rise to this saying (d)? When traveling, or even when walking through the city, they wore Crosses as a testament of the religious love owed to our Savior. Consequently, they used nothing but ornaments enriched with precious stones, just as ladies now wear diamond crosses. Crosses were also carved onto gravestones and at the entrances of chapels. The pectoral cross had to be consecrated and sprinkled with holy water just like other Crosses.

The consecration of Crosses is very ancient and took place at least before the seventh General Council <note>The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 AD, which addressed the use of icons and images.</note>. Some writers believe it has been in use since the second century, and that oaths in legal matters had to be made before the Cross then; but this is without a semblance of truth, since the Church was then still under the yoke of Paganism.

<margin>and what a consequence this was.</margin> served before (a), and it is known that the priestly garment of the Jewish High Priest was equipped with small bells. However it may be, Sabinianus <note>Pope Sabinian (r. 604–606), successor to Gregory the Great</note> introduced the use of bells for the Mass and Canonical hours around the year 605, just as they are still used today. The practice of tolling bells for the dead was established in England (b) since the start of the eighth century, and this has remained in use in some non-Roman countries (c) despite their resistance to the Holy See. Besides this use, they are also (d) rung for the *Ave Maria* <note>The Angelus prayer</note> in the morning, at noon, and in the evening to invite the people to prayer. They were also rung (e) at the elevation of the Holy Sacrament, when it was brought to the sick, and carried in procession.

<margin>How in Holy Week the use of the Ratchet served for Bells.</margin> During Holy Week <note>The week preceding Easter</note>, instead of bells, a wooden instrument called a *Cresselle* <note>original: *Cresselle*; a wooden rattle or clapper used when bells are silenced in mourning</note> was used. In this *Cresselle* lay a hidden mystery; for example, it represented JESUS CHRIST praying on the Cross and inviting the people to his preaching. It represented the humility of the Savior, etc. It is believed that the use of the *Cresselle* is much older than that of bells (f), and that the first Christians used them to gather secretly for prayers in underground and remote places.

The Blessing is commonly (g) called the "Baptism of Bells," since at that time

<column-break/>

one gives them the name of some Saint (h) under whose invocation they are offered to God. *The blessing consecrates them to the service of God, so that they have the power not only to strike the ears—but to move hearts through the power of the Holy Spirit.—* This blessing also serves, when they are rung, to drive away demons, etc. It is usually the Bishop who performs this blessing. Before reaching that point, the parish priest, to whom the care of having the bells cast is entrusted (i), must take great care that the casting does not take place in a church or cemetery; that nothing unedifying is engraved on these bells; but only a Cross or image of the Saint or Patron of the church. One must also ensure that no superstition is mixed in during the melting and blessing of the bells.

<margin>With what solemnity the Bells are baptized.</margin> Once the bell is finished, it is soon placed in a condition to receive the blessing: namely, it is hung in such a position that one can walk around it, to reach both inside and outside, to wash it and perform the sacred anointing. Near the bell, a seat is placed for the officiating Bishop, a bench on his left side for the Deacon, and chairs to the side for the rest of the clergy. A lectern with the *Antiphonal* <note>original: *Antiphonaal*; a liturgical book containing the choral parts of the office</note> or the Church Customal Book is brought to the place where the ceremony will be held.

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc., of the ROMAN CHURCH.

If this takes place in the Church, a credence table <note>A small side table used for holding the vessels of the Eucharist or other rites</note> is placed to the side of the Epistle <note>The right side of the altar from the perspective of the congregation</note>, covered with a white tablecloth. Upon it are placed the aspergillum <note>A brush or sprinkler for holy water</note>, the holy water vat, the salt container, towels, the oil cruet, the jar of chrism <note>Consecrated oil used in baptism and other rites</note>, the censers and incense boats, the vessel of myrrh, some cotton, a dish, a ewer <note>A large jug</note>, and some breadcrumbs. All these things are brought to the site of the ceremony, after which they proceed to the Consecration of the Bell * in the following manner. The Bishop, dressed in an alb <note>A long white tunic</note>, stole, and white cope <note>A long ceremonial cloak</note>, and the Deacon, with his vestments of the same color, depart from the Sacristy in a procession. The censer-bearer leads the way, followed by two candle-bearers provided with their burning wax candles; the Clergy follow them in pairs, and then the Bishop, having the Deacon at his left side. Having arrived at the place where the blessing shall occur, the candle-bearers set their candles on the credence table, remaining there as the censer-bearers also do. The Clergy place themselves on either side, and the Bishop, seated in his chair placed near the Bell and covering his head, instructs the people regarding the Holy ritual he is about to perform, exhorted them to be as attentive as possible, and then stands up to sing a *Miserere* <note>original: *Miserere*; Psalm 51, "Have mercy on me, O God"</note> with the Choir, along with other Hymns indicated in the Ritual Book.

When the singing is finished, everyone stands and covers their heads, as does the Bishop. He exorcises (a) and blesses the water and the salt, saying these words: pray to God for both, and asks in one of his prayers that through the power of the Holy Water, the Bell may acquire the power to destroy the secret snares of the Devil, to drive away phantoms, to temper the force of storms, to awaken piety in the hearts of the faithful, etc. Next, the

<column-break/>

Bishop mixes the water and salt together, and after making three signs of the Cross in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he says each time (b) "The Lord be with you." In the prayer following the mixing, he prays to God that it may please Him (c) to look favorably upon the creature of salt and water—which might almost lead us to believe that these creatures consisting of salt and water possess intellect and judgment, much like the Count of Gabalis <note>A reference to a 1670 satirical occult novel by the Abbé de Villars</note> depicts the Gnomes † and Odins ‡ for us, etc. Finally, the Bishop takes the aspergillum, dips it into the Holy Water, and begins to wash the Bell: a task which his ministers complete. After the sprinkling, scouring, and washing of the interior and exterior, some linen is taken and the Bell is carefully dried off again, while certain Psalms are sung.

A jar containing what is called the last Anointing <note>Extreme Unction oil</note> is then opened by the Deacon. Into this, the Bishop dips the thumb of his right hand, with which he draws the Cross on the center of the Bell. Then the Deacon lifts the Bishop's cope on the right side of his hand, and does this every time something is done to the Bell. As soon as the Priest or Bishop has made this Cross, he repeats a prayer containing the previous prayers; after which he wipes the place where he made the Cross with some cotton. With the same oil, the Bell is marked with seven new Crosses, after which Psalm 29 <note>Numbered as the 28th in the Vulgate</note> is sung. Four other Crosses, made <margin>And a name given.</margin> by means of the Holy Chrism, set the seal upon the blessing of this metal. It is upon these four made Crosses that the officiating Bishop honors the Bell with a sort of Baptism, consecrating it in the name of the Trinity, and then names the Saint who serves as the Bell's Sponsor or Godfather, whose name is commonly given to this sounding metal.

->HISTORICAL DISCOURSE on the<-

<margin>How the bells are incensed.</margin>
The baptized or consecrated bell is also incensed, which takes place in the following manner. The thurifer <note>The person who carries the incense burner or censer</note> with the censer and the incense boat in hand approaches the Celebrant or officiating Bishop, who is seated near the bell. He takes incense from the boat, as well as myrrh and other aromatics, and throws these spices—without blessing them—into the censer. He then gives it to the thurifer, who places it beneath the bell so that it may be perfumed by the smoke. The prayer is performed with diligent devotion after a sung antiphon <note>A short sentence sung or recited before or after a psalm</note>; this perfuming is called the *dew of the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "dauw van den H. Geest"</note>. This solemn use of incensing is followed by the blessing of the incense, and they proceed with the thurifer in the middle of two candle-bearers, the Clerk or Sub-Deacon, and the Deacon—who carries the Gospel Book—to the place where the Gospel must be read. The Deacon gives the book to the Clerk to hold. The Clerk is positioned between the two candle-bearers in such a way, so says the Customary <note>A book containing the rites and customs of a particular church</note>, that they turn their backs toward the North; however, as for the Bishop, he has turned himself toward the Deacon. The thurifer at his right side offers him the censer to perform the usual incensing of the Gospel. After the Gospel has been read, the Clerk gives the book to the Celebrant to kiss. The Deacon incenses it. The Bishop turns toward the bell and makes the sign of the Cross over it with his right hand. Then the Clerk returns his biretta <note>A square clerical cap</note> to him, and they all subsequently go to disrobe.

By the decrees of the Council of Trent <note>A 16th-century ecumenical council that defined Catholic doctrine in response to the Reformation</note>, it is forbidden to place any unusual or uncommon image in the churches without the consent of the Bishop. One proceeds with the blessing of an image in the same way as with a new Cross. <margin>And what mysteries accompany the ceremony of the bells.</margin>
The Church Customaries teach us that the consecration of the bells represents that of the Teachers <note>The clergy or doctors of the church who "sound out" the truth</note>; that the washing, both inside and out, followed by the anointing with oil, expresses the holiness of Baptism; that the seven anointings in the form of a Cross testify (a) *that the Teachers must surpass common Christians in the grace of the Holy Spirit, and in demonstrating through the seven gifts that they possess the required perfection; that the anointing on the inside with the Chrism-oil signifies the absolute perfection of the Holy Spirit, which the Bishop finds shared with him through his confirmation.* It is easily believed that the incenses contain no small mysteries. The first representation they depict is that, just as the smoke of the incense rises to the bell and fills it, likewise the Teacher, adorned with the perfection of God's Spirit, receives the incense of the vows and prayers of the faithful. (b) If anyone desires to look up these mysteries, they will find many others in the Church Customaries.

<margin>When the veneration of images was introduced, and at times contested.</margin>
Protestant writers are of the opinion that the veneration of images <note>original: "Beeldendienst"</note> did not take hold until the fourth century, and that it subsequently increased extraordinarily, whereupon the zeal of the passionate *Iconoclasts* <note>Image-breakers; from the Greek 'eikon' (image) and 'klaein' (to break)</note> † gained much more ground than religion itself did. Nevertheless, there were those among them who brought forward good reasons for destroying the images. Of this opinion was Serenus, Bishop of Marseille, who had them removed in his diocese to prevent Christians newly converted from idolatry to the true faith from worshipping them as idols and honoring them as false deities. However, Pope Gregory ordered him to set them up again, while nonetheless praising his zeal and condemning the abuse of images; he believed that coarse and material representations were less effective than pastoral instruction, prescribing this latter means to present to his people the true use that one ought to maintain regarding images.

<margin>The reason given for the introduction of the veneration of images.</margin>
The use of images is almost as old as religion itself, and this is not surprising; since its origin is owed to the weakness of human intellect, which, being unable to devote itself for long or attentively to purely spiritual subjects, imperceptibly passes over to material things and seeks to make them tangible, to serve as the object of its religion. There is almost no one who would not speak to God as to a King, since the former is invisible, and on the contrary, the

<column-break/>

majesty of a King, through its visibility, masters the attention of the one who speaks. How many visible signs are used to teach children to pray to God and to help them understand His wonders? It is true that the use of these signs becomes dangerous. In former times, God was compelled to forbid them to the Jewish people; but nonetheless, Christians have believed they might follow the pagans, their ancestors, without danger. Thus it is that, to maintain devotions through objects that strike the senses, God the Father is depicted in churches as an old man, since He calls Himself the *Ancient of Days* <note>A title for God from the Book of Daniel</note>. The Son (a) is represented as a man, since He took on the human form. As for the Holy Spirit, He is depicted (b) under the form of a Dove, which is the symbol of simplicity. Angels are represented as youths with wings on their shoulders, since it is supposed that, being ministers of the Divinity, their activity cannot be better represented than by youths, and their swiftness by birds.

<margin>How the ancient Pagans viewed images, and what they understood by that service.</margin>
The ancient Pagans did not attribute supreme power to the great men whom they called Gods and demi-gods after their deaths, although they granted them a portion of the honor that seemed to belong only to the Supreme Being. They believed that these great men, through deification <note>original: "Vergodding"</note>, became Gods, Demons, or Guardian Spirits, which corresponds in some measure to the *Canonization* of the Roman Church, such that they were officials or helpers...

† [It was in the eighth century that those who resisted the veneration of images were called *Iconomachs* <note>original: "Iconomachen"</note>, image-fighters, or *Iconoclasts*, image-breakers, because they taught that it was unlawful to introduce images into churches for religious purposes; in this, the Emperors Leo III and Leo IV were favorable to them. Leo III had it proclaimed by his States that no one should worship any image made by hands, whether carved, cast, or painted, and that images already erected should be cast down and broken everywhere. Although Constantine *Copronymus* <note>Constantine V</note>, Leo's son, was no less inclined to oppose images than his father—since all worshippers of wooden, stone, and painted images were condemned during his reign at the Council of Constantinople—nevertheless, in the year 787, at the Second Council of Nicaea, a restoration of images was decreed; to which the Empress Irene and her son Constantine VI lent no small hand. Following this, the churches were again filled with statues and paintings.]

(b) This manner of depicting the Holy Spirit is very old, and in former times the *Eucharist* <note>The consecrated bread/host</note> was even kept in a box made like a Dove. Furthermore, the custom of painting Saints with certain things related to their deeds or status was also in use among the Pagans, of which the representations of their Gods and Demi-gods like Mercury, Apollo, Aesculapius, Diana, Minerva, Hercules, Bacchus, etc., are examples. Today, the fire of St. Anthony represents his Divine Love; the pig at his feet testifies that he trampled earthly lusts; his bell his diligence in prayer; the letter *Tau* the Cross of Christ. The giant stature of St. Christopher denotes the strength of a Christian; the small child he carries signifies the love of the Son of God, and the river he wades through is the flood of worldly cares. One can find many such examples in *Casalius, On the Sacred Ancient Christian Rites* <note>original: "Casalius de Sacr. Vet. Christ. <margin>Miracles performed by images, and how they are worked.</margin>
Few Christians are ignorant of the miracles and wondrous effects of the images of our Roman Saints. We shall, however, bring forward and recount some of them. The Image of Christ, wounded by a villain with a dagger-thrust, feeling itself thus hurt, placed

its hand upon the wound, is very famous in Naples: but that (c) of Our Lady, the work of St. Luke, a famous painter and Evangelist <note>St. Luke is traditionally considered the first icon painter of the Virgin Mary.</note>, is no less so; it is also said that the angels have often loudly sung the *Litanies* <note>A form of prayer consisting of a series of petitions.</note> around it. It would be unnecessary to recount here the histories of various other famous images, since books have been written on this subject: it is nevertheless noteworthy for the reader that long before Christianity, the pagans attributed to the images of their gods and heroes the power to perform miracles. Titus Livius <note>Livy, a famous Roman historian.</note>, an ingenious writer of pagan legends, adorned his history with many miracles and monstrous things, among which are many fabrications of images and decorative depictions of the pagans; Cicero, who otherwise was not the most light-hearted of believers, often tells us of these spiritual wonders; such as, for example, those consisting of the sweating (d) of certain statues. <margin>And with what solemnity the same are shown.</margin>
On the morning before the Easter Festival, three Canons went from the Chapel to the High Altar and sang: *who is it who shall roll away the stone of the grave for us?* <note>This is a reenactment of the "Visitatio Sepulchri," a medieval liturgical drama.</note> Then some children dressed as Angels came to them and asked: *Whom do you seek?* The Canons gave the Angels as an answer, *we seek Jesus the Nazarene.* The Angels answered, *he is not here.* Subsequently, the Cantor addressed the first of the Canons with these words: *Tell us, Mary, what you have seen on the way;* to which the Canon answered him: *I have seen the Grave of Christ who lives, and the glory of Him who has risen.* The second Canon added: *I have seen the Angels, witnesses of the Resurrection; I have seen the Holy Shroud and the garments;* at the same time this Shroud—
