Whoever reads the section of Chapter 16 of the *Psalmodia* by Cardinal Bona will take all that this Religious Cardinal says to the Cross as the poetic fervor <note>original: "Geestdryvery," which can mean fanaticism or spiritual intoxication; here used to mean poetic license or extreme devotion.</note> of a Poet. It is certain that these expressions and similar ones should never be taken in the strictest sense. It is even a crime to do otherwise. It is sufficiently believed that there is no one among the Christians who, after a little reflection, imagines that two pieces of wood, so arranged that they form a Cross, would have the power to protect those who address them to obtain Salvation, as Cardinal Bona has done, saying:

> Save us, fortified by your
> fearsome Sign. <note>original Latin: "Salva nos tremendo tuo / Signaculo munitos."</note>

But, some will say, he who addresses himself directly to a piece of wood from the true Cross, and would touch it at the same time, will undoubtedly feel the salutary effects; since it is to be presumed that the particles emanating from the wood to which JESUS CHRIST was attached would have the same effect on the human body as a lodestone <note>original: "Zeilsteen," a magnetic stone used for navigation.</note> on a needle.

Commonly, this name is attributed to a converted Jewish woman, called Berenice, who covered the Savior’s face with her handkerchief when he carried the Cross to Calvary, to dry his sweat and blood, which flowed from his face. It is claimed that this cloth was folded in three, and that the Savior's countenance was imprinted in each of these folds, of which one was kept in Rome, one in Spain, and the third in Jerusalem. In the Vatican Library, however, one finds a written Book containing the History of the transfer of the Holy Shroud to Rome, which it is believed occurred under the Reign of Tiberius; for Methodius says that this Emperor, having heard what miracles were performed by JESUS CHRIST in Judea, and finding himself infected with Leprosy, sent Envoys there, who brought Berenice with the Shroud to Rome, from which touch the Emperor was healed. <margin>What Miracles the Besançon Shroud performed.</margin>
The Besançon Shroud is famous for its miracles. It has even raised the dead, and this resurrection, which occurred in the fourteenth century, subsequently strengthened the esteem for the Shroud quite significantly. The Church of St. Stephen, where it was kept, soon became too small. The multitude of the devout coming from all directions to see this miracle-working Shroud required that a wooden stage be erected in front of the Church, which was afterwards replaced by a stone building, from where the Shroud was shown twice a year: specifically, on Easter Day and on the Sunday before Ascension Day. The aforementioned Chifflet (a) has, in his description, left the memory of the miracles performed by this *relic* <note>original: "Reliquie"</note> to posterity. It has on many occasions cured dangerous illnesses, made the blind see, and caused the plague to cease; and even the images <note>reproductions or prints</note> of this Holy Shroud have worked uncommon healings, as one can see and read in the work of our cited Author.

<margin>A Brotherhood established for the same.</margin>
The Brotherhood of the Holy Shroud was subsequently established in Besançon because of a severe plague from which it is asserted that this *relic* delivered the City in the year 1544. This Brotherhood holds a solemn Procession annually on the 3rd of May in the Church and Cloister of St. Stephen, and the Holy Shroud is then carried solemnly, enclosed in a small silver casket, attended by the most prominent citizens of the city. In the year 1579, Pope Gregory XIII granted great

<column-break/>

privileges to the Altar of the Holy Shroud. The Bull of this Pope assures that all the souls of the faithful for whom one performs the Mass at this Altar shall acquire Indulgences in the next World, and be delivered from the punishment of Purgatory through the merits of JESUS CHRIST, of the blessed Virgin, and those of the Apostles Peter and Paul.

<margin>The Shroud of Turin also famous for miracles.</margin>
The Shroud of Turin need not yield to that of Besançon. It was likewise brought from Jerusalem, and one can look up the circumstances in the History by Chifflet. He informs us that after changing its residence three or four times, it finally found a permanent place in Turin in the Chapel of the Holy Shroud, which is a part of the Cathedral. This *relic* is no less famous than the others for its miracles. Its presence alone delivered a possessed person from his ailment in the year 1534, and if a Father, seeing his Son in danger of drowning, had not (b) prayed to it, it would have been the end of the youth's life. This Holy Shroud is shown on the 4th of May, being its Feast day established by Julius II in the year 1506 (c). This Pope also founded the Brotherhood of this *relic* to satisfy the piety of Duke Charles and Duchess Claudia, his mother: He added Indulgences (d) for the faithful who visited the Chapel of the Shroud at certain times and practiced their devotion there.

<margin>Various other Shrouds and where they are found.</margin>

# CHAPTER XXIX.

## Concerning the Blessing of Priestly Garments, of Military Commanders, Banners, and Standards, etc.

<margin>How the priestly garments are consecrated.</margin>
This Blessing is performed only by the Bishop and is not permitted to any [ordinary] Priest. The one performing this blessing must wear the surplice <term>surplice: a white liturgical vestment worn over a cassock</term> and over it the stole of a color corresponding to the designated day. This Blessing does not differ from the preceding ones. It is performed by the light of wax candles with a sprinkling of Holy Water and several prayers found in the liturgy book. All the garments, from the miter to the soles of the feet, † receive the same blessing.

<margin>and the vessels of the Altar [are] blessed.</margin>
We refer the reader to the Consecration of the Altar for what is said there specifically regarding the blessing of the linens and other altar cloths; of the altar coverings, *chalice veils*, the *Tabernacle* \*, the *Ciborium* <term>ciborium: a chalice-like container used to hold consecrated bread</term>, and the pyx in which the *Eucharist* is kept; finally, the vessels containing the Holy Oils. To the blessing (a) of the chalice veil and the chalice, the anointing and the sign of the Cross with the Holy Oil are added: after which the chalice and chalice veil are scrubbed with breadcrumbs.

<margin>With what solemnity a man of war is blessed,</margin>
Regarding the blessing of those who are equipped for the Holy War, such as Knights, etc., as well as the army banners—both of which are depicted in the accompanying illustration—this is the most noteworthy part: When the Bishop (b) blesses the new (c) warrior, he gives him the Sword,

<column-break/>

which he has previously blessed and consecrated by the sprinkling of Holy Water. The Bishop, in giving him this sword, exhorts him to use it against the enemies of the Church and Religion, and for the protection of widows and orphans, etc., after which he places it in the scabbard, and the Bishop hangs it at his side. The warrior, having been kneeling during this ceremony, stands up, draws the sword from the scabbard, brandishes it three times through the air, and then lays it upon his left arm. The Bishop, who may be armed only with the Cross and Breviary as a warrior of the Gospel, then draws the material sword with steadfastness, giving three blows to the one who is to bear it, and exhorts him to be a (d) *Soldier of Peace*. Subsequently, he places it back into the scabbard, gives the military novice a gentle blow on the cheek, exhorts him to be watchful (e), and finally gives him the kiss of peace. The companions <note>original: "Spitsbroeders," referring to brothers-in-arms</note> of this newly trained man in military service put the spurs on his feet. The Bishop then has an Antiphon sung (f), after which he rises from his Seat and once more blesses the one he has consecrated for war. This warrior then kisses the Prelate’s hand and returns home in peace with his sword and spurs.

### CHAPTER XXX.

->Concerning the ADMONITIONS and SERMONS customary in the Church.<-

This part of the Divine Service is far too important not to be mentioned here. Under the name of this "Admonition," the *Ritual of Alet* <note>original: *Gewoonte-Boek van Alet*; referring to the influential 1667 liturgical guide by Nicolas Pavillon, Bishop of Alet</note> teaches us that we must understand the Instruction presented to the people regarding the necessity of their Salvation; the Prayers that the Church offers primarily for the Faithful; the announcement of Feasts, Fasts, Commandments or Proclamations, Holy Orders, Marriages, and other matters touching upon Ecclesiastical discipline. The Admonition is given after the Gospel, since this portion of the Spiritual Service is primarily established to explain the mysteries of God’s Word.

<margin>With what Solemnity</margin>
After the Gospel, when the Parish Priest, who must give the Admonition, has greeted the

<column-break/>

gle with death; likewise in the Cemeteries over the Corpses and the graves of the deceased. Finally, the religious use this also as their particular means, so that they find themselves protected from thunder and storms, and to ward off all the evils of the Demon, who commonly mingle in the effects of the air. Regarding the blessing of the Wax candles, there is nothing special to say.

<margin>the Admonition proceeds, explained.</margin>
Altar, he steps down the Altar steps on the side of the Epistle <note>the right side of the altar from the perspective of the congregation</note>, removes the *Chasuble* <term>chasuble: the outermost liturgical vestment worn by the priest</term> and the *Maniple* <term>maniple: an ornamental vestment worn over the left arm</term>, takes his Biretta, kneels in the center before the final step of the Altar, and offers to God that which he intends to perform. Subsequently, he goes to the pulpit; and if there is none, he delivers the Admonition at the entrance of the nave <note>original: *buik der Kerke*, literally "the belly of the church"</note> of the Church, standing and with his head covered: but whether there is a pulpit or not, he must be able to be seen by the Congregation (b), and be in a place where he can be heard and understood. Before his Sermon, he greets the Cross, making the sign (c) upon himself. Thereafter, he greets the most prominent Personages of the Congregation and the people. In Italy, the Angelic Salutation (d) <note>The "Hail Mary" prayer</note> precedes the start of the discourse; in France, it follows the beginning.

---

> (a) At the entrance of the Churches, vessels are placed, called Holy Water stoups, in which this Holy Water is to be found; a usage originating from Paganism, but subsequently introduced into the Christian Church.
> (b) Without entering into a long account to investigate whether those of Antiquity, who spoke in public, always chose an elevated place for their eloquence; nor whether, in the absence of Pulpits and elevated seats, they preferred to climb upon some Earth-mounds or benches rather than standing on the same level as those to whom they spoke: without all this investigation, we say, it must be admitted that a man who delivers a discourse in an Assembly must be seen by the entire Assembly, which cannot happen unless he stands elevated. This gave the Origin to the Pulpits. In the first centuries of the Church, the Bishop taught the People, or he preached seated or standing in a pulpit that was intended for him alone. Sometimes the Teacher climbed the steps of the Altar. One can find several noteworthy Remarks on this subject in the work of *Ferrarius, On the Rite of Ancient Church Sermons* <note>original: *Ferrarius de Ritu Veteris Ecclesiæ Concionum*</note> book 3.
> (c) It appears from a passage by *Corippus*, a contemporary Poet of the Emperor Justinian, that Christian Princes, when speaking in public, made a sign of the Cross before they began their discourse. The Scholars of the Church did likewise when they disputed with Heretics and Unbelievers: possibly to drive away the Devil, just as the Pope exhorted those who united with the Church to do.
> (d) In *Baudry’s Manual of Ceremonies* <note>original: *Baudry Manuale Cærem.*</note> one finds it noted: That it was the custom to repeat the Angelic Salutation before beginning the Sermon, and that this custom was not very old, if (as *Ferrarius* says in his Treatise already cited by us) *Vincent Ferrer*, who lived at the beginning of the 15th Century, is the first who spoke of it, or who introduced it. If during the Sermon, the Parish Priest or Preacher mentions the name of Jesus or of Mary, he tips his cap <note>original: *Bonnet*; specifically a biretta, the square cap worn by Roman Catholic clergy</note> and bows or curtsies. In Italy (a) the same is done when the name of the reigning Pope is expressed. The Sermon and the Admonition end with the blessing that the Parish Priest gives to the people: but if he preaches before his Bishop or before any other Superior of the Church, he pronounces the blessing before he begins the Sermon.

One preaches before the Bishop, or when the Holy Sacrament is solemnly displayed upon the Altar, with an uncovered head. The Greeting of the Angels <note>The *Ave Maria* or Hail Mary</note> is omitted on Good Friday: but in its place the Teacher kneels, (b) saying a Prayer before the Cross <note>original: *Crux ave, spes unica, hoc passionis tempore, &c.*; translated: "Hail the Cross, our only hope, in this time of passion, etc."</note>, which is on the Altar, or stands next to the lectern of the Pulpit. After finishing the Admonition, he shows the crucifix to the people; at that time he has two Acolytes in surplices at his side, each holding a burning wax candle. In the Church Ritual Books, one may, if desired, look up many other details on this subject, established more specifically for Parish Priests than for all other Clergy.

<margin>
The abuse in the Sermons in France abolished.
</margin>
As for the outward gestures of the Teacher, and the conduct during the Sermons of those who must preach the Gospel; it is well enough known that we no longer live in the age of *Barette* and *Menot* <note>Olivier Maillard, Jean Raulin, and Michael Menot were 15th-century preachers known for their coarse, often comical and "burlesque" style of preaching</note>. Nowadays one does not know much of these extravagant windbags, who brought forth all kinds of whims according to the Author (c) of the *Defense of Herodotus*. France has cleansed itself of this refuse, even if there were some Field-Priests who had the impropriety, or might be so blunt, as to fall into these excesses; *Bourdaloue*, *Massillon*, *Cheminais* and all the excellent Teachers, who are now spread throughout the entire Kingdom, undeniably confirm the contempt that has been conceived for these unworthy bluster-

<column-break/>

ers, who make of the Gospel a subject of mockery for the Freethinkers. The Decrees of the Councils command that the Teacher be clothed with an Apostolic dignity; and forbid everything that opposes the propriety with which a Teacher must serve the Gospel.

<margin>
How this is still in vogue in Italy.
</margin>
Nevertheless, in Italy this necessary decency for the seriousness of Religion has not yet been put into effect. Their Sermons are not only prickly, ambiguous, and full of cold allusions; but their outward gestures also closely resemble stage buffoonery. They are uncommonly restless in their movements, stamping with their feet, clapping and striking with their hands, rolling their eyes, and stepping with an irregular speed from one end of the Pulpit to the other (d).

# HISTORICAL DISCOURSE on the

„ that were suited to a Teacher. <note>This sentence fragment continues from the previous page's discussion on the requirements of a preacher.</note>

The Sermons of the Italian Teachers are, as has already been said, begun with the Greeting of the Angels <note>The *Ave Maria* or "Hail Mary"</note>. After this greeting, the Preacher reads the Text, and if he subsequently treats the subject of that Text, it is nonetheless in an unusual manner, and almost always involved without any coherence: however, such Sermons commonly consist of two Divisions, of which the first is more serious than the other, and filled with a Scholastic Divinity, entirely unpalatable to a Frenchman; after which one (a) goes around for alms for the poor. The second Division is entirely trifles, and often burdened with tales and strange Histories, which amuse the people more than they edify them: yet these tasteless beauties are called a sufficient edification.

<margin>When and how one preaches in Italy.</margin>
One usually preaches in Italy only during Advent and Lent: but in compensation for this, the Teachers prepare themselves some Months in advance so as to then more zealously (b) excel in all the dignity of their eloquence, so that the harvest of these Evangelical Masters may be the more fruitful. At all other times, one seldom hears preaching in the Parish churches: but rather the Service of Masses in Music. The Monks preach in their Cloisters over subjects that one might well call endless; for they seldom deviate from the Founders of their Order, and from certain Religious duties approved by these Founders, consisting of the Rosaries, the Scapular, and St. Francis’s Girdle <note>Devotional items: a scapular is a garment worn over the shoulders; the girdle is a cord worn around the waist</note>.

<margin>Market-preachers and their behavior observed.</margin>
In some Cities of Italy, one sees Market-preachers. Ear-witnesses are those who assure us that they entirely imitate the Rope-dancers and Stage-fools, by a manner in which they display themselves

<column-break/>

in their Orations of the Evangelical Truth, (c) of which they make a sort of Merchandise, which they hawk to the people, after having mixed the same with farces, just like the Quack-salvers <note>Traveling sellers of supposed medicines or "snake oil"</note>. The Clergyman takes a large Cross, which has been carried before him with a small bell, climbs up the portable Pulpit, to there dispose of this his Merchandise—as harmful to the soul as the adulterated herbs of the Quack-salvers are to the body.

<margin>What a conduct is kept in Spain and Portugal.</margin>
The Preachers of Spain and Portugal preach the Gospel in just as strange a fashion as the Italians do. „ The Teachers, says the Writer of the *Delices de l'Espagne* or *Delights of Spain*, preach there in public places and in great Streets; and however little skill they have, they nonetheless have a great number of listeners. Their custom is slightly different from that of other Peoples. They primarily aim to rebuke sinners, and at the end they make great gestures, and in some places they beat their breasts or give themselves blows, which the entire Assembly then follows. Some save the most vehement exclamations until the ending of their Sermon, and those who know how to shed the most tears have preached the best.

Rabelais mocks, in a pleasant manner, this coughing and the mixing of French and Latin, through a ridiculous discourse which he has his *Janotus de Bragmardo* deliver. <note>A character from François Rabelais’s *Gargantua* who represents the old-fashioned, bumbling academic style.</note> One saw in it puns, witticisms, and contrasts in abundance. Wild scholastic blather also had its place. An over-wrought emotionalism, accompanied by strange gestures, was even considered pleasing. This buffoonish impulsiveness, much more entertaining than Christian, moved the hearts of our Ancestors: now this is left only to the Capuchins. A familiar and simple instruction, or the mere reading of the Gospel followed by some remarks in a common style, without being low or groveling, produces

<column-break/>

greater fruit, provided that it is not unpleasant to an ear that prefers consistency; and it is this very distastefulness that custom has introduced. It is true that this is also supported by the pride of the Preacher, who commonly follows the course of eloquence and does not labor for the conversion of his Listeners, except to make himself prominent in the World.

The Devotion of the Listeners also takes this use and custom into account. It is quite true that this custom runs the risk of never being universal, as men cannot find the means to pair the *Exercise of the fear of God* with that of making their *fortune*. Nevertheless, there are Lands where one sees the People pairing their Devotion with their passions with impunity. Faithful observers of the introduced custom among them, following the commands of the Church, they are considered good Christians; yet they holily stab or poison their Enemies. The Priest himself, after he has performed the Service, will not fail to maintain amorous conversations with a *Signora* <note>Italian: Lady</note> or Maiden. On the other hand, Piety is of little use in those Lands where the looseness of sentiments takes hold: but it becomes customary when a Prince, having grown old, takes it into his mind to convert. Such a Prince, being inclined toward Devotion, fills his Palace with Crosses, Books of Hours, and Rosaries; he will grant no audience until after having prayed to God before an Image; sign no decrees except after having made the sign of the Cross and sprinkled himself with Holy Water: such a Prince will, as far as the outward appearance is concerned, soon see himself transformed into a very Holy Court: but besides that, it could be very wicked, as the Prince's Devotion would bring about the effects of subservience or mimicry. Examples of this are found in private Households. A Father of the household takes no pleasure other than that which smacks of Devotion, making of his house a Nursery of the Pious. The Family feels a revulsion for everything that smells of Worldliness, and condemns all the more those who appear worldly. They spend all the time in Masses and Prayers which they [take] from their...

(b) This is drawn word for word from *Piscara, Practice of Ceremonies* <note>original Latin: "Piscara Prax. Cærem."</note> Book 1, Section 3, Chapter 1, & Book 2, Section 1, Chapter 1. Venetian edition of the year 1681.

(c) Cardinal *Bona* <note>Giovanni Bona (1609–1674), a Cistercian cardinal and author on liturgy.</note> seeks to derive the origin of Altars from ancient times; for he believes that Adam was the inventor of them. *Liturgical Matters* <note>original Latin: "Rerum Liturg."</note> Book 1, Chapter 20. It seems that the use of them was established among Christians since the earliest times of the Church: but it is not known whether they were of wood or stone. The invention of these is attributed, though without proof, to Saint Sylvester.

* [To give the reader a somewhat broader account of the origin of Altars, we find it recorded that they formerly consisted of some heaped-up Earth. It is believed that the Egyptians were the first inventors of them; but Holy Scripture points us to a much older time; for long before the Flood, Cain and Abel sacrificed on Altars. *Gen. 4:20.* Holy Scripture also tells us that Jacob erected an Altar in memory of God having preserved him from the wrath of his brother Esau. *Gen. 33:20.* Moses also erected an Altar in memory of the victory obtained against the Amalekites. *Exod. 17:15.* The tribes of Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh built an Altar of remembrance, though they lived across the Jordan, yet still belonged among the Israelites. *Josh. 22:10.*

The Hebrews had two Altars both in the Tabernacle and in the Temple: an Altar of Incense and an Altar of Burnt Offering. The Altar of Incense stood in the Holy Place and was made of Cedar wood overlaid with gold, for which reason it was also called the golden Altar of Incense. On this Altar, twice daily, the golden censer with incense was placed and burned before the Lord. *Exod. 30.* The Altar of Burnt Offering stood in the Court of the Tabernacle and Temple, also made of Cedar wood, but overlaid with brass <note>original: "koper"</note>, for which reason it was called the brass Altar. *2 Chron. 1:5.* Some believe that this Altar was hollow inside and filled with earth, since in *Exod. 20:24* mention is made of an Altar of Earth: but Spencerus <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English theologian who studied Hebrew rituals.</note> believes that this must be understood as another Altar, which was used and erected in the Wilderness for a short time. On the Altar of Burnt Offering an ever-burning fire had to be kept, which God had first ignited with Heavenly fire, and he did not desire that one should bring strange fire before his face.

The material of the ancient Altars consisted of this: the Jews had them, as already mentioned, of gold or overlaid with gold and also of unhewn stones, likewise of brass. *2 Chron. 4:1, Exod. 20:25.* The Altars dedicated to the Olympian Jupiter consisted of ashes of the sacrificed animals, which like clay were prepared with water; the Altar of Apollo on the Island of Delus consisted solely of the Horns of the sacrificed animals, without any clay or anything else being used. Some were round, others square, and commonly half a man's height. Some could also be moved from one place to another.

In former times, Altars were used for three specific purposes. The primary use seemed to be to sacrifice to the Gods on them, since they were seen placed on all corners and public roads; and since some of the deceased were placed among the Gods, or at least shown some Divine honor, it was also customary to erect Altars by the graves; as happened in honor of Leonidas and his soldiers when they fell at the pass of Thermopylae in the battle against Xerxes' army, so that their memory was maintained thereby. *Berthold. de Ara. C. 24.* In the time of the Roman Emperors they even built...

<meta>This page continues the specific instructions regarding the construction and maintenance of the Altar. RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH.
<meta>catchword: one</meta>

one must ascend to it by three stone steps covered with a carpet. The Clerks must take care to cover the table with a *Chrismale* <note>original: *Chrismal* — a waxed linen cloth placed directly on the altar stone to prevent the consecrated oils from soaking into the altar linens</note>, upon which a clean white cloth is spread, so that *everything may be honorable and pure*, according to the command of Paul to the *Corinthians* <note>Referring to 1 Corinthians 14:40: "Let all things be done decently and in order."</note>. All of this must be observed with the utmost precision in regards to the High Altar, where the consecrated Body of **JESUS CHRIST** is commonly preserved; and to this end, to decorate this High Altar and care for everything, two of the most capable Clerks are chosen, who are bound never to approach it except in their surplices <note>original: *Koorrokken*</note>; as soon as they have reached it, they kneel, adore the Holy Sacrament, and pour out some prayers before God. When the altar decorations must be changed, it happens in this manner: before it is decorated anew, this waxed linen, called the *Chrismale*, is removed; the carpet is spread before the Altar; the cloth and the linens used for the Altar are neatly folded. These decorations are locked away, after which the Clerks wipe away the dust from the Altar with a brush or duster made for that purpose. Subsequently, they spread the covering appropriate for that day, in such a way that the Cross comes in the middle; three cloths are then spread, one of which covers the perimeter of the Altar, while the other two are not as long. Everything must be blessed, accompanied by the sign of the Cross and the sprinkling of Holy Water. Regarding the Tabernacle of the Altar, the *Ciborium* <note>original: *Ciborie* — the vessel used to hold the consecrated hosts</note>, the pyx <note>original: *bus*</note> in which the **Holy Sacrament** is enclosed, the Altar cloths upon which one *consecrates*, etc., the same care is taken; and to glorify God (a) one shall be careful to provide everything

<column-break/>

which can serve as decoration for the Altar.

We have said that the Altar decorations are changed according to the solemnity of the Feast Day. Also, the Altars are decorated with living and artificial flowers according to the season of the Year.

Daily (b) one must wipe the dust from the Altar. As for the carpets, the Clerks must take care that they are beaten out at least once a week. When the Clerk who sweeps the floor of the *Presbytery* <note>original: *Presbyterium* — the area of the church surrounding the altar</note> comes near the Holy Sacrament, he must be bareheaded.

The *Tabernacle* of the Holy Sacrament is placed upon the Altar. Neither gold nor silver, nor even precious stones, are spared upon it. Everything that art can invent in its most magnificent form serves to enhance its luster: but one must especially take heed that the *Eucharist* is not kept in a damp place. The wax candles are placed to the right and left sides of the *Tabernacle*. These wax candles must be of white wax, except during Funeral Masses and those of the last three days of Holy Week; then one uses those made of yellow wax. We have already spoken of the Canopy.

One must have a Crucifix of raised sculpture on the Altar, even if there is a *Tabernacle* there, and the Cross should be painted or carved in bas-relief on the door of the *Tabernacle*. The Crucifix must be placed in such a way that the foot reaches the height of the candlesticks, and that it appears entirely above them. It is not necessary to say that everything must be blessed, even the Cross and the Image. The Candlesticks must be of a particular shape, different from those used

---

<margin>Notes on the history of Altars.</margin>
...during their lives, to flatter them, built some Altars, since some desired to be honored as Gods; Altars were also erected in the fields and on the roads, and sacrifices were offered upon them when meeting a General returning home from battle, or also when the Emperor had been abroad, although this offering was not made for the sake of the men, but for their Gods. The second use of Altars was when entering into a Covenant, confirming a Marriage, or swearing a solemn oath; such occurred before the Altar, which one touched, and then called God to witness that one would fulfill what was promised, and that, on the contrary, the breaker of it might be punished. Thus Hannibal had to make vows and swear to be an enemy of the Romans to his father Hamilcar <note>original: *Amilkar*</note> while touching the Altar. The third use of these Altars consisted in this: when someone had committed a crime, or a servant had offended his Master, they served as places of sanctuary if they went thither; yet in cases of high crime this was not permitted, as God expressly commands that the willful murderer be taken even from His Altar. Exod. 21:14.

The ancient Christians also had a use for Altars, which was introduced in the time of Constantine the Great. They were used only for the administration of the Holy Supper. Subsequently, superstition introduced another use: the Relics of the Saints were kept near them; and finally, in later times, as many Altars were built as there was space found for them in the Churches. In later times, these Altars were granted certain properties and incomes by laying the sealed letters of the same upon them; and when someone laid his head upon the Altar, he indicated thereby that he made himself tributary to it, and was obliged to a yearly payment. *Pitiscus, Danet, Spencer, Reland’s Hebrew Antiquities, Du Cange, etc.* <note>Referencing various 17th and 18th-century scholars of antiquities and law.</note>

(a) Piscara, *Praxis Caeremoniarum* <note>Practice of Ceremonies</note>, ibid. (b) Idem, ibid.

HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

->which are used in houses.<-
Upon every Altar one must have a sheet of pasteboard, which is called the *To Thee, Therefore* <note>original: *Te Igitur* — the opening words of the Roman Canon of the Mass</note> (a) or the Canon of the Mass. The letters must be somewhat large, so that the Priest can read them easily, and this writing is placed at the foot of the Crucifix.
We shall make no mention of the cruets, nor the basin, nor the towel which are used in the *I shall wash* <note>original: *Lavabo* — the ritual washing of the priest's hands</note> after one has washed the hands, nor of the gilded nail at the side of the Epistle, which serves to hang the Priest's biretta <note>original: *bonnet* — a liturgical cap</note>: but we must not forget the bell, which must serve to ring at the *Holy, Holy, Holy* <note>original: *Sanctus*</note> and the two other elevations. The Clerk must ring twice at every *Holy, Holy, Holy*, and nine times at every elevation, namely, three times when the Priest kneels, three times when he lifts the Host, and three times when he sets it upon the Altar and even upon the Chalice.
Before every Altar there must be a screen or rail, whether of iron, marble, or

<column-break/>

wood, which separates the people and prevents them from approaching the Altar.
On both sides of the Altar (b) and before the lowest step, two wax candles are placed on two silver candlesticks, if the resources of the Parish allow; and this is done in honor of the Holy Sacrament when it is elevated. Three, or even five lamps hang there (c) to illuminate it for that purpose.
The High Altar must have a length (d) of twelve palms <note>A "palm" is an old unit of measurement, roughly 3 to 4 inches or the width of a hand</note>, a height above the footstool of four and two-thirds palms, and a width from the steps to the edge of four palms. The footstool must consist of a hard wood and be well-polished.
The portable Altar, or the Consecrated stone, which serves in the absence of a consecrated Altar, must be of hard stone or marble. It must be hollow inside, provided in the middle with a small opening, in which one places the *Relics* of the Holy Martyrs as if in a grave, sealed by the Bishop. If this Seal is found broken, the power of the Altar's Consecration is lost.

<margin>Which vessels must serve for the Altar service.</margin>
The description of the Altar would be deficient if we did not mention the Vessels and other things belonging to it, serving for the decoration and the solemnity of the Service, such as those that must serve for the use of the Eucharist. Both the one and the other lift the soul (e) toward the contemplation of Heavenly matters and oblige her to bless God. Thus expresses himself a Roman Pre-

<column-break/>

late, who adds that the arrangement of these things is an *Act of Latria-service* <note>original: *Latrie-dienst* — from the Greek *latreia*, meaning the supreme worship offered to God alone</note> †.
It is not permitted for laypeople to make use of consecrated Vessels. It belongs to no one but the Clergy to lay a hand upon them, and it is a custom which the Christians have borrowed from the Jews.

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH.

<margin>Description of the Chalice.</margin>
The Chalice must be made of gold or silver. Its height is most commonly nine inches, with three for the cup and six for the base. A veil made of a precious white fabric, fringed all around, covers the precious Host-casket <note>The vessel used to hold the consecrated bread or "Host".</note>.
Likewise, there must be a Pyx <note>original: *Bus* — a small round container</note> to bring *Communion* to the sick; it must be of silver and gilded on the inside. When one must travel far and use a difficult path, it is placed in a white silk bag, which is hung around the neck. The Pyx and *Ciborium* <note>A covered container for holding the consecrated Hosts</note> must be blessed. Another Pyx for holding (c) the large Hosts must be round and a little larger than the Hosts themselves. Inside this Pyx, a thin red plate covered with taffeta must lie, upon which the Hosts rest. One must take great care to store these Hosts in a place that is neither too dry nor too damp. Also, one must not make use of those that are too old.

<column-break/>

The Chalice [must] be of gold or silver. We shall pass over [certain details]. The cup has... Bishop Boniface, a martyr, instilled a thought which we express in Note (a). Proclus was little edified by the dissoluteness of the clergy of his time. (b) In the infancy of the Church, the Chalices were made of wood; likewise, she was then like nothing more than a fisherman's boat. Subsequently, Chalices were made of glass and marble, and finally of silver and gold. It was required that the Chalices be blessed by the Bishop, as well as the Patens <note>original: *Kelkdekzels* — the shallow plates used to hold the Host during the Eucharist</note>. (c) The common height of the Chalices must be nine inches for the small ones, and eleven or twelve inches for the large ones. The Paten must consist of the same material as the Chalice. Its use is to hold the Consecrated Host. This Paten (d) must be proportionate to the size of the Chalice, namely, six or eight inches in diameter.
<margin>Observations on the Ciborium.</margin>
The Ciborium (e) in which the Holy Sacrament is kept must be at least of silver and gilded on the inside. Its base must be half a palm high; having the width in its diameter, or more, with the head or cup proportionate to the size; the bottom of the cup slightly raised to pick up the Hosts when there are not many, and so that they can be better distributed. One must purify them, being fearful of moldiness: (f) At the very least, one must also clean them every eight days. These are the smallest details for describing the Ciborium.
The Monstrance <note>original: *Sakramentshuisje* — literally "Sacrament House," a vessel used to display the Host</note> (g) must be of silver; the height of the base of the smallest must be one palm. The Monstrance must have two crystals, having a width of one palm in diameter, or more, so that a large Host can easily be placed within, resting on a small half-moon <note>known as a *lunette*</note> of the same material, but it must be gilded. One crystal is [attached] by a small chain, like a cover-glass of a pocket... [the top of] the monstrance must be a Cross.

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH.

<margin>Description of the Chalice.</margin>The Chalice must be made of gold or silver. It is a rule intended to suggest the thought that the Church is rich. The material of the Chalices inspired a thought in Boniface, Bishop and Martyr, which we express in Annotation (a). This Prelate was little pleased by the licentiousness of the Clergy of his time. (b) In the infancy of the Church, the Chalices were made of wood; likewise, she was then like nothing more than a fisherman’s boat. Subsequently, Chalices were made of glass and marble, and finally of silver and gold. It was required that the Chalices be consecrated by the Bishop, as well as the Chalice covers <note>the paten</note>. (c) The usual height of the Chalices must be nine inches for the small ones, and eleven or twelve inches for the large ones. The Chalice cover must consist of the same material as the Chalice. Its use is to place the Consecrated Host upon it. This Chalice cover (d) must be proportionate to the size of the Chalice, namely, six or eight inches in diameter.

<margin>Remarks on the Ciborium.</margin>The Ciborium (e) <note>a covered container for holding the consecrated hosts</note> in which the Holy Sacrament is kept, must be at least of silver and gilded on the inside. The foot of the same must be half a palm high; the bottom of the cup slightly raised to receive the Hosts, over which a thin red cover-glass must be turned to better fit them. One must not leave them in the Ciborium for too long without purifying them, being fearful of mold: (f) At the least, one must also clean them every eight days. The smallest details for describing the Ciborium

<column-break/>

shall be skipped. Its height must usually be nine inches, namely, three for the cup and six for the foot. A veil consisting of a precious white material, fringed all around, covers the precious Host-casket.

Likewise, there must be a Pyx <note>a small round container</note> to bring Communion to the Sick; the same must be made of silver and gilded on the inside. When one must travel far and consequently use a difficult path, one places it in a white silk bag, which is hung around the neck. The Pyx and Ciborium must be blessed. Another Pyx to place the large Hosts in must be round and slightly larger than the Hosts. In this Pyx must lie a thin red plate covered with taffeta, upon which the Hosts rest. One must take great care to keep these Hosts in a place that is neither too dry nor too damp. Also, one must not make use of those that are too old.

<margin>The Monstrance.</margin>The Monstrance <note>original: "Sakramentshuisje," a vessel used to display the Host</note> (g) must be made of silver; the height of the foot of the smallest must be one palm. The Monstrance must have two crystals, having a diameter of one palm or more, so that a large Host can easily be placed within, resting on a small crescent moon <note>a "lunette," which holds the Host upright</note> of the same material, but gilded. One crystal is fastened by a small chain, like the cover-glass of a pocket-watch. On top of this Monstrance there must be a Cross.

<margin>Likewise the Thurible.</margin>The Thurible <note>original: "Wierookvat," a metal censer for burning incense</note> (h) may be of silver or brass, and provided with four chains. One makes use of two incense-boats <note>vessels for holding unburned incense</note>.

The altar cloths (b) must be made of fine white linen, not too transparent, without embroidery or lace. If there is lace, it must be very small and positioned about two fingers' width from the front edge. In the place where the priest usually kisses the altar, a small cross of white silk or thread in this shape ✢ must be stitched. The altar cloths must be folded in such a way that all the ends are tucked inward and are not visible, etc.

<margin>Chalice covers.</margin>
The chalice palls <note>original: "Kelkdekzels"; the stiffened square of linen used to cover the chalice</note> (c) must be made of the same linen as the altar cloths; they must be filled

<column-break/>

with a piece of cardboard placed between the linen. No wool or silk fabric, nor any cross or images, may be placed upon the chalice palls. Likewise, no lace may be sewn onto them; only four "acorns" or four small tassels at the four corners, so they may be more easily grasped. They must be blessed along with the altar cloths, and it must be at least a sub-deacon who touches them.

<margin>Towels, etc.</margin>
The towels (d) are made of linen, two palms in length, and are folded into three. In the middle of them, a small cross of blue thread must be sewn.

The burses <note>original: "Beurzen"; a pocket-like case for holding the corporal</note> (e) for the altar linens consist of the same fabric as the vestments; on the inside, they are lined with fine white linen, with a sturdy piece of cardboard in between. The width must be one palm. They are closed with a button and a silk cord, and on the burse there must be a stitched cross about three-quarters of a palm long.

The chalice veil must consist of silk fabric in the same color as the vestments, three palms square; but without a cross or any other image.

<margin>and what further pertains to the altar service.</margin>
In the churches (f) where solemn service is performed, the veils for the sub-deacon—when he holds the chalice cover <note>here likely referring to the paten</note> during the solemn Mass—must be ten palms long and wide, consisting of fabric in the four colors, which are (g) white, red, green, and violet; but never black, unless they are used for Requiem Masses or on Good Friday. These veils <note>the humeral veil</note> must consist of silk fabric and be bordered with lace, etc.
The Customary of Alet adds that in the principal churches, there is another veil of the same size, which should be white and very costly, to be placed on the shoulders of the celebrant when he must carry the Holy Sacrament in procession. Likewise, in the parish churches, there must be a canopy <note>original: "Verhemelzel"</note> where...

These metaphors and many others are more than sufficient to prove that incense should be used in the Church to honor the Divinity, and St. Ambrose says very well that an angel attends this ceremony.

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc., of the ROMAN CHURCH.

<sig>Rr 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

under which the Holy Oil for the sick is carried, should be five or six palms long and at least four palms wide, and the hangings with the fringes should be one and a half palms; they must consist of a white silk fabric. There must be two poles to carry it, at a height of five or six palms, covered with the same fabric as the Canopy, unless they are painted or gilded. This Canopy, which serves in the procession for the Holy Sacrament, is larger than that used for the sick.

Furthermore, one needs Veils (a) or covers for the Crosses and Images during the time of the Passion or the Suffering of the Savior; namely, from the Saturday Vespers of Passion Sunday until Easter Eve after the blessing of the Holy Water. They must be made of Camlet <note>a costly fabric made of silk and camel hair or wool</note> or other violet-colored fabric, without any Images, nor Cross or other instruments of the Passion.

<margin>The Church banner described.</margin> In every parish church (b) one must have a Church banner, of a color corresponding to the Patron of this Church. It must be nine or ten palms high and six wide. The Image of the Patron must be embroidered in the middle. This Church banner must be made of Satin, or Damask, Taffeta, or lined Camlet, or a light fabric. The pole to carry this Banner must be at least one and a half cubits long.

Regarding the Missal <note>original: "Misboek"; the book containing the prayers and instructions for the Mass</note> we shall make no lengthy discourse; its use is well known, and

<column-break/>

it contains the prayers and lessons that serve piety before the Altar.

Those who rely on the authority of the *Institution* <note>original: "Instelling"; referring here to the Apostolic Constitutions</note> and of St. *Clement* <note>Clement of Rome, traditionally the fourth Pope</note>, do not doubt that St. *Peter* was the Institutor of the Missal, and that he recommended this use to Clement, his successor.

Having already spoken of the sacred Vessels of the Altar and their use, it is not necessary to mention here the attention that the Ministers must have for the Holy Sacrament: since this is not our primary aim, and since one should further regard it as evidence of the esteem held for the *Eucharist*, as well as the care taken to practice this, along with the precautions that must be maintained in purity through Holy and other spiritual means, etc. Although *Calvin* strips the Sacrament of all its glories, regarding it as nothing more than a sign of the bread which he points out to his fellow believers; the Catholics, however, believe it together with the most precious ornaments as befits the body of Him who is the King of Kings. The Faithful kept the *Eucharist* for themselves when traveling, and also preserved it in (c) their homes. Nevertheless, one also finds in these practices (d) things that seem to conflict with the Church's thoughts regarding the Holy *Eucharist*.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.

#### Concerning the BLESSING of the FIRST STONE used for the construction of a Church, as well as its Foundations.

The Assembly of the Faithful is called the Church, as is the place where they assemble. This place must be intended solely for Spiritual Service, of which the most essential and most pleasing part to God is prayer, along with meditation, devotion, and the lifting of the heart to the Supreme Being. These qualities are essential to Christianity, which professes to call upon God in the Spirit: This is why the name of "Church" must be assigned to the Christian Assemblies and also to their Temples.

Before one builds a Church (e), such must be authorized by the Bishop.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.
->Concerning the Blessing of the First Stone used for the building<-
->of a Church, as well as its Foundations.<-

The Assembly of the Faithful is called *Church*, and also the place where they assemble. This place must be intended solely for the *Spiritual Service*, of which the most essential and the most pleasing part to God is prayer, alongside meditation, modesty, and the lifting up of the [soul]; [these] qualities are essential to [Christen]dom, which professes to call upon God in *Spirit*: This is why the name of *Church* must be assigned to *Christian Assemblies* and likewise to their *Temples*.

Before one builds a *Church* (e), this must be approved by the *Bishop*.

<meta>This page continues the liturgical instructions for the Roman Catholic Church, moving from the description of processional banners and veils to the formal rites for founding a new church building. # HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

<margin>
How the Bishop must perform the Dedication of the construction of a Church, and with what solemnity it is accompanied.
</margin>

It belongs to him to designate the place, to determine the space, to find the income for the Church and its Ministers, and everything necessary for the lighting, the ornaments, and the maintenance of the Church. It is he who erects the Cross on the ground where the Church is to be built and lays the first stone; or, if he does not attend to this himself, it nevertheless depends on his pleasure and consent that a lesser Clergyman performs this sacred ministry.

The day before the first stone is laid, a wooden Cross is set in the place where the Altar shall be. The following day, a rectangular stone is taken, which shall serve as the First Stone and the foundation of the building. To complete the ceremony of the Blessing \*, the Pope—if he wishes to perform this clerical duty himself in Rome—clothes himself in the Priestly High-Vestments and the ornaments corresponding to the stateliness of this action: but a (a) Clerical Person of lesser rank <note>original: "Geeſtelyk Perſoonaadje"; referring to a lower-ranking member of the clergy such as a priest or deacon</note> must, in addition to the Surplice <note>original: "Koorkleet"</note>, be provided with the Head-covering <note>a biretta or skullcap</note>, the *Alb* <term>Alb: a long white linen robe reaching to the feet</term>, *Girdle*, *Stole*, the white *Cope* <term>Cope: a long mantle or cloak, open in front and fastened at the chest</term>, and the simple Mitre. He must hold the Bishop’s Staff in his left hand; and thus attired, he places himself on the ground prepared for the new Church building, blessing (b) the salt and the water; beginning with the salt, expressing himself thus:

> that he adjures it by the living God, etc. <note>original: "dat hy 't door den levendigen Godt bezweert enz."</note> So that, being thus adjured for the Salvation of the faithful, it may bring forth Health of body and Soul to those who shall use it, and that it may have the power to drive away the plagues of Satan.

Next, the Pope or Bishop removes his Mitre and pronounces the Blessing over the salt. To adjure the water, he puts the Mitre back on, so that it, like the salt, may have the power to drive away the power of the Devil and his—

<column-break/>

—Angels, and completes the same ceremony as was done with the salt. Having finished these two Blessings, he sprinkles the salt in the form of a Cross into the water, says the prayers corresponding to the subject, takes the Mitre, and has an *Antiphon* (c) <term>Antiphon: a short sentence or verse sung or recited before or after a psalm</term> and the 83rd Psalm <note>Psalm 84 in modern numbering, beginning "How lovely are thy tabernacles"</note> sung according to the common Latin Translation. While they sing, the Bishop, covered with his Mitre, sprinkles the place where the Cross stands: after which, when the bystanders have sung the *Antiphon* and the Psalm, he proceeds to the place which he sprinkles with Holy Water, and taking off his Mitre, offers a Prayer to God under the direction of the Saint to whom the New Church is to be dedicated.

Then, removing his Mitre once more, he blesses the Stone. The Blessing is then followed by prayers, and the prayers by a sprinkling over the Stone. The sprinkling being performed, the Officiating Bishop makes several (d) Images of the Cross on the Stone with a knife *in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost*; upon which an *Oremus* <note>Latin: "Let us pray"</note> and several Litanies follow; and after this performance, the Bishop, who had previously knelt on a spread carpet, stands up again and offers a prayer while turning toward the Stone.

Meanwhile, the Cement is prepared, and when it is ready, the Bishop puts his Mitre back on and begins an *Antiphon* regarding the Stone that Jacob erected as a monument when he was on his journey in the Wilderness <note>A reference to Genesis 28, where Jacob uses a stone as a pillow and later sets it up as a pillar</note>. This *Antiphon* is followed by the 126th Psalm <note>Psalm 127: "Except the Lord build the house..."</note> according to the common Latin translation. Finally, the Bishop, being mitred, takes this first Foundation Stone in his sacred hand and lays it in its place (e) through faith in Jesus Christ, etc. While the mason then sets the stone firmly in the lime, the Bishop is busy sprinkling it with Holy Water...

[Bottom notes:]
...to build, except by the Bishop’s order and authority. He must designate the place and entrance thereof, etc. See the Church Custom Book of *Alet*.

(a) The Pontifical says *Religiosus*.
(b) This refers to the Blessing of the water and salt, in the manner that is always customary.
(c) Thus in the sense of the Antiphon: *Lord, set a sign of salvation in this place, and do not permit the destroying Angel to enter therein.*
(d) He marks the sides of the stone with the Cross. See the Custom Book of *Alet*.
(e) This is the beginning of the prayer which he then prays.

another Prayer, after which the Antiphon and the 121st Psalm are sung again. With the third sprinkling for the last third of the consecrated building, the Prelate returns to the place where the first stone was laid. The Antiphon is resumed, the mitre removed, and prayer is offered again, after which the Bishop raises the hymn <term>Come, Holy Spirit, Creator Blest <note>original Latin: "Veni Creator"</note></term>, and kneels while the first verse is sung. He stands up again during the second verse and remains uncovered until the end of the Hymn †: after which he prays to God that the Holy Spirit may deign to dwell in this consecrated building; that this House of Piety may remain inviolate, and that He may judge it worthy to enjoy the benefits of His grace, etc. One of these benefits undoubtedly consists of the Faithful favoring this building with charitable gifts. Then the Bishop sits down, covered with the mitre, to exhort the assembly to contribute funds. This exhortation then ends with a Blessing and the granting of Indulgences <note>remissions of temporal punishment for sins</note> on behalf of the Pope.

---

> (a) *Sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Asperges me Domine Hyssopo &c."</note>
> \* [A song beginning with the words: *Come God Creator etc.*]
> † [A Hymn is a song of praise, which is also called *Thee, O God, we praise* <note>original Latin: "Te Deum Laudamus"</note>.]
> (b) This is taken from the *Roman Pontifical* and the *Manual of Alost*.
> (c) If by dedication one understands the Sanctification of a certain building through prayer to God, one must consider this practice as very ancient and even established by the Apostles: but as far as the sequence of ceremonies is concerned, they undoubtedly began to be introduced when the Church was delivered from the persecution of her enemies and saw herself elevated in the prosperity and worldliness of her ministers. It is noteworthy that the ancient Christians built their churches in a manner corresponding to the Temple of Jerusalem: but that later the shape of the Cross was given to them in memory of the Savior. See *Bona, Book I, Chapter 20. Keruin Liturgy, and Casalius on Ancient Christian Rites, Chapter 33.*
> (d) This happens the day before the Blessing of the Church.
> (e) It is believed that the custom of placing Relics under the Altar has its origin in the honor shown by early Christians in cemeteries and at graves to the Martyrs resting there. When the Christian Church triumphed over Heathenism, the first Temples were built in these places—built, so to speak, upon these Believers and Confessors of the Truth. The Roman Church was the first to adopt the custom of placing Relics under the Altar. This custom is very old, since St. Ambrose and Prudentius speak of it: but it may nonetheless be that it arose by chance. If meetings were held at the graves of the Martyrs, this perhaps happened not out of love for them, but because one found oneself safe there from the rage of the Heathens. However it may be, it later happened that it was ordered that those who dedicate churches without first having provided some Relics should be deposed and viewed as transgressors of Ecclesiastical Tradition. See further in *Bona*.

As soon as the singing starts, he puts the *Mitre* back on and goes around to the right side, making a circuit around the Church, preceded by the Sub-Deacon who carries the Cross between two candle-bearers, alongside the Clerk carrying the Holy Water vessel. ### RELIGIOUS DUTIES etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH. 319

on both sides, they must lift his cope <term>Cope: a long, ornate cloak (pluvial) worn by bishops and priests during processions</term>, and the holy water bearer must take care to stay a little to the side of the Bishop’s right hand, so that whenever he needs holy water, he may make use of it.

Having returned to the previous place and having repeated the antiphon <term>Antiphon: a short chant or sentence sung or recited before or after a psalm</term> at the end of the Psalm, the Bishop, standing with head uncovered, says the "Let us pray" <note>original: "Oremus"</note> and turns toward the church door. The first assistant says (a) "Let us kneel" <note>original: "Flectamus Genua"</note>. Then they all kneel except for the Bishop, alongside the cross-bearer and the two candle-bearers. The other assistant says "Rise" <note>original: "Levate"</note> and stands up, after which they all stand up together again. This spiritual exercise is quite difficult because of the various details that accompany it, and it is for this reason that all the church customs are performed with the Manual <note>a book of church rites</note> in hand.

We ask Christians for forgiveness for the comparison we have made, since it has no bearing on the essence of the religion.

The prayer which follows "Rise" in the Pontifical <term>Pontifical: a liturgical book containing the prayers and rites performed specifically by a bishop</term> is of a mystical nature. After finishing this, the Bishop puts the mitre back on and, approaching the church door, knocks on it with his crosier <note>the Bishop's staff</note>, saying: (b) "Lift up the gates, and the King of Glory shall enter" <note>original: "Attollite portas & introibit Rex Gloriæ"</note>. The Deacon, who had remained inside the church, hearing that knocking at the door, asks him "Who is this King of Glory?", to which the Bishop responds: "It is the Lord, the Almighty God, the God of Hosts." Is this to accommodate human weakness, and as Charron <note>Pierre Charron (1541–1603), a French Catholic philosopher</note> says: (c) *since folly must be tolerated as one does with small children, that a ceremonial custom is practiced which by no means flows from the Apostolic Spirit?* Those who invented these spiritual ceremonies sensed very well that the

<column-break/>

human mind, in matters of religion, has power only over secondary things.

After having made this procession to the right side around the church, the Bishop likewise makes one to the left, sprinkling the walls of the church from the outside at about his own height. The antiphon sung then is not the same as the one sung before, nor is the prayer; but the ceremony is the same, except that when the Deacon inside the church asks "Who is the King of Glory?", the clergy with the Bishop respond: (d) "It is the Almighty Lord" <note>original: "Dominus virtutum"</note>, it is he "who is the King of Glory," and they collectively cry out three times (e) "Open up." The Bishop makes the sign of the Cross on the church door and meanwhile recites (f) a Latin verse from the Breviary <note>a book containing the daily office or prayers</note>, which terrifies the Devil and all the powers of hell no less; the meaning of which is: *that all evil spirits must flee at the sight of this Cross*. The church door finally being opened, the Bishop enters the church alone with his ministers, without being followed by the people attending this ceremony, except for some masons who must seal the tomb of the relics <note>original: "Reliquiën"</note> and seal the table of the Altar with cement. Upon entering the church, the Bishop says: "May peace be in this dwelling," and the Deacon responds: (g) "When you shall enter it." While the words of Scripture that correspond with this wish are being sung, the Bishop approaches the heart of the church and, kneeling and uncovered, begins the "Come, Holy Spirit" <note>original: "Veni Creator"</note>, with his face turned toward the High Altar. Then one of the sub-deacons takes the ash and scatters it in the shape of a cross upon the floor, just as the illustration (h) shows. Then the Litany is sung, in which the Saint is named twice.

(b) Open up, eternal doors, so that the King of Glory may enter. Psalm 23 [24], according to the Latin translation.
(c) Book 1, *Of Wisdom* <note>original: "de la sagesse"</note>, section 8. (d) Lord of Hosts <note>original: "Dominus virtutum"</note>.
(e) This Bishop's staff with which the Bishop knocks on the church door represents the priestly power that JESUS CHRIST shared with his disciples, which their successors acquired through arms and which religion grants them. The blows given to the church door inform us that Heaven, Earth, and Hell must bow entirely under the power of the Vicar of Jesus Christ. We have drawn this explanation from Casalius, *On the Rites of Ancient Christians* <note>original: "de Ritub. Vet. Christ."</note>, Chapter 33.

# HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

...calls, [is] dedicated to this Church and the Altar.
We must also note here that similar honor should be given to those whose *relics* <note>The physical remains of a saint or objects they touched, considered holy.</note> are kept under the Altar. This occurs each time to say to God with three repetitions: <note>original: "Te rogamus audi nos"</note> *We beseech thee, hear us*; while at the same time naming the Saint of the Church and making the sign of the Cross. These ceremonies are followed by a prayer <note>original: "Oremus"</note>, an Antiphon <note>A short sentence sung or recited before or after a psalm.</note>, and the Song of Zechariah; and while the ministers sing in the choir, the Bishop puts on his miter and writes a double alphabet <note>original: "A. B. C."</note> in large letters, in Greek and Latin, with his pastoral staff upon a cross of strewn ashes. The reader will have sufficiently understood what this ceremony entails from the accompanying illustration *, as shown in the first two figures.

After the Bishop has written the aforementioned alphabet in the ashes, he moves a certain distance toward the High Altar, removes his miter, kneels, and prays. To which the choir responds. This is repeated three times, each time with a raised voice and tone. Then the Bishop covers his head and blesses the water, salt, ashes, and wine. The exorcism <note>original: "bezweering"</note> of the salt and water, etc., along with the prayer that is said, are different from those we spoke of regarding the blessing of the first stone. During the blessing of the ashes, one prays to God that He

<column-break/>

might send His angel to hallow and bless them, 
> so that they may become a healing remedy for those who call upon the holy name of God and confess their sins.

Likewise, one prays, 
> that those who call upon His holy name shall feel the redemption and acquittal of their sins, and receive health of body and salvation of soul.

Once the prayer is ended, the Bishop takes the salt, mixes it in the shape of a cross with the ashes, and then takes a handful of this material, throwing it into the water in three intervals, repeating the blessing each time. He then blesses the wine and mixes it crosswise with the water. This blessing, like the previous ones, is accompanied by several appropriate prayers, and ends with an account of the benefits the water produces and the miracles performed through it. The consecration of the Altar does not follow immediately; instead, the Bishop again makes the sign of the cross with his pastoral staff at the top and bottom of the church door, praying to God <note>original: "Sit positis crux invicta liminibus"</note> that the cross be invincible, and that those who visit the Church be favored with blessings, etc. Finally, he returns to the place where he blessed the water, and turning toward the High Altar with his head covered, he exhorts the assembly to pray to God, 
> that He, through Jesus Christ, may bless and preserve this place by the sprinkling of water mixed with wine, salt, and ashes, 

etc.

(a) *We beseech thee, hear us.* <note>original: "Te rogamus audi nos"</note>
(b) This alphabet represents the first principles of the Christian religion. The Cross signifies that the first thing a Christian must know is **JESUS CHRIST** crucified. See Casalius, *On Rites*, etc.
(c) See the first two figures of the adjacent illustration. We do not doubt that this ceremony and several others present something unusual; it is not surprising that Judaism was the source of these mysteries and temple customs, and that Paganism is not far behind on this subject. One might say that the ceremonies have, to some extent, mirrored the essence of these two temple services; but it is surprising that Christianity, whose principles are uncommonly simple, has chosen to burden itself with such a difficult and heavy load as these rites, which one is thus obliged to maintain and which entail endless effort. It is to be believed, and not without reason, that it takes far more labor to learn all this than to understand what religion actually is.
(d) *See the <term>Roman Pontifical</term><note>The official liturgical book containing the rites performed by bishops.</note>.*
(e) When he says <note>original: "Deus in adjutorium"</note> *O God, come to my assistance*, the choir responds; he says <note>original: "Gloria Patri"</note> *Glory be to the Father*, etc., and the choir responds: <note>original: "sicut erat in principio"</note> *as it was in the beginning*. All this must be done in an orderly fashion, for usage is the soul of the prescriptions. The slightest attention to ecclesiastical and worldly affairs will convince the reader of this.
(f) The Pontifical calls these things <note>original: "Creatura Salis, Creatura aqua"</note> *Creature of Salt, Creature of Water*, etc. <note>In liturgical Latin, "creature" refers to an element of creation that is being addressed or purified.</note>
(g) <note>original: "Sit positis crux invicta liminibus"</note> *May the cross be invincible upon these thresholds*, etc. *Roman Pontifical*.

etc. (a) This is followed by an <term>Antiphon<note>A short sentence sung or recited before or after a psalm.</note></term>, which is frequently repeated. At the start of the Antiphon, the Bishop stands before the Altar, dips the finger of his right hand into the water he has previously blessed, and makes a cross on the center of the Altar’s table. He consecrates this Altar (b) *to the honor of Almighty God, of the Virgin Mary, and of all the Saints, in the name and memory of Saint . . . etc. and does so in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.*

Likewise, upon returning, he sprinkles toward (d) the four quarters of the world. Then he places his hands on his chest and repeats with the Choir that which the Church (f) calls the *Preface* or Introduction.

After this Introduction, the Bishop or the officiating Priest mixes the <term>mortar<note>original: 'sement'</note></term> with Holy Water, which serves to secure the stone covering the tomb of the *Relics*: he blesses it, and after the blessing, a prayer follows.

# CHAPTER XXXV.

->How the RELICS are brought in a PROCESSION to the CONSECRATED CHURCH; and how the CHEST with these RELICS is placed in the ALTAR.<-

---

<margin>How the Relics are transported, and with what solemnity this is accompanied.</margin>
The Bishop proceeds solemnly to the *Relics*, followed by many Clergy and preceded by the Cross carried between two candle-bearers. The Holy Oil is brought to the entrance of the Church, and arriving at the place where the *Relics* are, they sing an *Antiphon* and the Psalm which, according to the Latin Translation, is the 94th. Sometimes they are content to sing a <term>Responsory<note>A type of chant where a soloist and choir alternate.</note></term> in honor of the Saint from whom the *Relics* are taken. After this song, the Bishop uncovers his head, remaining before the *Relics*, and offers a—

<column-break/>

prayer (g) in honor of the same. Then incense is cast into the censer, and the Procession begins in this order.

The Cross-bearer leads the way between * two candle-bearers, and the other Clergy follow, singing. After them come the Priests, carrying the *Relics* on a litter, magnificently covered.

Likewise, in returning, he sprinkles toward (d) the four corners of the world. After this Introduction, the Bishop or the officiating Priest mixes the cement with Holy Water, which must serve to fix the stone that covers the tomb of the *Relics*: he blesses it, and after the blessing, a prayer follows.

<margin>Transfer of the Relics from the</margin> Before placing the **Relics** in the Sepulcher <note>A small cavity in the altar table intended to hold relics</note>, the Bishop—or whoever else is performing this service—marks the casket or reliquary with the **Holy Oil**, after having previously sealed the vessel containing the **Relics**. He takes great care that the mark of the **Holy Chrism** is accompanied by four signs of the Cross, which are made on the four sides of the Sepulcher in the name of the Father, etc. This is what the consecration of the Sepulcher consists of. Then the reliquary is placed in its designated spot with all possible reverence, and to further demonstrate this to the assembly, this is done with heads uncovered. This action is followed by an **Antiphon**, which is also repeated, while the Bishop, without his miter, censes the **Relics** with incense; after which he puts the Miter back on, takes the Stone that is to close the sepulcher in his left hand, and dips the finger of his right hand into the **Holy Oil**, with which he paints a sign of the Cross in the middle of the Stone and on the side facing the Holy **Relics**, in order to consecrate them with this blessing. Following this, the **Antiphons** and the **Let us pray** <note>original: "Oremus"</note> (c) must follow according to custom. Thereafter, the Bishop lays the Stone upon the sepulcher; and the Mason completes his work. Then the Prelate sanctifies it with a sign of the Cross, which he must draw upon the Stone.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

(a) This address covers the respect one owes to God and the Church; likewise concerning the Liberties of the Churches; and the respect that Jewish Princes and subsequently Christian Powers have had for these Holy places. One also does not forget to praise the fact that the guilty who may enjoy the advocacy of the Clergy who serve these Churches. Furthermore, he exhorts the Christians to enter it only with decency: "The Holy Saints," he adds, "have granted these privileges to the Church, which we [dedicate] to the honor of the Almighty, of the blessed Virgin Mary, of all the Saints and particularly of Saint [Name]. We declare that we have placed the Relics of the Saints [Names] beneath his Altar, and that the bodies of these Saints and of Saint [Name] rest in this place. Those who visit them shall enjoy an Indulgence, granted by [Name]. We exhort you to the maintenance of the same and of those who shall serve this Church, for God's Blessing depends upon this, etc. See: *Roman Pontifical* <note>original: "Pontific. (c) Through this prayer, one testifies before God that one embraces with spiritual love the **Relics** of the Saints, which is the essence of this ceremony; etc.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.

*How the **INCENSING** of the **ALTAR** is performed; the **ANOINTING** of the twelve **CROSSES**, and the **CROSS** before the **ALTAR**; as well as the **BLESSING** of the **VESSELS** and **ALTAR ORNAMENTS** completed.*

<margin>How the incensing of the Altar is performed.</margin>
When the aforementioned Stone <note>The "altar stone" or "sepulchre" which holds the holy relics.</note> is blessed, finished with the signs of the Cross, and sealed, the Altar must be incensed. The Bishop casts the incense into the Censer, giving (a) it the Blessing and making the sign of the Cross over it. Then he incenses the Altar to the right and left, from the front and the back, while the choir sings. After the incensing he prays, and when the prayer is finished, the Ministers rub the Altar table with a clean linen cloth. The Prelate incenses it in the form of a Cross; just as he also does the four sides of the Altar, and this incensing is repeated each time.

After the incensing, the Bishop makes five Crosses with the Holy Oil, namely, one in the middle of the Altar, and the others on the four sides, and this in the very same places where he had previously made them with Holy Water. Having resumed the five Crosses with the Oil, he begins the incensing once more.

<margin>Anointed signs of the Cross made, and how they are handled.</margin>
The *Antiphons*, *Psalms*, and the *Oremus* <note>Latin: "Let us pray."</note> being repeated each time, accompany the abundant fragrances and all the signs of the Cross which the Prelate makes for the third time with the Holy Oil. Finally, without expanding further upon this action, we must also say that the (b) Bishop simultaneously pours some Oil and Chrism together upon the Altar. He smears these everywhere and then rubs them in with his right hand. Meanwhile, the Choir sings the Blessing that the Patriarch Isaac gave to his son Jacob, which is followed by a Psalm: thereafter the Prelate exhorts the Assembly (c) to pray to God

<column-break/>

that it may please him to bless and sanctify the Stone upon which the Anointing has occurred, etc.

While the Clergy and the Choir are intent on the singing of the *Antiphons* and *Psalms*, we shall interrupt the thread of the incensing of the Altar for a moment to proceed to the Anointing of the twelve Crosses, which the Bishop has made upon the walls of the Church *. He begins behind the Altar and continues to the right side, anointing these Crosses one after the other. At each Anointing, he repeats the prescription for the Consecration (d) of the Church. Each Cross is incensed individually after the Anointing is completed.

This Incensing of the twelve Crosses being finished, the Bishop returns again to the incensing of the Altar, has singing performed, and then prays to God, with the usual signs (e) of the Cross, that it may please him to sanctify the Altar and to Bless the Offerings of his Servants, etc. He also does not neglect to bless the incense, this Creature (f), which through its (g) scent not only drives away all fainting and ill-health: but also especially turns away the secret snares of the Enemy (the Devil). He also does not neglect to make five new Crosses upon the Altar, each of five Grains of incense, in the same place where he had previously made them with the Holy Water, as well as with the Holy Oil, and the last Anointing. Upon each Cross of incense, he places one of wax, exactly as the Illustration (h) shows. Subsequently
