<margin>How the incensing of the Altar is performed.</margin>
When the aforementioned Stone has been blessed, finished with the signs of the Cross, and sealed, the Altar must be incensed. The Bishop throws the incense into the thurible <note>a metal vessel for burning incense</note>, giving (a) it the Blessing and making the sign of the Cross over it. Then he incenses the Altar to the right and left, from the front and back, while singing is performed. After the incensing he prays, and once the prayer is ended, the Attendants rub the Altar table with a clean linen cloth. The Prelate <note>a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop</note> incenses it in the shape of a cross; just as he also does the four sides of the Altar, and this incensing is repeated each time.

After the incensing, the Bishop makes five Crosses with the Holy Oil, namely, one in the middle of the Altar, and the others on the four sides, and this in the same place where he had previously made them with Holy Water. Having resumed the five Crosses with the Oil, he begins the incensing once more. <margin>Anointed Cross-signs and how they are handled.</margin> The *Antiphons* <note>short chants sung before or after a psalm</note>, Psalms, and the *Let us pray* <note>original: "Oremus"</note> repeated each time, accompany the abundant perfumes and all the signs of the Cross which the Prelate makes for the third time with the Holy Oil. Finally, without expanding further upon this action, we must also say that the (b) Bishop simultaneously pours some Oil and Chrism <note>a mixture of oil and balsam used in church sacraments</note> upon the Altar. He smears it everywhere and then rubs it with his right hand. Meanwhile, the Choir sings the Blessing that the Patriarch Isaac gave to his son Jacob, which is followed by a Psalm: then the Prelate exhorts the Assembly (c) to pray to God

<column-break/>

that it may please him to bless and sanctify the Stone upon which the Anointing has occurred, etc.

While the Clergy and the Choir are attentive in the singing of the Antiphons and Psalms, we shall break the thread of the incensing of the Altar for a moment to proceed to the Anointing of the twelve Crosses, which the Bishop has made on the walls of the Church \*. He begins behind the Altar, and continues to the right side, anointing these Crosses one after the other. At each Anointing he repeats the prescription for the Consecration (d) of the Church. Each Cross is incensed individually after the Anointing is completed.

This Incensing of the twelve Crosses being finished, the Bishop returns again to the incensing of the Altar, having the Antiphons and Psalms sung attentively, with the usual signs (e) of the Cross, that it may please Him to sanctify the Altar and to Bless the Offerings of His Servants, etc. He also does not neglect to bless the incense, this creature (f), which by its (g) scent not only drives away all weakness and unhealthiness: but also especially turns away the secret snares of the Enemy (the Devil). He also does not neglect to make five new Crosses on the Altar, each of five Grains of incense, in the same place where he had previously made them with the Holy Water, as well as with the Holy Oil, and the final Anointing. ...then he lights this, kneels before the Altar, invokes the Holy Spirit, and prays (a) *to kindle the fire of his love in the hearts of the faithful.* The Antiphon <note>a short chant or sentence sung or recited before or after a psalm</note> is preceded by a *Hallelujah*. The Choir continues the song and the Priest concludes this small pious action with a prayer, while the Crosses of wax and incense burn. The Bishop orders this sacred ash to be carefully preserved. One of his Attendants carries this out, placing it in a Vessel designated for that purpose; after which he washes his hands in the *Piscina* <note>original: "Piscina"; a stone basin in a church used for draining water used in rituals</note> *.

The general conclusion of this ceremony consists of a *Let us pray* <note>original: "Oremus"</note> performed by the Prelate on the step of the Altar (b), spoken in the required order. The *Let us pray* being ended, according to the rules indicated in the Remarks, the Bishop begins the *For ever and ever* <note>original: "Per omnia"</note> in a moderately high tone, with hands upon his chest, as we have already spoken of.

On Thursday and Friday in Holy Week, the Altar is stripped of its decorations, and in *Rome* it is washed with water and wine. This stripping of the ornaments signifies the despondency of Christians due to the suffering of the Savior, or represents how JESUS CHRIST was undressed to be scourged. The washing with water and wine represents the water and blood that flowed from his side.

After the Bishop has blessed, consecrated, sanctified, and dedicated the Altar with all the Crosses, it seems that there is nothing more for him to do: But by no means; he must still make another on the front part of the Altar. This is done with the Holy Oil <note>specifically the Oil of Chrism</note>, which is accompanied by a prayer. Subsequently, he makes others in the places where the Altar table is joined to the Pillars or posts: after which he says a prayer again.

<column-break/>

Finally, the Sub-deacons come to rub the Table of the Altar with towels serving solely for that purpose. The Prelate <note>a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop</note> sits near the Altar and rubs his hands with breadcrumbs, washes them, and dries them again solemnly. Then the Acolytes <note>altar servers</note> offer him the altar cloths and other linens for the Altar, besides the vessels, and everything that serves for decoration. This now is the most particular part used in this Ceremony: there is nothing more to note regarding the consecration of the portable Altar, nor such an Altar which one blesses specifically without the Consecration of the Church. Regarding the portable Altar, one only observes that one must begin preparing it with some small *Relics* and three grains of Incense, and this at the place where the Consecration occurs, and what is more, it must be carried out while fasting. After this Consecration, the Priest then says the Mass, if he judges it necessary.

The Officiating Priest (c) sprinkles these Vessels and Decorations with Holy Water. Then those who serve spread the *Chrismal* <note>a waxed linen cloth</note> over the Altar, dress it with its usual decorations, place the Cross upon it, etc. Standing, the Priest begins the first verse of an *Antiphon*; after which a Psalm is sung, and he steps before the Altar, greets the Cross, and then incenses the Altar three times. Hereafter the Priest prays, and the prayer being ended, he goes to the *Sacristy* <note>a room where vestments and sacred items are kept</note>, takes off the *Cope* <note>original: "Pluviaal"; a long, ornate cloak</note>, (d) and returns wearing Slippers. Then he washes his hands and dresses himself in all his white vestments. The Church is decorated, the wax candles on the Altar are lit, and the Officiating Priest performs the Mass, if he is not too exhausted by his duties; otherwise, this is done by someone else.

# ROMAN CHURCH.

## Second Section.

### CHAPTER I.

->*How the* BLESSING *of the* AGNUS DEI <note>original: "Agnus Dei"; Latin for "Lamb of God," referring here to wax medallions bearing the image of a lamb</note> *takes place, and the origin of this* CEREMONY.<-

---

<margin>The *Agnus Dei* and its preparation described.</margin>
The Pope (a) is accustomed, in the first year of his Papacy, to solemnly (b) baptize <note>original: "doopen"; the author notes that in Rome, this blessing of the wax is referred to as a "baptism"</note> or bless the *Agnus Dei*, and continues to do so every seven years during his reign. We are pleased to describe this *Agnus*. It consists of wax and certain materials made in the form of an oval commemorative medal, upon which *Jesus Christ* is depicted under the representation of a Lamb holding a Cross; it is for this reason that this material, prepared in this way, is called an *Agnus*. In former times (c), this wax was managed by the Pope's (d) Chamberlain <term>Master of the Wax of the Apostolic Palace</term>, whose office was under the Master of the Sacred Palace. Whoever desired to be provided with these *Agnus Dei* placed themselves before the Altar of St.

<column-break/>

Peter; an Apostolic Sub-Deacon then led them from the Altar to a chamber in the Papal Palace. This Sub-Deacon and his colleagues, assisted by some Acolytes <note>minor ministers who assist the priests during ceremonies</note>, worked this wax and gave it the form of the *Agnus* (e) according to the wording of the Roman Ceremonial, with great piety, respect, and cleanliness. The Apostolic Chamber <note>the administrative department of the Papal treasury</note> provided all the necessary expenses for the preparation of this sacred material. They made the wax, which was the primary substance of it, malleable through a mixture of Holy Oil and Chrism <note>original: "Zalfoly"; a mixture of oil and balsam used for anointing</note> from the previous year. When they had the mixture ready, they presented the *Agnus Dei* to His Holiness in one or more dish- <note>The catchword "ſcho-" indicates the word "schotels" (dishes or basins), which would continue on the following page.</note>

---

(a) See *Ecclesiastical Ceremonies of the Roman Church, Book I, p. XXXVII*, printed in the year 1516.
(b) In Rome this ceremony is called the Baptism.
(c) *Eccl. Ceremonies of the Roman Church, ibid.*
(d) <note>original: "Magister Ceræ Palatii Apostolici"</note> *Master of the Wax of the Apostolic Palace.*
(e) <note>original: "Cum magna devotione, reverentia & munditia"</note> *With great devotion, reverence, and cleanliness.*

dishes, which were then blessed by this Holy Father: But now (a) the Prelate Sacristan of the Pope has the charge of the preparation of the *Agnus Dei* <note>original: "Agnus Dei"; Latin for "Lamb of God," referring to wax medallions blessed by the Pope</note> through his Chaplains and Clerks of the Chapel. The wax from which they are made is taken from the leftovers of the Paschal wax candles of the previous year, and as this cannot reach far enough, the Apostolic Chamber <note>the administrative department of the Papal treasury</note> provides the rest.

<margin>How the Blessing is performed.</margin> On Easter Tuesday (b) the Sacristan blesses the water, and the following day at the conclusion of the Papal Mass, the Pope—clad in his head-covering, the *Albe* <note>a white linen liturgical tunic</note>, a stole of white damask bordered with silver lace, and having on his head a Mitre <note>the tall, pointed ceremonial hat worn by bishops</note> of gold cloth—consecrates the water that the Sacristan blessed the previous day. This water is in a large silver dish: the sanctification occurs with the usual blessings, to which His Holiness adds a prayer to God, asking Him to hallow these things (c) that wash away sins, etc. Subsequently, the Pope takes the Balsam, pours it crosswise into the water, and likewise adds the Anointing Oil crosswise. All this occurs amidst repeatedly voiced prayers to God. Thereafter he turns toward the *Agnus Dei*, (d) blesses them, incenses them, and prays to God to grant them such powers as are commonly attributed to them. A second and third prayer follow this, after which the Holy Father goes to sit in an armchair he has placed, (e) with a towel tied before him and having the Mitre on his head; he takes the *Agnus Dei* one after another, which are handed to him in silver-gilt dishes by the Chamberlains, and throws them into the Holy Water, from which the Cardinals, clad in the fine linen *Albe*, immediately take them out again with a spoon used for this purpose. Their *Eminences* bring these *Agnus Dei* to a table covered with a white cloth, and dry them there with a towel that they wear as an apron before their bodies. The Assisting Prelates arrange them in order on this table, where they are left to dry thoroughly. After the Baptism (f) <note>The author uses "baptism" here to describe the immersion of the wax medallions in holy water</note> of the

<column-break/>

*Agnus Dei* is finished, the Pope stands up and offers a prayer to the Holy Spirit to obtain the Blessing over them; just as he likewise does to **Jesus Christ**; after which they are laid back into the dishes, and His Holiness departs with the Cardinals who have served him (g) in this, to hold the midday meal with them. This work is resumed the following Thursday and continued until all the manufactured *Agnus Dei* are blessed. This work usually ends on Friday; and this ceremony is performed in the presence of Ambassadors and many foreigners, who are curious to see this baptism of the *Agnus Dei*.

On the following Saturday, a day on which the *Agnus Dei* are presented in the chapel, the Mass is sung by a Cardinal Priest. The Pope attends in his Papal vestments. “(h) When the *Agnus Dei* has been sung, an Apostolic Sub-Deacon, dressed in his ceremonial robes and preceded by the Cross-bearer, two candle-bearers, and the thurifer <note>the person who carries the incense burner</note>, receives from the hands of the Pope’s Sacristan a silver dish with *Agnus Dei*, newly blessed and wrapped in Chinese cotton wool of various colors. The Sub-Deacon is followed by a Clerk of Ceremonies and by two Chaplains in their choir robes. When they have come to the door of the chapel, they kneel; the Sub-Deacon (i) sings in a loud voice these words in broken Latin <note>meaning a liturgical Latin formula that may not follow classical grammar</note>: (k) *Holy Father, here are the new Lambs, whom you have announced, Alleluia.* Recently they have drunk from the fountain of blessed water. *They are now greatly enlightened; Praise the Lord.* Upon this, the Choir responds in music: *God be blessed, Alleluia.* The music being ended, the Sub-Deacon stands up again and continues his way. Having come to the door of the chapel screen, he repeats the aforementioned words; and likewise for the third time, when he has come before the Papal Throne and kneels down before St. Peter’s feet, who, sitting and wearing a mitre...

# LAMB OF GOD
<note>original: "AGNUS DEI"; these are wax medallions blessed by the Pope, impressed with the figure of a lamb.</note>

# EXPLANATION
## AND
# DEPICTION
## THE POWERS OF THE LAMB OF GOD

->Consisting of a mixture of the Holy Oil, the Balsam, and pure White Wax,<-
->blessed by the hand of the High Priest <note>the Pope</note>, on one Wednesday or another<-
->after Easter Day, in the first or seventh years after the restoration<-
->of the people, in one or another pious manner.<-

---

It can bend the penalty of death;
What sins have wrought,
God’s protection will still permit,
That no water shall stain
The faithful holy heart;
The blood shall serve as a shield for you;
It puts the Devil to flight,
While carrying the world's burdens.

<column-break/>

There is no mother so anxious
For her child, whose care and fear
As you hover and watch in guilt,
Or if you must bear upon your head
The retribution for what you did;
Though the renown of this is small,
It can rescue you from much misfortune.

---

->The Prayer which the Pope says at the Blessing of the Lamb of God.<-

That sins may be blotted out; that the removal of the need for baptismal liberation and the cleansing of the conscience, and the grace of pious works may be granted to the hearts of the faithful.

That the noise of the air, hail, lightning, and storms, and the violent winds and tempests, may have no power over the hearts of the faithful.

That the evil Spirits may not rule over us, nor the pestilence, nor any diseases, nor water or fire, which could destroy the life, the property, and the bodies of men.

That the pious, after death, may obtain eternal salvation, and rejoice with the Divine Majesty of the Angels in heaven, through Jesus Christ, our Lord, Amen.

That the pious, in the transition of soul and body <note>referring to the moment of death</note>, may be delivered from all evil and the Devil’s assaults through the help of this holy <term>Lamb of God</term> <note>Agnus Dei</note>, and be led into heaven by the Angels of God.

---

->At Rome, at the Press of the Apostolic Chamber. 1661.<-
->With the permission of the Spiritual Authorities.<-

# EXPLANATION
->of the Adjacent<-
## DEPICTION.
### THE POWERS of the LAMB OF GOD,
<note>original: "AGNUS DEI"; these are sacred wax medallions blessed by the Pope.</note>

->Consisting of a mixture of the Holy Oil, Balsam and pure Wax,<-
->extracted from the book called the *Ceremonial*, wherein the Blessing<-
->of the same is spoken of, and of which one finds the following words<-
->noted at the end in this manner.<-

->ONE READS THEREIN HOW POPE URBAN V SENT TO THE GREEK<-
->EMPEROR THREE LAMBS OF GOD, WITH THIS VERSE, AND<-
->THE FOLLOWING WORDS.<-
<note>Pope Urban V (r. 1362–1370) famously sent these medallions to Byzantine Emperor John V Palaiologos as part of diplomatic and religious exchanges.</note>

It can subdue the power of thunder;
It washes sins purely away;
Fierce fire shall never penetrate,
Nor shall any water be your grave.
It guards you from a sudden death;
It puts the Devils to flight,
And it causes the enemy's plot to fail.

It brings a mother no distress
For her child, though laden with care.
As you labor, toil, and struggle,
May prosperity be your guarantee
Of the enjoyment at which you aim.
Though its form is small in parts,
It can heal you of much sorrow.

->The PRAYER which the POPE says at the BLESSING of the LAMB OF GOD<-

That it may blot out sins, that one may obtain forgiveness, and become a partaker of grace.
That Christians, touching and beholding it, may be encouraged to praise God.
That the noise of the air, hail, snow, and the storm, the violent winds and claps of thunder may be softened and stilled.
That the evil Spirits may be terrified and flee before the Wholesome and Blessed Standard of the Cross, which is depicted upon it.
That the bearer be strengthened against the delusions, deceits, ruses, and craftiness of the Devil and the evil Spirits.
That no storm, nor accident, nor pestilential air <term>pestlucht: historically believed to be "bad air" that carried disease</term>, nor destruction, nor falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note>, nor any plagues, and sea-storms, no danger of fire nor other temporal disasters, can damage, destroy, or harm those who shall wear it religiously.
That the mother in childbirth <note>original: "kraambedt"</note> be preserved from accident.
That all who wear it may be constantly out of danger; that they have no misfortune to fear; that they be not afraid of any phantoms; that no violence of the Devil harm them; that they cannot be deceived by men; that they are not subject to any dangers of fire, lightning, storm, and tempest; and that the pregnant women give birth without pain, and are freed from all accident and danger.

->At Rome, by the Printer of the Apostolic Chamber. 1662.<-
->With the consent of the Spiritual Authorities.<-

A. An exact copy of the printed paper which the Pope gives with the Lamb of God, being a sort of wax-printed commemorative medal, representing a Lamb as one sees at the letter B. and this Commemorative Medal has on the other side some image of a Saint.
C. The Arms <note>heraldic coat of arms</note> of Pope Alexander VII, who granted the original of the aforementioned copy A.
D. The Scapular <term>Scapulier: two small pieces of cloth joined by strings, worn over the shoulders as a sign of devotion</term>.
E. The Rosary or Pater Noster <note>Latin: "Our Father"</note> consisting of 15 decades.
F. A common Pater Noster, decorated with Relics.
G. A Ring which the Knights of Malta use to pray their Rosary; the Rose that is on top points the way with a small black dot on the 15 numerals around it, and the number of decades already mentioned.
H. A Decade <note>original: "Tienling"</note> to read the Pater Noster.
I. The Bread of St. Genevieve, or a sort of biscuit, which the Clergy of St. Genevieve distribute for fevers.
K. A blessed copper commemorative medal that the Sisters of Charity in Paris wear on their Rosary to preserve their virginal state.

<note>The "Agnus Dei" is a small disc of wax, usually blessed by the Pope during the first year of his reign and every seventh year thereafter. It is made from the wax of the previous year's Paschal candles mixed with holy oil and balsam.</note>

->Composed of Holy Chrism, Balsam, and pure wax. Extracted<-
->from the book called the *Ceremonial*, where, speaking of the<-
->blessing of these items, the following words are found<-
->recorded at the end in this manner.<-

Surrounding it are various aids for prayer: a scapular (D), several styles of rosaries (E, F, H), a specialized rosary ring (G), blessed bread for healing (I), and protective medals (K).</note>

->It is read that Pope Urban V sent to the Emperor of the Greeks<-
->three *Agnus Dei*, with these verses and words.<-
<note>Pope Urban V (reigned 1362–1370) sent these to Emperor John V Palaiologos to encourage his conversion and as a sign of papal favor.</note>

The thunder it drives away;
Sins it wipes away;
It saves from conflagration;
And from drowning,
It guards against sudden death,
It puts the Devils to flight,
And subdues all enemies.

<column-break/>

Placed out of danger are
Both the child and the Mother,
Who labors in childbirth;
It gives many powers,
To those worthy to have it.
A part, however small,
Avails as much as the whole.

---

->The Prayer that the Pope says at the Blessing of the Lamb of God.<-

> That it may erase sins, that one may obtain pardon, and that it may confer graces.
> That upon touching and seeing it, Christians may be moved to praise God.
> That the noise of the air, hail, snow, and tempests, the fury of the winds, and the thunders may be moderated and stilled.
> That before the Saving and glorious standard of the Cross, which is depicted thereon, the evil spirits may be terrified and flee.
> That he who carries them may have power against the illusions, deceptions, ruses, and frauds of the Devil and of evil spirits.
> That no tempest, adversity, pestilential or corrupt air, nor the falling sickness <note>original: "mal caduc"; an old term for epilepsy</note>; no storm, sea-tempest; no fire, or other injuries of the weather, may be able to offend, harm, or prejudice him who shall devoutly carry it upon himself.
> That in childbirth, the Mother and the child may be preserved.
> That all those who carry it may always be in safety, that they fear no peril, that they have no fear of shadows <note>perhaps referring to ghosts or spectral illusions</note>, that no cruelty of the Devil may harm them, that they may not be deceived by men, and that they be exempt from all perils of fire, lightning, storm, and tempests. And that women may give birth without labor, and be delivered from evil and all danger.

->with permission of the Superiors.<-

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc., of the ROMAN CHURCH.

<margin>and how the Distribution of the Lambs of God takes place.</margin>
Two Auditors take a towel that is clean and white, and offer it to two Assisting <term>Cardinal Deacons|High-ranking officials who assist the Pope in liturgical functions</term>, who spread it over the knees of His Holiness. The two Auditors, kneeling, hold both ends of this towel while the Sacred College participates in the Holy Father’s generous gifts. Their Eminences, after the customary expressions of respect and esteem, offer the Pope their upturned, horned mitres; then His Holiness places as many of these sacred **Lambs of God** into the horned caps as he pleases. (a) In former times, he gave no more than three to each member of the College, two to other prelates, and one to the rest of the clergy, etc. Their Eminences then kiss the hand and knee of the Holy Father. After the distribution of the **Lambs of God** to the Cardinals and other clergy is finished, the Ambassadors and other prominent personages approach with their white towels to take their turn in sharing these spiritual benefits. The Holy Father treats these, his latest-arrived children, a little less generously than the others. Nevertheless, he distributes a fair portion of the **Lambs of God** into their towels.

When the distribution is finished, the Pope washes his hands, the Sacred College removes their ceremonial vestments, the officiating Bishop returns to the altar, and (b) the Mass being ended with a double *Hallelujah* <note>original: "Helleluja"</note>, Saint Peter <note>Referring to the Pope as the successor of St. Peter</note> gives the blessing to his children with a proclamation of many indulgences. The *Roman Ceremonial* states that in former times, at the conclusion of the meal, the Popes had a dish

<column-break/>

filled with **Lambs of God** brought to the table, which they distributed to the Apostolic Court.

<margin>Means prescribed to preserve them.</margin>
> "All the remaining **Lambs of God** (c) from the great multitude that were blessed, are kept by the Prelate who is the Master of the Pope’s Wardrobe.... This Prelate distributes them daily at certain hours to the pilgrims and strangers who desire them. By an ordinance of Pope Gregory XIII from the year 1572, it is forbidden for those who have not received Holy Orders to touch the **Lambs of God**, unless required by certain unusual circumstances; and to ensure the most precise care is taken in this, it is commanded to keep them enclosed in glass or crystal, or other transparent materials; and that the wealthy should have them covered with some precious embroidered fabric, yet in such a way that the **Lambs of God** can always be seen from one side, as if in a reliquary. Likewise, by the same ordinance, it is forbidden to paint them, under penalty of excommunication <note>original: "Ban"</note>. This is because the white color of the wax, of which these relief images consist, was judged by this Pope to be the most fitting of all that could be used... to represent the *spotless Lamb of God*. Such are the expressions which the Popes, from Gregory XIII until now, have used... when speaking of the miraculous effects of the **Lambs of God**."

<margin>How they serve as charms, compared with the usage of the Romans.</margin>
Regarding the origin of this ceremony, it is as follows. (d) In the first centuries of the Church, new converts <note>original: "Doopeling," literally 'baptized one'</note> were given a small wax image representing JESUS CHRIST in the form of a Lamb. The **Catechumens** <note>original: "Catechumenen"</note> or beginners in the faith \* wore it hanging around the neck. This custom seems to have followed the practice of the amulets or charms of the ancient Pagans. By <meta>catchword: the</meta>

---

(b) *The "Ite Missa est" [Go, the Mass is ended] is said with a double Hallelujah. Ceremonial etc. Ibid.*
(c) *See the "Picture of the Roman Court."*
(d) *Casalius, On Rites, etc.*

\* [In the ancient Church, the **Catechumens** were those who passed from Heathenism to the Christian religion and allowed themselves to be instructed for that purpose. First, they had to present themselves to a Christian and request help in approaching the clergy. Subsequently, they were exhorted not to undertake this salutary work lightly: but when the petitioner persisted in his intention, he was presented to the clergy, who laid hands on him and had his name, as well as the name of the one who presented him, recorded in the Church book. Then the **Catechumens** were instructed in the Christian faith, and they were placed among the penitents, as they had to remain in a separate place in the church called the **Narthex**, which was a kind of chapel, usually separated from the nave of the church by a gate, in which the **Catechumens, the Initiated**, and the **Candidates** <note>original: "Competenten"</note> stayed; as for the first group, they had to depart after the sermon was finished, since they were not permitted to hear the public church prayer... <meta>catchword: hear-</meta>

<margin>and how the distribution of the *Agnus Dei* is performed.</margin>
Two *Auditors* <note>High-ranking officials of the Apostolic court.</note> take a towel that is clean and white, and offer it to the two assisting Cardinal Deacons, who spread it over the knees of His Holiness. Both *Auditors* remain kneeling, holding both ends of this towel, while the Sacred College participates in the Holy Father’s generosity. Their *Eminences*, after the customary expressions of respect and esteem, offer the Pope their upturned horned mitres; then His Holiness places as many of these sacred *Agnus Dei* into the horned caps as he pleases. (a) Formerly he gave no more than three of them to each Member of the College, two to other Prelates, and one to the remaining Clergy, etc. Their *Eminences* furthermore kiss the hand and knee of the Holy Father. After the distribution of the *Agnus Dei* to the Cardinals and other Clergy is completed, the Ambassadors and other prominent personages approach with their white towels to likewise take their turn in sharing these spiritual benefits. The Holy Father treats these last-arrived children a little less generously than the others. Nevertheless, he distributes a fair portion of *Agnus Dei* into their towels.

The distribution being finished, the Pope washes his hands, the Sacred College removes their ceremonial vestments, the officiating Bishop returns to the Altar, and (b) the Mass being ended with a double *Hallelujah* <note>original: *Helleluja*</note>, St. Peter <note>Referring to the Pope as the successor of St. Peter.</note> gives the blessing to his children with an announcement of many Indulgences. The *Roman* Ceremonial says that in former times, at the end of the meal, the Popes had a dish

<column-break/>

filled with *Agnus Dei* brought to the table, which they distributed to the Apostolic Court.

<margin>Means prescribed for preserving them.</margin>
> “All the remaining *Agnus Dei* (c) from the great multitude that were blessed, are kept by the Prelate who is Master of the Pope’s Wardrobe.... This Prelate distributes them daily at certain hours to the Pilgrims and Strangers who desire them. By a Decree of Pope Gregory XIII from the year 1572, those who have not received Holy Orders are forbidden to touch the *Agnus Dei*, unless required by certain unusual circumstances; and to provide for this with the utmost care, he commanded the laity to take care to keep them enclosed in glass or crystal, or in other transparent materials; and that those who were wealthy should have them covered with some precious embroidered fabric, yet in such a way that the *Agnus Dei* could always be seen from one side, as if in a reliquary <note>original: *Reliquikasje*</note>. Likewise, by the same Decree, it is forbidden to paint them, under penalty of Excommunication. For the white color of the wax, of which these raised-relief images consist, was judged by this Pope to be the most appropriate of all that could be used... to represent the *spotless Lamb of God*. Such are the expressions which the Popes from Gregory XIII until now have used... speaking of the miraculous effects of the *Agnus Dei*.”

## CHAPTER II.
### *Concerning the CANONIZATION or MAKING OF SAINTS, and with what PAGEANTRY this is performed.*

<margin>Council meetings held by the Pope regarding the Canonization, and how.</margin>
Before (a) the inscription among the number of the blessed Saints occurs, for which the Canonization or Sanctification is requested, the Pope holds four Council meetings. The first two are secret, the third is public, and the fourth is semi-public. In the first meeting, the Holy Father has three *Auditors of the Rota* <term>Auditors of the Rota: Judges of the highest ecclesiastical court in the Catholic Church.</term> examine the petition of those who desire that their Saint be recognized as such in the Roman Church in general. He commands the Cardinals to carefully review the documents pertaining to the case. In the second, the Cardinals report to His Holiness on their findings; the third is held in public (b) as has already been mentioned. The Cardinals offer their submission to the Pope there, after which a Consistorial Advocate bellows the eulogy of the one who is to be declared a Saint and gives a detailed account of the life and miracles of that faithful servant of God: sometimes he even deals with the secrets and most hidden deeds of the new Saint. Continuing with these thoughts, he picks apart the slightest motivations with such cautious and necessary accuracy when the dispute concerns recognizing him before God as a new Mediator and accepting him into the Society of Intercessors, established now and then for the faithful of the Church.

<column-break/>

The fourth Meeting is held semi-publicly, namely in the Ducal Hall, and the Pope attends it wearing a mitre and a simple *Pluvial* <term>Cope (Pluvial): A long, ornate liturgical mantle worn by clergy.</term>. No act of submission is shown to him there. Patriarchs, Archbishops, Bishops, *Protonotaries*, and *Auditors of the Rota* are admitted. The *Caudatarii* <term>Train-bearers who assist high-ranking prelates.</term> perform their duties there in violet; but after the *Extra* <note>The formal closing of the public portion of the session.</note>, everyone must stand outside, except for the Prelates mentioned above. The Council is then occupied with taking the votes for and against the Canonization, and when the majority of the electors reach a decision, the Holy Father appoints (c) the exact day for this solemn inauguration.

<margin>Preparation for the Canonization, and the splendor that accompanies it.</margin>
On the day of the *Canonization*, the Pope is dressed in white, and the Cardinals likewise. St. Peter's Church is decorated with uncommon magnificence. One sees upon the tapestries the coat of arms of the Pope, and those of the Prince or the State requesting the Canonization, embroidered in gold and silver. Infinite torches illuminate the Church everywhere, where thousands of Christian souls wait, perhaps with a godly impatience, for the sanctified one to make his public entry into Paradise, so that they may subsequently present their supplications to him without danger of rejection. We shall [continue] regarding the details of the *Canonization*...

RELIGIOUS DUTIES etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH.

<margin>Which qualities are required for Canonization.</margin> *Canonization* costs Princes an unbelievable sum of money to obtain the honor of Canonization for a Saint. What is called Beatification <note>Original Dutch: "Gelukzaliging"</note> is, in a sense, a prerequisite for it. Beatification actually leads to Sainthood and fosters the thought that those seen as Blessed here on Earth must be recognized as such in Heaven. However, many of the Blessed have not been able to reach the rank of Sainthood; either because the necessary testimonies and assurances could not be provided for them, or because enough miracles could not be gathered to declare them Holy. For it is much the same as with soldiers who would like to see themselves promoted in military rank. Thus, it is required that the one as well as the other produce at least some signs of outstanding worth or bravery. And since the Great Ones of this world are not always able to judge merit, intercessors are required to present their virtue to the Princes, and Advocates who plead in their favor.

<margin>Origin of the same.</margin> The birth of the Martyrs, the thoughts held in their honor on solemn days, and the general feast days of the Martyrs which were testified to, have for many centuries meant the Canonization of the Saints of the Church had no eternal value. Nevertheless, it appears that Pope John XIV or XV usually did not satisfy a *Constitution* or a *Decree*, but many years before a canonization, the first Saint who solemnly enjoyed this honor exists. There are those who have attributed the institution of a Saint to a Pope Alexander III.

The Protestant writers say that the *Canonization* of the Church corresponds with the Apotheosis <note>Original Dutch: "Vergoeding" or "Vergoding" — the process of deifying a human.</note> of the Saints of the ancient Romans, and possibly had its birth from such a source.

<columns>
Taking up the wax candle once more, he seated himself again in the sedan chair and had himself carried before the Altar of the Apostles. There, the Holy Father handed the wax candle to a server <term>Schenker: Literally a "pourer" or cupbearer, here referring to a ceremonial attendant</term>, who held it until the end of the ceremony; His Holiness knelt in his chair and prayed for some time, after which he distributed several new blessings to the assembly of the faithful, ascended his Throne to fulfill his office as Vicar <term>Stedehouder: A title for the Pope meaning "representative" or "vicar"</term> of JESUS CHRIST, and received the submission of the Sacred Society <note>The College of Cardinals</note>, etc. After this submission, the eldest of the Cardinal Bishops ascended the Papal Throne and took his place on the right side, positioned so that he turned his face toward the left side. The Cardinal sent to request the Canonization presented himself before the steps of the Throne, having on his left the Cardinal-Legate of Bologna and a Consistorial Advocate on his right. The Master of Ceremonies who accompanied the Cardinal Petitioner was on the left of the Legate. They greeted the Altar and the Pope; after which the Cardinal Petitioner stood up, and the Advocate, turning to the Pope in the name of His Eminence, requested that it please His Holiness (a) *to have the four Blessed inscribed in the Register of the Lord's Saints.* Hardly had this request been made when one of the Pope's chamberlains and Secretary of His Holiness's Briefs <term>Brevetten: Official papal letters or decrees</term>, having stood up, spoke and gave a short eulogy of the merits and virtues of these Blessed, all four born in Italy, who had become immortal through their spiritual undertakings. Italy has always excelled in the renown of many Saints. The dignity of Saint *Francis* of *Assisi* and of *Paul*, of *Anthony* of *Padua*, etc., is sufficiently known there. (b) *These brave and noble soldiers of the Lord’s hosts, who with the help of Christian virtues won the Kingdom of Heaven, and earned a glory in their Fatherland infinitely more magnificent than that of the heroes of ancient Rome.* But it seems now that for some time Italy has turned away from this latter glory.

<column-break/>

<margin>and how the Canonization was completed.</margin>
The Chamberlain, having ended his speech, further exhorted the assembly on this so tender occasion to implore the light of the Spirit of God: then the Pope rose from his Throne, and all the clergy knelt; two choirmasters of the chapel, wearing surplices, also sang while kneeling the *Litany of the Saints*; after which the request to resume the *Canonization* was continued by the Cardinal who had requested it. A prayer to God followed these repeated requests: they implored Him for His Holy Spirit, and the Holy Father sang the *Come, Creator Spirit* <note>original: "Veni Creator Spiritus" — a traditional hymn invoking the Holy Spirit</note>, which is a hymn attributed to the third Person of the Trinity. The two choirmasters sang the verse beginning with the words: *Send forth thy Spirit* <note>original: "Emitte Spiritum"</note>. The Pope invoked the Holy Spirit while the two Voters of the Signature stood before the steps of the Throne, each with a wax candle in hand. A third and very last petition, which occurred in the same order as the previous ones, followed this invocation. Subsequently, the Secretary of Briefs took the floor again and declared (c) that it was time to submit to the commands of God; the Holy Father, he continued, *grants an Apostolic Decree to elevate to Sainthood PIUS V, ANDREW AVELLINO, FELIX OF CANTALICE, AND CATHERINE OF BOLOGNA, serving the honor of God and His Catholic Church, so that their names may be invoked in the coming ages, etc.* After saying this, the Secretary withdrew, while all the Cardinals stood up, and the Vicar of JESUS CHRIST, strengthened by the Holy Spirit <note>original Latin: "Cæleſti Spiritu afflatus"</note>, (c) proclaimed the decision of the *Canonization*; ordering that henceforth they shall be held as Saints in the Catholic Church, and that their feast shall be celebrated on the day of their birth <note>Referring to their "heavenly birthday," the date of their death and entry into heaven.</note>. The Protonotaries and Apostolic Notaries then immediately prepared a copy of this *Canonization*, and the *Thee, O God, we praise* <note>original: "Te Deum" — the ancient hymn of thanksgiving</note> was sung to thank God.
<margin>Demonstration of joy upon the completion.</margin>
While the chapel music was still singing the *Te Deum*, the signal was given by a Master of Ceremonies to inform the City of the completed solemn elevation.

The company of Trumpets, the noise of Drums, the sound of Bells, the thundering of Cannon, and the firing of small arms announced in all the quarters of Rome the triumph of the **Church Militant** <term>Strydende Kerke: The part of the Christian Church on earth, seen as engaged in spiritual warfare</term> under the leadership of the Vice-Commander of JESUS CHRIST on Earth. Men spoke of nothing but the illustrious deeds of the new Saints, of their austere lives, of their Piety and virtues. Already the people placed their trust in them and chose them as their Patrons, and in the rapture caused by the joy of the Pious in Rome, thousands of Vows were heard which they made to God for the prosperity of the Pope.

<margin>Papal decree regarding the classification of the new Saints.</margin> When the Choir music had concluded with the singing of the *Te Deum* <note>original: "Te Deum" — "To Thee, O God," a traditional hymn of praise</note>, the Assistant Cardinal Deacons <term>Kardinaal Noothelpen: Historically, the Cardinal Assistants who flank the Pope during ceremonies</term> on the right side sang the *Litanies* in honor of the new Mediators, calling each of them by name. The Canonization being finished, a solemn Mass followed. His Holiness was brought there between two Assistant Deacons and drawn by two *Auditors* of Rome, brought from the great Throne to the small throne where he led the service; in the attached Depiction of the new Saints, it is shown who it was. Moving from the great Throne to the small one, and from the Holy Father moving to either side, the Holy Father gave several blessings over the Apostolic Council. Shortly thereafter, His Holiness took off his Mitre, stood up, embraced the Altar, saying softly the *Pater* <note>The Our Father</note> and the *Ave Maria* <note>The Hail Mary</note>, made the sign of the Cross, and began the third hour, *Deus in adjutorium* <note>original: "Deus in adjutorium" — "O God, come to my assistance"</note>. We shall not elaborate further on the account of this Mass, since it differs almost not at all from other Papal Masses. We shall only note that the Holy Father delivered a discourse, which was a sort of familiar lesson. One of the most remarkable parts of 
<margin>The Pope's sermon concerning the invocation of the new Saints.</margin> his talk was that the calamitous times necessarily required that new examples of virtue be shown to the people, to reawaken their already cooled Religious fervor, so that one could be assured of obtaining new help from Heaven for the defense of Religion; for this purpose, one could find no better subjects, nor any of greater effect, than the power of St. Pius the Fifth and His three companions in Holiness. Approximately in the middle of his discourse, the Holy Father turned his Christian words toward the four Saints of his creation, so that they might look upon the distress of the Church with eyes of compassion, and he commended to them with all possible zeal the *new Sion* <note>Rome</note>, the Mother and Mistress of all other Churches. After this delivered lesson and granting of Indulgence, the Assistant Cardinal Bishop requested of the Holy Father that it please him to grant Indulgence to those who would offer their devotion before these new Saints; then the Pope turned to the people and declared a seven-year Indulgence for the pious who annually visit their graves.

### Regarding the offerings (a) that are in How one [is]

(a) It is well known that offerings were in use among the ancient Jews. Likewise, one is no less aware of how they were in vogue among the ancient Idolaters. The Christians followed a custom which has only degenerated into an error, and such a one that one can hardly refrain from laughing. In the time of Constantine the Great, one was not permitted to approach the Altar except with a gift in hand. This was indeed a primary matter of importance. It increased the Ecclesiastical income significantly and was paired with the Articles of Religion. _**27** Going to Church, praying, for-_

The first also carried a small Wax Candle and the other two Doves in a silvered basket. Next came two Noblemen of Cardinal *Pamphili* in clerical robes, carrying two small flasks, one gilded and the other silvered, one of them filled with wine and the other with water, both provided with the Coat of Arms of the Pope and the *Postulants* <term>Postulanten: Those petitioning or requesting the canonization</term> or Petitioners on the base. The Cardinal followed

<column-break/>

them, after whom also followed the Reverend Father Secretary of the Congregation of the Index, as well as the Reverend Provincial of the Holy Land. The Secretary of the said Congregation carried a gilded cage with small birds, and the Provincial a small Wax Candle, as we have already described, under which he held a beautiful white towel, so that not a single drop of the wax was lost. When they had reached the steps of the Papal Throne, the Staff-bearers and Noblemen placed themselves in a row on the right and left sides; and Cardinal *Abdua*, alongside Cardinal *Albani* as Procurator of the Canonization, stepped to the right side of the Pope after having greeted him. Those who carried the large Wax Candles offered them to Cardinal *Abdua*, who, after having kissed them, offered them to His Holiness. Cardinal *Albani*, as Procurator, offered the small Wax Candles and the (b) Offerings carried in the small baskets. The other Cardinals likewise served to offer the Holy Father the bread, the water, and the wine (c); after which the Bearers of these Sacred Gifts were admitted to the kissing of the Pope's foot. They descended on the left side of the Throne, and all these Offerings were subsequently brought back to the Tables from which they had been taken.

<margin>The Scene and the Papal Throne described.</margin>
It would now be required to give a description of the Throne’s decorations; but as the reading of this account would be too dry and tasteless, one may be satisfied with finding the most remarkable parts thereof explained alongside the Illustration. We shall say in general,

---

> "...forgiveness to sinners, attend the Mass, and bring your offerings:" thus Nicholas I expresses himself, in a passage cited by Mr. Chiapponi in his treatise on Offerings.
> 
> These Offerings were of many kinds; some were common, such as the bread, the wine, and the water for the Eucharist <note>original: "Eucharistie" — the central rite of the Mass</note>. There were those intended for the Ceremonies and for the necessities of the Church and her Ministers; such were the incenses, perfumes, wax candles, the oil, sacred vessels, the firstfruits of the earth and the livestock: but especially the Money, the Inheritances, the possession of Lands, Lordships, and many fine National Revenues, which the pious Ministers of the Church have gradually taken from devout souls.
> 
> In the Church of Milan, a kind of Offering is still in use today, having regard to those of bread and wine that occurred in the ancient Church of Rome. Two old men of the School of St. Ambrose <note>Referring to the Ambrosian Rite, a unique liturgical tradition in Milan</note> offer three Hosts on a dish, and a small silver flask full of wine. Two old women make a similar offering. It is clearly a remnant of Communion under two kinds <term>Communie onder de twee gedaanten: Receiving both the bread (Body) and wine (Blood) of Christ</term>, of which the Roman Church has also preserved the idea in the Canonization of Saints, the Consecration of a Bishop, and the Blessing of an Abbot; likewise the Ceremonies where bread, wine, and water are offered. Antiquity also offered Wax Candles to the Popes and Prelates; a custom that still exists in many Ecclesiastical Church practices, such as the taking of Orders and the Blessing of Virgins. In the Annual Ceremonies in Rome, offerings are still made by the City Officials, and upon the Altars of the principal Churches, of chalice covers, chalices, Wax Candles, etc.
> 
> (a) This is a particular Description of the Offering made for St. Pius V, drawn word for word from the drafted Acts by Mr. Chiapponi.
> 
> (b) The Author of the "Tableau of the Roman Court" <note>original: "Tafereel van ’t Roomſche Hof"</note> says that the Pope opens the birdcages offered to him and lets one bird fly away, while the others must remain captive: claiming that this is a symbol of the Outskirts of Hell <term>Helsche Voorburgen: Often referring to Limbo</term> and of Purgatory, from which the Pope releases those whom he pleases to lead into Heaven, etc.
> 
> (c) Namely the Flasks in which this liquid is contained.

...say, that the stage was covered with magnificent tapestries, and one could not imagine anything more stately than the great Papal Throne was. On one side of the Throne, one saw a figure representing the Church, and on the other side, Justice. The center of the Throne was fifty-five Roman palms <note>A Roman palm was a unit of measurement roughly equal to 22 centimeters</note> high, and the width was thirty-six. Figures of Faith and Hope were placed at both ends of the stage.

Countless wax candles illuminated the Church and the stage. The writer, who serves us a very extensive account of what we have shortened here, has also recorded a long list of things necessary to complete a well-regulated and magnificent <term>Canonization</term> <note>The formal process by which the Catholic Church declares a deceased person to be a saint</note>. Likewise, we shall make no mention of the particular favors and gifts of grace which the Holy Father attaches to <term>Rosaries</term> <note>original: "Paternosters"; prayer beads used to count a sequence of prayers</note>, chapels, images, crosses, commemorative medals, and other such things, and which he hallows and blesses on the occasion of the solemnities, or performed during the triumphal entry of the four Saints into Heaven. All this was expressed in a decree <note>original: "Afslaat"</note>, with promises of forgiveness of sins to those who visited seven churches in one year, or at least as many as were found in the city of their residence: provided, however, that if there were only one, they must visit all the altars of that same church. 

The same promise was granted to those who, in memory of the suffering of our Savior <term>Jesus Christ</term>, should kiss the earth seven times, or perform some duties of virtue in imitation of these our four Saints, or read some chapters of their lives, visited their altars, or honored their <term>Relics</term> <note>Physical remains or personal effects of a saint preserved for veneration</note>: praying alongside these for the glory of the Church, the conversion of sinners, etc.

The monks and <column-break/> brothers followed one another before the altar, all kneeling, except for the cross-, banner-, and candle-bearers. The Brothers of the Holy Sacrament, who carried the standard of the Saint, stood still near the altar of the choir to hear the <term>Antiphon</term> <note>A short sentence or verse sung or recited before or after a psalm</note> which was sung in music in honor of St. Pius V, and was followed by a <term>Litany</term> <note>A series of petitions for use in church services, usually recited by the clergy with responses from the congregation</note>. 

Subsequently, the Canon of the week sang the prayer of the Saint and went straight to the standard, upon which the image of the newly-sanctified Pope was painted, which he censed three times. Meanwhile, the clergy of the Church appeared in the wake of the cross with the wax candles. They proceeded toward the Dominicans. Then the standard of Pius V was placed into the hands of four fathers of the Dominican Order by the Canon of the week, who then religiously knelt to honor the holy image. When they stepped out of the church with the standard, the clergy and the Chapter placed themselves in rows on either side to honor the image, and with a genuflection, they paid their homage before the representation of the sanctified Pope.

It was fitting to grant the <term>Dominicans</term> <note>A Catholic religious order founded by Saint Dominic; Pope Pius V was a member of this order</note> the honor of carrying the standard of the Pope who had come from their Order. These peaceful clergymen walked with burning candles, followed by drums and trumpets, the Roman people, and the members of the brotherhood likewise armed with candles, mingled with a large number of music masters, and carrying the cross, the standard of the brotherhood, and lanterns. The banner of St. Pius was accompanied by twenty <term>Grooms</term> <note>original: "Palfreniers"; papal attendants who managed the horses and assisted in ceremonies</note> of the Pope and thirty Swiss Guards of his life-guard. 

The bells of all the churches they passed were rung; the windows of the houses everywhere were decorated with religious emblems and filled with lights, while the thunder of cannon was heard. At the expense of the Dominican Order, fifty small pieces of artillery had been placed before St. Mary of Minerva, and it was seen then that the thunder of the cannons caused no alarm to the hermits <note>referring to the monks</note>, though their solitude was accustomed to nothing but embracing the cross and holding the <term>Rosary</term>. When the procession arrived at St. Mary of Minerva, they passed through this church in two rows. <margin>Of what significance the offerings at the Canonization have been.</margin> Everything offered for a <term>Canonization</term> <note>The formal process by which the Catholic Church declares a deceased person to be a saint</note> is full of mystery; the wax candles represent (b) the humanity of JESUS CHRIST, and are also the symbol of the purity of the Saints, and of the good works that were excellent before men. The bread, the water, and the wine represent the idea of the spiritual life. Besides that, the bread signifies the gratitude one owes to God, and these three things together are the images of the Sacrifice that JESUS CHRIST made of his body at the Supper held with his Apostles. As for the turtle-

<column-break/>

dove; this bird is the symbol of marital fidelity, and is also a symbol of duty in the <unclear>married state</unclear>. It represents very well to us the inviolable faithfulness that the Saints have sworn to God. Likewise, the turtle-dove is the symbol of the contemplative life of the Saints, for it also loves solitude. Its sighs express wonderfully well the distress that the faithful servants of God feel because of the sins of men. However, the good qualities of the turtle-dove must not compel us to despise common pigeons; these birds, which love company and fly in flocks, are the speaking symbol of the active life of the Saints. What is more, the Holy Spirit is represented to us by the form of a dove. As for the small birds offered in this ceremony, they also represent the Saints, who, taking flight to Heaven through the power of contemplation, enjoy an <unclear>intimate</unclear> fellowship with God there. The baskets in which the loaves lie, the perceived loaves of understanding, the silver bowls in which the baskets of bread lie, the painted wax candles, the gold and silver with which the loaves are adorned, are all hidden matters; about which the reader can find further report in the author who composed this narrative for us.

### CHAPTER IV.

Concerning the CEREMONY of the CONSECRATION of the BLESSED; and the PIETY shown to the Saints.

<margin>What an investigation regarding church laws is required for the new Saints.</margin> A believer may not be beatified until fifty years after his death. Then, in the Council Meeting <note>The Congregation of Rites, the Vatican body responsible for supervising the canonization process</note> regarding Church laws, all the testimonials brought forward regarding his virtues and miracles are examined. This investigation sometimes lasts several years: after which His Holiness decides upon the <term>Beatification</term> <note>original: "Zaliging"; a declaration by the Pope that a dead person is "Blessed" and may be venerated in a particular region</note>; for the esteem of a believer is never disappointed, since confirmation always follows.

After the Council Meeting has carefully examined the petitions of the petitioners as well as the life of the future Saint, the Holy Father grants a Decree of Beatification. (c) Then the <term>Relics</term> <note>Physical remains or personal effects of a saint</note> of the Saint may be put on display to be honored by the faithful. His images are subsequently seen radiating light <note>Depicted with a halo or "glory"</note>. Forgiveness of sins is granted to him <note>An indulgence granted to the public on his feast day</note> on the day of his ceremony.

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc., of the ROMAN CHURCH.
V v 2

<margin>The various types of Saints.</margin> ...elevate [them] to the State of Beatitude.

One finds various kinds of Saints. First, they become so through the help of temporal goods, and through benefits bestowed upon the Church or her Ministers; others, by the authority they have acquired, are declared to be Protectors and Patrons. Again, there are others who have been [recognized] for their Learning and their great intellect; however, this has never been lacking after their death, or they have acquired the gifts of miracles. Of this, one is convinced in Rome, where the piety attributed to unknown Saints has great authority.

Such Saints are found in the ancient and modern Legends, in which their lives are described with praise as an example for the Faithful, appearing suspicious enough if they were intended for worldly-minded people. One finds nothing but great, miraculous, outstanding, and rare matters related therein.

Besides the Saints known by deeds and by name, there are thousands who do not possess these qualities: but it is suspected, however, that they are true and legitimate Saints, since the Pope declares them as such after their corpses have been retrieved from the burial places that are called <term>Catacombs</term> <note>Ancient subterranean cemeteries, particularly in Rome, where early Christians and martyrs were buried</note> or underground Burial places. Although one imagines that these new Protectors were an example during their life in the World, however, this has never been lacking after their death, or they have acquired the gifts of miracles. Of this, one is convinced in Rome, where the piety attributed to unknown Saints has great authority.

<margin>How the Scholars view and critique the [veneration of] Saints.</margin> It seems that the Faithful, after the pronouncement of the Apostolic Court, made no difficulty in commending themselves to the protection of these unknown Saints; nevertheless, some Scholars have undertaken to undermine the grounds of this worship. Mr. Thiers <note>Jean-Baptiste Thiers (1636–1703), a French theologian known for his critiques of popular superstitions</note>, one of these Scholars, has not described this piety to attack it or to answer him, that one without danger... See * how he expresses himself on this.

A piety that is currently most esteemed is this, which one shows to the new Saints, whose bodies are taken from

<column-break/>

the --- <term>Catacombs</term> or underground Burial places, and which are given out of affection to powerful Personages who request them, after the Cardinal Vicar <note>original: "Kardinaal Stedehouder"</note> of the Pope, or Bishop Sacristan of the Apostolic Chapel, has given them the required names: --- People run from all sides to the Churches where the bodies of the new Saints rest; they bring Offerings there, or make Vows, likewise Pilgrimages and nine-day Prayers <note>A "Novena," a series of prayers held over nine consecutive days to seek a specific grace</note>; they have Masses performed and Gospels read there; they bring and commend the sick there for the healing of various diseases, as well as stillborn children or those who have died unbaptized, in expectation that they shall be raised again through the intercession of these new Saints; they hasten to kiss the Reliquaries <note>original: "Reliquikafjes," the small chests or containers used to hold sacred remains</note>, to rub their <term>Rosaries</term> <note>original: "Paternoster"</note> against them, as well as commemorative medals and some linen for the use of the sick; they then cry out "miracle" --- Everyone wants to be a witness to it, and it is spread abroad that these Saints are of more power, and stand in high esteem with God. One would not wish to guarantee that the People, always lovers of novelties, might not easily fall into this irregularity. It appears to them that it is with God as it is with men, and that the latest arrival must be regarded by the Supreme Being as the first favorite.

<insert>Mr. Thiers believes that the piety shown to the ancient Saints is more regulated, more certain, and better established. He is free to hold to that: but one must answer him that one can, without danger, equate one of these ancient Saints with anyone whom the Pope has recognized in recent centuries through a solemn <term>Canonization</term> <note>The formal process by which the Catholic Church declares a person a saint</note> or through other legitimate means. The piety shown to the Saints is grounded upon their power, which a witness—</insert>

# HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

<margin>...that accompany the miracles of the Saints;</margin>
deeds performed in life, or those proven after death: Thus, miracles are the incontestable witnesses of the holiness of those whom the Pope (a) places among the number of the Saints; since God would not communicate these essential marks of His supreme authority except to those who have excelled through their virtue. In former times, all supernatural effects were called miracles, such as those that arrested the course of nature and resisted the laws by which it was meant to work. These effects were, so to speak, an act of violence committed against nature: since God did not permit them except for extraordinary reasons, such as, for example, the destruction of error and the maintenance of the true religion, etc. As for those miracles which Heathenism formerly used to defend error, these have been placed in the rank of delusions, deceptions, and blindness, of which we shall make no further mention.

<margin>Ideas conceived regarding</margin>
For several centuries, another conception of miracles has been adopted.
<column-break/>
They have become more general, less difficult, and more common than in the times of the early Church. They have ceased to have only religion and truth as their objects: but in compensation for this, one has been able to console oneself by seeing how the laws of nature are overturned to satisfy the request which a Saint makes to God according to his pleasure, or to obtain his particular necessities. Birds (b) have been made to fall silent to listen to the sermons of the Saints, and fish (c) have been made to come out of the water to attend their exhortations. This change of conception, without a word being said, has allowed the Saints to prove their status with less effort than custom used to require. All these changes have necessarily been followed by a great number of miracles, which have not yet ceased, nor shall they cease until the end of the ages. However powerfully the unbelievers may set themselves against this, the faith of pious hearts is never exhausted: it is a spring that shall by no means run dry.

## CHAPTER V.
### What sort of CONCEPTION one has of the POWER of the SAINTS in these RECENT CENTURIES.

IF faith found nothing but reason for its support, it would not be able to exist for long. It must have more perceptible aids than the fruits of the brain, which consume themselves in brooding over the truth of religion. To cut off all reasoning; it requires, so to speak, striking examples that leave one amazed. See how the heart of some religious devotees shall find itself strengthened by the necessity of the miracles of the recent centuries. We have already given some examples of these miracles, to which we (d) shall still add the following.

<margin>A rare miracle by</margin>
St. Raymond of *Peñafort* <note>Spanish Dominican friar and patron saint of canon lawyers</note>, after he had for a long time rebuked the dissolute life of the King of Spain without being able to divert him from his blameworthy practices, decided to leave him on account of his wicked inclinations. He wished then to take ship to return again to Barcelona: but the King forbade him from crossing over to Catalonia; hereupon Raymond renewed the miracle of *Jesus Christ* such that he walked upon the water. He threw his choir-robe <note>original: "koorkleedt," likely referring to the cappa or habit</note> into the sea, and taking his staff in hand, he stepped upon this new vessel and arrived safely at land; whereupon the door of the Monastery opened at the arrival of this Saint.

<margin>Miracles of Francis of Paola.</margin>
St. Francis of Paola was an uncommonly powerful Saint: the likes of whom had not been heard of since Samson. He single-handedly lifted a rock of enormous size that lay in the way of the foundation of a monastery dormitory he was building. He carried on his shoulders what four men would not have been able to move. He held up in the air a piece of a rock that, having broken loose from a mountain, threatened to crush his building along with a portion of the workers. Subsequently, he supported it with his staff and held it up in such a manner for some time in the sight of a multitude of people who came to see this miracle. Thereafter, this rock was used for the completion of the monastery of that Saint: but history does not tell us that any relics were made from it, which is something unusual. <note>The author finds it "unusual" because objects associated with such great miracles were typically broken up and sold or kept as holy relics.</note>

<margin>What occurred regarding Agnes of Monte Pulciano.</margin>
Often, manna was seen falling in the shape of a cross upon the Holy Agnes of Monte Pulciano. On a Feast of the Assumption of Mary, the Holy Virgin appeared to her, holding her child Jesus in her arms, whom she permitted her to embrace and even press against her breast. (a) Upon departing, she left Saint Agnes a cross, which the little Jesus wore around his neck. We shall make no mention of the rose which was presented on a dish by Agnes to two hermits in the middle of winter: but we cannot pass by mentioning what a courtesy she showed after her death to St. Catherine of Siena, who went to visit her grave. When she wished to kiss the feet of the deceased, the latter brought her foot to the mouth of St. Catherine, in order to anticipate her through a polite humility. Nevertheless, St. Catherine did not judge it proper to venture this a second time; for wishing to visit Agnes again, she kissed her head instead of her feet.

<margin>Likewise Bonaventure.</margin>
The Holy Bonaventure, an excellent writer of the *Psalter of Our Lady*, <note>original: "Lieve Vrouws Pfalmboek"</note> (b) being unable to receive Communion in the usual manner due to an uncommon chest disease, placed (c) the Holy Ciborium <note>The vessel used to hold the consecrated bread or "Host".</note> upon his chest, whereupon the Holy Host soon penetrated through to the innermost part of his entrails, in order to allow his soul to attain life.

<column-break/>

<margin>Ignatius.</margin>
St. Ignatius, abandoned by the physicians, was visited by St. Peter, who miraculously healed him by the touch of his sanctified hands. His illness laid the beginning of his rebirth. Subsequently, the Holy Virgin came to visit him and offered him a Heavenly ointment, which one may call the Balm of Chastity, since it withdrew his senses and purified even his soul from all thoughts of fleshly lusts. It is to be suspected that Sts. Ignatius left the power of this Balm to his spiritual children. Father Alegambe tells us extraordinary things of fleshly struggles and victories achieved against the flesh. For Father Gillis, a man of 73 years, could behold no woman unless he took care that his thoughts were withdrawn from such subjects. He mistrusted himself and was therefore averse to it, thanking God that the failing of his eyes served him as a remedy for his senses. Father Costerus declared that he had never felt any disorderly movements, and that his imagination knew nothing that had the power to draw it toward seduction. Father Coton, Confessor to a Prince whose brain very easily received an impression from a moving object, preserved purity in such a way that he even had an aversion for everything which caused the least struggle against this virtue: moreover, he was so fine of smell that he smelled the impurity of those who had violated the rules of chastity. Father Spiga, who died at the age of 74, could not distinguish his nieces from one another, because he had accustomed his eyes never to behold the charming sex: But to return to St. Ignatius; when he went on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, he decided to go visit the Mount of Olives, in which Jesus Christ served him as a guide. He healed the falling sickness, <note>epilepsy</note> delivered the possessed, and many felt a healing power by touching the hem of his garment. Finally, at least two hundred such miracles are told of him.

<margin>*St. Teresa*</margin> *Teresa* appeared to many after her death (a), which was caused by an excessive Divine Love, in order to show them the exalted rank of honor to which she had been snatched away. We shall not mention her wonderful visions, nor the wound of love that a **Seraph** <note>A high-ranking angel often associated with fiery love and light.</note> gave her in the heart with a golden arrow, armed with a fiery iron point.

<margin>*St. Didacus*</margin> *Didacus* <note>Known as San Diego de Alcalá.</note> healed the sick with the oil from the lamp that burned before an image of Our Dear Lady. It once happened that while traveling to a Monastery with one of his companions and being destitute of provisions, he made a fervent prayer to God; whereupon immediately the Table was set for them in the field, and they enjoyed a good meal.

<margin>*St. Francis Xavier*</margin> *Francis Xavier* raised several dead people during his Mission in the East Indies. Having arrived near **Amboina** <note>Ambon Island in modern-day Indonesia.</note>, he stilled the storm by dipping the Crucifix into the sea: in the zeal of this action, the Crucifix slipped from his hand: but a helpful fish <note>The legend usually identifies this "helpful fish" as a crab that returned the lost crucifix to the shore.</note> brought it back to him immediately, and it was noticed, in offering it to the Saint, that it was held upright and raised, to show the triumph of the Cross over the unbelievers.

<margin>*St. Thomas Becket*</margin> *Thomas Becket*, Archbishop of Canterbury, was richly rewarded for the violent death he had suffered through a great number of miracles he performed after his death, and which he still does now, if one may believe Father Giry. Hardly was this Saint buried when he declared himself a Physician of many diseases. He was not satisfied with just healing these ailments: but also raised the dead. From this we can observe that the Saints of the latter centuries, in matters of bringing the dead to life, uncommonly surpass the Saints of the Apostles' century.

This custom is still observed today by the Servants of the Holy Virgin, as
<margin>How goods were formerly sacrificed to the Saints.</margin>
(a) testifies to us. In a more religious age than the one we live in now, a Christian Prince had formerly made his States tributary to some Saint, which happened more often then: but these times have changed. One finds no Sovereign now who conducts himself so piously that he is satisfied to be a subject of the Church. The Saint to whom one yielded the income of his Property obtained by this means Houses, Lands, and rich incomes, which the Monks and Clergy needed to cover their costs for him: but the Christians of our time have become a little cooler on this subject. In the fourteenth century, one finds a formal ceremony for how the Pious person acts when bequeathing his Property to the Church. He took a knife with a handle and a clod of earth, in which a small tree shoot was planted. He offered these three things to the Saint whom he had chosen as his Protector, or rather he offered this to the Monks and Clerical Caretakers of the Saint. The clod of earth represented the Fields and other immovable property, the shoot the fruits of the earth, and the knife with the handle the movable property.

The Saints have their Offices and *Litanies* <note>A form of prayer consisting of a series of petitions or invocations.</note> in the Church. These *Litanies* attribute all due praises to the Saint, and give the faithful an accurate Idea of his power.
<margin>Devotional duties to the chosen</margin>
It is common for the Pious to favor the Saint whom they have

<column-break/>

chosen as Protector above all other Saints of Paradise, and to place him entirely in all their interests, without much prejudice to the other Saints, etc.
<margin>Saints, and how these were shown.</margin>
(b) “They imagine that God has given this Saint particular Privileges, to certainly and infallibly obtain from him all requested favors, whether spiritual or temporal, through his intercession, without concerning themselves much with any repentance to satisfy the Law of God.” This excess of particular piety gives rise to other excesses.

> “Some,” says the Author we quote, “believe that when they dedicate their devotion to St. Barbara—called in many places the *Mother of Confession*—they will never die without having made confession, regardless of how they have lived.
> “Others subject their devotion to St. Christopher, and they imagine, if they look at his image in the morning, that they will not die that day nor the following night — To find again stolen, lost, or scattered things, many Pious people imagine that one has nothing to do but think of St. Anthony of Padua, and say in his honor the eighth *Responsory* (c) of the Matins <note>The early morning service of the Divine Office.</note> of his Feast.”
> “Again, others imagine that by repeating the Little Crown of St. Anne daily for an entire Year, God will infallibly grant them one of the three things they request of him at the end of the Year.”

Let this be enough to give the Reader an Idea of some excesses in the devotion shown to Saints.

# CHAPTER VI.

## On the Manner in Which One Totally SACRIFICES Oneself to the SAINTS.

<margin>How one formerly sacrificed oneself to the Saints.</margin>
In former times (a) one sacrificed oneself to the Saints, which still occurs today in various Roman Catholic lands. One paid (b) a yearly tribute to the Saint whom one chose as a Patron Saint, and the vassal often stood in for himself and for his descendants, or at least for his children. We shall provide here a brief account of a formula, showing how this spiritual obligation was performed in the year 1030.

->IN THE NAME OF THE HOLY TRINITY.<-

<margin>Formula for such a sacrifice.</margin>
> I, *Ghisla*, born in Ghent and orphaned, testify through the example and the admonition of the Saints that humility is the first of all Christian virtues, and have decided to give an example of this humility by sacrificing myself entirely to the service of one of these Saints, so that under their protection and with their help I may share in the Divine Mercy. To that end, I offer both myself and my descendants to St. Gertrude, whom I have chosen for my protectress and for that of my

<column-break/>

-quitoes; and as these were a hindrance to her contemplation, she judged it necessary to enter into a peace with them, which was concluded on this condition: She promised the mosquitoes a residence in her cell during the greatest heat or cold; and the mosquitoes bound themselves not to treat *Rose* poorly anymore, and even to leave her when her presence was too troublesome for her. However, the peace was nearly broken by the imprudence of a clergyman who came to visit *Rose*. This modest account can be read in the beautiful eulogy by *Father Oliva*; but let us not forget to note that the largest trees in the garden bowed their branches and even their trunks when *Rose* went to her cell.

> household, so that through this voluntary servitude we may obtain the forgiveness of our sins; in which trust I bind myself and my descendants to pay yearly on the 17th of April at the High Altar of St. Gertrude the sum of.... And fearing that someone might violate our obligation, we subject ourselves to the sentence of the Ban <note>Excommunication from the Church.</note> proclaimed in the Church of Nivelles against the transgressors of the same, that there befall them what befell Dathan and Abiram <note>original: "Dathan en Abiron"; Biblical figures from the Book of Numbers who were swallowed by the earth for rebelling against Moses.</note>. This signed in the presence of witnesses, Nivelles 1030.

There are other customs of sacrificing oneself or giving oneself over to the service of a Saint, and the signs of this Spiritual Servitude consist of a necklace worn around the neck, or a chain wound around the arm, which is not laid aside except with life itself. Two decrees of the Inquisition <note>original: "Onderzoek des Geloofs" (Investigation of the Faith).</note> in Rome, issued in the year 1673, condemn all the Brotherhoods of the Slavery of the Holy Virgin, and forbid the use of chains, images, and commemorative medals that represent this Slavery, as well as the books that deal with this form of devotion. In a more religious age than the one we now live in, a Christian Prince had formerly made his States tributary to some Saint, which happened more often then: but these times have changed.
