In the fourteenth century, one finds a formal ceremony for how the pious person acts when bequeathing his goods to the Church. He took a knife with a handle and a clump of earth in which a sapling was planted. He offered these three things to the Saint whom he had chosen as his Protector, or rather he offered this to the monks and clerical administrators of the Saint. The clump of earth represented the fields and other immovable property, the sapling represented the fruits of the earth, and the knife with the handle represented the movable property.

The Saints have their Offices and **Litanies** in the Church. These *Litanies* attribute to the Saint all rightful praises and give the faithful a precise idea of his power.

By reducing the perceived excesses found in the Holy Virgin and the Saints, one could also reduce the piety of many people who believe in good faith that everything in Heaven happens just as on Earth, and that one absolutely cannot pass the Saints by before one can come to God. They also imagine that the Saints are proud, headstrong, fickle, and irritable; that access to them is very difficult, and that one must win them over and anticipate their needs. There are no honorable titles that the theologians of the Church, and especially those of the last centuries, have not given to the Blessed Virgin. After taking what was most excellent and magnificent in Paganism to appropriate it for the Mother of the Savior, they have invented even more high-flown names, which the most fertile imaginations of the poets were never able to invent.
<margin>What kind of expressions have been invented in honor of the Holy Virgin.</margin>
The heresies against the Holy Virgin produced gradual effects of respect and devotion for her. In the early times of the Church, she was called *Queen of Angels and Mother of God*; subsequently, due to the disputes that arose on this occasion, her defenders favored everything that could be of any use against heresy, and the pious became accustomed to all sorts of far-fetched expressions, which were natural in polemics. She was regarded as the *Dispenser and Possessor of the Grace of God*; the *Treasurer* and even the *Queen of Heaven*; the *Fountainhead of Salvation*, and of *Life*; the *Door of Paradise*; the *Mother of Light*; the *Mediatrix between God and Men*; the *Hope of the human race*; the *Ocean* (a) of Divinity, etc. Notorious writers treat her as a *Goddess* (b); and at the end of the 16th century it was declared—

We shall conclude with a popular, or rather superstitious, form of worship, which is the custom of magnificently dressing up Our Lady, crowning her on her feast day, and on other solemn days lighting one or more wax candles before her images, and presenting her with flowers and fruits. ## CHAPTER VIII.

->Of the Feasts established in honor of Our Lady.<-

<margin>
When and how Candlemas is celebrated.
</margin>
**W**e shall follow the order in which the Church celebrates these feasts. On the 2nd of February, one celebrates *Candlemas* <note>original: "Vrouwlichtmis," literally "Lady-Light-Mass."</note> or *The Purification*. This feast was formerly called the feast of Saint Simeon and Saint Anna, because these two holy persons met each other in the Temple when the Holy Virgin Mary came there to offer her Son JESUS CHRIST to God. For the same reason, the Greeks called this *The Meeting* <note>original Greek: "Hypapante"</note>, a word which signifies "meeting." Nowadays, this feast is known in the Church only under the name of *Candlemas* or *Lady Day*, and among the people by that of *Chandeleur* <note>The French name for Candlemas, derived from "chandelle" (candle).</note>, which has the same meaning, since a procession is then made around the church with wax candles.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Correspondence of this feast with those of the Romans indicated.
</margin>
This feast (a) corresponds with the *Amburbia* <note>original: "Amburbales"</note> or the processions that the Romans held at the beginning of February, established in honor of the goddess *Februa*, and with the night-walks performed with torches to represent the wandering of Ceres, when this goddess wandered through the land seeking her daughter Proserpina, whom Pluto had abducted. Since these Roman devotions were the true origin of licentiousness, and the Christian Popes wished to untie the snares of pagan superstition, it was required to provide some equivalent to compensate the people for the loss of a ceremony that, in truth, was no longer an act of religion for Christians. The *Lustrations* <note>Rituals of purification.</note> $\dagger$ of the Month

> *...praiseworthy is the love one has for me when my images are adorned with precious ornaments and gemstones, while one is not mindful of the poverty of* JESUS CHRIST. *Before you decorate the churches, clothe* JESUS CHRIST *in his poverty, adorn him in the adorable mystery of his sanctified body, which you keep upon your altars. Do not, like the idolaters, place your trust in my images and likenesses; though they may be miracle-working, they have no power in themselves. It is to God that the miracles must be attributed. Blessed is he who confesses with the Apostle to know nothing but* JESUS CHRIST. *This booklet is provided with many fine approvals, among which is that of the Lord of Choiseul, Bishop of Tournai, who declares it to be very much in accordance with the Spirit of the Church, fit to instruct the simple, etc.*

(a) The institution of this feast is attributed to Pope Gelasius, who lived in the year 492. Others claim it was Pope Vigilius, saying he did nothing but renew it around the middle of the sixth century. According to some writers, Pope Sergius I, who held the Papal See at the end of the seventh century, was the institutor of the procession with wax candles. He changed, says the ancient legend, the custom of the heathens into a better one; namely, that Christians should go around the church with consecrated and burning wax candles in honor of the Mother of God; so that this ceremony remained, but was performed with a different intent.

$*$ [The *Amburbia* were sacrificial feasts performed in procession around the City. These sacrificial feasts were nearly identical to those of the *Ambarvalia*. The word *Amburbium* consists of *Urbs*, a City, and *Ambire*, to go around. Thus they also called them Amburbial Victims <note>original Latin: "Amburbiales Hostiae"</note>, which were led around the walls of Rome or some other city. Lucanus. Festus. The *Ambarvalia* were also processions used in the months of April and July, when the Roman citizens went thrice around the fields with certain sacrificial cattle, whereby they called upon Ceres for the fertility of the land, as well as for the warding off of all harm and storms. Then, for the sacrifice, pigs, sheep, and calves were slaughtered, which offerings were called the *Sacrifice of the pig, sheep, and bull* <note>original Latin: "Suovetaurilia"</note>. Danet. Pitiscus I p. 79.]

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc. OF THE ROMAN CHURCH.

In the month of February, [candles] were consecrated: it was turned into Candlemas <note>original: *Vrouwenlichtmis*, literally "The Lady’s Light Mass," referring to the Feast of the Purification of the Virgin Mary</note>. Out of love for the Holy Virgin, the people carried torches or wax candles, which were previously carried out of love for Februa and Ceres <note>Februa and Ceres were Roman deities; the author suggests the Christian feast replaced pagan Roman processions</note>. It was permitted to mix these pious acts with the pleasures that the Feasts never failed to inspire.

<margin>
Ceremonies of distributing consecrated wax candles, and how.
</margin>
The wax candles (a) for the Feast of Candlemas are blessed with the usual ceremonies. The Bishop (b), or his deputy, distributes them to the most prominent members of the Clergy, then to the most prominent Laymen, Priests, Acolytes, etc., and finally to the principal members of the congregation. It is one of the youngest Canons (c) <note>original: *A Seniore Dignitate* — meaning by the senior dignitary</note> who distributes them to women of rank; but as for the common people, after the distribution of the largest wax candles to the most distinguished of the assembly has taken place, they receive the remaining small ones (d) <note>original: *Aliquis de Capitulo distribuit candelas minutiones populo utriusque Sexus* — "Someone from the Chapter distributes smaller candles to the people of both sexes"</note> from the hand of an ordinary Priest, without distinction of rank or honor.

The Procession (e) is performed, as has already been said, around the Church. The Singers go first, followed by the Censer-bearer, then the wax candle-bearers on either side of the Cross-bearer, and the Clergy follow the candle-bearers. Those walking on the left side hold their candles in their *left* hand, and those on the right side in their right hand. The Bishop appears here between two Assistant Deacons, holding the wax candle in his left hand and giving the Blessing to his people with his right. All of them carry burning wax candles, and the reason given for this is that they (f) represent JESUS CHRIST, who is the light of the nations. "Before they depart, they bow "their knees before the Altar or bow toward

<column-break/>

"it, if they are Canons and when there is no Tabernacle." This is shown more fully in the Illustration of the Ceremonies of the Lady’s Day <note>referring to Mary</note>, on the Plate depicting those of Easter.

<margin>
When the Feasts of the Annunciation and the Visitation of Elizabeth are celebrated.
</margin>
On the 25th of March, the Feast of the Annunciation <note>original: *Maria-boodschap*</note> is celebrated. The origin of this feast is placed before the third century.
On the 2nd of July, the Visitation of Elizabeth by Mary <note>original: *Mariäs bezoeking*</note> is celebrated. St. Bonaventure, Minister General of the Order of Friars Minor, introduced this within his Order in the year 1263. Pope Urban VI issued a Bull in the year 1389 by which he recommended this Feast to the entire Church. The Council of Basel confirmed this Feast and fixed the day on the second of July. St. Francis de Sales and Mother Jeanne de Chantal established an Order of Clergy <note>The Visitation Sisters</note> in memory of this Visitation of Mary.

<margin>
Likewise those of Our Lady of Carmel and of the Snow; from what origin these feast celebrations arose.
</margin>
Our Lady of Mount Carmel is celebrated on the 16th of July. This Feast particularly concerns those who hold a devotion to the *Scapular* †.
The Feast of Our Lady of the Snows is celebrated on the 5th of August. We are assured that a miracle caused this celebration. Under (g) the Papacy of Liberius, there was a Son of a Counselor, one of those called *Patricians* ‡, or a Roman Nobleman, who, having grown old and seeing himself without children, decided with the mutual consent of his Wife to name the Holy Virgin as their sole and general heir to all their property. The vow was then performed with great piety, and in such a manner as might be most pleasing and acceptable to Our Lady. Now, to know what her desire might be regarding the use of her inheritance,

[The couple] fasted, prayed, supported the poor, and visited the sick. Finally, the Holy Virgin appeared to both of them in a dream, declaring: "that it was her Son’s desire as well as her own, that they use these goods to build him a Church on a certain place on the Esquiline Hill * <note>original: *Esquilinus*</note> which they would find covered with snow." The pious man revealed his dream to his wife, who likewise declared that she had had a similar dream on that same night: but even though both their dreams had not turned out exactly the same, their zeal was powerful enough to inspire in them all the required agreements. Both these pious people declared their dreams to the Pope, who had received the same revelation. It was then no longer doubted (a) that this was a Heavenly command. The Pope gathered the Clergy; to confirm the miracle, they went in Procession to the Esquiline Hill, and there they found the place indicated in the dream covered with snow. The area was of the exact size needed to build a Church. This Church (b) is the one subsequently called the *Head Church of Liberius* and the *Holy Mary at the Manger* <note>original: *H. Maria ad praesepe*</note>, named for the crib that served as the Savior’s cradle and was brought there from Bethlehem; it is currently known by the name of *St. Mary Major* <note>original: *St. Maria Maggiora*</note>. On the Day of the Feast of *Our Lady of the Snows*, this miracle is renewed in this Church in remembrance, by artistically letting the petals of white jasmine fall, mimicking how snow falls upon the earth.

<margin>When the Assumption of Mary and the Feast of her birth are celebrated;</margin>
On August 15th, the Assumption of Mary is celebrated; but it is not likely that this Feast was established before the sixth century. Before this time, there had yet been no revelation concerning the bodily Assumption of the Holy Virgin.

The birth of Our Lady is celebrated on September 8th. This Feast first became known after the eleventh century. It was in the twelfth century that Pope Innocent IV established it universally.

<margin>Likewise that of the Rosary,</margin>
On October 7th, the solemnity of the Rosary is dedicated. We shall speak of it when we deal with the Rosary.

<column-break/>

<margin>The Presentation of Mary,</margin>
*P. Giry* assures us (c) that "from the moment the Holy Virgin came into the world, she offered herself to God as an everlasting Servant. The sacrifice of her heart and soul was even older than her birth. It occurred in her Mother’s womb." Nevertheless, it is not this secret Presentation <note>original: *Inwying*, referring to the Presentation of Mary in the Temple</note> that the Church celebrates on November 21st; it is the dedication of the Holy Virgin to God by her parents Joachim and Anna. This Feast originates from the East, and they began to introduce it into Europe at the end of the fourteenth century.

<margin>and her Conception.</margin>
The *Conception of Our Lady* is celebrated by the Church on December 8th. This Conception is called *immaculate*, since it is believed that the Holy Virgin was conceived without sin. The Feast of the Conception was introduced earlier among the Greeks than among the Latins. It first became known in Europe at the beginning of the twelfth century. A Bull from Sixtus IV, who had been a Franciscan monk and consequently a defender of the Immaculate Conception, confirmed this Feast in the fifteenth century.

<margin>As also that of her Expectation,</margin>
On December 18th, the Feast of Our Lady of *O*, or the Expectation of the Holy Virgin <note>original: *Kraambedt*, literally "childbed"</note>, is celebrated. It was established in Spain under the Papacy of Vitalian, in the middle of the seventh century. It was also called the Feast of the *Expectation of the Birth* of our Savior. The name of Our Lady of *O* comes from the *Antiphons* <note>The "Great O Antiphons" sung at Advent</note> called the *O*s, because the exclamation *O!* is frequently repeated in them. Through these Antiphons, the Church requests that Eternal Wisdom descend to earth.

<margin>The Pregnancy.</margin>
In Italy and Spain, nine days are set aside before the Expectation of the Birth, in memory of the nine months of the Holy Virgin’s pregnancy. During this time (d), the Altar is decorated in the most appropriate manner, and the Statue of Our Lady is placed upon it.

<margin>and the Betrothal.</margin>
Formerly, the Feast of Our Lady’s Betrothal <note>original: *ondertrouw*</note> was celebrated. It is believed that it was established in France in the year 1532, and that the celebration was fixed for January 12th.

In Rome, a Feast called *St. Mary of the Martyrs* is celebrated on May 13th.

RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc., of the ROMAN CHURCH.

## IX. CHAPTER.

### *On the famous PLACES distinguished by service to OUR BLESSED LADY, or made famous by her MIRACLES; RELICS of the HOLY VIRGIN and in what they consist.*

<margin>Explaining how the Chapels of Our Lady were built and why: such as at Zaragoza,</margin>
It is claimed that the Apostle Peter (a) himself dedicated a chapel to the Mother of God: but we have reason to doubt this. The Spaniards say that the Holy Virgin appeared to St. James <note>original: "St. Jacob"</note> at Zaragoza, and that after this apparition, the Apostle had a chapel built for her, which was subsequently named *Our Lady of the Pillar* <note>original: "Nuestra Sennora del Pilar"</note>. Some chroniclers suggest (b) that angels were the architects of this chapel. The Holy Virgin, magnificently adorned, stands there atop a marble pillar, holding the Child Jesus in her arms. Several silver angels surround her with torches in their hands, not to mention the fifty silver lamps and a great number of candlesticks of the same metal that shine day and night. The walls of this sacred place are hung with tapestries (c) depicting hands, feet, arms, hearts, etc., which the faithful have offered to the Holy Virgin in recognition of the miraculous healings she has performed upon those parts of the body.

<margin>Madrid,</margin>
Our Lady of *Atocha* is illuminated in a chapel in Madrid (d) by a hundred gold and silver lamps. She performs no fewer miracles there than at Zaragoza, Loreto <note>original: "Lorette"</note>, etc. This Our Lady of *Atocha* is usually dressed as a widow and holds her Rosary <note>original: "Paternoster"</note> in her hand: but despite this pious attire, she is nonetheless crowned with a Sun, and on solemn Feast Days, she displays herself in a Queen’s robes, with all her adornments decorated with precious stones.

<margin>and in Picardy.</margin>
For five or six hundred years, Our Lady has established herself at Liesse in Picardy. It was during the time of the Crusades that an Egyptian Princess,

<column-break/>

having heard of the Miracles of the Holy Virgin, requested an image of her: for this reason, she approached three noblemen from Picardy who were held prisoner in Cairo. None of them could paint, yet one of these noblemen presumed to undertake the painting of the Image. After he had labored in vain to fulfill his promise through the help of an art he did not understand, he turned to the Holy Virgin. His two companions joined their prayers to his, after which they fell asleep. Having woken up again, they found a beautiful Image of Our Lady, which they sent to the Princess. In recognition of the gift, she secured the release of these three prisoners. We intentionally pass over the rest of this history: it is enough for the reader to know that the Princess was converted to Christianity by means of this Image, and that the noblemen who had obtained this from Heaven through their prayers found themselves miraculously delivered from their prison in Egypt, and that as a result of the same miracle, they immediately found themselves in Picardy, at the place where the Church of Our Lady of Liesse was built.

<margin>How Our Lady of Neuburg became famous through Marco d'Aviano.</margin>
Our Lady of Neuburg <note>original: "Nieuburg"</note> would have remained forever unknown if the piety of the Capuchin <note>term: Capuchin; a reform branch of the Franciscan order known for their brown robes and long pointed hoods</note>, Father Marco d'Aviano <note>original: "Marcus de Aviano"</note>, had not lured the religious there. This pious monk took it very poorly to see that this Our Lady had been so entirely forgotten for a period of 40 years, which moved him to take the interests of the miracle-working statue to heart; of which many elderly pious folk became eyewitnesses, which was not surprising.

Likewise those of the Mount of *Guardia*, which have become no less famous, and various others, notorious for miracles.

Our Lady of the Mount of *Guardia*, situated about five miles from Bologna <note>original: "Boulonje"</note>, needs not yield to the previous ones. Her image being the work of St. Luke, it is carried in procession through the city of Bologna for three consecutive days every year.

In the continuation of this Treatise, we shall find occasion to speak of *Our Lady of Loreto*: but for now, we shall content ourselves with naming only Our Lady of Mount Montserrat in Catalonia, and those of *Halle* and *Aspermont* in Flanders and Brabant; likewise that of Mercy in Naples, of Healing in Gascony, etc. The miracles performed by her in all these places are almost innumerable. No less difficult is it to name her images (a). As a result of the miracles these have worked, the devout must take care of her images; her statues are decorated with flowers, dressed in silk or some other costly fabric; wax candles are lit before them, they are kissed and viewed with a loving countenance, rosaries <note>original: "Paternosters"</note> and handkerchiefs are rubbed against them, etc., and they are greeted with all respect.

<margin>
Which Relics of her are preserved in various places,
</margin>
It now remains to mention the *Relics* of Our Lady. One is provided with almost all of her head-hair. As for her milk, we are assured that not a drop of it was ever lost,

<column-break/>

<margin>
and in what they consist.
</margin>
and that immediately after the Savior’s birth, *Relics* were made from it. One finds them in many places throughout Christendom. The wedding ring of Our Lady is carefully preserved in Perugia <note>original: "Perusa"</note>. The miracles of this Ring are described in a book (b), printed at the beginning of the seventeenth century. The clothes of the Holy Virgin are shown in Rome and other places; her shifts at Chartres and Aachen <note>original: "Aken"</note>; one of her head-coverings at Trier; her belts at Our Lady of Montserrat, at Prato, etc. One of her combs at Rome, another at Besançon; her shoes at Our Lady of Le Puy and at St. Flour, and one of her slippers in Brittany. Her foot-measure (c) is in the hands of the Spaniards. To put it in a word, one must not doubt that all the kitchen utensils, her table linens, and household ornaments have been carefully preserved. One also finds her gloves, caps, veils, her bed, the chair, the stones upon which she washed the Savior's diapers; her candlesticks, the lamp oil, and her earthenware vessels. It is true that these things were lost and went missing for several centuries: but the monks have had the kindness to find them all again little by little. No relics (d) of her body are to be found, since she ascended into Heaven, as we have already said.

# CHAPTER X.

### On the PREPARATION for the celebration of the JUBILEE YEAR, and with what CEREMONIES this is accompanied.

---

<margin>
The origin of the Jubilee festival indicated, and to what it may be compared.
</margin>
The Jubilee festival is of a Jewish and Heathen origin. Among the Jews, freedom was proclaimed to slaves, the needy were relieved of their debts, and property was returned to those who had been forced by necessity to pawn it. Even the fields were left fallow during the Jewish Jubilee year. Through the Christian Jubilee year—of which the first was but the image—the Pope granted similar privileges to Christian souls. It was for them a year of rest. The Holy Father forgave sins, met the spiritual poverty of the penitent by opening to him (e) the treasury of Divine mercy, forgiving him his debts and sharing heavenly goods. On the other hand, it seems that the Jubilee year is a framework in imitation of the Secular Games of the Romans, and that, in order to the <meta>catchword: the</meta>

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc., OF THE ROMAN CHURCH

<margin>Who was the first Founder of the Roman Jubilee Year.</margin>
To lead the Christian people away from this heathen ceremony <note>original: "Heidensihe Plichrighrit"</note>, Pope Boniface VIII wished to introduce a better one, accompanied by many praiseworthy and godly actions.

Pope Boniface was then the first who (a) established this great Jubilee Year, expressly declaring with his Bull that those who in the year 1300, and every hundred years thereafter, visited the Head-Churches of St. Peter and Paul, after having confessed their sins with sincere repentance, would obtain a full forgiveness and indulgence <note>A grant by the Pope intended to remit the temporal punishment for sins.</note>, extending as far as possible to relieve repentant sinners. It did not seem, says Mr. *Turrin*, (b) that this Pope had the slightest regard for the Jewish Jubilee, since he not only gave the name of Jubilee to his institution, but on the contrary, doubled the time prescribed to the Jews. Pope Clement VI did likewise; he called the institution the Jubilee Year and ordered that it should be celebrated every fifty years.

<margin>The Jubilee Year in accordance with the Secular Games of the Romans.</margin>
Several Roman-minded writers have found a correspondence between the Jubilee Year of the Christians and the Secular Games <term>Secular Games: Known as *Ludi Saeculares*, these were ancient Roman celebrations involving sacrifices and performances, theoretically held once every century (a *saeculum*).</term> of the ancient Romans. We shall quote two (c) passages on this subject, without however seeking to oppose the solemnity of the Jubilee festival. The evil consists not in the correspondence found between an introduced practice of a false religion and this practice being adopted by the true religion: but in the abuse and superstition, in which the goals of interest and ambition infallibly take the lead.

Onuphrius <note>Onuphrio Panvinio (1530–1568), an Augustinian friar and historian.</note> explicitly compares the Jubilee festival to the Secular Games. "They worked there," he says, "for the erasure of sins in Rome; they converted and promised a better life. Our Jubilee festival grants us a general forgiveness of our

<column-break/>

duties of sins." Mr. *Turrin* provides us in his Treatise with a precise comparison of these two particular ceremonies. We shall quote his words here: "One must seek both the one and the other in Rome. The Secular Games were solemnly proclaimed, just as the Jubilee Year is now proclaimed by Bulls sent to all Christian peoples. In the Secular Games, one visited the Temples of two great heathen deities, just as one now visits the Churches of St. Peter and Paul, of St. John Lateran, and St. Mary Major during the Jubilee festival. The Erasures and *Lustrations* <term>Lustrations: Ritual purifications used in ancient Rome to cleanse individuals or the state from pollution or bad luck.</term> of the Secular Games were seen as necessary to obtain the forgiveness of sins; to appease the Gods and ward off their punishments! The subject of the Jubilee festival is to erase sin, etc. The offerings that the people made during the ceremony of the Secular Games can be seen to some extent as a sufficient value for the money which is offered for the Indulgences. Formerly the Emperor, as absolute High Priest <note>original: "Opperpriefter," referring to the title *Pontifex Maximus*.</note>, was the first moving cause and the Head of the Ceremony; just as the Pope is now! Some commemorative medals <note>original: "Gedenkpenningen"</note> show us the Emperor of the Romans, as the Director of the Secular Games, knocking with a rod at the door of a Temple; the Pope likewise uses his hammer: after which the sacred gates open for the one as well as the other. The solemnity of the heathen ceremony was accompanied by hymns of praise, just as those of the Jubilee festival are now likewise accompanied. Finally, the Emperors often changed the designated time to celebrate the Secular Games (d). Augustus did not wait that—

<margin>How the Jubilee Year has been changed four times.</margin>
the hundred years had passed, and Emperor Claudius celebrated his own <note>The author is likely referring to the Roman Secular Games, which Emperor Claudius held in 47 AD, disregarding the traditional 100-year interval.</note> after about seventy years. In the 12th [century?], the Feast was celebrated nine years thereafter, and subsequently, a Bull from Sixtus IV determined the period to be twenty-five years. His predecessor, Paul II, had determined it for the same timeframe through a decree in the year 1470. Nevertheless, Sixtus IV celebrated a Jubilee feast in the year 1475; and Pope Alexander VI, not satisfied with having celebrated it in the year 1498, renewed it again in the year 1500.

The Decrees of Paul II and Sixtus IV do not prevent the Popes from proclaiming a general Jubilee feast in the year of their elevation to the Papacy, and even upon certain unusual occasions. Nevertheless, one never opens the **Holy Doors** except for the twenty-five-year Jubilee, which, if one may say so, brings with it a general Indulgence, (a) *which refreshes the hearts of the Faithful and leads them into the Hall of Joy of the Lord.*

The Jubilee year grants the power to the Confessors, authorized by their Cloister Superior, to absolve all suspended cases, exclusions, and great Excommunications; to revoke the suspensions of Offices and Ecclesiastical services, and to lift prohibitions. It also allows them to commute vows, provided they do not concern religion, nor chastity, nor the nature of those vows by which one binds oneself to certain pilgrimages, such as those of Rome, Jerusalem, and St. James in Galicia <note>The famous pilgrimage site of Santiago de Compostela.</note>.

<margin>Jubilee Year announced.</margin>
and has [decreed it], he gives notice thereof to all the usual Prelates of Christendom, and such by those means which are by them in their Dioceses proclaimed, along with the required exhortations, so that the faithful Father—the Churches that must be visited are designated; certain rules of piety are prescribed which are always accompanied by proper Indulgences, and a manual of *Litanies* and prayers is printed, appropriate for the solemnity of the Jubilee feast and the subject it promotes. No Brotherhoods, nor Religious Orders, may excuse themselves from the ordained Processions or neglect the celebration of this devotion. The people, the Authorities, and other leaders of the people are requested to attend the same with all humility, which is proper to an act of religion. On the designated Fasting and Penance days, it is commanded to the Bishop and his Clergy to demonstrate an inner solemnity and perfect humility. They must pray to God with heart and mouth, to show them the fruits of their upright religious exercises, and to forsake all inclinations toward sin, as well as to perform a proper prayer, and to take a firm resolution to live in peace with God.

## HISTORICAL TREATISE

<columns>2</columns>

...him with wax tapers in his hand, and the Holy Father, knocking three times upon the Gate <margin>* *Open for me the gates of righteousness* <note>original: "Aperite mihi portas justitiae"</note>; that is: Open for me the Gates of Justice, and the Choir adds these words: here is the Gate of Eternity, righteousness shall dwell there, etc.</margin> says with a loud voice: *Open for me the gates of righteousness* <note>original: "Aperite mihi portas justitiae"</note>, that is: *Open for me the Gates of Justice*, and the Choir adds these words: *here is the Gate of Eternity, righteousness shall dwell there*, etc. (a) Meanwhile, the Master Masons break down the wall that closes the Holy Gate, and the debris is shared among the devout, who create a great throng to obtain a piece of it and preserve it as the most precious *Relics*. They imagine that these pieces possess a hidden power, and that something Divine always accompanies them and everything else used in the ceremonies of Religion. While the broken-down wall is being cleared away, the Pope seats himself again upon his Throne.

After the wall has been demolished, the Confessors of St. Peter <note>These are the "Penitentiaries," priests authorized to hear confessions and grant absolutes for specific sins</note> come with their brooms to sweep out the gate, removing the remaining rubble and mortar, which are not viewed as lowly materials, since one

<column-break/>

makes *Relics* of them, and they wash the foliage-work and the entire perimeter of the Gate with Holy Water. After this performance, the Holy Father descends from his Throne, beginning the *Antiphon*: *This is the day the Lord has made* <note>original: "Haec dies quam fecit Dominus"</note>, etc., which the Choir continues to sing. Having arrived before the Holy Door, the Pope says several prayers, takes up the Cross, and kneels before the Gate; he begins the *Te Deum* <note>A traditional hymn of praise: "Thee, O God, we praise"</note>, and standing up, he passes through this Holy Gate, followed by his Clergy. Everyone then proceeds into the Church to see this magnificent Church ceremony, or to attend the *Vespers* <note>Evening prayers</note> of the Papal Chapel. After the conclusion of the *Vespers*, the Cardinals take off their white ceremonial robes and dress themselves again in their red garments, accompany the Pope to the door of his chambers, and then depart. On Christmas Day, after the Mass is finished, the Holy Father goes to the place of *Blessing* and blesses the faithful according to the custom of the Jubilee Year.

*to earn. Likewise, it is prescribed to the Romans to visit them thirty times. Christians who are fearful of being unable to fulfill the difficulty of such a heavy and burdensome piety nevertheless enjoy the same Indulgence <note>A remission of temporal punishment for sins</note>. One must cover twelve miles to visit the four Churches only once a day: Therefore, the believer who wishes to be precise in his devotion must reckon that, for the love of God, he piously visits these places during the Jubilee feast. There are small prayer books, arranged by order of the Pope, to guide the devotion of the faithful Pilgrim, serving for the Churches he is commanded to visit: and if he should happen to die before he has completed all his visits, there is a promise contained in the Bull of the Jubilee <note>An official papal decree</note> that favors the intention of this pious person and places him in possession of all the associated advantages of the Indulgence.

<margin>How piously one visits the Holy Stairs, and of what origin this may be.</margin>
There is another meritorious devotion, which is to climb the *Holy Stairs* <note>original: "Heilige Trappen" or Scala Sancta</note> on one’s knees; this is the name given to the twenty-eight steps by which it is said that JESUS CHRIST ascended to Pilate or to Caiaphas. It is even asserted that a small copper grate covers a drop of the Savior’s blood. It is added that we owe the preservation of the Holy Stairs to Helena, the mother of Emperor Constantine the Great. Having reached the top of the Holy Stairs, the Pilgrim must offer a short prayer before he enters the Holy of Holies. As for the women, they are not permitted to enter; nevertheless, they gain the Indulgence by viewing this chapel through an iron grate. All these pious treatments provide the Pilgrims with a complete forgiveness of their sins, and the Confessors affix the seal to this forgiveness by touching them with their rods <note>A ritual gesture where a priest taps a penitent with a wand to signify absolution</note>. The Prelates and Roman

<column-break/>

Barons come in penitential robes to wash their <insert>the pilgrims'</insert> feet; the Pope, clothed in the robes of his dignity, and the Cardinals serve them at the table. After which the Holy Father presents them with *Paternosters* <note>original: "Paternosters"; rosary beads used for reciting the Lord's Prayer</note>, Holy Medallions, and *Agnus Dei* <note>original: "Agnus Dei"; wax discs blessed by the Pope, often depicting the "Lamb of God"</note>, allowing them to kiss his foot. †

<margin>Ceremonies that accompany the closing of the Holy Door, noted.</margin>
The Jubilee Year ends with the closing of the Holy Doors. They are closed on the day before Christmas, being one year after they were opened. The Pope and his Cardinals, along with the Clergy and the most prominent personages of the Roman Court, proceed in ceremonial robes to St. Peter’s. *Vespers* <note>Evening prayers</note> are said there; after which the Clergy, with wax candles in hand, show their homage to the Holy Face, known under the name of Veronica. Then the Pope begins the *Antiphon* <note>A short sentence sung or recited before or after a psalm</note>, which starts with the words: *presented with joy* <note>original: "cum jucunditate exhibitis"</note>, "you shall depart with joy." As soon as the *Antiphon* has begun, everyone hastens to pass through the Holy Door. The Holy Father approaches the Door after everyone has passed through, and turning toward them, he says: *Our help* <note>original: "Adjutorium"</note> etc. *is in the name of the Lord*, along with some prayers with which he blesses the stones and the mortar, prepared to *close* the Door that was opened for the Jubilee Year. His Holiness himself lays the first stone ‡ to this structure, and under this stone are placed several commemorative medals, which serve to preserve the memory of this pious ceremony for posterity.

After this stone is laid, the Holy Father washes his hands and returns to his Throne, at which time they sing <gloss>(a)</gloss> *Save thy people* <note>original: "Salvum fac populum"</note> etc. While the masons wall up the Door, in the middle of which a copper Cross is fastened, the Pope says several prayers, with which he continues until the opening is closed. # CHAPTER XIII.
## *Of the INSTITUTION and USE of INDULGENCES*

---

<margin>Origin of Indulgences indicated.</margin>
Observe here the stumbling block which the Holy Father uses to test the faith of the believers. Many of the pious imagine that Indulgences <note>A remission of temporal punishment for sin</note> ensure the conquest of Paradise. It appears that the origin of these means—however beneficial the institution may once have been, though it has since degenerated into an abuse—is pointed out in a passage (a) by Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258), an early Christian bishop and writer</note>: but however that may be, the softening of punishment was not associated with the name "Indulgence" until long afterward. In the seventh and eighth centuries, it was very common. In the year 884, Pope Sergius granted three forty-day Indulgences at once to those who (b) visited the Church of St. Martin of the Mountains on the day of his Feast.

<margin>and what they have reportedly achieved.</margin>
If one attributes to the Indulgence (c) *a forgiveness of temporal punishments, which active sinners must atone for*, it will be easy to understand that access to Heaven is no more free to the pious who have earned them, unless
<column-break/>
they are made more worthy by the effects of virtue. Nevertheless, no one is ignorant of the actual power attributed to Indulgences, nor the significant services they have rendered to greed, false zeal, and pride. One must not think, however, because we express ourselves thus, that we intend to diminish the advantages of Indulgences. We are not unaware of the miracles performed by St. Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a major leader in the reform of Benedictine monasticism</note> when, preaching the Indulgences of Pope Eugenius III, (d) he simultaneously inclined men's minds toward war and awakened the spirit of repentance in the hearts of the faithful of his time, showing them the erasure of their crimes and the forgiveness of their sins, tied to the Cross and the sword, with which he encouraged them to arm themselves against the infidels. We are also not ignorant of how St. Bridget declares in her Revelations, and the vision she had of JESUS CHRIST, who informed her "that the shortest means to..."

One can add to this that there is no more suitable City than this for the religious who wish to arrange their piety according to this subject, for these its Main Churches provide daily perpetual Indulgences, which are also doubled on solemn Feasts.

<margin>
*The abuse of Indulgences demonstrated,*
</margin>

Mr. *Thiers* <note>Jean-Baptiste Thiers (1636–1703), a French theologian known for criticizing ecclesiastical abuses</note> has expanded on the abuse of Indulgences: we shall here present his words on this matter in a more abbreviated manner, as he expresses himself in his Book (a). It is not necessary, according to his thoughts, that we speak of the well-known false or fabricated Indulgences; nor of those that are beyond the power of those who grant them; those given without a just and reasonable cause; those that are very abundant and too great in excessive number; those that do not flow from the Holy See, nor from Bishops who have the power to grant them; those presented to the faithful after they have been revoked, or after their time has expired; those given on false declarations, on false deeds, on particular visions, and on Bulls of mere authority, or on Bulls that contain matters contradictory to the doctrine of the Church. For example: *that certain persons shall be released from punishment and guilt <note>original: "straf en schult" / Latin: "a poena et a culpa"</note> (which is even beyond the power of the Popes) if they are found to belong to a certain Religious Order, to a certain Brotherhood, or if they wear a certain garment or instrument of piety.* All these Indulgences are useless, as they are found to be defective. Such are also those that pass to some extent, yet are of no better value, such as those granted for a hundred years, two hundred years, yes a thousand years etc.; which the Cardinals give for more than a hundred days, and the Bishops for forty. Finally, it is required that the cause, or to say better, the works that one must do to earn the Indulgences, have some proportionality with them. This proportionality is not found in many low-value exercises of piety, such as praying a *Paternoster* <note>The Lord's Prayer</note>, an *Ave Maria* <note>The Hail Mary</note> or some prayer at a certain hour;

<column-break/>

the carrying of a Memorial Medal, an image, and a Rosary or *Paternoster* <term>prayer beads used to count devotions</term>, a Cross, or some blessed Grain; the kissing of these objects of piety; the looking upon them with a penitent eye, accompanied by some sighs, which one is able to produce at regular times when one is accustomed to behold these sacred things—after which the religious nonetheless pride themselves that they may equal the greatest Saints of the Church. They flatter themselves that visiting a Church, a Chapel, an Altar, and attending Masses gives them the same right.

<margin>
and how one must earn them presented.
</margin>

Mr. *Thiers* gives us in the same place a short account of exercises brought into use to earn Indulgences, given for the deliverance of souls from Purgatory. See how he expresses himself:
"They have," he says, "become so abundant since about a century and a half, that one may not trust them too much, unless one examines and purifies them well. The application consists in reading prayers, or in visiting Churches, Chapels, or Altars; saying, having said, or hearing Masses; attending certain Church services and Processions; confessing and going to Communion; giving alms or wearing certain garments, Crosses, *Paternoster*, Crowns <note>A chaplet or circular prayer string</note>, blessed Grain etc."
Roman Catholics have much regard for the privileged Altars, (b) of which there was no talk in the Church except since the decree of the Council of Trent. This decree, which was taken there, is fatal for some souls; and consists of this: *Every time one performs a Requiem Mass for the Soul of a deceased person at such an Altar, one shall acquire an Indulgence, by virtue of which Indulgence this soul shall be delivered from Purgatory or freed from its punishment.* Mr. *Thiers* says, not without reason, that the Pope, for the refreshment of all Souls, should have privileged all Altars. Is it, for example, just that a person's soul, whose virtue possessed nothing praiseworthy in the World, enjoys relief much sooner than that of a perfect Pious person, simply if one offers JESUS CHRIST <note>referring to the Eucharist</note> for her at a privileged Altar?

# CHAPTER XIII.

## On the INSTITUTION and USE of INDULGENCES

<margin>Origin of Indulgences indicated.</margin>
Behold here the stumbling block <note>The author uses "steen des aanstoots" (stumbling block) to describe how Indulgences—payments or actions to reduce punishment for sins—became a point of intense theological conflict.</note>, which the Holy Father uses to test the faith of the believers. Very many Pious souls imagine that Indulgences ensure the conquest of Paradise. It appears that the origin of these means—however wholesome their Institution may once have been, though it has since degenerated into an abuse—is pointed out in a passage (a) by Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), an early Christian bishop and writer.</note>: but however it may be, the mitigation of punishment was not associated with the name "Indulgence" until long after. In the seventh and eighth centuries, it was very common. In the Year 884, Pope Sergius granted three forty-day Indulgences at once to those who (b) visited the Church of St. Martin of the Mountains on the day of his Feast.

<margin>and what they subsequently brought about.</margin>
If one attributes to the Indulgence (c) *a forgiveness of temporal punishments, which actual sinners must atone for*, it will be easy to understand that access to Heaven is no more free for the Pious who have won them, unless they are

<column-break/>

made worthier through the effects of virtue. Nevertheless, no one is ignorant of the actual power attributed to Indulgences, nor of the considerable service they have rendered to greed, false zeal, and pride. Yet one must not think, because we express ourselves thus, that we intend to curtail the benefits of Indulgences. We are not unaware of the Miracles performed by St. Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a key figure in the Cistercian order who preached for the Second Crusade.</note> when he preached the Indulgences of Pope Eugenius III, (d) simultaneously inclining minds toward War and awakening the Spirit of repentance in the hearts of the believers of his time, showing them the blotting out of their crimes and the forgiveness of their sins, tied to the Cross and the sword, whereby he encouraged them to arm themselves against the infidels. # XIV. CHAPTER.

### Concerning various PIOUS TOOLS; and SOCIETIES OF PIETY instituted.

---

<margin>Who was the first Introducer of the use of Paternosters.</margin>**W**e have already described the *Agnus Dei* <note>original: "Lamb of God"; a wax disc blessed by the Pope.</note> and how they are made. It now requires that we speak here of the *Paternosters* <note>Prayer beads used to count repetitions of the "Our Father" (Pater Noster).</note>. The Historians of the wars commonly called the Crusades say that Peter the Hermit was the first who taught the Crusaders to pray by counting, and that for this purpose he invented a tool, which was called a *Paternoster*, and the use of which soon became very common. St. Dominic, the

<column-break/>

Founder of the Order named after him and of the Holy Office of the *Inquisition* <note>The ecclesiastical tribunal established to suppress heresy.</note>, gained much luster from this Pious Tool, spreading the word that the Holy Virgin had brought him one from Heaven, being a spiritual composition of a certain number of beads, which he called the *Rosary* <note>original: "Rozekrans" (Rose-wreath).</note>. The people received this with much respect and zeal; and it is still one of the most religious exercises of piety among the great-

(a) It is unnecessary to seek proof of this here prior to the Papacy of Leo X. We offer Maimburg <note>Louis Maimbourg (1610–1686), a Jesuit historian.</note> as our guarantee for it. "See what he says of it in his *History of Lutheranism*. Leo X, elevated to the dignity of the Head of the Church at the age of 37, displayed all the perfections of a great Prince and no less of an eminent Pope; but having undertaken to complete the magnificent building of St. Peter's Church ----- he took recourse, following the example of Pope Julius, to Indulgences, which he had proclaimed everywhere, with permission to eat eggs and cheese during Lent and to choose a Confessor for those who contributed what was requested for the construction of St. Peter's Church. One must confess in good faith (and we confess it with some exception according to Maimburg) that the Popes who have since occupied the Chair have been much more regular in the distribution of these treasures, and that certain things were done then which one would not do now, and which were also hateful, especially in Germany, because of the Indulgences of Leo --------- There are Writers who assure us that these Indulgences were to some extent sold in lots, and to have quick ready money, everything that could be drawn from them was farmed out to those who gave the most, and who subsequently were not only reimbursed; but enriched themselves with such a shameful trade, through chosen Indulgence-Preachers and Treasurers whom they believed to be the most capable, and finding themselves well satisfied, whereby the people, to obtain forgiveness, put forward everything that these greedy and sacrilegious Tax-farmers desired to enjoy ----- it is certain that these Treasurers, who were appointed at the same time as the Indulgence for the Crusades began to be proclaimed under Urban II, have since this time quietly acquitted themselves of it, being overcome by their greed -----" *Truly an estimate was made to stem the course of such a shameful trade: but Maimburg adds*, "notwithstanding this precaution, great abuses crept into the proclamation of these Indulgences of Leo --- Some of the Indulgence-Preachers raised the price and value so much that they gave the people cause to believe that one was assured of his salvation, and that Souls were released from Purgatory as soon as money had been advanced, which was demanded for the letters certifying that one had earned the Indulgence. ----- One saw the Deputies of these Tax-farmers, who had leased the profit of these Indulgences, daily making good cheer in Taverns and Inns, and squandering in all kinds of pleasures a portion of this money, which the needy said was violently robbed from them, etc."
(b) See the Book *Tax of the Chancery* <note>original: *Taxe de la Chancellerie*.</note> etc.
(c) Likewise, Indulgences brought in incalculable profits in the Old and New World; for a great trade was driven in Bulls <note>Official papal edicts.</note> which the Pope of Rome sent to the Indies; it was believed then that the Apostolic Court distributed nothing out of love; and this was the more unreasonable, "since there were children of good families who, as Coreal <note>Francisco Coreal, purported author of a travelogue to the West Indies.</note> Vol. I of his *Voyages to the West Indies* p. 81 says to us, could hardly find themselves provided with two Reals <note>Spanish silver coins.</note> or Pieces of Eight, although many of them had been very rich. The Spaniards forced their people to buy them." Was it greed that carried this out, or concern for the salvation of the poor Indians? If the Bull worked upon the hearts of these Indians—which much more naturally should have happened through teaching supported by good examples—the Spaniards have this evil principle to blame.

the greatest number of Catholics. As for this Rosary or *Paternoster* <note>Latin for "Our Father"; here referring to the string of prayer beads</note>, there is no doubt that it originates from the Muslims. Peter the Hermit (a) undoubtedly taught it to those Crusaders who could not read, nor make use of books to recite their prayers. The intention was laudable: but from where and from whom did the Muslims borrow this custom? Possibly they owe it to the East Indians, who also made use of a type of Rosary. It also appears from commemorative medals, which are depicted in the *Treatise on the Religion of the Ancient Romans* by *Du Choul*, that the use of *Paternosters* existed among them as well. It was no less necessary for the Pagans than for the Christians and Muslims, since the prayers of the former were at least as (b) burdensome and difficult to remember as those of the others. It is believed that the same Peter the Hermit of whom we have spoken invented the Hours <note>The Liturgy of the Hours; a set of daily prayers</note> and the Office of Our Lady.

<margin>The Rosary and the use thereof described.</margin>
Four instruments of piety have produced four powerful Brotherhoods. This one, of the *Rosary*, owes its birth to that of St. Dominic. The *Rosary* is a large *Paternoster* * of one hundred and fifty beads which make up as many *Ave Marias* <note>The "Hail Mary" prayer</note>. Sets of ten are distinguished by a slightly larger bead or pearl, which makes a *Pater* <note>The "Our Father" prayer</note>. The fifteen large beads represent fifteen mysteries (c), which
> "are like beautiful Images, in which one
> "sees the purpose of the Eternal Father in the
> "temporal birth of His Son,
> "the misfortunes that befell Him in His childhood,
> "in His hidden and unknown life, in
> "His suffering and industrious conduct, and in
> "His Glorious and immortal life."

The common *Rosaries* have no more than fifty *Ave Marias* and five *Paters*. Before one recites one's *Rosary*, one must make a Cross <note>The Sign of the Cross</note>. One must then read the Article of Faith

->PART I.<-

<column-break/>

of the Apostles <note>The Apostles' Creed</note> to prepare oneself for prayer: after which one must say one *Pater* and three *Ave Marias*, regarding the three correspondences of the Holy Virgin with the three persons of the Trinity. After this preliminary piety, one shall proceed to the fifteen sets of ten. The pious Christian must take care to introduce himself into the mysteries of each set of ten through a prayer, to be found in the books that deal with the customary devotion of the *Rosary*. The fifteen mysteries are divided into three sections, of which the first comprises the five joyful mysteries; the five following mysteries are sorrowful, since they deal with the suffering of the Savior; and the last five are Glorious, as they relate to His Resurrection and Ascension etc. After the *Rosary*, the Brotherhoods, who have the honor of bearing its name, must recite the Litanies and Prayers for the afflicted etc. They shall lift up their hearts to the Holy Virgin, (d) who is the *Queen of the Rosary*, the *Empress of Heaven and Earth*, the *Absolute Sovereign of the Treasures and Heavenly Riches*: and just as the faithful must pray for one another, and even request in their prayers the expansion of the religion they profess, so those of the *Rosary* must never forget this last article, and always strive to bring *Proselytes* <note>Converts from another faith or opinion</note> to the faith of St. Dominic.

<margin>When and by whom this use was introduced.</margin>
This Saint, of whom the legend-writers tell many wonders, was of noble birth. In the year 1170, he first saw the light in Spain. While still a child (e) the Holy Virgin began to give him instruction in the devotion of the *Rosary*, which shortly became the great object of the Saint's religious practice. HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

<margin>A Brotherhood of the Rosary established.</margin>
to establish the Brotherhood of the Rosary (a), and subsequently he preached about it everywhere he traveled. We shall mention nothing of the miracles during his mission against the Heretics of Languedoc <note>A region in Southern France</note>, nor of the Holy persecutions that he brought upon them, believing it necessary to join temporal weapons <note>Physical force or military power</note> to spiritual ones against the People who, it was claimed, maintained their teachings with a stubbornness capable of provoking the greatest patience of all the godly. This Saint, authorized by the Pope, disputed their errors, preached the Crusade against their followers, and had those who refused to submit to his arguments condemned and damned: but the *Rosary* alone—uncommonly more powerful than the temporal sword—and the charitable sermons of St. Dominic, caused many hundred thousand souls (b) to return to the bosom of the Catholic Church. All other wonders told of this pious instrument we leave untouched: yet one must give this Saint the credit for an act that has no equal in the life of *Jesus Christ*; this is, that he miraculously caused a great number of Heretics to drown during the crossing of the Garonne <note>A major river in Southwest France</note>.

<margin>When this Feast is solemnly celebrated.</margin>
The solemnity of the Rosary is celebrated on the first Sunday of October. This Feast owes its institution to the piety of Pope Gregory VIII <note>The text likely refers to Gregory XIII, who formalised the feast in 1573 following the Battle of Lepanto</note>. Various Popes (c) have, through Bulls <note>Official papal edicts</note>, confirmed the manner of praying with the Rosary and granted all appropriate Indulgences <note>Remissions of temporal punishment for sin</note>, both plenary and specific, to those who made a pious use of it.

<margin>How this Brotherhood has divided into two branches.</margin>
As for this Brotherhood; the Legend Writers <note>Authors of hagiographies or lives of the saints</note> of the Order of St. Dominic and many others assert that it owes its origin to the Holy Institutor of the Rosary. He established it, they say, by command of the Holy Virgin, while he worked to subdue the Albigensians <note>A dualist religious sect in southern France targeted by the medieval Inquisition</note> and root out the Heretics. After the death of the Saint, the devotion of the Ros-

<column-break/>

ary was entirely neglected: but *Alanus de Rupe* <note>original: "Alanus van la Roche"; a 15th-century Dominican monk</note> (d) revived it with much fruit, and worked for fifteen years to encourage the pious toward it. This Brotherhood is divided into two branches, one of which—the common Rosary—obliges itself to recite the fifteen decades weekly, to confess, and to receive Communion every first Sunday of the month. The Brothers are also required to attend the Processions of the Brotherhood. The other branch is that of the *Perpetual Rosary*: the faithful of this Brotherhood are very strongly devoted to it. The first duty of these Brothers is to read the Rosary continuously: namely, that there is always someone among them who daily greets the Holy Virgin in the name of the entire Brotherhood.

<margin>How and by whom the Scapular was brought into use;</margin>
The *Scapular* * <term>Scapular: A devotional garment consisting of two small pieces of cloth joined by bands, worn over the shoulders</term> produced another group, which in matters of piety in no way yields to the exactness of the one we have described. After many prayers and pious requests, the Holy Virgin gave the *Scapular* to *Simon Stock*, Prior General of the Carmelites, in the same century and nearly at the same time as she gave the Rosary to St. Dominic. She assured the Blessed of her protection, promised to be favorable to the faithful who bound themselves to the devotion of the Scapular, and to look upon them as her children. She pledged herself to save those who were found provided with such a precious pledge at the hour of death.

<margin>The same described.</margin>
The *Scapular* of the Carmelites is a small woolen garment, of a brown, dark gray, or tan color, which hangs over the chest, the back, and the shoulders. It also consists of two small patches of cloth, three or four inches square, attached by two bands. Thus do the Brothers of the devotion of the *Scapular* wear it. We shall not expand upon the miracles of this excellent preservative against all the inconveniences of life. One can find satisfaction on this subject from the Legend Writers, who

<margin>When the Feast of the Scapular is celebrated,</margin>
The devotees of the *Scapular* celebrate their Feast on July 16th, the day likewise dedicated to *Our Lady of Mount Carmel*. Papal Bulls have, from time to time, guaranteed them innumerable indulgences; but what especially set the *Scapular* above all other pious exercises is the famous Sabbatine Bull <note>original: "Zaturdagfche Bulle"</note> of John XXII. This Pope declared that the Holy Virgin had certainly promised him, while he was in prayer, that she would deliver the Carmelite disciples and Brothers of the *Scapular* from Hell on the Saturday after their death, and this upon three conditions: I. That they should wear the *Scapular* during their
<margin>and what must accompany this devotion.</margin>
lives. II. That they must maintain chastity, or at least temperance, and observe conjugal purity. The Carmelite monk had to fulfill the first two points. The lay Brother satisfied the requirement if he observed the first point within marriage. III. That they recited the Canonical Hours, or if they could not read, that they should then fast on the days established by the Church, and eat no meat on Wednesdays or Saturdays, except on Christmas Day when it fell on one of these days. This practice was burdensome: which cannot be denied. Temperance is indeed the principal point, the neglect of which could have nullified the power of the *Scapular*. What power must a Carmelite not have over himself, who is compelled by his Order to bear this burden, on the condition of simultaneously subjecting himself to the yoke of chastity? Could one sufficiently express the sorrow of a Brother who has made a vow to provide himself with this, in order to deliver himself from Hell? How many temptations is he not forced to combat?
As for the faithful of the Brotherhood of the *Scapular*, several Popes have forgiven them a third of their sins. The Archconfraternity of Our Lady of Mount Carmel in Rome dresses in a peculiar

<column-break/>

manner. A sack of tanned color is attached to a monk's hood <note>a cowl</note>, which covers the face of the devotee of the Archconfraternity and hangs down, tapering to a point, as far as the belt. The hood has two holes positioned for the eyes. The sack is tied with a leather strap, and the shoulders of the disguised devotee are covered with a priest's cape (a) made of white serge.
<margin>A Brotherhood of St. Francis of the Girdle established, and by whom.</margin>
The *Girdle of Saint Francis* constitutes the third Brotherhood. Those who know the outstanding merits of this Saint, and all his perfections (b) which correspond to **JESUS CHRIST**, will easily be able to imagine that the believer who unites himself through the Girdle is the happiest of all men. We shall consider St. Francis (c) as an example of patience, chastity, and humility. The Impressions of the wounds of **JESUS CHRIST** <note>the Stigmata</note> which he received from a Seraph on his hands, feet, and in his side, in memory of the wounds of the Savior, prove the first of these virtues. Furthermore, his poor and needy conduct is not unknown, nor how he treated the wretched *Brother Ass* (d). As for his chastity, who does not know how he rolled his body in the snow, likewise on thorns and thistles and in the fire (e) to preserve his spotlessness. Finally, his wisdom and humility were undoubtedly very famous, as when he preached to the Birds and Fish (f); and when he felt a movement of impatience or pride, he forced Brother *Bernard of Quintavalle* to set his foot upon his throat.
<margin>The same described, and of what power it has been.</margin>
The large cord of the clergy, who lived according to the Rule of this Saint, was called *the Girdle of Saint Francis*, and it is shared among several Orders by all followers of St. Francis. This Cord, after it serves as a belt for the monk's body, hangs down a little way to the feet, and also serves him as an instrument for discipline <note>self-flogging</note>, being armed with an interval of very large knots, especially at the end of the

<margin>When the Scapular Feast is celebrated,</margin>
The devotees of the *Scapular* celebrate their Feast on the 16th of July, a day likewise dedicated to *Our Lady of Mount Carmel*. (f) He treated a raging Wolf as a brother and made him promise never to kill anyone. The Wolf, very happy to be released so cheaply, promised it to him solemnly, and to gain belief in this, he gave him his paw. ibid.

The Girdle of St. Francis has at times healed the sick, aided in childbirth, strengthened health, granted children, and performed infinite other edifying miracles.

Among the Societies dedicated to St. Francis, that of the Impressions of the Five Wounds of Jesus Christ in Rome is the most prominent. A surgeon gave birth to it at the end of the sixteenth century and soon gathered a large number of devout followers. After the rules of the Brotherhood were finalized, it was named the Archbrotherhood. The author of the *History of the Religious Orders* has accurately cited everything concerning this Brotherhood in the 50th Chapter of the 5th volume of his work, to which we direct the reader. We shall only say here that the faithful of the Brotherhood clothe themselves in humility with an ash-colored sackcloth; they bind this sack with a large cord equipped with a large wooden *Paternoster* <note>The "Our Father" beads, or rosary</note>; they wear a coat of arms (b) on which the arms of the Order of St. Francis are depicted; they walk barefoot in procession wearing wooden soles and holding a wooden cross; and finally, they cover their faces with a (c) hood <note>original: "regenkap"; a pointed cowl used by penitents to remain anonymous</note>.

The Girdle of St. *Augustine* also unites a large number of the devout under the name of an Archbrotherhood. It is made of leather. The Augustinian clergy assert in a book dealing with their Brotherhood: *That the Holy Virgin, Empress of angels and men, wore it around her loins. The Law of Nature, the Written Law, and the Law of Grace have all three made use of the Girdle.* <note>The "Law of Nature" refers to the time before Moses; the "Written Law" to the era of the Ten Commandments; and the "Law of Grace" to the Christian era.</note> It is

<column-break/>

probable that our first ancestors, who lived under the Law of Nature, clothed themselves in skins and wore a Girdle of the same material. (They were perhaps members of St. Augustine's Order.) As for its use under the Written Law, it is forbidden to doubt this: the Prophet *Elias* <note>Elijah</note> also wore it around his loins, since it is written that he was girded with a leather belt. John the Baptist wore it under the Law of Grace, and this provides sufficient proof, without the slightest doubt.

The hip-belt of St. *Monica* <note>The mother of St. Augustine</note> must not be forgotten. It is of no less power than the Girdle of St. *Francis of Paola*. <margin>and other Brother-hoods.</margin> This Girdle has five knots which all correspond to those of St. *Francis*. We leave to the lay-followers of St. *Francis of Paola* the honor of profiting from all the advantages of their Girdle. It suffices for us here to have shown how the same is judged necessary for the edification of the devout, placing them under its protection. The Brotherhood (d) of the Holy Sacrament in Rome recognizes St. *Francis of Paola* as one of their patrons and wears the Girdle of the Spiritual Friars Minor or Franciscans over their violet sacks.

Let us pass from Girdles to clothing. <margin>What common use was made of the Monk's habit.</margin> Formerly (e) it was believed that one did not die as a good Christian unless one was wrapped in a Franciscan robe during the throes of death, or drew one's last breath in a monk's hood; but this piety has slackened; now a believer dies without being dressed up like a monk: one now takes one's leave in ordinary attire. # CHAPTER XV.

## CONTINUATION of the proposed SUBJECT; how (a) the BROTHERHOODS are constituted.

---

We have already said of some of these Brotherhoods <note>Also known as confraternities: groups of laypeople organized for religious or charitable purposes</note> that their founders have set themselves against the Societies of the flesh and the *Demon*. No one is ignorant that the purpose of the Brotherhoods is to unite under the same Livery <note>A distinctive uniform or dress identifying the group</note>, and to take service under one Banner, to wage war against the Enemy of the human race. He is fought with a courage that outwardly promises much: but it often turns out with the Fellow-brothers as it does with auxiliary troops taken over from a foreign Prince. They fight an Enemy who is no enemy to them. Every Brotherhood has its Rules, Exercises, and Prescriptions of Piety, likewise its stratagems, clever inventions, and military discipline. The most important thing is to constantly wear the tokens of the Society into which one has entered. The new Fellow-brother receives from the Head of the Brotherhood a *Letter of Sonship* <term>A formal certificate granting a layperson spiritual membership in a religious order, allowing them to share in the order's spiritual merits</term>, after which he shares in the Scourgings, the Prayers, Mortification of the Body, and all the good Works of the Brotherhood.
We shall present here various details regarding the Brotherhoods of Christendom, without however overstepping our specific purpose; for the Account would indeed require a large book. Our century has brought forth many new Brotherhoods, of which we

<column-break/>

shall treat. The Previous ones no longer had the scent of novelty, which at once struck both the Pious man and the Worldling. It was required to recapture the taste of this Heavenly manna, which during some centuries had become all too tasteless. Nothing seems more fitting than to pray to God by oneself and with one's family, or to join other Believers in public devotions: but it is more glorious to call the Christians to their Banner and to march toward Heaven with unfurled Banners. Possibly this was the origin of a great number of these Brotherhoods.
<margin>How time has gradually produced an extraordinary number of Brotherhoods.</margin>
Italy, Spain, and Portugal are the principal countries of Europe where one finds the greatest number of Brotherhoods, of which many have adopted the name of Arch-brotherhoods, as we have already said. These are, so to speak, the Mothers or Heads of others. They (b) communicate to them their Rules and Institutions, their Dress and Privileges. Rome alone contains in her bosom a considerable number of these Pious Societies, of which each has its Church or its House of Prayer. The Occupations, Arts, and Trades divide themselves into Brotherhoods in this Capital of Religion, and each places itself under the protection of

(a) A Brotherhood of Black Penitents established in the year 1488. They assist criminals at their
executions, bury them, and have Requiem Masses performed for them.
(b) Established in the year 1600 by a Dominican Master of the Sacred Palace, holding the office of Overseer

(c) *John of God* <note original: "Jan de Dieu"></note> lived at the beginning of the sixteenth century. He had been a
shepherd until the age of 22, and subsequently became a soldier. Because he had neglected the Rosary and his other
religious duties, he fell from his horse and injured himself while out for provisions. See Giry's
*Life of the Blessed John of God*. It appeared through the account of his life that he had less aptitude
for being a good soldier than for becoming a great Saint. His negligence nearly cost him his
life. He was discharged; he wished to return to the life of a shepherd, but he ventured a
second time to become a soldier, and was more successful, says Father *Giry*, since this war
was just. In a sea storm, he wished to imitate Jonah and desired to be thrown into the sea. They took him at his
word: but having said a well-timed *Ave Maria*, he saved himself. Thereafter, for a long time, he led a
holy life; when he traveled, he sold books, or rather he became a peddler of news.
He sold paper, prints, catechisms, and simultaneously gave exhortations to virtue. This
pious bookseller, who possibly had no equal, sanctified such a trade, of which his
piety did not make much noise in the world. He subsequently set up a shop in Granada, left it
again some time later, going through the streets crying out "*Mercy*." It was believed that he was mad,
for he did everything that could confirm this opinion. It once happened that he sang the *Salve Regina*
before the Virgin Mary, upon which she pushed away the curtain that covered her, to honor him with the sight
of her. The sacristan, rushing forward, wanted to beat him, thinking he was a thief: but his
leg became stiff and was only restored by the prayer of the Blessed man.
(d) Established in the year 1571.

tapestry-makers are often subject.

fire <note>Referring to the fire of devotion or spiritual fervor</note> that is primarily necessary for the Masses of the faithful who are still on Earth; those of St. *Marcellus* and St. *Giles*; of Our Lady of the People, of the Resurrection, of St. *Salvator* in the *Lateran*, of St. *Salvator* in the *Sancta Sanctorum* <note>Latin: "Holy of Holies," a chapel in Rome</note>; the Archconfraternity (a) of the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin; those of (b) the Holy Sacrament and the five wounds of the Savior; those (c) of the Trinity of the Pilgrims. The Brotherhood (d) of the Piedmontese regards the Holy *Sudarium* <note>original: *Zweetdoek*, referring to the Shroud of Turin</note> as a great object of piety; those of (e) the *Annunciation* honor the Holy Virgin primarily, doubling their homage on the day of this Feast.

The Brotherhood of the *Gonfalon* <note>Italian for "Banner"</note> received as its Founder St. *Bonaventure*, who in the year 1264 gave it the name of Recommendation of the Virgin, and prescribed a white habit (f) with a red and white cross in a circle on the shoulder, by which the Brothers received the name of White Penitents. They (g) adopted the name *Gonfalon* to demonstrate their zeal for the Fatherland and Liberty on an occasion when they executed justice against the oppression of the Roman Lords.

It was around the middle of the past century that *Michael Buch*, called "Good *Henry*," a poor Shoemaker by trade, took upon himself the care of restoring the piety of the Shoemakers, his fellow-brothers. He was a Luxembourger. We leave all the wonders of his conduct unmentioned, to speak only of the Guild established by him. With all zeal, he spent his life in silence with a reborn nature and in the forgetfulness of his fellow shoemakers, had he not had the fortune of being sought out by a prominent Nobleman.

<column-break/>

It was the Baron of Renti <note>original: *Vryheer van Renti*</note> who made him known, without him stopping his humble trade, however. This Baron secured his mastership for him. Good Henry set up shop in Paris; he took on boys and apprentices with no other aim than to teach them to pray to God: thus the Shoemaker’s Shop was soon transformed into a school of practice, where the apprenticeship was spent in piety. His Society decided to establish itself in the year 1645. Mr. Renti was declared the Protector of this new Company, and Good Henry, the Father of this institution, immediately rose from the rank of Shoemaker to that of Headmaster. Such was the origin of the Guild of the Brother Shoemakers, which was followed in the year 1647 by the Brother Tailors, likewise entrusted to the management of Good Henry. Subsequently, some similar ones were also established in other cities of France.

The Brotherhood (h) of Mercy in *Lisbon* <note>original: *Irmandade da Misericórdia*</note> is too well-known not to mention. It consists of the most prominent personages of the State, and the King himself is enrolled in it. This Brotherhood, which is very numerous, extends its branches through the entire Kingdom, having many Masses said for the faithful: but primarily for those who are under their jurisdiction.

The account which we have given of all these Brotherhoods will be sufficiently satisfying. Many pious people believe that enrollment alone brings much assurance of Salvation; that certain signs on the livery are essential marks of true Christianity, and that there is no true piety other than that of their Society. Therefore, it must be distressing for some Religious Orders that the devotees allow themselves to be instructed otherwise.
