### XVI. CHAPTER.

### On PENANCES, PRAYERS, and PILGRIMAGES.

<margin>The differences between the Penance of the ancients and that of today considered.</margin>
**O**ne would not do well to compare the Penitents of our century with those of the first Christians. The practice of publicly whipping oneself and calling upon Divine Mercy with a masked face and a rope around the neck was unknown to them. Likewise, those Christians (a) who strip naked to the waist in their undergarments, repeatedly tearing open their shoulders, and—what is more—are burdened with a cross and chains, their arms tied to a piece of wood of excessive weight (b) to holily represent the Cross of the Savior, seem a thousand times more like idolaters than followers of Apostolic simplicity. We shall make no mention of those who wear crowns of thorns on their heads in honor of JESUS CHRIST, who scourge and pierce themselves with sharp barbs (c) and steel prongs, place the points of bare swords against their chests, or who inflict heavy wounds upon themselves for the love of God. Can one carry Christianity any further than by willingly suffering that pain which the Savior of the Human Race did not demand?

<margin>Some put into use</margin>
In Spain and Portugal (d) many

<column-break/>

<margin>by proxies, and how this occurs.</margin>
pious people perform Penance through proxies <note>A proxy is someone authorized to act on behalf of another; here, it refers to hiring someone to undergo physical punishment in one's place</note>. There are those who, for profit, take the place of the Penitents and discipline themselves with all the severity of a devout person who chastises himself for his sins, and who wishes to pay with his body what he believes he owes to God. During these harsh penances, the women, who religiously examine all the merit therein (e), cry and wail with all their might. They also bruise themselves by beating their breasts and faces, pull out their hair, and reproach with all possible zeal those who do not chastise themselves severely enough. On the other hand, the Penitents try to strengthen their hearts again by drinking, and while they refresh themselves slightly during their pious actions, the wine bottle swings from hand to hand, by which the penitents regain new strength; then they begin to weep again, beseeching God for His Mercy, and calling upon all the Saints of Paradise. This mixture of penitence and drunkenness is, however, not offensive in those lands where it is believed in good faith that the Christian Religion

(a) *This Penance is practiced in Italy and in Spain during Lent <note>The 40-day period of fasting and prayer before Easter</note> and Holy Week.*
(b) *This is done in Catalonia.*
(c) *See, Travels of S. Dellon. Vol. I. printed 1709.*
(d) It is not only in Spain and Portugal that Penance occurs through proxies; but one also sees it introduced in Provence and Italy. Some years ago, there was a certain Jacob Zéger who performed this charitable trade in several cities in Brabant <note>A historical region in the low countries, now part of Belgium and the Netherlands</note>. This fellow whipped himself until he bled in the presence of the Sinner, if he was only given enough to buy some "strengthening waters" <note>likely referring to spirits or cordials</note> before he began the discipline; in addition to what he was paid for the Penance itself. It is also said that he had two daughters who hired themselves out for such chastisements, not only for young ladies, but also for wives and common women who had anything to pay. A set price had been established for when one had to fast, depending on whether it was more or less difficult. Ten stivers <note>a small Dutch coin</note> was what was given if one was not allowed to eat meat, and thirty to fast on water and bread: but as for the Penances in which one had to whip oneself, and for other pious acts of that nature, there was no fixed price, so that a deal had to be made beforehand. One laid open his Register for the Penitent, and read the account of the obligations that custom had dictated. A penance of four common Fasts, the reciting of 52 Hail Marys <note>original: *Ave Marias*</note> a day, a penance of 25 lashes on Friday after midnight, along with a "Have mercy on me, O God" <note>original: *Miserere mei Deus*, the beginning of Psalm 51</note>, a fast on water and bread on a Wednesday, along with three "My soul magnifies" <note>original: *Magnificats*</note> said before sunrise, a penance of five Rosaries at the midnight hour, along with seven Penitential Psalms and the Litany of all Saints read, were then sufficient. Other Penitents heard three Masses one after another in the Church of the Jesuits before St. Ignatius, on bare knees on the marble; one agreed to stand with both arms outstretched before an image of the Holy Virgin; from one to two hours after midnight one went around the Sacrament of the Miracle, limping barefoot, without being allowed to rest except every hundred paces; one pulled 150 hairs from one's head before the church door of the Carmelites, or one had to be there in the morning between two and three o'clock and recite 150 Hail Marys, giving oneself twenty-five rod-strokes, saying the "O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger" <note>original: *Domine ne in furore*, Psalm 6</note> up to "Blessed are those" <note>original: *Beati quorum*, Psalm 32</note>, and this on bare knees, and on a board strewn with sand 250 Hail Marys, with five times the "Praise the Lord" <note>original: *Laudate Dominum*</note>; on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Saturdays at night to sleep without a shirt and entirely naked between sheets strewn with horsehair, etc. But enough of this, we shall leave many other such examples unremarked, since it gives no benefit to true Christianity; for these exercises, entirely without command, are contemptible to true Christians and forbidden by their Teachers who wish to honor Religion.
(e) *Dellon ibid.*

<margin>
When the Scourging of Penitents first arose.
</margin>
Abbot Boileau (a) does not go back further than the eleventh century to find the origin of Scourgings in penitential practice. It was then, he says, that chastened men armed themselves with rods and whips to appease the Divinity through very severe floggings. It seemed that people then took upon themselves a task of the most difficult Piety and excessive penance. Finally, this Scourging was carried so far that in the thirteenth century a Sect of <term>Flagellants</term><gloss>Latin: *Flagellantes*; those who whipped themselves publicly</gloss> was introduced, who went through the Cities in pairs and scourged themselves in public in a completely unedifying manner that deserved some pity. The devotion toward this Scourging soon passed to women. They also scourged themselves: but so as not to offend the public, they did so in private chambers. (b) Twenty-five years after this Sect of Flagellants took hold, another arose, which imagined it had received a command from God to scourge itself for the Sins of the human race. Even Children established a Society of Flagellants among themselves. It appears from the cited Author that these Religious people rebuked the crimes and irregularities of Christians openly enough: yet one cannot deny that this admirable Piety was accompanied by much extravagance.

Such roughly was the origin of the Scourging which (c) the Nations

<column-break/>

of Italy, Spain, and Portugal have adopted in their public and private Penitential exercises, and which many Religious Orders practice in their Cloisters. We shall find occasion hereafter to speak of Repentance when we move on to the Sacrament of Confession; and of the Procession of the <term>Disciplinants</term><gloss>Those who practice self-flagellation as a "discipline"</gloss> of Spain: when dealing with Processions.

<margin>
What manner of things solemn Prayers are.
</margin>
Nothing seems more necessary than prayer; for it is practiced in all Religions: but if the outward form of prayer is not accompanied by an inward feeling of virtue, all its regularity must be viewed as a habit, or regarded as a ceremony, and it is in this form that it finds a place in our Treatise. One must then regard the prayer of those as a ceremony who are enrolled in a Brotherhood, viewing all its institutions as spiritual, yet not shrinking from surrendering themselves to wrongdoing; and of those who, at the hour of Death, clothe themselves in a Monk’s habit and give to the Cloisters the inheritance which they withhold from their closest friends; of those who turn to Piety only when they perceive that their senses can no longer serve them. This sample gives a sufficiently just Idea of what we shall call Solemn Prayers, and what could be treated as a FORMAL ADDRESS GIVEN TO THE DIVINITY. We leave the account of it to the Confessors.

In the rank of Customs one must place (d) the practice of carrying certain Prayers in one's pocket; a practice which one can view as a superstitious remnant of Amulets; likewise the practice of praying precisely at a set hour and always in the same posture, or in the most difficult

---

(a) *History of the Flagellants, Chapter VII.*
(b) *See the cited Chronicle by Abbot Boileau. Ibid.*
(c) The Penitents in Italy distinguish themselves by Colors. They form many Brotherhoods under the names of blue, green, violet, gray, black, and white Penitents. During Holy Week, the Brothers scourge themselves in time to a rhythm with whips which, it is said, make more noise than they cause pain. If this is so, their penances are not carried out with as much confidence as those of the <term>Brahmins and Fakirs</term><gloss>Hindu and Muslim ascetics often cited in this period as examples of extreme physical penance</gloss>, nor those of the Pagans of Antiquity. We shall not cite the comparison, fearing to make them hated: but since we have come to the Article on penance, the Reader must be informed that it is, if one may call it so, the most wonderful and outward thing in Religions where the Service requires a great apparatus, many Priests, and customs. It shows the same mark in those who withdraw from the World to become friends of God, and strive to be enemies of men. Finally, it is the same in countries where heated brains are easily burdened with unusual ideas by the warmth of the Region. It is from this principle that one can derive the penitents of the Mexicans and East Indians; likewise those of the Greeks and the ancient Romans, whom *Minutius Felix* <note>A 2nd-century Christian apologist</note> reproaches: that they, offering their own blood to the Gods and praying through the gaping of their wounds, were not of sound mind. As for modern Scourgings, *Polydorus Virgilius* <note>An Italian humanist scholar</note> takes the liberty of comparing them to the *Lupercalia* <note>An ancient Roman festival involving ritual whipping</note>, which were celebrated with whip in hand and a masked face. He adds that the Egyptians scourged themselves with rods at certain openings <note>original: "zekere openingen," likely referring to temple festivals</note>.
(d) *See Thiers, "On the most necessary of all devotions," Ch. 21.*

<margin>How Pilgrimages are judged as an Ancient custom, and of what utility they were thought to be.</margin>
"The Vows and Pilgrimages made to and upon the graves of the Martyrs and other Saints, to Churches, Chapels, and other places of Piety, are of great antiquity, which is confirmed by the testimony of the Church Fathers and other Ecclesiastical Writers. Thus Mr. **Thiers** expresses himself (b): but he adds that to imagine one could not be perfect without making Pilgrimages to Holy places, or that because one performed such pilgrimages and offered up Vows and Prayers there, one would certainly obtain from God what was requested through the intercession of the Saints—or that one would be released from the inconveniences and difficulties one suffered, or that, except for the crime, one died in God’s Grace and would see oneself saved despite leading a common life—would certainly be a great error."

"We believe that one could very well be mindful of the Saints within oneself without these Pilgrimages; following their virtues without going from place to place, and could pray zealously to God without visiting all the Churches of a City."

We have said that the famous Pilgrimages formerly made to the Holy Land, Rome, Compostela, Loreto, etc., are currently the most renowned. We have already spoken of the Pilgrimage to Rome under the name of the Jubilee Year. The Devout betake themselves to Compostela to visit the Relics of St. James the Great, commonly known by the name of St. James in Galicia: likewise, they go to Loreto to visit Our Lady.

<column-break/>

<margin>The behavior of the Pilgrims going to visit St. James, patron saint of Spain.</margin>
See what a good writer (c) tells us regarding the Apostle who is the object of the Pilgrims' piety. "St. James, (d) Patron Saint of all Spain, has rested in the Archepiscopal church of Compostela for nine hundred years. The image of this Holy Apostle stands upon the high Altar; it is a small wooden bust, always illuminated by 40 or 50 wax candles. The... Pilgrims kiss the image three times, and with a very esteemed devotion place their hat upon its head. One sees hanging in the church some thirty silver Lamps, which always burn, and six large silver Candlesticks five feet high, gifted by King Philip III. Around the Church, one sees beautiful flat floors of large stones upon which one walks, and above one sees another likewise, where the Pilgrims climb up and fasten a scrap of their clothing to a stone cross which has been erected there. They have yet another ceremony there which is no less singular. They crawl three times under this cross, through a hole which is so narrow, <margin>accompanied by a strange ceremony,</margin> that they are forced to strike their chests against the floor; wherefore those who are a little stout of body must suffer much discomfort. Nevertheless, it is necessary that they crawl through there if they wish to earn the <term>Indulgence</term><gloss>A promise of the removal of temporal punishment for sins</gloss> that is attached to it."

"A rare gate of the Gospel through which the Pilgrims come upon the path of Salvation!" One has seen there, says the Author of the *Delights of Spain*, those who had forgotten to crawl under this stone cross, having traveled back a distance of 500 miles to complete this solemn religious act. The French Pilgrims also have a Chapel in the same church.

(a) Ibid. where the Author speaks of the 30-day and 33-day prayers, etc.
(b) Ibid. Ch. 23. The wandering which one calls Pilgrimages took its beginning under the reign of Constantine the Great. This was introduced much more commonly around the end of the fourth century: but this is in no way to be compared with the Pilgrimages of the following centuries. The tenth century became notorious for those to the Holy Land, which gave birth to the Crusades. One may also count among Pilgrimages the solemn religious acts that the dispersed Jews of Jerusalem performed at least once a year to this Capital of Judea, and the journeys of the Devout of ancient Paganism to ask advice from the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi, of Jupiter Ammon in Africa, of Serapis in Egypt, and of Trophonius in Boeotia in the Cave which bears his name.

(a) The House called *Santa Casa* has been given the most exalted titles in Italy; it is, so it is claimed, the same House in which the Holy Virgin was born, betrothed, and married; where also the Annunciation of the birth of the Son of God and His Incarnation took place. For more than thirteen centuries this House had stood in Nazareth; then, in the year 1291, angels transported it from there to Dalmatia. After the passing of three years and seven months, they transported it again and brought it to the region of Recanati, situated under the jurisdiction of Ancona. If one may believe the writers of legends, heavenly music was often heard there, the sweetness of which brought wonder to the inhabitants of the neighborhood; these writers add further that all of nature rejoiced over this transport, and that even the trees of the forest greeted the Holy House. Nevertheless, it took up its residence in this place for only eight months, after which it was transported a little further. But hardly had four months passed when the angels transported it for the fourth and final time. Then they placed it where it is still seen today, and where a magnificent Church has been built, in which this Holy House is enclosed. Besides that, it is further surrounded by four walls that encompass it without, however, touching it. The legend writers add a miracle to give the reason for this separation: at which one must not wonder, since the building, the materials, the decorations, and statues are all miraculous. The **Paternosters** that are rubbed against it, the handkerchiefs and any other linen that has touched it, or anything belonging to this Holy structure, likewise become miracle-working instruments. We must not forget to say that all original testimonials of Loreto come from people who saw the Holy House being transported, and it is almost certain that they themselves have become quite capable Saints.
(b) The Mohammedans who go on pilgrimage to Mecca must make a circuit seven times around the famous Mosque of this city. See Reland, *On the Mohammedan Religion* <note>original: "de Relig. Maho:"; referring to Adriaan Reland's "De religione Mohammedica," 1705.</note>.
(c) *Regia* <note>original: "Regia"; Latin for Royal or Palace-like.</note>; thus an Italian writer expresses himself.
(d) *Travels in Italy by Misson* <note>original: "Voyage d'Italie par Misson"</note>. Vol. I. 1702. Dutch edition.
(e) See that which we have already spoken of here before.
(f) There are some, says the writer cited in a marginal note, made of gold, silver, ebony, ivory, floral-work, and several that are set with pearls and precious stones.

(a) It is added that the cleric leaves his slippers at the door, to notify the husband thereby that he must not hinder the devotion of the wife.
(b) Just as in certain Christian lands one does penance through Proxies <note>Paid representatives who performed religious rituals or pilgrimages on behalf of wealthy patrons.</note>. There are also pilgrimages from which one can be excused without harm to salvation, provided one pays one of these devotees for it, and as has already been said here before, who takes this burden upon themselves to carry it out. A certain Walloon from Liège, named **Klaasje**, had, so they say, been very notorious for some years for accepting this kind of power of attorney, and the common saying in Brussels was that if Klaasje did not succeed through her spiritual conduct in acquiring what was requested, one had no priest nor monk to use for this subject. Her room was always full of household members, who requested pilgrimages to be done for their masters or mistresses, and to go visit male or female Saints. No small trade had she fostered among the citizens, who came to consult her on what one had to request from the Holy Virgin; she spoke sensibly of the power of the Saints, and of what she had done for them. This pious and godly woman was the Mother of a son and daughter raised in the same trade: they were always at work for the penitents and pilgrimages. Mistress Klaasje kept, like Jacob Segers, a daily register of the debts she agreed upon with Heaven to relieve the sinners. See how she recorded the items: a pilgrimage barefoot from my house to the **Our Lady of Halle**; to have three Masses said in succession, and to offer at each Mass a wax candle of good weight, etc. To do a **Novena** <note>A nine-day sequence of prayers.</note> to Our Lady of Good Success, with the wax candle in one hand and the **Rosary** in the other; to recommend oneself to the Young Lady of whom I spoke before, to go visit **St. Bricus** <note>St. Brice.</note>, and to pray to him on behalf of a noble Lady that he have the goodness to lead her husband away from his irregular life; a prayer to **St. Eloi** <note>St. Eligius, patron of horses and metalworkers.</note> for a young lady; to make a visit to **St. Marcon** <note>St. Marculf, traditionally invoked to heal skin diseases.</note>, to pray to him that he heal an old lady of the scurvy; a penance for a lady, sentenced to keep her mouth as wide as she can without closing it, from midnight until one o'clock, and then to recite 52 *Hail Marys* with an *Inviolata Integra* <note>original: "Inviolata, integra et casta es Maria" — a Gregorian chant meaning "Untouched, whole, and chaste are you, Mary."</note> etc., because she had slandered some clerics, etc.
(c) This Saint excelled even from her childhood. Subsequently, her mother having become a widow, she became a religious and desired this also for her daughter. It was in this state of seclusion that **St. Gertrude** completed the dedication of herself to God, and became one of the most beautiful ornaments of the Church. A legendary writer <note>An author of hagiographies (lives of the saints).</note> has very ingeniously noted that this Saint came into the world at the same time as **Muhammad**: a wonderful proof of the Providence of God, who wished to use St. Gertrude to support religion in the West, while that in the East was wavering: Another proof of the truth of this remark is the name of Gertrude (*Gartrout*), which means "entirely faithful" <note>original: "ganch getrouw"</note>. See Ryckel already cited.

Following, after the Mass has been sung, the Reliquary <note>A container, often made of precious metals, used to hold and display holy relics.</note> of St. Gertrude is carried to the Western entrance of the Church of the Beguines or Spiritual Daughters <note>The Beguines were lay religious women who lived in community without taking perpetual vows.</note>. It is placed on a wagon decorated with painted panels containing emblems and proverbs, which the most gifted minds of the city try to produce as wittily as they can in honor of the Patroness of the place. The wagon is drawn by six magnificently adorned horses: but before the transfer of this Saint begins, this ceremony must be observed.

While they are busy decorating the horses that must pull the wagon, the Reliquary of St. Gertrude is placed under the keeping of the Abbess <note>Original: *Kloostervoogdesse*, a title for the noblewoman who governed the abbey; she held both religious and secular authority.</note> of the aforementioned Spiritual Daughters of Nivelles, a Lady who is simultaneously secular and spiritual. The City Authorities receive this Heavenly treasure from the Abbess, after having previously requested the honor of solemnly carrying it in procession. Then a start is made on the procession in the following order.

Three companies of Citizens accompany the Triumphal Wagon of the Saint. At the head of the procession go the boys of St. Francis with the cross in the attire of spiritual soldiers, and with their hoods on; likewise the Williamites <note>A religious order following the Rule of St. Benedict or St. Augustine.</note>, Singers, Canons, and Canonesses of St. Gertrude. The Abbess follows with some elderly Canonesses, dressed in white, in a carriage. During the march, the hymns of the Saint are sung, and when they have arrived before Mountain Street [Bergstraat], they take up the *Veni Creator* <note>Original: *Veni Creator Spiritus*, a traditional Latin hymn: "Come, Holy Spirit, Creator Blest."</note>, which is answered by a choral song. This music having ended, an almost innumerable multitude of people comes rushing from all sides, both citizens and strangers, to join the procession. The most devout, pressed by the crowd, come barefoot to beg the help of this Saint. Everyone tries to obtain the first favor; they all flatter themselves to have obtained it, and it is undoubtedly related to what the Scripture calls *taking the Kingdom of Heaven by force* <note>A reference to the Biblical passage in Matthew 11:12.</note>. The Authorities, Nobles, and the prominent citizens of the city appear on horseback in the procession. They resume the singing: they sing the Hymn of the Trinity, etc. After a short distance, another band of believers is met. This is the procession of St. Barbara. The Nivelles procession thus continuing—

<column-break/>

—singing the hymns and responses in honor of the Virgin, of St. Michael, and all the Angels. Thus singing, they arrive before the Chapel of St. Anne, where they begin the seven Penitential Psalms and the Litanies, which they continue to sing until they have come before Our Dear Lady of Seven Sorrows, and here they halt until the worshippers have refreshed themselves a little.

The signal for the march being given, they resume their ranks; this onward march lasted at least two more hours, having lasted five hours in total. Then the Reliquary of the Saint was handed back to the Abbess with all required solemnity. Another circuit is made around the Church, into which they finally enter to sing the *Te Deum* <note>Original: *Te Deum Laudamus*, Latin for "Thee, O God, we praise," a hymn of thanksgiving.</note>. After which the Abbess delivers the Reliquary entrusted to her back to the Chapter <note>The governing body of the collegiate church.</note>.

During the eight-day service of St. Michael, the Canonesses must perform the service for the Relics <note>Original: *Reliquiën*.</note> of St. Gertrude by day and night: But on the ninth day, they are put back in their place. Six Canons, dressed in white stoles <note>Original: *Stolen*, liturgical vestments consisting of a long band of colored cloth.</note>, perform this ceremony. These precious parts, in which a pure soul once resided, are neither shown nor processed except in cases of highest necessity. Our Author notes that such processions have often appeased the wrath of the Divinity. Truly, is there anything more worthy of the Supreme Majesty than such a march of a countless band of worshippers, who cast their eyes upon the Reliquary of a Blessed one, and with holy patience expect that the grace of God flowing from this hallowed body should spread over them like a saving balm?

On the day following Pentecost <note>Original: *Pinxter*.</note>, the Brotherhood of St. Gertrude performs another procession in honor of the Patroness, of which we must say something due to its singularity. The march is opened by a well-mounted rider, who has a beautiful girl seated behind him, religiously dressed, representing St. Gertrude. A nimble Devil and jester <note>Original: *poetzemaker*, a prankster or comedian.</note> performs some crooked leaps before the supposed Saint, and constantly does his best to upset her grave dignity. After her appear the young girls carrying the image of the Holy Virgin; these are followed by the Crossbowmen of St. Catherine,

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc., of the ROMAN CHURCH.

<margin>
How among the Processions in Spain, that of the Disciplinants is the most prominent,
</margin>
Among a great number of Spanish Processions, that of the *Disciplinants* <note>Also known as flagellants, these were individuals who publicly whipped themselves as a form of penance or devotion.</note>, which is held on Good Friday (a), is one of the most remarkable. It perfectly reveals the nature of that nation, which is naturally inclined toward a proud piety, contenting itself (b) with that which has an appearance of religiousness. All the Religious Orders, all the magistrates of Madrid, all the guild masters, and even the stage actors—whom the Church nonetheless regards as contemptible people—are required to attend.

<margin>
and with what a rare solemnity it is accompanied.
</margin>
The King is often found there, accompanied by the entire Court. Every Lord is followed by his valet bearing a torch. The arrangement of the ceremony is truly very mournful: the Bodyguard of his Catholic Majesty leads the procession with their weapons in mourning. Masked men, likewise in mourning, play upon various instruments. The drummers, dressed in black, beat a mournful drum-roll to announce the death of the Savior of mankind, and the lamentable tone of the trumpets awakens the grief of the Penitents; the banners and the cross, covered with crepe, together produce a mournful effect on the pious heart. But nothing arouses more devotion than the heavy machines serving as stage decorations of the Savior’s passion; they are dragged in the Procession to be subsequently erected on stages, expressly with the intention of representing the physical death of the Savior. A kind of pious Tragedy is performed there, divided into several acts, and during the performance of the play, people weep, sigh, and beat their chests.

All the Penitents of Madrid take part in this Procession. (c) „They wear a high bonnet covered with linen

<column-break/>

„to the height of three feet and shaped like a sugarloaf, from which a piece of cloth hangs down, covering their faces in front. There are those who take this pious exercise as a true motivation for religion: but others, again, do this only to please their mistresses, this being a new kind of gallantry <note>The author highlights a unique Spanish custom where self-flagellation served as a form of romantic courting to impress women.</note>, unknown to other nations. These Penitents wear white gloves and shoes, and (d) a camisole <note>A short, sleeveless jacket or doublet.</note> whose sleeves are tied with ribbons; they wear a ribbon on their bonnet or on their whip in the color that most pleases their mistresses. (e) They scourge themselves according to measure and rules, with a discipline <note>A small whip used for religious penance.</note> of cords, to which small wax balls are attached at the ends, fitted with sharpened glass. He who scourges himself most bravely and skillfully is regarded as the most courageous. When they meet a well-favored Lady, they know how (f) to scourge themselves so skillfully that they cause their blood to spray over her: and this is an honor for which they do not fail to thank the Penitent. When a Penitent has come before the house of his Mistress, he then redoubles the blows more violently, such that he tears open his back and shoulders. The Lady, who sees him from her balcony and knows with what intention he does this, is all the more favorable to him, and does not fail to take good account of it. Those who behave thus are obliged to come every year, or by neglect a sickness would seize them; and it is not only the common people or even the Citizens who perform this: but it is also persons of great stature - - - - One sees on such an occasion in Seville as many as seven or eight hundred Penitents at once, and these have the fame of scourging themselves more severely than those of Madrid.

If they assign these reported accounts to them, it is nonetheless certain that they are not naturally burdened with many oddities that could be devised by the human wit in matters of religion: but possibly the imagination of various writers has amused itself to their disadvantage, and has not shrunk from placing infinite absurdities on the account of the Spaniards. For this reason, we shall not engage ourselves in a broad narrative regarding the subject of their religious practices.

# HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

<margin>
How the Procession of the Sacrament is conducted in Spain;
</margin>
The Penitents (a) <note>original: "Boetelingen"</note>, having returned home from the Procession, find a grand feast prepared for them, provided it is not one of the most solemn days of Holy Week:
"But after having performed such a good work,
"they believe it is permitted for them to
"endure a little more pain. Soon, the
"Penitent allows his shoulders to be rubbed
"for some time with sponges dipped in salt
"and vinegar, in order to stem the seeping
"blood." Afterward, he sits down at the table and enjoys himself with his friends. This Procession (b) begins at four o'clock in the afternoon and hardly concludes before eight o'clock in the evening.

The Procession of the Blessed Sacrament <note>The "H. Sakrament" refers to the Eucharist carried in a monstrance during the feast of Corpus Christi.</note>, as it occurs in Spain, also has many unique characteristics. It consists (c) of all the parish churches and clergy, who, as is well known, are very numerous and very powerful in Spain. The streets through which the Procession travels are decorated with the most precious tapestries. All the balconies are left open and likewise hung with tapestries. Canvas awnings are stretched from one side of the street to the other to prevent the sun's heat from being too burdensome for the faithful, and these are moistened with water to make the air cooler; the streets are also strewn with sand, watered, and scattered with many flowers. The stations <note>Temporary altars or resting places for the Sacrament.</note> are large and adorned with the utmost splendor.

The Blessed Sacrament is carried under a costly canopy. The King and his entire Court attend the Procession, as do the Councils and Judges: but without any order of precedence, and each with a wax candle in hand. His Majesty follows immediately behind the Blessed Sacrament <note>original: "Hoogwaardige"</note> and walks just like his subjects, armed with a wax candle. They rest from time to time according to the established custom of the Processions. During the progress of the Blessed Sacrament and all the religious entourage, one sees the Ladies on the balconies in summer attire, perhaps more curious and moved by the merit of a well-equipped

<column-break/>

Penitent than by the religious nature of the custom, which they nevertheless strive to pair with their hearts. They are provided with flowers, which they scatter over the Procession, and bottles of perfume, which are poured over the delegates of the Church Militant—just as Holy Water resists the secret snares of the Devil, while the fragrant waters of this fair sex sprinkle the participants.

<margin>
and performed with strange acts.
</margin>
Jesters <note>original: "Poetsemakers"</note> are also mingled among these pious folk; they dance alongside the Blessed Sacrament and perform countless clever tricks during the progress. These pranksters, who mostly consist of Biscayans <note>People from the Basque region of Spain, often depicted in literature of this era as energetic or eccentric.</note>, are of a surprising disposition: but what is even more surprising is how Spanish dignity can coexist with such a different temperament. The Procession lasts several hours, and it is sometimes two hours past noon before it is finished. This being done, the faithful take their midday meal so that they may subsequently find themselves at the *Sacramental Acts* <note>original: "Autos Sacramentales"</note>. These *Autos* are a kind of pious farce (d) performed in broad daylight in honor of the Blessed Sacrament, although by torchlight and in the middle of the street. The *Autos* last for a month and form the conclusion of the devotion to the Blessed Sacrament.

<margin>
How the Procession of the Sacrament is handled more seriously in Genoa.
</margin>
The Procession of the Blessed Sacrament on Corpus Christi is carried out more seriously in Genoa. There, as in France, the streets and houses are hung with tapestries; the roads are strewn with greenery, and the young ladies scatter flowers and perfumes upon the heads of those who have the honor of following the Blessed Sacrament: but here, gallantry is not mixed with buffoonery. They wisely reject those religious farces which, if one is to believe travelers, are still zealously practiced in Milan, where it is claimed (e) that people even practice a little beforehand to appear more Christian at the Feast.

(b) Ibid. (c) Idem ibid and *The Wonders of Spain* <note>original: "Delices de l'Espagne"</note>.

Many are favorable to him: but the Elders point out to the others the injustice they would commit by allowing a person of low birth among them; that St. Joseph his Father had been a poor carpenter, and the Holy Virgin earned her living by sewing. Our Lord awaits with much sorrow the decision they will take; which is decided, with some difficulty, to refuse him: but they nonetheless see fit to institute the Order of Christ for him, and by this means everyone is satisfied.

### RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc. OF THE ROMAN CHURCH.
<sig>Bbb</sig>
<meta>VOLUME I.</meta>
<meta>catchword: precede-</meta>

<margin>
A strange Rosary Procession used in Venice, and the solemnity with which it is accompanied.
</margin>
The Rosary Procession organized by the Dominican Fathers in Venice is quite remarkable. Following the Cross, one sees a great number of little Angels and Saints, consisting of the most beautiful and well-formed young children of both sexes. One of these girls represents St. Apollonia <note>St. Apollonia is the patron saint of dentistry, often depicted with pincers; here she is part of a living tableau.</note>, another St. Lucy, and yet another St. Agnes: in a word, they are clever copies of the "female citizens of Paradise." These feigned Saints are accompanied by several small black Devils, provided with tails, horns, and claws; they lack nothing to perform what they represent. They perform all sorts of crooked leaps and make ridiculous faces at the Saints to try, if possible, to distract this Blessed Youth from their godly conduct; however, the children maintain their required dignity, covering themselves with the shield of a borrowed holiness, and believing themselves perhaps armed with all the "Saving Weapons" <note>A theological term referring to spiritual defenses against temptation.</note>, they despise all the tricks of the Devils. The more one labors to distract them from their devotion, the less heed they pay to the dangerous mockeries produced by Hell to lead them astray; mockeries in which only the common believers in the Procession find themselves amused. St. Catherine of Siena <note>A 14th-century mystic and doctor of the church, highly revered by the Dominicans.</note> attends this exercise with a child by her side. It represents a little *Jesus* (a) holding a broom in one hand and a bellows in the other. After these Holy Daughters, a train of Pious Women appears, chosen from the most beautiful among them, to represent various Saints of the Old Testament. The Music then mingles with this procession: the *Castrati* * sing hymns of praise and other vocal pieces. A Holy Virgin, magnificently adorned and dressed in Royal ornaments, follows these Pious Matrons. She holds an uncommonly large Rosary in her hand, of which the beads and grains are of the very largest size. It is said that the Holy Virgin had a particular regard for the devotion of the Rosary during her life: at least, this is what the Dominicans claim. The young girl who represents the Holy Virgin is carried on a litter. At a short distance

<column-break/>

from her, they carry a wooden Our Lady <note>A statue of the Virgin Mary.</note>, of which the Dominicans make an uncommonly great deal of fuss. The people humble themselves and throw themselves on their knees with an uncommon zeal around this miracle-working image, imagining that by this means they will gather an abundant harvest of blessings. The Dominicans, armed with their Rosaries, surround Our Lady.

<margin>Thoughts on this.</margin>
Christians of a "thick-skinned" or particular taste <note>A reference to those with more stoic or perhaps cynical viewpoints on such elaborate displays.</note> do not take pleasure in accompanying these solemn parades, where the Saints are stripped of the state of humility they had chosen on Earth to make themselves pleasing to God; but however that may be, these sorts of exercises are regarded as excellent by some people, as long as superstition and passion continually assert this: a dispute always advantageous to the leaders of the Church Militant <note>The "Church Militant" refers to the body of living believers on earth struggling against sin and the devil.</note>. As for the mysteries (b) of the Processions, we shall leave them to be searched out by those involved, since it is a secret to no one but them.

We shall not enter into a broader account of the subject of Processions here. In the continuation of this work, we shall describe two or three others, the least of which can be said to appear very unusual to the Reader.

<margin>Of what nature processions were formerly regarded among the Heathens.</margin>
Processions are of a Heathen <note>Pagan</note> origin. They were formerly carried out very solemnly in honor of false Gods. On this subject, one may consult *Polydorus Virgilius* <note>Polydore Vergil (c. 1470–1555), an Italian humanist scholar who wrote on the origins of things.</note>: but to satisfy the Reader, we shall describe a Heathen Procession to him, such as *Apuleius* presents to us in the 11th Book of his *Metamorphoses*. It contains a procession in honor of Diana. First, one saw some men equipped for war, and others as hunters armed with hunting knives and boar spears. Next, one saw people disguised in women's clothing, with braided hair and elegantly dressed from head to foot, adorned with every conceivable lady’s finery.

One represented a Magistrate, another a Philosopher. They carried on a litter, in honor of the Goddess of the Woods, a tamed Bear, as a living emblem of the hunt, over which Diana held her authority among the Heathens. ---- Such then were the precede-

# HISTORICAL DISCOURSE on the

Nor did they neglect to carry in this Procession certain "mysteries" <note>In this context, 'mysteries' refers to hidden sacred objects or symbolic relics revealed only to initiates of ancient cults.</note>, which constituted a portion of the most essential, and the most precious or dear elements of the religion. These things were enclosed in a small casket, carried by a Minister of the Gods, and with such a solemnity as was required to captivate the minds of the people and to impress a blind faith upon the devout.

<margin>Likewise in use among the ancient Jews.</margin>
Processions were also in use among the ancient Jews (a). It is believed that they were introduced into Christianity during the reign of Constantine the Great. The use of wax candles had already taken hold, but they were not used in Processions until long afterward.

<margin>The meaning assigned to Processions indicated.</margin>
The <term>Mystagogues</term> <note>Literally 'teachers of mysteries'; here referring to liturgical commentators who interpret the symbolic meaning of church rituals.</note> assure us (b) that Processions remind Christians of the various Journeys of JESUS CHRIST, undertaken for our Salvation, and the Christian life that we are obliged to suffer on earth. We believe, however, that the Christians who introduced their use in the first centuries of the Church did not make this observation; but that they merely had to imitate Paganism in their

<column-break/>

Ceremonies, which gave much luster to religion, and that even the Jews made no difficulty in adopting them. Furthermore, it is easy enough to understand how the Christians, living in the midst of the Pagans, gradually borrowed many customs from them which they believed they could appropriate to their own religion without harm.

The Cross which is carried before the Procession teaches us that the faithful must always keep JESUS CHRIST before their eyes; and the Image of the Saint, when carried, teaches that they are obligated to follow their Holy Predecessors, who were followers of the Savior. The people who follow after the Priests and the Clergy serve to instruct the faithful that they must trust in their teachings and follow them blindly on the path they show them to attain Salvation.

Regarding the manner of attending the Processions, the Clergy must let their thoughts dwell only upon the mysteries; and when this does not happen, there is perhaps no harm in piously assuming that it does. They must also not aim for any temporal advantages in them, such as the profits of a parish church might be, or of a Monastery, through a desire to introduce some particular devotion, etc., and to involve themselves in their superiority <note>The Dutch 'Opperhoofdigheit' suggests a display of rank or ecclesiastical authority.</note>, as JESUS CHRIST did when He held fellowship with His Disciples. Finally, they must arrange their private lives according to the purpose of the Procession. As for the people, one must make them observe the excellence of the Ceremony and explain its mysteries to them, so that they appear with such a spirit as the Church chooses to see in the faithful.

<margin>Order for conducting Processions established, and how it is found.</margin>
Since it is not enough to have described some noteworthy Processions regarding their subject matter, we proceed to speak of the general order that must be observed in Processions instituted by the Church. „ quired, except in those of the **Holy**
„ **Sacrament** <note>referring to the Eucharist or the consecrated Host</note>: but the first two Can-
„ tors, clothed in Chasubles, walk on either
„ side of the Mass-priest. The Authori-
„ ties and the most prominent men of the place follow
„ here, and after them the rest of the people: first
„ the men, then the women and young
„ maidens.” The Reader can look up the rest in
the standard Book.

The procession of the delegates of the
**Church Militant** <term>original: *strydende Kerke*; a theological term for the body of Christians on earth who are still "battling" against sin and temptation</term>, who make
up a Procession, is always destined for a Church:
but sometimes they halt during the progress,
in order to subsequently visit several others;
this being an act of extraordinary Piety,
always accompanied by certain **Indulgences** <term>the remission of temporal punishment for sins</term>, which
His Holiness the Pope grants to en-
courage the Faithful. In Rome, one calls
this act of devotion **Church-visitation**
or **Statio** (a) <note>original Latin: "Station" or stopping place</note>: this word formerly
signified a stay that one found in a
place, also a Harbor or a place where ships
stayed, an Army Camp, etc. All these
concepts correspond with the Church Mili-
tant.

**Retreats** <note>original: *Afzonderingen*; literally "separations" or withdrawals from the world</note> exist in all Reli-
gions, if one understands by this word
a voluntary separation from the rest of man-
kind, in order to practice one's religious duties
in private and without any distrac-
tion. Anyone can perform such Retreats by
themselves: but it is much more sol-
emn, and we only use the term **Retreats**,
for a stay that one takes for some

<column-break/>

time in a **Seminary** <note>original: *Queekschool*; literally a "nursery" or training school for clergy</note> or in a Monastery,
to better pray to God, to be free from
temptations, and without giving oneself
over to earthly cares.

<margin>What must be observed in the Novenas.</margin>
We have already said that the **Nove-**
**nas** <note>original: *Negendaagsche Gebeden*; "nine-day prayers"</note> originally come from
Paganism: to observe this devotion
well, one must take care that it is
strictly limited to the number of nine.
Some devout people be-
lieve that nine solemn Masses performed on nine
consecutive days are more pleasing to God
than twelve Masses said over
twelve days. If it is true that these
Novenas take place in honor of the nine
Orders of Angels; can one doubt that
they will be well received?

<margin>Observations on the Devout person, introduced by custom.</margin>
There is nothing that more flatters the human heart
than what are called **Pious Works**,
since they are seen as an
absolute contract, or, to express it in
other words, as a truce between one's passions
and the duties that Religion itself
prescribes. (b) There is someone who
has said, „ that a devout person prays to God,
„ and does not pay his debts; that he robs
„ his neighbor, and gives the tithe to the poor;
„ that he builds a Hospital and tears down
„ good houses; that finally, for the devout
„ person, Religion is the counterweight to in-
„ justice.” We shall not examine
whether this characterization is indeed true;
this is not the place to moralize:
but one can say boldly enough,
that many people view good Works as
the great highway to Salvation.
We may also add that, what-
ever these good Works may be, the Cler-
gy always employ them fruitlessly,
under the plausible pretext of lead-
ing many Christians to Heaven:
above all, they have wanted to pave a
way for their annual income, which,
according to Mr. **Thiers** <note>Jean-Baptiste Thiers (1636–1703), a French theologian known for his work on superstitions and liturgical history</note>,
(c) had its beginning in the fourth or fifth
century. This, however, mattered nothing to the cause:
for the custom, gradually introduced,
subsequently became entirely a Law. One then
saw nothing but people of all Stations,
Age, and Sex, who gave their goods
and their interests to the benefit of the
Churches

...and sacrificed to churches and monasteries. From
all sides, new exercises of
humility were introduced; the pious

seemed too weak to them. The priests and monks

maintained a close negotiation with the

measures were taken against the Devil, who 
became terrifying. Crosses were unearthed; 
many previously unknown *Relics* <term>original: *Reliquiën*; physical remains or personal effects of a saint preserved for veneration</term> were found. 
They even discovered several mouths of 
Hell and two or three of Purgatory. The 
maps of the monks indicated their exact 
elevation, and this discovery was not 
one of the least essential of the century. 
An innumerable multitude of souls were 
saved from Purgatory, and many of the 
Damned were released. The wealthy were 
soon mindful of their relatives: 
new means were devised to refresh 
the dead to whom one felt 
obligated.

<margin>Numerous Masses for Souls, and for what purpose they were established.</margin>
Masses were multiplied. A 
single Offering could not suffice; but 
ten, twenty, or thirty were required. 
Sometimes this number rose to thirty thousand. 
The high authorities of the Church chose 
new Patron Saints. 
Countless Altars and Churches were founded. Swarms 
of monks covered the earth. 
It was, as they said, a work of God. 
Dwelling places were assigned to them, 
and their incomes were secured: but 
pious souls increased them. 
They were not very favorable toward the houses where 
piety had at all times found its 

<column-break/>

refuge. It was judged sufficient 
that the monasteries multiplied 
with religious devotion, and that those 
who had surrendered their inheritance to the Servants of the Church 
found no means to save themselves, 
except under the monk's hood or 
the nun's veil. Finally, people were then 
strongly convinced that God could not 
be better served than by monks and priests: 
one saw nothing but monk's

of piety and leaving the world, 
such that one prayed to God more fervently 
with the monks and hermits.

Besides the annual income of 
the Churches, Monasteries, and Masses, there 
were still others very remarkable. (a) People 
contracted for these to put the Holy Sacrament on display, 
or to carry it in procession 
outside the usual days that 
the Church had designated, or to celebrate 
a day better than according to the 
original Institution of the Church. 
Such is the annual gift by

on the day of the Feast of the Patron of a 
parish church; the day of the 
Feast of the one whose name was celebrated, or 
for whom one had some special 
devotion. They also contracted 
annual gifts of services and prayers 
in honor of the Saints, when they 
had enjoyed some uncommon favors 
from them.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

### Concerning PIETY for HOLY RELICS.

<margin>What has been understood regarding the veneration of Relics.</margin>
On this subject we must again 
quote Mr. *Thiers* (b). He 
assures us that the faithful in all 
ages of the Church have had much 
reverence for the true *Relics* of the 
Saints, and that from time to time they 
have enjoyed great benefits from them: 
but he adds that this devotion 
in recent times has been carried so far 
that a great number of people ---- have 
imagined that nothing more was required 
than to be religious toward certain *Relics*, 
to carry them on one's person, and 
to visit places where they are kept, 
in order not to die in sin. 
Mr. *Thiers* has reason to express 
himself thus: however, he would have 
done better to remain silent on this subject. 
Why should a multitude of pious souls not 
be helped out of their slumber, who 
labor for their salvation with more 
powerful zeal and affection for the head or 
the arm of a Saint, since they 
especially [regard] this Holy 
Relic as the object of their love...

(a) *Thiers Ch. 24. ibid.* (b) *Thiers Ch. 23. ibid.*

<page-num>381</page-num>
<header>RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH.</header>

...have chosen that which, deprived of sensory objects and occupied with spiritual thoughts, leads those who practice it straight to God? Christian Charity shuns overly bold sentiments: a believer assures himself that a small portion of a Holy Relic, <term>original: *Heilig Overblyfzel*; physical remains or objects associated with a saint</term> which he carries with him in a small reliquary, is for him an excellent antidote against the temptation of the flesh, a spiritual balsam that strengthens him, and a fragrant oil that makes him live in God. Let us take him at his word.

<margin>And how one tries to find these among the Ancient Jews, narrated along with their effects.</margin>
One seeks to prove the antiquity of the veneration of *Relics* by (a) the transport of the bones of the Patriarch Joseph during the Exodus from Egypt: it is certain that under the Old Testament, just as now, it was believed that whoever touched the body of a Holy person acquired uncommon qualities. The first Christians were of the same mind, and one sees examples of this in the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles: from which one must conclude that even the bodies of Saints can produce many miraculous effects. Consequently, the implications of this opinion regarding power and holiness have been extended much further. It was believed (b) that it was necessary to collect everything that had served the Saints; to exhume their bodies, to seek out their bones and ashes, in order to establish a respected, lawful, and just confidence in them, since the Saints had earned such during their lives. Then Temples, Chapels, and Altars were built for them. (c) Even the Angels concerned themselves with this; for they gathered the bones of St. Catherine and buried them on Mount Sinai. In the fourth century, the transfer of *Relics* began to be carried out with great solemnity. The use of reliquaries was introduced at the same time.

<margin>The use of reliquaries introduced.</margin>
The Church solemnly blessed these cases in which the Holy Remains were enclosed. Nothing unusual occurred during this ceremony. (d) In a Prayer, God was

<column-break/>

<margin>...brought into use, and what power was attributed to the Relics.</margin>
entreated to grant His protection to those who honored the merits of the Saints and humbly embraced their *Relics*, so that these supplicating believers might be shielded from the power of the Devil, from the force of lightning, from the plague, from tainted air, from blinding and harmful beasts, and from the hostilities of malicious men. This enumeration shows to what use the *Relics* could serve. Another Prayer, which the Officiating Priest said before sprinkling Holy Water on the cases intended to enclose the precious remains of the Saints, is at least as powerful.

<margin>How one solemnly swears upon them.</margin>
One is made to swear upon the *Relics* of the Saints; an example is the Ecclesiastical Custom of the oath which the King of the Romans <note>The "King of the Romans" was the title used by the heir-apparent or the elected ruler of the Holy Roman Empire before being crowned Emperor.</note> takes upon the blood of St. Stephen at Aachen on the day of his Coronation.

<margin>Established times for the exhibition of Relics brought into use.</margin>
The believer who visits the *Relics* out of piety must fulfill his duty with all zeal and touch the Sacred Limbs of the Saints with confidence. A set time exists to publicly present them to the God-fearing. Every seven years, (e) the *Relics* that are in the Church of Our Lady at Aachen are shown. The exhibition is accompanied by an announcement, which serves to prepare the devotion of the believer. We present here to the Reader a copy of this Announcement, so that he may have a better idea of this Ceremony.

->The Announcement is regarding the HEAD<-
->and the RIGHT ARM of St.<-
->CORNELIUS.<-

### CHAPTER XIX.

(a) *Exodus 13 verse 19.* <note>The OCR text lists verse 29, but Exodus 13:19 is the correct reference for Joseph's bones.</note> The ancient Heathens also honored the ashes of their Heroes. By order of the Oracle of Apollo, the Athenians gathered the bones of Theseus and preserved them holily after having carried them magnificently in Procession, and solemn Sacrifices were performed for them on that occasion. One could bring forward other Examples, if such were required.
(b) *Bozius* <note>Tommaso Bozio (1548–1610), an Italian priest and writer who defended the Church against Machiavelli and Protestant critics.</note> grounds the merit and the incorruptibility of *Relics* in one of his works on these Scripture passages: *Not a single hair shall fall from your head. The Lord preserves the bones of his own; they shall not be subject to corruption. He who eats my flesh has eternal life.* These Texts prove, he says, that the smallest parts of the Saints (even their hairs) have been preserved for us; that their bones must be enclosed in cases to arouse our homage; that the *Relics* of the Saints have an eternal life, a living power, and that they have preserved the ability to perform miracles, just as the Saints had in their lives.
(c) *Casalius, On the Ancient Rites of Christians.* <note>original: *Casal. de Vet. Christ. Ritib.*</note> (d) *Ritual of Alet. Roman Pontifical.* <note>The "Rituel d'Alet" was a famous liturgical book issued by Bishop Nicolas Pavillon of Alet in 1667.</note>

### CHAPTER XIX.

### Concerning the TRANSLATION of RELICS and their Miraculous Works Solemnly Celebrated.

<margin>Council meeting held regarding the translation of Relics.</margin>
The solemnity of the translation <term>original: *overvoering*; the formal moving of a saint's remains from one place to another</term> of *Relics* is a matter of weight and requires much observation and care. Before (a) the translation takes place, the Bishop must recognize them. For this translation, a meeting of Clergy and Teachers of Divinity <term>theology</term> is held. One must also not neglect to consult with Physicians, especially those experienced in Anatomy, so that they may give their judgment on the state and nature of the *Relics*, without which a great mistake might be committed. After investigating their power, one proceeds to create an official record, and the Clerk prepares a certificate; subsequently, they are kept in the designated place. Everything is noted down; the Bishop provides his proof, which is followed by a Decree ordering the faithful to honor them. Finally, this sacred treasure is locked up. Before the testimony of the *Relics* is drawn up, the Bishop solemnly blesses them.

<margin>How this translation is performed by a solemn Procession, and with what preparation;</margin>
The translation of the *Relics* is performed by a Procession: the pious who attend can be assured of a sufficient number of Indulgences <term>original: *Aflaaten*; the remission of temporal punishment for sin</term> granted by the Holy Father <note>The Pope</note> to those who attend this spiritual act. On the day of the translation, the streets through which one passes must be cleaned, and the houses decorated with Tapestries. The church (b) and the Altar are magnificently adorned, and the Statues of the Saints are put on display. He who must perform the Ritual of the transfer is dressed in his ceremonial vestments. Accompanied by his Ministers, he proceeds to the place where the *Relics* rest; he prays kneeling before them; he rises again and blesses the incense with which he must cense; he censes three times, then bows, and has them brought to the designated place while singing Psalms. The people, naturally inclined toward that which is accompanied by outward splendor, surround them

<column-break/>

often with wax candles in hand. When they have arrived at the appointed place, the Clergy must keep watch day and night. This watch is relieved in turns. Let us not forget to mention that prayer must be the only exercise of the faithful who are tasked with keeping the watch.

The Mass for the Procession of the translation of the *Relics* having been performed, the Procession begins in the following manner. <margin>Order observed in the Procession.</margin> (c) Two Staff-bearers lead the march and make way; the Master of Ceremonies arranges the faithful according to their rank; the Official of the bells has them rung, and the faithful soon prepare themselves for the march.

One then sees some Musicians appear, followed by the Brotherhoods according to their rank; thereafter follow the Images of the Saint or Saints, if there are multiple Saints to be transferred. Some laymen of distinction carry these images just as one carries war banners in battle, the ends of which are held up by two persons. A choir of Singers precedes these images; the children and youths, well-dressed, follow the choir with uncovered heads. The most prominent and distinguished citizens follow the Images with a wax candle in hand. The Religious Orders <note>Monastic orders like the Franciscans or Dominicans</note> are present in groups or by delegates, and after these follow the wealthy laymen. We shall not detail the following order of how the secular Clergy <note>Priests who live in the world rather than in a monastery</note> march—namely, the Censer-bearers at the head, the Cross-bearer between two Candle-bearers, etc.—for we have already said enough of that.

The *Relics* are carried under a canopy. The Bishop must, if he attends the Solemnity, be in all his Episcopal robes. Some Singers, elegantly dressed, precede the *Relics*, singing the Hymns of the Saint whose transfer is being made. Durin- <note>original: *Geduu-* (catchword for *geduurende*); indicates the text continues with "During..."</note>

# RELIGIOUS DUTIES etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH.

<page-num>383</page-num>

during the procession, two incense-bearers <term>thurifers</term> are occupied with incensing.

When one has arrived in the Church with the *Relics*, one must sing the *Te Deum* <note>A traditional Latin hymn of praise: "Thee, O God, we praise"</note>; they are then placed upon the Altar to be honored by the people. Before they are locked away, the Bishop gives his blessing over them. Some prayers are instituted in their honor, and a lamp is left to burn night and day before the place where they rest.

The *Relics* of the Saints (a) may not be carried by laypeople under the pretext of any Brotherhood. The transfer of Images <note>Statues or icons</note> is performed in the same manner as that of the *Relics*.

<margin>How and why Rome and all of Italy possess so many, especially those consisting of the Blood of the Martyrs.</margin>
Regarding the miraculous works of the *Relics*, we shall not expand further, for this would be nearly inexhaustible. We shall speak only of the blood of the Martyrs, which is preserved in various places throughout Christendom. Rome especially and Italy may boast of finding many on this subject; and it is not to be wondered at, given the persecutions that the first Christians suffered under the tyranny of Heathenism <note>The Roman Empire before the adoption of Christianity</note>. The soil of Rome is entirely soaked with the blood of the believers. This city, says a certain writer (b), has drunk it so greedily that she has become drunk from it. He adds that the Pope makes gifts of this consecrated earth to strangers; wishing thus to satisfy the pious desires of the faithful, who have come to Rome moved by godly motives and do not wish to return to their country without bringing back the salutary signs of their journey. This Holy Remnant is believed to possess at least a portion of the properties that the Saints always communicate when one touches them; and this is what we shall prove through a miracle, drawn from the cited Writer.

<margin>A rare incident involving a Polish Envoy related here.</margin>
A Polish Envoy fervently petitioned Pope Pius V to grant him a Holy Relic: whether it was that the Holy Father did not wish to open his treasury to the Poles, or that he believed a small amount of gathered earth from the floor had as much power as any detached bone from a Saint's body,

<column-break/>

he took his handkerchief, placed a little of the Roman earth into it, and then tying it shut, gave this gift to the Envoy, who thought the Pope was mocking him. However, upon his return to his Court, the Envoy opened the handkerchief and seemed intent on throwing the material therein away; but he found that both the earth and the handkerchief were soaked with blood, and this was the Blood of the Martyrs.

<margin>Miracles performed by the Blood of the Martyrs, and by whom.</margin>
The Blood of the Martyrs has performed a multitude of Miracles. The cited Writer relates many kinds thereof; to which we refer the Reader.

As for the miraculous manner in which, as he says, it has been seen at all times that the Blood of the Martyrs has become liquid, pious souls flatter themselves that God has wished to give this satisfaction to the faithful for their comfort and as a reward for their piety. "One has now, and especially in Italy, many of these uncommon liquefactions <term>original: *vloeibaarmakingen*; the miraculous turning of dried blood into liquid</term>. (c) On the day of the Feast of St. Eustatius, one sees the Blood of that Saint boil in Rome. The Blood of St. John the Baptist works no less in Naples, and even in three different Churches. It concerns (d) primarily the honor of JESUS CHRIST; it seems to wish to proclaim the coming of the Savior once again. In the same city, the Blood of St. Bartholomew yields in no way to that of St. John the Baptist, nor to the Blood of St. Stephen, which does not fail to flow on the day when the finding of the body of that Saint is celebrated. Some unbelievers mean that all these liquefactions are more trickery than a miracle, and we would likewise believe it, were we not convinced by infinite examples, and by the good faith of the Priests and Clergy of this land. We shall present one of these that proves this entirely.

<margin>The Head and the Blood of St. Januarius displayed in Naples, and what follows.</margin>
On the eighteenth of September, the Head and the Blood of Saint Januarius <note>San Gennaro, the patron saint of Naples</note>, Patron Saint of the city, are solemnly displayed to the faithful in Naples. A solemn Procession (e) is also held in honor of that Saint, in which

# HISTORICAL TREATISE on the

<margin>Possession of remains, as indicated.</margin>
Is it possible that the clothes of JESUS CHRIST and his Apostles have been preserved, as well as some instruments of their suffering; that some have obtained the chains of St. Peter, and others the stones with which St. Stephen was stoned? Far be it from me to claim these are forgeries; perhaps the devout have been led to believe that enough believers were found—or to put it better, people clever enough to turn a profit—at the very moment when St. Joseph was chopping wood, that they managed to capture his breath (a) and seal it in a bottle. However this may be, without faith and miracles, one could not say for certain how these *Relics* and (b) others, which are at least as old, have been passed down to us without falsification, after the states of the world have been subject to so many upheavals over seventeen centuries.

<margin>How the custom of carrying Relics was anciently practiced, and why they served as a protective charm.</margin>
The custom of carrying Holy *Relics* on one's person, whether out of piety or as a means to deliver oneself from sad encounters, ailments, accidents, etc., is very old in the Church, (c) as St. Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century Greek bishop and theologian</note> speaks of one which his sister wore in a ring on her finger. This custom could have partly taken its origin from the behavior of the Heathens, to protect themselves against enchantments and poisoning. It is believed that the objects the children of the Romans wore around their necks <note>The "bulla," an amulet given to free-born Roman children</note> served as a protective measure against present and future evils; Amulets and *Abracadabras* * have the same origin. But however it may be, it is St. Helena <note>Mother of Emperor Constantine, credited with finding the True Cross</note> to whom *Relics* owe the origin of their great esteem. Nevertheless, at that time it was only the Cross which actually came into use. This pious Princess, foreseeing that the discovery of the Cross would awaken the devotion of Christians, took only a portion with her and left the rest in Jerusalem to be the object of the zeal of Pilgrims. But one must not think that this Holy Wood was imperceptibly lost due to the continuous distribution made to the devout; for St. Paulinus <note>St. Paulinus of Nola, who wrote about the miracle of the "growth" of the Cross</note> assures us (d) that from then on the remainder stayed in the same state; that the faithful repeatedly took from this Divine Wood, and yet it was always seen to be undiminished. In the course of time, people carried all sorts of *Relics* with them, primarily around the neck (e) and on the chest.

<margin>Relics formerly carried in War.</margin>
In former times, *Relics* were carried in military undertakings, and this custom was practiced as early as the century of Theodosius the Great <note>Roman Emperor, reigned 379–395 AD</note>. Long after that, the Templars and Crusaders made their processions with them against the enemy of the Christian name. Kings, having set out for War, provided themselves with the choir-robe <note>The "Cappa," from which the word "chapel" is derived</note> of St. Martin, and had the reliquary chests carried at the head of their Armies. The Monk (f) of the Val de Cernay assures us that in a dangerous situation, a group of Clergy and Priests, having the Cross at the head of their procession and...

---

(a) Somewhere a portion of the breath <note>original: "Aamhyging" — literally the "panting" or "sighing"</note> of St. Joseph, the betrothed husband of the Holy Virgin, is preserved.
(b) Such as, for example, a piece of the tablecloth which was spread for JESUS CHRIST when he held the Last Supper. This Holy Relic is kept at Vienne in the Dauphiné <note>A former province in southeastern France</note>. Also preserved are the manger of the Savior; the table at which he held the Holy Supper; the linen with which he dried the feet of his Apostles; his seamless robe; his purple coat; the veil he had around his body on the Cross; the sponge used to give him vinegar mixed with gall; the rod with which he was beaten; the blood mixed with water that flowed from his side; the hair and the clothing of the Holy Virgin; as well as those of St. John the Evangelist; the belt of Our Lady, and the cloak of St. Joseph. 
The Carthusian Monks in Cologne have the Hem of Jesus Christ's Robe, which the woman afflicted with the issue of blood touched to be healed. The young ladies of Cologne, so it is said, send wine to the Carthusians so that they may dip the *Relic* into it; after which, when this ailment befalls them, they drink of the same and are healed.
(c) *Observations on the Cemeteries, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Osservazioni Sopra i Cimiteri"</note>
\* [These protective charms called *Amulets*, or *Abracadabras*, or as others read *Abraxas*, with which the Learned have so racked their brains, were of many uses, whether hung around the neck or worn as a ring on the finger, which worked wonders; among which the ring of Gyges <note>A mythical ring mentioned by Plato that granted invisibility</note> may well be counted, which could make him (who can believe it?) invisible. Of such a kind must also have been the ring of the Jew Eleazar, who healed a great number of possessed persons in the presence of the Emperor Vespasian, for which the Devils took to their heels. Whoever is inclined to study further into these rarities can read the author *Thiers* <note>Jean-Baptiste Thiers, a French priest who wrote a famous treatise on superstitions</note>, where he treats of superstitions. *Herodotus, Memoirs of Literature of the Royal Academy, Bataviæ Sacra, etc.*]
(d) *Observations, same title and place.*
(e) St. Charles Borromeo wore a tooth of St. Sabina around his neck. Gregory XII wore one of St. Catherine of Siena. Some centuries before, St. Dunstan, having broken his walking stick on the back of the Devil (who had appeared to him in the form of a Bear), had another much stronger one made, in which he had a tooth of the Apostle St. Andrew embedded.
(f) Cited by the Author of the *Observations, etc.*

### RELIGIOUS DUTIES, etc. of the ROMAN CHURCH. 387 ###

accompanied by some *Relics*, marched against the Albigensians <note>The Albigensians were a medieval religious sect in Southern France deemed heretical by the Catholic Church; they were the target of the Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229).</note>. After singing the *Come, Creator Spirit* <note>original: "Veni Creator"</note>, which was their battle cry, they found that upon the third repetition of a verse from that hymn, the rebels against the Church fled the battlefield. The Bishop of Cominges displayed no less courage. Without the slightest regard for the small number of the Faithful who stood exposed before more than a hundred thousand Albigensians, he armed himself with the Wood of the Cross, and showing it from a hill, (a) he blessed the soldiers of the Catholic Army by setting the Cross before their eyes.

<margin>The customs performed with *Relics* during timely occasions to prevent threatened disasters.</margin>
In times of general disaster, piety dictates that one take refuge in the Holy *Relics*. (b) The Blood of Saint Januarius <note>San Gennaro, the patron saint of Naples; his blood is famously said to liquefy miraculously.</note>, shown to the erupting flames of Mount Vesuvius, has never failed to extinguish them. (c) Enough is known in Paris of the miraculous effects of Saint Genevieve, whenever it is deemed necessary to carry her *Relics* in procession; and if one believes the religious of Reims, the shroud-cloth <note>original: "Zweed-doek," likely referring to a sudarium or burial cloth</note> of Saint Remi has had no less power whenever it is judged necessary to 

<column-break/>

bring it forth to ward off general calamities. It shall now suffice to justify this usage. We have already spoken of the custom of swearing upon the *Relics* of the Saints. They were used as witnesses to misfortunes, or as instruments of defense against the wrongs of one's enemies, and these uses were no less edifying.

In former times, it was permitted to offer *Relics* as a pledge in cases of extraordinary necessity; they were made to, so to speak, wear mourning for grievances, as someone would throw them to the ground in this state, strewn with thorns <note>This refers to the medieval practice of the "humiliation of relics," where monks would place relics on the floor to shame the saint into intervening during a crisis.</note>, but this custom was abolished. The Pagans maintained such practices, since they punished their Gods whenever they were not favorable to them. They were given the duty of protecting the lands and fields against the harassment of robbers. This custom was also a remnant of the Idolatry of the Pagans, who recommended the preservation of their pleasure gardens to certain deities. Finally, the *Relics* were religiously carried through the cities and at crossroads to increase the collection of alms.

---

> (a) The Catholic soldiers, encouraged by the presence of the Cross, defeated the army of the King of Aragon, who was found among the dead.
> (b) In Venice, a bone of Saint Lawrence is used to extinguish fires. In one of the Churches of this State, Holy Water is made with great power using a bone of Saint Liberalis. In Sicily, the Veil of Saint Agatha, carried in procession by the Clergy of Catania, very quickly causes the fire-flood of Mount Gibel <note>Mount Etna</note> to stop. A little cotton rubbed against this Veil produces the same effect. *Observations Upon* &c. <note>original: "Offer-vazioni Sopra"</note>
> (c) Saint Genevieve is the Protectress of the Parisians. In times of general anxiety, the casket of her *Relics* is lowered, owing to some miracle-working power that has been observed from it. After it has been lowered, it is carried in procession to Our Lady <note>Notre-Dame de Paris</note> alongside Saint Marcel and several other Saints. The ceremony usually begins at midnight. All the Guilds of the city, preceded by the Clergy, attend the procession. The Abbot and Clergy of Saint Genevieve walk barefoot from their Church to that of Our Lady, where a High Mass is sung, which does not end until four o'clock in the afternoon. Often one is satisfied with merely uncovering the casket of this Saint: but whether it is uncovered or carried in procession, it is always accompanied by the attention of the Pious, and it fulfills their expectations.
